innovations.raw_text:
Bunja – kraina możliwości
Charakter innowacji
Produkt
Problem, na który odpowiada innowacja
Innowacja odpowiada na problem niedostosowania przestrzeni publicznej do potrzeb dzieci i młodzieży, które nie są włączane w działania miastotwórcze i nie mają wpływu na otaczającą ich przestrzeń. Negatywne konsekwencje braku partycypacji dziecięcej to obniżenie poczucia sprawczości, mały związek emocjonalny z otoczeniem czy niewykształcenie się postaw obywatelskich, przejawiających się m.in. dbaniem o przestrzeń publiczną. Brak głosu dzieci w dyskusji i planowaniu funkcjonowania miasta ma także swoje odzwierciedlenie w niskim poziomie bezpieczeństwa młodych osób, a także braku czytelności przestrzeni miejskiej i jej przebodźcowaniu. Gra odpowiada na potrzebę wzmocnienia samostanowienia najmłodszych mieszkańców miast, sprzyja budowaniu ich odpowiedzialności, sprawczości i poczucia przynależności.
Jak działa innowacja?
Innowacja ma postać gry, w ramach której dzieci zostają podzielone na kilka plemion. Ich zadaniem jest zaplanowanie i zrealizowanie pomysłu drobnej interwencji w bliskim im otoczeniu, np. poprawienia zielonej infrastruktury, zapewnienia czystości i porządku, organizacji wydarzeń integrujących grupę. Do przeprowadzenia gry konieczne jest uzyskanie zgody właściciela miejsca (np. dyrektora szkoły czy urzędu miasta) na wprowadzenie zmian w przestrzeni. Dobrą praktyką jest również poinformowanie rodziców dzieci o tym, na czym polega działanie.
Komu służy innowacja?
Dzieci i młodzież w wieku 10-15 lat, uczniowie klas 4-8 szkoły podstawowej. Istotne jest posiadanie przez uczestników gry rozwiniętych umiejętności czytania, analizy, abstrakcyjnego myślenia. Grupę biorącą udział w rozgrywce można stworzyć w każdym miejscu, w którym dzieci spędzają czas, np. w szkole, świetlicy środowiskowej, klubie młodzieży.
Kto może wdrażać innowację?
Jednostki samorządu terytorialnego działające w obszarze partycypacji i włączania mieszkańców w procesy kształtowania przestrzeni;
organizacje pozarządowe;
liderzy społeczni i aktywiści związani z działaniami na rzecz przestrzeni publicznej, wsparcia dzieci i rodzin, partycypacji;
szkoły, biblioteki, świetlice środowiskowe – wszystkie miejsca, w których młodzież spędza czas;
architekci, urbaniści – mający bezpośredni wpływ na zmianę przestrzeni publicznej.
Miejsce testowania innowacji
Gdynia
Szkoła podstawowa z oddziałami integracyjnymi
Świetlica socjoterapeutyczna
Produkty powstałe w wyniku testowania
Gra Bunja - kraina możliwości (m.in. Karty Mistrza Gry, Karty Misji, Karty Plemion);
podręcznik dla użytkowników.
Rezultaty osiągnięte w wyniku testowania
W kreatywnej ankiecie dla dzieci uzyskano informację, że 20 na 23 dzieci odczuło, że ma wpływ na bliskie miejsce, przed rozgrywką takiej odpowiedzi udzieliło 13 na 25 dzieci. 11 na 23 przebadanych dzieci po rozgrywce czuje się odpowiedzialne za bliskie im miejsce, przed uczestnictwem w grze takiej odpowiedzi udzieliło 4 na 25 dzieci.
Komentarz do oceny
Przeprowadzone z dziećmi badania wskazały, że innowacja ma realny wpływ na wzrost u dzieci poczucia sprawczości i odpowiedzialności za otaczającą je przestrzeń. Zmiany dokonane po etapie testowania w pełni odpowiadały na zgłoszone przez dzieci niedoskonałości – dzięki czemu ostateczny produkt spotkał się z pozytywnymi opiniami zarówno młodych osób, jak i dorosłych (np. pracowników urzędów). Uczestnicy gry, wypowiadając się przy użyciu jednego słowa, określali grę m.in. jako: ,,ciekawa”, ,,wciągająca”, ,,cool”.

https://innowacje.rops.poznan.pl/project/bunya/
Kto jest niezbędny do wdrożenia innowacji?
Właściciel miejsca, w którym przeprowadzane są zmiany;
mistrz gry;
dorosły, który będzie wspierać dzieci w realizacji zadań;
dzieci z grupy docelowej.
Co jest niezbędne do wdrożenia innowacji?
Zgoda właściciela przestrzeni na dokonanie w niej zmian;
instrukcja;
fundusze i materiały niezbędne do przeprowadzenia zmian.

innovations.name: Powitalnik
innovations.lead: Przewodnik dla rodziców mierzących się z diagnozą dziecka
innovations.problem: Moment diagnozy niepełnosprawności narodzonego dziecka jest dla rodziców często traumatycznym doświadczeniem – powoduje poczucie dezorientacji, zagubienia, niewiedzy. Rodzice nie wiedzą co robić dalej, gdzie szukać pomocy, do kogo się zwrócić. Ponadto gdy okazuje się, że wyczekane dziecko mierzy się z poważnymi wyzwaniami zdrowotnymi, rodzice często pozostawieni są sami sobie. Brakuje wsparcia, dostępu do informacji, przestrzeni do dzielenia się trudnymi emocjami i wymiany doświadczeń.
innovations.target_group:
Rodzice dzieci z niepełnosprawnością;
personel medyczny na oddziałach położniczych.
innovations.evidence: W „Powitalniku” opisane zostały najważniejsze rodzaje pomocy terapeutycznej i finansowej, które przysługują rodzinom mierzącym się z diagnozą dziecka. Ponadto wskazane zostały dane kontaktowe do osób znajdujących się w podobnej sytuacji. Dzięki temu narzędziu rodzice uzyskali szybki dostęp do kompleksowego kompendium wiedzy, które wspiera ich w przetrwaniu trudnego okresu, co pozytywnie wpłynęło na ich poczucie bezpieczeństwa i komfort psychiczny.

innovations.name: Przenośne modularne łazienki
innovations.lead: Projekt przenośnych, modułowych zestawów łazienkowych dla osób, które mają ograniczony dostęp do podstawowych udogodnień sanitarnych
innovations.problem: Wiele domów i mieszkań, zwłaszcza położonych na obszarach wiejskich lub miejskich o niższym standardzie życia, może nie mieć dostępu do podstawowych udogodnień sanitarnych. Innowacja pomaga rozwiązać ten problem, umożliwiając szybkie dostarczenie podstawowej infrastruktury sanitarnej w miejsca, gdzie wcześniej nie było to możliwe.
innovations.description: Innowacja oferuje dostęp do projektu przenośnych modułów łazienkowych, które są łatwe w montażu i demontażu i można je zainstalować w różnych przestrzeniach. Materiały użyte do ich produkcji są lekkie, trwałe i łatwe w transporcie. Gotowe moduły są transportowane do miejsc przeznaczenia, gdzie następuje ich instalacja.
innovations.target_group:
Osoby ubogie;
osoby zamieszkujące lokale nieposiadające łazienki.

innovations.name: Asystent studenta z ASD
innovations.lead: Skalowanie innowacji „Tłumacz/adwokat społeczny – asystent osoby z ASD”, poprawiającej komunikację przedstawicieli uczelni wyższych z osobami z ASD
innovations.problem:
Według badań przeprowadzonych m.in. przez rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich studenci z niepełnosprawnościami psychicznymi są praktycznie niewidoczni na uczelniach wyższych, a ich specjalne potrzeby rzadko są brane pod uwagę w działaniach na rzecz zapewnienia równego dostępu do nauki. Dzieje się tak dlatego, że studenci neuronietypowi często unikają zauważania, starając się uniknąć negatywnych reakcji otoczenia oraz stygmatyzacji. Rzadko też korzystają z usług biur ds. osób z niepełnosprawnościami, próbując radzić sobie na swoich wydziałach samodzielnie lub z pomocą swoich bliskich. W związku z tym, wielu z tych studentów zostaje bez wsparcia i często rezygnuje z kontynuowania nauki.
Opis innowacji przed skalowaniem znajduje się
tutaj.
innovations.description: W ramach projektu zaoferowano studentom i studentkom z ASD poradnictwo oraz usługi asystenckie. Zakres i częstotliwość wsparcia ustalana jest indywidualnie i może dotyczyć różnych obszarów związanych ze studiowaniem, np. załatwianie spraw w dziekanacie, poruszanie się po mieście, relacje z osobami prowadzącymi zajęcia, planowanie nauki oraz czasu wolnego. Korzystanie ze wsparcia nie wymaga orzeczenia o niepełnosprawności i diagnozy spektrum zaburzeń autystycznych. Każda studentka i każdy student, którzy podejrzewają u siebie ASD, mogą wziąć udział w projekcie i otrzymać wsparcie. W ramach projektu prowadzone są również prace nad rozpowszechnieniem wiedzy o spektrum zaburzeń autystycznych.
innovations.target_group: Studenci oraz osoby zakwalifikowane do rozpoczęcia studiów, którzy w okresie ostatnich 5 lat korzystały (bądź korzystają aktualnie) z pomocy specjalistycznej, psychologicznej bądź też są pod opieką organizacji zrzeszającej osoby z ASD.
innovations.evidence:
W ramach testowania udało się realnie poprawić sytuację wielu studentów ze spektrum autyzmu. 79 studentów z ASD otrzymało wsparcie w komunikacji ze środowiskiem akademickim, co pomogło zrekompensować ich trudności społeczne i ograniczyć zakłócenia w procesie studiowania. U 68 nastąpił wzrost kompetencji społecznych i umiejętności radzenia sobie w życiu zawodowym. Przyczyniło się to do zwiększenia pewności siebie i poziomu samodzielności osób z ASD.
W czasie trwania projektu 42 osoby zdobyły wiedzę w zakresie lidera adwokata studenta z ASD. Powstało też 48 sieci adwokatów studentów z ASD.

Zakres i częstotliwość wsparcia ustalana jest indywidualnie i może dotyczyć różnych obszarów związanych ze studiowaniem, np. załatwianie spraw w dziekanacie, poruszanie się po mieście, relacje z osobami prowadzącymi zajęcia, planowanie nauki oraz czasu wolnego. Korzystanie ze wsparcia nie wymaga orzeczenia o niepełnosprawności i diagnozy spektrum zaburzeń autystycznych. Każda studentka i każdy student, którzy podejrzewają u siebie ASD, mogą wziąć udział w projekcie i otrzymać wsparcie. W ramach projektu prowadzone są również prace nad rozpowszechnieniem wiedzy o spektrum zaburzeń autystycznych.
Komu służy innowacja?
Studenci oraz osoby zakwalifikowane do rozpoczęcia studiów, którzy w okresie ostatnich 5 lat korzystały (bądź korzystają aktualnie) z pomocy specjalistycznej, psychologicznej bądź też są pod opieką organizacji zrzeszającej osoby z ASD.
Kto może wdrażać innowację?
Uczelnie wyższe.
Produkty powstałe w wyniku testowania
Raport końcowy;
model asystenta studenta z ASD;
scenariusz warsztatu
szkoleniowego dla przyszłych asystentów;
materiały informacyjne skierowane do studentów i pracowników uczelni.
Rezultaty osiągnięte w wyniku testowania
W ramach testowania udało się realnie poprawić sytuację wielu studentów ze spektrum autyzmu. 79 studentów z ASD otrzymało wsparcie w komunikacji ze środowiskiem akademickim, co pomogło zrekompensować ich trudności społeczne i ograniczyć zakłócenia w procesie studiowania. U 68 nastąpił wzrost kompetencji społecznych i umiejętności radzenia sobie w życiu zawodowym. Przyczyniło się to do zwiększenia pewności siebie i poziomu samodzielności osób z ASD.
W czasie trwania projektu 42 osoby zdobyły wiedzę w zakresie lidera adwokata studenta z ASD. Powstało też 48 sieci adwokatów studentów z ASD.

innovations.name: Model Dom – skalowanie innowacji społecznej
innovations.lead: Kompleksowe wsparcie rodzin dzieci w trakcie leczenia onkologicznego lub po przebytej chorobie onkologicznej
innovations.problem:
Najczęstszymi nowotworami u dzieci jest białaczka – stanowi ok. 30% zachorowań, kolejnymi są: guzy mózgu (16%), chłoniaki (13%), nowotwór układu współczulnego (7%), nowotwór nerek (7%). Według danych krajowego konsultanta w dziedzinie onkologii pediatrycznej, w Polsce co roku na raka choruje ponad 1000 dzieci (co daje 1000 rodzin rocznie dotkniętych problemem choroby onkologicznej), co stanowi około 1% ogółu zachorowań na nowotwory w społeczeństwie. Każdego roku 2000-2200 dzieci poddawane jest leczeniu przeciwnowotworowemu, a około 10 000 dzieci wymaga monitorowania stanu zdrowia. Ponad 85% małych pacjentów chorujących na białaczki zostaje wyleczona. Wyleczalność dla wszystkich nowotworów dziecięcych wynosi ok. 80% (
Złota Wstążka
, dane za rok 2020), co daje ogromną roczną liczbę dzieci i rodzin, które potrzebują wsparcia w zakresie powrotu do funkcjonowania w rzeczywistości poza szpitalnej. Ich stan zdrowia i jakość życia jest wyzwaniem do działań lekarzy, psychologów, socjologów.
innovations.description:
Innowacja opiera się na publikacjach merytorycznych, głównie poradnikach, dotyczących tematyki związanej z problemami dzieci chorych onkologicznie lub po przebytym leczeniu oraz ich rodzin. Rozesłano je w formie papierowej do wszystkich ośrodków biorących udział w projekcie jako jedno z narzędzi wsparcia rodzin. Publikacje są również dostępne w formie elektronicznej na stronie
www.wsparciezdrowiadzieci.pl
.
W ramach projektu Model Dom – skalowanie innowacji społecznej zaoferowano 30 rodzinom wsparcie w 15 ośrodkach środowiskowej opieki psychologicznej i psychoterapeutycznej (I poziom referencyjny nowego systemu ochrony zdrowia psychicznego dzieci i młodzieży)
z terenu całej Polski.
Ośrodki poprzez zatrudnienie psychologów i edukatorów zapewniały wsparcie w zgodzie z Modelem DOM dla rodzin biorących udział w projekcie. Oferowane wsparcie było zindywidualizowane i nastawione na pomoc konkretnej rodzinie, co zapewniała przeprowadzona diagnoza oraz indywidualny plan wsparcia dla każdego z członków rodzin. Zatrudniony przez Grantobiorców personel miał za zadanie prócz wsparcia psychologicznego czy wytchnieniowego, włączenie do opieki nad rodziną instytucji środowiska lokalnego tj. MOPS, GOPS, placówki oświatowe itd. Grantobiorcy otrzymywali przez cały okres projektu wsparcie merytoryczne, publikacje merytoryczne stworzone na potrzeby projektu, zakupiono pakiety terapeutyczne dla rodzin oraz ośrodków jako dodatkowe wsparcie w terapii oraz zapewniono szkolenia dla psychologów i edukatorów związane z tematyką projektu.
innovations.target_group: Odbiorcami innowacji są dzieci w trakcie leczenia onkologicznego lub po przebytej chorobie onkologicznej oraz pośrednio instytucje środowiska lokalnego, tj. instytucje pomocowe, instytucje oświaty (w szczególności przedszkola, szkoły) , podmioty organizujące zajęcia dodatkowe dla dzieci itd.
innovations.beneficiaries: Ośrodki środowiskowej opieki psychologicznej i psychoterapeutycznej (I poziom referencyjny nowego systemu ochrony zdrowia psychicznego dzieci i młodzieży) oraz podobne instytucje zajmujące się wspieraniem zdrowia psychicznego.
innovations.evidence:
Rezultaty osiągnięte w wyniku wdrażania na szerszą skalę:
W ramach skalowania udało się realnie poprawić sytuację wielu rodzin dzieci w trakcie leczenia onkologicznego lub po przebytej chorobie onkologicznej oraz pośrednio zaktywizować i wyedukować instytucje środowiska lokalnego we wsparciu osób z podobnymi problemami.
Grantobiorcy – ośrodki środowiskowej opieki psychologicznej i psychoterapeutycznej (I poziom referencyjny nowego systemu ochrony zdrowia psychicznego dzieci i młodzieży) dzięki projektowi miały możliwość wprowadzenia modelu wsparcia pod nadzorem ekspertów z Fundacji Wspierania Zdrowia Dzieci i Młodzieży oraz osób współpracujących przy tworzeniu innowacji (autorem innowacji jest Fundacja Pomocy Dzieciom z Chorobami Nowotworowymi w Poznaniu).

innovations.name: koMIX życiowy
innovations.lead: Terapeutyczna gra planszowa dla nastoletnich wychowanków placówek opiekuńczo-wychowawczych
innovations.problem: Innowacja jest odpowiedzią na wyzwania związane z trudnościami w rozumieniu i radzeniu sobie z silnymi emocjami przez podopiecznych placówek opiekuńczo-wychowawczych. Dodatkowo rozwiązuje problem braku narzędzi, które mogłyby wesprzeć opiekunów w prowadzeniu edukacji emocjonalnej młodzieży z tych placówek.

innovations.target_group: Wychowankowie placówek opiekuńczo-wychowawczych w okresie dojrzewania.

Problem, na który odpowiada innowacja
Innowacja jest odpowiedzią na wyzwania związane z trudnościami w rozumieniu i radzeniu sobie z silnymi emocjami przez podopiecznych placówek opiekuńczo-wychowawczych. Dodatkowo rozwiązuje problem braku narzędzi, które mogłyby wesprzeć opiekunów w prowadzeniu edukacji emocjonalnej młodzieży z tych placówek.
Jak działa innowacja?
Innowacja działa dzięki interaktywnej, angażującej grze planszowej, która jest dostosowana do potrzeb i wyzwań młodzieży przebywającej w placówkach opiekuńczo-wychowawczych.
Komu służy innowacja?
Wychowankowie placówek opiekuńczo-wychowawczych w okresie dojrzewania.

Placówki opiekuńczo-wychowawcze typu rodzinnego i instytucjonalnego;
szkoły publiczne i niepubliczne;
psychologowie/psycholożki;
pedagodzy/pedagożki;
terapeuci/terapeutki;
letnie i zimowe turnusy terapeutyczne;
ośrodki socjoterapeutyczne.
Produkty powstałe w wyniku testowania
Projekt gry planszowej;
instrukcja;
film instruktażowy.

innovations.name: Les Héritiers de la Récup'
innovations.problem:
The association addresses a dual social and environmental challenge: the overproduction of waste and intergenerational isolation. On average, every French person produces 4.6 tonnes of waste per year, whilst overconsumption and waste are depleting natural resources. Beyond raising awareness of the need for moderation, the development of a more circular economy is desirable. This is based on the reuse, repair and transformation of materials.
At the same time, a survey carried out by Petits Frères des Pauvres in 2021 indicated that 530,000 elderly people were in a state of ‘social death’ in France in 2021, whilst 52 per cent of 18–30-year-olds would like to have closer ties with their elders.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Since its foundation in 2021, Les Héritiers de la Récup has organised nearly 350 workshops, raised awareness amongst more than 3,000 people and helped prevent more than 3.5 tonnes of waste. Today, the association organises 95 workshops a year and reaches nearly 950 beneficiaries, with 75 members and a growing network of local authorities and partner organisations.
Its impact is based on two key drivers: building bridges between generations and passing on skills, whilst giving materials a new lease of life and reducing waste.

innovations.raw_text:
Les Héritiers de la Récup'
The association addresses a dual social and environmental challenge: the overproduction of waste and intergenerational isolation. On average, every French person produces 4.6 tonnes of waste per year, whilst overconsumption and waste are depleting natural resources. Beyond raising awareness of the need for moderation, the development of a more circular economy is desirable. This is based on the reuse, repair and transformation of materials.
At the same time, a survey carried out by Petits Frères des Pauvres in 2021 indicated that 530,000 elderly people were in a state of ‘social death’ in France in 2021, whilst 52 per cent of 18–30-year-olds would like to have closer ties with their elders.
Since 2021, Les Héritiers de la Récup has been organising craft workshops that bring different generations together around the reuse of materials.
Its model is based on a number of complementary aspects:
travelling craft workshops: sewing, DIY, gardening and cooking, run at partner venues such as community centres, retirement homes, care homes, schools, library centres and alternative community spaces;
integrated environmental awareness: each workshop begins with a quiz on the challenges of reusing materials and achieving zero waste, followed by practical sessions and discussions;
the collection and reuse of materials: raw materials come from donations by individuals and businesses, as well as from local recycling centres. They are transported, in particular, using a lorry funded by a crowdfunding campaign.
Recognised by the State as being in the public interest since 2022, the association relies on a network of volunteers, half of whom are older people, who are particularly involved in running the workshops.
Since its foundation in 2021, Les Héritiers de la Récup has organised nearly 350 workshops, raised awareness amongst more than 3,000 people and helped prevent more than 3.5 tonnes of waste. Today, the association organises 95 workshops a year and reaches nearly 950 beneficiaries, with 75 members and a growing network of local authorities and partner organisations.
Its impact is based on two key drivers: building bridges between generations and passing on skills, whilst giving materials a new lease of life and reducing waste.

innovations.name: Alim'Mater
innovations.problem:
Nutrition during the first 1,000 days of life (from pregnancy to the child’s third birthday) is crucial for the mother’s health and the child’s development. Poor-quality nutrition during this period is associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes, preterm birth, reduced cognitive abilities and obesity. These risks primarily affect the most vulnerable families. Indeed, social inequalities in health begin on the plate, right from pregnancy.
In France, figures show that one in three children aged between 2 and 7 is overweight, according to a survey by the League Against Obesity. According to DRESS, childhood obesity is three to four times more common in nursery schools in priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy (QPV). Yet there are no prevention programmes specifically targeting diet throughout this period amongst the most vulnerable groups. As for healthcare professionals, they lack the time and training to address the issue.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
In 2025, Alim’Mater reached 553 families through 119 workshops aimed at pregnant women and parents of children aged 0 to 3. The association also distributed €5,000 worth of organic food (fruit, nuts, baby food, and vouchers) to the most vulnerable families.
Alim’Mater brings together 197 healthcare professionals as members, offers 18 webinars available for replay, and has participated in four conferences. Its app, ‘9 mois à croquer’, has been downloaded 10,000 times. This work is carried out thanks to three staff members, around thirty volunteers, a board of directors and a multidisciplinary scientific advisory board.

innovations.raw_text:
Alim'Mater
Nutrition during the first 1,000 days of life (from pregnancy to the child’s third birthday) is crucial for the mother’s health and the child’s development. Poor-quality nutrition during this period is associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes, preterm birth, reduced cognitive abilities and obesity. These risks primarily affect the most vulnerable families. Indeed, social inequalities in health begin on the plate, right from pregnancy.
In France, figures show that one in three children aged between 2 and 7 is overweight, according to a survey by the League Against Obesity. According to DRESS, childhood obesity is three to four times more common in nursery schools in priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy (QPV). Yet there are no prevention programmes specifically targeting diet throughout this period amongst the most vulnerable groups. As for healthcare professionals, they lack the time and training to address the issue.
Founded in 2023 by a doctor specialising in nutrition and public health, Alim'Mater runs the ‘1,000 Days to Crunch’ prevention programme. The aim is to provide free resources accessible to all families, with a particular focus on those most in need.
Its work is organised around three key areas:
promoting a healthy, sustainable and affordable diet amongst the most vulnerable families, starting from pregnancy. This is achieved through workshops led by dietitians and nutritionists, as well as free resources: illustrated fact sheets written in simple language and the ‘9 Months to Crunch’ app;
tackling food insecurity during pregnancy and early childhood by providing families with financial support through vouchers or fresh, organic produce. This aspect relies on partners such as Action contre la Faim, the Racines social grocery shop and VRAC Marseille;
equipping professionals in the fields of nutrition, perinatal care and early childhood (maternal and child health centres (PMI), health centres, and primary health insurance funds (CPAM)), who are on the front line in conveying prevention messages to families.
In 2025, Alim’Mater reached 553 families through 119 workshops aimed at pregnant women and parents of children aged 0 to 3. The association also distributed €5,000 worth of organic food (fruit, nuts, baby food, and vouchers) to the most vulnerable families.
Alim’Mater brings together 197 healthcare professionals as members, offers 18 webinars available for replay, and has participated in four conferences. Its app, ‘9 mois à croquer’, has been downloaded 10,000 times. This work is carried out thanks to three staff members, around thirty volunteers, a board of directors and a multidisciplinary scientific advisory board.

innovations.name: Le Réseau Éco Habitat
innovations.problem:
The energy and environmental crisis is hitting the most vulnerable households particularly hard: according to the National Observatory on Precarity, in 2022, 4.8 million households – representing 12 million people – were affected by energy poverty in France, including 350,000 very low-income owner-occupier households living in substandard accommodation. Cold in winter, hot in summer, excessive energy consumption and deteriorating health are the main consequences.
Yet it is the lowest-income households that find it hardest to access public renovation schemes, despite increased financial support.
innovations.description:
Since 2014, Le Réseau Éco Habitat has been providing end-to-end support to owner-occupiers on very low incomes with the comprehensive energy-efficiency refurbishment of their homes.
Through its support, it removes the social, financial and technical barriers that often prevent these households from undertaking such work. Its support is based on a community-focused approach: each family receives personalised support from the initial contact right through to the end of the works, with the help of a volunteer and a team of staff.
The organisation identifies the household’s needs, helps them access public grants and additional funding, ensures the renovation project is properly managed, and oversees the works. This approach enables the most vulnerable households to take an active role in their project and carry out renovations that lead to a sustainable reduction in their energy consumption.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Since 2014, Le Réseau Éco Habitat has supported 424 families and successfully completed 175 renovation projects in the Hauts-de-France region, achieving an average energy saving of 64.8 per cent per renovated home.
The Social Impact Bond, carried out in partnership with the National Housing Agency (Anah) and Secours Catholique between 2020 and 2024, has enabled the organisation to support 111 very low-income households, with the average energy saving rising from 49 per cent to 66 per cent over the period, thanks in particular to the involvement of 58 volunteer support workers.

innovations.name: L'Alternative Urbaine
innovations.problem:
Priority neighbourhoods under urban policy (QPVs) are characterised by a combination of precarious living conditions, distance from employment and a negative public image. The unemployment rate there exceeds 26 per cent, compared with 11.7 per cent nationally, whilst one in three residents believes that their neighbourhood is viewed unfavourably by the rest of the city, according to the National Observatory for Urban Policy. Furthermore, fewer than one in four residents of a QPV consider their neighbourhood to be ‘a very pleasant place to live’.
At the same time, over 90 per cent of the integration schemes offered to the unemployed are in the construction, maintenance or personal care sectors.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence:
In 2025, with three branches, L’Alternative Urbaine supported 24 urban guides who were distanced from the labour market and organised 238 walking tours in 13 priority neighbourhoods, bringing together 1,600 participants.
90 per cent of participants reported having greater self-confidence after the training, compared with 30 per cent at the start of the programme, and 93 per cent felt comfortable speaking in public, compared with 56 per cent at the outset. 60 per cent of those completing the programme went on to find a job, undertake further training or set up their own business.
For the walkers, the main impact lies in a change in perspective: 90 per cent say they now view the neighbourhoods visited more positively, 65 per cent would like to return there, and 30 per cent say their relationship with these areas has changed.
The association thus operates on two fronts: re-engaging people who are distant from the labour market by highlighting their skills and giving them a voice, whilst helping to change the image of and foster a sense of ownership in working-class neighbourhoods.

innovations.raw_text:
L'Alternative Urbaine
Priority neighbourhoods under urban policy (QPVs) are characterised by a combination of precarious living conditions, distance from employment and a negative public image. The unemployment rate there exceeds 26 per cent, compared with 11.7 per cent nationally, whilst one in three residents believes that their neighbourhood is viewed unfavourably by the rest of the city, according to the National Observatory for Urban Policy. Furthermore, fewer than one in four residents of a QPV consider their neighbourhood to be ‘a very pleasant place to live’.
At the same time, over 90 per cent of the integration schemes offered to the unemployed are in the construction, maintenance or personal care sectors.
Since 2016, L’Alternative Urbaine has been transforming walking and cultural mediation into tools for professional integration and the revitalisation of working-class neighbourhoods.
Its work is based on three complementary activities:
a programme for integration through cultural mediation: people who are distant from the labour market undertake the ‘Becoming an Urban Guide’ programme, a vocational training course in cultural mediation and public speaking, and then lead paid walking tours as part of a socio-professional integration programme run in partnership with the intermediary association ARE 33. The programme also combines individual and group support, particularly addressing barriers related to mobility, digital literacy and health;
cultural walking tours in working-class neighbourhoods: offered to the general public on a pay-what-you-can basis or commissioned by businesses, local authorities and social organisations, these tours enable participants to discover little-known neighbourhoods through the eyes and stories of their residents. The aim is to foster a sense of ownership of these neighbourhoods, enhance their appeal and change the way they are perceived;
practical training programmes leading to employment: the association also develops innovative training courses aimed at re-engaging people in the labour market, particularly in the fields of cultural mediation and theatre.
The programme is supported by the European Union, the Nouvelle-Aquitaine Region, the Gironde Department and Bordeaux Métropole, alongside private partners such as Vinci.
In 2025, with three branches, L’Alternative Urbaine supported 24 urban guides who were distanced from the labour market and organised 238 walking tours in 13 priority neighbourhoods, bringing together 1,600 participants.
90 per cent of participants reported having greater self-confidence after the training, compared with 30 per cent at the start of the programme, and 93 per cent felt comfortable speaking in public, compared with 56 per cent at the outset. 60 per cent of those completing the programme went on to find a job, undertake further training or set up their own business.
For the walkers, the main impact lies in a change in perspective: 90 per cent say they now view the neighbourhoods visited more positively, 65 per cent would like to return there, and 30 per cent say their relationship with these areas has changed.
The association thus operates on two fronts: re-engaging people who are distant from the labour market by highlighting their skills and giving them a voice, whilst helping to change the image of and foster a sense of ownership in working-class neighbourhoods.

innovations.name: La Jardinière
innovations.problem:
French agriculture is facing a crisis that is at once social, economic and ecological: nearly half of all farmers will retire within the next ten years, whilst 18 per cent live below the poverty line. At the same time, the dominant agricultural models are damaging the soil, water and biodiversity, and are contributing to the decline of rural areas.
Collective and cooperative farms offer a solution to these challenges by pooling means of production, responsibilities and resources, whilst promoting agroecological practices and short supply chains. They also serve as hubs for cooperation and community life, re-establishing links between agriculture and society.
innovations.description:
Founded in 2012, La Jardinière has, since 2022, focused primarily on developing community-run agroecological farms, which it regards as a catalyst for transforming the agricultural system. It is currently building a network driven by the farms themselves, promoting mutual support, the sharing of best practice and the emergence of new projects.
Its work is based on a collaborative approach: the farms and project leaders are both beneficiaries and active participants in the network. The organisation facilitates meetings between collectives, encourages peer-to-peer exchanges and develops shared resources (a wiki, feedback on experiences, training courses and working groups) to support the creation and long-term sustainability of collective farms.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The association’s dissemination strategy is based on these replicable models, which are capable of fostering autonomous local initiatives. Inter-collective meetings, in particular, serve as a key driving force: the third edition, held in March 2026, brought together 115 participants from 22 collective farms and 19 project leaders over three days. In particular, it helped to spark plans to establish networks in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté and Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur.
La Jardinière is also part of the ‘Fermes Partagées’ network, to which it contributed by helping to set up the SCIC Les Fermes Partagées in 2019–2020.

innovations.name: La PASS de ville Marseille
innovations.problem:
In France, access to healthcare remains characterised by significant social inequalities. According to France Assos Santé, nearly two in three people say they have already foregone or postponed treatment for financial or administrative reasons, or because of the complexity of the healthcare system. The failure to claim entitlements exacerbates this situation: nearly 30 per cent of those eligible for the supplementary solidarity health cover do not make use of it. Only about one in two people make use of the State Medical Aid.
Barriers such as a lack of awareness of entitlements, administrative red tape, language barriers, stigma and out-of-pocket costs lead to delays in care and to repeated and inappropriate use of A&E services. This exacerbates health situations already weakened by precarious living conditions. Yet general practice, the first point of contact under the standard healthcare system, remains largely under-utilised by these groups.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
In 2025, la PASS de ville Marseille supported 1,343 people and processed 1,269 applications for the introduction or reinstatement of health insurance cover. This enabled many people to re-engage with the healthcare system.
La PASS de ville Marseille provided 720 in-person accompaniment services to medical appointments over the course of the year. In 2025, the organisation drew on a network of 133 partner healthcare professionals, compared with 45 when it was first established.

innovations.name: Social Innovation in Multidisciplinary Field-Based Intervention
innovations.problem: The project addresses the issue of inadequate and fragmented community-based health and social care for socially excluded individuals experiencing homelessness or at risk of losing their housing. They face serious health issues, barriers to accessing assistance, and often violence, which hinders their social inclusion. The goal is to improve the active inclusion of these individuals by developing an integrated system of multidisciplinary outreach assistance (TSSKI, healthcare, assistance in cases of violence and/or human trafficking). The system responds to the needs of vulnerable groups and increases their chances of improving their health, safety, protection of rights, housing, and socio-economic integration. The project fulfills the call’s objectives: supporting active inclusion, developing innovative approaches in social work, healthcare, and protection against violence. It focuses on overcoming barriers, improving access to services, and supporting reintegration. A multidisciplinary approach allows for an effective “one-stop” response to the client’s complex needs, with trust and respect for their situation. It prevents duplication, gaps, and inconsistencies in approaches.
innovations.description: The aim of the project is to contribute, through systemic changes in the support and development of integrated, multidisciplinary fieldwork, to improving the quality of life and increasing the social inclusion of socially excluded and vulnerable groups in Slovakia, particularly those experiencing homelessness or at risk of losing their housing, including victims of violence, people from marginalized communities, members of minority groups, and migrants. The project aims to overcome existing barriers to accessing integrated health and social care through an innovative multidisciplinary field-based approach. This comprehensive support system not only improves the health and social situation of individuals but also contributes to reducing social exclusion and to a more efficient use of existing resources in society. Ultimately, the project aims to contribute to systemic changes in the field of support for homeless people in Slovakia through proven methods, the dissemination of best practices, and advocacy for better integration of services and legislative support for multidisciplinary fieldwork.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
1. Results of work with clients (quantitative and qualitative outputs) At least 200 homeless individuals or those at risk of losing their housing will be involved in multidisciplinary outreach interventions in the BSK and BBSK regions during the project’s duration.
2. Project outputs (material, systemic, advocacy, and data).
3. Networking, system integration, and social impact Strengthening cooperation between organizations and institutions from various sectors in fieldwork and enhancing its multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary nature. (Measurable by the number of joint interventions and cooperation agreements).

innovations.name: L'Économe
innovations.problem:
According to ADEME, around 10 million tonnes of food are wasted in France every year. A significant proportion of this occurs as early as the agricultural production stage. Between overproduction, sizing requirements and a shortage of labour during the harvest, a large quantity of perfectly edible fruit and vegetables is left to go to waste. It is estimated that a third of the fruit and vegetables produced never reach the consumer.
At the same time, food insecurity is on the rise. According to the Centre for Research into the Study and Observation of Living Conditions, one in six people in France do not have enough to eat. Charities are struggling to provide fresh, local produce to their beneficiaries. Added to this is the lack of processing facilities accessible to small and medium-sized producers, who have no straightforward way of making use of their surplus produce.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Since its creation, L’Économe has saved 58 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from going to waste. In 2025, the organisation diverted 12.7 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from being destroyed, of which 8.8 tonnes were redistributed to ten partner charities in the Var region and 3.6 tonnes were turned into 12,682 jars thanks to its mobile canning facility.
Its work has benefited around 13,000 people, including nearly 10,000 recipients of food aid. L’Économe has also reached 2,768 people through 77 awareness-raising events across 32 local authorities.

L'Économe
According to ADEME, around 10 million tonnes of food are wasted in France every year. A significant proportion of this occurs as early as the agricultural production stage. Charities are struggling to provide fresh, local produce to their beneficiaries. Added to this is the lack of processing facilities accessible to small and medium-sized producers, who have no straightforward way of making use of their surplus produce.
Since July 2017, L’Économe has been tackling food waste at source and organising the charitable redistribution of salvaged fruit and vegetables.
Its model is based on four complementary activities, all of which form part of its scaling-out strategy:
charitable collections at markets: weekly collection of unsold produce from market gardeners;
solidarity-based harvesting in the fields: organised gleaning at producers’ farms involving volunteers and food aid recipients;
processing via the mobile canning facility: a travelling kitchen that visits producers to turn their surplus produce into jars;
awareness-raising events: cookery workshops, ‘smoocyclette’ (a food bike), and anti-waste buffets for schoolchildren, older people, families and businesses.
Since its creation, L’Économe has saved 58 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from going to waste. In 2025, the organisation diverted 12.7 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from being destroyed, of which 8.8 tonnes were redistributed to ten partner charities in the Var region and 3.6 tonnes were turned into 12,682 jars thanks to its mobile canning facility.
Its work has benefited around 13,000 people, including nearly 10,000 recipients of food aid. L’Économe has also reached 2,768 people through 77 awareness-raising events across 32 local authorities.

innovations.name: Réfugiés Bienvenue
innovations.problem:
In France, refugees (more than 689,000 in 2024) are expected to be able to secure housing and employment independently. In reality, however, the complexity of the asylum process, their distance from the labour market, support schemes that are often inadequate, and social isolation hinder this independence.
At the same time, the labour market is experiencing persistent pressures: in the third quarter of 2025, there were around 458,000 vacancies in the private sector, particularly in sectors facing labour shortages, such as construction and the hospitality and catering industries.
innovations.description:
Since 2015, Réfugiés Bienvenue has been working in the Île-de-France region to promote the reception, inclusion and self-reliance of refugees.
The organisation runs two separate accommodation schemes:
‘citizen-hosted accommodation’, which involves refugees staying with private individuals in the Île-de-France region, supported by a network of volunteers;
the ‘Réfugiés Bienvenue’ Houses, established in 2022: shared accommodation for 3 to 4 people for 12 months, each linked to a sector facing labour shortages. Those accommodated benefit from stable housing as well as social and professional support aimed at helping them access employment and independent housing.
In addition to its accommodation schemes, the organisation offers personalised social and professional support, as well as the Créations de Liens InterCulturels (CLIC) programme, which promotes social and intercultural ties through cultural, sporting and leisure activities.
Réfugiés Bienvenue is a member of the international network Refugees Welcome International.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence:
Since 2020, more than 90 per cent of those supported by the association have secured independent accommodation, following an average support period of twelve months.
Five ‘Maisons Réfugiés Bienvenue’ centres are now open in Paris and Neuilly-sur-Marne, and nearly thirty people have been supported there. By the end of 2025, over 80 per cent of those who had completed the programme had secured a long-term employment contract (a fixed-term contract of more than one year or a permanent contract) and found independent accommodation. In 2025, the association supported 40 beneficiaries and relied on around thirty volunteers.

innovations.name: CARE+ - Tools and Community Support for Informal Caregivers of Older Adults
innovations.problem:
A key tool of the project is the SILVERGON careplan digital app, which enables families to:
• identify the changing needs of older adults,
• create and customize individual care plans,
• involve the wider community in the caregiving process.
The project targets people at risk of poverty and social exclusion, particularly informal caregivers of older adults (often women) and older adults over 65 who are facing a loss of autonomy and need support from both their families and community services.
innovations.description:
The CARE+ project brings innovation in four areas:
• app customization incorporating personalized recommendations, AI support, and digital tools for effective coordination,
• community support a volunteer program in pilot locations focused on interpersonal connections and social inclusion,
• collaboration with employers: creating workplaces that are accommodating to employees with caregiving responsibilities,
• building local ecosystems: connecting communities, local governments, experts, and services.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Improving informal caregivers’ access to digital tools and practical information to help them better manage the day-to-day care of older adults.
• Strengthening the capacity of local organizations and institutions to create a more welcoming and supportive environment for informal caregivers.
• Increasing family and community involvement in the care of older adults, with an emphasis on intergenerational solidarity and shared activities.
• Reducing stress and emotional exhaustion among informal caregivers through accessible support, the sharing of experiences, and the sense that they are not alone.
• Expanding caregiver-friendly approaches in the workplace through flexible working conditions and greater understanding on the part of employers.

innovations.name: Social Entrepreneuership for Rural Development
innovations.problem: Many rural areas face an interconnected set of challenges: demographic decline, young and qualified people leaving, limited employment opportunities, long commuting distances, declining services and fewer places for social interaction. This can create a cycle in which shrinking opportunities make rural areas less attractive, leading to further population and infrastructure decline. At the same time, digitalisation and remote work have reduced the need for many jobs to be located in cities. However, rural communities often lack the professional infrastructure, networks and social environments needed to benefit fully from this transition. Coconat addresses this gap. It creates local opportunities to work, start projects and businesses, build professional networks and participate in community life. It also responds to social isolation among remote workers and to the disappearance of traditional rural meeting places. The underlying challenge is therefore not only employment, but equal access to opportunities, networks, services and participation. Coconat aims to turn digital transformation into an instrument for rural inclusion rather than another factor increasing the urban-rural divide.

innovations.name: Cooperative archipelago for coastal habitability
innovations.problem: Low-lying coastal territories face a convergence of accelerating threats: sea-level rise, coastal erosion, marine flooding — and a near-total absence of tools, skills and community frameworks to adapt in time. Gâvres peninsula illustrates this blind spot: physically vulnerable, socially fragile, economically seasonal, yet without the infrastructure to turn local exposure into collective capacity. Beyond Gâvres, 10,000 km² of French coastline and 500,000 homes face submersion by 2100.
innovations.description: 3 interlocked innovation ecosystems and projects : First, a permanent convivial infrastructure — open year-round, economically self-sustaining through activity cross-subsidisation — that makes coastal adaptation a lived, everyday reality rather than an expert debate. Second, a pioneering training ecosystem: France's first sail-work maritime programme, first flood rescue course for the general public, and an incoming university degree in coastal resilience — building the professional and citizen skills territories urgently need. Third, an expanding cooperative archipelago: a Submersion Witness House exploring legal and economic frameworks for coastal heritage adaptation, and a Campus of Coastal Transitions on Bailleron island — designed as a shared infrastructure for cross-territorial learning, replication and European cooperation.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Other target groups
innovations.evidence: From Maison Glaz (historical project since 2019) to the upcoming Coastal Transition Campus on Bailleron island (2026) For participants: 150 people trained in coastal resilience in 2025, including 30 job-seekers; 15 permanent jobs maintained year-round on a seasonally fragile territory; measurable pathways from exclusion to qualified employment. For the territory: 35,000 annual visitors, 100+ events per year, €1M in locally circulated value over three years — sustaining social cohesion and economic activity on a peninsula otherwise emptied off-season. For the social economy field: a documented proof-of-concept that non-lucrative governance, inclusion, hybrid financing and territorial rootedness are the key engine of genuine adaptation to climate change
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Les Bricolades
innovations.problem:
The project operates in a context of socio-economic deprivation within disadvantaged urban neighbourhoods (Priority Urban Areas).
It addresses three major local needs:
Housing improvement and purchasing power
Many residents lack the means to maintain or renovate their homes.
The project enables tenants to reduce costs through self-renovation and environmentally friendly practices, including waste reduction and energy savings.
Social inclusion and mental wellbeing
Local assessments revealed high levels of social isolation, particularly among retired people and single parents.
The project rebuilds social connections and strengthens self-confidence and empowerment.
Local ecological transition
The project contributes to environmental sustainability by promoting circular economy practices, reuse, and environmentally friendly DIY solutions.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: La Banque Solidaire de l'Équipement
innovations.problem: Drawing on the experience of its social workers, who support people undergoing social and professional integration on a daily basis, Emmaüs Défi has identified financial and material difficulties in accessing long-term housing. Indeed, whilst access to housing is a crucial step that offers hope to people in difficulty, it also raises issues regarding household furnishings, which can act as a barrier to them settling into their new home.
innovations.description:
The Banque Solidaire de l'Équipement (BSE) has five shops in France, in Paris, Toulouse, Lyon and Lille. In these shops, beneficiaries – who have been referred by social workers from partner organisations – are welcomed by BSE staff, who assist and advise them with their purchases.
The products on offer in BSE shops are new, high-quality items at prices that are, on average, 71 per cent lower than market prices. Indeed, BSE’s aim is to enable everyone to personalise their home so they can make it their own and feel ‘at home’.
The logistics involved in handling the items – both upstream (receiving donations) and downstream (preparing orders and home deliveries) – are managed by employees on work integration programmes at Emmaüs Défi.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
43,000 people supported by the BSE
1,700 social workers who refer clients
60 partner companies that make donations

innovations.name: Le RECHO
innovations.problem: The refugee crisis we are currently facing is an unprecedented situation. By the end of 2022, there were 12.4 million refugees, fleeing the horrors of war and destitution, on the soil of a weakened Europe. Then there was the photograph in September 2015 of the body of little Aylan, aged 3, washed up on that Turkish beach… Then there were the attacks of 13 November 2015, which shook France and the whole of Europe to the core. This ordeal further fuelled fear of ‘the foreigner’, intensified the state of emergency, encouraged isolationism and the closing of borders… Yet it also strengthened the spirit of citizenship and solidarity, characterised by resistance and resilience.
innovations.description:
Le Recho operates through various actions:
Cookery workshops for businesses
Guided by professional chefs and refugee cooks training with RECHO, participants work together to prepare recipes that will be distributed as part of a food aid programme.
Workshops with Secours Populaire de Paris
Every Monday, RECHO brings together around twenty people – either recipients of food aid or referred by the project’s partner associations – in the kitchen of the Secours Populaire solidarity food shop in the 18th arrondissement to cook together recipes that are economical, easy, tasty and healthy.
O2R Re-engagement Programme
This re-engagement programme is aimed at people living in exile in France who are far from the labour market. It combines cookery workshops, social support and group activities.
Cookery workshops for children
Supervised by a professional chef and a refugee cook on a work integration programme at our restaurant, our cookery workshops enable children to meet and interact whilst preparing recipes from around the world.
Les Tables des Voisin·es
Over lunch, thanks to valuable partnerships with several associations, people facing hardship or isolation are invited to the restaurant to come together around the table.
Cookery workshops for the general public
RECHO organises inclusive cookery workshops followed by large charity banquets bringing together those receiving support and those providing it, with the aim of fostering connections and a sense of community through the universal language of cooking.
Social integration restaurants
Since 2019, RECHO has continued its commitment to promoting social inclusion and supporting the professional integration of refugees through the opening of several social integration restaurants.
Tables Ouvertes
Thanks to the support of chefs who share our commitment, RECHO organises charity dinners known as ‘Tables Ouvertes’: over the course of a meal, guest chefs come to cook alongside our team – made up of refugee chefs – to offer them kind support on their journey towards professional development.
Itinéraires Solidaires
Since 2022, Le RECHO has been putting its experience to good use in welcoming cities across France, such as Lyon, Strasbourg and Bourges, to bring together local authorities, associations and the cities’ reception services around a solidarity marathon!
Le Grand RECHO
Conceived as a true hub for community life within a city, Le Grand RECHO is a pop-up restaurant based on solidarity that fosters connections through food, highlighting the hospitality and generosity of an entire region.
Humanitarian missions
In 2016, as our initiative began to take shape, Le RECHO launched a crowdfunding campaign that enabled us to buy a food truck: this gave us the opportunity to travel to reception centres to meet refugee and local communities, so that we could cook together to heal the world!
Advocacy
Given the situation in France and Europe over the past decade or so, and drawing on our expertise on the ground, Le RECHO believes it has a role to play in raising public awareness and advocating to institutions and political authorities.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence: 37,832 Meals prepared and shared together 5,215 Participants in our cookery workshops, from both refugee and host communities 1,100 Volunteers since 2016 4 Social enterprises established since 2019 43 Refugees employed and trained in the catering sector
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: La Ferme de Moyembrie
innovations.problem: A spell in prison deeply undermines a person’s confidence and will to live. Regaining one’s place within a community, breaking free from the routine of prison life, and taking responsibility for oneself once again are all challenges that must be anticipated. Discovering or rediscovering one’s life plan, and returning to the outside world and its rules of social life, are key challenges of reintegration for which prisoners nearing the end of their sentences are still far too ill-prepared.
innovations.description:
La Ferme de Moyembrie is unique in that it takes in people who are still in custody but nearing the end of their sentences, with a view to facilitating their return to society. The residents are exclusively men. The project is structured around three key areas:
> work: market gardening and livestock farming, carried out in accordance with the principles of organic farming, with six AMAPs as clients.
> accommodation: each prisoner has their own accommodation on the farm and pays a monthly rent. They are not permitted to leave the farm’s 20-hectare grounds without being accompanied by a supervisor or a volunteer coordinator.
> Support: assistance with social and administrative issues, as well as support in finding employment and new accommodation upon completion of the programme.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Men and women
25 workers on a work integration programme, including 20 residents on external placements who are accommodated at the farm.
8 paid supervisors, 2 night watchmen and around 40 volunteers committed to the Farm and to helping the residents achieve their life goals.
500 people have been supported since 2000. 150 applications for admission are received from prisoners each year, and 50 people are admitted annually.
The residents’ journey
An average stay of 9 months on the farm: a period that allows residents to settle back into life after prison and prepare for the future, and which is deliberately limited to ensure it remains a stepping stone to leaving the programme.
On average, 70 per cent of residents receive visits or visit their loved ones during temporary leave, thereby gradually preparing for their future after leaving the farm.
60 per cent of leavers are actively engaged in employment: three months after leaving the farm, they are in work, on a training course, living in an Emmaus community or retired. All leave with a housing or accommodation solution.
Agricultural production
140 baskets of vegetables distributed to 6 AMAPs every week.
40 goats for milk production and the making of cheese and yoghurt.
200 laying hens.
The economic model
25 per cent of the budget is covered by the farm’s own resources.
€35 per day: a work placement outside the Ferme de Moyembrie costs the prison service a third of the cost of a prison place.

> accommodation: each prisoner has their own accommodation on the farm and pays a monthly rent. They are not permitted to leave the farm’s 20-hectare grounds without being accompanied by a supervisor or a volunteer coordinator.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
Men and women
25 workers on a work integration programme, including 20 residents on external placements who are accommodated at the farm.
8 paid supervisors, 2 night watchmen and around 40 volunteers committed to the Farm and to helping the residents achieve their life goals.
500 people have been supported since 2000. 150 applications for admission are received from prisoners each year, and 50 people are admitted annually.
The residents’ journey
An average stay of 9 months on the farm: a period that allows residents to settle back into life after prison and prepare for the future, and which is deliberately limited to ensure it remains a stepping stone to leaving the programme.
On average, 70 per cent of residents receive visits or visit their loved ones during temporary leave, thereby gradually preparing for their future after leaving the farm.
60 per cent of leavers are actively engaged in employment: three months after leaving the farm, they are in work, on a training course, living in an Emmaus community or retired. All leave with a housing or accommodation solution.
Agricultural production
140 baskets of vegetables distributed to 6 AMAPs every week.
40 goats for milk production and the making of cheese and yoghurt.
200 laying hens.
The economic model
25 per cent of the budget is covered by the farm’s own resources.
€35 per day: a work placement outside the Ferme de Moyembrie costs the prison service a third of the cost of a prison place.

innovations.raw_text:
APREVA
Today in France, nearly 13 million people face mobility difficulties. One in three French people also say they have had to turn down a job opportunity because of travel problems.
Since 2010, our mission has been to support people in vulnerable circumstances by offering them tailored transport solutions. Our aim is to ensure that a lack of transport is no longer a barrier to accessing, returning to or retaining employment, but also to independence and maintaining a social life.
Our support is based on four main areas of activity:
1. Vehicle hire at subsidised rates;
2. Vehicle maintenance and repairs at our Social Integration Workshop and our community garage, both located in Aiguillon;
3. Social Transport Services (TUS);
4. Vehicle sales.
This social micro-transport service is aimed at people facing mobility difficulties, particularly older people, those with visual impairments or those with reduced independence. It enables them to access essential everyday services: medical appointments, healthcare, administrative procedures, access to entitlements, shopping or activities that help maintain social connections.
Our entire fleet consists of donated vehicles. We collect cars that are no longer needed by private individuals, businesses or local authorities, and then repair them at our Social Integration Workshop.
Each vehicle is thus given a new lease of life and a new social purpose, enabling people to travel to work, attend training courses, access healthcare or maintain their independence.

300 Repairs per year

innovations.name: Toutenvélo
innovations.problem:
The transport sector is the largest emitter of greenhouse gases (GHGs), with urban logistics alone accounting for 30 per cent of emissions. The environmental impact of travel is now a key issue. Sustainable transport solutions therefore play a major role in the fight against climate change.
Before Toutenvélo there were no environmentally friendly and secure transport solutions for parcels.
innovations.description:
For Toutenvélo, the development of local projects lies at the heart of our ambition. Our mission is to establish independent, resilient organisations with democratic governance.
This same mission enables us to tailor our services as closely as possible to the needs of local authorities, economic stakeholders and residents, whilst taking into account the specific characteristics of the area in question.
The cooperative status of Toutenvélo’s organisations enables us to:
strongly involve all employees in the entrepreneurial process
ensure the long-term sustainability of the collective enterprise beyond the individuals involved
guarantee the integrity of our economic, social and solidarity-based values
From logistics to trailer manufacturing
Our added value at Toutenvélo is that we are able to offer our customers a comprehensive range of logistics solutions, as we are both cycle couriers and trailer manufacturers.
We offer a comprehensive solution dedicated to the last mile, with a focus on quality of service:
Expertise developed over more than 10 years
Suitable and robust transport equipment
Reliability and expertise of our operational teams

innovations.name: GRAP
innovations.problem:
Two needs have been identified:
Firstly, there is a need to structure the organic food sector, small-scale farming and short supply chains in the Rhône-Alpes region, particularly with regard to supply.
Secondly, there is a need to develop economically viable, socially just and environmentally friendly activities.
innovations.description:
The GRAP cooperative has set itself the mission of bringing together various organisations within the sector around a shared project based on two pillars: the pooling of a number of tasks inherent to their activities as food business owners (HR, legal, accounting and tax, financial, administrative and IT management) and support for the establishment and development of businesses and their projects.
This pooling of resources therefore applies to every GRAP member, including organic grocery shops, chocolate shops, bakeries, farmers’ markets, restaurants, caterers, retailers of Italian products, wine merchants, small-scale processing workshops, delivery services and organic meal preparation facilities supplying nurseries – totalling around sixty businesses today.
The support provided, meanwhile, covers professional expertise, overall strategy, project set-up and any other needs that may aid a business’s development. It applies to each entity individually and can take place from the actual establishment stage (i.e. once the project is sufficiently concrete to ensure a high degree of certainty regarding its integration into the cooperative) right through to the development of the business. GRAP also organises training courses, open to all cooperative members, which help to improve everyone’s professional practices.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The direct beneficiaries of the project are the entrepreneurs themselves, who benefit from a secure framework in which to run their businesses. The strength of this consortium’s model lies in the fact that the entrepreneurs are both beneficiaries and active participants in it.
The social impact of the cooperative is therefore seen, on the one hand, in the development and sustainability of its activities and, on the other, in the employment conditions of the entrepreneur-employees. Pooling resources aims to achieve self-sufficient funding, with public subsidies covering the shortfall (in the region of 10 per cent to 15 per cent). Environmental impact is also a priority for GRAP, which has developed tools to assess its performance in this area and raise consumer awareness. One of its initiatives, for example, involves a product-by-product rating system based on four criteria (local origin, social impact, production methods and packaging).
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Pistyles
innovations.problem: The Pistyles project was set up to address the under-use of environmentally friendly techniques in the landscaping sector and to highlight the human, social and entrepreneurial qualities of gardeners, whose profession has become increasingly technical in recent years and has lost its original purpose: caring for nature.
innovations.description:
Pistyles’ role is that of both a gardener (someone who looks after the garden, a space of human-shaped nature) and a mediator (that is to say, someone who facilitates dialogue and rebuilds close-knit relationships).
The project is structured around three key areas:
Putting residents back at the heart of their gardens and customer relations
Putting nature and respect for it back at the heart of the professional landscaping and gardening sector
Restoring the gardener’s full role as a passionate professional and entrepreneur
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
In terms of environmental performance, the organisation has succeeded in:
Achieving virtually zero waste, meaning zero export of materials and zero use of plant protection products (no pesticides)
Eliminating virtually all bare ground (to combat soil depletion, erosion, etc.)

innovations.name: RézoSocial
innovations.problem: The RézoSocial project was set up to meet the need to create pathways to employment for people excluded from the labour market.
innovations.description:
As an accredited social integration enterprise, RézoSocial is committed to promoting integration through economic activity. Employees on integration programmes are hired, for a maximum period of two years, in roles as IT maintenance technicians or junior developers.
The success of the objective of helping these employees return to work is based on:
The acquisition of advanced IT skills throughout the programme
Practical training and direct experience working with clients
Social and professional support
Preparation for leaving the programme, facilitated by targeted initiatives (career planning, work placements, job-search techniques)
The trust placed in them by the whole team
The high staff-to-participant ratio is a key factor that forms an integral part of the model and contributes to its success.
As a social integration enterprise, RézoSocial itself employs staff on subsidised contracts and also develops the software, Siham, which is primarily intended for use by other social integration enterprises. This enables it to maximise its social impact in two ways – directly and indirectly – as a social integration organisation providing services to the social integration sector.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence:
Qualified professionals to support you with your projects. 91 per cent customer satisfaction (2025 figure).
50 per cent of our staff are on a work integration programme.
Over 350 client organisations, including businesses, charities and local authorities.
75 per cent of our staff on work integration programmes secure a permanent contract after two years with us.

innovations.name: Croc La Vie
innovations.problem: On average, a child eats three to four times as much as an adult, relative to their weight. They are therefore more vulnerable to pesticides, and a poor diet can have significant consequences for their development. It is therefore essential to provide them with a healthy, high-quality diet.
innovations.description:
Founded in 2009, Croc la vie has made this its mission and set out to develop a high-quality catering service, tailored to young children and full of flavour. For Croc la vie, getting a child used to a healthy, flavourful diet means educating both children and parents in good eating habits; it means investing in the future and preparing the child to become an adult who is mindful of food-related issues.
To this end, Croc la vie selects fresh, flavourful fruit and vegetables, as well as local and seasonal produce, but above all strives to offer a wide variety of dishes and flavours to develop children’s palates and curiosity.
Whilst Croc la vie initially chose organic farming to provide the best nutrition for children’s mental and physical development, the organisation also wished to make an environmental and economic commitment.
According to Croc la vie, organic farming is the only method of production that is mindful of natural resources and respectful of the environment and biodiversity. This form of agriculture is therefore the only one that can be considered sustainable in the long term, enabling future generations to enjoy a rich and high-quality diet.
The organisation therefore quickly established partnerships with local organic producers who are mindful of their production methods and the quality of their products. For example, the partner bakery sources its organic flour from a grain collector who uses granite millstones to produce exceptional wholemeal flours.
More broadly, respect for the environment is integrated throughout the entire supply chain at Croc la vie and is the subject of constant consideration. Significant measures are already in place: prioritising local and seasonal produce, selecting producers who recover and reuse their packaging, minimising and sorting waste, and reducing transport routes to farms and nurseries.

innovations.name: Plateau Urbain
innovations.problem: In 2013, Simon Laisney observed a structural vacancy in the property market. Indeed, nearly 4 million square metres of office space stood empty in the Île-de-France region, 800,000 of which had been vacant for more than five years and were therefore off the market. He then came up with the idea of prioritising the utility value of these premises over their market value, thereby saving owners unnecessary expenses (maintenance, security, insurance and taxes).
innovations.description:
Plateau Urbain is a cooperative specialising in social housing and transitional and temporary urban planning, offering affordable workspaces and, where possible, emergency accommodation solutions in vibrant, creative and community-focused third places with a social purpose, in the Île-de-France region and in several major cities (Lyon, Bordeaux, Marseille). It also provides consultancy and support services throughout France.
Support Plateau Urbain’s services go beyond simply providing affordable workspaces. Whether you are a local authority, a developer, a landlord or a community group, we support you in designing your transitional and temporary urban planning projects, and ensure the successful implementation of your third-place initiatives.
Setting up and managing third places We manage and oversee fixed-term third-place projects from start to finish: leasing, bringing the premises up to standard, technical and administrative management, events and activities, programming, security and building maintenance.
Consultancy and studies We support local authorities, property owners and community groups in setting up their projects involving temporary occupation, transitional urban planning and third places. Taking into account the specific characteristics of the sites, ecosystems and areas under consideration, the support we offer is based on a bespoke methodology.
A platform for making premises available
Plateau Urbain offers a platform to publicise your calls for applications and connect you with the 12,000 organisations registered on the platform that are looking for affordable workspaces.

innovations.name: AGORAé
innovations.problem: The financial insecurity faced by students is a major social issue: according to the latest survey by the Observatoire de la Vie Etudiante (OVE), 54 per cent of students report experiencing financial difficulties and 45 per cent work whilst studying, often taking on jobs that come at the expense of their studies. In order to cope with these difficulties, spending on food and healthcare is often the first to be cut back.
innovations.description:
The AGORAé project aims to provide services to students and to foster social connections. It is a space for inclusion, exchange and solidarity, run by students for students, comprising:
a student hub open to all, which hosts activities organised by volunteers and participants. Furthermore, this space enables students to find out about their entitlements, obtain advice on everyday life (nutrition, responsible consumption, etc.), develop project management skills, gain an introduction to the voluntary sector and foster solidarity.
a solidarity grocery shop accessible on the basis of social criteria, where students can stock up on food, cleaning products or school supplies at reduced prices (between 10 and 30 per cent below standard prices). Thus, an AGORAé is a social innovation project within the field of the social and solidarity economy. It provides a local response to a real and identified need. This project embodies fundamental values such as solidarity, citizenship and commitment.
Management of AGORAé
AGORAé are run at local level by a team of volunteers from the federation or association responsible for the local AGORAé. The volunteers are supported by young people on civic service placements, as well as by the FAGE’s national team.
At national level, the AGORAé project is led by the FAGE’s national team, which ensures the project’s development and sustainability, and helps to overcome any difficulties that local teams may encounter.
This dual structure enables the creation of a strong and sustainable network, and ensures a positive impact for the beneficiaries.

innovations.name: VRAC
innovations.problem:
In 2012, association activists and committed professionals came to a shared realisation regarding the decline in purchasing power – and consequently in consumption – amongst residents of these neighbourhoods: what people buy, consume or use has an impact on many aspects of their personal, family and social lives. The idea of proposing an alternative way of consuming – to boost people’s ability to cope with precarious circumstances, enhance their self-esteem and promote individual and collective agency – was born.
A study was then undertaken by the association, confirming the following findings: 1. A widening of socio-economic inequalities between residents of working-class neighbourhoods and the rest of the population. 2. Increased discrimination regarding access to consumer goods. 3. A diet leading to health and social problems amongst vulnerable groups. 4. Marked social isolation in working-class neighbourhoods
innovations.description:
The VRAC project arose from the idea of developing a cooperative approach to group buying of food and household products, as well as services. VRAC thus addresses, on the one hand, the demand for affordable, high-quality products amongst local residents and, on the other, the shortfall in food supply (a lack of local shops and an under-representation of discount stores) in some of the working-class neighbourhoods of the Lyon metropolitan area.
Indeed, by cutting out various intermediaries, developing short supply chains, offering bulk delivery, and involving local residents in the process of converting bulk goods into retail units and distributing the products, the VRAC concept enables goods to be sold at the producer’s purchase price.
The VRAC project thus lies at the intersection of several areas of intervention: consumption and food, social cohesion, citizenship, individual and collective empowerment, and the social and solidarity economy.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: 23 areas covered thanks to the work of 22 organisations 143 buying groups 12,300 member households and around 36,450 people reached 2,515 volunteer members 90 staff members
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all
