innovations.name: Article 1
innovations.problem: According to the OECD, it would take six generations in France to escape poverty. Fewer than 10 per cent of children from working-class families go on to become managers, compared with 47 per cent of children from managerial families. 35 per cent of young people from working-class backgrounds go on to higher education, compared with 90 per cent of those from more affluent backgrounds.
innovations.description:
From an academic journey to a path to success
From career guidance to entry into the world of work, we support young people from working-class backgrounds, aged 15 to 25, on their journey to success.
Article 1's action is organised around three key areas: career guidance, academic success and personal development, and finally, preparation for entry into the world of work.
CAREER GUIDANCE: Fostering academic ambition
This area is aimed at Year 11 and Year 12 pupils in general, technological and vocational streams throughout France.
Objectives:
To overcome self-doubt and barriers to continuing one’s studies
To shed light on career guidance options and future prospects
To support sixth-formers in choosing their course of study
SUCCESS: Ensuring students have every opportunity to succeed
This area is aimed at students in preparatory classes, grandes écoles, BTS/IUT programmes and universities.
Individual mentoring, the cornerstone of our work:
Helping students build self-confidence;
Raising their ambitions and helping them develop an academic plan;
Introducing them to the world of business, its professions and its codes of conduct;
Laying the foundations for their career plans and preparing them for entry into the labour market.
PERSONAL DEVELOPMENT: Identifying, assessing, recognising and developing transferable skills.
This programme is aimed at young adults aged 16 to 25.
Its objectives are to enable them to:
Recognise the richness of their life experiences;
Develop and make the most of their key soft skills to enrich their life experiences and improve their employability;
Encourage their commitment to help them take control of their future;
Foster the mindset and skills needed to reinvent themselves, take the initiative and contribute to transforming the world, in their own way.

innovations.name: Bou'Sol
innovations.problem: The project addresses three key issues: helping people with few or no qualifications to return to work; producing organic bakery products for groups who have had little or no access to them until now; and supporting the local organic farming sector (with a focus on short supply chains).
innovations.description:
Bou’Sol supports projects to set up organic social enterprise bakeries and coordinates the network thus formed. Bou’Sol provides a full range of services to the bakeries: establishing and developing local supply chains; developing specific tools for the operational management of social enterprise bakeries; creating communication tools; and implementing initiatives to develop new market opportunities for the bakeries.
What sets Bou’Sol apart is:
the way the bread is made, based on traditional baking methods using additive-free organic flour, with a focus on quality, health and nutrition
its alignment with public policies: the Grenelle II Environment Forum, socially responsible procurement, the ‘Ambition Bio 2017’ initiative, and the National Nutrition and Health Plan
its collective organisational structure, designed to foster autonomy, the involvement of various stakeholders in governance, and solidarity amongst its members.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)

innovations.name: CAIRE13
innovations.problem: In France, the self-employed and entrepreneurs (retailers, craftspeople, micro-entrepreneurs, independent professionals, etc.) account for 99 per cent of businesses and 52 per cent of salaried jobs; yet there is no comprehensive support scheme to assist them when they are faced with illness, particularly cancer. Faced with family, financial and professional challenges, these individuals find not only their ability to remain in employment but also the long-term viability of their businesses severely jeopardised.
innovations.description:
To support the self-employed, CAIRE 13 works in collaboration with a range of local partners, including cancer care centres (the Centre for the Fight against Cancer, hospitals, radiotherapy centres) as well as private healthcare professionals (doctors, nurses, etc.) who refer their patients to the association.
This group, comprising equal numbers of men and women from all socio-professional backgrounds and occupational sectors, is then supported by CAIRE 13 through a socio-professional assessment carried out by a multidisciplinary team, enabling the individual to identify the relevant resources. The association’s volunteers then monitor the self-employed person’s progress and regularly organise group activities to discuss the challenges and issues encountered both before and after their illness, particularly in relation to their professional life.
In addition to this bespoke support, the organisation runs a dedicated drop-in and information centre, the Maison du Rebond, which enables self-employed people to meet up and access a computer room, a library and a resource centre.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
tags: Modernising labour market institutions and services

innovations.name: RoseUp
innovations.problem:
Every year, around 174,000 cases of cancer are diagnosed in women, but medical advances are leading to many remissions or cures. Indeed, according to the Fondation Contre le Cancer, nearly 70 per cent of patients are still alive five years after their diagnosis (all types of cancer combined).
However, according to a study by the National Cancer Institute (INCA), three in five people report continuing to experience the after-effects of the disease two years after diagnosis, whilst 8.5 per cent feel they are subject to discrimination. Furthermore, the growth in outpatient treatments and therapies administered outside hospital settings is heightening the sense of isolation, the need for information and the need for support amongst patients who find themselves alone at home.
innovations.description:
The association's mission is to enable women facing cancer to continue living their lives as women, mothers and professionals both during and after treatment, and also to help them feel less alone in the face of the illness by enabling them to be part of a community, in particular by providing them with information and psychological support throughout the various stages of their illness.
To achieve its objectives, RoseUp has developed several initiatives, including:
Rose Magazine: A women’s magazine with a print run of 180,000 copies, combining in-depth features with lighter topics. It is distributed free of charge in cancer centres and departments and is available online.
Maison RoseUp: This centre aims to break the cycle of isolation, combat recurrence and empower women with cancer to take control of their own journey. Bringing together local organisations (charities, healthcare centres and other professionals), this centre is a true haven in the heart of Bordeaux, open to all women and free of charge. Here, they can find the resources they need (information, talks, etc.) to address all the challenges of living with and after the disease, and take part in workshops (beauty and wellbeing, nutrition, sport, creative arts, career coaching).
RoseCar: a free car-sharing platform for journeys between home and hospital, aimed at fostering solidarity amongst patients, helping to reduce the cost of medical transport, easing the burden on carers and alleviating congestion in hospital car parks.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised

sections.question: Problem
sections.answer:
Every year, around 174,000 cases of cancer are diagnosed in women, but medical advances are leading to many remissions or cures. Indeed, according to the Fondation Contre le Cancer, nearly 70 per cent of patients are still alive five years after their diagnosis (all types of cancer combined).
However, according to a study by the National Cancer Institute (INCA), three in five people report continuing to experience the after-effects of the disease two years after diagnosis, whilst 8.5 per cent feel they are subject to discrimination. Furthermore, the growth in outpatient treatments and therapies administered outside hospital settings is heightening the sense of isolation, the need for information and the need for support amongst patients who find themselves alone at home.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:
The association's mission is to enable women facing cancer to continue living their lives as women, mothers and professionals both during and after treatment, and also to help them feel less alone in the face of the illness by enabling them to be part of a community, in particular by providing them with information and psychological support throughout the various stages of their illness.
To achieve its objectives, RoseUp has developed several initiatives, including:
Rose Magazine: A women’s magazine with a print run of 180,000 copies, combining in-depth features with lighter topics. It is distributed free of charge in cancer centres and departments and is available online.
Maison RoseUp: This centre aims to break the cycle of isolation, combat recurrence and empower women with cancer to take control of their own journey. Bringing together local organisations (charities, healthcare centres and other professionals), this centre is a true haven in the heart of Bordeaux, open to all women and free of charge. Here, they can find the resources they need (information, talks, etc.) to address all the challenges of living with and after the disease, and take part in workshops (beauty and wellbeing, nutrition, sport, creative arts, career coaching).
RoseCar: a free car-sharing platform for journeys between home and hospital, aimed at fostering solidarity amongst patients, helping to reduce the cost of medical transport, easing the burden on carers and alleviating congestion in hospital car parks.

innovations.name: Habit'âge
innovations.problem:
The ageing of the population in Maine-et-Loire is particularly pronounced, especially in rural areas, and is set to increase significantly. Today, 20 per cent of the department’s population is aged 65 and over, and 3,500 people join the over-65s category every year.
There is a high level of vulnerability amongst this section of the population, who are often isolated and whose homes are falling into disrepair due to a lack of maintenance. Nearly 6 per cent of homes occupied by people aged 65 and over are thus identified as ‘potentially unfit for habitation’, amounting to 3,500 homes across the entire department.
Furthermore, whilst new-build construction continues to rise, the department has more than 25,000 vacant or unoccupied homes, the upkeep of which is poorly managed or neglected. Consequently, an entire built heritage is falling into disrepair and requires decisive action to safeguard it.
innovations.description:
Since 2013, the association has been creating shared living spaces designed in collaboration with local residents – spaces that foster connections and independence – so that housing can support a happy and independent old age in rural areas! Since 2018, it has also been running discussion workshops to enable everyone to reflect on and choose their living arrangements for today and tomorrow. Supporting and guiding pensioners as they consider their housing choices seems essential.
Supporting the decision-making process:
Through its commitment to enabling everyone to consider and choose their current and future housing, the association develops initiatives to support older people as they consider their housing options.
Furthermore, it now supports local councillors in developing housing for older people within their local areas.
The three Habit'âge homes:
The association is responsible for the design and project management of the Habit'âge homes in all their aspects: social and local, architectural and financial.
This process is supported by a local steering committee actively involved at every stage, broad community involvement and trusted partnerships.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
In practical terms, Habit’âge involves:
The creation of three homes recognised as inclusive housing
The restoration of three historic buildings in the heart of the village
The raising of nearly 3 million euros (from over 30 funders)
14 people to be housed in the long term
More than 50 local residents involved in the Habit’âge housing projects
1,000 people supported through 60 preventative initiatives in Maine-et-Loire
including more than 500 in the workshops entitled ‘Ageing gracefully and planning for your future home’

innovations.name: E-Fabrik'
innovations.description:
Through its ‘E-Fabrik’ challenges, Traces brings together, at a local level, organisations working with people with disabilities and young people, and innovative digital creativity hubs such as fablabs. It provides spaces for collaboration between young people who are distant from the labour market and people with disabilities, enabling them to devise and create, together, practical solutions relating to disability, whilst acquiring the skills needed to master new digital tools.
Once recruited, the young E-Fabrik’ apprentices meet the E-Fabrik’ mentors – experts in education, disability, digital creation and design – during discussion and training sessions. At the same time, the young apprentices begin working with their E-Fabrik’ partner, a person with a disability who has chosen to get involved in the project. Together, they identify and describe a problem that the partner experiences in their daily life and for which they will seek a solution: their challenge for the next six months is set! It is then within a fablab, and with the support of the E-Fabrik’ mentors, that they will be able to devise and develop a prototype of their solution.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion

innovations.raw_text:
E-Fabrik'
At the heart of the Traces association’s thinking is the belief that experience of science and technology should serve as a vehicle not only for the individual’s empowerment, but also for sparking curiosity and helping people to grasp concepts. The E-Fabrik’ challenge was born out of this philosophy.
Through their various activities and collaborations, the members of Traces made three key observations that sparked the design work for the E-Fabrik’ project:
many young people aged 15 to 25 from working-class neighbourhoods are still excluded from the digital world;
digital manufacturing is a sector under pressure, in which many jobs are currently vacant and will continue to be so;
people with disabilities report a range of needs that could be met through digital manufacturing.

innovations.name: Le Paysan Urbain
innovations.problem: Guided by the values of cooperation, transparency and realistic idealism, the association Le Paysan Urbain is dedicated to the development of environmentally friendly, socially responsible urban agriculture and healthy eating.
innovations.description:
The association focuses its work on two areas: raising public awareness of the challenges facing sustainable agriculture and high-quality food, and establishing urban agroecological farms that are economically viable, socially responsible and firmly rooted in their local communities.
In light of the observed deterioration in social ties in urban areas, the disconnect between city-dwellers and the environment, and the growing desire for access to high-quality local food, the association runs workshops in its educational garden to help and encourage city-dwellers to rediscover a connection with the land, and to raise awareness amongst young and old alike of environmental issues – such as the use of chemicals in conventional agriculture, significant food waste, the considerable distances food is transported over, and pollution caused by production and consumption patterns – as well as social issues, such as the precarious working conditions faced by farmers.
In July 2015, Le Paysan Urbain set up its first eco-friendly and socially responsible urban micro-farm, La Belle Pousse, in Romainville, to grow microgreens.
On a 6,000 m² site, the charity has set up its greenhouses and grows microgreens – plants that are slightly more developed than a sprout but much smaller than a mature plant, and which are tasty and fresh. These organically grown microgreens are sown in natural compost, enriched with compost produced from local organic waste, and distributed locally by bicycle. To round off its environmental project, the association has, of course, connected its farm to a renewable and cooperative energy source by partnering with EnerCoop.
Today, the association is recognised as an organisation promoting social integration through economic activity and already employs several people on integration programmes, both in the cultivation of the sprouts and in their packaging and distribution.
Finally, it is here that Le Paysan Urbain has set up its educational garden to carry out the bulk of its work raising awareness of environmental issues such as organic farming, short supply chains, the fight against food waste and responsible consumption, by sharing expertise on growing edible plants in urban areas.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
3 farms in France
Nearly 100 employees including 70 on work integration programes
7 tonnes micro-sprouts produced each year

innovations.name: Utopia 56
innovations.problem: The story of Utopia 56 begins in the Calais jungle. Whilst on a voluntary mission, Gaëdig, Yann and Liza noticed a lack of coordination on the ground. They therefore decided to put their organisational skills to good use to supervise the volunteers and act as a link between the various charities. They thus founded Utopia 56 in January 2016.
innovations.description:
In April 2017, the association launched its network of solidarity-based hosts to help refugees in distress. The main focus of this initiative is the care of unaccompanied minors. Indeed, more than two in three asylum seekers are refused the status of unaccompanied minor by the state authorities, a status which guarantees long-term support for these individuals who are particularly vulnerable to insecurity and financial and social hardship. In response to this situation, Utopia 56, in partnership with Médecins Sans Frontières, has set up a network of accommodation centres to support these young migrants with their administrative, health and social procedures.
Originally, Utopia 56 focused its activities on organising and coordinating outreach patrols designed to help and support refugees. It was through experience on the ground that the association gradually refined its work and came to dedicate itself specifically to assisting unaccompanied minors not in state care.
The association operates on a decentralised basis, which enables it to find solutions tailored to local problems, whilst taking volunteers’ initiatives into account. This open approach has, in particular, enabled inexperienced members of the public to make a contribution without having to commit to the long term.
In order to raise awareness amongst the public and policy-makers about the plight of migrants, Utopia 56 has also sought to engage directly with the public authorities. The association states that its ‘work cannot be carried out without vigorous and proactive advocacy towards the institutions which we are stepping in to replace as citizens’. Taking on, in its view, a role that falls to the state but which the latter refuses to fulfil, the association denounces the degrading treatment suffered by migrants and the national and European legal framework which, according to Utopia 56, constitutes a ‘policy of non-reception’.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence: In 2018, the association provided shelter for 12,500 families and single women, including 4,100 children.

innovations.name: Biocycle
innovations.problem:
1/3 of the food produced worldwide is wasted
20 per cent of French people are food insecure
10 million metric tonnes of food are thrown away every year in France
25 per cent of food waste can be prevented through simple actions
innovations.description:
Biocycle has set up a system for collecting unsold food. These products are first collected from restaurants, shops, supermarkets and local authorities, and are then redistributed via short supply chains – by cycle couriers on reintegration programmes – to charities working to tackle food insecurity.
As well as tackling food waste and food insecurity, Biocycle is committed to an environmentally friendly approach by using bicycle deliveries. The association is also committed to a social mission, as its two delivery riders are employed as part of a work-based reintegration programme.
Their work involves innovative tools, such as the ‘cargo bike’ used by the delivery riders to transport food, or the ‘VéloMixeurs’ – created from scrap bicycles – which allow food to be blended using leg power, enabling them to offer delicious fruit and vegetable juices. This ‘participatory awareness-raising tool’ is used to maintain their range of artisanal products (juices, compotes, etc.) designed to make use of food that is unsuitable for direct distribution because it is too damaged or there is too much of it.
To take the ‘AntiGaspi’ cause as far as possible, Biocycle’s work also includes an educational component through awareness-raising initiatives and institutional advocacy. Raising awareness amongst the general public is also a key aspect: the association’s participatory events reach over 6,000 people a year. The ‘VéloMixeurs’ are at the heart of this initiative and are involved in all sorts of workshops: beer brewing, an introduction to composting, making natural dyes… these activities enable even food unfit for consumption to be repurposed, all in a fun and engaging way. These public events take place just as easily in public spaces as they do at corporate events or with young children.
The expertise developed by Biocycle now enables it to offer advice to local authorities, particularly regarding the identification of sources of unsold food and the needs of vulnerable people within their areas.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Over 80,000 recipients of our food aid
5 successful consultancy projects
8 bicycle delivery jobs created as part of a social integration programme
45,000 citizens reached

The expertise developed by Biocycle now enables it to offer advice to local authorities, particularly regarding the identification of sources of unsold food and the needs of vulnerable people within their areas.

innovations.name: Énergie Partagée
innovations.problem: The association was founded in response to the observation that the production of renewable energy is controlled by companies that are often out of touch with the realities and needs of local communities. Yet it is precisely the involvement of local stakeholders in the implementation of such projects within their own communities that drives development: renewable energy does, in fact, contribute to economic and social vitality at a local level.
innovations.description:
Énergie Partagée was therefore set up to support and finance the development of renewable energy generation sites harnessing solar, wind and hydro power, or energy from waste treatment. Its aim is to develop community-led renewable energy projects by involving all local stakeholders – citizens, local authorities, farmers and SMEs – from the design stage right through to the operation of the facilities.
The association thus offers support to residents’ groups, local authorities and farmers: it contributes its knowledge and expertise in collective organisation, legal and economic structuring, and support for local savings schemes, amongst other areas. It also trains intermediary organisations such as local energy agencies and runs national communication campaigns, such as the ‘Juin citoyen’ initiative, a major national event focusing on community-led energy.
By supporting citizens’ reclaiming of ownership over energy issues through solidarity-based finance, Energie Partagée also strengthens social cohesion and contributes to the transition towards a more sustainable model of society.
To carry out its mission, Énergie Partagée operates through regional networks, run either by the association itself or by local associations, which mobilise and support local stakeholders in setting up projects.
Énergie Partagée is also organised at national level to coordinate working groups, pool services and tools, and represent the interests of local stakeholders. It is currently the only national network carrying out this type of work in the field of renewable energy.
Whilst Énergie Partagée Association is responsible for project and network coordination, SAS Énergie Partagée Coopérative (EPC), an ESUS-certified SCIC, manages the various funding schemes: Énergie Partagée Investissement, Énergie Partagée Études and Énercité.

innovations.name: ANTS
innovations.problem:
To make adapted physical activity accessible to people with mobility impairments by using new technologies
To develop links with healthcare organisations to ensure continuity of support for adapted physical activity whilst improving quality of life
To support the research and development sector through technological innovation relating to physical activity and health
To raise awareness amongst the general public and elected representatives about mobility impairments, as well as technological and sporting innovations.
innovations.description:
Founded in 2015 in Lyon, the association’s main mission is to make the latest advances in the field of neurorehabilitation available to as many people as possible. To this end, ANTS supports research into the development of innovative rehabilitation methods and promotes access to these innovations for people with disabilities. The association also aims to raise awareness amongst the general public and elected representatives of mobility issues, as well as the technological advances that can help overcome them.
ANTS is developing genuine expertise in neuro-rehabilitation therapies, spanning both scientific research and medical practice: two founding members are part of the neurological rehabilitation team at the physics laboratory of the École Normale Supérieure (ENS) in Lyon, whilst another founding member holds a PhD in neuroscience and practises at the functional rehabilitation centre at Henry Gabrielle Hospital.
In October 2018, ANTS opened France’s first adapted fitness centre in Lyon, open to the general public: the S.P.O.R.T. (Stimulating People and Organising Recreational Therapies) centre.
The aim is to rekindle a love of sport among people with disabilities, using innovative technologies and adapted equipment. Physical activity enables members to regain maximum physical independence, help reduce the risk of chronic conditions associated with various types of disability, and support rehabilitation outside a hospital setting.
Within the S.P.O.R.T. centre, adapted physical activity instructors create personalised programmes for each member. Specialised equipment also enables electrical muscle stimulation, thereby facilitating lower-limb exercise for people with paraplegia.
In addition, ANTS organises an annual scientific and sporting event: Lyon Cyber Days. Dedicated to showcasing the latest technological advances in support of people with physical disabilities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: 2 fully equipped adapted fitness rooms 5 electrostimulation devices 10 weight training machines 170 members

innovations.name: Permis de construire
innovations.problem: In France, nearly 80 per cent of prison releases are so-called ‘unassisted releases’, meaning that no support has been offered to the prisoner in terms of integration into the labour market or healthcare.
innovations.description:
The association promotes a genuine social reintegration programme based on empowering each individual and on giving every prisoner the freedom to choose and invest in their own personal projects. To this end, the support offered by Permis de Construire is structured around the ‘Building Ourselves, Together’ programme, centred on four fundamental pillars: physical wellbeing, mental wellbeing, living well and doing well.
This personalised support focuses on the health and psychological challenges faced by prisoners, whilst highlighting the talents of each participant. It includes weekly one-to-one sessions, group socio-educational activities and training programmes that provide a structured framework for supporting individuals.
The ‘Permis de construire’ programme enables work to begin well in advance of release from prison, which is essential for defining a career plan. It thus complements approaches directly focused on vocational integration and is the subject of numerous partnerships with prison services, accredited justice organisations, accommodation centres, Pôle Emploi and healthcare organisations.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Every year, nearly 65 per cent of those supported by the association have successfully achieved their goals (returning to work, long-term recovery, re-engagement with local life, social harmony, etc.), and behavioural changes have been observed, such as giving up alcohol, regaining a sense of well-being, or volunteering with associations. Permis de construire also estimates that, following the support provided, the three-year reoffending rate amongst these beneficiaries is less than 10 per cent.

innovations.name: Coopcoloc
innovations.lead: l'Association de Coopération pour le Logement des Etudiant·es de France (ACLEF)
innovations.problem: A student on a moderate or modest income who wishes to move to a major university town faces a major problem these days: the very high cost of rent. As CROUS student accommodation is already at full capacity, many young people give up on the idea of moving out of their parents’ home or are forced to live in substandard accommodation.
innovations.description:
Coopcoloc therefore runs a solidarity-based rental agency scheme: the association rents large flats – which its four partner social housing providers struggle to let due to their size – and houses several students in shared accommodation, at a rent approximately 20 per cent below the traditional rental market rate.
The Coopcoloc project was conceived as a means of empowering students: moving out of their parents’ home is the first step for students towards building a life for themselves. Having accommodation close to where they study also helps to reduce journey times and the associated inconveniences. Finally, by enabling these students to save an average of €100 per month, CoopColoc makes it easier for them to access better-quality food and leisure activities.
Beyond property management, the association organises activities designed to foster a sense of community amongst students and combat isolation, such as creating a collective mural and staging a play.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: l'Association de Coopération pour le Logement des Etudiant·es de France (ACLEF)
innovations.evidence:
85 per cent of students say they are satisfied with their experience, and the rate of non-payment is low, confirming the viability and appeal of the scheme for the target audience.
More than a thousand applications were submitted via the website in 2018.

innovations.name: DAHLIR
innovations.problem: Even today, access to regular leisure activities remains difficult for children and adults with disabilities. For example, it is estimated that only 1 per cent of people with disabilities take part in regular physical activity, compared with nearly 50 per cent of the general population (source: Association Rénovons le sport français – 35 recommendations – July 2018).
innovations.description:
The Programme to Support People in Accessing Integrated and Regular Leisure Activities (DAHLIR) was established in 2012 in Le Puy-en-Velay. It is aimed at all sections of the public: people with disabilities, older people, jobseekers, people on probation, etc. Its aim is to act as a facilitator, enabling all these people to access sports clubs and leisure organisations in their local area. The support provided through this scheme is free, personalised and locally based.
The association works closely with a wide range of organisations across the area. At an operational level, the association liaises with around 700 to 800 organisations, including sports, cultural and leisure centres. These are essential to DAHLIR’s work as they enable the association to cater for its diverse range of participants. The association also has numerous referral partners, such as clinics, hospitals and local employment support organisations.
DAHLIR wanted some of these partners to be represented on its board of directors, which is therefore composed of individual members (people with an interest in the project) and organisational members (associations or organisations working within DAHLIR’s field of activity).

innovations.name: Les Concerts de Poche
innovations.problem: In France, isolation within different regions is a particularly pressing issue in rural areas. The situation faced by farmers is a good illustration of this reality. In 2020, according to an Ipsos survey, 45 per cent of farmers ‘feel more isolated than ever’.
innovations.description:
The association’s aim is to forge connections and bring people together through classical music, opera and jazz. The idea is to reach out to an audience that is, for various reasons – such as limited mobility, lack of financial means, disability, age or a lack of familiarity with the sector – very distant from the world of music. Les Concerts de Poche manage to bring together a diverse audience, even going so far as to put local residents on stage alongside renowned concert performers.
Beyond organising concerts and workshops, the association helps to revitalise villages and has become one of the cornerstones of local cultural policy. It breaks down barriers between residents and helps to foster a sense of community within a local authority and with neighbouring villages.
The association Les Concerts de Poche organises workshops and travelling concerts in the mountains and the countryside. In consultation with local councils, they offer the workshops to organisations working with those who are hardest to engage. Participation in the workshops is free, and admission to the concerts – excluding any tiered pricing – is a maximum of €10.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The association currently reaches 45,000 beneficiaries through 2,400 workshops and 125 concerts every year.
Recognised as a public-interest organisation and renowned within the national artistic, cultural and social landscape, the association has an agreement with the Ministries of Culture, Regional Planning and Decentralisation (via the National Agency for Territorial Cohesion), and Agriculture and Food Sovereignty; and is accredited by the Ministry of National Education, Higher Education and Research.
The association is also accredited for civic service programmes and by the DSDEN 77 for youth and community education. Finally, it holds ‘Social Solidarity Enterprise’ accreditation.
Les Concerts de Poche also enjoys recognition from key private sector stakeholders in the voluntary and cultural sectors. The association was awarded the ‘Éclaireur 2030’ prize by the Foundation for the Co-construction of the Common Good in 2023. Furthermore, it was a winner of the ‘La France s’engage’ award, a scheme that recognises innovative initiatives serving society and offers programmes to support those behind socially innovative projects in their development strategies.

innovations.name: Recyclerie Sportive
innovations.problem:
Of all the social and environmental issues surrounding sport, three major ones have been identified: - sports waste - ‘fast sport’ and energy-intensive modes of transport - access to sport for all.
Moreover, According to the Regional Institute for the Development of Sport, one in five young people in the Île-de-France region does not take part in sporting activities. Participation is particularly low in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, due to geographical barriers (difficulty accessing sports shops) and economic barriers (expensive equipment).
In light of this, La Recyclerie Sportive aims to tackle the dual challenge of making sport more accessible to all and reducing waste in the sporting sector (‘zero-waste sport’).
innovations.description:
The association is establishing itself in priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy (QPV) to be as close as possible to residents who face difficulties in accessing sport. La Recyclerie Sportive also caters to the beneficiaries of other member organisations of La Recyclerie, such as Les Apprentis d’Auteuil and Secours Populaire. It also develops partnerships with local authorities and companies such as Decathlon.
Beyond collection, sorting and resale, La Recyclerie Sportive runs workshops on repairing sports equipment together (bicycles, scooters, rollerblades, etc.) and organises activities to encourage participation in sport and raise awareness of zero-waste sport. These events (creative workshops using sports waste, ‘bicycle blender’ workshops on the importance of healthy eating, etc.) take place at the foot of blocks of flats and are organised at the request of local authorities, businesses or sports associations.
Finally, the historic Recyclerie Sportive site in Massy serves as an experimental laboratory where the organisation trials activities such as a community café, ‘slow sport’ activities (activities combining sport, ecology and social inclusion), a cycling school and a co-working space.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups

innovations.name: Caracol
innovations.problem:
The Caracol association was founded on the realisation that the majority of refugees leave accommodation centres without any housing arrangements, which acts as a real barrier to their social and professional integration. Furthermore, many people – both local residents and refugees – are looking for a place to live that fosters intercultural exchange, enables them to pursue their aspirations, and supports an eco-friendly and community-minded way of life.
On the other hand, property vacancy is a major issue in large cities and can sometimes prove costly for property owners.
innovations.description:
The Caracol association offers solidarity-based, multicultural shared accommodation accessible to people on low incomes. These shared arrangements bring together refugees and long-term residents of France for an average period of 1 to 3 years in vacant properties, in partnership with the owners. Caracol undertakes to renovate and maintain the properties in exchange for the owners making them available free of charge. For their part, in addition to saving on caretaker costs, landlords are able to make their properties available to a project that is meaningful and beneficial to the local community.
The association manages the running of these shared accommodation schemes by organising communal activities and involving the residents in the Caracol project.
Beyond housing, a multi-partner social integration programme is being implemented. Caracol thus offers support towards secure housing, access to rights, French language lessons and cultural and leisure activities to enjoy together.
Caracol’s support complements that provided by other organisations working, in particular, on employment integration. As a result, Caracol works in collaboration with social service providers and local organisations in the areas where the shared accommodation schemes are based. This partnership-based approach enables the organisation to monitor housemates as they work towards their integration goals.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
35 shared accommodation schemes launched since 2018
400 flatmates since 2018
27,688 m² of space brought into use since 2018

innovations.name: Educate for Independence
innovations.problem:
Young people with intellectual disabilities face significant barriers in the transition from education to adult life. After completing school, many have limited access to employment, vocational training and meaningful opportunities for participation in community life. As a result, they risk becoming NEETs and remaining dependent on traditional, centre-based support services that may offer limited opportunities to develop autonomy in real-life contexts.
The problem is not limited to access to employment. Young people may also lack opportunities to strengthen essential life skills, including time and money management, mobility, communication, decision-making, domestic autonomy, teamwork and the ability to carry out tasks with increasing independence. At the same time, employers and community organisations may have limited experience of working alongside people with intellectual disabilities and may continue to be influenced by stereotypes about their abilities.
The Diffuse Learning Model addresses these interconnected barriers by creating individualised learning pathways across ordinary community, social and work-related settings. It enables participants to practise skills, assume meaningful responsibilities and build relationships outside segregated services, while supporting local organisations and communities in recognising them as active contributors.
innovations.description:
The Diffuse Learning Model transforms the Local Educational Unit approach into a flexible, community-based learning system. Rather than concentrating support in a single day-care centre, it distributes educational activities across ordinary community settings, including municipal spaces, libraries, museums, sports facilities, agricultural cooperatives, shops, school canteens and workshops.
Small groups of young people participate in practical activities selected according to their individual life projects, interests and support needs. Through progressive task assignment, they develop life skills, autonomy, social competencies and work-related abilities in real-life situations. Individual and group sessions complement practical learning when specific skills or difficulties need to be addressed.
The coordinating organisation retains educational responsibility and provides the staff who accompany participants across the different settings. Local organisations contribute spaces, equipment, expertise or meaningful tasks, while their personnel may cooperate with the group. This arrangement creates learning opportunities without requiring each community setting to become a specialised disability service.
The innovative element lies not only in using multiple locations, but in connecting individual development with community participation. Participants are recognised as active contributors who provide useful services, while local organisations gain direct experience of inclusion. The model can therefore be adapted to different territories by building on existing community resources and progressively expanding the network of learning environments.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
The Spanish pilot involved 12 young people and achieved an overall attendance rate of 84.2% , indicating sustained engagement despite differences in individual schedules and pathways. Progress was particularly visible in social participation, leisure, use of community resources, home living and employment-related skills.
Participants developed a cohesive peer group that provided mutual support and a safe environment in which to practise communication, self-determination and social skills. Educators and families also observed greater independence, responsibility and confidence, improved social and communication skills and, for some participants, increased self-esteem and emotional stability. Some participants accessed training or employment opportunities during the pilot; however, these transitions proved fragile, confirming the importance of maintaining educational support during the initial stages.
The pilot also produced changes within the participating organisations. Professionals reported that direct experience with the young people challenged their initially limited expectations. Relationships gradually became less protective and more natural, reciprocal and inclusive.
The Italian scaling-up phase involved 30 young people in eight municipalities , generating 8,885.5 hours of participation over 2,134 participant-days . Each participant experienced different tasks across ordinary community settings rather than remaining in a single service environment. Activities included product and dairy packaging, work in a reuse shop, library services, care of public spaces, preparation of meals and shopping, and management of uniforms for a local football association.
Concrete examples illustrate the benefits of this approach: one participant learned to use public transport independently; another progressively carried out library volunteering duties with greater autonomy; and the sports-uniform activity created regular interaction with players and families.
Beyond individual skill development, participants provided visible and useful services to municipalities, libraries, cultural venues, shops and community organisations. This helped shift their perceived role from recipients of care to active contributors. The scaling-up phase also strengthened IL RAMO’s territorial network and demonstrated that the model can be adapted to different local settings while linking individual learning objectives with concrete community needs.

innovations.name: A vos soins
innovations.problem:
Following the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, Noémie Brégeon, a nurse, went on a mission there with Médecins sans frontières. She returned with a critical perspective on the impact of NGOs’ work on the ground and decided to refocus on more local projects that were better aligned with the needs of the areas in which she was working.
To identify unmet needs in her local area, the healthcare professional brought together volunteers to discuss issues surrounding access to healthcare in Loire-Atlantique. “We realised that Saint-Nazaire was facing significant challenges,” explains Nicolas Blouin, the association’s current coordinator and co-founder. In Saint-Nazaire, 17 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line.
innovations.description:
The ‘A vos soins’ association project is based on several key principles:
Access to healthcare for all, with the widespread introduction of direct billing (social security and supplementary health insurance);
All forms of care, whether or not they generate income, and all patients are accepted;
Any budget surpluses are reinvested in developing the health centre’s activities and in free preventative initiatives open to all.
The ‘A vos soins’ association also differs from other, more traditional organisations in its relationship with patients. Nurses take the time to explain the options available throughout the care pathway. Patients, regarded as active participants in their own healthcare, are represented on the association’s board of directors.
The team at the association A vos soins has designed and fitted out a former occupational health van, which is now equipped with a shower, a surgery and a space for discussions: the MarSOINS, which was launched in October 2017. Its aim is to facilitate access to screening (for HIV, eye tests, dental checks, hearing tests, etc.), contraception and health check-ups.
Whilst the mobile team pays particular attention to those furthest from healthcare, it is open to everyone. Depending on the screening results, the MarSOINS can target populations at higher risk, such as people experiencing homelessness, always in collaboration with grassroots organisations.
The purchase and refurbishment of the van were funded through a crowdfunding campaign and volunteer work. Numerous local businesses, local authorities and foundations have also provided financial support. The project’s annual budget stands at around €70,000 and is funded both by the profits generated by the nursing health centre and by public and private funding: corporate sponsorship, foundations, urban development programmes, etc.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Today, the organisation has seven staff members, including five nurses and two coordinators. It treats more than 15,000 patients a year.
In 2018, MarSOINS carried out nearly 900 screening tests (dental, eye, nursing, HIV, etc.). 60 per cent of those seen were women and 34.45 per cent were from priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy.

She returned with a critical perspective on the impact of NGOs’ work on the ground and decided to refocus on more local projects that were better aligned with the needs of the areas in which she was working.
To identify unmet needs in her local area, the healthcare professional brought together volunteers to discuss issues surrounding access to healthcare in Loire-Atlantique. “We realised that Saint-Nazaire was facing significant challenges,” explains Nicolas Blouin, the association’s current coordinator and co-founder. In Saint-Nazaire, 17 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:
The ‘A vos soins’ association project is based on several key principles:
Access to healthcare for all, with the widespread introduction of direct billing (social security and supplementary health insurance);
All forms of care, whether or not they generate income, and all patients are accepted;
Any budget surpluses are reinvested in developing the health centre’s activities and in free preventative initiatives open to all.
The ‘A vos soins’ association also differs from other, more traditional organisations in its relationship with patients. Nurses take the time to explain the options available throughout the care pathway. Patients, regarded as active participants in their own healthcare, are represented on the association’s board of directors.
The team at the association A vos soins has designed and fitted out a former occupational health van, which is now equipped with a shower, a surgery and a space for discussions: the MarSOINS, which was launched in October 2017. Its aim is to facilitate access to screening (for HIV, eye tests, dental checks, hearing tests, etc.), contraception and health check-ups.
Whilst the mobile team pays particular attention to those furthest from healthcare, it is open to everyone. Depending on the screening results, the MarSOINS can target populations at higher risk, such as people experiencing homelessness, always in collaboration with grassroots organisations.
The purchase and refurbishment of the van were funded through a crowdfunding campaign and volunteer work. Numerous local businesses, local authorities and foundations have also provided financial support. The project’s annual budget stands at around €70,000 and is funded both by the profits generated by the nursing health centre and by public and private funding: corporate sponsorship, foundations, urban development programmes, etc.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
Today, the organisation has seven staff members, including five nurses and two coordinators. It treats more than 15,000 patients a year.
In 2018, MarSOINS carried out nearly 900 screening tests (dental, eye, nursing, HIV, etc.). 60 per cent of those seen were women and 34.45 per cent were from priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy.

innovations.name: Latitudes
innovations.problem:
Digital technology is part of everyday life for almost all French people: 98 per cent of those aged 12 and over own a mobile phone, one in two people now use AI, and we spend several hours a day in front of our screens.
‍Digital technology is everywhere. And the more it becomes ingrained in our lives… the less we understand it. We use it every day to work, communicate and organise our lives, without always realising the impact it has on our surroundings. As long as everything works, it seems simple, but all it takes is for a service to change or be discontinued for us to suddenly realise just how dependent we are on it.
This dependence comes at a cost: digital technology also means a 9 per cent increase in our ecological footprint each year, growing screen overexposure, infringements on our freedoms, fake news spreading six times faster than other information, artificial intelligence that is transforming our relationship with the world, and technologies which, due to a lack of diversity, perpetuate the very inequalities they promise to resolve.
innovations.description:
The organisation is working to create a model for technology education that places civic engagement at the heart of training, to enable tech professionals to get involved in projects with a social and/or environmental impact, and to support public-interest organisations in harnessing new technologies to maximise their impact.
Through a range of programmes, Latitudes connects students, professionals and companies with technological expertise who wish to engage with organisations running social and environmental projects.
Latitudes has launched ‘Tech for Good Explorers’, an innovative educational programme within engineering and computer science schools and universities. This programme offers courses on ‘Tech for Good’, engages mentors to support students, and raises awareness of impact projects to encourage civic engagement. Students can then apply their skills, as part of their course, to projects addressing social or environmental challenges.
The ‘Tech for Good Enthusiasts’ programme is aimed at organisations and professionals wishing to get involved in practical initiatives to develop the use of technology for the public good. It enables companies to establish a policy of volunteering and skills-based sponsorship and provides access to a community of peers working towards a common goal. This expertise is harnessed to help public-interest organisations capitalise on the potential of technology to maximise their impact.
Latitudes also offers freely accessible resources for all audiences, covering a wide range of topics: digital moderation, AI, cybersecurity, disinformation, systems thinking…
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Our catalogue of resources is aimed at all audiences and at every stage of life: secondary school pupils, higher education students, professionals, organisations, the general public, and so on. Since 2017, these resources have helped train 80,000 people!
Today, the Latitudes association brings together several thousand people trained to use our resources, 700 of whom are active each year.
Latitudes also comprises several hundred partner organisations and stakeholders, a permanent team of around fifteen people and a budget of one million euros, which, taken together, enable us to reach 30,000 people each year.

innovations.name: Silver Geek
innovations.problem: Silver Geek aims to improve the health and wellbeing of older people, to foster social and intergenerational connections, whilst bridging the digital divide
innovations.description:
To promote digital inclusion amongst older people, the Silver Geek association offers two complementary activities:
Digital workshops tailored to older people, run by young people on civic service placements in organisations catering for older people (nursing homes, independent living facilities or sheltered accommodation, CCAS, social centres or community centres, MJC, rural community centres and senior citizens’ clubs). These workshops are free of charge and come with no obligation for older people. Their content is co-developed by the young volunteer facilitators and the older participants, based on their skill levels and interests; The organisation of e-sports competitions for older people. The regional finals of these competitions take place during major e-sports events such as Paris Games Week. Through these activities centred on digital technology and gaming, the Silver Geek project also forms part of an initiative promoting intergenerational exchange and sharing, enabling older people to break out of their isolation and young volunteers to gain a new perspective on the world of older people. Finally, the association's decision to use exergames (movement-based games) helps to get older people active again and combat the harmful effects of a sedentary lifestyle on this population.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: ETIC Emballages
innovations.problem: In Toulouse, 10,000 meals are ordered every day, generating 3 tonnes of disposable packaging. This packaging, which is often manufactured far away using fossil fuels, causes massive pollution from the production stage right through to the end of its life.
innovations.description:
The ETIC Emballages association was set up in response to two observations:
The social, economic, environmental and health impacts caused by the widespread use of single-use packaging in the catering sector are significant and a cause for concern;
There are currently few, if any, concrete, practical and affordable alternatives to disposable packaging available to restaurants and their customers, despite the enactment of several laws aimed at reducing waste (notably the French law banning disposable plastic tableware from 1 January 2021).
The association’s aim is to curb the damage caused by the use of single-use packaging by organising a network of returnable glass jars made available to shops. To encourage sharing, these jars can be returned by customers after use to any of the network’s partner shops. The glass jars are then collected and washed before being returned to the system for reuse.
By promoting this deposit-and-return scheme, the association aims to bring about changes in behaviour and a broader shift in consumption patterns across the region.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: 3,533,541 pieces of single-use packaging avoided since 2019.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.raw_text:
Terre de Liens
By 2030, 40 per cent of farmers will have retired, representing a quarter of France’s agricultural land. This structural change carries the risk of accelerating trends towards farm consolidation, speculation and the expansion of intensive farming. Furthermore, farmers switching to organic farming struggle to gain access to land, particularly if they do not come from a farming background.
In the face of these challenges, Terre de Liens works to ensure the practical preservation of agricultural land by acting as a land management organisation: identifying land, acquiring farms, letting them out, and then managing them as part of its property portfolio and rental operations. The organisation also supports prospective farmers in setting up their businesses.
At the same time, it has developed and coordinates a network of local organisations (citizens, local authorities, decision-makers and stakeholders in the agricultural sector).
The association is aimed at a range of stakeholders, including:
Local authorities struggling to provide a coherent response to interrelated issues (climate, biodiversity, food, rural depopulation, etc.);
Project leaders from outside the agricultural sector who are running small-scale, sustainable, environmentally friendly and diversified projects;
Farmers who are retiring and wish for their land to be used under a different agricultural model.
The Terre de liens federation now comprises 19 regional associations across mainland France, with over 6,000 members and 1,100 volunteers.

innovations.name: ÉCHOBAT
innovations.problem: The construction sector accounts for over 40 per cent of energy consumption in France and emits more than 120 million tonnes of CO₂ per year. Sustainable construction therefore has a vital role to play in creating resource-efficient buildings and improving the energy performance of the built environment.
innovations.description:
The ECHOBAT association carries out a number of initiatives aimed at private individuals, local authorities and project owners:
Bringing together a network of professionals to provide a comprehensive service to private individuals interested in green building; Carrying out awareness-raising activities amongst local authorities on green building; Connecting network members with one another and with a project management support team to assist with the design and delivery of building projects. By targeting both the supply side of the construction sector (construction professionals) and the demand side (private individuals, local authorities, etc.), the ECHOBAT network provides a collaborative and cross-sectoral response to project leaders committed to achieving energy, environmental and economic efficiency.
The association aims to reduce the environmental impact of buildings whilst promoting social inclusion. To this end, it facilitates and encourages cooperation within its network between businesses and organisations promoting social integration through economic activity (SIAEs). ECHOBAT also offers training courses for employees on integration programmes to help them make the most of their experience. Finally, the association is committed to sustainable development by promoting the use of eco-friendly materials and exploring the circular economy in the construction sector (optimising the management of construction site waste).
innovations.target_group: Other target groups

innovations.name: Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble
innovations.problem: The association aims to reduce feelings of social isolation. Indeed, in 2021, 44 per cent of French people felt they did not have the opportunity to take part in activities with people from different backgrounds (2021 Fraternity Barometer), and 7 million people were experiencing social isolation (Fondation de France).
innovations.description:
Since 2014, the Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble association has been organising a new kind of get-together for local residents: surprise meet-ups that bring together people from diverse backgrounds in a ‘blind’ setting for activities organised by one of the participants (local residents or community organisations). Participants take turns as hosts and guests and are connected via the association’s online platform, kifkif.org.
These surprise meet-ups and activities primarily involve people from priority neighbourhoods under urban policy (QPVs) in the Île-de-France region and bring together people of all ages (between 18 and 87).
Beyond the Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble digital platform, the association relies on its outreach work on the ground and its strong local roots to ensure its visibility and long-term sustainability. This strong local presence enables Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble to forge partnerships with local stakeholders: social housing providers, local organisations and facilities (community centres, cultural and sports venues, artists, specialist prevention groups, etc.) as well as local authorities, particularly those responsible for youth services, social cohesion, urban policy and culture. For these organisations, which may organise or host activities, these gatherings serve as an innovative means of diversifying and further engaging local residents, whilst upholding the values of fraternity and inclusion.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: 93 per cent of surprise meet-ups take place in public places. Those taking part (Kiffeuses and Kiffeurs) are aged between 18 and 85, come from over 60 different nationalities, and live in 114 different cities.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

Since 2014, the Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble association has been organising a new kind of get-together for local residents: surprise meet-ups that bring together people from diverse backgrounds in a ‘blind’ setting for activities organised by one of the participants (local residents or community organisations). Participants take turns as hosts and guests and are connected via the association’s online platform, kifkif.org.
These surprise meet-ups and activities primarily involve people from priority neighbourhoods under urban policy (QPVs) in the Île-de-France region and bring together people of all ages (between 18 and 87).
Beyond the Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble digital platform, the association relies on its outreach work on the ground and its strong local roots to ensure its visibility and long-term sustainability. This strong local presence enables Kif Kif Vivre Ensemble to forge partnerships with local stakeholders: social housing providers, local organisations and facilities (community centres, cultural and sports venues, artists, specialist prevention groups, etc.) as well as local authorities, particularly those responsible for youth services, social cohesion, urban policy and culture. For these organisations, which may organise or host activities, these gatherings serve as an innovative means of diversifying and further engaging local residents, whilst upholding the values of fraternity and inclusion.
93 per cent of surprise meet-ups take place in public places. Those taking part (Kiffeuses and Kiffeurs) are aged between 18 and 85, come from over 60 different nationalities, and live in 114 different cities.

innovations.name: Traces de Vies
innovations.problem: Drawing on her own personal experience, the founder of Traces de Vies has observed that people who are vulnerable and isolated as a result of illness sometimes need to reflect on their life journey and share their story with those around them. Hospital-based biography is therefore a way of meeting this need to be listened to and heard, whilst enabling those receiving support to feel valued and not merely seen as objects of care. This process encourages people to speak freely, whilst also helping to combat the isolation of those receiving support and improve their mental health and self-esteem.
innovations.description:
The hospital biography service offered by Trace de Vies is aimed at children and adults who are seriously ill or at the end of their lives, and who find themselves isolated due to care protocols or have little contact with their loved ones. They are identified by the care teams looking after them (hospital departments, care homes, home care workers) and who then contact the association’s biographers, whose role is to listen to and faithfully transcribe the words of the people they support. Trace de Vies offers this service to patients and their families, making it accessible to all. The association also prints 10 books and sends them to recipients chosen by the beneficiaries.
The association has developed a training programme to professionalise new hospital biographers, thereby enabling them to support as many people as possible.
Recognition of the profession of hospital biographer is a key priority for the association. To this end, Traces de Vies carries out awareness-raising and communication initiatives aimed at highlighting this profession at local and regional levels. Advocacy work to secure recognition of hospital biography as a fully-fledged form of supportive care still needs to be undertaken.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: + 360 people supported as at 31 January 2026 + 3,600 people who have benefited from support since 2013

innovations.name: Re-Belle
innovations.problem:
In France, food loss and waste amount to 10 million tonnes of produce per year (Ministry for Ecological Transition and Territorial Cohesion, 2022). More specifically, 45 per cent of fruit and vegetables from local producers do not end up on our plates (ADEME, 2016).
Furthermore, the department of Seine-Saint-Denis is the poorest in the Île-de-France region, with a poverty rate of 28.4 per cent and 11 per cent of the population receiving the RSA (INSEE, 2020).
In light of these two findings, the Re-Belle association was established as a Atelier Chantier d’Insertion (Social Integration Workshop) and has developed two strands of activity:
The production of jams;
The organisation of awareness-raising initiatives and workshops on food waste and sustainable food.
innovations.description:
As a social integration workshop, Re-Belle offers personalised social and professional support based on the method of vocational and personal development activation, enabling the employees it supports to take back control of their career paths. Throughout their time with the organisation, employees are trained in various roles: anti-waste production officer, collection and delivery driver, and administrative assistant.
Re-Belle’s main activity is the production of jams. Every week, unsold fruit and vegetables from supermarkets, restaurants, hotels and partner farmers in the Île-de-France region arrive at Re-Belle’s kitchens in Stains. The food collected is sorted, washed, chopped and processed in the organisation’s workshop.
At the same time, Re-Belle runs workshops to raise awareness of healthy and sustainable eating amongst residents of priority neighbourhoods in Seine-Saint-Denis and company employees. Participants are given tips that are easy to replicate at home, teaching them how to cook delicious, balanced meals on a tight budget whilst minimising food waste on an individual level.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: 30 tonnes of fruit and vegetables are repurposed by Re-Belle every year.

innovations.name: Locaux-Moteurs
innovations.problem:
The Locaux-Moteurs association has chosen to focus its work on the under-utilisation of housing policies relating to energy-efficiency refurbishment and housing adaptations (support for those with reduced independence). Combating energy poverty lies at the intersection of the quest for a better quality of life, the reduction of social inequalities and the fight against global warming. 20 per cent of French people say they suffered from the cold for at least 24 hours during the winter of 2021–2022. Today, the ‘lower middle classes’ are bearing the brunt of energy costs, and energy-efficient refurbishment goes beyond the mere notion of quality of life. 11.9 per cent of households are in energy poverty. With regard to housing, a study by the Ministry for Ecological Transition highlights the link between energy-efficient refurbishment and health benefits. According to this study, ‘the average annual health cost of these Category F or G homes is €7,500 (€400 in social security costs, €1,400 in lost well-being and €5,700 in mortality-related costs)’, so ‘renovation is socially cost-effective’. According to Locaux-Moteurs, tackling under-take-up is a matter of urgency for public policy.
The association focuses in particular on rural areas, which face the challenges of socio-economic vulnerabilities exacerbated by the health crisis; areas where scattered settlements and the distance from urban centres and places where public services are available (despite the presence of France Services) reinforce the ‘invisibility’ of households in precarious circumstances
innovations.description: The Locaux-Moteurs association has opted to use the ‘outreach’ approach, with door-to-door visits organised by local residents acting as liaisons from the rural areas where the scheme operates; households’ needs are then channelled to housing providers. To inform and support households, Locaux-Moteurs volunteers are recruited to help them access housing improvement support schemes. The strength of Locaux-Moteurs and the effectiveness of their visits lie in their role as peers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Nearly 4,200 owner-occupiers (between 2017 and 2024) received an initial information pack accompanied by explanations. Between 7 and 8 out of 10 doors are opened when the Locaux-Moteurs teams visit. Nearly 400 tenants were contacted (between 2017 and 2023) Nearly 1,000 application forms submitted 20 to 25 per cent of households are taking part in the scheme Over 1,200,000 euros’ worth of works (projects completed since 2020)

innovations.name: Sira
innovations.problem:
Accessing training or employment may require temporary or long-term relocation, sometimes involving two successive places of residence. Many people may abandon their plans when faced with the difficulty of finding and affording a new rental property. Furthermore, there is growing pressure on urban areas, with a sharp rise in prices that makes it more difficult for the most vulnerable to access housing, and a rise in the number of unscrupulous landlords.
At the same time, in suburban areas, the stock of rental accommodation suited to people on the move (small flats, furnished or unfurnished) is rather limited. Finally, a further challenge is the near-total digitisation of many administrative services, which for many people results in a failure to claim financial assistance designed to help them secure and retain accommodation. This is why, for over 60 per cent of those who approach SIRA, information on available financial assistance and administrative support in putting together applications is the main reason for their enquiry.
Based on these findings, SIRA has set itself the mission of securing pathways to training or employment by removing peripheral barriers, and of combating both the failure to access support and poor housing conditions.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Over 3,000 contacts per year
Over 4,000 referring partners and landlords
Over 3,000 housing solutions listed across mainland France
Over 1,600 people follow us on social media

innovations.name: Lève les yeux !
innovations.problem:
Over the past decade or so, screen addiction has become a key issue for virtually every society around the world, and all the more so in France, where daily screen time has literally skyrocketed with the advent of smartphones and tablets.
The ASNAV estimated the average screen time for adults in France at 10 hours a day in 2019 (compared with 5 hours 40 minutes in 2012), and we know that usage has increased further during the lockdowns linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Children and teenagers are the most vulnerable: imitating their elders, engrossed in social media which has become an essential space for socialising, addicted to video games designed for this purpose, and watching entertainment videos on a continuous loop, they are highly exposed at all ages.
‘Lève les Yeux !’ raises awareness of these issues amongst all audiences (children, teenagers, parents and educational staff) through participatory, fun and supportive workshops. The association's education approach aims to make participants aware of their screen use and its effects; it also promotes offline activities that can strengthen independence, critical thinking and creativity, in order to help them reduce their dependence.
innovations.description:
Lève les Yeux ! has developed around two main areas of awareness-raising work, which reinforce one another: grassroots activities (at local level) and advocacy work (at national level). The organisation also stands out for its educational approach, notably a board game designed to raise awareness called ‘Planète déconnexion’.
Community-based activities mainly involve running community education workshops for children and teenagers in schools and community centres, as well as for parents and teaching staff. Lève les Yeux ! also trains professionals working with children. ‘Disconnection Challenges’ are launched at neighbourhood or school level. Finally, the association runs workshops and talks in companies on the theme of ‘Mindfulness and wellbeing at work in the digital age’.
The association’s second area of focus encompasses advocacy work, notably the coordination of the Collectif Attention, a coalition of around ten organisations committed to combating excessive screen time. Lève les Yeux ! monitors news and developments relating to the role of digital technology in society and, based on this, produces a weekly press round-up for its members. Some active members of the association also publish articles, book reviews or in-depth works. Finally, meetings and coffee-table discussions are occasionally organised.
In addition, a ‘Label’ for ‘disconnected’ venues has been introduced: a network of venues and artists who support the association’s project, with mutual promotion.
