innovations.name: Énergie Solidaire
innovations.problem:
In France, 12 million people are experiencing energy poverty in their homes – one in five people – according to the National Observatory on Energy Poverty.
Although public funding for energy-efficiency renovations is available, the application processes are lengthy and complex, and the ‘out-of-pocket costs’ for the work are often too high for households to afford, given that their financial situation is already untenable. Whilst there are specialist organisations attempting to tackle this social and environmental emergency, they lack the resources to cope with growing demand and the ageing of housing and infrastructure, against a backdrop of inflation.
innovations.description:
Énergie Solidaire brings together local communities and strengthens the capacity of associations to reduce the number of households experiencing energy poverty.
The Fund is aimed at all individuals and businesses involved in the energy transition (producers, suppliers, consumers, local authorities, etc.) to enable them to contribute to the fight against energy poverty in their local area and to increase their commitment.
Énergie Solidaire implements innovative fundraising solutions. These include financial donations as well as micro-donations based on energy consumption, sourced from various stakeholders: private companies, foundations, members of the public, local authorities, and so on. The Fund then redistributes these donations via annual calls for proposals organised for locally-based public-interest organisations committed to tackling energy poverty and supporting low- and very low-income households.

innovations.name: Ikambere
innovations.problem:
Ikambere aims to contribute to health equity, a concept which means that everyone has equal access to the opportunities to live a healthy life, regardless of their social, economic or demographic circumstances. To achieve equity, it is essential to address the social determinants of health, such as income, housing and food insecurity, and to ‘reach out’ to those populations furthest removed from the healthcare system and information.
In France, cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among women, claiming the lives of 200 women every day. Those most affected are women living in precarious circumstances. Furthermore, 54 per cent of women living in priority neighbourhoods (QPVs) are overweight, compared with 38 per cent of women outside QPVs, and 41 per cent of women living in QPVs forgo at least one medical treatment for financial reasons.
This is why Ikambere offers comprehensive support to women living in precarious circumstances and with a chronic illness. By addressing the social determinants of health, its approach promotes sustainable improvements in the living conditions, well-being and empowerment of this highly vulnerable group.
innovations.description:
Ikambere’s activities are divided into three main areas of work. All the services offered by the organisation are provided free of charge to beneficiaries.
Support towards self-reliance: each woman receiving support benefits from individual support (social, health and employment integration) and can take part in group activities organised according to a fixed weekly schedule. The approach is structured around four main areas: social support and responses to urgent needs, physical health, mental health, and social and professional integration.
‘ Outreach and health mediation: community-based mediation in hospitals for female patients living with HIV (individual support, support groups, information workshops), screening and awareness-raising initiatives on sexual health and rights in migrant accommodation centres and in public spaces, and monthly workshops in community centres on topics related to the prevention of diabetes and obesity.
Training and research: training courses delivered to medical and social care professionals across France, where Ikambere presents its methodology and equips professionals to support vulnerable populations.

innovations.name: Règles élémentaires
innovations.problem:
As periods have a daily impact on the lives of half the population, they are a matter of public concern. In France, 4,000,000 people experience period poverty, and one in two French people believe that periods are a taboo subject, according to the Period Poverty Survey published by Règles élémentaires and OpinionWay. This taboo remains very real and has negative consequences in many areas. Indeed, period poverty can have an impact on social inequalities, starting at school and continuing into the world of work. It is estimated that one in three adults has missed work, and that nearly one in two young people has missed school because of their periods.
The taboo surrounding periods has implications for education: one in two people first hear about periods only at puberty, and many have received no formal education on the subject; this often affects the self-esteem of those concerned, as well as their health. In fact, one in two people suffer from painful periods, and many find themselves facing a medical odyssey.

innovations.raw_text:
Règles élémentaires
As periods have a daily impact on the lives of half the population, they are a matter of public concern. In France, 4,000,000 people experience period poverty, and one in two French people believe that periods are a taboo subject, according to the Period Poverty Survey published by Règles élémentaires and OpinionWay. This taboo remains very real and has negative consequences in many areas. Indeed, period poverty can have an impact on social inequalities, starting at school and continuing into the world of work. It is estimated that one in three adults has missed work, and that nearly one in two young people has missed school because of their periods.
The taboo surrounding periods has implications for education: one in two people first hear about periods only at puberty, and many have received no formal education on the subject; this often affects the self-esteem of those concerned, as well as their health. In fact, one in two people suffer from painful periods, and many find themselves facing a medical odyssey.
Règles Élémentaires is France’s leading association working to tackle period poverty and the taboo surrounding periods. Its mission is to enable everyone affected to manage their periods in good conditions, so that they no longer act as a barrier to their daily lives. It aims to put an end to period poverty, to make period education and awareness-raising more widespread, and to improve the quality of life for people who have periods, by taking action at various levels.
The organisation operates in three areas:
collection and redistribution: facilitating the collection of sanitary products via an online platform, then redistributing these products to its 1,000 partner organisations across France;
awareness-raising and training: workshops, events and outreach sessions (in schools, sports clubs, businesses and medical and social care organisations). The organisation also trains medical and social care staff in menstrual hygiene and related health conditions;
public engagement: advocacy campaigns to make menstruation a topic of public debate (transparency regarding the composition of sanitary products, greater consideration of menstruation in education and the workplace, and an end to period poverty).

sections.question: Description

innovations.raw_text:
L'Alterfixe
In ten years, France has lost 100,000 farms, and by 2030, half of all farmers will have retired. More than two in three farms have no guaranteed succession plan. The average size of farms has increased by 25 per cent over the last ten years, rising from 55 hectares in 2010 to 69 hectares in 2020.
At the same time, there is a trend of people from non-farming backgrounds returning to the land. These individuals, who are often changing careers, face two major challenges when setting up: finding partners for their farm and finding a farm on which to settle.
Alterfixe plays a key role in bringing together existing and aspiring farmers. It builds bridges between local expertise and the new generations of farmers. Through networking weekends or extended placements, future farmers are not only trained in the realities of the profession, but also benefit from a genuine transfer of skills from local stakeholders. These opportunities for exchange are not limited to technical learning: they play a vital role in integrating newcomers into the local community. The approach is clear and focused on self-management, with the aim of supporting farmers’ long-term autonomy.
The training programme is based on three main pillars:
living together: getting to know the local area and its stakeholders;
working together: learning to cooperate with stakeholders on local issues;
thinking together: learning to draw up action plans with other farmers.
Alterfixe also organises awareness-raising sessions for elected representatives and members of the public to encourage reflection on the transfer of knowledge and agricultural land, and to give farmers a stronger voice within the local ecosystem.

innovations.name: Territoire Zéro logement passoire
innovations.problem:
In France, 62 per cent of households experiencing energy poverty are tenants. There are 3 million low-income tenants who struggle to pay their energy bills and suffer from discomfort in their homes. They have no say in the renovation of their homes, and current state support is focused mainly on homeowners, thereby leaving tenants in energy-inefficient homes behind.
They are therefore affected by landlords’ ‘renovation procrastination’ – the tendency to put off renovation work due to regulatory uncertainty and the lack of guaranteed returns on such work. The cost of this delay is borne by tenants in the form of high energy bills that could have been avoided. Whilst 50 per cent of the rental stock is owned by a minority of multi-property owners with at least five properties, the public authorities lack the tools to identify those who are best placed (and have the greatest responsibility) to change the situation.
innovations.description:
Territoire Zéro Logement Passoire (TeZeLoPa) has a twofold aim: to empower tenants to initiate renovations and to develop tools for eco-friendly planning and support provided by local authorities.
Data analysts, cartographers, thermal engineers, community organisers, lawyers, local councillors and local authority departments are thus working together in a pioneering initiative to make the goal of a ‘Zero Substandard Housing Area’ tangible and achievable, and, first and foremost, to eradicate substandard housing from the private rental sector.  The method combines the mapping of substandard housing, the collective organisation of tenants, the provision of expert advice, engagement with landlords, and support and assistance schemes for the tenants concerned.
The project is part of a highly local and experimental approach, designed to enable rapid positive outcomes and to create a space for experimentation that can subsequently be replicated and scaled up.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: This innovative project has proven its concept and has now completed its first two pilot schemes in partnership with the cities of Grenoble and Lyon. Following the presentation of the pilot scheme, a similar project has been underway in Charleroi, Belgium, since April 2024.

innovations.name: Territoire des possibles
innovations.problem:
According to INSEE, by 2030 people aged over 65 will account for a quarter of the French population. This highlights the need to plan for this ageing population in all its dimensions, taking into account the various challenges associated with ageing: economic, social, health-related, and so on.
85 per cent of people hope, if they are forced to leave their home, to have access to accommodation that is as similar as possible to their original home. At present, institutional approaches do not meet these needs, and alternative housing options are limited, particularly in rural areas.
innovations.description:
To address these challenges, Territoires des possibles has set itself the mission of broadening the range of possibilities for retired people living in rural areas, so that they can freely choose where to live, through discussion and awareness-raising workshops, and by working with them to design shared and accessible housing.
In 2022, it opened its first shared and inclusive housing scheme, an innovative shared-living solution designed to meet the needs of many retired people. Designed to enable people living in rural areas on modest incomes to continue their retirement in a home that meets their need for social connection, their health requirements and their financial means, these small-scale shared homes ensure a balance between independence, freedom, the need for social interaction and security.
They are co-developed with residents and local authorities, with the involvement of local healthcare and social care providers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The first shared housing scheme, located in Lestiac-sur-Garonne in southern Gironde and conceived during a participatory feasibility study in 2017–2018, now comprises eight independent private studio flats and 220 m² of shared spaces. All the homes are designated as social housing. The participatory approach lies at the heart of the project: a total of 43 workshops have been organised since 2017, bringing together 200 participants.

innovations.name: Happiness Lessons Integrated Programmes – A Whole-School Well-being Programme with Scalable Impact on Mental Health Promotion
innovations.problem:
Educational institutions play a central role not only in academic development but also in children’s and young people’s emotional, social and psychological well-being. However, many educators and institutions lack a coherent, age-appropriate and practically applicable framework for promoting mental health and well-being as part of everyday education. Support is often limited to isolated activities, short-term interventions or the involvement of external professionals after difficulties have already emerged.
Children and young people need regular opportunities to learn how to recognise and regulate emotions, manage stress, develop self-confidence, use their personal strengths, build supportive relationships, resolve conflicts and navigate digital environments consciously. Access to such development may depend heavily on the resources, professional capacity and geographical location of the individual institution. Educators also need practical methods, professional preparation and ongoing peer support to respond confidently to students’ emotional and social needs without being expected to act as therapists.
The challenge is therefore both individual and systemic. Mental health promotion cannot remain solely the responsibility of individual children, families or specialists. It requires an educational culture in which well-being, emotional literacy, supportive relationships and healthy coping strategies become shared priorities and part of everyday practice. The programme addresses this gap by making preventive mental health promotion accessible in the everyday environments where children and young people learn and develop, while actively supporting educators in implementing and sustaining these practices.
Within the programme, happiness does not mean a permanently positive mood or the avoidance of difficult emotions. It refers to a set of psychological and social capacities that can be developed—including emotional regulation, positive orientation, optimism, perseverance, healthy relationships and adaptive coping—and which can function as protective factors throughout life.
Difficulties in emotional regulation may be expressed through impulsivity, aggression, withdrawal or anxiety. They may also negatively affect peer relationships, conflict management, school readiness, concentration and academic engagement. Without early and systematic support, children may reach adolescence without the internal resources needed to manage increasing social, educational and psychological pressures.
innovations.description:
Happiness Lessons Integrated Programmes translates research-based well-being promotion into an educational model that trained educators can implement within the day-to-day life of kindergartens and schools. Its innovation lies in moving beyond isolated interventions and combining structured curricula, educator capacity-building, age-specific experiential learning, institutional commitment, family engagement, professional networking and continuous development within one scalable framework.
Rather than functioning as a conventional school subject, the programme creates experiential learning situations in which children and young people practise evidence-informed behaviours and mental strategies through discussion, play, movement, music, creative activities, reflection and shared experiences.
The integrated model comprises seven complementary programme pathways covering more than 50 developmentally adapted topics:
Happiness Lessons Core Programme: Over a ten-month cycle, children and young people explore and practise happiness-enhancing strategies such as gratitude, optimism, positive relationships, acts of kindness, goal-setting, coping, forgiveness, physical activity and sustainable well-being.
Character Strengths Programme: The programme helps students recognise, appreciate and consciously apply their own character strengths in learning, relationships, everyday challenges and conflict situations.
Competence-Based Self-Confidence Programme: Built on the scientific foundations of growth mindset and self-compassion, the programme strengthens positive self-image, self-efficacy, perseverance and a constructive response to mistakes and difficulties.
Mindfulness Programme for Emotional Regulation and Attention Control: Designed for children aged 3–10, the programme develops attention control, emotional awareness and age-appropriate self-regulation through playful and experiential activities.
Stress Mindset Programme: Young people learn to understand their responses to stress and mobilise the energy associated with stress so that it supports rather than paralyses them in challenging situations.
Positive Communication and Conflict Resolution Programme: By developing assertive communication and restorative approaches to conflict, the programme aims to prevent peer bullying, strengthen cooperation and contribute to a supportive institutional climate.
Digital Well-being Programme: The programme supports children and young people in developing a more conscious, balanced and responsible relationship with digital devices, online platforms and social media.
Together, these pathways address happiness-enhancing strategies, character strengths, self-confidence, growth mindset and self-compassion, emotional regulation and attention control, adaptive responses to stress, positive communication, restorative conflict resolution and conscious digital engagement. The seven programmes and their main objectives are consistent with the programme’s current integrated framework.
Educators receive practice-oriented professional training and structured resources that can be adapted to the developmental level, educational setting and specific needs of their groups. The activities use stories, games, movement, music, relaxation, creative work, reflection and collaborative projects, making preventive mental health promotion accessible without turning educators into therapists or the programme into clinical treatment.
The programme also changes relationships among stakeholders. Educators move from being primarily recipients of external support to becoming trained facilitators of well-being development within their own institutions. Children and young people become active participants who practise, reflect on and discuss strategies relevant to their own lives. Parents, school leaders, researchers, mentors and professional communities are connected around a shared responsibility for well-being.

innovations.name: More appreciation of nature and food - Educational programmes for schools and kindergartens
innovations.problem: As natural spaces become increasingly rare in everyday life and food production becomes more industrialised, many young people are losing the opportunity to experience where their food comes from. The social consequences of this are significant: around 30% of food produced is wasted. The lack of engagement with food also leads to unhealthy eating habits. In Germany, more than 20% of children are overweight, putting them at high risk of subsequent diseases.
innovations.description: To address this, our vision is to promote a deep appreciation of nature and food, encourage healthy eating habits, and reduce the growing disconnect between society and the natural world. Central to this vision is our belief that every child has the right to a natural learning environment. To make this a reality, we develop educational programmes that enable participants to explore, understand, and value the process of growing food. At the heart of our work are the educational programmes GemüseAckerdemie and AckerRacker, tailored for schools and kindergartens as a train the trainer approach. These programmes equip teachers and educators with the necessary tools, resources, and support to implement nature and nutrition education. Through growing their own vegetables, children gain valuable hands-on experience and develop a deeper understanding of sustainability, nutrition, and biodiversity.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
At Acker, we have been impact-oriented since our beginnings. This means that the ultimate goal of our educational programmes is to bring about sustainable and holistic change - in the participants of our programmes and in our society. Our impact analysis proves it: Participants in our educational programmes acquire a basic understanding of food production and agricultural interrelationships and develop conscious and sustainable consumer behavior. Participating children acquire new knowledge about food, eat more healthily and spend more time outdoors. To name some examples we can say that in 2024, 58 % of children have increased their vegetable consumption and 59% have developed a greater appreciation for vegetables. Our work is not an end in itself, but aims to bring about a positive change in our target groups - as holistically and permanently as possible! That is why we use our impact results to guide our strategies and future goals.
Replicated in Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein Scaled-up and programmes adapted in new sectors such as universities, colleges, companies, retirement homes.

innovations.name: From dreams to impact with Start-Up de Territoire
innovations.problem: Many French territories face pressing social and environmental challenges — social isolation, lack of local services, ecological transition — yet struggle to mobilise citizens and local actors around collective solutions. At the same time, research shows that 94% of French citizens want to contribute to solving societal issues, but only 20% have done so concretely (Ticket for Change & Occurrence, 2016). This gap between civic willingness and actual engagement reflects a lack of accessible, structured frameworks for collective action at the local level. Additionally, locally-rooted entrepreneurial projects often lack the community support, visibility, and accompaniment needed to emerge and grow. Existing incubation models tend to focus on individual entrepreneurs rather than collective, citizen-led initiatives that respond to shared territorial needs.
innovations.description: Start-Up de Territoire introduces a pioneering model of citizen-led territorial innovation combining community organising, collective intelligence, and social entrepreneurship support. The approach is innovative in several ways: 1. A structured 4-step territorial methodology: Step 0: Building a core team and shared vision Step 1: Collecting dreams, ideas, and needs from inhabitants and local actors Step 2: Co-designing solutions during large-scale open creativity events (from 30 to 1,492 participants) Step 3: Selecting projects and forming collective teams Step 4: Accompanying project development within the local ecosystem 2. Joyful collective intelligence : The approach deliberately combines rigour and celebration, making participation accessible and attractive to a wide diversity of citizens. 3. A replicable model with local adaptation: Each territory adapts the methodology to its specific context, culture, and resources, while benefiting from a shared toolkit, peer mentoring, and a national learning network. 4. Inclusive by design: The model creates space for all — including people experiencing social exclusion, unemployment, or marginalisation — to contribute and take action in their community.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Start-Up de Territoire operates through a network model designed for replication, adaptation, and scaling: - Replicated: The core 4-step methodology has been transferred to 29 independent local teams across France and Luxembourg, maintaining its fundamental approach. - Adapted: Each territory customises the model to its specific context (urban, rural, overseas...) - Scaled-up: From 6 pilot territories in 2018 to 29 territories today, with 3 successive cohorts trained and a 4th launching in autumn 2026.
Quantitative results: 20,750 citizens mobilised to share their dreams and ideas 638 projects supported and accompanied 832 non-relocatable local jobs created 24 territories officially labelled, 5 in the launch phase 3 cohorts of new territories trained (Promotion 1, 2, and 3) Qualitative benefits: Strengthened social cohesion and inter-actor cooperation within territories Increased civic engagement and empowerment of citizens, including those usually excluded from decision-making Development of local entrepreneurship ecosystems combining social economy, public authorities, and civil society Transfer of facilitation skills to local teams, enabling them to independently animate future creativity events Creation of a national learning network fostering inter-territorial solidarity and knowledge sharing

innovations.name: Network of Future Places
innovations.problem: Rural regions across Germany—especially in the former East—are living through a compounding crisis that is both material and social: demographic shrinkage, physical decay, the thinning of civic life, and political radicalization feed each other. They accumulate into a pervasive sense among rural and small town residents of being left behind by the mainstream economy, by infrastructure decisions, and by national attention. The most concrete symptom is the quiet disappearance of shared or “third” places. A former school that no longer has children, a village pub that cannot survive without regulars, a church or farm building that sits locked and unheated—these are not just “properties.” They are where people once met, argued, worked, organized help, and experienced a sense that their town was more than just a loose collection of houses. When those spaces go dark, the loss is both tangible and symbolic: it is the loss of the everyday infrastructure through which a community recognizes itself. With the collapse of such places, where civic participation is a habit rather than an event, political conversation migrates to digital platforms that reward outrage and simplify complex realities into camps and enemies. Germany’s growth-oriented economic logic concentrates capital, infrastructure, and opportunity in urban centers. As the population in many rural areas thins and ages, “critical mass” disappears: schools close, doctors relocate, buses run less often or not at all. Each closure makes the next one more likely. Resulting vacancies turn this demographic story into one of physical landscape abandonment. Around 16% of residential units in East Germany are vacant—often in poor structural condition requiring full renovation—compared to roughly 2–3.5% in urban and western regions. Beyond housing, disused schools, manor houses, and train stations stand as permanent markers of neglect. Repurposing is complex: long-neglected structures can be expensive to stabilize, and heritage protections or permit requirements can make timelines uncertain and financing difficult. In practice, vacancy becomes a category of “burden”—something to be disposed of—rather than a civic infrastructure resource worth  developing for the future. The political consequences are obvious: in national and state elections, the right wing forces are becoming more and more powerful - threatening to overtake whole states in the next elections. This democratic erosion is also spatial: vacant buildings are increasingly contested as organizing infrastructure. Far-right groups have recently included reviving third places in the countryside such as village pubs as a strategic priority to reshape local loyalties. There have been attempts at rural renewal. Across structurally weak regions, people and collectives, many of them coming from urban backgrounds, have tried to revive former infrastructure and vacant buildings in the countryside. Most have fallen into bankruptcy or stalled, with little sign of them today: a German researcher described a “long history of failure” from lack of resources and internal conflicts. Interest in countryside living has grown again since the Covid pandemic, but it does not automatically repair social fabric: newcomers can bring values and aesthetics that long-rooted residents experience as foreign or moralizing, or a kind of “land consumption,” renovating vacancies for private use without creating any shared benefit and risking a “us versus them” dynamic that is precisely the emotional terrain in which authoritarian narratives thrive. Meanwhile, community-led alternatives struggle to take root because there is no shared knowledge infrastructure for rural pioneers to learn cooperative ownership, financing, building permits, and community integration without starting from zero; only about 6% of EU startups are located in rural areas, and most initiatives collapse after the initial round of funding ends or a founder leaves. The crisis is therefore n
innovations.description: Founded in 2018, Netzwerk Zukunftsorte connects, inspires and shares knowledge for the development of community-based places in rural areas as resilient spaces for social innovation as well as economic and ecological resiliance. Community-based living and working projects in villages and small towns serve as models and experimental hubs for practical climate protection, social cohesion, social entrepreneurship and regional development through the revitalisation of vacant spaces as well as nature and climate protection. As a network, we make good examples visible ( www.zukunftsorte.land/orte ), connect actors and stakeholders, organise knowledge transfer and provide recommendations to policy makers. So far, we have around 80 projects on our map across Germany. In our scaling strategy we want to add several hundred Future Places in the DACH region within the next 3 years and aim at transferring the knowledge and network infrastructure to other European countries. VISIBILITY AND AWARDS FOR IMPACT PLACES In order to identify future locations, we have developed our own criteria to ensure that projects have a positive impact on their region. These criteria relate to standards in terms of the attitude to the common good and its implementation within the projects: Establishment of open meeting places and facilities, integration into the region, sustainable construction, regenerative lifestyles and much more. We recognise projects that meet these criteria as Impact Places and put them with an attractive profile on our Map. Our community reports that the Impact Place label is a great help in gaining the support of government decision-makers and potential investors. We are currently working on linking the criteria to an impact measurement for Impact Places. This should make it even easier to communicate the impact of projects in the future. This year we are also launching the Future Places Award. These will be visible as outstanding model projects and thus inspire imitation. ENABLEING EXCHANGE One of the core tasks of our network is to organise exchanges between creators of Impact Places. We do this through countless digital meet-ups, where project makers talk about their places, processes, challenges and solutions, and experts give tips on relevant topics. There is also an annual networking event that brings together hundreds of people from the future places community. These events are cited by our Impact Places community as essential in giving them the strength, energy and support to continue with their challenging projects. ORGANISING KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER Knowledge is essential to the successful development and operation of Impact Places. Our knowledge platform ( https://wissen.zukunftsorte.land ) provides project developers, local authorities and owners with access to tried and tested practical knowledge. In addition to instructions, checklists and model projects, you will also find personal experiences in the form of videos and audio contributions. Our publications, at least one per year, share specific expertise that has become highly valued and popular in the field of urban and regional development. ADVOCACY AND POLITICAL DIALOGUE We see it as our task to engage in dialogue with local, state and federal politicians to promote better framework conditions that facilitate the development and operation of Impact Places. For example, in terms of building law, commercial regulations or public-interest operator structures. With regard to financing and funding opportunities, we advocate low-threshold loans and funding programmes that take into account the social impact of projects. At the local level, we lobby for administrative support for Impact Place players.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Since 2020 our organisation has been instrumental in raising public and political awareness of the potential of community-focused property development in rural areas. We coined the term 'Future Places' to describe impact-driven co-living and co-working projects in the countryside - a term now adopted by many other organisations and government bodies. Thanks to the visibility of our Future Place projects, our publications and the policy dialogue we lead, funding programmes now include more and more of what we promote as crucial to their development. With our help, many Future Places have been founded and stabilised. sections.question: Problem
sections.answer: Rural regions across Germany—especially in the former East—are living through a compounding crisis that is both material and social: demographic shrinkage, physical decay, the thinning of civic life, and political radicalization feed each other. They accumulate into a pervasive sense among rural and small town residents of being left behind by the mainstream economy, by infrastructure decisions, and by national attention. The most concrete symptom is the quiet disappearance of shared or “third” places. A former school that no longer has children, a village pub that cannot survive without regulars, a church or farm building that sits locked and unheated—these are not just “properties.” They are where people once met, argued, worked, organized help, and experienced a sense that their town was more than just a loose collection of houses. When those spaces go dark, the loss is both tangible and symbolic: it is the loss of the everyday infrastructure through which a community recognizes itself. With the collapse of such places, where civic participation is a habit rather than an event, political conversation migrates to digital platforms that reward outrage and simplify complex realities into camps and enemies. Germany’s growth-oriented economic logic concentrates capital, infrastructure, and opportunity in urban centers. As the population in many rural areas thins and ages, “critical mass” disappears: schools close, doctors relocate, buses run less often or not at all. Each closure makes the next one more likely. Resulting vacancies turn this demographic story into one of physical landscape abandonment. Around 16% of residential units in East Germany are vacant—often in poor structural condition requiring full renovation—compared to roughly 2–3.5% in urban and western regions. Beyond housing, disused schools, manor houses, and train stations stand as permanent markers of neglect. Repurposing is complex: long-neglected structures can be expensive to stabilize, and heritage protections or permit requirements can make timelines uncertain and financing difficult. In practice, vacancy becomes a category of “burden”—something to be disposed of—rather than a civic infrastructure resource worth  developing for the future. The political consequences are obvious: in national and state elections, the right wing forces are becoming more and more powerful - threatening to overtake whole states in the next elections. This democratic erosion is also spatial: vacant buildings are increasingly contested as organizing infrastructure. Far-right groups have recently included reviving third places in the countryside such as village pubs as a strategic priority to reshape local loyalties. There have been attempts at rural renewal. Across structurally weak regions, people and collectives, many of them coming from urban backgrounds, have tried to revive former infrastructure and vacant buildings in the countryside. Most have fallen into bankruptcy or stalled, with little sign of them today: a German researcher described a “long history of failure” from lack of resources and internal conflicts. Interest in countryside living has grown again since the Covid pandemic, but it does not automatically repair social fabric: newcomers can bring values and aesthetics that long-rooted residents experience as foreign or moralizing, or a kind of “land consumption,” renovating vacancies for private use without creating any shared benefit and risking a “us versus them” dynamic that is precisely the emotional terrain in which authoritarian narratives thrive. Meanwhile, community-led alternatives struggle to take root because there is no shared knowledge infrastructure for rural pioneers to learn cooperative ownership, financing, building permits, and community integration without starting from zero; only about 6% of EU startups are located in rural areas, and most initiatives collapse after the initial round of funding ends or a founder leaves. The crisis is therefore n

sections.question: Description
sections.answer: Founded in 2018, Netzwerk Zukunftsorte connects, inspires and shares knowledge for the development of community-based places in rural areas as resilient spaces for social innovation as well as economic and ecological resiliance. Community-based living and working projects in villages and small towns serve as models and experimental hubs for practical climate protection, social cohesion, social entrepreneurship and regional development through the revitalisation of vacant spaces as well as nature and climate protection. As a network, we make good examples visible ( www.zukunftsorte.land/orte ), connect actors and stakeholders, organise knowledge transfer and provide recommendations to policy makers. So far, we have around 80 projects on our map across Germany. In our scaling strategy we want to add several hundred Future Places in the DACH region within the next 3 years and aim at transferring the knowledge and network infrastructure to other European countries. VISIBILITY AND AWARDS FOR IMPACT PLACES In order to identify future locations, we have developed our own criteria to ensure that projects have a positive impact on their region. These criteria relate to standards in terms of the attitude to the common good and its implementation within the projects: Establishment of open meeting places and facilities, integration into the region, sustainable construction, regenerative lifestyles and much more. We recognise projects that meet these criteria as Impact Places and put them with an attractive profile on our Map. Our community reports that the Impact Place label is a great help in gaining the support of government decision-makers and potential investors. We are currently working on linking the criteria to an impact measurement for Impact Places. This should make it even easier to communicate the impact of projects in the future. This year we are also launching the Future Places Award. These will be visible as outstanding model projects and thus inspire imitation. ENABLEING EXCHANGE One of the core tasks of our network is to organise exchanges between creators of Impact Places. We do this through countless digital meet-ups, where project makers talk about their places, processes, challenges and solutions, and experts give tips on relevant topics. There is also an annual networking event that brings together hundreds of people from the future places community. These events are cited by our Impact Places community as essential in giving them the strength, energy and support to continue with their challenging projects. ORGANISING KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER Knowledge is essential to the successful development and operation of Impact Places. Our knowledge platform ( https://wissen.zukunftsorte.land ) provides project developers, local authorities and owners with access to tried and tested practical knowledge. In addition to instructions, checklists and model projects, you will also find personal experiences in the form of videos and audio contributions. Our publications, at least one per year, share specific expertise that has become highly valued and popular in the field of urban and regional development. ADVOCACY AND POLITICAL DIALOGUE We see it as our task to engage in dialogue with local, state and federal politicians to promote better framework conditions that facilitate the development and operation of Impact Places. For example, in terms of building law, commercial regulations or public-interest operator structures. With regard to financing and funding opportunities, we advocate low-threshold loans and funding programmes that take into account the social impact of projects. At the local level, we lobby for administrative support for Impact Place players.

innovations.name: An innovative approach to working with homeless individuals with substance use disorders in a new type of service (alcohol management)
innovations.problem: The project itself builds on nearly 20 years of work by Depaul Slovakia with homeless people in its services and addresses the lack of low-threshold residential services. The applicant has extensive experience working with homeless people with substance use disorders; it was the first organization in Slovakia to establish the very first low-threshold night shelter in Bratislava, which currently has a capacity of 200 beds.
innovations.description: The purpose of the project is to create a sufficiently adequate and safe space for working with homeless individuals struggling with addiction who are repeat clients of the applicant, as their addiction prevents them from taking the next step toward integration. Upon completion of the project, a new social service will be established, which will complement the range of low-threshold crisis intervention services in Slovakia while implementing an innovative approach to working with homeless individuals with substance use disorders. The main output of the project—the implementation of an innovative method for managing alcohol consumption within a new type of social service—will support the proposals in the approved National Concept, which mentions the need for the creation of this type of service. Based on the applicant’s internal statistics, some clients of residential services repeatedly return, as a condition of their stay is managing their addiction, yet the services provide almost no support in this regard. After their condition improves and they subsequently leave the service, their addiction resurfaces; they are unable to stop drinking alcohol overnight. The project will create a space to address the needs of this marginalized group of homeless people, whose lives are constrained by addiction, and one of the steps toward integration is the gradual reduction of that addiction. The idea of providing residential services for homeless people with addictions in Slovakia is groundbreaking, given that residential services are typically conditional on merit and complete abstinence. The main activity of the project was inspired by data from our partner, Depaul Ireland, which began providing this service in 2004. The outcome of the project will be the implementation of alcohol management in the Slovak context.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The project proposer expects that clients receiving comprehensive support (social, psychological, and community-based), through the application of alcohol management methods, will gradually begin to work toward changing their life circumstances with the long-term goal of reintegration. The project will support that group of homeless people who are motivated to change their life situation but are limited by addiction.

innovations.name: Social Accelerator
innovations.problem: the project aims to reduce structural inequalities, promote social cohesion, and enable a green, digital, and inclusive transition across the region.
innovations.description: Key activities within the project include: - Mapping existing social innovation initiatives and opportunities in 10 countries. - Establishing Social Labs for co-creation, pilot testing, and knowledge exchange. - Incubating and accelerating startups focused on social and environmental impact. - Delivering training in sustainability, digital skills, gender equity, and impact investment. - Organising contests and hackathons to foster innovation. - Providing competitive funding to third parties, focusing on territorial and sectoral diversity. - Launching a digital platform for e-learning, impact tracking, and community building. - Hosting public-private dialogue spaces to align local strategies with national and regional priorities
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: 1.Enhanced institutional capacities (public sector, CSOs, BSOs, academia) and the development of tools (such as roadmaps and country strategies) to establish social innovation hubs in the LAC region, drawing from successful EU models. 2.Strengthened entrepreneurial capacities (with a focus on youth, women, and vulnerable groups) and the development of companies offering services to vulnerable populations in the LAC region, enabling sustainable, digital, and socially innovative initiatives. 3.Increased financing/investment opportunities and enhanced support mechanisms to help social innovation projects access funding, promoting equity and sustainable development in line with the EU-LAC Global Gateway Investment Agenda. 4. Improved collaboration and networking opportunities among EU-LAC public-private initiatives and global social innovation programmes, creating a robust framework for the Global Gateway.

innovations.name: Pinhal ImPACT – Itinerant Incubator for Impact Entrepreneurship in the Pinhal Interior
innovations.lead: ADXTUR – Territorial Development Agency for Aldeias do Xisto (Schist Villages)
innovations.problem: The Pinhal Interior faces structural challenges common to many rural European regions: population decline, ageing, low density, difficulty in attracting and retaining people, limited access to support structures and weak connections between local ideas, institutions, entrepreneurs and investment opportunities. At the same time, the region has strong natural, cultural, social and entrepreneurial assets. The problem is not the lack of ideas or resources, but the lack of continuous support, coordination and pathways to transform these assets into sustainable initiatives with measurable impact.
innovations.description:
Pinhal ImPACT builds on previous territorial innovation and social incubation experience, including the I3Social Beiras e Serra da Estrela itinerant social innovation incubator developed by Aldeia dos Girassóis, and adapts this approach to the specific challenges and opportunities of the Pinhal Interior region.
Pinhal ImPACT uses an itinerant incubation model, bringing support directly to different municipalities and communities rather than concentrating services in a single location. The project combines ecosystem mapping, community mobilisation, hackathons, capacity-building laboratories, mentoring, incubation, acceleration and impact monitoring. Its innovation lies in connecting territorial development, social innovation and impact entrepreneurship through a collaborative regional support structure. It brings together municipalities, associations, entrepreneurs, social investors, knowledge institutions and local communities to co-create solutions rooted in the territory.

innovations.evidence: Expected results include 280 direct participants, 20 institutions involved in social innovation and experimentation, and 40 incubation, acceleration and capacity-building processes. The project is already mobilising a regional ecosystem through interviews, events, stakeholder engagement and project incubation. Benefits include stronger local collaboration, increased entrepreneurial capacity, better connection between ideas and implementation, support for rural impact projects, and greater visibility for social innovation in low-density territories.

At the same time, the region has strong natural, cultural, social and entrepreneurial assets. The problem is not the lack of ideas or resources, but the lack of continuous support, coordination and pathways to transform these assets into sustainable initiatives with measurable impact.
Pinhal ImPACT builds on previous territorial innovation and social incubation experience, including the I3Social Beiras e Serra da Estrela itinerant social innovation incubator developed by Aldeia dos Girassóis, and adapts this approach to the specific challenges and opportunities of the Pinhal Interior region.
Pinhal ImPACT uses an itinerant incubation model, bringing support directly to different municipalities and communities rather than concentrating services in a single location. The project combines ecosystem mapping, community mobilisation, hackathons, capacity-building laboratories, mentoring, incubation, acceleration and impact monitoring. Its innovation lies in connecting territorial development, social innovation and impact entrepreneurship through a collaborative regional support structure. It brings together municipalities, associations, entrepreneurs, social investors, knowledge institutions and local communities to co-create solutions rooted in the territory.
Expected results include 280 direct participants, 20 institutions involved in social innovation and experimentation, and 40 incubation, acceleration and capacity-building processes. The project is already mobilising a regional ecosystem through interviews, events, stakeholder engagement and project incubation. Benefits include stronger local collaboration, increased entrepreneurial capacity, better connection between ideas and implementation, support for rural impact projects, and greater visibility for social innovation in low-density territories.

innovations.name: How can we foster integrated, cross-sector approaches to child health and parenting support in order to promote children's well-being and thriving families?
innovations.problem: Families today face increasingly complex challenges, including parental burnout, mental health issues, social isolation, behavioural difficulties, disability, and major life transitions. Yet support services remain fragmented across healthcare, social services, education, and parenting support, making access difficult and reducing the effectiveness of interventions. This fragmentation limits prevention, delays appropriate support, and places an additional burden on families, who must navigate multiple organisations with little coordination between professionals.
innovations.description: L'Étoile des familles has developed an innovative hybrid multidisciplinary coordinated pathway that brings together professionals from healthcare, parenting support, education, social services, and well-being around the needs of each family, regardless of the child's age and the family dynamics at play. Each personalised pathway combines: individual consultations; parent-child and family workshops; group activities; coordination between regulated and non-regulated professionals. Developed through a Social R&D approach, the model is co-designed with local stakeholders and supported by the creation of a health-focused community hub ("third place"). It promotes prevention, early intervention, and integrated support from preconception through adolescence.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project delivers benefits at several levels: -For families: easier access to coordinated services, personalised support, stronger parenting confidence, improved family relationships, and enhanced mental well-being. -For professionals: improved multidisciplinary collaboration, better communication, and reduced fragmentation between services. -For the community: stronger social cohesion, more efficient use of local resources, and a preventive approach that may reduce the need for more intensive interventions later.

innovations.name: L'école comestible
innovations.problem:
Food production methods and diet have a major impact on our health, on society and the environment. According to ADEME, diet accounts for between 20 and 50 % of the environmental footprint of the French population. Furthermore, diet is the leading risk factor for the loss of healthy life years, ahead of tobacco, as highlighted by Santé Publique France. Diet is a significant factor in health inequalities, which are linked to socio-spatial inequalities.
The lack of high-quality, affordable food shops in many working-class neighbourhoods increases the risk of food insecurity and health risks for their residents. In light of these findings, it is essential to tackle these inequalities and food waste, whilst raising awareness amongst citizens from a young age about the impacts of food. This approach aims to preserve our environment, protect our health and promote social justice.
innovations.description:
In collaboration with stakeholders in the school and out-of-school sectors, as well as local and national public authorities, l'école comestible offers a series of workshops on healthy and sustainable eating during school hours, mainly in priority neighbourhoods under the urban policy.
Each participating class takes part in 4 to 6 workshops a year, following a structured educational programme and the ‘La bouche pleine et les mains sales’ (Mouths full and hands dirty) methodology, based on hands-on learning (learning through handling, preparing and tasting) and working together (a sense of sharing and community). The workshops are structured around major cross-cutting themes: plants, the seasons, the plant life cycle, tastes and the senses, reducing food waste, world cuisines, etc.
L’école comestible bases its teaching approach on ecological, human and social values.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Since 2019, the association has built up a strong regional network comprising local and regional producers, associations that share its values, and public sector partners, including local authorities and schools. Thanks to this growing network, it has run more than 2,900 workshops, reaching over 20,000 children in 105 schools. L’école comestible also involves 150 dedicated volunteers.

innovations.name: CyclAvenir
innovations.problem:
The association, based in Île-de-France, operates in a region where cycling is one of the preferred modes of transport. However, access to cycling remains uneven, as not everyone has had the opportunity to learn how to ride a bike.
This divide creates barriers for some people, forcing them to turn to more expensive and polluting transport options. In 2023, mobility difficulties were ranked as the second biggest obstacle to returning to work.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Thanks to short- and long-term programmes, more than 88 % of female beneficiaries say they now feel confident cycling around town.
In total, more than 320 women took part in the training programmes, 150 of whom acquired a bicycle at the end of the programme. Among the programme’s beneficiaries, more than 62 % say they have seen an improvement in their quality of life thanks to regular cycling.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

CyclAvenir
The association, based in Île-de-France, operates in a region where cycling is one of the preferred modes of transport. However, access to cycling remains uneven, as not everyone has had the opportunity to learn how to ride a bike.
This divide creates barriers for some people, forcing them to turn to more expensive and polluting transport options. In 2023, mobility difficulties were ranked as the second biggest obstacle to returning to work.
CyclAvenir is a social inclusion project that promotes cycling through improved access.
Through its cycling training courses, CyclAvenir enables people in vulnerable situations – particularly women, those who have experienced homelessness, exiles, refugees and asylum seekers – to reconnect with the city in a healthier way. By teaching people to cycle, the organisation supports projects aimed at helping people enter the workforce and promotes access to culture for groups who are often excluded from these two fundamental rights.
CyclAvenir offers three key programmes:
En S’Elles ! supports women in vulnerable situations as they discover and master urban cycling;
Tou(r)s à vélo is a programme offering everyone a guided tour of Paris and its cultural sites, centred on socially engaged themes such as gender equality, decolonisation and the Republic;
Cycl-à-lire is aimed at families and children, deploying a mobile Japanese reading and theatre unit to provide a unique, travelling cultural experience.
Thanks to short- and long-term programmes, more than 88 % of female beneficiaries say they now feel confident cycling around town.
In total, more than 320 women took part in the training programmes, 150 of whom acquired a bicycle at the end of the programme. Among the programme’s beneficiaries, more than 62 % say they have seen an improvement in their quality of life thanks to regular cycling.

innovations.problem: The low-tech approach offers everyone the means to meet their needs whilst respecting both people and the planet. It aims to answer the question: ‘What do we really need to thrive in a world of constraints?’. For over 10 years, numerous initiatives have emerged across the country. To spread the low-tech approach more widely, it is necessary to support and guide the development of these local initiatives.

innovations.raw_text:
Low-tech Lab
The low-tech approach offers everyone the means to meet their needs whilst respecting both people and the planet. It aims to answer the question: ‘What do we really need to thrive in a world of constraints?’. For over 10 years, numerous initiatives have emerged across the country. To spread the low-tech approach more widely, it is necessary to support and guide the development of these local initiatives.
Low-tech Lab’s mission is to explore and test low-tech solutions, and then share them with as many people as possible. By acting as a champion for these ideas, it aims to contribute to the emergence of more frugal, more respectful and more resilient ways of living, producing and consuming. It thus seeks to bring about a more sustainable and desirable society.
Low-tech Lab has three main objectives:
to coordinate all existing low-tech communities across the regions;
to create and maintain shared collaborative tools to promote the low-tech approach;
to raise the profile of the low-tech approach by devising simple and appealing narratives.
The Low-tech Lab wiki has been viewed more than 2 million times to date. It lists more than 300 low-tech systems and techniques, the result of 10 years’ work. There are also 28 documentaries available. The Low-tech Lab also provides the general public with a directory listing more than 950 low-tech initiatives .

innovations.name: Robin.e.s des bennes
innovations.problem:
Les Robin.e.s des Bennes was founded in Amiens, where more than 36,000 residents are living in precarious circumstances. In the Hauts-de-France region, 15.5 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line.
Faced with difficulties in accessing food and clothing, even as many goods and foodstuffs are thrown away, the Robin.e.s des Bennes offer practical solutions to make better use of these resources and meet the basic needs of the most vulnerable members of society.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
According to an impact study carried out in 2023, for every euro invested in the charity, 4.30 euros of social, environmental and economic value will be generated in the local area.
To date, more than 44 tonnes of food, 17 tonnes of textiles and 9 kilograms of plants have been recovered and redistributed free of charge. 82 % of beneficiaries say they have gained purchasing power thanks to these solidarity-based, anti-waste initiatives, and 90 % say that their mindset has changed as a result of their involvement with the association.

Robin.e.s des bennes
Les Robin.e.s des Bennes was founded in Amiens, where more than 36,000 residents are living in precarious circumstances. In the Hauts-de-France region, 15.5 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line.
Faced with difficulties in accessing food and clothing, even as many goods and foodstuffs are thrown away, the Robin.e.s des Bennes offer practical solutions to make better use of these resources and meet the basic needs of the most vulnerable members of society.
Les Robin.e.s des Bennes are working to reduce waste through community initiatives that are free and open to everyone.
Their model, which is based on the principles of the circular economy, has three main components:
food;
clothing;
plants.
In practical terms, they organise solidarity-based food harvesting, food distributions, soup parties, ‘freeperies’ (free second-hand clothes shops), sewing workshops and plant donations. These initiatives directly involve beneficiaries in the fight against waste and precarious living conditions.
According to an impact study carried out in 2023, for every euro invested in the charity, 4.30 euros of social, environmental and economic value will be generated in the local area.
To date, more than 44 tonnes of food, 17 tonnes of textiles and 9 kilograms of plants have been recovered and redistributed free of charge. 82 % of beneficiaries say they have gained purchasing power thanks to these solidarity-based, anti-waste initiatives, and 90 % say that their mindset has changed as a result of their involvement with the association.

innovations.name: Travaux suspendus
innovations.problem:
The climate crisis highlights the urgent need to scale up the renovation of energy-inefficient homes. Yet many owner-occupier households continue to face poor housing conditions and energy poverty.
The construction sector alone accounts for 28 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions in France, whilst more than 2.2 million people are energy-excluded and 1.3 million live in homes that expose them to health and social risks. As existing state support does not always meet the needs of the most vulnerable households, Travaux Suspendus was set up to provide a complementary and tailored solution.
innovations.description:
Travaux Suspendus works to make decent, refurbished housing accessible to everyone.
The association runs a community of socially-minded building craftspeople who volunteer on renovation projects for substandard housing. These projects, which are free for households in precarious circumstances, are made possible by fundraising from individuals and businesses.
Furthermore, the creation of a dedicated fund enables better remuneration for the building craftspeople, thereby strengthening the social and solidarity-based nature of the initiative.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Since Travaux Suspendus was founded in 2023, more than 50 craftspeople have volunteered for community building projects and more than 100 craftspeople have been involved in collecting donations.

innovations.name: Toit à moi
innovations.problem: The issue of poor housing is one of the major challenges our society has long faced. Today, particularly as a result of the financial and migration crises, it has become an even more pressing issue: between 2001 and 2012, the number of homeless people rose by 50 per cent, reaching 141,500 people without a fixed abode in the latter year ( Infographie Les personnes à la rue , Fondation pour le Logement des Défavorisés, September 2017). Despite a strong commitment from the voluntary sector to the issue of housing support, not all needs can be met and many approaches still need to be developed.
innovations.description:
In 2006, when they founded the association Toit à Moi in Nantes, Denis Castin and Gwenaël Morvan were determined to transform the small, informal donations that people make on a daily basis into a collective, regular and impactful sponsorship scheme. Their calculation was simple: it would take fewer than 100 people donating an average of €20 a month to finance a flat within five years. They therefore launched a campaign to recruit sponsors, volunteers and patrons, which culminated in 2008 in the securing of a loan and the purchase of their first flat.
The Toi à Moi model is truly built on a principle of cooperation and complementarity between various forms of giving: regular donors help to repay the loans taken out to purchase the flats; volunteers regularly devote their time to activities organised jointly with those who have been rehoused; and corporate sponsors fund the organisation’s fixed costs and staff salaries, contribute their expertise or open up their networks to facilitate the beneficiaries’ return to work.
What sets Toi à Moi’s work apart is that it combines rehousing with a highly effective programme of psychosocial support for beneficiaries, as the loss of a home is, first and foremost, a major driver of social exclusion. The association therefore offers very close support to individuals, helping them on a day-to-day basis as they rebuild their lives until they are able to leave the scheme and move into standard accommodation. Three types of support are therefore provided: a professional support worker assists beneficiaries in developing and implementing their strategy for re-entry into the labour market; volunteers help rebuild social ties by sharing daily, cultural or leisure activities with those receiving support; and specialist organisations (training centres, psychologists, social workers, doctors) make their expertise available. The association’s work aims to achieve the genuine integration of individuals into society, both economically and on a human level.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Since 2016, the organisation in Nantes has settled into a comfortable rhythm, with a dedicated community of volunteers and staff working to bring this community of stakeholders to life.
Today, the association owns 18 apartments, which have enabled it to rehouse more than 50 people over the past 10 years.

innovations.name: Association Zoein
innovations.problem:
There are many entrepreneurial citizen-led initiatives working towards the ecological transition, but they still receive too little support from public or private funding.
Those leading transition projects often use their own funds to support their activities and sometimes struggle to make a decent living in a stable environment.
innovations.description:
Association Zoein provides guidance and financial support to project leaders through the Ecological Transition Income (RTE). Aimed at those committed to the ecological transition, the RTE helps to ensure the long-term sustainability of socially and environmentally innovative initiatives.
The association targets two groups:
project leaders who wish to implement their initiatives and meet with peers;
social and solidarity economy organisations and local authorities that are exploring new ways to revitalise their local areas in an environmentally friendly manner.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Today, seven RTE experimental groups welcome project leaders and their teams so that they can pool their skills and experiences with their peers.
This community brings together more than 70 project leaders across the various experimental fields.

innovations.name: Topophone
innovations.problem:
In priority neighbourhoods and rural areas, young people are particularly affected by a lack of access to musical culture.
In France, around 50 per cent of pupils in state schools take part in musical activities, whether at school or outside school hours. However, this average masks significant inequalities: the figure drops to 30 per cent in the most disadvantaged areas, whilst it reaches 70 per cent in more affluent areas.
innovations.description:
In order to address inequalities in access to musical culture, Topophone offers a range of music learning and introductory activities aimed at young people:
music workshops and lessons, enabling young people facing social, educational or family difficulties to play a full part in artistic discovery;
music programmes in schools and medical-social settings, aimed at fostering young people’s creative development.
Topophone also organises outreach initiatives to promote local artists through the organisation of concerts.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
tags: Equal access to education and training

In priority neighbourhoods and rural areas, young people are particularly affected by a lack of access to musical culture.
In France, around 50 per cent of pupils in state schools take part in musical activities, whether at school or outside school hours. music workshops and lessons, enabling young people facing social, educational or family difficulties to play a full part in artistic discovery;
music programmes in schools and medical-social settings, aimed at fostering young people’s creative development.

educational and social, with the aim of fostering young people’s personal development and self-confidence;

innovations.name: Innovative Solutions for Refugee Integration and Crisis Mitigation in EU Member States (ISRICM-EU)
innovations.problem: Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has resulted in the displacement of millions of people, creating significant challenges for host communities across the European Union. Displaced Ukrainians often face barriers to employment, education, social inclusion, access to services, and community participation, while public authorities and civil society organisations require innovative approaches to respond effectively to these evolving needs. The project addresses these challenges by developing and promoting social innovation solutions that strengthen integration, improve employability, foster community cohesion, and enhance cooperation among key stakeholders.
innovations.description: ISRICM-EU applies a transnational social innovation approach that combines education, employability support, entrepreneurship, community engagement, policy dialogue, and stakeholder cooperation into a single integrated framework for refugee inclusion. Rather than addressing individual needs in isolation, the project strengthens collaboration among public authorities, civil society organisations, educational institutions, employers, and local communities to co-create sustainable and transferable solutions. Through knowledge exchange, capacity building, awareness-raising activities, and the testing of innovative practices across multiple EU countries, the project promotes long-term social inclusion and strengthens the capacity of communities to respond effectively to the challenges arising from forced displacement.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: ISRICM-EU delivered significant results by strengthening the social inclusion and resilience of displaced people from Ukraine through coordinated actions implemented across nine European partner organisations. The project enhanced beneficiaries' access to education, vocational training, entrepreneurship support, social services, and community engagement opportunities, while increasing awareness of refugee inclusion among public authorities, employers, civil society organisations, and local communities. Strong stakeholder cooperation was established through transnational collaboration, knowledge exchange, and multi-sector partnerships, contributing to the development and transfer of innovative social inclusion practices. Evaluation findings demonstrated stakeholder and beneficiary satisfaction levels exceeding 85% across consortium activities, confirming the quality, relevance, and effectiveness of the project's interventions. The project also strengthened the capacity of participating organisations to design and implement sustainable, evidence-based solutions, creating lasting benefits for both displaced people and host communities while promoting the transferability of successful practices across Europe.
tags: Social integration of those at risk
