innovations.name: #radikalanders – New Work in the Social Economy
innovations.lead: Arbeiterwohlfahrt Mönchengladbach und im Rhein-Kreis Neuss e.V. (AWO)
innovations.problem: Before the transformation, the organisation was close to insolvency. Rigid hierarchies, central control and heavy bureaucracy produced long decision paths, an elaborate reporting system, overloaded managers – especially middle management – and frustrated teams. The consequences were high sickness-absence rates, poor decisions and a dangerous financial and cultural imbalance. At the same time the whole social and care sector faces a severe shortage of skilled workers, constantly changing client needs and external shocks – pandemics, uncertain public budgets – that centralised, top-down structures cannot react to quickly enough. In the social economy these effects of outdated working cultures show up as if under a magnifying glass.
innovations.description: Instead of reforming the old structure, AWO Mönchengladbach made a radical break and moved to a self-organised, hierarchy-free model based on the BetaCodex. Today the organisation works like a network of mini-enterprises (“cells”). Decisions are made where the work is – without committees or approval chains – by the colleagues and situational peer groups who hold the relevant knowledge and responsibility; what counts is evidence and competence, not status. The organisation rests on two complementary structures: a value-creation structure, in which cells decide autonomously, close to clients and impact, and a compliance structure that does not control but enables – setting the safe legal, financial and ethical frame within which self-organisation can work; where a decision binds the whole, it is taken jointly and visibly, with no votes but reasoned by evidence. Cells manage their own value flows with no budgets and no approvals (a value-flow accounting makes impact visible for orientation, not control; sustained deficits trigger more visibility, not permission). Crucially, the system has matured into shared, written frameworks rather than ad-hoc practice: how we decide, how we create value, and – since January 2026 – how we set pay. Salaries are no longer fixed cell by cell but follow one transparent, organisation-wide model: market-based bands per role, set yearly by a peer market round, from which each individual salary is calculated (never negotiated, no bonuses) on the basis of two impact dimensions – “skill & responsibility” assessed by the cell and “contribution to the whole” assessed by an organisation-wide peer round. A simple, real example of everyday autonomy: if an educator needs new sandpit toys, she simply buys them – no application, no form, no approval layer – because she is closest to the children, the parents and the situation. The logic of every model is radically transparent and accessible to all, so that transparency enables responsibility without control.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Arbeiterwohlfahrt Mönchengladbach und im Rhein-Kreis Neuss e.V. (AWO)
innovations.evidence: The organisation moved from the brink of insolvency back to stability, with faster, more flexible decisions taken close to the people it serves. A key measurable outcome concerns staff health: in a joint analysis with the health insurer AOK, colleagues at AWO Mönchengladbach had on average around 10 fewer sick days per year than the sector average, and the share of colleagues with no absence at all was notably higher. Lower staff turnover and a more attractive employer profile have made the organisational model a real advantage in recruiting and retaining skilled workers – decisive in a sector facing severe labour shortages. Self-organisation and trust have proven to work in practice, even in a complex welfare organisation. Transparency is supported by radically open figures and a value-creation accounting approach, and continuous improvement is anchored through regular annual cell reviews, thematic knowledge conferences, all-hands meetings and an annual OpenSpace congress with more than 100 colleagues. The experience is shared widely – through the “radikal anders” podcast, talks to other organisations and a nationwide AWO barcamp. The approach has also matured from practice into durable, codified frameworks – for how the organisation decides, how it accounts for value, and, since January 2026, how it sets pay – showing that the change is firmly anchored rather than a temporary experiment.
authors: Arbeiterwohlfahrt Mönchengladbach und im Rhein-Kreis Neuss e.V. (AWO)
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Climate and Environmental Literacy
innovations.problem: The Adult Literacy for Life programme is a national initiative in Ireland to improve all types of literacy. Notably, over 1 in 5 adults in Ireland does not have a functional level of literacy. Alongside this, many adult learners and adult education tutors do not feel confident engaging with topics of climate change, sustainability, and environmental action.
innovations.description:
This project, led by ECO-UNESCO in collaboration with Kilkenny and Carlow ETB and Laois and Offaly ETB, comprised several key stages:
Focus groups with adult literacy learners and adult education tutors in target areas
ECO-UNESCO workshops with adult literacy learners; these workshops served to improve participants' climate and environmental literacy, as well as providing valuable feedback on the development of activities for the resource pack
Development of a resource pack, provided in both digital and physical formats, for the use of adult education tutors. The resource pack takes an Education for Sustainable Development approach to building confidence in climate and environmental literacy within adult literacy learning contexts.
Training sessions were delivered by ECO-UNESCO to adult literacy tutors in target areas
The final resource pack was launched in December 2025 with a launch event in Tullamore, Ireland, bringing together all stakeholders including tutors and learners.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The resource pack, designed with an Education for Sustainable Development approach in mind, has been disseminated through Education and Training Boards across Ireland. Future development of this project includes training sessions to be delivered to ETB staff.
Over 40 individual adult learners were impacted through the workshop sessions for this project, helping to build their climate and environmental literacy.

innovations.name: UNITE Ukrainian Newcomer’s Integration Towards Employment!
innovations.problem: UNITE responds to several challenges faced by Ukrainian refugees when rebuilding their lives in a new country: Loss of stability and networks — people arrive without their familiar support systems, professional contacts, or community ties. innovations.name: Inclusive Recruitment Programme
innovations.problem: People with disabilities continue to experience significant barriers when seeking employment, despite having the skills, qualifications and motivation to work. Traditional employment initiatives often focus on preparing individuals for work and adapting to the workplace but do not sufficiently address the barriers that exist within recruitment systems, workplace cultures and employer practices. Many employers have positive intentions regarding inclusion but lack the knowledge, confidence or practical understanding required to recruit and support employees with disabilities effectively. This can lead to missed opportunities for both employers and jobseekers. The Inclusive Recruitment Programme addresses these challenges by tackling the systemic and societal barriers that exist within recruitment and employment processes, helping to create a more inclusive labour market for all.
innovations.description: The Inclusive Recruitment Programme takes a different approach to disability employment by focusing on employers as well as jobseekers. Rather than viewing disability employment solely as a challenge for individuals to overcome, the programme recognises that inclusion is a shared responsibility. It shifts the focus towards preparing workplaces, recruitment systems and hiring professionals to become more accessible and inclusive. The programme provides practical training covering every stage of the employment journey, including accessible recruitment practices, inclusive interviewing, workplace accommodations, onboarding and employee retention. By equipping employers with practical tools and confidence, the programme helps create lasting organisational change rather than one-off recruitment outcomes. This dual approach bridges the gap between job-ready candidates and inclusive employers, creating sustainable pathways into employment.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The Inclusive Recruitment Programme delivers benefits for individuals, employers and the wider community. For people with disabilities, the programme helps create greater access to meaningful employment opportunities, increased independence, improved confidence and enhanced quality of life. For employers, it provides practical knowledge and tools that support inclusive recruitment and retention practices. It also helps organisations access a wider and often underutilised talent pool, strengthen workplace culture and improve diversity and inclusion outcomes. The wider community benefits from increased workforce participation, stronger local businesses and economy and greater social inclusion. By removing barriers to employment, the programme contributes to a more equitable society where people with disabilities can participate fully in economic and community life.

innovations.name: Youth Impact Säffle
innovations.problem: Many young people in rural communities feel excluded from decision-making and lack opportunities to influence the present and future of their communities. This contributes to disengagement, outmigration and a loss of valuable perspectives in local development.
innovations.description: The project brings young people and decision-makers together to co-create solutions to local challenges. Unlike traditional consultation processes, youth-generated ideas are developed into concrete actions and embedded into municipal structures for lasting impact.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project aims to engage hundreds of young people in shaping their community, strengthen trust between youth and local authorities, and ensure that at least two youth-generated solutions are implemented. Youth impact Säffle also educate decision-makers and creates more inclusive and effective local decision-making processes.

innovations.name: Specialsitter
innovations.problem:
People with disabilities and their families should have the same opportunities in society as every one else.
Article 1 UN-CRPD and other international and EU treaties are the foundation and guidance of our work. According to the German Institute for Human Rights, people with disabilities remain disadvantaged across nearly all areas of life, despite the Convention having been in force for 16 years (Deutsches Institut für Menschenrechte (2025), file:///C:/Users/Anne/OneDrive%20-%20Specialsitter%20GmbH/Desktop/Nebenprojekte/Social%20Innovation/Eckpunkte_Bundestagswahl_2025_MST_UN-BRK.pdf). We aim for the goal to support people in Germany who don’t have the same access and participation in society. This is where our work comes into focus. People with disabilities have the right to equal participation in society, and it is our mission to support them in exercising and fully enjoying this right.
innovations.description: There are multiple ways we intake clients. The vast majority of new requests are arranged through municipal agencies like the Social Welfare Department or the Youth Welfare Department (Youth Welfare Department = 96,81 % and Social Welfare Department = 3,19 %). Some clients find us through online research, and others recommend us to their friends and acquaintances. The first contact of a new client is the coordinating team of the respective site. The coordinating team conducts the admission interview, which covers the entirety of the client’s situation: their diagnosis, their character, their preferences, hobbies, the day-to-day tasks as well as special wishes such as the preferred background or gender of the assistant. After the admission interview, the matching begins. Part of it is digitalized: our dashboard allows us to filter employees, or sitters, according to their qualifications, location, no-gos and special interests. The site coordinating team makes the first connection between the potential assistant and the client and/or their family. Candidates meet the families first and get to know each other so they can build a trustful relationship before they start working together. Only after a successful meeting in real life and an enthusiastic agreement to start collaboration is a match confirmed. The qualifications of our sitters range from kindergarden teachers, to social workers, to special eds teachers, to occupational therapists down to experienced career changers. Which qualification is necessary depends on the requirements of the respective departments and the clients’ needs. For us, it’s important to not only find qualified employees, but people with a good sense of the impact of their work and empathy for the client. Newly employed sitters take part in an onboarding process, including a mandatory first-aid class and a child-protection class. Submitting an extended certificate of conduct is an indispensable requirement, as well. Through our digital learning platform and online courses we offer continuous advanced training. For example clinical pictures or soft skills. Training, supervision, and team meetings contribute to maintaining a high quality of work and provide employees with the opportunity to continuously develop their skills and competencies. Regular employee surveys help ensure that people in our organization are heard, enabling improvements to be identified and implemented.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
With our inhouse digital platform we digitalized the administration of assistant services both within and outside our organization, we have transformed the way support services for people with disabilities are delivered. This has streamlined processes and reduced administrative burdens for public authorities. The positive experience with our digital way of working is that our central administration consisted of four employees in 2019 and remained at the same size in 2021, even though the organization had tripled in scale. We attribute these efficiency gains to the implementation of our software. In 2020 we implemented our app for the employees to digitalize the daily processes of documentation and obtaining signatures from our employees for the commitments with the client. In addition to our organization, 15 extern companies are currently using our self-developed digital platform, benefiting approximately 300 employees. The platform has since been spun off into an independent company.
Since the founding of Specialsitter in 2015, we have so far supported 6.740 families in 528.138 commitments. In the last 52 weeks, we have provided 15.552 support hours. The working areas are as different as the people’s life situations. We provide our services in multiple settings, always according to the clients’ needs: in schools and kindergardens, in the workplspace, in the free time and in a domestic setting, at night, on a school trip or during doctors’ or agency visits. The main outcome of our work is the improved quality of life and self-determination of people with disabilities who we support. Even though disability or sickness are commonplace, the environmental barriers in different settings are still substantial: kindergartens, schools and companies are often overwhelmed due to a lack of personnel, skills and knowledge on the specifics and practicalities of disabilities. Our services fill the gaps, so that people with disabilities can participate in social life, education and employment on their own terms. We also provide relief to the families of our clients by taking care of their loved ones with special needs, so that the carers can take a breather, find time for themselves to recharge or simply go to work knowing their relatives are in good hands.
The following chart illustrates the growth and development of our organization. It shows the development of jobs created, people supported, and service hours provided since 2023.
What our employees and families we support say about working at or working with Specialsitter:
„ They are open-minded and understanding when you have a lot going on in your personal life and need to take a short break. You don’t have to worry about losing your job if you are unable to work for an extended period. Thank you, Specialsitter. ”
“Specialsitter invests not only in acquiring new clients but also in employee retention and supporting its clients.”
“ A caring employer where you are not just a number as an employee, with direct points of contact. Better pay. The freedom to make your own decisions .”
“ What sets Specialsitter apart from others is its incredibly kind staff, flexibility in day-to-day work, extremely supportive location managers, efficient communication and collaboration within the team, and above all, the wide range of activities and events on offer. ”
“ The appreciation and recognition. The gender-inclusive language—which is especially meaningful to me because it always makes me feel addressed and included. The mindfulness tips, the way communications are addressed with “Dear all,” the regular expressions of gratitude, the attitude toward my questions and concerns (“at Specialsitter, almost nothing is impossible”), and the caring team meetings .”

Regular employee surveys help ensure that people in our organization are heard, enabling improvements to be identified and implemented.
With our inhouse digital platform we digitalized the administration of assistant services both within and outside our organization, we have transformed the way support services for people with disabilities are delivered. This has streamlined processes and reduced administrative burdens for public authorities. The positive experience with our digital way of working is that our central administration consisted of four employees in 2019 and remained at the same size in 2021, even though the organization had tripled in scale. We attribute these efficiency gains to the implementation of our software. In 2020 we implemented our app for the employees to digitalize the daily processes of documentation and obtaining signatures from our employees for the commitments with the client. In addition to our organization, 15 extern companies are currently using our self-developed digital platform, benefiting approximately 300 employees. The platform has since been spun off into an independent company.
Since the founding of Specialsitter in 2015, we have so far supported 6.740 families in 528.138 commitments. In the last 52 weeks, we have provided 15.552 support hours. The working areas are as different as the people’s life situations. We provide our services in multiple settings, always according to the clients’ needs: in schools and kindergardens, in the workplspace, in the free time and in a domestic setting, at night, on a school trip or during doctors’ or agency visits. The main outcome of our work is the improved quality of life and self-determination of people with disabilities who we support. Even though disability or sickness are commonplace, the environmental barriers in different settings are still substantial: kindergartens, schools and companies are often overwhelmed due to a lack of personnel, skills and knowledge on the specifics and practicalities of disabilities. Our services fill the gaps, so that people with disabilities can participate in social life, education and employment on their own terms. We also provide relief to the families of our clients by taking care of their loved ones with special needs, so that the carers can take a breather, find time for themselves to recharge or simply go to work knowing their relatives are in good hands.

innovations.name: Ro(o)tation - sustainable integration of the long-term unemployed into the labour market
innovations.problem: RO(O)TATION addresses the growing challenge of long-term unemployment, particularly among neurodivergent individuals and people on the autism spectrum, who often face multiple barriers to labour market participation. The project responds to limited access to tailored support, low financial literacy, mental health challenges, employer stereotypes and insufficient cooperation between key stakeholders by developing innovative, community-based and person-centred employment solutions.
innovations.description: RO(O)TATION combines psychotherapy, financial education, career coaching and subsidised employment into one integrated support pathway for long-term unemployed people. By engaging employers, public institutions, academia and civil society through the Quadruple Helix model, it creates inclusive employment communities and promotes sustainable labour market integration for neurodivergent individuals.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: RO(O)TATION supports 120 long-term unemployed people (including 40 neurodivergent participants) through integrated employment pathways. Key outputs include 24 Diversity Celebration events, 24 Rooted Rooftop employment community meetings, financial education tools, mental wellbeing materials, reports on neuro-friendly workplaces and a sustainable local employment network connecting employers, public institutions and NGOs. The project enhances participants’ employability, mental wellbeing and financial skills, while fostering inclusive workplaces, stronger local partnerships and greater awareness of neurodiversity among employers and communities.
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Connecting Artists Europe
innovations.problem: The project addresses significant challenges experienced by artists with intellectual disabilities, including social isolation, unequal access to arts opportunities, limited professional progression pathways, and ongoing under-representation within the cultural sector. These challenges are evident both in Ireland and across Europe. Census 2022 found that 56% of people with an intellectual disability in Ireland experience difficulties participating in work, education, and other aspects of daily life, highlighting the barriers that continue to limit inclusion and participation. Similar patterns exist across Europe, where research spanning 28 countries has identified persistent physical, educational, financial, and attitudinal barriers that restrict disabled people's participation in cultural life.
innovations.description: The Connecting Artists Programme responds to these challenges through an innovative, artist-centred model that combines accessible creative development, one-to-one mentoring, peer support, networking, and public engagement opportunities. The programme supports artists with intellectual disabilities to develop their creative practice while building the professional skills required to participate more fully in the arts sector. Participants receive training in areas such as presenting and discussing their work, valuing and pricing artwork to professional standards, framing, and preparing for exhibitions and public showcasing opportunities such as artists talks and workshops. Each artist is paired with an mentor who provides tailored one-to-one support throughout the programme, helping them to identify goals, build confidence, and navigate preparing for exhibition. Through this combination of creative, professional, and personal development, the programme enables artists to expand their networks, increase their visibility within the cultural sector, and strengthen their capacity to sustain an artistic practice. As a practical and scalable model, the programme offers an effective approach to increasing cultural participation, representation, and professional opportunities for artists with intellectual disabilities, with potential for replication in other regions and European contexts.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Since its launch, the programme has supported 40 artists nationally, generated over €33,000 in artwork sales, delivered exhibitions and public events across Ireland, and created a thriving artist collective. For CAC, engagement reflects how visible our artists are within the broader arts landscape, and how actively they are participating in it. We assess this through: The exhibitions we co-create with participating artists. The development of their artistic portfolios For those pursuing a professional pathway, the sales they generate From 2022 - 2024 12 exhibitions and showcases have been delivered. 21 workshops, talks and demonstrations. During 2025: 13 exhibitions and showcases were delivered. 14 workshops, talks and demonstrations. These extended beyond Dublin, including Kildare, Mallow and our third annual exhibition in Belfast, in collaboration with the University of the Atypical. Expanding Artist Opportunities in 2025: 3 artists from the Collective held individual exhibitions. 5 artists delivered workshops as public events in The Royal Hibernian Academy of Arts,  The Royal College of Surgeons and The Project Arts Centre. This brings the total number of workshops delivered by Collective artists to 29. CAC also participated in Art Source, Irelands biggest art fair, with an estimated 15,000 attendees and exhibited at the Royal Hibernian Academy of Arts (RHA) with approximately 20k attendees. Supporting Professional Pathways: For artists who wish to pursue a professional career, CAC provides a supported sales channel. This provides a tangible pathway for artists to develop their practice as a source of income, where they choose to do so. To date, approximately 132 individual artworks have been sold. Generating over €33,000 in sales

innovations.name: Re:Match
innovations.problem: Ukrainian protection seekers often face relocation pathways that do not sufficiently consider their skills, preferences, family needs, or long-term employment prospects. At the same time, German municipalities need better tools to connect available places, local services, housing, and labour-market opportunities with people who are likely to integrate successfully. Re addresses this gap by moving beyond place-based allocation towards needs-based and individualized matching. It responds to the lack of coordinated systems that align individual agency, municipal capacities, and job-market integration, creating safer, more informed, and more sustainable relocation pathways.
innovations.description: Re introduces a human-centred, data-supported approach to refugee relocation that matches people not only to available places, but to municipalities where their skills, preferences, family circumstances, and employment prospects are most likely to lead to successful integration. The project combines algorithm-based matching with human support, bringing together individual profiles, municipal capacities, housing availability, local services, and labour-market opportunities. Through outreach, informed decision-making, municipal coordination, relocation support, and follow-up after arrival, Re creates more sustainable integration outcomes for both participants and host communities. By linking labour-market needs with individual aspirations and local capacities, the project offers a scalable model for needs-based and employment-oriented relocation that can be adapted across Europe.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence: Re enables Ukrainian protection seekers to make informed relocation decisions and access employment opportunities that better match their skills and professional experience. Participants benefit from increased agency, improved access to information, and stronger prospects for long-term economic and social integration. Municipalities benefit from better matching outcomes, improved retention, and stronger alignment between local labour-market needs and incoming residents. Employers gain access to qualified talent, helping address labour shortages in key sectors. The project demonstrates that relocation can be organised in a more needs-based, transparent, and effective way by combining individual preferences, municipal capacities, and labour-market opportunities. The resulting methodology provides a transferable model for labour-market-oriented relocation that can support integration and regional development across Europe. Re:MatchJob strengthens individual agency, improves employment and integration outcomes, supports municipalities in addressing labour shortages, and demonstrates a scalable model for needs-based, labour-market-oriented relocation. The project generates practical evidence for how data-supported matching can create better outcomes for protection seekers, host communities, and employers, while contributing to a future European standard for relocation and integration.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Community Centre
innovations.problem: The Chiojdu community lacked a dedicated, accessible space for social activities that could strengthen community cohesion and support local development. At the same time, there was a need to preserve local architectural identity, engage community members in decision-making processes, and create opportunities that would stimulate the local economy in a sustainable manner. The project responded to these challenges through a participatory process that identified community needs and priorities directly with local stakeholders.
innovations.description: The Chiojdu Community Center was conceived through a collaborative and participatory design process involving local community members, students and teachers from the “Ion Mincu” University of Architecture and Urbanism, local authorities, artisans, and businesses. The center combines contemporary architecture with elements inspired by traditional wooden architecture specific to the area, creating a contemporary yet locally rooted intervention. The project applies circular economy principles by prioritizing local resources, engaging local craftsmen and companies in the construction process, and supporting knowledge transfer between generations. Through three international ArhiPera Summer Schools, architecture students actively participated in the construction process, developing innovative applications of traditional, eco-friendly materials while working directly with community members. Educational workshops further introduced local pupils to sustainable architecture and environmentally responsible building practices.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: - Creation of a multifunctional community facility that addresses local social needs. - Enhanced collaboration between academia, public authorities, civil society, and the local community. - Strengthened community engagement through participatory planning, design, and implementation processes. - Preservation and contemporary reinterpretation of local architectural heritage. - Support for the local economy through the involvement of local contractors, artisans, and businesses. - Development of practical skills and knowledge among architecture students through hands-on construction experience. - Increased awareness among local children and young people regarding sustainable architecture and ecological materials.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: VEM mobility with dignity
innovations.problem: Millions of older adults, people with disabilities, and individuals with reduced mobility face significant barriers when accessing healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and community life. While transport systems may exist, many people cannot use them independently and lack reliable human support. As a result, they often miss appointments, reduce social interactions, become increasingly isolated, and experience a loss of autonomy, wellbeing, and quality of life. Families and caregivers frequently struggle to provide the necessary support, creating additional emotional and practical burdens. With Europe's ageing population and growing demand for inclusive services, the lack of accessible, human-centred mobility support remains a major barrier to social participation and independent living.
innovations.description:
VEM was inspired by existing independent living, mobility assistance and community accompaniment approaches that support people with disabilities and older adults. It also draws on sighted guiding practices used by organisations supporting people with visual impairments. However, VEM combines these principles into a professional, on-demand, door-to-door mobility support model tailored to the Portuguese context, with a strong focus on autonomy, dignity and social inclusion.
VEM introduces a new approach to inclusive mobility by focusing on the human support that many people need to move safely and independently within their communities. While existing solutions typically focus on transportation, VEM addresses the gap between transport availability and actual accessibility. Through a network of trained companions, the service provides door-to-door assistance before, during, and after each journey, enabling users to access healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and everyday tasks with confidence and dignity. The model combines social impact with economic sustainability by creating flexible employment opportunities for young people while supporting older adults and people with disabilities. It also strengthens connections between citizens, communities, healthcare providers, and social organisations. By transforming mobility from a transport challenge into a human-centred inclusion solution, VEM helps people remain active, independent, and connected to society.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: VEM enables older adults and people with disabilities to access healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and community life with greater independence and confidence. Key benefits include reduced social isolation, improved wellbeing, increased autonomy, better access to essential services, and reduced burden on families and caregivers. The model also creates meaningful employment opportunities for young people while promoting disability awareness and social inclusion. Since launching, VEM has already supported dozens of beneficiaries through more than 300 assisted mobility missions, demonstrating both social impact and operational viability. The model has strong potential for replication in other regions facing challenges related to ageing, disability, and social exclusion.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.raw_text:
VEM mobility with dignity
Millions of older adults, people with disabilities, and individuals with reduced mobility face significant barriers when accessing healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and community life. While transport systems may exist, many people cannot use them independently and lack reliable human support. As a result, they often miss appointments, reduce social interactions, become increasingly isolated, and experience a loss of autonomy, wellbeing, and quality of life. Families and caregivers frequently struggle to provide the necessary support, creating additional emotional and practical burdens. With Europe's ageing population and growing demand for inclusive services, the lack of accessible, human-centred mobility support remains a major barrier to social participation and independent living.
VEM was inspired by existing independent living, mobility assistance and community accompaniment approaches that support people with disabilities and older adults. It also draws on sighted guiding practices used by organisations supporting people with visual impairments. However, VEM combines these principles into a professional, on-demand, door-to-door mobility support model tailored to the Portuguese context, with a strong focus on autonomy, dignity and social inclusion.
VEM introduces a new approach to inclusive mobility by focusing on the human support that many people need to move safely and independently within their communities. While existing solutions typically focus on transportation, VEM addresses the gap between transport availability and actual accessibility. Through a network of trained companions, the service provides door-to-door assistance before, during, and after each journey, enabling users to access healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and everyday tasks with confidence and dignity. The model combines social impact with economic sustainability by creating flexible employment opportunities for young people while supporting older adults and people with disabilities. It also strengthens connections between citizens, communities, healthcare providers, and social organisations. By transforming mobility from a transport challenge into a human-centred inclusion solution, VEM helps people remain active, independent, and connected to society.
VEM enables older adults and people with disabilities to access healthcare, public services, cultural activities, and community life with greater independence and confidence. Key benefits include reduced social isolation, improved wellbeing, increased autonomy, better access to essential services, and reduced burden on families and caregivers. The model also creates meaningful employment opportunities for young people while promoting disability awareness and social inclusion. Since launching, VEM has already supported dozens of beneficiaries through more than 300 assisted mobility missions, demonstrating both social impact and operational viability. The model has strong potential for replication in other regions facing challenges related to ageing, disability, and social exclusion.

innovations.description:
The CICF in Maia joins an existing national ecosystem. CDI Portugal's Digital Citizenship Centre in Valongo, for instance, is already in its 8th edition (2024/25), having been inaugurated in 2018, demonstrating that this model can achieve long-term continuity and institutionalisation. This approach, rooted in CDI Portugal's internationally recognised methodology, builds not only technical skills but also resilience, creativity and collaboration. innovations.name: IMMERSED
innovations.problem: Together, as the IMMERSED consortium, these partners identified a gap: although many organizations in host countries provide valuable support, initiatives often operate in isolation. This means that Ukrainian refugees have fragmented access to services, particularly in important areas such as employment, financial literacy, and mental health. Working together to provide sustainable, long-term impact for refugees is the cornerstone of the project.
innovations.description: The IMMERSED project is dedicated to empowering Ukrainian refugees in Poland, Slovakia, and Romania by fostering lasting employment, financial independence, and meaningful community participation. By combining innovative training, psychological support, and communitybased initiatives, the project addresses both the professional and personal needs of refugees. IMMERSED brings together partners from public, private, academic, and civil society sectors in a dynamic Quadruple Helix partnership to create a comprehensive support model that can be adapted across different local contexts.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The IMMERSED project successfully identified and consolidated intervention solutions for the inclusion of Ukrainian refugees. Validated by experts and participants, these models provide a foundation for future social and professional integration initiatives. Key Intervention Models • Transnational Piloting & Expertise Transfer: Utilizing the "Quadruple Helix" model, teams in Romania, Poland, and Slovakia exchanged knowledge to create a regional integration support ecosystem tailored to local realities. • "Train the Trainers" (ToT): Workshops in Palermo and specialized ESC&FR sessions prepared 17 coaches and multidisciplinary teams. They utilized creative tools like art therapy and storytelling to manage cultural sensitivities and trauma. • Integrated Educational Resources: The project produced a Trainers' Manual, Mental Well-Being Guides for beneficiaries, and an inclusive recruitment Booklet for Employers, bridging the gap between emotional balance and professional stability. • Active Community Involvement: By involving 133 Ukrainian refugees and hiring Ukrainian specialists as facilitators, the project ensured high trust and cultural relevance. • Social Cohesion & Well-being: The "Discussion & Barter Clubs" mobilized 353 participants from refugee and host country to reduce isolation & foster social cohesion. 184 individuals participated in programs integrating psychosocial resilience into the employment process. • Employment Sustainability (ES) & Financial Resilience (FR): Training for 133 participants emphasized that economic autonomy requires both labor market navigation skills and effective money management. • Initiative Mapping & Expertise Transfer: Networking events connected 89 participants to local resources, while coaching methodologies were transferred to 140 frontline professionals to ensure long-term impact. Through dissemination events involving 848 participants, the project’s methodology has been integrated into local university, business, and public sectors, transforming deliverables into living resources for regional policy improvement.

innovations.name: Web4Kids
innovations.lead: PROBRANCA- Association for the Sociocultural Development of Branca
innovations.problem: WEB4Kids, hereinafter referred to as WK, aims to address the problem of digital illiteracy and digital mental health—risks and internet addiction—by promoting the acquisition of digital skills and reducing and minimizing adherence to risky online behaviors. The recognition of this social problem, its current relevance, and the social and individual impact it introduces is visible in global, European, and national regulations. Aligned with United Nations General Comment No. 25, which, in February 2021, updated the Convention on the Rights of the Child (which covers children under 18), taking into account the new digital context. We follow the European Commission's guidelines for a Better Internet for Children, approved in May 2022 and based on three pillars: safe digital experiences; digital empowerment; and active participation. In Portugal, we emphasize the purposes of the National Strategy for Children's Rights (2021-2024) in promoting children's well-being, their access to information and participation, the prevention and combating of violence, as well as support for families. We align ourselves with the purposes of the INCoDe 2030 Program, which intervenes with the population, aiming in particular at deconstructing stereotypes in the technological area and promoting equal opportunities. We base our intervention on Law No. 27/2021 of May 17 - which promulgates the Portuguese Charter of Human Rights in the Digital Age, enshrining: Article 2 - Rights in the digital environment - the recognition of the global process of transforming the internet into an instrument for achieving freedom, equality and social justice and into a space for the promotion, protection and free exercise of human rights, with a view to inclusion in the digital environment; Article 3 - Rights of access to the Digital environment. (...) point b) The definition and execution of programs to promote gender equality and digital skills in different age groups; (...) point g) The implementation of programs that guarantee access to technological and digital tools and resources for the population, to enhance digital skills and access to electronic platforms, particularly for the most vulnerable citizens; Article 11 - Right to the development of digital skills. Point 1 - Everyone has the right to education for the acquisition and development of digital skills. Item 2 - The state promotes and implements programs that encourage and facilitate access, by the various age groups of the population, to digital and technological means and tools, in order to ensure, in particular, education through the internet and the increasing use of digital public services. Article 15 - Right to Cybersecurity - Item 1 - Everyone has the right to security in cyberspace, and it is the State's responsibility to define public policies that guarantee the protection of citizens and information networks and systems, and that create mechanisms that increase security in the use of the internet, especially by children and young people. Article 20 - Rights of children. Point 1 - Children have the right to special protection and the necessary care for their well-being and safety in cyberspace. Point 2 - Children can freely express their opinions and have the freedom to receive and transmit information or ideas, depending on their age and maturity. The goal of the WK (Cybersecurity Week) is to address this particularly acute problem among children and adolescents with underlying vulnerabilities in the municipality of Albergaria-a-Velha. Children and young people with identified vulnerabilities see the negative consequences of this social problem amplified because they find themselves in a situation of inequality and without access to a targeted specialized response, which increases the social impact of the problem. Capacity building and empowerment contribute to guaranteeing the rights provided for by law and to reducing the social, cultural, and health impact of the social problem.
innovations.description: The WEB4Kids initiative is the result of a journey that began several years ago by PROBRANCA. In 2020, with the awarding of the BPI Infância Prize, SafeWeb was developed - a pilot project for digital literacy and capacity building aimed at students and families of the Branca School Group. During the COVID-19 Pandemic, SafeWeb adapted the training and capacity building methods to the public health constraints, integrating the measures for prophylaxis and containment of the virus. The target audience was approximately 100 students from the 1st to the 3rd Cycles of Elementary Education, in a free attendance modality to training workshops, among other training initiatives for educational agents and the general community. The results in terms of students' digital skills were an indicator of success, as at the end of the intervention the students had a higher level of literacy than at the beginning. At the entity and project team level, there was a consolidation and exponential increase in know-how, as well as an expansion of its institutional network of contacts in the area of ​​digital literacy and training. The SafeWeb project is recognized as a benchmark pilot project, and the team was invited to participate in the 89th edition of the Antena 1 program, Ouvido Crítico, and was featured in the DigiMedia - UA newsletter on May 21, 2021, receiving numerous words of recognition for the merit and distinction of the initiative. The pilot project also gave rise to two presentations at symposia: one at the VIII National Seminar Investigating Teaching Practices (SNIPE) and another at the III International and VI National Symposium on Digital Technologies in Education (Brazil); and also to the publication of an article in the e-Curriculum journal. The outcome was extremely positive, and the need to implement the intervention in other territories (clusters) was the driving force to continue. In 2022, PROBRANCA had its SafeWeb 2.0 project approved – Partnerships for Impact – under the Operational Programme for Social Inclusion and Employment – ​​POISE – Operation No. 0093. sections.question: Problem
sections.answer: WEB4Kids, hereinafter referred to as WK, aims to address the problem of digital illiteracy and digital mental health—risks and internet addiction—by promoting the acquisition of digital skills and reducing and minimizing adherence to risky online behaviors. The recognition of this social problem, its current relevance, and the social and individual impact it introduces is visible in global, European, and national regulations. Aligned with United Nations General Comment No. 25, which, in February 2021, updated the Convention on the Rights of the Child (which covers children under 18), taking into account the new digital context. We follow the European Commission's guidelines for a Better Internet for Children, approved in May 2022 and based on three pillars: safe digital experiences; digital empowerment; and active participation. In Portugal, we emphasize the purposes of the National Strategy for Children's Rights (2021-2024) in promoting children's well-being, their access to information and participation, the prevention and combating of violence, as well as support for families. We align ourselves with the purposes of the INCoDe 2030 Program, which intervenes with the population, aiming in particular at deconstructing stereotypes in the technological area and promoting equal opportunities. We base our intervention on Law No. 27/2021 of May 17 - which promulgates the Portuguese Charter of Human Rights in the Digital Age, enshrining: Article 2 - Rights in the digital environment - the recognition of the global process of transforming the internet into an instrument for achieving freedom, equality and social justice and into a space for the promotion, protection and free exercise of human rights, with a view to inclusion in the digital environment; Article 3 - Rights of access to the Digital environment. (...) point b) The definition and execution of programs to promote gender equality and digital skills in different age groups; (...) point g) The implementation of programs that guarantee access to technological and digital tools and resources for the population, to enhance digital skills and access to electronic platforms, particularly for the most vulnerable citizens; Article 11 - Right to the development of digital skills. Point 1 - Everyone has the right to education for the acquisition and development of digital skills. Item 2 - The state promotes and implements programs that encourage and facilitate access, by the various age groups of the population, to digital and technological means and tools, in order to ensure, in particular, education through the internet and the increasing use of digital public services. Article 15 - Right to Cybersecurity - Item 1 - Everyone has the right to security in cyberspace, and it is the State's responsibility to define public policies that guarantee the protection of citizens and information networks and systems, and that create mechanisms that increase security in the use of the internet, especially by children and young people. Article 20 - Rights of children. Point 1 - Children have the right to special protection and the necessary care for their well-being and safety in cyberspace. Point 2 - Children can freely express their opinions and have the freedom to receive and transmit information or ideas, depending on their age and maturity. The goal of the WK (Cybersecurity Week) is to address this particularly acute problem among children and adolescents with underlying vulnerabilities in the municipality of Albergaria-a-Velha. Children and young people with identified vulnerabilities see the negative consequences of this social problem amplified because they find themselves in a situation of inequality and without access to a targeted specialized response, which increases the social impact of the problem. Capacity building and empowerment contribute to guaranteeing the rights provided for by law and to reducing the social, cultural, and health impact of the social problem.

innovations.name: Job Navi
innovations.problem:
Long term unemployed persons need more continous support in order to access the labor market - support which is not provided due to the lack of ressources.
The number of long-term unemployed in Austria is currently rising significantly, particularly among those who have already gone through a wide range of measures offered by the Public Employment Service but have still not been successfully integrated into the labour market. In our project, long-term unemployment is not an individual problem, but a multifactorial one. We do not see the problem as lying with the long-term unemployed, but rather in the circumstances that prevent them from overcoming long-term unemployment. With a view to empowerment, the aim is to support the long-term unemployed in such a way that they, who often feel ‘labelled’, actually become jobseekers.
innovations.description:
Job Navi provides continous case management in order to prevent drop outs when long term unemployed persons transits from alabour market related service to a job in the labour market, for instance. Job Navi starts with an comprehensive assessment checking not only labor market related dimensions of the target group.
The case management service for long-term unemployed persons, operating at the interface between the AMS (Public Employment Service), labour market policy measures and the labour market, is a new initiative in the region.  The following elements are new to the project concept:
• The scaling of the approach “Unterstützte Beschäftigung” (supported employment) into the region
• Continuous case management for members of the target group, including whilst they are participating in a labour market policy measure, as well as follow-up support to ensure labour market integration
• Job search designed to avoid further experiences of failure, such that, through assessments by case management, at least a work trial is likely
• The provision of comprehensive support options for companies to enable sustainable integration into the workplace
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Since Job Navi started just at the beginning of 2026 it is to early to state key results yet. After some more time it will become clear if the innovative approach leads to better results in the labour market related system of stake holders.
The main objective is to pilot a new approach in Tyrol (Austria) that addresses the highly diverse circumstances and needs of people who are extremely distant from the labour market and face a wide range of barriers to employment.
At an individual level, the benefit of the project lies in having designed, implemented and further developed an approach that addresses the diverse circumstances and needs of the target group and identifies feasible pathways to labour market integration through: continuous case management with intensive individual assessment to identify the most suitable measure for each individual, enabling the target group to secure jobs that are appropriate to their capabilities. For the individuals in the target group, the benefit lies in avoiding frustration caused by unsuitable job offers, whilst at the same time strengthening their self-efficacy and enabling them to participate in working life.
The benefit at a societal level lies in having, ideally, developed an approach to tackle rising unemployment among the long-term unemployed, to help reduce social inequality within the target group.

innovations.name: Small Scale Entrepreneurial Support for Community Development
innovations.problem: For more than 20 years Land Source of Income Foundation/LSIF/ strives to support income generation initiatives of financially disadvantaged families mainly in the rural areas of Bulgaria by developing its Land Program and applying the Integrated Model for Entrepreneurship Support. In that way our team contributes to a more inclusive market economy in Bulgaria. We share the understanding of the Rockefeller Foundation that Inclusive Economies have 5 inter-related characteristics: participation, equity, growth, sustainability, and stability. We also think that communities should play crucial role in this process. The LSIF team believes that inclusive market economy opens real opportunities for more broadly shared prosperity especially for those facing the greatest barriers to advancing their well-being.
innovations.description: Farm4us.eu platform allows us to offer distant interactive specialized consultancy needed. It reduces costs and increase the number of people being served. All agricultural producers interested have access to it for specialized information (technological maps, business plans, information for RDP etc.).  The platform provides agrometeorological information from the specially installed station in Perushtiza. This information is of help not just to our beneficiaries, but also to many other agricultural produces in the area. Installed in the secondary Vocational school it also serves the training process and allows students to be acquainted with the benefits of digitalization. ( http://farm4us.eu/ )
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: By the end of 2025, the project supports 204 families in rural areas in Plovdiv region. It provides income to 667 people, out of which 374 are members of the supported families and 297 part-time workers (non family members). They cultivate 2247 dca land in total. For the period 2024-2025 the project has supported 35 business initiatives with the total amount of BGN 33 492. We have also helped the families in the program to get accesses to BGN 352 917 from EU direct payments schemes. During our work on the Land Source of Income Program, we began asking ourselves to what extent the program has changed the lives of the families we support. Visually, their standard of living has improved, but it is difficult to determine how much of this improvement is due to the overall economic development in Bulgaria and how much can be attributed to our intervention. We found that impact evaluation is a difficult and challenging task. The Theory of Change framework is often recommended as an approach to evaluating impact. However, in practice, its application is frequently limited to comparing planned and achieved levels of predefined indicators. While such comparisons can demonstrate progress, they do not necessarily show whether the observed changes were caused by the program itself or by external factors. In 2023 we publish an article, where attempt was made to evaluated the impact of Land program. Before publishing we discussed the issue with colleagues from Economics department of Agricultural University-Plovdiv; Entrepreneurialship centre at the Technical University -Sofia Branch Plovdiv; Institute of Agricultural Economics-Sofia. innovations.name: Inno4Ufo - Innovative tools to support business succession in rural areas
innovations.problem: The issue of business succession, particularly in rural areas, threatens economic and social structures.
innovations.description: Our solution: co-creative processes and solidarity-based, participatory business models that involve and empower employees. We viewed the transition to business succession as an opportunity for a paradigm shift. We designed a participatory process to transform traditional businesses into socially responsible, democratically organized enterprises. For two years, we provided co-creative and people-centered support to two businesses undergoing succession planning and worked with them to develop practical solutions for successful business succession.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
A follow-up project, GENOTRAFO, was approved based on the Inno4Ufo approach, focusing specifically on the cooperative model in business succession. This approach is being further developed in the project both scientifically and practically in the rural area of Brandenburg.
In this way, we created future-proof structures that promote economic and social stability and strengthen democratic participation. In practice: - A bakery and an auto repair shop developed employee-centered succession models; 14 other businesses applied for succession support from Inno4Ufo; chambers of commerce, stakeholders, and companies are seeking out these approaches - Over 700 people were informed for the first time about collaborative, co-creative succession planning - Networking for stakeholders in East Brandenburg; collaborative/co-creative cooperation with approximately 10+ practitioners from rural and urban regions in the fields of law, taxation, and organizational development; exchange and knowledge transfer with the East Brandenburg Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK), the Frankfurt/Oder Chamber of Crafts (HWK), and the District Craftsmen’s Association - Magazin: "Succession. Co-creatively guided—cooperatively lived" -> https://nachfolgemagazin.carrd.co/ In academia: - Involvement of students in research; project topics are used in master’s theses - Presentation of project results at conferences - Welland, J., Walk, H., Krebber, S. (2026). Mitarbeitendengenossenschaften: ein Zukunftsmodell für die Unternehmensnachfolge!. In: Blome-Drees, J., Degens, P., Göler von Ravensburg, N., Picker, C., Schmale, I., Schulz-Nieswandt, F. (eds) Handbuch Genossenschaftswesen. Springer VS, Wiesbaden. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-18639-5_109-1

innovations.name: St. Leo the Great Mental Health Center: Restoring Safety, Trust and Dignity for People Affected by War-Related Trauma
innovations.problem:
People who have survived captivity, torture and severe war-related trauma often face complex and long-term consequences. These may include post-traumatic stress, anxiety, depression, cognitive difficulties, chronic pain, loss of trust, reduced sense of safety, difficulties in rebuilding relationships and challenges in returning to everyday life.
Standard medical or psychological services are often not sufficient for this target group. Many former prisoners of war return with untreated injuries, neurological symptoms and other health complications, while also carrying deep psychological trauma. Certain procedures, closed spaces, physical contact, unfamiliar equipment or pressure to talk about traumatic experiences too early can trigger traumatic memories and undermine recovery.
Ukraine therefore needs specialised services that combine medical stabilisation, psychiatric assessment, psychotherapy, rehabilitation, family support and trauma-informed practice. The challenge is not only to treat symptoms, but to restore safety, dignity, trust, emotional stability, cognitive functioning and the possibility of social reintegration.
innovations.description:
The St. Leo the Great Mental Health Center introduces a specialised multidisciplinary and trauma-informed model of care for people released from captivity and affected by severe war-related trauma. The model combines inpatient and outpatient mental health care with medical, neurological, psychotherapeutic, rehabilitative, creative and family support.
The patient pathway is structured and gradual. Upon admission to the First Lviv Territorial Medical Union, former prisoners of war first undergo comprehensive medical assessment and stabilisation. Because many return from captivity with untreated injuries, chronic pain, neurological symptoms or other health complications, they may first receive treatment in therapeutic, neurological or other relevant departments. A multidisciplinary diagnostic workup may include consultations with ophthalmologists, otolaryngologists, urologists, traumatologists and other specialists, as well as laboratory and imaging examinations.
At the same time, all patients undergo psychiatric assessment and mental health screening using standardised tools such as PCL, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 to identify symptoms of PTSD, depression, anxiety and other trauma-related conditions. After physical stabilisation, patients are transferred to the Center, where the average inpatient stay lasts four to six weeks, depending on individual needs. Some patients may need two to three admissions before achieving long-term stabilisation and recovery.
Each patient receives an individualised treatment plan and a personalised therapy schedule developed by a multidisciplinary team. The Center employs psychiatrists, neuropsychologists, EMDR therapists, prolonged exposure therapists, art therapists, body-oriented therapists and sleep specialists. Treatment combines psychiatric care, medication management, individual psychotherapy, group interventions, neurocognitive rehabilitation and creative therapies.
Because cognitive difficulties are common after captivity, treatment often begins with intensive neuropsychological support focused on attention, concentration and memory. Patients may also participate in art therapy, clay therapy and other creative activities that support emotional regulation and recovery. As patients become more stable, treatment can progress to evidence-based trauma processing approaches, including Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing and Prolonged Exposure Therapy.
Family involvement is an important part of the model. Family members receive psychoeducation and psychological support. The weekly “Women’s Circle” support group within the UNBROKEN ecosystem provides additional support for wives and mothers of defenders. After discharge, many patients continue outpatient follow-up and may return for additional treatment episodes if needed.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Since opening in June 2025, the St. Leo the Great Mental Health Center has provided specialised care to 85 patients who survived captivity, torture and severe war-related trauma: 8 patients in 2025 and 77 patients during the first half of 2026. The Center currently combines inpatient and outpatient services and is expected to reach an annual capacity of up to 1,000 patients.
The Center is already demonstrating tangible recovery outcomes. Former patients have successfully re-engaged in economic activity, education, creative initiatives and community life. One former patient established his own greenhouse business and is now participating in the development of a therapeutic gardening initiative at the Center. Another former patient is studying psychology and plans to support future patients through social work and creative rehabilitation activities. Several former patients have become involved in theatre and arts initiatives within the UNBROKEN ecosystem, helping them regain confidence, self-expression and social connections. Three former prisoners of war who underwent treatment together are developing plans to establish a small business and are participating in entrepreneurship training programmes.
Patients and families have also reported improved relationships, restoration of trust, greater emotional stability and renewed confidence in planning their future lives together.
The main benefits are specialised trauma-informed support for people released from captivity and affected by torture or severe war-related trauma; improved psychological stability, dignity and sense of safety; better cognitive functioning, emotional regulation and social reintegration; support for families to understand and respond to trauma; and stronger capacity of the Ukrainian healthcare system to address the long-term psychological consequences of war.

innovations.name: My Yearbook (on inclusion)
innovations.problem: This tool helps individuals think about what they want. It helps them put their thoughts into words or pictures, come up with ideas, and maybe even try something that hadn’t even crossed their mind before. Friends’ ideas and peer support also help them feel included and get involved in activities they enjoy. Professionals and family members have provided feedback that it brings to light wishes and needs that previously hadn’t been expressed or made visible as part of daily life. My Yearbook is, in fact, a tool for everyone to strengthen inclusion.
innovations.description: The approach of My Yearbook is quite simple. It offers many illustrated examples of activities for different seasons. It enables personalized life planning. It serves also a tool to support professionals and family members as they help others to build a fulfilling life for themselves. The monthly layout and very simple question format bring together a life-sized picture of the past year. It helps you plan well into the future or look back on what you did last year. In other words, it helps you manage your life and daily routine and supports your decision-making. Perhaps the most important feedback has been that “we didn’t know he/she/they wanted to...” Based on the feedback we’ve received, we’ve learned that it’s also used to plan group activities. It’s a great task also for summer workers that can be used together with the client. And in creating the service implementation plan.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: My Yearbook strengthens an individual’s inclusion by activating a support network around and help to make it happen.

It helps them put their thoughts into words or pictures, come up with ideas, and maybe even try something that hadn’t even crossed their mind before. Friends’ ideas and peer support also help them feel included and get involved in activities they enjoy. Professionals and family members have provided feedback that it brings to light wishes and needs that previously hadn’t been expressed or made visible as part of daily life. My Yearbook is, in fact, a tool for everyone to strengthen inclusion.
The approach of My Yearbook is quite simple. It offers many illustrated examples of activities for different seasons. It enables personalized life planning. It serves also a tool to support professionals and family members as they help others to build a fulfilling life for themselves. The monthly layout and very simple question format bring together a life-sized picture of the past year. It helps you plan well into the future or look back on what you did last year. In other words, it helps you manage your life and daily routine and supports your decision-making. Perhaps the most important feedback has been that “we didn’t know he/she/they wanted to...” Based on the feedback we’ve received, we’ve learned that it’s also used to plan group activities. It’s a great task also for summer workers that can be used together with the client. And in creating the service implementation plan.
My Yearbook strengthens an individual’s inclusion by activating a support network around and help to make it happen.

innovations.name: Peer support
innovations.lead: Foundation for the Development of the Education System, Ministry of National Education, Fundacja „Instytut Edukacji Pozytywnej”
innovations.problem: The project responds to the growing mental health challenges faced by young people and to the difficulties schools experience in providing long-term and accessible support. Many students in emotional distress do not immediately turn to adults or professional services; they often prefer to talk to their peers first. At the same time, schools need practical tools for prevention and early intervention, especially before problems become more serious.
innovations.description:
The innovative solution is a structured peer support method implemented in secondary schools. It prepares selected student volunteers, called schoolworkers, to notice signs of emotional distress, start supportive conversations, provide basic emotional support and guide peers towards appropriate help. They do not replace psychologists or teachers and do not provide psychological interventions. Their role is to be a trusted first point of contact and a bridge between students and trained adults in school. The entire school program is supervised by school coordinators, who are also responsible for recruiting school workers and ensuring safety.
The model includes training for school coordinators, mainly school psychologists and pedagogues, as well as mentoring, supervision, handbooks, toolkits and digital learning support. A key innovative element is that the project uses the natural strength of peer relationships in a safe and organised way. It combines youth participation, prevention, early intervention, school culture change and cooperation with local psychological and pedagogical support institutions. The peer support method is a new way of conducting mental health prevention in Poland.

innovations.beneficiaries: Foundation for the Development of the Education System, Ministry of National Education, Fundacja „Instytut Edukacji Pozytywnej”
innovations.evidence:

The expected benefits include better school climate, stronger trust between students and adults, reduced stigma around mental health, earlier identification of students in difficulty, and more open communication about emotional and social needs. The project also supports the development of empathy, communication skills, responsibility and a sense of belonging among students.
Early achievements already observed include stronger appreciation of students’ interpersonal talents, more lively discussions about student needs, meaningful bonds across age and class groups, and the identification of cases requiring adult intervention.

innovations.name: “Family wins” in the Praga-Południe District of Warsaw
innovations.lead: The Capital City of Warsaw, South Praga Social Welfare Centre of the Capital City of Warsaw, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw
innovations.problem: Project’s goal is to scale up in the Praga-Południe District of Warsaw the cohesive and comprehensive Model of Counteracting Transgenerational Transmission of Poverty called “Family wins”. The model supports an entire family by its closest neightbourhood. The project’s premise was for a set family, and local entities, to be aided by a cooperating team of specialists.
innovations.description:
The beneficiaries of the project are cared for by a team of specialists representing various fields such as for example social care, psychology, education or functioning in the local environment. These specialists accompany families in the process of change, set goals that match the family's capabilities, strengthen agency and the sense of control over their own life,  shift the perspective from survival to quality of life and everyday well-being as well as open space for joy, relationships, rest, and positive experiences.
An individualized support program is developed for each family. This program is implemented for several months during which family members participated in various activities and received various assistance. Participants can use the following forms of suport:
1. Support of a family assistant
2. Help of other supporting families (aid in organizing free time activities for children, tutoring, receiving advice regarding raising children)
3. Support of a health visitor
4. Childcare services
5. Special care services (support for children provided by a physiotherapist, speech therapist, psychotherapist and other specialists)
6. Support within the Talent Development Academy – accordingly with a Child’s Individual Development Plan – which encompassed: help from child and teenage development mentors and psychologists; extracurricular classes matching children’s talents and interests; languages, computer or entrepreneurship courses; tutoring; social competence classes.
7. Family Education (educational support on the topic of raising children and financial literacy)
8. Support of Mutual Neighbourhood Aid (spending time and establishing relationships within the local community, organising events in the neighbourhood)
9. „Get Back The Child” programme (individual meetings and classes aided at developing parental skills)
The implementation of the support program is based on cooperation between local government authorities and local non-governmental organizations.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: The Capital City of Warsaw, South Praga Social Welfare Centre of the Capital City of Warsaw, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw
innovations.evidence:
Thanks to the obove desribed approach, the family (15 families, around 60 people participate in the project) will be equipped with tools that will, first of all, contribute to a change in awareness. Then, the social and educational competences of families will be strengthened. And the involvement in the activities of the local community means that the family is not alone in the process of change, the immediate surroundigs supports it in striving to better fulfill its functions and motivates it to work that will lead to the improvement of its life situation.
Hard outcomes:
- restoration of full parental rights
- maintaining constant contact with a child who is staying in an orphanage or foster family or  keeping children in families (no referral to foster care)
- systematic participation in psychological therapy and addiction therapy
- making changes in your immediate surroundings (taking care of the apartment)
- increasing neighborly contacts
- putting your legal situation in order or repayment of all or part of the debt
- cessation of the use of physical violence and - making people aware of the use of psychological violence
- increasing the ability to ask for help and benefit from it (to people or institutions).
authors: The Capital City of Warsaw, South Praga Social Welfare Centre of the Capital City of Warsaw, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw
