innovations.name: Centro de Inovação Carlos Fiolhais
innovations.problem: Across Europe, the digital divide remains one of the most pressing social challenges of our time. In 2025, only 60% of EU citizens aged 16–74 had at least basic digital skills, with stark disparities linked to education level — ranging from 82% among those with high formal education to just 38% among those with low or no formal education. In Portugal, basic digital skills remain unevenly distributed across society, and according to the 2023 International Computer and Information Literacy Study, 37% of Portuguese eighth-graders have a low level of digital skills. But the problem goes deeper than access or basic literacy. Young people are heavy consumers of technology yet rarely learn to use it as a tool for creation, problem-solving, or civic participation. Formal education, constrained by curriculum rigidity and resource gaps, often fails to bridge this gap — particularly for young people from less privileged backgrounds. CDI Portugal was founded precisely to address this reality: to transform communities and redefine life trajectories for people from socioeconomically disadvantaged contexts, using technology and its full potential. The municipality of Maia — a mid-sized urban area in northern Portugal — identified the same challenge locally: a disconnect between the digital future young people are entering and the creative, critical and collaborative skills they need to navigate it with confidence and agency. The CICF was created to address this gap, promoting technology as an essential tool for inclusion, innovation and social transformation — not as a luxury for the few, but as a right and a resource for all young people, regardless of their background.
innovations.description: The CICF's innovation lies not in any single technology or tool, but in a comprehensive model that reimagines how, where and for whom learning happens. A "choose your own journey" learning architecture. Rather than following a fixed curriculum, participants choose from seven thematic universes — Code, Bot, Play, Make, Green, Voice and Link — covering areas from AI and robotics to media literacy, digital fabrication and community engagement. Within each universe, projects vary in duration and depth, from shorter tasters to three-month commitments, allowing each young person to set their own pace. This learner-driven model stands in sharp contrast to the rigid, standardised format of traditional education. Learning by doing — and by failing. The CICF actively fosters critical thinking, experimentation and teamwork in an environment where curiosity and discovery are valued. The pedagogy is built on a cycle of experimenting, failing, reflecting and trying again — normalising failure as a driver of growth rather than a source of shame. This approach, rooted in CDI Portugal's internationally recognised methodology, builds not only technical skills but also resilience, creativity and collaboration. The Digger journey and Digital Passport. Each participant becomes a "Digger" — someone who digs deep, discovers, builds and transforms with technology. Everything they learn is recorded in their Digital Passport, tracking the projects completed, the skills developed, and the impact created. This portable record gives young people ownership of their learning journey and makes their growth visible and legible beyond the classroom. Real projects with real community impact. The CICF goes beyond simulation exercises. Projects like 3D for a Cause see young people design and print 3D objects for local social institutions; City Data has participants collect and analyse real urban data to inform decisions about their municipality; and the Repair Café brings the community together to fix electronic devices, combining digital skills with sustainability and circular economy values. A whole ecosystem approach. The CICF invites participants to learn in practice, use technology meaningfully, develop critical and creative thinking, and collaborate with leading companies and specialists. Teachers receive dedicated training through the CAE (Centre for School Support), and community mentors — professionals who volunteer their expertise — provide role models and bridges to the world of work. Programmes are also available for young people who are NEET (not in education, employment or training), ensuring the most vulnerable are not left behind. Municipal integration and scalability. Integrated in CDI Portugal's national network of Digital Citizenship Centers, the CICF bets on a smart and human cities model, where technology is placed at the service of the community. The co-promotion model — pairing local government with a civil society organization — offers a blueprint that other municipalities can replicate, making the CICF not just a local solution but a potential national and European reference.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The CICF in Maia joins an existing national ecosystem. CDI Portugal's Digital Citizenship Centre in Valongo, for instance, is already in its 8th edition (2024/25), having been inaugurated in 2018, demonstrating that this model can achieve long-term continuity and institutionalisation. The CICF represents an evolution of this approach — more structured, thematically richer and co-branded — that can serve as the new benchmark for future centres.
Reach: 1,500+ student and teacher participations across all 7 school clusters in Maia; 515+ hours and 45+ activities delivered in Year 1, across 7 thematic universes (Code, Bot, Play, Make, Green, Voice, Link). Digital competences (DigComp 3.0): Measurable gains in Problem Identification & Solving, Communication & Collaboration, and Safety, Wellbeing & Responsible Use among participating youth (ages 12–18). Teacher capacity: Educators trained in emerging, learner-centred methodologies (Paulo Freire approach; pedagogical autonomy). Youth-led innovation: Tech solutions built by student teams addressing real community problems. Ecosystem: Active public–private model (Maia Municipality + CDI Portugal, NORTE 2030) with industry partners (Synopsys, Lenovo, Google, Kyndryl, Stempura, Tecmaia, FabLabs Portugal); a documented, replicable lab model. Youth: Stronger digital literacy and critical thinking that narrow the digital divide and open STEM and employability pathways; greater agency, belonging, and digital wellbeing. Teachers & schools: Access to innovative, hands-on methodologies and continuous professional development, free of formal-curriculum bureaucracy. Community & municipality: Improved social inclusion and cohesion; reinforced local talent and Maia's position as an innovation territory. Ecosystem & EU level: A scalable, transferable social-innovation model with multi-stakeholder governance (local authority + NGO + industry), aligned with national digital strategy and EU inclusion goals. Guiding principle: Technology as the means, people as the end — opportunity for all, placing equity at the centre.

innovations.name: Digital works for youth
innovations.lead: Bucovina Institute for Social Partnership Association
innovations.problem: Vulnerable young people, especially NEETs, often remain outside education, training and employment because existing support mechanisms do not fully respond to their complex and individual needs. Many face a combination of barriers such as low confidence, limited professional orientation, weak employability and digital skills, lack of access to relevant networks, social exclusion, long-term unemployment, low qualifications, disability or other forms of vulnerability. A key challenge is that standard labour market services are often too general, institutional or fragmented. They may provide information, but not enough personalised guidance, motivation, practical preparation or direct connection with employers. As a result, many young people do not feel seen, supported or ready to take the next step toward training or work. At the same time, purely digital solutions can reach many young people, but they risk excluding those who need personal encouragement and trust-based support. On the other hand, only face-to-face support can be resource-intensive and difficult to scale. DigiW addresses this gap by combining the scalability of digital outreach and online activities with the “personal touch” of mentoring, in-person meet-ups, bootcamps and tailored support. The project builds on the digital experience of Go Remote and the personalised supported-employment approach of SEPAL, which worked with vulnerable NEETs facing barriers such as low skills, disabilities and long-term unemployment. The problem is also linked to the distance between vulnerable youth and employers. Young people may lack interview experience, confidence and understanding of real labour market expectations, while employers may have limited contact with disadvantaged youth. DigiW therefore addresses not only the lack of skills, but also the missing bridge between young people and companies, using mentoring, practical training and job speed-dating events to create safer, more accessible pathways into employment. In this context, DigiW responds to the need for an integrated, youth-friendly and scalable model that can identify vulnerable young people, motivate them to participate, support them through personalised mentoring and training, validate their progress, and bring them closer to real employment opportunities in Latvia and Romania. The project aims to support 600 vulnerable young people, including at least 240 through mentoring, 360 through training, 400 through job speed-dating, and at least 120 into employment.
innovations.description:
DigiW is inspired by two previous and complementary approaches developed in different national contexts. The first is Go Remote, an initiative developed by Visas Iespējas in Latvia, focused on using digital tools to reach young people, promote opportunities, deliver online mentoring and training, and connect participants with employers through accessible job-matching formats. The second source of inspiration is SEPAL, implemented by Bucovina Institute in Romania, which focused on the inclusion of vulnerable NEETs through personalised support, mentoring, individual guidance and preparation for employment. SEPAL showed the importance of direct human support, especially for young people facing complex barriers to education, training or work. DigiW brings these two experiences together in a new blended model. It keeps the scalability and accessibility of the digital approach developed through Go Remote, while integrating the personalised, trust-based support methods tested through SEPAL. In this way, the project adapts proven practices from Latvia and Romania into a joint social innovation model for vulnerable youth, combining digital outreach, mentoring, training, bootcamps and job speed-dating in one coherent pathway toward employment.

Instead of offering isolated services, the project creates a full pathway for vulnerable young people: from digital and offline outreach, to mentoring, practical training, bootcamps, skills validation and direct interaction with employers through job speed-dating events. The innovation lies in combining two complementary approaches: the digital outreach, online training and job-matching experience of Go Remote, developed by Visas Iespējas, and the personalised support model for vulnerable NEETs from SEPAL, developed by Bucovina Institute. This creates a blended intervention that is both scalable and inclusive, reaching large numbers of young people online while still providing individual guidance and trust-based support for those facing deeper barriers. The project also innovates by making recruitment less intimidating for young people. Through structured job speed-dating events, participants meet employers in short, accessible interviews, helping them reduce fear, gain confidence and better understand real labour market expectations. At the same time, employers are brought closer to vulnerable youth in a practical and low-barrier format. DigiW therefore offers a replicable social innovation model that can be adapted by public institutions, NGOs and employers in other regions. Its strength is the combination of digital scalability, personalised mentoring, practical skills development and direct labour market access in one coherent support pathway.

These results show that the project is designed not only to improve skills, but also to create measurable labour market outcomes. Through mentoring and bootcamps, participants will also receive individual guidance, peer support and direct contact with professionals and employers. For employers, DigiW creates a structured way to meet motivated young candidates, including young people who may not usually access formal recruitment channels. The job speed-dating format helps reduce barriers between companies and vulnerable youth, creating short, accessible and practical interactions focused on real employment opportunities. For partner organisations, public institutions and the wider social innovation ecosystem, DigiW will deliver a tested and documented model that can be replicated or adapted in other regions. The project will also produce monitoring tools, impact data, research findings and final recommendations, supporting future initiatives in youth employment, NEET activation and social innovation.

innovations.name: Travelhive
innovations.problem: Tourism destinations often suffer from fragmented governance. Public bodies, destination managers, operators, associations, residents, volunteers and visitors hold valuable knowledge, but their contributions remain dispersed across informal channels, physical meetings, emails, social media and messaging apps. As a result, decisions are often based on partial information, local communities have limited influence over tourism development, and the economic value generated by tourism is not always redistributed locally. The problem is especially visible in small destinations, rural areas, islands, inner areas and emerging destinations where local organisations may lack professional digital tools, staff and data capacity. Senior volunteers, residents with low digital skills, young people at risk of leaving their communities and local micro-enterprises are frequently excluded from structured planning processes. This produces weak coordination, low trust, duplication of initiatives, limited accountability and difficulty in transforming tourism into a lever for social inclusion, employment, local identity and regeneration.
innovations.description: Travelhive combines social networking, AI, blockchain verification and participatory governance into a single platform designed specifically for destination management and community-led tourism. Unlike generic CRM, civic participation or tourism marketing tools, Travelhive is built around the daily life of a territorial community: discussion spaces, stakeholder groups, proposals, voting, shared maps, dashboards and verified local data. Its AI Voice-to-SWOT module allows people to contribute through voice, text, photos and local language inputs, including dialects. This lowers barriers for senior citizens, volunteers, local artisans, small operators and people with lower digital literacy. Contributions are processed into SWOT analyses, strategic priorities and actionable roadmaps. A permissioned blockchain layer can notarise decisions, minutes, territorial data and community-generated content, increasing transparency and trust. The innovation is not only technological. It changes the governance model: local communities become producers and validators of their own knowledge, while Travelware supports the monetisation of verified territorial data and the reinvestment of value into locally co-created projects and rewards for active members.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Travelhive has been adapted to different local and national contexts. It is being validated in more than 10 Italian territories and has active international implementations or pilots in Boavista, Cape Verde, Mossuril, Mozambique, Mexico, Colombia, and Bulgaria. The core model remains the same - participatory destination governance and community data - but it is adapted to each territory, language, stakeholder structure, tourism maturity and local development priorities.
Key results achieved so far include an operating MVP, pilot activities in more than 10 Italian territories, active experimentation in Boavista in Cape Verde and Mossuril in Mozambique, and a mapped base of more than 390 Italian historical-cultural destination areas. Travelhive has also developed original intellectual property around Token Joint and DAO/fractal governance models, and is supported by a team and advisory network combining tourism, AI, blockchain, community development and institutional expertise. A particularly relevant early example is Boavista, Cape Verde, where the Travelware model is connected to a concrete local welfare action: part of the value generated through tourism-related activities is used to support local childcare/kindergarten services, with an estimated social contribution of around €6,500 per year. This case shows how Travelhive is not only a digital governance platform, but also a mechanism to translate tourism flows into tangible community benefits, especially in contexts where tourism development must be linked to education, care services and local quality of life. The main benefits are social, organisational and economic. Communities gain a direct channel to participate in tourism governance. Destination managers and public bodies gain structured data, dashboards and a more transparent way to coordinate multiple stakeholders. Local associations and Pro Loco reduce administrative and communication friction. Young people can become digital leaders in their communities, while senior residents and non-technical volunteers can participate through voice-first interfaces. The model supports overtourism reversal by making smaller and lesser-known destinations more visible and coordinated, while promoting local value chains, authentic experiences and redistribution of value through community-led projects. In Boavista, this redistributive logic is already visible through the support to kindergarten services; in other destinations, the same model can be adapted to fund locally selected priorities such as education, cultural heritage, youth employment, environmental care or community services.

The core model remains the same - participatory destination governance and community data - but it is adapted to each territory, language, stakeholder structure, tourism maturity and local development priorities.
Key results achieved so far include an operating MVP, pilot activities in more than 10 Italian territories, active experimentation in Boavista in Cape Verde and Mossuril in Mozambique, and a mapped base of more than 390 Italian historical-cultural destination areas. Travelhive has also developed original intellectual property around Token Joint and DAO/fractal governance models, and is supported by a team and advisory network combining tourism, AI, blockchain, community development and institutional expertise. A particularly relevant early example is Boavista, Cape Verde, where the Travelware model is connected to a concrete local welfare action: part of the value generated through tourism-related activities is used to support local childcare/kindergarten services, with an estimated social contribution of around €6,500 per year. This case shows how Travelhive is not only a digital governance platform, but also a mechanism to translate tourism flows into tangible community benefits, especially in contexts where tourism development must be linked to education, care services and local quality of life. The main benefits are social, organisational and economic. Communities gain a direct channel to participate in tourism governance. Destination managers and public bodies gain structured data, dashboards and a more transparent way to coordinate multiple stakeholders. Local associations and Pro Loco reduce administrative and communication friction. Young people can become digital leaders in their communities, while senior residents and non-technical volunteers can participate through voice-first interfaces. The model supports overtourism reversal by making smaller and lesser-known destinations more visible and coordinated, while promoting local value chains, authentic experiences and redistribution of value through community-led projects. In Boavista, this redistributive logic is already visible through the support to kindergarten services; in other destinations, the same model can be adapted to fund locally selected priorities such as education, cultural heritage, youth employment, environmental care or community services.

innovations.name: Inspire PA. INtroducing Social Practices to Improve the REsilience of Public Administrations
innovations.problem: Public Administrations are increasingly required to address complex societal challenges such as demographic change, social inequalities, environmental transitions, and declining public trust. While many modernization efforts have improved administrative efficiency, they have not sufficiently strengthened the capacity of institutions to collaborate across sectors, engage citizens, and generate sustainable social impact. Contemporary challenges demand a different governance approach: one that moves beyond traditional bureaucratic models and enables Public Administrations to act as facilitators of collective problem-solving and innovation. However, many public institutions still lack the specialised competences, organisational culture, and professional profiles needed to integrate social innovation into everyday policymaking and service design. Connections with civil society organisations, social innovators, and local communities often remain fragmented and dependent on individual initiatives rather than institutionalised practices. INSPIRE PA addresses four interconnected systemic challenges: the lack of social innovation competences within Public Administrations; weak and non-structured collaboration with innovation ecosystems; limited capacity to assess social impact beyond traditional performance indicators; and difficulties in scaling and transferring successful innovation practices across different territories. By addressing these barriers, INSPIRE PA helps Public Administrations develop new ways of understanding societal needs, building partnerships, and co-creating resilient solutions with citizens and stakeholders.
innovations.description: Rather than treating social innovation as a process led exclusively by external actors, INSPIRE PA embeds innovation capacity directly within Public Administrations through the Social Innovation Officer. The Social Innovation Officer is conceived as an internal change agent capable of connecting departments, facilitating collaboration across sectors, mobilising stakeholders, and introducing new approaches to policy design and public service delivery. By positioning innovation within institutions themselves, INSPIRE PA promotes a structural and long-term transformation of administrative culture. The initiative is built around three interconnected pillars: A certified European curriculum for Social Innovation Officer, developed through extensive research on social innovation practices and skills gaps within Public Administrations. The curriculum equips civil servants with practical methodologies, tools, and frameworks for collaborative governance and public value creation. A recognised professional profile for public innovation, supported by a certification framework aligned with ISO/IEC 17024 principles. This contributes to the long-term recognition and professionalisation of social innovation competences within the public sector. A transnational Community of Practice, bringing together Public Administrations, training providers, researchers, and social innovators to exchange knowledge, share experiences, and support the replication of successful practices across Europe. Together, these elements create a sustainable ecosystem for embedding social innovation within public institutions and strengthening their capacity to respond to emerging societal challenges.

Delivery of a pilot training programme involving 90 civil servants and public managers from Italy, Greece, and Romania, representing different levels of governance and policy fields. Creation of a growing transnational Community of Practice involving more than 500 members, including public officials, social innovators, researchers, training providers, and civil society organisations. Development of Replicability Guidelines supporting the adaptation and implementation of the model in different territorial and institutional contexts. Formulation of Policy Recommendations aimed at integrating social innovation competences into recruitment, training, and professional development pathways within Public Administrations. Beyond individual capacity building, INSPIRE PA contributes to a broader cultural shift by empowering public servants to act as facilitators of collaboration, innovation, and public value creation.

innovations.name: Turning Labour Market Exclusion into Skills Supply
innovations.problem: Region Gotland is addressing the Gotland labour market paradox with the two models. Employers are experiencing significant skill shortages, while some members of the labour reserve are unable to find work through the regular system. The ESF project addresses the early system gap between healthcare, social services and the labour market through low-threshold guidance, social prescribing and pre-rehabilitation progression. The IOP with Tillväxt Gotland builds on this by strengthening employer-focused matching, broadening recruitment pathways, and creating more sustainable transitions to internships, work training, employment, and self-sufficiency. Collectively, these initiatives establish a unified regional framework for transforming social vulnerability and underutilised labour potential into increased labour market participation, enhanced skills supply, and social sustainability.
innovations.description: Gotland faces a structural labour market challenge that is both urgent and demographic. By 2040, the share of citizens aged 80 and over is forecast to grow by 40 percent. The working-age population, meanwhile, remains flat or shrinks. Fewer people will fund an expanding welfare system — and the margin for wasted human potential is gone. The paradox runs deeper still. Employers report persistent skills shortages across key sectors. Yet 75 to 80 percent of those registered as unemployed belong to groups with limited employability in the regular system — individuals whose accumulated barriers, whether health-related, social or cognitive, place them outside the reach of standard active labour market programmes. Supply and demand exist side by side. The system between them is broken. Gotland Forward was created to adress these challenges. Two complementary models now form a unified regional framework for inclusion and workforce development. Inclusion to Work targets the early system gap between healthcare, social services and the labour market. Drawing on social prescribing, low-threshold motivational support, cognitive accessibility and work-oriented rehabilitation, it creates the functional and social preconditions people need before labour market measures can take meaningful effect. This is not a waiting room. It is a progressive, clinically informed pathway towards employability. Matcha Alla operates at the other end of the same challenge. As a formalised public-civic-business partnership between Region Gotland and Tillväxt Gotland, it strengthens employer-driven skills matching, widens recruitment pathways and supports sustainable transitions into internships, subsidised employment, work training and lasting self-sufficiency. The innovation is in the architecture. Both models address different points of the same exclusion-to-employment continuum, and together they replace fragmented, short-term interventions with a regionally anchored system built to last. In a region where demography and skills mismatch converge, Gotland Forward turns underutilised labour potential into workforce participation, social sustainability and economic resilience.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: For individuals, the results are concrete. People with severely limited employability have developed functional capacity, rebuilt self-reliance and progressed along structured pathways toward active labour market programmes, education, internships, work training or open employment. Progress that the regular system had repeatedly failed to generate. Employers have seen equally tangible gains. Recruitment support has widened, skills matching has improved and more job placements have proved durable. The difference is not volume — it is quality of match and sustainability of transition. At the regional level, something more fundamental has shifted. Gotland now has a coherent operational framework in which social inclusion and skills supply are governed as interdependent policy objectives rather than separate administrative responsibilities. Health, social services and labour market actors share a common logic, joint referral structures and a mutual accountability that simply did not exist before. The systemic results may be the most consequential of all. The chronic revolving-door pattern between healthcare, social services and the labour market — costly, demoralising and deeply entrenched — has been directly targeted by both models. Sustained inter-agency collaboration, shared methodology and permanently embedded working practices mean that the capacity built during the project period does not disappear when funding ends. The framework holds. In a region where demographic trends leave no room for systemic waste, that is not a minor achievement. It is the foundation on which long-term social and economic resilience is built.

innovations.name: Magos
innovations.problem: Educational poverty represents a severe social challenge across the Iberian Peninsula, characterized by systemic gaps in foundational learning and unequal academic opportunities that heavily penalize children from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds and neurodivergent learners. In the transition to formal primary schooling, this crisis manifests through a critical pedagogical gap where children entering the education system without pre-reading skills are three times more likely to fall behind within their first two years. The broader consequences of this issue are reflected in high early school leaving rates and declining reading literacy, with over 25% of 15-year-old students in Portugal failing to reach the minimum level of functional reading proficiency, a trend mirrored in disadvantaged areas of Spain. Class of Wonders directly addresses this problem, transforming the educational paradigm from expecting a child to be ready for school to ensuring that the school is structurally ready for every child. The current context is shaped and aggravated by 3 elements, such as: 1) the sudden  expansion of non-native speaker populations in domestic classrooms, which creates immediate communication  and comprehension barriers; 2) the persistent academic underachievement in historically marginalized  territories; and 3) the scarcity of practical, daily tools for teachers to manage highly heterogeneous classes  without sacrificing the pace of the official curriculum. When educational frameworks remain static, these  vulnerable groups suffer from early academic exclusion, leading to long-term social and economic  marginalization.
innovations.description: Magos provides a dynamic digital infrastructure that integrates directly into the daily operations of public education networks. Rather than forcing diverse student profiles to adapt to a rigid teaching method, our platform modifies the delivery of the curriculum to suit the specific cognitive and linguistic realities of each classroom. The intervention is structured around 3 concepts, such as: 1) interactive pedagogical modules that use game mechanics to sustain high levels of focus and participation among younger audiences; 2) adaptive progression systems, supervised by educators, that automatically adjust the difficulty and content delivery to match the individual proficiency of the user; and 3) shared classroom interfaces designed to foster peer-to-peer interaction and reduce the isolation of newly arrived or struggling students. By deploying this adaptable technology, we enable public administrations to swiftly respond to sudden demographic shifts and special educational needs. Current implementation metrics validate this approach, showing significant improvements in daily academic engagement and a measurable reduction in learning deficits across foundational subjects.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Following its initial success in Portugal, the platform expanded into Spain, a transition that required a comprehensive alignment with a highly decentralized educational landscape. To achieve effective integration across the country, the methodology was adapted not only to the official Spanish language but also tailored specifically to the localized curricula and cultural contexts of the different territories, allowing the intervention to establish a presence across all 17 autonomous communities. Building upon this European expansion, the innovation has been successfully replicated and adapted for the Latin American educational context, specifically within Brazil. To ensure structural and cultural alignment, this international expansion relies on 4 execution steps, such as: 1) the comprehensive adaptation of the platform's pedagogical content to meet the official requirements of the Brazilian national curriculum; 2) the strategic rebranding of the solution from MAGOS to "Fantásticos" to maximize cultural resonance and user acceptance among local students; 3) the establishment of a co-development and piloting partnership directly with the schools of the SESI SENAI educational network; and 4) the implementation of a rigorous initial testing phase designed to validate educational outcomes before mass distribution. Following the successful completion of this current piloting phase, the organization aims to scale this localized version of the intervention to reach hundreds of thousands of students across the Brazilian educational system by the year 2028.
The deployment of the Magos platform yields validated educational outcomes that directly mitigate the risk of early academic failure among vulnerable student populations. On a systemic level, the primary benefit is the successful integration of adaptive digital resources into the daily routines of public schools across the Iberian Peninsula, currently reaching one hundred thousand active students in twenty percent of Portuguese public school clusters and ten percent of Spanish public schools. The intervention's effectiveness is demonstrated through 5 key results and benefits, such as: 1) a documented eighty percent increase in student motivation to learn, driven by the platform's evidence-based gamification engine; 2) an eighty-four percent rate of students improving their overall academic performance in foundational subjects like language and mathematics; 3) a ten percent decrease in performance gaps concerning essential literacy and numeracy indicators when compared to standard learning tracks; 4) the active enrollment of thirty-three percent of the user base in personalized skill recovery paths that automatically adjust to individual competency levels; and 5) the structural empowerment of the teaching body, with sixty-five percent of educators reporting a higher frequency of digital resource integration, which enables them to autonomously manage classroom diversity and provide individualized support. Furthermore, in targeted demographic interventions, such as the adaptation for migrant students in Portugal, the model establishes concrete academic targets. The current implementation framework requires that at least eighty percent of participating migrant students achieve a positive final grade in the subject of Portuguese as a Non-Native Language, a metric that is subject to independent academic evaluation by the Nova School of Business and Economics and formal validation by the Directorate-General for Education. By delivering these verifiable metrics, the project proves its capacity to generate a tangible reduction in educational poverty.

innovations.raw_text:
Magos
Educational poverty represents a severe social challenge across the Iberian Peninsula, characterized by systemic gaps in foundational learning and unequal academic opportunities that heavily penalize children from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds and neurodivergent learners. In the transition to formal primary schooling, this crisis manifests through a critical pedagogical gap where children entering the education system without pre-reading skills are three times more likely to fall behind within their first two years. The broader consequences of this issue are reflected in high early school leaving rates and declining reading literacy, with over 25% of 15-year-old students in Portugal failing to reach the minimum level of functional reading proficiency, a trend mirrored in disadvantaged areas of Spain. Class of Wonders directly addresses this problem, transforming the educational paradigm from expecting a child to be ready for school to ensuring that the school is structurally ready for every child. The current context is shaped and aggravated by 3 elements, such as: 1) the sudden  expansion of non-native speaker populations in domestic classrooms, which creates immediate communication  and comprehension barriers; 2) the persistent academic underachievement in historically marginalized  territories; and 3) the scarcity of practical, daily tools for teachers to manage highly heterogeneous classes  without sacrificing the pace of the official curriculum. When educational frameworks remain static, these  vulnerable groups suffer from early academic exclusion, leading to long-term social and economic  marginalization.
Magos provides a dynamic digital infrastructure that integrates directly into the daily operations of public education networks. Rather than forcing diverse student profiles to adapt to a rigid teaching method, our platform modifies the delivery of the curriculum to suit the specific cognitive and linguistic realities of each classroom. The intervention is structured around 3 concepts, such as: 1) interactive pedagogical modules that use game mechanics to sustain high levels of focus and participation among younger audiences; 2) adaptive progression systems, supervised by educators, that automatically adjust the difficulty and content delivery to match the individual proficiency of the user; and 3) shared classroom interfaces designed to foster peer-to-peer interaction and reduce the isolation of newly arrived or struggling students. By deploying this adaptable technology, we enable public administrations to swiftly respond to sudden demographic shifts and special educational needs. Current implementation metrics validate this approach, showing significant improvements in daily academic engagement and a measurable reduction in learning deficits across foundational subjects.
Following its initial success in Portugal, the platform expanded into Spain, a transition that required a comprehensive alignment with a highly decentralized educational landscape. To achieve effective integration across the country, the methodology was adapted not only to the official Spanish language but also tailored specifically to the localized curricula and cultural contexts of the different territories, allowing the intervention to establish a presence across all 17 autonomous communities. Building upon this European expansion, the innovation has been successfully replicated and adapted for the Latin American educational context, specifically within Brazil. To ensure structural and cultural alignment, this international expansion relies on 4 execution steps, such as: 1) the comprehensive adaptation of the platform's pedagogical content to meet the official requirements of the Brazilian national curriculum; 2) the strategic rebranding of the solution from MAGOS to "Fantásticos" to maximize cultural resonance and user acceptance among local students; 3) the establishment of a co-development and piloting partnership directly with the schools of the SESI SENAI educational network; and 4) the implementation of a rigorous initial testing phase designed to validate educational outcomes before mass distribution. Following the successful completion of this current piloting phase, the organization aims to scale this localized version of the intervention to reach hundreds of thousands of students across the Brazilian educational system by the year 2028.
The deployment of the Magos platform yields validated educational outcomes that directly mitigate the risk of early academic failure among vulnerable student populations. On a systemic level, the primary benefit is the successful integration of adaptive digital resources into the daily routines of public schools across the Iberian Peninsula, currently reaching one hundred thousand active students in twenty percent of Portuguese public school clusters and ten percent of Spanish public schools. The intervention's effectiveness is demonstrated through 5 key results and benefits, such as: 1) a documented eighty percent increase in student motivation to learn, driven by the platform's evidence-based gamification engine; 2) an eighty-four percent rate of students improving their overall academic performance in foundational subjects like language and mathematics; 3) a ten percent decrease in performance gaps concerning essential literacy and numeracy indicators when compared to standard learning tracks; 4) the active enrollment of thirty-three percent of the user base in personalized skill recovery paths that automatically adjust to individual competency levels; and 5) the structural empowerment of the teaching body, with sixty-five percent of educators reporting a higher frequency of digital resource integration, which enables them to autonomously manage classroom diversity and provide individualized support. By delivering these verifiable metrics, the project proves its capacity to generate a tangible reduction in educational poverty.

innovations.name: PRODIGY – PROmoting Digital and Green skills for Youth
innovations.problem: Many young people who are not in employment, education or training (NEET) face significant barriers to entering the labour market, including limited digital and green skills, low self-confidence and restricted access to quality training opportunities. These challenges are particularly acute in disadvantaged areas of Italy, Greece and Bulgaria, where unemployment and youth unemployment rates remain high. PRODIGY specifically targets NEET young people with different educational backgrounds, with a particular focus on vulnerable groups such as Roma communities, migrants and young people with disabilities, who often face multiple forms of exclusion and discrimination. Without tailored support, these young people are at greater risk of long-term unemployment, social exclusion and poverty. The project addresses the mismatch between labour market needs and the skills of vulnerable youth by providing inclusive and personalised pathways that strengthen employability and support active participation in society.
innovations.description:
DIG4All was a project funded by the Fondo per la Repubblica Digitale and implemented by Fondazione L’Albero della Vita and Fondazione Mondo Digitale across six regions in Central and Northern Italy. The project supported vulnerable NEET, including those with semi-structured skills, through an innovative and multi-stakeholder approach that brought together local services, educational providers, employers, employment agencies and public institutions. Its objective was to provide training, career guidance and employment support through a structured digital learning pathway, personalised coaching and concrete opportunities for labour market integration. DIG4All developed and tested a comprehensive model combining tailored digital training, one-to-one career coaching, employer engagement and territorial outreach activities, addressing both skills gaps and the broader social barriers faced by vulnerable young people. The project also strengthened collaboration among local stakeholders, creating sustainable networks to support youth inclusion and employment. Building on the successful results and methodology of DIG4All, PRODIGY was conceived as its European-scale transfer and expansion. Funded under the ESF+ Social Innovation+ Initiative, PRODIGY adapts and scales the DIG4All model to Italy, Greece and Bulgaria, extending its focus from digital inclusion to the development of both digital and green skills. By transferring proven practices across countries and strengthening collaboration among civil society organisations, training providers, universities and private-sector employers, PRODIGY demonstrates how a successful local social innovation can be transformed into a scalable European model for youth employability and inclusion.
PRODIGY addresses the needs of vulnerable NEET youth through an innovative educational approach that combines digital and green skills development with personalised one-to-one support and the strengthening of multi-stakeholder social networks. The project delivers tailored training pathways designed to develop digital, green and job-related competences aligned with current labour market demands. By bringing together youth organisations, educational institutions, employers and local stakeholders, PRODIGY creates an enabling ecosystem that supports participants throughout their learning and employment journey. The project also generates concrete employment opportunities through close collaboration with the private sector, helping young people gain access to internships and job placements. This integrated model promotes both individual empowerment and sustainable labour market inclusion.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: PRODIGY is expected to generate significant benefits for both participants and the wider community. Through tailored training pathways, 240 NEET young people will strengthen their digital, green and job-related skills, improving their employability, career readiness and access to professional networks. The project will also enhance the capacity of youth organisations to deliver innovative and inclusive training programmes while fostering stronger cooperation among employers, educational institutions and local stakeholders in Italy, Greece and Bulgaria. A key expected outcome is the successful labour market integration of at least 120 participants through employment and internships. Beyond employability, PRODIGY aims to strengthen participants’ self-confidence, aspirations and sense of belonging, enabling them to become active contributors to their communities and agents of positive change in their own lives. Through this holistic approach, the project promotes not only economic inclusion but also greater social participation, resilience and long-term empowerment.

innovations.name: Digital Career Program
innovations.problem: Germany faces a talent shortage in many sectors, yet a large pool of capable individuals remains systematically excluded from the labor market. Many people with forced migration backgrounds and marginalized locals — disproportionately women — have relevant credentials, but lack the opportunity to advance their technical skills in a fast-moving field. Newcomers face additional structural barriers: often they lack professional networks in Germany, and the German labor market is difficult to navigate without guidance. The digital gender gap deepens this challenge. Women from underserved communities face a dual disadvantage — underrepresented in tech broadly, and further marginalized by migration status, socioeconomic barriers, and cultural expectations that steer them away from technical careers. The human cost is real: years of unsuccessful job searching erode confidence and reinforce exclusion from both the labor market and society. This is a serious social failure — and an overlooked economic opportunity. Germany's companies and institutions stand to benefit greatly from the talent and diverse perspectives this community brings. The potential is there; what is missing is the structured pathway to unlock it.
innovations.description: ReDI School offers a free, high quality tech education program targeting newcomers and marginalised individuals aimed at opening new opportunities in the digital industry. The ReDI program includes: - Tech courses taught by tech professionals: we are offering semester-long courses across the ReDI locations, including on Data Analytics,  Software Development, Cloud Computing, AI Fundamentals, and more. Each course is taught by expert volunteer teachers that dedicate their time and knowledge to supporting our learners. - Soft skills training and career support: Our learners get access to a huge array of trainings aimed at enhancing their employability and understanding the professional market in their new host country. In addition to this, they have access to a personal mentor and to career counseling by the ReDI team. - Access to a professional network: ReDI operates with more than 400 partners across locations, which are connected to the learners through a Talent Pool, multiple Job Fairs, and different networking events. - Provision of refurbished hardware: ReDI provides learners with the hardware needed for the course to ensure accessibility.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The digital career program started in 2016 in Berlin, based on the requests of newly arrived refugees who wanted to advance their digital education. The program has since been replicated in other parts of Germany, namely Hamburg, Munich, and the region of North Rhine-Westphalia, and in different locations in Denmark and Sweden. Over the past decade, the program has significantly scaled up in Berlin (as in the other ReDI locations in Germany, Sweden, and Denmark), reaching many more learners and engaging volunteers as teachers. The program was adapted to offer more modules online to facilitate the scaling and reach more students, and has been tailored to the specific local context. Elements of the program have further been adapted to other target groups in new projects. We have created projects more specifically targeted at youth and their career orientation, and to the specific needs of women* wanting to advance their (basic) digital  skills.
The programme delivers impact at three levels. For students: up-to-date digital skills, reduced time to employment, hands-on project experience with industry partners, personal mentorship, and a professional network that makes entry into the labour market tangible. For the tech industry: access to a motivated, diverse talent pool that strengthens the workforce. For society: greater social integration through a supportive community of learners and volunteers. Since 2023, ReDI Germany reached over 4.400 learners in our Digital Career Program alone and engaged over 2.000 volunteers.

innovations.name: Rural Revive
innovations.problem: Long-term unemployment in rural areas poses significant economic, social and infrastructural challenges that are structurally distinct from urban unemployment. In the project's target regions of Crete in Greece and Cavan/Monaghan in Ireland, adults aged 45+ face compounding barriers rooted in geographical isolation, inadequate infrastructure and reliance on declining industries and seasonally dominated sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, retail and tourism. Ireland's LTU rate stands at 26.3%, with rural areas most affected. Those who are long-term unemployed in Ireland tend to have been out of work for over a decade, a troubling trend driven by insufficient wages, lack of effective supports and a declining availability of local jobs. In Greece, LTU stands at 52% nationally, with Crete recording a rate of 16%. This demographic (LTU aged 45+) is consistently overlooked by traditional employment programmes and as such face compounded difficulties due to age, skill degradation and economic barriers. Poor connectivity and limited job availability, particularly for those with outdated skills, create a persistent mismatch between the available labour force and modern industry needs. At the same time, the small rural businesses best placed to offer local employment are deterred from hiring LTU jobseekers by financial risk and a lack of knowledge around inclusive hiring practices. Without targeted interventions, these regions risk further economic and social decline, perpetuating unemployment and limiting social mobility for those who need support most.
innovations.description:
Rural Revive builds directly upon two proven models from Austria that have demonstrated measurable success in addressing long-term unemployment through employer engagement and guaranteed employment schemes.
The first is the MAGMA Model, which provides unconditional job guarantees for long-term unemployed individuals, matching them with suitable jobs while offering ongoing support including training, counselling, and health services. The success of MAGMA lies in its comprehensive approach, which integrates not only job creation but also social support, leading to sustainable employment outcomes. The project has helped over 112 long-term unemployed individuals secure employment through customised support services and job guarantees.
The second is the V/Faktor Initiative, which focuses on employer engagement and skills development, equipping employers with the tools and knowledge to create inclusive workplaces and ensuring the long-term integration of marginalised workers.
Both models were selected for their proven success in addressing unemployment through employer engagement and guaranteed employment. What makes Rural Revive distinctive is that it is the first time these approaches have been transferred and adapted specifically for rural contexts. Previous applications of these models have been largely urban-centric and Rural Revive addresses this gap by orientating their core methodologies to suit the unique economic, social and infrastructural barriers faced by long-term unemployed individuals in rural communities across Ireland and Greece.
Rural Revive's innovation lies in its tailored approach to rural challenges, an approach that previous efforts have largely failed to deliver, as existing employment programmes have been predominantly urban-centric. The project introduces a comprehensive support system combining financial incentives for employers, personalised career coaching for jobseekers and workshops on inclusive hiring practices, transferring proven models namely Austria's MAGMA Model and V/Faktor Initiative and orientating them specifically to suit rural long-term unemployment for the first time. At the heart of this is the Guaranteed Job Placement Scheme (GJPS), which guarantees 100 long-term unemployed individuals a minimum of 12 months of fair and decent employment, with wages 30+% above minimum wage. Employers access the Employment Subsidy Scheme, which covers minimum wage costs for the full 12 month period, only after completing mandatory Inclusive Hiring Practices Workshops covering age-diverse hiring, skill adaptation and workplace accommodations. This prerequisite ensures lasting cultural change within participating businesses rather than simply incentivising short-term recruitment. The project also addresses structural rural barriers such as transport and isolation through personalised supports and uses the Quadruple Helix Model, engaging the consortium, public authorities, private entities and educational institutions, to align with local needs and ensure broad support and scalability across EU regions.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Rural Revive directly targets 100 long-term unemployed individuals aged 45+ across Ireland and Greece, providing them with stable employment, fair and decent wages and personal development through career coaching and training - rebuilding confidence, improving employability and addressing skill gaps. A minimum of 30 rural employers will be engaged across both countries benefiting from subsidised employment costs, access to trained workers and improved inclusive hiring practices that broaden their talent pool. At least 50% of participants are targeted to be offered contract extensions or to transition into new roles upon completion of their 12-month employment supported by Rural Revive. For partner organisations, Rural Revive will build lasting capacity to tackle LTU and sustain employment schemes beyond the project period. Employment Support Officers will remain available as resources to help rural businesses apply the skills and practices developed during the project. At a community level, Crete and Cavan/Monaghan will see reduced LTU rates, revitalised local economies through increased market participation and a reduction in pressure on public finances and social services. The project's structured Quality Assurance and Evaluation Plan, real-time digital dashboard and biannual reporting will ensure that results are rigorously tracked, evidenced and made available to partners, funders and the wider public.

innovations.name: I want to work
innovations.problem: People facing poverty, homelessness, low education, long-term unemployment, migration backgrounds or other vulnerabilities often encounter multiple and interconnected barriers to employment. Conventional employment measures rarely provide the long-term, individualised support needed to overcome these challenges, resulting in persistent exclusion from the labour market and society.
innovations.description:
The project was inspired by other Work Integration Social Enterprise (WISE) models that combine paid employment, personalised support and skills development for people facing barriers to employment. Ateliere Fără Frontiere adapted this approach to the Romanian context, integrating circular economy activities with socio-professional inclusion pathways.
The programme applies a Work Integration Social Enterprise (WISE) model that combines real paid employment, personalised socio-professional support and skills development within circular economy activities. By integrating economic activity with social support, participants gain work experience, professional skills and confidence in a protected yet realistic work environment, preparing them for transition to the open labour market.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The model was adapted and scaled within Bio&Co, AFF’s organic farm in rural Romania. While following the same socio-professional integration methodology and personalised support pathway, the programme was adjusted to local labour market realities by removing the standard two-year time limit, as employment opportunities in the area are significantly more limited than in urban settings.
Since 2008, the programme has supported over 8,000 people towards labour market integration and provided employment opportunities for 360 people within Ateliere Fără Frontiere’s circular economy workshops. In 2025 alone, 600 people received employment counselling, 225 benefited from in-depth individual support, and 46 people from vulnerable backgrounds secured employment through the socio-professional integration programme. Beyond employment outcomes, the programme strengthens autonomy, self-confidence and social inclusion, while generating environmental benefits through circular economy activities such as WEEE refurbishment, reuse and recycling.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Youth Aware of Mental Health (YAM)
innovations.problem: In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of an increase in mental health problems among adolescents, ranging from clinical disorders to broader emotional distress and well-being difficulties. These issues often emerge during adolescence and may persist into adulthood, where they can become more severe and consolidated, generating significant personal suffering as well as long-term costs for healthcare systems and society as a whole. At the same time, there is an increasing sense of disconnection between young people and key social environments, particularly schools and community support services. Many adolescents report feeling that existing resources are not designed for them, are difficult to access, or do not adequately respond to their needs. This can contribute to reduced engagement, limited help-seeking behaviour, and a growing perception of isolation. Taken together, these factors highlight a critical need for early, accessible, and school-based mental health promotion and prevention strategies that foster inclusion, strengthen protective factors, and improve young people’s connection to supportive environments.
innovations.description:
The project is based on the SEYLE study (Saving and Empowering Young Lives in Europe), a large-scale European research initiative focused on the promotion of adolescent mental health and suicide prevention in school settings across several European countries. SEYLE provided evidence on the effectiveness of school-based, universal prevention programmes and served as a key reference for the development of YAM (Youth Aware of Mental Health).
The innovative solution of the programme is based on bringing mental health promotion directly into the adolescents’ most familiar environment: the school setting. By working within the educational centre, the programme ensures accessibility and reduces barriers to participation. The sessions are delivered by professionals with experience in mental health who are specifically trained in the programme methodology. Their role is not to provide answers, but to facilitate dialogue, ask open questions, and actively listen to students, fostering a space of trust, safety, and participation. A key component of the approach is the creation of a safe environment where young people feel free to express themselves without judgement. The programme also provides information about existing social, cultural, and sports resources available in the community, helping students to identify accessible support networks. In addition, participants are encouraged to share their own interests and activities in their free time, allowing peers to learn from one another, strengthen social connections, and promote positive, healthy alternatives. This peer-sharing dynamic helps students to better know each other and reinforces a sense of belonging within the group.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The programme has demonstrated positive outcomes in increasing mental health awareness and reducing stigma among adolescents. Students show greater willingness to talk about emotional well-being and to seek help when needed. The participatory approach fosters student engagement and empowers young people to take an active role in their own well-being. Overall, YAM contributes to prevention, improved emotional literacy, and better connection between young people and available social and community resources.
The YAM (Youth Aware of Mental Health) programme has been replicated and implemented in multiple countries

innovations.name: “Bridges Beyond Bars” – Supporting Children of Romanian Prisoners Across Europe
innovations.problem: Many tens of thousands children across Europe experience the negative consequences of parental imprisonment. In the Romanian context, a significant number of citizens (over 10.000) are incarcerated in other European countries while their children remain in Romania, often under the care of relatives or extended family members. These children face multiple challenges, including increased risk of school dropout, emotional distress, social stigma, reduced parental support and limited access to specialised services. Despite their vulnerability, they often remain invisible to public authorities and social support systems. Currently, there is no coordinated transnational mechanism that allows authorities, prisons and civil society organisations to identify these children, assess their needs and connect them with appropriate support services. As a result, many children affected by parental imprisonment receive little or no assistance and are at greater risk of social exclusion and educational failure. The project addresses this gap by creating an integrated cross border framework that links imprisoned parents, support organisations and children in Romania, ensuring that vulnerable children are identified early and receive the assistance they need.
innovations.description:
The project is based on the SEYLE study (Saving and Empowering Young Lives in Europe), a large-scale European research initiative focused on the promotion of adolescent mental health and suicide prevention in school settings across several European countries. SEYLE provided evidence on the effectiveness of school-based, universal prevention programmes and served as a key reference for the development of YAM (Youth Aware of Mental Health).
The innovative aspect of the proposed project lies in its transnational and child centred approach. While support services for prisoners or vulnerable children exist in many countries, there are currently very few mechanisms that connect imprisoned parents abroad with support services for their children in their country of origin. The project introduces a coordinated model involving prisons, civil society organisations, schools and local authorities across multiple European countries. Through structured cooperation, Romanian prisoners detained abroad will be identified and invited to participate voluntarily in the programme. Information about their children in Romania will be collected in compliance with GDPR requirements and used to facilitate tailored support interventions. Each child will benefit from an individual support plan that may include educational tutoring, psychological counselling, mentoring, material assistance and community based support. The project will also generate practical tools, cooperation protocols and policy recommendations that can be transferred and replicated in other European contexts. By combining cross border cooperation with personalised intervention, the project creates a new pathway for protecting children affected by parental imprisonment and reducing the long term consequences of social exclusion.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The project is expected to generate both immediate benefits for children and long term systemic impact at national and European levels. The SVASTA Foundation brings more than ten years of experience in supporting children affected by parental imprisonment and has already helped over 350 pupils and university students successfully continue their education despite being at risk of school or university dropout. This experience demonstrates the effectiveness and sustainability of the proposed intervention model. Key results include: • Identification of at least 150 Romanian prisoners detained in partner countries. • Mapping and assessment of children and young people remaining in Romania. • Delivery of personalised support plans for at least 120 children and young adults. • Improved school attendance, educational performance and retention among beneficiaries. • Reduced risk of school and university dropout. • Increased emotional wellbeing, resilience and social inclusion of participating children. • Strengthened cooperation between civil society organisations, educational institutions, local authorities and prison administrations across participating countries. • Development of a transnational referral mechanism compliant with data protection requirements. • Publication of a practical methodology, cooperation protocols and recommendations for policymakers. The project will directly improve the lives of children affected by parental imprisonment by providing access to educational, psychological and social support that would otherwise be unavailable. Families, schools and local communities will also benefit from stronger support networks and improved coordination of services. In the longer term, the initiative will contribute to reducing educational inequality, preventing social exclusion and promoting equal opportunities for vulnerable children across Europe.
Since 2014, the SVASTA Foundation has implemented a project ”Alone to school”, implemented in partnership with the VELUX Foundations from Denmark, aimed at supporting children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds and with parents behind bars in Penitenciary from Romania. Over 350 such cases, at risk of dropping out of school, have been helped to successfully complete their studies. Many of them are today engineers, IT specialists, economists, doctors, teachers and are actively involved in the present projects of the SVASTA Foundation.
The proposed project aims at a category of children and young people in extremely vulnerable situations. Approximately 4 million Romanian citizens work and live in other European countries, in many cases their families remaining in Romania. According to European statistics, out of the 4 million, approximately 10,000 Romanian citizens are in detention, most of them in countries such as: Italy, Spain, Germany, France and the UK. Identifying these cases, contacting the prisons in the respective countries and obtaining the contact details of the families in Romania requires collaboration with other specialized institutions in other European countries, as well as with civil society organizations concerned in this field. Currently, June 2026, the SVASTA Foundation has managed to identify several cases of children in situations of extreme vulnerability and whose parents are behind bars in prisons in Germany or Italy. These cases have been taken over by the Foundation and are supported from its own resources. This pilot stage needs to be extended, given the large number of such cases often in extreme situations. This is also the main reason why the SVASTA Foundation is interested in a pan-European collaboration.

This experience demonstrates the effectiveness and sustainability of the proposed intervention model. Key results include: • Identification of at least 150 Romanian prisoners detained in partner countries. • Mapping and assessment of children and young people remaining in Romania. • Delivery of personalised support plans for at least 120 children and young adults. • Improved school attendance, educational performance and retention among beneficiaries. • Reduced risk of school and university dropout. • Increased emotional wellbeing, resilience and social inclusion of participating children. • Strengthened cooperation between civil society organisations, educational institutions, local authorities and prison administrations across participating countries. • Development of a transnational referral mechanism compliant with data protection requirements. • Publication of a practical methodology, cooperation protocols and recommendations for policymakers. The project will directly improve the lives of children affected by parental imprisonment by providing access to educational, psychological and social support that would otherwise be unavailable. Families, schools and local communities will also benefit from stronger support networks and improved coordination of services. In the longer term, the initiative will contribute to reducing educational inequality, preventing social exclusion and promoting equal opportunities for vulnerable children across Europe.
Since 2014, the SVASTA Foundation has implemented a project ”Alone to school”, implemented in partnership with the VELUX Foundations from Denmark, aimed at supporting children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds and with parents behind bars in Penitenciary from Romania. Over 350 such cases, at risk of dropping out of school, have been helped to successfully complete their studies. Many of them are today engineers, IT specialists, economists, doctors, teachers and are actively involved in the present projects of the SVASTA Foundation.
The proposed project aims at a category of children and young people in extremely vulnerable situations. Approximately 4 million Romanian citizens work and live in other European countries, in many cases their families remaining in Romania. According to European statistics, out of the 4 million, approximately 10,000 Romanian citizens are in detention, most of them in countries such as: Italy, Spain, Germany, France and the UK. Identifying these cases, contacting the prisons in the respective countries and obtaining the contact details of the families in Romania requires collaboration with other specialized institutions in other European countries, as well as with civil society organizations concerned in this field. Currently, June 2026, the SVASTA Foundation has managed to identify several cases of children in situations of extreme vulnerability and whose parents are behind bars in prisons in Germany or Italy. These cases have been taken over by the Foundation and are supported from its own resources. This pilot stage needs to be extended, given the large number of such cases often in extreme situations. This is also the main reason why the SVASTA Foundation is interested in a pan-European collaboration.

innovations.evidence:
The socio‑educational innovation Ajungem MARI was launched in Bucharest in 2014, starting with zero financial resources, and beginning the following year it was replicated and expanded nationwide. Today, the program operates in 29 counties (Arad, Argeș, Bacău, Bihor, Bistrița‑Năsăud, Botoșani, Brașov, Buzău, Călărași, Cluj, Constanța, Dâmbovița, Dolj, Galați, Gorj, Hunedoara, Iași, Ilfov, Maramureș, Mehedinți, Mureș, Olt, Neamț, Prahova, Sibiu, Suceava, Timiș, Vaslui, Vrancea) and in Bucharest (in all districts), in partnership with local DGASPC institutions, adapting its intervention model to the specific needs of children and young people in the protection system. From a local initiative, Ajungem MARI has grown into a national network of over 12000 trained volunteers and specialists who provide educational, emotional, and moral support each year to 3500 institutionalized children and young people. Its scalable model — based on standardized training, long‑term support, support groups, and periodic training sessions for volunteers and DGASPC staff — enables coherent implementation of the program in both urban and rural communities, in state‑run and private centers, while maintaining the quality and impact of interventions. Through weekly activities such as homework support, school recovery, creative workshops, general knowledge courses, personal development, vocational counseling, psychotherapy, sports and recreational activities, camps focused on developing independent living skills, and career orientation visits, the program reduces educational gaps, mitigates the effects of trauma, and strengthens self confidence. The stable, trusting relationships built between volunteers and children significantly increase their chances of social and professional integration and contribute to developing the skills needed for independent living.
In 2025, the Ajungem MARI program generated significant national impact, strengthening its role as a social innovation initiative with direct effects on institutionalized children and young people. Through the involvement of the Lindenfeld Association and its volunteer network, 3500 children and young people from 323 residential centers and social homes benefited from consistent educational and emotional support. This impact was made possible by the involvement of 1400 volunteers, who contributed over 61852 hours of volunteering, becoming role models, mentors, and active support in educational, recreational, and personal development activities. These interventions included homework support, workshops, trips, camps, counseling, and mentoring, helping build stable and trust‑based relationships. The program supported the personal and professional development of beneficiaries through specialized activities: 223 children participated in vocational courses, 20 young people in qualification courses, 50 in career counseling, and 600 in professional orientation workshops. At the same time, 216 children received exam preparation through tutoring, and 128 benefited from therapy and speech therapy, contributing to their emotional and cognitive development and recovery. The program also created development opportunities through 1104 outings and trips, 58 camp participations, 37 charitable events, and 54 training sessions for volunteers, strengthening both the beneficiaries’ experiences and the capacity of the intervention network. The program’s major benefits include reducing educational gaps, increasing access to development opportunities, improving the emotional well‑being of children and young people, and preparing them for independent living by strengthening self‑confidence and personal and professional skills. Through its scale and consistent impact, Ajungem MARI is an initiative with visible and measurable results, generating real and lasting change within the community.
