innovations.name: Gamechanger - Junge Männer gestalten ihre Zukunft durch peer-gestützte Ansprache und Angebotsformate
innovations.problem: In the context of the first project year, we have experienced that in the defined target group there is a great mistrust of public institutions and of external influences in general. The job center is often perceived as a place that can sanction and use certain information against clients (especially refugees). There is furthermore a major concern that data could be abused. Concrete fears are often not possible to name. This makes engaging the target group difficult once MainArbeit is mentioned as a cooperation partner. The numerous minor cases show that many potential participants would rather forego support from Joblinge and MainArbeit than take up the offered support formats. Not infrequently, participants are willing to receive advice and support, but refuse to fill out and sign project documents. In addition, although the target group has often been socialized in Germany, knowledge of the dual training system and understanding of the added value of training are hardly present. Many participants can barely identify with society, which frequently leads to feeling excluded and, at times, even despised by it. Active social and cultural participation in society is often not present. In 2025, 16 out of 17 participants were under 25. This was partly because the project’s focus last year was more on placement into vocational or academic training. This is currently being adjusted to also reach older representatives of the target group. Furthermore, it is often difficult to convey the tools and goals of the project to the target group. As described, our training ambassadors as well as the provider’s staff frequently encounter strong resistance, as official and external counseling is often rejected. Especially when potential participants have been in a support system or not connected to anything for a long time, it is difficult to break up the existing structures. In addition, many potential participants have numerous other difficulties, such as debt or problems within their families. These problems make placement in the job market difficult, as the young men are already overwhelmed by the existing barriers and do not have the necessary resources to take care of themselves. The connection to existing counseling services, MainArbeit, and the labor market is often perceived as unimportant.
innovations.description: To better reach the target audience and address the aforementioned activation issues, we have already taken measures. We have learned that our training ambassadors need closer supervision and more intense support in their work. Negative experiences in outreach have unfortunately led to most ambassadors from the previous spring to quit shortly after starting. As a result, a lot of work already invested in the project has fallen by the wayside. Specifically, outreach to MainArbeit customers is now handled by the social pedagogical staff of the organization, who are also taking on clarification regarding data protection and monitoring. In these cases, outreach is either accompanied by training ambassadors or contact with the training ambassadors is established by Joblinge staff only afterwards. In addition, the recruitment of ambassadors has been revised. Ambassadors are now deployed according to their individual skills. Promoters, networkers, and content creators are in use, each taking on different tasks according to their suitability. Moreover, more ambassadors who have already completed their training are now being deployed, and they are also more solidified in their personal development. We have learned that young people, even those who are already in vocational training, also struggle with targeted barriers (commitment, challenges in training, etc.). Furthermore, we have recognized that we must provide stronger supportive scaffolding for potential participants to identify known barriers and actively assist them. This includes addressing debt, difficulties in communicating with authorities and job centers. In many cases, sanctions from the job center have already occurred. We want to stabilize the participants in general and support them to such an extent that positive and goal-oriented communication with the job center staff becomes possible again.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Currently, 38 participants are officially registered in Gamechanger. This means that these 38 participants have filled out the necessary and relevant ESF documents and have been extensively supported by the provider’s educational staff as well as the training ambassadors. In addition, 21 MainArbeit clients have been assigned to the project, who have either already been successfully contacted or are being continuously contacted by the provider. Nine participants have already been placed into work, training, or school. The other, already registered participants have participated in extensive counseling sessions, which has partly significantly increased their employability. Placement of participants is challenging because multiple barriers often exist that hinder placement. The group of potential participants with whom we have spoken so far, but who refused to sign official documents, is considerably larger. MainArbeit clients have not yet been placed into work or training. However, we would like to point out the particularity of the target group: clients assigned through MainArbeit are considered difficult even within the job center and typically have an existing history of sanctions. Many clients are connected to MainArbeit but are unknown to the counselors there. Many have never attended counseling meetings or have not attended for months. Of these 21 assigned participants, seven are now being intensively supported by the provider. That may not sound like much, but counselors at MainArbeit regard it as a great success, since other projects and standard activation processes have not been able to contact and engage the clients successfully. Moreover, we have been able to adjust our processes and the form of our communication and outreach several times to work more effectively with the target group. Working with the target group—whether MainArbeit clients or participants addressed across sectors—gives us many useful and important insights into the target group and how this group perceives our society and public actors. This enables us to continuously adapt and improve our processes. In the context of other labor market policy measures, we do not have these opportunities. Lastly, I want to emphasize again that we often work with young men who categorically reject support from public authorities and do not wait for someone to help them.

innovations.name: Community Lunch
innovations.problem: Community Lunch responds to a deeply entrenched and multi-layered crisis affecting children in disadvantaged communities across Romania, one of the most acute in the European Union. Child poverty and food insecurity. Over 32% of Romanian children — more than 1.16 million — live in risk of poverty or social exclusion. In the past year there has been a worrying increase in the number of families that cannot afford a meal with meat or fish even once every two days. School dropout and educational exclusion. In 2024, over 400,000 children aged 7 to 17 were outside the education system, representing 18.7% of the resident population of that age. Romania has one of the highest early school leaving rates in the European Union — 16.6% in 2023, with a particularly acute vulnerability in rural areas — nearly double the EU target of under 9%. The dropout rate among secondary school-age adolescents has grown from 23% to over 27% in just three years, suggesting that existing measures have not only failed to reduce dropout but have actually allowed it to worsen. Functional illiteracy —  Even among children who remain in school, the capacity to read, understand and use information remains critically low. According to PISA 2022 data, over 42% of 15-year-olds in Romania do not reach the minimum level of competence in reading. Romania ranks second to last in the EU, with 33.2% of students falling below the functional literacy threshold across all three PISA domains — mathematics, science and reading — compared to an OECD average of 16.4%. When school dropout is factored in, functional illiteracy in Romania exceeds 50% of the child population — and studies show a direct correlation between functional illiteracy and low self-confidence in children, which inevitably affects their quality of life and future employment prospects. Only 11% of children in primary and lower secondary education reach a functional level of literacy, demonstrating the ability to locate, understand and synthesise written information. This is precisely why Community Lunch pairs every shared meal with literacy workshops and structured debates — creating recurring spaces where children practise reading comprehension, critical thinking and public expression in a safe, non-formal setting, building the foundational skills that the formal school system alone is failing to provide. Social isolation and the collapse of community bonds. In rural and peri-urban areas where Community Lunch operates, children face not only material poverty but the absence of safe, stimulating social spaces. Families are isolated, community ties are weak, and children lack access to non-formal learning, cultural experiences and positive adult role models outside the school system. Food waste. Romania generates significant food waste at the production and distribution level, while families in the same regions go hungry — a paradox that Community Lunch directly addresses by sourcing 70% of its ingredients from food banks and local producers. These problems are deeply interconnected: hunger undermines learning; poverty causes dropout; isolation reinforces exclusion; and poor literacy closes every door that education is meant to open. Community Lunch addresses all five simultaneously, through a single, recurring, community-rooted intervention.
innovations.description: Community Lunch is not a food aid programme. It is a community activation model that uses the shared meal as a catalyst — a deliberate social technology for rebuilding trust, stimulating learning and generating local educational ecosystems in communities where institutional support has largely failed. What makes it innovative is not any single element, but the integration of all of them. 1. The meal as a pedagogical tool. Rather than distributing food packages or vouchers, Community Lunch organises the cooking and eating of meals together — children, elderly people, volunteers and community members side by side. This transforms a basic survival need into a recurring ritual of socialisation, dignity and belonging. The table becomes a classroom without walls. 2. Non-formal learning embedded in every event. Every Community Lunch includes structured workshops on literacy and reading comprehension, financial education, personal development, critical thinking and debate, creativity, ecology and digital media. These are not add-ons — they are co-designed with the meal as a single, coherent experience. Children who struggle to engage with formal schooling participate actively in these sessions precisely because the setting is safe, informal and built around positive relationships. 3. Literacy and debate workshops as a systemic response. In a country where over 50% of children are functionally illiterate when dropout is factored in, and where only 11% of primary and lower secondary students reach a functional level of literacy, the association deliberately organises literacy workshops and structured debates after each meal. Children practise reading comprehension, learn to formulate arguments, listen to opposing views and express themselves in front of peers — skills that are foundational for civic participation and employability, and deeply absent from the communities where Community Lunch operates. 4. Community co-production, not service delivery. Local community members, parents and young volunteers co-cook the meals alongside the association's team. 70% of ingredients come from food banks and local producers, embedding the programme in the local economy and reducing food waste simultaneously. This co-production model means the community is not a passive recipient of charity — it is an active co-author of its own social infrastructure. 5. Recurrence as a design principle. Unlike one-off interventions, Community Lunch returns to the same communities repeatedly, building trust over time, tracking individual children's progress and generating the sustained relationships that are the prerequisite for any meaningful educational or social change. In 2025, the programme operated across 19 communities in 10 counties, with over 2,200 children and adolescents directly involved. 6. Cross-generational inclusion. By bringing children and elderly people together around the same table, the programme rebuilds intergenerational bonds that poverty and migration have eroded — creating natural mentoring relationships and a sense of shared community identity that extends well beyond each event. 7. Low-cost, high-replicability architecture. The model requires no permanent infrastructure, no specialist facilities and no proprietary technology. It runs on trained volunteers, local partnerships and food bank networks — making it highly adaptable and replicable in any European rural or peri-urban context facing similar challenges of child poverty, educational exclusion and community fragmentation. The innovation of Community Lunch lies in treating a hot meal not as an end in itself, but as the beginning of something larger: a local educational ecosystem built from the ground up, one table at a time.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Since its launch in January 2021, Community Lunch has grown from a two-community pilot into a national network active across Romania, with documented, measurable results across five dimensions: food security, education, community cohesion, environmental impact and institutional leverage. From pilot to national network — growth over 4 years. The programme started in 2 communities in 2 counties. By 2025 it operated across 19 urban and rural communities in 10 counties — Hunedoara, Ialomița, Ilfov, Gorj, Vâlcea, Giurgiu, Tulcea, Bacău, Prahova and București — and had prepared hot meals for at least 10,000 children in total since its founding.
Community Lunch was not designed as a fixed programme to be exported wholesale, but as an adaptable community activation framework — and its replication history reflects exactly this. Each new community has adopted the core model (shared meal + educational workshops + local co-production) while adapting content, format and partnerships to local context. Geographic replication — from 2 to 19 communities in 4 years The programme launched in January 2021 in two communities: Slobozia (Ialomița County) and Lupeni (Hunedoara County). By 2025 it had been replicated — largely by community request — across 19 urban and rural communities in 10 counties. Each of these represents a distinct replication context — post-industrial towns (Valea Jiului), remote Delta villages (Sulina, Letea), rural agricultural communities (Puieni, Vladimir, Măciuca) and urban peripheries (București, Petrăchioaia) — demonstrating the model's adaptability across very different social, geographic and economic environments.
The most significant programmatic adaptation in 2025 was the collaboration with Liceul Tehnologic Constantin Istrati in Câmpina, Prahova County — a vocational high school with a food specialisation. Here, the Community Lunch model was adapted so that students cook the community meals as part of their practical vocational training, integrating dual education with community service. This represents a structural innovation on top of the original model: it removes the need for external volunteer cooks, embeds the programme within the formal education system and simultaneously addresses vocational training, food production and community inclusion. This adaptation is directly replicable in any European country with vocational schools in food, hospitality or catering.
In Aninoasa — a small post-mining town with extreme socioeconomic challenges — the Community Lunch framework was adapted into a three-day Summer School (29–31 July 2025), with 87 children participating and the entire programme designed and facilitated by 16 adolescent volunteers. This peer-education adaptation demonstrates that the model can evolve from a monthly meal-and-workshop format into an intensive educational intervention, co-created and delivered by young people from within the community itself.
In Enisala (Tulcea) and Puieni (Giurgiu), Community Lunch events were combined with the physical transformation of kindergarten spaces — equipping them with furniture, carpets and educational materials, and creating reading corners. This adaptation connects the programme's community activation logic with permanent infrastructure improvements, extending impact beyond the event itself and into the daily educational environment of young children. What replication has taught us. Every new community has reinforced the same finding: the model works precisely because it does not impose a standardised programme, but activates what already exists locally — people who want to cook together, spaces that can host a shared meal, local producers willing to donate ingredients, teachers and parents ready to contribute workshops. The role of Asociația Copii pentru Viitor is coordination and quality assurance, not delivery. This distinction is what makes the model genuinely replicable — by other NGOs, by local authorities, by schools, and ultimately by communities thems

innovations.name: Kopfsachen – Mental Health Prevention in Schools
innovations.problem: Research shows that 75% of all mental health conditions emerge before the age of 25. Yet most young people never receive support (Molecular Psychiatry, 2023). The gap is widest among those from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, where access to private therapy is limited, schools are under-resourced, and mental health remains stigmatised. Schools are the one institution that reaches all young people regardless of background but educators lack the training, tools and structures to respond effectively. Without early prevention, mental health challenges translate directly into educational disengagement, school dropout and reduced life chances.
innovations.description: Most school mental health initiatives rely on external experts who deliver a session and leave. Kopfsachen takes the opposite approach: rather than importing support from outside, it builds lasting capacity from within the school itself. Five staff members per school are trained as Mental Health Ambassadors over one year. We are equipping them to recognise warning signs, lead preventive programmes and build peer support networks. They are not therapists, but skilled first responders embedded in the everyday life of the school. Age-specific workshops reach every student cohort: younger students explore emotions and transitions in peer-led clubs, middle schoolers develop self-care strategies, older students build resilience for key life transitions. Parents are brought in as partners, not afterthoughts. Older students support younger ones through structured peer mentoring. And when the project period ends, the school continues — independently, with its own certified staff, its own structures, and a quality seal that makes its commitment to mental health visible to the whole community. The innovation is not a programme that visits schools. It is a transformation that stays.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: By end of 2028, the programme will have directly reached 12,900 people: 6,000 students through workshops, 750+ students through peer clubs, 1,500 teachers through training, 4,500 parents through awareness events, and 150 staff trained as Mental Health Ambassadors. A further 12,000 students benefit indirectly through the structural changes embedded in their schools. But the numbers only tell part of the story. The programme's deepest impact lies in what remains after it ends: 150 trained Mental Health Ambassadors embedded in their schools, equipped with practical skills, and connected through cross-school networks. They continue to deliver prevention work independently. They are not merely programme participants but a permanent, growing infrastructure for mental health in their communities. Scientific evaluation in partnership with the University of Marburg and Humboldt University Berlin demonstrates significant improvements in emotional self-efficacy and openness to professional support among participating students.

innovations.name: ZekkiPro
innovations.problem: Measures and digital tools are rare in social work globaly. However, digitalization is becoming more and more popular with the advent of artificial intelligence for the use of social welfare. Often, data collections with meters appear to respondents from traditional forms and it is not motivating for the customer, especially young people, to answer administrative queries. There is therefore a clear need for customer-oriented user interfaces that strengthen agency and inclusion. If support cannot be accessed on time, problems become more complex and prolonged. This can lead to social exclusion (loneliness), marginalisation and resentment towards society. At the same time, the society loses the young person’s potential.
innovations.description:
ZekkiPro is based on the experiences from open zekki.fi website.
ZekkiPro offers support for strengthening wellbeing in three ways. First, an understanding of one's own life situation becomes clear to the respondent when he or she does a quick but comprehensive life situation survey which highlights both problems but also strengths. Often, one's own resources are hidden if there are difficulties in some area of life. Seeing areas of life that are in good shape supports in trouble. Second, ZekkiPro can be used to generate verbal, encouraging feedback for each area of life. This way, a professional can use ZekkiPro to give their customers the kind of feedback they think is best. Third, ZekkiPro also offers the organization's own services based on the self-assessment of the clients. ZekkiPro is integrated into the national Suomi.fi Service Data Reserve and picks up from there suitable public services for the customer as well as support provided by NGOs. In the screening of services, the employee is assisted by artificial intelligence, but services are always provided by human decision.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The roots of ZekkiPro are in 3X10D measure and open Zekki.fi website. 3X10D is widely used in projects and social services nationwide. The measure is validated before, and validating studies are going on. Zekki.fi is nominated in 2021 European innovation council's the best European social innovation (EUSIC) award and it has also been awarded in national competitions. ZekkiPro is also integrated into the organization's customer information system and its results have been taken to the organization's information management dashboard.
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: The Magic Locker
innovations.problem: Children from disadvantaged rural communities often lack the basic school supplies needed to participate fully in class. Many come from families facing financial hardship, including large families, single-parent households or families in which children are raised by grandparents. The problem is not limited to the beginning of the school year: notebooks, writing instruments, backpacks and other materials must be replaced continuously as they are used, lost or damaged. Previous support initiatives showed that one-time donations do not always provide a lasting solution. Even when pupils receive individual school-supply packages, the materials may be left at home, lost or returned to school in poor condition. When children arrive in class without the necessary supplies, they may feel ashamed, excluded or unable to take part in lessons. Over time, this can contribute to absenteeism and increase the risk of early school leaving. The issue also places additional pressure on teachers, who frequently purchase missing supplies from their own resources, and on families that cannot consistently cover school-related costs. A reliable, school-based and recurrent support mechanism is therefore needed to ensure that pupils can access essential materials whenever they need them throughout the school year.
innovations.description: The Magic Locker replaces one-off school-supply donations with a recurrent, school-based support mechanism. A dedicated locker is installed inside each participating school and stocked with the materials pupils need throughout the year, including notebooks, writing instruments, drawing supplies, pencil cases, backpacks and reusable items such as geometry sets. Consumable supplies are replenished periodically, ensuring that support remains available after the beginning of the school year. Each locker is managed by a volunteer teacher who distributes supplies fairly, according to the pupils’ needs. This simple system ensures that essential materials are available at the right place and at the right time, while reducing the risk that they are lost, damaged or left at home. It also removes the stigma associated with arriving at school without the supplies needed to take part in lessons. The pupils are actively involved in unpacking the supplies, organising the shelves and decorating their locker. They learn to use shared resources responsibly, take only what they need and leave reusable materials available for classmates. In this way, the project combines material support with responsibility, solidarity and community participation. The innovation lies not only in the physical locker, but also in the delivery model: a visible, accessible and continuously replenished resource integrated into everyday school life. The model is practical, cost-efficient and adaptable to different schools, age groups and local needs. It can be replicated in other underserved communities through partnerships with schools, teachers, companies, donors and local stakeholders.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Since its launch in 2021, The Magic Locker has developed into a recurrent educational support programme. More than 50 fully equipped lockers have been installed in rural schools across four Romanian counties: Arad, Bihor, Timiș and Vaslui. Existing lockers are replenished throughout the school year, while additional schools are included as new partnerships and funding become available. The project has expanded steadily: In 2021, approximately 700 pupils received support. In 2022, around 1,400 children from 12 schools benefited from the supplies available through the lockers. In 2023, 9 lockers supported more than 1,500 children. In 2024, a further 11 lockers were equipped. In 2025, 9 more lockers were established The most important benefit is that children can access essential school supplies whenever they need them, not only at the beginning of the school year. Pupils can attend lessons with the appropriate notebooks, writing instruments, backpacks and learning materials, even when their families cannot afford to replace items that have been used, lost or damaged. According to feedback collected by the organisation, children feel more secure knowing that the locker is available inside their school, and they are more likely to return to class even when they no longer have the necessary supplies at home. The project also helps reduce the shame and social exclusion experienced by pupils from disadvantaged backgrounds. Because materials are accessed through a shared school resource, children receive support discreetly and can participate in lessons on more equal terms with their classmates. This contributes to improved attendance and helps prevent early school leaving. The Magic Locker creates additional benefits for the wider school community. Families face less financial pressure, while teachers no longer need to purchase missing supplies as frequently from their own resources. Reusable items, such as geometry sets, are shared and returned after use, increasing the efficiency of each donation. Finally, the model encourages responsibility and solidarity. Pupils help unpack supplies, organise the shelves and decorate their locker. They learn to take only what they need and to preserve shared resources so that other children can benefit as well. This makes The Magic Locker more than a donation mechanism: it is a practical, scalable and community-based tool for educational inclusion.
tags: Equal access to education and training

innovations.name: "Coach for Inclusion". Training coaches with disabilities for a more inclusive society
innovations.problem: There are approximately 957,000 people with disabilities (various abilities) in Romania. All of them, down to the last one, have valuable life experiences and extraordinary resilience, and many of them also have extraordinary empathy. Because it is not easy for them to make it in a country where accessibility is often non-existent, and inclusion is still seen as an obligation.
innovations.description:
We transform people with disabilities from simple beneficiaries into authors of change. Our company previously offered the opportunity for 3 people with disabilities to complete the coaching training program. Seeing the impact on them, we decided to take the project to a much higher level.
We have confirmed a fundamental need: there are people who do not want to be defined by their limitations or viewed exclusively through the prism of compassion. Beyond these, they seek real opportunities for development, autonomy and contribution. They want to be part of a more united and inclusive “we”, a community where differences do not separate, but complement. And now we want to develop the first coaching training groups dedicated to people with disabilities, conducted entirely online and adapted to the needs of the participants. In a pragmatic sense, our project creates: ✔ Leaders of inclusion People with disabilities who become facilitators of development processes, offering support and guidance to people facing various life challenges. ✔ Representation Who can better understand the challenges of discrimination, lack of accessibility or social limitations than someone who has experienced them? ✔ Changing a social paradigm People with disabilities are still often underestimated, perceived through the lens of things they cannot do or do differently. The project changes this perspective, training professionals and leaders who inspire through competence and authenticity. ✔ Multiplied impact Each participant subsequently undertakes a minimum of 20 hours of pro-bono coaching for people with disabilities, which means that the impact of the investment continues to grow. We form a future support for dozens or even hundreds of people.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Our company previously offered the opportunity for 3 people with disabilities to complete the coaching training program. Seeing the impact on them, we decided to take the project to a much higher level.
Our program offers: New skills, professional development - for some being the first career opportunity; Increased self-confidence; Education, Communication and Leadership Tools; Education, professional training in the coaching profession. Opportunities for professional and social integration; Autonomy and independence; The possibility of transforming difficult experiences into valuable resources for others. For many participants, coaching will be the only profession in which disability is not a barrier. Being an online program, it even eliminates one of the biggest barriers they face: the inaccessibility of transportation and physical spaces. We give them the necessary resources, we have mentors ready to accompany them and we can't wait to work together!

innovations.name: AGRI-CIRC SocInoLab: Developing an innovation ecosystem and tools to support social innovation in agriculture and the circular economy.
innovations.lead: Slovenská poľnohospodárska univerzita v Nitre, 1. Regionálne Sociálne Družstvo, AGRO SOCIÁLNY PODNIK s. r. o., Druživa, o. z., Farma u Felixov s. r. o., Národná recyklačná agentúra Slovensko, Regionálna rozvojová agentúra Levicko, Služby občanom mesta Levice, s. r. o., r. s. p. (SOM Levice)
innovations.problem: Less-developed rural regions across Slovakia face severe socio-economic decline, depopulation, and limited municipal capacity, exacerbated by high structural long-term unemployment rates often exceeding 10%. Vulnerable populations, including individuals with disabilities, long-term unemployed youth (NEETs), and marginalized groups, face immense barriers to labor market integration. While social farming and the circular economy offer tremendous local development potential, their implementation has been stifled by a total absence of cross-sectoral collaboration. Standard approaches isolate farmers from social workers and disconnect waste management entities from the enterprises that could recycle and revalue those waste streams.
innovations.description: The project introduces a highly novel framework that breaks traditional sector silos by combining social farming and the circular economy into a unified, cross-sectoral regional ecosystem. Departing from traditional top-down integration models, it utilizes cutting-edge tools including gamification, artificial intelligence (AI) for innovation scouting, hybrid (online/offline) decentralized incubators, and scientific modeling. innovations.name: Empatic-HUB – Anonymous Early Listening and Restorative Intervention Model for Schools
innovations.problem: School violence, bullying and emotional vulnerability among children are increasing challenges in Romania, affecting students’ wellbeing, sense of safety and educational participation. Although the national legal framework regarding school safety and child protection has significantly improved in recent years, many schools still face difficulties in the practical implementation of prevention, reporting and intervention mechanisms. Field experience revealed inconsistent procedures, limited early intervention capacity, administrative pressure on school staff and insufficient functional anonymous reporting systems. As a result, many situations are identified late, managed reactively and escalated before coordinated support can be provided.
innovations.description:
The project was inspired by restorative education approaches, child protection frameworks and community-based prevention models promoted in the fields of education, mental health and child protection at European and international level. Relevant sources of inspiration include anti-bullying and restorative practices developed by organisations such as UNICEF, World Vision, Terre des Hommes and educational wellbeing initiatives focused on early intervention, emotional safety and participatory approaches in schools. The initiative adapted these principles to the Romanian educational context through the development of an integrated operational model combining anonymous early listening mechanisms, restorative educational interventions, teacher training and interinstitutional collaboration.
The initiative developed an integrated, community-based and restorative intervention model that combines: -anonymous early listening and reporting tools (Empatic-HUB), -emotional climate mapping, -restorative educational interventions, -applied teacher training, -parental engagement, -and interinstitutional collaboration. One of the most innovative components is Empatic-HUB, a digital anonymous listening mechanism that allows students to safely express emotional distress, conflicts or risk situations while generating aggregated data that support preventive and evidence-based interventions. The model shifts the approach from reactive and punitive responses toward early identification, emotional support, prevention and coordinated community intervention. It is designed as a scalable and replicable mechanism that helps schools operationalise existing child protection and school safety legislation in a practical and accessible way.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The initiative generated both direct community impact and practical institutional outcomes. Key results include: -over 400 teachers trained in school violence prevention and intervention; -more than 2000 student participations in awareness and restorative educational activities; -around 900 parent participations in dialogue and prevention activities; -development and pilot testing of Empatic-HUB in schools from Dolj and Olt counties; -creation of an operational guide and practical intervention tools aligned with Romanian legislation; -strengthening collaboration between schools, child protection services, social workers, psychologists, police representatives, NGOs and universities. The project contributed to: -earlier identification of emotional vulnerabilities and conflict situations; -increased awareness regarding bullying, cyberbullying and emotional wellbeing; -improved practical understanding of intervention procedures among school staff; -promotion of restorative and preventive approaches instead of exclusively punitive responses; -increased institutional dialogue regarding the operational implementation of school safety legislation. The model also generated a broader advocacy process aimed at supporting the development of more functional, preventive and community-based school safety mechanisms at national level.
The innovation was progressively scaled-up during the implementation of two complementary projects developed within the SAVE Programme (School Anti-Violence Ecosystem), coordinated by World Vision Romania and co-funded by the European Union. Initially implemented through the project “Without Barriers in a Borderless World” in schools and communities from Dolj and Olt counties, the model was later expanded through the project “From Emotions to Solutions, Beyond Barriers”, which introduced the Empatic-HUB digital early listening mechanism, extended teacher training activities, strengthened interinstitutional collaboration and supported the development of a broader advocacy process addressed to national educational authorities. The initiative also reached professionals from multiple Romanian regions through online training activities and generated interest regarding future replication and adaptation in other educational contexts.

innovations.name: FORTIFY: Empowering Greek Systems to Protect and Prevent Delinquency in Unaccompanied Minors
innovations.problem: The project addresses the need to prevent juvenile delinquency among unaccompanied minors in Greece by strengthening the capabilities of Greek practitioners and improving existing prevention systems. It responds to identified challenges, gaps, and training needs in current juvenile delinquency prevention efforts and seeks to enhance child protection measures through technical cooperation and knowledge transfer. The project also addresses the need for a better understanding of current prevention challenges, stronger professional capacities, and the adoption of effective practices tailored to the Greek context. More specifically, the project tackles: Gaps in existing juvenile delinquency prevention efforts for unaccompanied minors in Greece. Training and capacity-building needs of frontline professionals working with unaccompanied minors. Limited knowledge and understanding of current challenges and intervention needs. The need for effective child protection measures and evidence-based practices adapted to the Greek context. The need for stronger cooperation, expertise exchange, and professional networks between Greek and Norwegian stakeholders. The project’s needs assessment and mapping activities are specifically designed to identify these challenges and gaps and provide recommendations that will support future training modules and policy development.
innovations.description: The project’s innovative solution lies in its integrated approach that combines a comprehensive needs assessment and mapping of existing juvenile delinquency prevention efforts with international knowledge transfer and best-practice exchange between Greek and Norwegian partners. This approach enables a detailed understanding of the real needs and challenges faced by unaccompanied minors in Greece and supports the development of tailored child protection measures. The project further innovates by organizing study visits to Norway, compiling best-practice reports and participatory work guidelines, and translating the findings into training modules and future policy recommendations. Through collaboration with NORCAP, Greek practitioners gain exposure to effective prevention models and methodologies, helping create a robust framework for preventing juvenile delinquency among unaccompanied minors in the Greek context. In summary, the innovation stems from combining evidence-based needs mapping, cross-country expertise transfer, participatory methodologies, and capacity building into a single framework designed to strengthen prevention systems and improve outcomes for unaccompanied minors.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The key results and benefits of the FORTIFY project include: -Improved understanding of current challenges and needs related to juvenile delinquency prevention among unaccompanied minors through a comprehensive needs assessment and mapping process. -Enhanced skills and knowledge of Greek practitioners through exposure to Norwegian best practices, expertise transfer, study visits, workshops, and seminars. -Strengthened bilateral relations and professional networks between Greek and Norwegian stakeholders, promoting long-term cooperation and knowledge exchange. -Development of best-practice reports and participatory work guidelines to support the adoption of effective child protection measures tailored to the Greek context. -Actionable recommendations for addressing identified gaps and training needs, providing a foundation for future training modules and policy development. -Creation of stable, safe, and supportive environments for unaccompanied minors transitioning to adulthood, helping prevent offending behaviour. -Standardized protocols and good practices that better equip professionals to respond to the needs of unaccompanied minors. Overall, the project strengthens Greece’s capacity to prevent juvenile delinquency among unaccompanied minors by combining needs-based interventions, professional capacity building, and international knowledge transfer.

innovations.name: Educational Hub – The Art of Being Together
innovations.problem: The local community of Anina lacks a modern and inclusive space dedicated to educational, cultural, and personal development. Children, young people, adults, and seniors have limited access to non-formal learning opportunities, artistic activities, and intergenerational programs that promote social inclusion, active citizenship, emotional well-being, and community engagement. This gap reduces opportunities for personal growth, cultural participation, and meaningful connections between generations.
innovations.description:
The inspiration for the project came from the direct work with students in a school environment and from the identified need for a dedicated space where young people can learn, express themselves, and develop through non-formal education, arts, and collaborative activities. The idea emerged from practical experience within the local educational context in Anina, Romania, under the guidance of teacher Ruva Valentina Ancuța, where the lack of such a space for students was clearly observed.
The project introduces a multidisciplinary Educational Hub that combines non-formal education, arts, culture, volunteering, and intergenerational learning in a single inclusive space. By bringing together children, young people, adults, and seniors through creative, educational, and community-based activities, the Hub fosters lifelong learning, social cohesion, emotional intelligence, and active participation. This integrated approach creates a sustainable model that can be replicated in other communities facing similar challenges.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The Educational Hub approach was implemented as a pilot in the community of Anina, Romania, through five completed educational and cultural activities. The model was adapted to the local context, involving children, young people, adults, and seniors in intergenerational learning and community engagement. The experience provides a practical example of how non-formal education, arts, and volunteering can be combined to strengthen social cohesion at local level.
The project will establish a modern Educational Hub serving as a community center for learning, creativity, and social engagement. At least 50 direct beneficiaries and more than 50 volunteers will participate in educational, cultural, and artistic activities, developing civic, digital, cultural, and interpersonal skills. The project will strengthen community cohesion, encourage active citizenship and volunteering, promote social inclusion, and create lasting opportunities for intergenerational collaboration and personal development.

innovations.name: WISE – Supporting Ukrainian Refugee Women’s Socio-Economic Integration and Wellbeing
innovations.problem: UA refugee women face unique socio-economic integration challenges in IT and BG. Their higher education and skills contrast with the low-skilled, part-time jobs they secure due to language barriers and a mismatch between qualifications and available jobs (European Commission, 2023). In the context of forced displacement and forced conscription of UA men, women have no choice but to be fully responsible for caring responsibilities of children and elderly relatives. This limits women's labour market participation (UN Women and UNFPA, 2022), with 33% of women unable to work due to care obligations (FRA, Eurofound, 2023). Refugee women socio-economic integration is strongly correlated to their MH: on the one hand difficulties in accessing the labour market negatively impact their MH, by hindering their self-esteem and sense of belonging to their community (FRA, Eurofound, 2023). innovations.name: Design for Change România
innovations.problem: Romanian schools continue to prioritise academic performance and standardised outcomes, often leaving limited space for students to develop agency, empathy and the confidence to act on the challenges they see around them. As a result, many young people move through education as recipients of information rather than active contributors to their communities. At the same time, teachers face increasing pressure to prepare students for a rapidly changing world while lacking practical tools that foster collaboration, problem-solving, civic engagement and student participation. This challenge is particularly visible in vulnerable communities, where educational disparities, low literacy levels and school dropout rates remain significant concerns. Design for Change Romania responds to this need by equipping teachers with a proven framework that transforms students from passive learners into changemakers, helping them identify real-life challenges, develop solutions and take meaningful action in their schools and communities.
innovations.description:
Design for Change (DFC) is a global educational movement founded in India in 2009 by educator and social entrepreneur Kiran Bir Sethi. Today, the movement is active in more than 70 countries, empowering children and young people to become changemakers in their schools and communities through a simple yet powerful framework: Feel, Imagine, Do and Share (FIDS). Rather than positioning students as passive recipients of knowledge, DFC encourages them to identify challenges that matter to them, develop solutions and take meaningful action while building empathy, creativity, collaboration and civic engagement.
Design for Change Romania combines a globally validated methodology with a scalable national implementation model that enables teachers to bring student-led changemaking into everyday classroom practice. At the core of the programme is the FIDS framework (Feel, Imagine, Do, Share), which helps students identify challenges that matter to them, develop solutions and take action in their schools and communities. Rather than positioning students as passive recipients of knowledge, the methodology encourages agency, empathy, collaboration and civic participation through real-life projects. What makes the Romanian model innovative is the ecosystem built around the methodology. Teachers are supported through face-to-face training, mentoring, implementation resources, an online learning platform and a growing community of practice. Through dfc.raa.ro, educators can access learning materials, connect with peers and share their Stories of Change, contributing to a national and global network of changemakers. By combining teacher capacity building, digital learning, peer support and storytelling, the programme creates a sustainable and highly adaptable model that can be implemented across different educational levels, subjects and community contexts.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
During the first phase of implementation, Design for Change Romania engaged more than 60 schools, 872 registered teachers and over 12,000 students. More than 615 teachers participated in face-to-face training activities, while 755 educators enrolled in the online course and over 300 Stories of Change were shared through the national platform. Beyond these figures, the programme helped teachers adopt more student-centred approaches and created opportunities for children and young people to become active participants in their learning process. Students developed skills such as empathy, collaboration, communication, problem-solving and civic engagement by addressing real challenges in their schools and communities. Teachers reported increased curiosity, initiative and confidence among their students, as well as a greater willingness to listen to others, work together and take responsibility for improving their environment. Many educators observed that children became more attentive to the needs of those around them and more confident in expressing their ideas. In some cases, parents also noticed positive changes, describing their children as more empathetic, aware of others and motivated to contribute to their communities. The project also created a growing national community of educators connected to the global Design for Change movement, enabling teachers and students to learn from one another, share practices and inspire new Stories of Change across different regions of Romania.
The methodology has gained international recognition for its contribution to student agency and participatory learning. Its impact has been explored through research conducted by institutions such as Harvard Project Zero and Stanford University, highlighting its potential to strengthen problem-solving, empathy, confidence, collaboration and students’ belief in their ability to create change. More info about DfC: https://dfcworld.org/SITE

innovations.name: MOVE Methodology: Turning Local Ideas into Lasting Change
innovations.problem: MOVE addresses the structural cycle of poverty and economic exclusion affecting vulnerable communities in Portuguese-speaking developing countries.MOVE addresses the structural cycle of poverty and economic exclusion affecting vulnerable communities in Portuguese-speaking developing countries. In the regions where MOVE operates — rural Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé e Príncipe, and Timor-Leste — the dominant development model has historically relied on passive assistance: one-off donations, food distribution, and subsidy dependency. While these interventions address immediate needs, they fail to generate lasting change. Communities remain trapped in cycles of dependence, with no tools to create stable, autonomous income. The root causes MOVE targets are threefold. First, the near-total absence of financial literacy and basic business management skills among the adult population, compounded in contexts like Guinea-Bissau by high illiteracy rates and complex linguistic barriers. Second, the complete lack of access to business development support — the incubation, mentorship, and market-access infrastructure that entrepreneurs in developed economies take for granted simply does not exist in these communities. Third, the absence of formal market connections, meaning that even when local people develop viable products or services, they have no structured channel to reach customers, validate demand, or grow sustainably. The result is a paradox: communities with enormous human potential, resilience, and entrepreneurial drive, but no ecosystem to convert that potential into economic stability. MOVE exists precisely to build that ecosystem — from the ground up, inside the community, one entrepreneur at a time.
innovations.description: MOVE's innovation lies in a radical departure from the traditional aid model — replacing passive assistance with an integrated, community-embedded entrepreneurship system that accompanies each person from first idea to full business independence. innovations.name: HuSI - HUB sociálnych inovácií (Social Innovation HUB)
innovations.lead: Katolícka univerzita v Ružomberku, Focus Hub s. r. o., INOVIA, OZ „Partnerstvo pre MAS Dolný Liptov“
innovations.problem: The Žilina Region, particularly the Lower Liptov sub-region, faces a long-term structural absence of coordinating infrastructure and methodological support for social innovation development. Local communities, non-profit organizations, and social entrepreneurs struggle with a lack of expert know-how, professionalization, and networking platforms, preventing them from transforming good concepts into viable, sustainable projects. This systemic deficit directly worsens the status of vulnerable groups in the labour market – particularly inactive youth (NEETs) who have fallen out of both the education and employment systems, elderly individuals (seniors) at risk of isolation, and people experiencing social exclusion.
innovations.description: The innovative approach consists of introducing a structured, cross-sectoral model based on the "Six Stages of Social Innovation" methodology (Murray et al., 2010), deployed via a quadruple helix partnership (academia-NGOs-private sector-local action groups). The support flow is split into two sequential phases: the Incubator (idea generation, prototyping, and small-scale validation) and the Accelerator (focused on intensive development, commercialization, and scaling to achieve a measurable social impact). This entire framework is anchored by the launch of a digital Solutions Portal (acting as a knowledge base and digital library of best practices) and five extensive interactive facilitation workshops executed directly in the field, breaking down traditional boundaries between academic research and practical community application.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: Katolícka univerzita v Ružomberku, Focus Hub s. r. o., INOVIA, OZ „Partnerstvo pre MAS Dolný Liptov“
innovations.evidence:
The key results and benefits of the project include:
The establishment of a functional physical and digital HUB infrastructure, serving as a primary contact and consulting hub for regional innovators.
The elaboration of an in-depth, data-driven regional analysis focused on the key drivers behind the NEETs situation in the Žilina Self-Governing Region, including the formulation of targeted preventative measures.
Enhanced professional capacity and skills (project management, social entrepreneurship, creativity) of dozens of employees and ecosystem actors through specialized seminars.
The deployment of a permanent online platform (Solutions Portal), ensuring open access to and transfer of verified best practices and know-how for other municipalities and regions across Slovakia, thereby verifiably increasing the market readiness and employability of target groups.
authors: Katolícka univerzita v Ružomberku, Focus Hub s. r. o., INOVIA, OZ „Partnerstvo pre MAS Dolný Liptov“

innovations.name: Rainbow Urban Garden – Growing Communities Through Nature-Based Learning
innovations.problem: Children and families are increasingly disconnected from nature, while urban communities often lack accessible spaces that promote environmental awareness, wellbeing, social interaction and experiential learning. At the same time, educational systems frequently provide limited opportunities for hands-on, outdoor and community-based learning that supports social-emotional development, environmental responsibility and active citizenship. Rainbow Urban Garden addresses these challenges by creating an inclusive urban learning ecosystem where children, families, educators and community members can reconnect with nature, learn together and contribute to a more sustainable and resilient community.
innovations.description: Rainbow Urban Garden transforms an urban green space into a living laboratory for education, wellbeing and community engagement. The initiative combines nature-based learning, Montessori-inspired education, permaculture principles, nonviolent communication and community participation into a single integrated model. Children learn through direct experience, exploration and environmental stewardship, while families, educators and volunteers actively contribute to the development of the space. The project demonstrates how underutilised urban areas can become vibrant educational ecosystems that simultaneously support learning, wellbeing, sustainability and social cohesion.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: • Established one of the first urban educational gardens in Cluj-Napoca dedicated to nature-based learning. • Engaged hundreds of children, parents, educators and community members through educational, cultural and environmental activities since 2019. • Created a permanent outdoor learning environment that supports social-emotional development, environmental awareness and active citizenship. • Developed practical learning experiences based on gardening, biodiversity, sustainability and community participation. • Increased opportunities for intergenerational learning and community involvement. • Demonstrated a replicable model for transforming urban green spaces into educational and community assets.

innovations.name: A New Life in the Lumea Nouă
innovations.problem: The project addresses a complex set of social, economic, educational, health and housing-related challenges affecting people and families at risk of poverty and social exclusion in the marginalized urban community of Lumea Nouă, Alba Iulia. The community faces low employment levels, insufficient professional skills required by the labour market, limited access to social, medical and educational services, poor housing conditions, reduced participation in education and a high risk of discrimination and social marginalization. A significant number of adults are unemployed or economically inactive and lack qualifications aligned with labour market demands. Their limited access to career guidance, counselling, training and employment support services reduces their chances of obtaining stable income and contributes to the persistence of poverty and dependency. Children and young people experience barriers in accessing and participating in education, which increases the risk of school dropout, low educational attainment and reduced opportunities for future social and professional integration. At the same time, poor housing conditions and the lack of integrated social, medical, educational and community-based services contribute to the persistence of vulnerability and exclusion. Limited awareness of employment opportunities, housing-related rights and responsibilities, anti-discrimination measures and the benefits of multiculturalism further restricts the community’s ability to actively participate in local social and economic development.
innovations.description: The project introduced an integrated, family-centred model of social inclusion, combining employment, education, healthcare, social services, housing and community development measures within a single coordinated intervention. Instead of addressing individual needs separately, the project focused on the entire family unit, recognising that poverty and social exclusion are generated by multiple interconnected challenges affecting children, young people, adults and elderly family members at the same time. A key innovative element of the project was the combination of direct support services with a major housing intervention. To address inadequate living conditions and housing insecurity, the project included the construction of a social housing building with 21 apartments, providing safe, adequate and sustainable accommodation for vulnerable families from the Lumea Nouă community. This housing investment was not implemented as an isolated infrastructure measure, but as part of a broader pathway towards social inclusion. Beneficiaries were also supported through educational assistance, employment counselling, vocational guidance, healthcare services, social support, anti-discrimination measures and community participation activities. The integrated approach allowed families to benefit simultaneously from tailored services addressing their specific needs. Children and young people received support for education and social participation, adults were assisted in improving their employability and access to the labour market, while vulnerable family members benefited from social, medical and community-based support. By combining housing, essential services and active inclusion measures, the project addressed both immediate needs and structural causes of vulnerability. The solution contributed to improving living conditions, strengthening family resilience, increasing access to opportunities, reducing social exclusion and supporting the long-term integration of vulnerable families into the social and economic life of Alba Iulia.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: KEY RESULTS The project delivered a comprehensive package of integrated interventions addressing employment, education, healthcare, social inclusion, housing and community development challenges in the marginalized urban area of Lumea Nouă, Alba Iulia. More than 720 vulnerable individuals participated in integrated support measures. 360 participants received career guidance and professional counselling services aimed at identifying employment opportunities and developing individualized pathways towards labour market integration. 180 participants attended vocational training courses in occupations relevant to local and regional labour market demand. 180 participants benefited from employment mediation services, including job matching, employer engagement and support during the recruitment process. 90 participants successfully entered employment. 455 individuals received social and socio-medical services tailored to their specific needs. 200 individuals accessed specialized medical services and health-related interventions. 30 children benefited from integrated educational support, including after-school activities and educational therapy designed to improve school participation and educational performance. 720 community members participated in awareness-raising campaigns, educational activities, sports events, volunteering actions and initiatives promoting multiculturalism and non-discrimination. A multifunctional centre was established to provide integrated social, medical, educational and cultural services at community level. A social housing building comprising 21 apartments was constructed, creating improved housing opportunities for vulnerable families living in inadequate conditions. Strong local cooperation mechanisms were developed between public authorities, educational institutions, social service providers, healthcare professionals and community stakeholders. BENEFITS The project generated long-term benefits extending beyond the immediate outputs achieved during implementation. Increased employability and labour market participation among vulnerable adults through improved skills, qualifications and access to employment opportunities. Higher household incomes and improved economic stability for families whose members obtained employment. Reduced dependence on social assistance and increased capacity for self-sufficiency among beneficiaries. Improved access to healthcare services, contributing to better health outcomes and increased awareness of preventive care. Enhanced educational participation and development opportunities for children, reducing the risk of school dropout and intergenerational poverty. Improved housing conditions and greater residential stability for vulnerable families through access to social housing. Strengthened family resilience through a family-centred approach that addressed multiple needs simultaneously. Increased social inclusion and community participation among vulnerable groups, including people facing discrimination and social marginalization. innovations.name: Living Heritage for Social Inclusion
innovations.problem: Many rural communities in Europe face social isolation, ageing populations, limited access to cultural and social services, weak intergenerational links and a lack of meaningful participation opportunities for children, older people and people with disabilities. At the same time, local cultural heritage, traditional skills and community knowledge often remain underused as practical resources for wellbeing, inclusion and resilience.
innovations.description: The innovative programme solution is a community-based “living heritage” model that integrates social services, cultural education, traditional crafts, folklore, local food, nature-based activities and intergenerational learning into one practical inclusion programme. Instead of treating cultural heritage as a separate cultural activity, the model uses it as a method for strengthening wellbeing, participation, skills, identity and community resilience among children, families, older people and people with disabilities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The main results include stronger social inclusion, improved emotional wellbeing, increased participation of children, older people and people with disabilities, and better intergenerational cooperation in the rural community. The programme also preserves and activates local cultural heritage, develops practical skills, strengthens community identity and creates a transferable model that can be adapted by other rural communities in Europe.

innovations.name: Língua do Vagar
innovations.lead: Alves & Ferreira – Business Consulting and Solutions
innovations.problem: The project addresses the gradual loss of linguistic expressions, oral histories, and cultural knowledge associated with the Alentejo concept of Vagar. As demographic change, urbanization, and globalization reshape communities, many words, stories, and ways of understanding time and social life are disappearing without being documented or transmitted to younger generations. At the same time, existing linguistic and heritage initiatives tend to document language in a technical or archival way, without capturing the lived experiences, personal testimonies, and artistic expressions that give these concepts meaning. Língua do Vagar responds to this gap by creating a participatory, intergenerational process that preserves, interprets, and shares this unique cultural heritage through both physical and digital formats, ensuring its accessibility for future generations.
innovations.description: Língua do Vagar introduces an innovative approach to safeguarding cultural heritage by using a cultural concept—Vagar—as the starting point for linguistic and artistic exploration, rather than focusing on language documentation alone. The project combines community participation, oral history, audiovisual storytelling, artistic creation, and digital technologies to create a living, multimedia archive of cultural knowledge. Unlike traditional dictionaries or heritage inventories, each entry is enriched with personal testimonies, audio and video recordings, and connections to literature, music, theatre, and visual arts. The project's intergenerational methodology brings together different age groups to co-create knowledge, while its digital platform ensures long-term accessibility and engagement. This model is designed to be replicable, allowing other communities and regions to document and celebrate their own cultural concepts using the same framework.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Alves & Ferreira – Business Consulting and Solutions
innovations.evidence: Língua do Vagar will deliver lasting cultural, social, and educational benefits by preserving a unique element of Alentejo's intangible heritage while creating new forms of community participation and cultural engagement. Key results include the creation of a multimedia Dictionary of Vagar, an open-access digital platform, the collection of more than 250 audiovisual testimonies, the documentation of 150–180 linguistic and cultural entries, and the active involvement of over 700 participants across multiple generations and communities. The project will also generate new artistic works, educational resources, podcasts, and public events, extending its reach far beyond the initial programme. The initiative strengthens intergenerational dialogue by connecting younger and older generations through shared cultural knowledge, helping to prevent the loss of local language, traditions, and collective memory. It also increases the visibility of Alentejo's cultural identity nationally and internationally through its connection to Évora 2027 European Capital of Culture. Beyond its immediate outputs, the project establishes an innovative and replicable methodology for documenting cultural concepts through language, storytelling, and community participation. This creates long-term value by providing a model that can be adapted by other regions and communities seeking to preserve and activate their own intangible cultural heritage. Expected outcomes include enhanced social cohesion, greater community pride and cultural participation, increased access to heritage resources through digital technologies, and the creation of a sustainable cultural asset with educational, research, tourism, and international collaboration potential.

innovations.name: Join Us on Board Your Career
innovations.problem: Many young people and adults across Europe face difficulties entering or re-entering the labour market due to a mismatch between the skills they acquire through education and those demanded by employers. Traditional education and training pathways often provide limited practical experience, insufficient career guidance, and weak connections with industry, resulting in delayed employment and underutilisation of talent. At the same time, the aviation sector faces recurring shortages of qualified cabin crew personnel and requires candidates who possess both specialised technical competencies and strong interpersonal skills. Access to these career opportunities is often limited by a lack of specialised training, recognised certification, and direct recruitment channels. Universifly addresses this dual challenge by reducing the gap between vocational education and employment. The initiative improves access to industry-relevant skills, enhances employability, and creates structured pathways towards stable and internationally recognised careers, particularly for young people, recent graduates, and individuals seeking professional reconversion.
innovations.description: UNIVERSIFLY introduces an innovative approach to vocational education by integrating training, certification, employability development, and direct access to recruitment opportunities within a single pathway. Rather than providing education in isolation, the project connects learners directly with labour market needs, ensuring that skills development leads to concrete employment outcomes. UNIVERSIFLY has developed an innovative, market-driven training and employment model that bridges the gap between vocational education and labour market needs in the aviation sector. The initiative combines professional cabin crew training, practical simulation-based learning, soft-skills development, and direct recruitment pathways into a single integrated programme. The innovation lies not only in the training itself, but in the creation of a complete employability ecosystem. Participants acquire industry-recognised qualifications while simultaneously developing transversal skills such as communication, teamwork, intercultural awareness, problem-solving, and customer service. Through close cooperation with airlines and industry stakeholders, training content is continuously aligned with current workforce demands. Unlike traditional vocational programmes that focus primarily on certification, UNIVERSIFLY supports learners throughout the entire journey from skills acquisition to employment. This integrated approach reduces barriers to labour market entry, accelerates professional integration, and increases access to international career opportunities. By transforming vocational training from a purely educational service into a comprehensive employability ecosystem, UNIVERSIFLY delivers a more effective and socially impactful response to workforce development challenges. By combining education, practical experience, and employer engagement, UNIVERSIFLY offers a scalable and replicable solution that addresses both skills shortages in the aviation industry and employability challenges faced by young people and adults seeking career transitions.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: UNIVERSIFLY has generated measurable outcomes in improving employability and facilitating access to international career opportunities in the aviation sector. Key results include: 1. Training and certification of a large number of aspiring cabin crew professionals through programmes aligned with European aviation standards. 2. Successful integration of graduates into the labour market through direct recruitment opportunities with national and international airlines. 3. Increased employability of participants through the development of both technical aviation competencies and transferable skills such as communication, teamwork, customer service, and intercultural awareness. 4. Creation of a sustainable link between vocational training and employer needs, reducing the gap between education and employment. 5. Support for professional mobility by enabling graduates to access career opportunities across multiple European and international markets. 6. Demonstration of a scalable training-to-employment model that can be adapted to other sectors facing skills shortages and workforce development challenges. In figures, there are the following numbers: - 1882 of people trained, out of which 569 through the European project; - 95% employed after graduation, the rest of 5% either followed another form of study or started a family; - 8 partner airlines (Ryanair, Wizz Air, Hisky, Emirates, Fly Dubai, Flynas, Gulf Air); - 25 countries where graduates are employed; - 12 years of operation.
