innovations.name: More than Boxing-Training for Life
innovations.problem: Vulnerable young people - in addiction recovery, refugees, Roma, young people with disabilities, those without family support or living with abuse - often remain trapped in marginalisation, isolation and sometimes crime, without any support they can trust. For many, the need for power and the built-up frustration find no healthy outlet and turn into violence, on the streets or against themselves. Conventional social programmes struggle to reach them for two reasons. First, because they require young people from the outset to see themselves as "beneficiaries" or "cases" and to enter dedicated services, separate from the rest of the community, which stigmatises them further instead of including them. Second, because they put forward specialists whom young people do not feel are close to their reality, so they do not open up and the support has no effect. The result is a paradox: the very young people who most need counselling, therapy and mentoring are the ones who reach them least. And beyond services, they lack exactly what can keep them on the right path: a real community that accepts them and in which they can belong.
innovations.description: The innovation of More Than Boxing lies not in the activities themselves, but in reversing the order and dismantling segregation. We reverse the order. Conventional programmes start with therapy; we start with sport. Through boxing, young people first gain trust in adults, in the coaches who train them, and only then does the way open towards counselling, therapy and mentoring. Sport is not the goal, but the gateway to real support. Moreover, boxing meets a need that other programmes ignore: it offers a healthy outlet for the need for power and for built-up frustration, including for those living with abuse, turning a force otherwise directed towards violence into a driver of discipline. We dismantle segregation. No one enters as a "beneficiary" or a "case". Vulnerable young people and young people from stable families train together, without labels, in an environment where everyone discovers they are more than a problem. Normality itself becomes the intervention: inclusion is no longer a service, but a reality lived every day. And the impact runs both ways: young people without difficulties learn from an early age to accept and include others, becoming a resource themselves. We replace the distant specialist with the relatable role model. Many of the coaches have been through similar struggles. Young people open up to them because they are facing people who understand from experience, not from theory, a trust impossible to gain any other way. All of this works because PHONEO acts as the coordination point of an ecosystem of specialised partners, building an integrated journey around each young person, instead of separate services.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Around 150 young people are currently in the programme, half of them in vulnerable situations, and the number is growing. For vulnerable young people: access to counselling, therapy and mentoring they would not otherwise have reached; reduced risk behaviours and violence, by channelling frustration in a safe setting; greater self-confidence and stability; real bonds within a community that accepts them. For young people without difficulties: learning, from an early age, to accept and include others, becoming a resource for them themselves. At community level: real integration of young people in recovery, refugees, Roma and marginalised youth alongside the others, without segregation; a generation that learns to include. Recognition and validation: First Prize at the Cluj Youth Gala 2025 and the trophy for the "Social Inclusion and Diversity" category, awarded by the Cluj Youth Federation; PHONEO is a licensed Duke of Edinburgh's International Award centre since 2023; a team with lived experience and partnerships with specialised organisations. For those who wish, the programme also opens a path towards competitive sport, through professional partner clubs.

innovations.name: Maior Idade
innovations.problem: Like many European communities, the Municipality of Ílhavo faces the challenges associated with an ageing population. Many older adults experience social isolation, loneliness, reduced participation in community life and limited opportunities for lifelong learning and personal development. Age-related stereotypes and discrimination can also contribute to the exclusion of older people from social, cultural and civic activities. At the same time, ageing is often viewed through a deficit-based perspective, overlooking the knowledge, experience and contributions that older adults can bring to their communities. Maior Idade was created to address these challenges by promoting active ageing, social participation, intergenerational connections and opportunities for learning, creativity and community engagement throughout later life.
innovations.description: Maior Idade offers an integrated and community-based approach to ageing through three complementary spaces that address different dimensions of later life: research and knowledge, health and environmental awareness, and social participation and inclusion. Rather than focusing solely on care or recreational activities, the programme actively involves older adults in learning, research, creative projects, environmental initiatives and community life. Through the Ageing Lab, older adults engage with researchers, professionals and organisations to contribute to new knowledge and innovative approaches to ageing. Fórum Maior Idade promotes active lifestyles and environmental engagement, including the development of a community garden. Sala de Estar provides opportunities for social connection, digital inclusion and cognitive stimulation. By combining community participation, intergenerational exchange, research, creativity and lifelong learning, Maior Idade promotes a more positive, active and inclusive vision of ageing, recognising older adults as active contributors to society rather than passive recipients of support.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Maior Idade has established itself as a reference programme for active ageing within the Municipality of Ílhavo, reaching more than 400 participants through a wide range of initiatives developed across its three community hubs. Among its key achievements is the creation of the Ageing Lab, an innovative space dedicated to research, knowledge-sharing and creativity in the field of ageing. The programme also established a Gerontological Library, making books, publications and research on ageing and longevity freely accessible to professionals, students, researchers and the wider community. The programme has created opportunities for older adults to engage in activities that are rarely associated with ageing programmes, including environmental projects, community gardening, artistic creation, digital literacy, research initiatives and intergenerational experiences. By bringing together local authorities, social organisations, researchers, artists and citizens, Maior Idade has helped strengthen local networks and promote a broader understanding of ageing as a stage of life that continues to offer opportunities for learning, participation and contribution to society.

Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: AugmentAble - Digital Accessibility Tool
innovations.problem: Millions of people with disabilities encounter barriers when accessing websites, online services, education platforms, and public information. Despite existing accessibility standards, many organisations lack the expertise, resources, or awareness needed to identify and address accessibility issues effectively. Accessibility evaluations often require specialist knowledge and can be difficult for non experts to interpret. As digital services become increasingly essential for participation in society, inaccessible design can contribute to exclusion from education, employment, public services, and everyday life. Augmentable addresses this challenge by making accessibility evaluation and understanding more accessible to a wider audience.
innovations.description: Augmentable combines AI assisted accessibility evaluation with clear explanations and educational support. Instead of only identifying technical issues, the platform helps users understand why accessibility barriers matter, who is affected, and how they can be resolved. By making accessibility knowledge more understandable and actionable, the project lowers barriers to improving digital inclusion.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Augmentable has successfully developed a functional prototype that demonstrates the potential of AI assisted accessibility evaluation. The solution has been tested with the Institute for Integration at Johannes Kepler University Linz and with the Upper Austrian Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired, providing valuable feedback from both accessibility experts and representatives of the target group. The project has increased awareness of digital accessibility, demonstrated practical applications of AI for inclusion, and shown how accessibility findings can be communicated more effectively to non experts. The solution has the potential to help organisations improve digital accessibility while reducing barriers for people with disabilities.

innovations.name: Hacker School @yourschool
innovations.problem: Digital Skills & Pedagogical Gap: Schools struggle to integrate practical, up-to-date IT education into the curriculum. Teachers often lack the specialized technical knowledge, resources, and time to teach modern programming and AI concepts. Lack of Industry Exposure: Young people rarely have direct contact with real IT professionals. This leads to abstract, often skewed perceptions of tech careers and perpetuates the IT skill shortage. Socio-Economic Entry Barriers: Extracurricular IT courses often exclude students who lack intrinsic motivation, supportive home environments, or financial means. This disproportionately affects girls and youth from disadvantaged backgrounds (e.g., schools with a low social index).
innovations.description: Hacker School @yourschool addresses the digital education gap through an expert-led volunteering model that brings active IT professionals, university students, and apprentices directly into classrooms as authentic role models. To ensure inclusivity, these modular 4-hour workshops take place during regular school hours and are entirely free of charge for participating schools and students. This zero-barrier approach - funded through targeted fundraising, public grants, and corporate CSR partnerships - ensures the program reaches youth who might otherwise never participate in extracurricular IT activities. We utilize standardized, ready-to-use practical modules (such as MakeCode Arcade, HTML/CSS, or Python) paired with dedicated AI modules. In today's era of rapidly advancing Artificial Intelligence, foundational programming knowledge is essential. While AI tools are becoming ubiquitous, understanding underlying coding concepts is what enables young people to transition from passive consumers of algorithms to active, critical creators. Grasping this underlying logic empowers students to understand, evaluate, and steer AI outputs, allowing them to confidently participate in shaping the digital future rather than simply being shaped by it.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
For Students: By working directly with practitioners, students develop foundational computational thinking and problem-solving skills. Furthermore, the authentic interaction with industry professionals provides realistic career orientation, helping young people - especially those from underrepresented groups - visualize themselves in technical roles. This practical success fosters a sense of self-efficacy in digital environments. For Teachers & Schools: The project actively relieves the pressure on educators who often lack the capacity, time, or specialized technical know-how required for modern digital education. It enables teachers to facilitate authentic, cutting-edge industry insights for their students without having to prepare or deliver complex IT curricula themselves. This model bypasses the bottleneck of lengthy curriculum preparation while gradually building the schools' internal confidence to engage with computational concepts. For Society & Industry: The initiative offers a structured pathway for companies to engage in impactful Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) by allowing employees to volunteer during working hours. For the volunteers (the "Inspirers"), it enhances their own communication and mentoring skills. On a macro level, the project addresses the systemic shortage of IT professionals by structurally widening the talent pool and encouraging a more diverse generation of students to consider STEM pathways.
Our April 2024 expansion validates our international scalability. Driven by a critical shortage of 28,000 IT specialists, the move was spearheaded by Stefanie Susser. A former core team member of Hacker School Germany, she relocated to Austria to ensure direct knowledge transfer. By establishing a 100% subsidiary (Hacker School Austria gGmbH) and forging local partnerships - like training FH Salzburg students as volunteer "Inspirers" - we successfully adapted our zero-barrier workshops to a new national framework, proving the model's potential for broader European adoption.

innovations.name: Work Aid Kit — Neurodiversity Inclusion for the Workplace
innovations.problem: In Romania, neurodivergent adults — including those with autism, ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions — face near-total exclusion from the labour market. A 2025 national study by Autism Voice and MKOR research agency found that approximately 90% of neurodivergent adults in Romania are unemployed or economically inactive, significantly above the European average (where only 10% of autistic adults are in full-time employment, compared to 74% of the general population). This exclusion is driven by four interconnected problems: At the individual level, neurodivergent people often lack structured support to identify their strengths, navigate recruitment processes and transition into the workplace. Standard hiring practices — unstructured interviews, implicit social communication expectations, sensory-unfriendly environments — systematically disadvantage them, regardless of their actual capabilities. innovations.name: Social Innovation: A Hospice Care Day Centre as a Community-Based Social Service for Palliative and Hospice Care Patients
innovations.problem: The problems this project addresses are - social isolation of the target group, excessive burden on relatives, insufficient availability of support at home, and an underdeveloped end-of-life care system.
innovations.description:
Integrated, interdisciplinary and human approach to palliative care, filling a crucial gap between inpatient and home care services.
The inspiration is rooted in experience exchange visits that were made to Austria (HOSPIZ AUSTRIA model (ÖBIG 2004)) where a well-developed and diverse hospice care system is in place.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
The main result we are seeking to achieve is – a paradigm shift in how we, as a society, perceive end-of-life care. Practical results and benefits: 1. At least 660 social care episodes of the target group (adults with an incurable illness whose life expectancy has been assessed by a medical council as up to 6 months and retirement-age people, including people with dementia) 2. Not less than 20 unique individuals that have received Hospice day care center services; 3. Fully functioning multi-disciplinary team and support network of social care staff, medical care staff and volunteers 4. Elaborated and adapted group training programmes as for professionals to be in palliative care as well as for relatives of patients in palliative or hospice care on the subjects of holistic care, psychological, spiritual support in the care process and practical care approaches and instruments.
This innovation has been modified in scale and the services that are provided have been slightly modified to fit the needs of the target group that has never before in Latvia experienced this kind of holistic care services outside their living space. Currently the project is located in the heart of the capital city of Latvia - Riga, near the Monument of Freedom, the Cabinet of Ministers and the most beautiful parks of the city - to place the patients in the center of attention that they deserve.

innovations.name: Digital Pathways to Employment: Tech Your Future & DigitHer
innovations.problem: The projects address a set of interconnected and structural challenges affecting both individuals and labour markets in Italy’s digital transition. First, many young people, particularly those classified as NEET and women, face persistent barriers to accessing quality employment. These barriers go beyond technical skill gaps and include limited professional networks, low confidence, weak job-search capabilities, and difficulties navigating recruitment processes. As a result, a significant share of young talent remains disconnected from emerging opportunities, even in sectors with strong demand. Second, there is a systemic mismatch between labour market demand and available talent. While companies across Italy report shortages of entry-level digital profiles (1 in 3 positions is hard-to-fill in 2025 - source: Unioncamere, Italy is 18th out of 28 EU countries for “above” basic digital skills - DESI), many young people lack access to pathways that provide not only relevant technical skills, but also a direct connection to employers (0,7 mln young people unemployed, and almost 2 mln NEET - source: Istat). Traditional education and training systems often fail to bridge this gap, resulting in parallel trends of unfilled vacancies and underemployment. Third, the projects address the underrepresentation of women in digital and technology careers, which remains a persistent challenge across Europe (17pp in employment rate gender gap, with only 16% of women among ICT specialists in Italy - source: Eurostat). Women face a combination of structural and socio-cultural barriers, including gender stereotypes, lack of exposure to role models, confidence gaps, and unequal access to targeted training and career pathways. These factors limit both individual opportunities and the diversity of the digital workforce. These challenges reinforce each other, creating a system in which disadvantaged groups are excluded from labour market opportunities, while employers struggle to access diverse and job-ready talent. The key problem is therefore not only a lack of skills, but the absence of an effective, inclusive system that connects training, support, and employer demand into a coherent pathway to employment. The innovation of the projects lies in addressing this system-level failure holistically, by designing an integrated approach that simultaneously tackles skills development, employability barriers, and labour market access, with a strong focus on inclusion and measurable employment outcomes.
innovations.description:
The projects build on Generation's global training-to-employment methodology, launched to reduce the gap between education systems and labour-market needs through short, intensive, profession-specific programmes linked to employer demand. The approach was adapted to the Italian context and to the specific objectives of the Fondo per la Repubblica Digitale. DigitHer also integrated Valore D's experience on gender empowerment and women's participation in the labour market.
The projects introduce a practical and scalable way to connect digital training with real employment opportunities, focused on groups that are often excluded from traditional pathways into the labour market. At the core is Generation Italy’s training-to-employment model, which integrates all key steps required to move learners into jobs within a single, coherent pathway. The model starts from a clear understanding of employer demand, identifying specific entry-level roles in the digital economy where there are concrete hiring needs. Training programmes are then designed (together with the employers) around these roles and delivered as intensive, full-time bootcamps, accessible free of charge and fully online, enabling participation from across the country. The implementation of the model is supported by a public–private–philanthropic funding structure through the Fondo per la Repubblica Digitale. This innovative mechanism brings together public policy objectives with public, private and philanthropic resources, enabling large-scale investment in digital skills while maintaining a strong focus on measurable outcomes and social impact. It also creates a framework for collaboration between institutions, training providers and employers, aligning incentives across actors involved in skills development and labour market integration. Other key distinctive and innovative elements of the Fund, from both a policy and an operational perspectives, are : i) Pay per performance mechanism, meaning the actual funding received was proportional to the target level reached, both in terms of training and employment outcome (i.e.  if you trained only an x% of the target, you will receive only x% of the agreed amount of funding); ii) Proof of scalability: clear focus on demonstrating that the model can scale: for wave 2 projects in the continuation call, the Fund required at least a +75% increase in ambition, we applied with a 3x objective vs first wave ; iii) Impact measurement taking into consideration placement outcome and characteristics (type of contract, salary earned, job role); iv) counterfactual analysis to prove whether projects are really delivering meaningful results (and adding value vs other initiatives) Another distinctive element of the approach is the combination of technical training with structured support on employability. Learners develop job-specific digital skills, communication, problem-solving and workplace readiness, supported by mentoring, coaching and continuous progress monitoring. For the DigitHer cohorts only, an additional module was added, focused on female empowerment, including also role model in-class testimony to instill self-confidence in their professional and personal potential. This allows participants with different starting points to remain engaged, complete the programme, prepare effectively for recruitment processes, and finally get placed into a job. Employer engagement is embedded throughout the model. Companies contribute to shaping the training content and are directly involved in the placement phase, creating a clear link between learning and hiring. Participants benefit from structured placement support, including interview preparation and direct access to job opportunities aligned with the skills acquired. Generation Italy operates within the wider Generation network, active across multiple countries and built around a shared methodology for improving employment outcomes at scale. innovations.evidence:
The innovation has been scaled up in scope and reach in Italy through follow-on initiatives and proposals, including Tech Your Future+ and DigitHer+ (calls for wave 2 of DigitHer and Tech Your Future: proposals have been submitted, awaiting outcome), expanding the number of classes, beneficiary targets and professional pathways. The broader Generation methodology is also transferable across countries and sectors, while the specific Italian model has been adapted across different target groups and digital professions
Across Tech Your Future and DigitHer, the model was implemented at national scale, reaching nearly 480 beneficiaries and delivering strong and consistent results in terms of training completion, employment outcomes and measurable impact. Both projects achieved the highest evaluation from the Fund and were recognized as the best projects of the two respective calls, especially in terms of employment outcomes significantly higher than the averages of the other projects supported  and net impact compared to the control group. Tech Your Future reached and trained 328 learners completing training (98.5% of target graduates), 199 employed after the programme (60.7% vs 60% target), and a dropout rate of 9.9%. DigitHer trained 147 young women, corresponding to approximately 98% of its 150-participant target. The project recorded a 12.5% dropout rate, significantly below the Futura portfolio average used for comparison (20.6%). The employment outcome previously consolidated for the project was 99 employed participants (67.3%), which was 3.6x the average of other projects in the Futura call. These results demonstrate the model’s ability to engage and retain participants who typically face barriers to completing intensive training programmes. Beyond these outcomes, both projects provide robust evidence of their effectiveness through independent counterfactual impact evaluations, which compare participants’ results to those of similar individuals who did not take part in the programmes (control group). This allows for a clear quantification of the added value generated by the intervention (which is the extra results attributable directly to the project). The findings show significant improvements across key dimensions: - Employment outcome is higher by around +15.7 percentage points for Tech Your Future and +37 percentage points for DigitHer vs employment outcome of the control groups - Monthly labour income increased by approximately +€236 and +€510 respectively (vs counterfactual) - Digital skills (DESI index) improved by around +6 points and +4.1 points - Access to digital employment also increased substantially, with a +43 p.p. for DigitHer and +26 p.p. for Tech Your Future These results indicate that participants not only accessed employment, but were more likely to secure jobs in the digital sector, with higher earnings and improved overall labour market prospects compared to what would have occurred without the intervention. The benefits extend beyond individual participants. For learners, the projects provide access to in-demand digital skills, increased confidence and clear entry points into growing sectors of the economy. For employers, they create a reliable pipeline of trained and motivated junior talent, while supporting more inclusive hiring practices. At system level, the projects demonstrate a practical and evidence-based way to connect social inclusion objectives with labour market needs, offering a model that can inform future investments and policy design. The quality and impact of both initiatives have been formally recognised within the evaluation framework of the Fondo per la Repubblica Digitale, where they received the maximum bonus coefficient, confirming their strong performance and potential for scaling. The projects address a set of interconnected and structural challenges affecting both individuals and labour markets in Italy’s digital transition. First, many young people, particularly those classified as NEET and women, face persistent barriers to accessing quality employment. These barriers go beyond technical skill gaps and include limited professional networks, low confidence, weak job-search capabilities, and difficulties navigating recruitment processes. As a result, a significant share of young talent remains disconnected from emerging opportunities, even in sectors with strong demand. Second, there is a systemic mismatch between labour market demand and available talent. While companies across Italy report shortages of entry-level digital profiles (1 in 3 positions is hard-to-fill in 2025 - source: Unioncamere, Italy is 18th out of 28 EU countries for “above” basic digital skills - DESI), many young people lack access to pathways that provide not only relevant technical skills, but also a direct connection to employers (0,7 mln young people unemployed, and almost 2 mln NEET - source: Istat). innovations.name: Red Salvia (Salvia Network): Innovation for improving the quality of life of older people
innovations.problem: Europe is experiencing an unprecedented demographic transformation. Population ageing, increased life expectancy, changing family structures and evolving patterns of social interaction are creating new challenges for social inclusion, wellbeing and long-term care systems. A growing number of older people face situations of social isolation, unwanted loneliness and reduced participation in community life. These challenges are particularly acute among people living alone, those with limited social networks, those experiencing digital exclusion and those facing economic, health or geographical barriers. In Spain alone, more than 2.1 million people aged 65 and over live alone, while around one in five older adults report persistent feelings of loneliness. Unwanted loneliness is increasingly recognised as a major social determinant of health and wellbeing, contributing to depression, anxiety, cognitive decline, reduced quality of life and higher risks of dependency and institutionalisation. At the same time, traditional responses often focus on care provision after dependency has emerged rather than on prevention and early intervention. Existing systems frequently underestimate the value of social participation, peer support and community engagement as protective factors against exclusion and institutionalisation. Research conducted within Red Salvia confirms that loneliness and social exclusion are complex and multidimensional phenomena that require integrated responses. They cannot be addressed solely through formal services but require stronger social connections, opportunities for participation, digital inclusion and supportive community environments. Red Salvia addresses these challenges through a preventive and community-based approach that combines social research, mutual-support methodologies, digital inclusion and active participation. The project strengthens social relationships, functional capabilities, autonomy and community engagement through accompaniment groups and mutual-support communities, while promoting digital literacy, health promotion, social participation and meaningful engagement in community life. By empowering older people as active contributors to their communities, Red Salvia helps prevent social exclusion, unwanted loneliness and institutionalisation while fostering active ageing, independence and improved quality of life.
innovations.description:
Red Salvia builds on Fundación Santa María la Real’s extensive experience in designing, testing and scaling social innovation initiatives in Spain that combine research, community participation and peer-support methodologies to address complex social challenges. A key source of inspiration was the Employment Shuttles (Lanzaderas de Empleo), a social innovation programme developed by Fundación Santa María la Real in the field of employment, social inclusion and community activation. Over more than a decade, this nationally recognised initiative has supported thousands of people through group-based methodologies focused on mutual support, empowerment, active participation and collective problem-solving. The programme demonstrated how peer learning, community engagement and collaborative action can generate sustainable social impact and strengthen individual and collective resilience. The project also draws on the experience of Hubs de Activación de la Empleabilidad, an ESF+ co-financed initiative developed in Spain by Fundación Santa María la Real within the employment and social inclusion sector. Hubs combines applied research, personalised accompaniment, group-based learning, digital inclusion, skills development and territorial collaboration networks to improve employability and social participation. The programme further reinforced the organisation’s experience in creating evidence-based methodologies, facilitating stakeholder collaboration and scaling innovative approaches across different territories. Building on these experiences, Red Salvia transfers and adapts proven social innovation principles to a new challenge: preventing unwanted loneliness, social exclusion and institutionalisation among older people. The project applies key elements such as mutual support groups, evidence-based intervention design, community activation, continuous evaluation, stakeholder collaboration and knowledge transfer within the fields of active ageing, social inclusion and community-based care. The design of Red Salvia has also been informed by an extensive benchmarking process involving 24 national and international initiatives focused on preventing unwanted loneliness, promoting social participation and supporting community-based care models for older people. This process identified 12 high-performing and transferable practices that informed the project’s intervention methodology and strengthened its replication potential.
Red Salvia introduces an innovative and evidence-based approach to tackling unwanted loneliness, social exclusion and the risk of institutionalisation among older people. The project’s core innovation lies in its mutual-support methodology, which transforms older people from passive recipients of support into active contributors to community wellbeing. Rather than focusing exclusively on service delivery, the project mobilises the experience, knowledge and capabilities of older people themselves, creating communities of solidarity, participation and shared responsibility. The innovation is built upon a comprehensive social innovation process that combines research, co-creation, experimentation, evaluation and transfer. The project began with an extensive diagnostic phase that included expert interviews, focus groups with older people, a large-scale survey and the analysis of national and international good practices. This evidence base informed the design of intervention methodologies tailored to the needs and realities of vulnerable older people. Through accompaniment groups and pilot experiences, participants work collectively to strengthen social connections, improve digital skills, promote active ageing, enhance functional capacities and increase participation in community life. The project simultaneously addresses individual wellbeing and broader community resilience. Another innovative aspect is the integration of multiple stakeholders within a collaborative ecosystem. innovations.evidence:
Since its launch in 2021, Red Salvia has achieved significant results by creating and validating an evidence-based framework for preventing unwanted loneliness, social exclusion and institutionalisation among older people.
Red Salvia was initially piloted in Manzanares El Real (Madrid, Spain), where the first accompaniment group tested the project’s mutual-support methodology with older people at risk of social exclusion and unwanted loneliness. Following the positive results obtained during this first implementation, the project was scaled up in 2026 through a second round of interventions in four additional Spanish territories: Ávila, León, Seville and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. This expansion increased the geographical reach of the project and extended participation from the initial pilot group to 60 additional older people. The scaling process has enabled the methodology to be tested and refined in different territorial contexts while strengthening its evidence base, transferability and potential for wider adoption.
One of the project’s major achievements was the development of a comprehensive research and diagnostic process. This included 12 expert interviews, three focus groups involving older people, and a national survey with 1,509 respondents, including 329 people aged 65 and over. This work generated valuable evidence on the psychosocial effects of loneliness, the factors contributing to exclusion, and the conditions required to promote active ageing and social participation. The project also carried out a benchmarking process analysing 24 national and international initiatives, identifying 12 high-performing and transferable practices. These findings informed the design of the intervention model and strengthened its potential for replication. Red Salvia has already implemented and tested its methodology through pilot projects in Spain. The first pilot was carried out in Manzanares El Real (Madrid), where the intervention model was initially tested and refined. Building on the positive results and lessons learned, the methodology was subsequently transferred and implemented in other regions, including Ávila, León, Seville and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. Among participants who completed the programme, 100% reported a reduction in unwanted loneliness. Participants also demonstrated an improved ability to identify risks within their homes, reorganise living spaces, reduce the risk of falls, and strengthen the conditions needed for independent living, thereby contributing to a lower risk of institutionalisation. A key achievement of the project has been the creation of the Red Salvia Network of Entities, a collaborative ecosystem that connects public authorities, social organisations, researchers, private-sector actors and community stakeholders committed to improving the quality of life of older people. The network already includes organisations from Spain and several international partners from Belgium, Estonia, Czech Republic, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Austria, Latvia and Japan. This international dimension strengthens peer learning, facilitates the exchange of good practices and increases the potential for future transfer and scaling of the model across different countries and contexts. innovations.name: STEAM Clubs
innovations.problem: Scientific literacy is increasingly recognized as a prerequisite for democratic participation, employability and informed decision-making. Yet Romania consistently ranks among the lowest-performing EU countries in scientific literacy. Access to quality STEAM learning is particularly limited for children from lower-income families and smaller communities, where extracurricular opportunities are scarce. At the same time, Romania maintains a nationwide public network of Children’s Palaces and Clubs that provides free non-formal education. Despite their extensive reach, many of these institutions lack the resources, equipment and specialized training needed to offer meaningful STEAM experiences. The result is a missed opportunity to engage children with science at an age when curiosity and interest in STEM subjects are most easily developed. STEAM Clubs addresses this gap by activating an existing public infrastructure and transforming it into a vehicle for scientific literacy and future-oriented skills development.
innovations.description:
The innovation was originally designed for Romania’s public network of Children’s Palaces and Clubs. It was subsequently adapted for implementation in public schools, including Școala Gimnazială Gălbinași (Călărași County) and Școala Generală Șag (Timiș County). These adaptations demonstrated that the framework can function effectively in both formal and non-formal education settings while preserving its core educational principles.
STEAM Clubs combines four complementary innovations. First, it leverages an existing nationwide public infrastructure rather than creating new educational centers. The project transforms Children’s Palaces and Clubs into local STEAM hubs, activating an underutilized network of public non-formal education institutions that already reaches tens of thousands of children throughout Romania. Second, it equips local teachers to become facilitators of hands-on STEAM learning through training, mentoring and access to structured educational resources. Rather than relying on external experts, the model builds local ownership and capacity, allowing participating institutions to deliver and further develop STEAM activities independently. Third, it uses a DIY and makerspace-based methodology that connects scientific concepts to practical projects, helping children learn through experimentation, construction and reflection. The project also creates local mini-makerspaces that provide children with new and varied learning experiences while expanding the educational tools available to teachers. These spaces and resources continue to support educational activities beyond the STEAM Clubs curriculum, enabling educators to introduce hands-on learning approaches into other courses and programs. Fourth, it focuses on institutional capacity building. Rather than delivering activities directly and leaving, the project strengthens participating institutions through equipment, curriculum, teacher development, implementation methodologies and community engagement mechanisms. This allows Children’s Palaces and Clubs to become long-term providers of high-quality STEAM education and creates the conditions necessary for sustainable growth. The project’s distinctive character lies in the combination of these four innovations. By combining public infrastructure, teacher development, institutional capacity building and experiential learning, the model achieves broad reach at relatively low cost while remaining adaptable to different communities and educational settings. The same methodology has already been successfully transferred to public schools, demonstrating its flexibility beyond the original implementation environment.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Key results achieved so far include: • Establishment of 10 STEAM Clubs and makerspaces within Romania’s public non-formal education network, as well as successful implementation in 2 (two) public schools, demonstrating the model’s adaptability across educational settings. Expanding to 16 locations in autumn through confirmed partnerships. • More than 420 children participating in the program and 44 teachers trained to facilitate hands-on STEAM learning. • Successful implementation in both large urban centers and smaller communities, demonstrating the model’s relevance across diverse socio-economic and geographic contexts. • Strong engagement and satisfaction levels among participating children, with evaluation data consistently showing high levels of enjoyment, curiosity, concentration, collaboration and willingness to continue learning. • Measurable improvements in children’s confidence when approaching scientific concepts and hands-on activities, as well as gains in knowledge and practical skills. • Demonstrated gender balance among participants, with equal participation of girls and boys in the newest implementation cohort. • Creation of a scalable implementation model combining teacher training, institutional capacity building, curriculum development, makerspace infrastructure and community engagement. • Recognition and support from the Romanian Ministry of Education, which recommended the initiative through its network of County School Inspectorates, facilitating nationwide visibility and engagement from Children’s Palaces and Clubs across Romania. A clear pathway for continued growth, with six additional clubs planned for the current year and a further eight clubs scheduled for expansion the following year. Beyond direct beneficiaries, the project has strengthened participating institutions, increased local capacity to deliver STEAM education and demonstrated a replicable model for improving scientific literacy through existing public infrastructure.
The model has been replicated across multiple Children’s Palaces and Clubs in different cities and towns from different regions of Romania, including Giurgiu, Călărași, Horezu, Câmpina, Tulcea, Măcin, Blaj, Timișoara, Jimbolia, Buziaș as well as 2 rural schools in Șag and Gălbinași . While local implementation varies according to context and available resources, all locations use the same core framework based on teacher training, makerspace development, hands-on STEAM activities, mentoring and continuous improvement through feedback.
Following its initial pilot phase, the project expanded and is still expanding into a growing national network of STEAM Clubs and makerspaces. The initiative currently reaches more than 420 children and 44 teachers through 10 STEAM Clubs and two public schools. The network continues to grow through confirmed partnerships with additional institutions, demonstrating both demand for the model and its capacity for sustainable expansion.

innovations.name: Magic Donkey Land
innovations.problem: Many children today experience increased stress, social isolation, excessive screen exposure and limited access to meaningful outdoor activities. Rural communities often lack innovative educational and therapeutic services that support children's emotional wellbeing and social inclusion. Vulnerable children, including those with special educational needs, frequently face barriers in accessing nature-based interventions. Magic Donkey Land addresses these challenges by providing accessible, inclusive and nature-centered experiences that improve children's wellbeing, confidence and social skills.
innovations.description: Magic Donkey Land offers a unique combination of donkey-assisted activities, outdoor experiential learning and social inclusion programs. Unlike traditional educational or recreational services, the project uses the natural bond between children and donkeys to encourage empathy, emotional regulation, communication and self-confidence. The activities take place in a farm-based environment where children learn through direct experience, interaction with animals and connection with nature. This innovative approach combines social impact, animal welfare, environmental awareness and rural development within a sustainable social enterprise model.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Since its establishment, Magic Donkey Land has engaged hundreds of children and families in educational, recreational and therapeutic activities. Participants report increased self-confidence, improved social interaction, stronger emotional wellbeing and a deeper connection with nature. The project has created local employment opportunities, promoted animal welfare and strengthened community involvement. It also contributes to raising awareness about alternative educational methods and the positive role of animal-assisted interventions in child development.

innovations.name: FLOW leerecosysteem
innovations.problem: Many young people struggle to identify their talents, interests and future opportunities. Those facing social, educational or economic barriers are particularly at risk of exclusion, low self-confidence and disengagement from learning and participation in society. FLOW addresses this challenge by creating accessible opportunities for young people to explore their strengths, connect with others and build meaningful pathways for their personal development and future.
innovations.description: FLOW’s innovation lies in its ecosystem approach. Instead of offering a single programme or service, FLOW connects youth organisations, cultural actors, social services and creative learning environments into one flexible network around the young person. Young people are not guided towards predefined outcomes but are encouraged to discover their talents, interests and intrinsic motivation through real-life experiences, creativity, participation and reflection. This personalised, strengths-based approach helps them build confidence, ownership and meaningful pathways for their future. By combining cross-sector collaboration with talent-oriented guidance, FLOW creates learning opportunities that are more accessible, engaging and responsive to the needs of young people.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: FLOW helps young people discover their talents, interests and strengths through creative, cultural and community-based experiences. Participants gain confidence, develop social and personal skills, expand their networks and become more engaged in learning and society. The project also strengthens collaboration between youth organisations, cultural actors and social services, creating more accessible and personalised opportunities for young people, especially those at risk of exclusion.

innovations.name: Providing Integrated Services in Rural Communities — Facilitating Access of Vulnerable Persons to Efficient and Quality Basic Services
innovations.lead: Ministry of Labor, Family, Youth and Social Solidarity
innovations.problem: A child at risk of dropping out of school may simultaneously need educational support, medical care, and social assistance. An elderly person living alone may need care, medical monitoring, and social support all at once. A person with disabilities needs not just a financial benefit, but access to healthcare, rehabilitation, counselling, and community integration. Yet public systems are organised by domain, and vulnerable people are left to navigate different institutions on their own. This is the daily reality for millions of people in rural Romania. Poverty in rural communities is not a single problem — it is multiple, overlapping deprivations: poor health, low school attendance, inadequate housing, absence of identity documents, lack of material resources, and exclusion from social life. Elderly people, Roma communities, children, young people, persons with disabilities, and their families face all of these at once. Vulnerabilities are geographically concentrated in isolated rural areas where public services are scarce, institutions are fragmented, and the people who need help the most are the least likely to find it. No single institution, working alone, can address interconnected needs. Fragmented interventions reach only part of the person and solve only part of the problem. What is needed is a shift — from institutions working in silos to professionals working together, from standardised bureaucratic responses to support built around each person's real situation. innovations.name: Edumetrix: From a 108-School Pilot to National Scale
innovations.problem: Many schools lack reliable mechanisms for understanding their strengths, challenges and development needs. Educational decisions are often based on fragmented information, while school leaders have limited access to tools that support evidence-based planning, stakeholder engagement and continuous improvement. These challenges are particularly significant in schools serving vulnerable communities, where inequalities in educational opportunities and outcomes are more pronounced. There is a need for scalable solutions that help schools collect, analyse and use data effectively to drive sustainable improvement and promote educational equity.
innovations.description: Edumetrix transforms a validated school transformation methodology into a scalable digital solution. Building on the experience gained through the School Transformation Programme implemented in 108 schools, the platform enables schools to assess organisational performance, educational quality and wellbeing through structured data collection and analysis. Schools receive tailored insights and recommendations based on feedback from students, teachers and school leaders. These insights support the development of evidence-based improvement plans and facilitate continuous monitoring of progress. The innovation lies in combining a proven school improvement methodology with digital technology, making high-quality diagnostics and school development processes accessible to a much larger number of schools while maintaining consistency and comparability of results.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The innovation was initially developed and validated through the School Transformation Programme implemented in 108 schools across Romania, engaging more than 50,000 students, over 4,000 teachers and 120 school leaders. Lessons learned from the pilot informed the development of Edumetrix, a scalable digital platform that standardises school diagnostics, improvement planning and progress monitoring.
The School Transformation Programme remains active, while Edumetrix represents the scaling mechanism developed from the pilot experience. The current scaling phase focuses on expanding access to the model through Edumetrix, with more than 200 public schools targeted for participation. The platform enables broader adoption of evidence-based school improvement practices while maintaining the core methodology tested during the pilot phase.
• Validation of the school transformation methodology in 108 schools across Romania, engaging more than 50,000 students, over 4,000 teachers and 120 school leaders. • More than 100 school diagnostic reports generated through a structured evaluation process supported by trained educational analysts. • Nearly 30,000 students participated in assessment and diagnostic processes that informed school development priorities and action planning. • More than 470 hours of professional development delivered to teachers and school leaders, supported by educational consultants, coaches and mentors. • Development of Edumetrix as a scalable digital platform based on evidence and lessons learned from the pilot phase. • Ongoing national scaling process, with more than 200 public schools targeted for participation through the Edumetrix platform.

innovations.name: Maurice & Nora
innovations.problem: Europe faces a growing care gap. In Flanders alone, the number of people over 80 is set to double to around 640,000 by 2040, while the pool of informal family caregivers shrinks. This squeezes the "sandwich generation", often women, between raising children and caring for ageing parents. Roughly one in two people over 50 provides informal care, frequently leading to reduced working hours or burnout, and care responsibilities fall disproportionately on women. At the same time, many seniors face loneliness and risk premature institutionalisation, and many young people lack meaningful, human work. Existing solutions are either expensive, hard to access, or rely on impersonal gig-economy models, leaving everyday non-medical care out of reach for most families.
innovations.description: We use technology for humanity, not to replace it. Three elements make the model distinctive. First, we perform the matching ourselves through a bias-free algorithm based on personality, interests, abilities, and logistics, rather than letting clients pick by photo or name. This gives every student equal opportunity regardless of background or appearance. Second, we automate the cognitive drudgery, scheduling, payments, contracts, intake calls, and routing, using AI and voice agents so coordination happens in minutes rather than weeks, and so the time between student and family stays purely human. Third, we use a B2B2C model: employers fund the service as a care benefit through existing cafeteria and flexible-pay plans, removing the cost barrier for families while protecting employee wellbeing and productivity. Together this makes trusted intergenerational care scalable and accessible to the many, not just the wealthy.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Maurice & Nora has grown into an active community of seniors, families, and students. To date the platform has over 3,900 registered clients and more than 3,800 screened students ready to help, with new registrations still coming in daily. The company closed a 1 million euro seed round in 2026 and ran a national launch campaign with broad press, radio, and television coverage. Recognition includes Business Startup of the Year and the Platforms category win at the Belgium Startup Awards, the HR Tech Startup Award 2025 by HR Magazine, and the Happy Aging Award 2025 by In4care, alongside a finalist place for Tech Startup of the Year at the Data News Awards. Early impact data shows the model reaches those who need it most: of an analysed client base, around two thirds of help-seekers are women, confirming the contribution to gender equity by professionalising care that otherwise falls on them. For seniors, the service supports ageing at home and reduces loneliness. For students, it provides meaningful income and human skills as an alternative to faceless gig work. For employers, it reduces care-related absenteeism and supports retention.

innovations.name: Savnet IT Academies - Connecting Skills to Opportunities. Together.
innovations.problem: 1. The digital skills gap that holds back people and economies. Demand for IT professionals far outpaces supply across Europe. Technology evolves faster than formal education can adapt, leaving roles unfilled, companies under pressure, and entire regions unable to keep up with digital transformation. We close this gap by training people in the exact, certified skills the labour market needs right now. 2. Youth unemployment and the academia-to-industry gap. Too many capable graduates leave university with strong theory but with less hands-on, job-ready skills and recognized certifications employers require — and they struggle to find their first role. We bridge that gap with practical, project-based academies, niched on certain IT roles that turn final-year students into employable professionals. 3. The cost barrier that locks people out of quality training. World-class IT education and international certifications are expensive, putting them out of reach for the students and young people who would benefit most, and reinforcing inequality of opportunity. We remove this barrier entirely: our academies are delivered at zero commercial cost to learners. 4. Talent shortages and brain drain in regional economies. Outside major hubs, employers cannot find qualified talent, and skilled young people leave their region or country in search of opportunity. By building a local pipeline of certified professionals, we strengthen the regional IT ecosystem and help retain talent where it is needed. 5. Underused corporate social responsibility budgets. Companies want measurable social impact but often lack a credible, high-impact channel for it. We convert their CSR investment into fully funded education that produces real, job-ready talent — turning private spending into shared public good.
innovations.description: Savnet IT Academies introduce a new model for closing the digital skills gap: high-quality, certification-based IT education delivered at zero commercial cost to both learners and employers, financed entirely by industry through corporate social responsibility. The innovation is not the training itself — it is who pays, why, and how the value flows back to society. A reversed financing model. Conventional IT education places the cost on the student or the employer, which excludes the very people who would benefit most. We reverse this: companies sponsor full cohorts as part of their CSR strategy, students learn for free, and the public good — a more employable, digitally skilled population — is produced as a direct result. Private investment is converted into shared social value. A self-sustaining, multi-stakeholder ecosystem. Rather than acting alone, we connect four actors that rarely work together effectively — universities, global education and certification partners, local employers, and an independent NGO — into a single aligned system. Each gains: students gain careers, universities gain employable graduates, sponsors gain a job-ready talent pipeline and measurable CSR impact, and the regional economy gains skilled professionals it can retain. Skills-to-Jobs by design. Every academy is reverse-engineered from real job roles. We bundle globally recognized courses and international certifications (Cisco, CompTIA, Python Institute and others) into the exact, validated skill sets the labour market requires — combining theory, hands-on lab work, and real projects so graduates are employable from day one. Modular and replicable. Because each academy is built from standardized, certification-based modules across cybersecurity, cloud, networking, DevOps, data, Python, Java and AI, the model can be transferred to new technologies, regions, and sectors across the EU without being rebuilt — making the social innovation scalable by design.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Proven results Over its activity, Savnet Training Center has delivered Network Automation, Java, Python, Python and AI, AI, Linux and Storage and Backup academies. Learning is hands-on, supported by three fully equipped labs with servers and 100+ routers and switches, and validated through 40+ internationally recognized certifications and badges. Quality is underpinned by world-class instructors — including trainers ranked in the global top 25% and top 10% best Cisco CCNA Instructors worldwide for over 30 times — backed by 4 partner universities and 5 international educational partnerships. Benefits delivered For learners: free access to world-class, certified IT education, practical job-ready skills, and a direct route into employment — regardless of their financial means. For employers and sponsors: a reliable pipeline of certified, job-ready talent, lower recruitment and training costs, the ability to shape curricula to real needs, and measurable, credible CSR impact. For universities and the education system: more employable graduates, stronger industry links, and curricula kept current with labour-market demands. For the region and society: a narrowed digital skills gap, increased youth employability, retained local talent that reduces brain drain, and a self-sustaining ecosystem that turns private investment into lasting public good.

innovations.name: Youngsters for the Future
innovations.problem: Every year, thousands of young people in Romania leave the child protection system and are expected to begin adult life with limited support. Many do so without stable family relationships, financial security, safe housing, trusted guidance, or access to consistent mental health services. This transition exposes them to poverty, unemployment, housing instability, social isolation, untreated trauma, and a high risk of long-term exclusion. The move into adulthood is often abrupt. Formal support can end at 18, while adult services are fragmented, under-resourced, and difficult to navigate. Mental health support is rarely connected to education, employment, housing, or social protection pathways. At the same time, stigma, low trust in institutions, and previous adverse experiences often prevent young people from asking for help early. This creates a critical service gap at the exact moment when emotional, social, and practical vulnerabilities are highest. Without consistent and trusted support, young people may struggle to remain in education, access or keep employment, manage stress and conflict, build healthy relationships, or live independently. Practical barriers and emotional distress reinforce each other, making the transition to adulthood unsafe, unstable, and unequal. The programme addresses this gap by treating mental health as a foundation for social and professional integration. The programme responds not only to material needs, but also to the emotional stability, self-confidence, relationships, and inner resources young people need to build a safe, dignified, and independent future.
innovations.description: Youngsters for the Future is innovative because it redefines social integration as both a practical and emotional process. The programme does not treat employment, education, housing and mental health as separate problems to be solved by separate services. Instead, it brings them together in one personalised pathway built around the real experience of young people leaving care. Its strongest innovation is the way mental health is embedded as a foundation for independence. Young people are not expected to become stable, employable or self-reliant while carrying untreated trauma, emotional distress, low trust or social isolation. The programme recognises that psychological safety, emotional regulation, self-confidence and healthy relationships are essential conditions for education, work and independent living. The model also introduces a prevention-to-care pathway. Young people can first engage through low-threshold, non-clinical support such as psychoeducation, group sessions, mentoring and informal check-ins. As trust grows, they can access psychological assessment, long-term psychotherapy or psychiatric referral when needed. This gradual pathway reduces stigma, respects each young person’s readiness, and makes help-seeking safer. Another innovative element is that the programme works not only with young people, but also with the ecosystem around them. It builds the capacity of social services, teachers, NGOs, employers, therapists and mentors to recognise distress, respond safely, use trauma-informed approaches and create clearer referral pathways. This shifts the programme from direct service delivery to system strengthening. In this sense, Youngsters for the Future is innovative because it combines personalised support, long-term mental health care, low-threshold prevention, employability, education, emergency support and ecosystem capacity-building in one coherent model. It addresses both the young person’s immediate needs and the wider conditions required for a safe, dignified and sustainable transition to adult life.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: In 2025, Youngsters for the Future / Tineri de Viitor delivered strong results across three levels: direct support for young people, strengthened capacity among professionals, and wider awareness of youth mental health. The programme reached 171 young people and provided a broad package of personalised support. Of these, 70 young people received psychological assessments and 31 entered individual therapy during the year. In total, the programme delivered 1,084 hours of psychotherapy and 275 psycho-emotional support sessions, offering young people consistent spaces to process distress, build trust, and strengthen emotional stability. The programme also supported education, employability and independent living. It delivered 65 workshops on topics such as financial education, psychoeducation, employability, sexual education, trafficking prevention, creativity and media. Young people also received 134 vocational counselling sessions, 157 hours of tutoring, 14 professional certifications, and access to 11 exploratory visits with employers. In addition, 20 emergency interventions responded to urgent needs related to health, housing, food and legal counselling. Beyond direct services, the programme strengthened the wider ecosystem around young people. Training activities reached social services, NGOs, teachers and corporate employees, helping professionals better understand youth mental health, trauma-informed support, early signs of distress, and safe referral pathways. The national mental health awareness campaign reached almost 150,000 people, contributing to the destigmatisation of seeking support. The most important benefits are qualitative. Young people reported improved emotional regulation, stronger self-confidence, clearer boundaries, better communication, and increased trust in themselves and others. Several participants connected therapy with better conflict management, stronger motivation to continue education, and greater stability at work. These results show that the programme creates value beyond individual activities. It helps young people build the emotional, practical and social foundations needed for independent living, while also helping employers, social services and communities respond more safely and effectively to the needs of vulnerable emerging adults.

innovations.name: ZINDR
innovations.problem: Zindr addresses the problem that decisions about marginalized groups are often made without their involvement, which can reinforce exclusion. It develops methods for inclusive knowledge co-creation and epistemic justice, so decisions become more grounded, effective, and fair. We believe that living and working together in a highly diverse world is essential to meeting today’s challenges, by creating spaces for equal collaboration, shared learning, and collective inquiry.
innovations.description: Zindr is innovative in shifting from participation to the co-production of knowledge, where people affected by exclusion become co-researchers and co-designers of solutions. Learning is treated as a collective practice rather than an individual activity, grounded in epistemic justice as a design principle that redistributes whose knowledge counts. Instead of fixed methods, Zindr works through emergent, practice-based processes where “Zindr spaces” function as a living research and learning infrastructure. Building on safe and brave spaces, it introduces generative spaces where shared insight and collective agency can unfold.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The main outcomes and benefits of Zindr can be summarized on three levels: 1. Better decisions and solutions By actively involving people with lived experience, insights become richer and more context-sensitive, leading to solutions that are more realistic, effective, and sustainable. 2. Redistribution of knowledge and power Zindr advances epistemic justice by recognizing and valuing the knowledge of people in situations of exclusion, making it meaningful in decision-making and design processes. 3. Stronger spaces for learning and agency It creates new forms of collective learning and collaboration where trust, ownership, and life energy can grow, strengthening both individuals and communities. In short, Zindr not only improves what we know, but also how we come to know, decide, and act together.

innovations.name: DIDACTIC MINE OF YOUTH WORK
innovations.problem: Across Europe, many young people — particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds — transition from education to adulthood without adequate preparation for the demands of the modern labour market or civic life. Youth workers and educators, who are often the primary support system for these young people, frequently lack structured, accessible, and engaging resources to develop entrepreneurial thinking, social responsibility, and critical life skills in non-formal settings. At the same time, the growing urgency of sustainable development challenges requires a new generation capable of understanding complex systemic problems and contributing to collaborative solutions. Existing educational tools often fail to bridge these two needs simultaneously, leaving a gap between skills development and real-world application.
innovations.description: The project addressed this gap through two complementary, practitioner-designed tools that make entrepreneurial and sustainability education tangible, engaging, and immediately usable. The e-book's 30 activities — each accompanied by a video presentation — are age-differentiated and ready to deploy in youth centres, classrooms, and non-formal settings without requiring specialised expertise. The interactive SDG game introduces a systems-thinking approach to social entrepreneurship, asking participants to forge connections between real-world problems and collaborative solutions, building competences such as strategic planning, communication, and teamwork in the process. Innovation lies in the integration of these two tools into a unified pedagogical framework that simultaneously targets individual skill development, organisational capacity building, and community-level impact — and does so in a format that is freely replicable across diverse European contexts.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: -An open-access e-book of 30 didactic activities, differentiated across three age groups, with accompanying video presentations produced by trainers from multiple countries. -An interactive game directly linked to the 17 SDGs, designed for use by youth workers, trainers, and young people in non-formal education settings. -Enhanced capacity of partner organisations to collaborate transnationally and develop innovative educational resources. -Improved competences among participating youth workers and trainers, including skills in content development, cross-cultural collaboration, and non-formal pedagogy. -Direct skills development among young participants in critical thinking, ethical decision-making, active citizenship, and entrepreneurial mindset. -A replicable, scalable methodology suitable for adoption by youth organisations, schools, and training providers across Europe. -Increased visibility and partnership opportunities for participating organisations through shared outputs published on open platforms.

innovations.name: Smart Social Hub: Optimizing Community Support through Real-Time Matching
innovations.problem: The core problem addressed is the inefficiency and fragmentation of traditional social assistance in Vrancea, Romania. We identify three systemic barriers: Resource Mismatch and Waste: Currently, humanitarian aid is often ad-hoc and reactive. There is a lack of real-time data correlation between the specific, urgent needs of vulnerable families and the supplies provided by donors, leading to resource waste and gaps in coverage. Delayed Intervention: Bureaucratic hurdles and the absence of a unified digital tracking system prevent rapid responses to acute social crises, leaving marginalized individuals without support when they need it most. Lack of Transparency and Coordination: There is a persistent 'silo' effect between local public authorities, private sector sponsors, and NGOs. This lack of a shared digital infrastructure hinders collaborative governance and prevents the scaling of social impact. Our project solves these issues by replacing manual, sporadic aid distribution with a 'Smart Social Hub' that acts as an agile, data-driven backbone for the entire community social support ecosystem.
innovations.description:
Our project is inspired by the European 'Digital Social Services' frameworks and various community-based resource-sharing models implemented in countries like Denmark and the Netherlands (e.g., 'Social Tech' initiatives for local resilience). While we do not follow a specific single-organization project, we drew on the best practices of 'Digital Solidarity' networks that bridge the gap between public social services and private resources. We adapted these principles to the context of Vrancea, Romania, specifically by tailoring the workflow to fit the collaboration between the Local Social Assistance Directorate, private sector CSR sponsors, and our organization (Asociatia Smart Group Solutions).
Our innovation lies in the 'Smart Solidarity Network', a model that digitizes the social support chain to move from reactive charity to proactive, data-driven inclusion. Data-Driven Precision: Unlike traditional models, our Hub uses real-time mapping to match verified social needs with the specific inventory of our local partners. This ensures that help is targeted, immediate, and waste-free. Digital 'Silo-Breaking': The Hub acts as a unified digital infrastructure that connects local authorities (who hold data on vulnerable populations) with private donors (who hold the resources) and NGOs (who provide the operational capacity). This creates a transparent ecosystem for collaborative action. Scalable Logistics: By digitizing the workflow, we transform social aid from a logistical challenge into a streamlined, automated process. This allows our small team to manage a high volume of interventions efficiently, proving that smart technology can significantly amplify the reach of local social initiatives. Ultimately, we are not just providing aid; we are providing a replicable digital framework that any community can use to modernize its social protection system.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Key Results: Systematization of Aid: Successfully transitioned from periodic, ad-hoc charity campaigns to a structured, data-supported distribution system that functions continuously. Multi-Stakeholder Synergy: Built a functioning community network involving 3+ key private sector sponsors, the Local Social Assistance Directorate, and local NGOs, creating a shared responsibility model. Improved Targeting: Developed a verified database of community vulnerabilities, which has increased the accuracy and speed of support interventions by ensuring the right resources reach the right families. Benefits: For the Community: Provides a reliable safety net that reduces social exclusion and addresses material deprivation with dignity and speed. For Private Sponsors: Offers high transparency and measurable impact for their CSR investments, encouraging long-term engagement. For Public Authorities: Provides a scalable digital tool (the Hub) that optimizes the efficiency of local social spending and human resource allocation. For the EU: Offers a replicable 'Digital Solidarity' template that directly contributes to the modernization of social protection systems and the strengthening of European social cohesion.

We scaled-up this model by integrating these sporadic efforts into a unified, technology-enabled 'Smart Social Hub'. This expansion involved moving from simple aid delivery to a structured digital network, effectively increasing our reach from individual neighborhoods to a county-wide framework involving local public authorities, private sector partners, and a growing database of vulnerable beneficiaries.
