innovations.name: Deep Inclusion: Unlocking Potential, growing Together in an Inclusive Society
innovations.problem: Every person is different. Disability is one of those differences, yet today it still too often leads to exclusion. People face barriers in all major domains of life. More than half (54%) report experiencing discrimination. Many also experience social isolation, with 44.2% reporting limited connectedness. Exclusion continues in education. Students with disabilities are twice as likely to leave school early, only 29% obtain a higher education degree. 6% of all children in Belgium are educated in segregated specialised settings. The situation is equally challenging in employment. Employment rates remain between 23% and 44%, people with disabilities face a 22% higher risk of poverty, and 38% experience long-term work incapacity due to mental health issues. The roots of this exclusion lie in persistent deficit-based thinking: focusing on limitations rather than possibilities, maintaining low expectations, and designing systems and environments around a single norm. It is reinforced by a society that too rarely sees care as a shared, collective responsibility. As a result, people with and without disabilities increasingly live, learn, and work in separate worlds. Both individuals and communities miss opportunities to grow together, learn from one another, and benefit from each other's strengths. Today, many people with disabilities are still not fully included in the fundamental domains of life, learning, and work. This is not only a loss for them, it is a loss for society as a whole.
innovations.description: The Deep Inclusion Model addresses exclusion by focusing on both the individual and the environment. Inspired by years of experience in strengths-based practice, it equips people with cognitive support needs, their families, professionals and communities with the tools to recognize and build on strengths rather than limitations. What makes the model distinctive is that it translates inclusion into concrete, practices on both sides of the loop- what individuals develop and what environments actively enable. The model combines two complementary perspectives: Yes I Can, which supports individuals to develop confidence, skills and meaningful social roles, and Yes We Care, which helps families, schools, workplaces and support services create the conditions in which people can thrive. By strengthening both people and their environments, the model promotes a shift from care and protection towards participation, contribution and shared growth. In doing so, it contributes to a broader systems change: a society where people with disabilities are not defined by their support needs, but recognized for their talents, potential and capacity to contribute.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
This model is grounded in more than a decade of practice across our programmes for young people with cognitive support needs. The Deep Inclusion Model builds directly on approaches that have already shown strong impact in real-life settings. We monitor around 300 participants annually, combining quantitative surveys, qualitative feedback and input from participants’ networks (family, peers, professionals). Our most mature impact data comes from Brake-Out, a three-year learning trajectory for young adults. We track development in the “yes I can” part: areas such as self-confidence, talent visibility, autonomy, social connectedness, resilience, role uptake and contribution to others. Over the last three years, we observe a consistent positive evolution. Overall positive scores among participants increased from 67.2% at intake to 83.4% in years 2–3. Network respondents increased from 46.9% to 71.7%, while coaches observed growth from 69.1% to 77.1%. The strongest improvements are visible in: • showing talents to others: 54.5% → 95.4% • taking up meaningful roles: 73.5% → 93.8% • future orientation: 75.8% → 87.7% • maintaining social contacts: 57.6% → 75.4% The data shows a clear development pattern: the first year mainly strengthens identity, belonging and talent awareness, while later years show stronger movement towards participation, role uptake and contribution. This reflects the core dynamic of the Deep Inclusion Model, where personal growth and supportive environments reinforce each other over time. While these results are promising, further longitudinal follow-up is needed to fully understand long-term impact after participants leave the programme. Over the next five years, Konekt aims to build on these proven practices by scaling the Deep Inclusion Model towards mainstream systems, supporting schools, organisations and communities to create inclusive environments from within.
Several of our practices have been directly replicated across different cities in Belgium. In addition, through participation in European projects, we have indirectly replicated our approach by inspiring and supporting partners in other countries to apply our practices in their own contexts. These experiences have informed the development of the Deep Inclusion Model.

innovations.name: Talents in Action
innovations.problem: The increasing precariousness of the labour market, the difficulties young people face in accessing stable employment opportunities, the growing incidence of social and economic vulnerabilities, and the rising risk of isolation and disengagement all highlight the need for a profound rethinking of public policy approaches. In Tuscany the 13% of young people is NEETs and even though NEETs are not an omogenous group, researches agree that the main problem is to reach them in order to reactivate them in a training or job context. TALENTI IN AZIONE was designed to create and strenghten local network to identify NEETs and include them in a process of empowerment and training.
innovations.description: In order to address the issue above, TALENTI IN AZIONE led to a perspective reversal in traditional approach: rather than expecting young people to adapt to the traditional modes of service delivery, policy instruments and support mechanisms must be redesigned around the target group's realities, taking into account their timing, languages, communication styles and the places they inhabit and frequent. Effective engagement is not associated with a single intervention; instead, it emerges from a combination of territorial proximity, educational relationships, clarity of the offer, personalised support, and a clear connection to tangible opportunities Breakthrough included: - building and strenghtening local networks of stakeholders (public services, municipalities, training agencies, cultural and youth associations, etc...); - focusing on innovative and active metodologies for training; - final evaluation and assessment in cooperation with all the stakeholders, in order to develope further initiatives aimet to the same target group.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
The TALENTI IN AZIONE initiative led to the development, in cooperation with all the relevant stakeholders, of specific guidelines for future projects aimed to the same target group.
Key issues are: - Reaching and engaging the target group within their everyday environments; - Using simple, clear and non bureaucratic language; - Strenghtening mentoring, guidance and active listenig support; - Tailoring pathways; - Making learning opportunities tangible, applicable and aligned with labour market needs; - Strenghtening local networks; - Investing in prevention measures and engaging young people at risk of becoming NEETs (“pre-NEETs”); - Using economic incentives in complementarity with trust-building, guidance and personalised support measures.

innovations.name: AI Literacy & Future Skills Initiative
innovations.problem: AI is rapidly changing education, employment and civic life, but many people lack the skills and confidence to engage with it critically and productively. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 highlights that employers expect almost 40% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, making upskilling and reskilling a central challenge for the labour market. At the same time, the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of AI systems to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and other persons dealing with AI systems. This creates an urgent need for practical AI literacy beyond technical experts. Young people often use AI tools without understanding their limitations, risks or effects on learning and decision-making. Educators, social organizations and SMEs frequently lack accessible formats to address AI in their own work. innovations.name: START MAJOR
innovations.problem: Romania faces one of the most severe youth disengagement crises in the European Union. Structural barriers, particularly within the vocational and technical education sector, translate into high rates of early school leaving, low financial literacy, and persistent exclusion from the labor market for young people from vulnerable backgrounds. Key data points that define the problem landscape: -Romania's youth unemployment rate is consistently 8 percentage points above the EU average. -Approximately 60,000 young people are active beneficiaries of the child protection system, and over 3,000 age out of institutional care every year with no preparation for independent adult life. -Only 1 in 70 youth leaving the child protection system finds formal employment a systemic failure of both the education and social support systems. -Financial literacy levels among Romanian youth rank among the lowest in the EU. Most students in vocational and technical schools receive no structured financial education. -Entrepreneurial thinking remains largely absent from curriculum, leaving students without the mindset or tools to create their own economic pathways. -Geography compounds the problem: vocational schools in rural counties and small towns have far less access to mentors, role models, and practical learning experiences than those in urban centers. The consequence is a deeply entrenched cycle of economic marginalization: young people who lack the financial knowledge to manage basic resources, the career skills to navigate a job market, or the entrepreneurial vision to identify and act on opportunities, end up trapped in patterns of dependence or poverty. The education system, as currently structured, does not bridge this gap. Systemic change requires interventions that go into schools, work directly with students and teachers, and build skills that are immediately applicable in real life.
innovations.description:
START MAJOR was originally conceived and funded by UniCredit Bank Romania as a financial literacy initiative targeting students in vocational and technical high schools. The first edition (2019–2020) was delivered by another NGO partner. From the second edition onward, Association The Social Incubator became the implementing partner, progressively expanding the program's scope. The original single-focus financial literacy model was developed into a three-module integrated curriculum: financial education (Module I), career and employability skills (Module II), and entrepreneurship camps (Module III).
START MAJOR 2025 addresses the above systemic gaps through a deliberately integrated, multi-layered, and experiential approach, one that operates at the intersection of formal education and non-formal learning. Module I – Financial Literacy (5,000+ participants | 90 live sessions) Interactive live sessions delivered directly in schools introduce students to practical financial concepts: budgeting, saving, responsible spending, credit and the use of digital financial tools. Facilitated by trained volunteers from UniCredit Bank and The Social Incubator, these sessions are designed to be immediately applicable rather than purely theoretical. The scale sessions is made possible by a network of corporate volunteers, making this one of the largest private-sector-supported financial literacy drives in Romanian secondary education. Module II – Career & Employability (5000+ participants | live sessions) Students engage in structured employability sessions that address: CV writing and job search skills, interview techniques, transferable skills identification, and career planning. The sessions bridge the gap between the vocational school environment and the real expectations of employers, using active learning methods, peer exercises, and direct interaction with professionals. This module responds directly to the documented disconnect between vocational graduates' skills profiles and labor market requirements. Module III – Entrepreneurship Camps (500+ participants | 15 counties | 15 camps x 3 days x 30 students) The entrepreneurship camps are the transformative heart of START MAJOR. Each 3-day immersive camp brings together 30 students from a given county in a structured learning environment where they work through the fundamentals of starting and running a business. Themes covered include: legal and regulatory basics, product strategy, market and customer analysis, competitive positioning, marketing, financial modelling, and the Business Model Canvas framework. Students engage in business simulations, practical exercises. The final day of each camp centers on pitching: students present their business ideas to panels of mentors and business representatives, preparing for the national Pitch Day competition. Hybrid Pitch Day – National Competition The national Pitch Day brings together the most promising ideas developed across all 15 camps in an online competition format open to all participants. Teacher Training Camp – Systemic Multiplier A dedicated teacher-training camp equips educators from participating schools with the skills, tools, and confidence to continue delivering financial literacy and entrepreneurship content beyond the program's funded cycle. This is the key systemic change mechanism: by investing in teachers, START MAJOR builds a durable infrastructure for ongoing impact that does not depend on external funding. What makes START MAJOR genuinely innovative is not a single feature but the combination: (1) integration of financial, employability, and entrepreneurship education in a single, coherent program; (2) national territorial deployment through county-level camps rather than centralized delivery; (3) private-sector co-design and volunteer delivery that embeds real-world knowledge into every session; (4) a competitive mechanism (Pitch Day) that elevates ambition and visibility; (5) teacher capacity-building that turns a time

Each edition brought meaningful adaptation, the three-module curriculum developed for START MAJOR has also informed broader program portfolio, with elements of financial literacy and entrepreneurship education integrated into other projects implemented by the association, including programs targeting NEET youth, young people leaving the child protection system and students in rural and underserved communities.

innovations.name: Engaging Youth in Digital Green Future 2.0 - GREENOVATE
innovations.problem: Young people are increasingly exposed to information about climate change and sustainability, but they often remain excluded from meaningful participation in policy discussions and local decision-making processes related to the green transition. Environmental debates are frequently communicated through institutional or technical language that is not accessible or engaging for youth audiences. At the same time, many schools and local communities still lack structured spaces where young people can connect digital communication skills with environmental literacy, advocacy, and civic participation. The challenge is even more visible in smaller communities and in the Western Balkans region, where opportunities for youth engagement in European sustainability debates are more limited. As a result, many young people feel disconnected from both European policies and their own potential role in shaping sustainable futures.
innovations.description:
The project “Engaging Youth in a Digital Green Future” served as the foundation and inspiration for the development of GREENOVATE 2.0. The original project was implemented within the youth and environmental sector through international cooperation between civil society organisations working on youth participation, sustainability, and digital engagement across Europe, including Western Balkan countries. The initial approach emerged during the post-pandemic period, when European societies were facing major social, economic, and environmental challenges connected to the green transition and the implementation of the European Green Deal. The project addressed the limited participation of young people in policy discussions and decision-making processes related to sustainability and climate action. Building on this experience, EY-DGF 2.0_GREENOVATE further developed the approach by introducing a stronger digital communication and advocacy dimension through the GREENOVATE platform. The project expanded the original methodology into a participatory digital ecosystem that combines youth engagement, green literacy, community-driven communication, and international cooperation.
GREENOVATE introduced a participatory digital ecosystem that combines youth engagement, green literacy, digital communication, and advocacy into one interconnected model. Instead of treating young people only as participants, the project positioned them as active contributors to the public conversation on sustainability. Through participation days, discussions, digital storytelling, online communication, and local green initiatives, young people gained opportunities to explore sustainability topics in accessible and practical ways. The project connected formal and non-formal learning approaches while using social media and digital platforms as tools for engagement, visibility, and peer-to-peer learning. An important innovative aspect of the project is its long-term communication structure through the GREENOVATE platform, which enables the continuation of youth-led communication and advocacy beyond the duration of the project itself.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The project strengthened young people’s understanding of the European Green Deal, climate action, and sustainable development while improving their digital communication and participation skills. It created new spaces for dialogue between youth, educators, civil society organisations, and local communities. GREENOVATE successfully developed an active digital communication ecosystem through its website, newsletters, and social media channels, reaching thousands of young people and stakeholders across Europe. The project also contributed to stronger international cooperation and increased visibility of youth perspectives in discussions about sustainability and the green transition. Beyond measurable outreach, the project encouraged a stronger sense of responsibility, participation, and ownership among young people regarding environmental and social challenges in their communities.
The GREENOVATE approach has been implemented through international cooperation between partner organisations from several European countries, including both EU Member States and Western Balkan countries. The project methodology was adapted to different local contexts through participation days, youth discussions, local sustainability initiatives, digital communication activities, and advocacy events organised in partner countries. The innovation was particularly scaled through the development of the GREENOVATE digital platform and its connected communication ecosystem, which enabled the participation of young people and stakeholders beyond the physical project activities. Through social media communication, newsletters, online discussions, and digital storytelling, the project reached wider audiences across different regions and created opportunities for transferability of the approach. The methodology also demonstrated adaptability across sectors, combining youth work, non-formal education, environmental awareness, digital communication, and civic participation. Elements of the approach can be further replicated by schools, youth organisations, municipalities, and civil society networks working on sustainability and youth engagement.

innovations.name: The Museum of Abandonment
innovations.problem: The project addresses the long-term social consequences of child abandonment, institutionalisation, and the exclusion of vulnerable children from public memory. Despite affecting hundreds of thousands of children in Romania and across Europe, these experiences remain insufficiently documented, understood, and integrated into public awareness, education, and policymaking. The lack of recognition of this history contributes to stigma, social exclusion, and limited understanding of how institutional care impacts individuals, families, and communities across generations. The project also addresses the need for innovative ways to engage citizens, survivors, and decision-makers in conversations about child rights, social inclusion, and democratic accountability.
innovations.description: The Museum of Abandonment is Romania's first fully digital and participatory museum and one of the few initiatives worldwide dedicated to documenting the history and legacy of child abandonment and institutional care. It combines a research hub, a digital archive of over 20,000 documents, participatory memory work, web and VR exhibitions, and immersive storytelling to transform collective memory into a tool for social inclusion and social change. Winner of the World Summit Awards 2025 (Culture & Heritage), the museum demonstrates how digital innovation can amplify marginalized voices, foster civic engagement, and address historical injustices.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The Museum of Abandonment initiated the first comprehensive research and public memory project on the history of child abandonment and institutional care in Romania. For more than 36 years after the fall of communism, the experiences of hundreds of thousands of institutionalised children remained largely absent from public discourse, education, and collective memory. The project was created as a form of social mediation, helping society engage with a difficult and largely silenced history. Over the past five years, the museum has built a unique digital archive containing more than 20,000 documents, photographs, testimonies, and historical records, becoming a reference point for researchers, journalists, artists, educators, survivors, and policymakers. Through its research hub, participatory methodologies, web exhibitions, and VR experiences, the project has made this history accessible to diverse audiences and fostered dialogue on child rights, social inclusion, and historical accountability. Beyond preserving memory, the museum has generated significant cultural and social impact. Since its launch, numerous films, documentaries, theatre productions, academic studies, and journalistic investigations addressing child abandonment and institutionalisation have emerged in Romania, contributing to a broader public conversation on the subject. In 2024, the museum's archive inspired Horror Vacui, the world's longest continuous theatrical performance. Over seven consecutive days, 505 actors performed non-stop testimonies about abandonment and institutionalisation, many drawn directly from the Museum of Abandonment's collections. The event attracted national attention and demonstrated the transformative potential of memory work in the public sphere. The museum has also become an international knowledge resource. Researchers, journalists, artists, and institutions from around the world regularly engage with its work, leading to collaborations with organisations and experts in Egypt, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the United States, and Serbia. In recognition of its contribution to memory, human rights, and social engagement, the Museum of Abandonment became a member of the International Coalition of Sites of Conscience, a global network of more than 350 museums, memorials, and human rights organisations dedicated to connecting history with contemporary social challenges. Through this work, the Museum of Abandonment demonstrates how collective memory, digital innovation, and participatory culture can become powerful tools for social inclusion, civic engagement, and long-term social change. The museum was shortlisted among the top five museum digital projects worldwide at the Museums + Heritage Awards 2024 (Best Use of Digital).

innovations.name: Project SEARCH Portugal
innovations.problem: Project SEARCH Portugal works to address the low rate of competitive employment among young people with disabilities caused by: - Lack of real internship and practical experience opportunities - Cultural barriers and corporate biases - Absence of effective school-to-work transition models - Lack of professional skills adapted to the current market - Fragmentation between schools, social services, families, and employers The program combats exclusion from work and creates real pathways to decent, stable, and competitive employment.
innovations.description:
Project SEARCH originated at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center (USA) in 1996 and served as the direct model for the Portuguese adaptation: a business‑led, workplace‑immersion transition programme that places young people with disabilities into employer‑based internships to achieve competitive employment.
Project SEARCH Portugal represents a systemic innovation in labor inclusion by transforming the workplace into a formal learning space. Instead of one-off internships or theoretical training, the model integrates an entire academic year within partner companies, with rotations through three practical internships, training in technical and social skills, and daily multidisciplinary mentoring. This combination creates an intensive, market-oriented learning path where assessment and adaptation are done in the work context itself—not in a classroom. The truly innovative element is the articulation between employer and educational team: companies cease to be mere recipients of candidates and become co-creators of the training process, receiving technical support to adapt positions and practices. This reduces institutional and cultural barriers, increases employer confidence, and improves the sustainability of hiring. Furthermore, the model incorporates scientific evidence and internationally tested implementation practices—including selection protocols, individualized learning plans, and post-placement follow-up strategies—allowing for faithful and measurable replication. Studies and implementation guides document high success rates when the model is applied faithfully.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
1. Key Results (Evidence): - Increased Competitive Employment Rate. Result:64,30% of participants obtain paid employment in the open market within 6 months of the program. -Retention and Sustainability of Placements. Result: high retention rate at 12 months, demonstrating that the hires are long-lasting. -Gain in Technical and Socio-Professional Skills. Result: measurable improvement in specific job tasks, communication, and autonomy. - Increased Functional Autonomy. Result: participants show progress in time management, commuting, and personal organization. - Employer Satisfaction and Predisposition. Result: positive feedback on productivity and adaptation; increased willingness to hire more participants. - Reduction in the use of social support. Result: average decrease in social support per placed participant, reflecting gains in economic independence. 2. Integrated Benefits for Stakeholders: - For young participants. Benefit: access to real employment pathways that increase autonomy, self-esteem, and income. The program transforms potential into competitive employment and a sustainable career. - For host companies. Benefit: access to motivated talent trained in their own work context; improved organizational culture; gains in productivity and social responsibility; technical support for adaptation and continuous integration. - For families and communities. Benefit: greater confidence in the transition to adulthood; reduced caregiving burden; strengthened local social inclusion. - For the public system and policies. Benefit: replicable proof of concept that reduces social costs in the medium term, contributes to inclusive employment goals, and offers a model that can be funded by ESF+ and national programs. Project SEARCH offers practical evidence, operational tools, and a scalable roadmap that can inform European policies and accelerate adoption in other Member States. The combination of measurable results, success stories, and replicable materials (operating manual, assessment toolkit, trainer training) makes the project an innovation ready for sharing and scaling up at the European level.
Since its inception, Project SEARCH has expanded from a single hospital site to an international network with hundreds of sites across the United States, Canada, the UK, Portugal Spain and other countries, reporting consistent rates of competitive employment and employer satisfaction where implemented with fidelity. These documented outcomes and the model’s replicability are central to its appeal as a basis for national adaptations. Project SEARCH provided a tested, employer‑driven blueprint that directly addresses the core barrier the Portuguese initiative targets: lack of real workplace experience and employer readiness to hire young people with disabilities. The combination of workplace immersion, employer capacity building and structured follow‑up made it an ideal, evidence‑based model to adapt to Portugal’s labour‑market and education systems.

sections.question: Problem

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:
Project SEARCH originated at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center (USA) in 1996 and served as the direct model for the Portuguese adaptation: a business‑led, workplace‑immersion transition programme that places young people with disabilities into employer‑based internships to achieve competitive employment.
Project SEARCH Portugal represents a systemic innovation in labor inclusion by transforming the workplace into a formal learning space. Instead of one-off internships or theoretical training, the model integrates an entire academic year within partner companies, with rotations through three practical internships, training in technical and social skills, and daily multidisciplinary mentoring. This combination creates an intensive, market-oriented learning path where assessment and adaptation are done in the work context itself—not in a classroom. The truly innovative element is the articulation between employer and educational team: companies cease to be mere recipients of candidates and become co-creators of the training process, receiving technical support to adapt positions and practices. This reduces institutional and cultural barriers, increases employer confidence, and improves the sustainability of hiring. Furthermore, the model incorporates scientific evidence and internationally tested implementation practices—including selection protocols, individualized learning plans, and post-placement follow-up strategies—allowing for faithful and measurable replication. Studies and implementation guides document high success rates when the model is applied faithfully.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
1. Key Results (Evidence): - Increased Competitive Employment Rate. Result:64,30% of participants obtain paid employment in the open market within 6 months of the program. -Retention and Sustainability of Placements. Result: high retention rate at 12 months, demonstrating that the hires are long-lasting. -Gain in Technical and Socio-Professional Skills. Result: measurable improvement in specific job tasks, communication, and autonomy. - Increased Functional Autonomy. Result: participants show progress in time management, commuting, and personal organization. - Employer Satisfaction and Predisposition. Result: positive feedback on productivity and adaptation; increased willingness to hire more participants. - Reduction in the use of social support. Result: average decrease in social support per placed participant, reflecting gains in economic independence. 2. Integrated Benefits for Stakeholders: - For young participants. Benefit: access to real employment pathways that increase autonomy, self-esteem, and income. innovations.name: Dentist for People with Disabilities
innovations.problem: People with disabilities face significant and persistent barriers in accessing adequate dental care services. In Romania, as in many other countries, dental healthcare is often not fully integrated into public health support systems, and available services are limited, especially for vulnerable groups. One of the main problems is the lack of accessible and specialized dental services for people with physical, intellectual, sensory, or multiple disabilities. Many dental clinics are not equipped with the necessary infrastructure, adapted equipment, or trained staff to properly treat patients with special needs. This results in frequent exclusion of these individuals from basic oral healthcare. Another major issue is the financial barrier. Dental treatments are often costly, and public healthcare coverage for dental services is minimal or insufficient. As a result, many people with disabilities are unable to afford regular check-ups or essential treatments, leading to untreated dental conditions, chronic pain, infections, and serious complications that affect overall health. In addition, there is a lack of awareness and training among some healthcare professionals regarding how to safely and effectively treat patients with disabilities. This further limits access and reduces the quality of care available. These combined barriers contribute to poor oral health, reduced quality of life, social exclusion, and loss of dignity for many people with disabilities. The project The Dentist for People with Disabilities, developed by the Drumul Independenței Association, addresses these challenges by creating a free, accessible, and inclusive dental care model designed specifically to meet the needs of this vulnerable group.
innovations.description: The project The Dentist for People with Disabilities, developed by the Drumul Independenței Association, offers an innovative and integrated solution to the lack of accessible dental care for people with disabilities by creating a free, inclusive, and patient-centered dental care model specifically designed for this vulnerable group. The core innovation of the project lies in its holistic approach, which combines free dental services with accessibility, adapted medical protocols, and a strong focus on empathy and individualized care. Instead of treating dental care as a standard service, the project redefines it as a tailored experience that responds to the physical, psychological, and social needs of each patient. A key element of the solution is the development of adapted dental services, including trained personnel capable of working with patients with diverse disabilities, as well as procedures adjusted to ensure safety, comfort, and trust. This includes longer consultation times, simplified communication methods, and a calm, supportive environment. The project also introduces a barrier-free access model, ensuring that financial constraints do not prevent beneficiaries from receiving treatment. By offering dental services free of charge, it directly addresses one of the most critical causes of exclusion in oral healthcare. Another innovative aspect is the emphasis on dignity and psychological comfort. Many people with disabilities experience anxiety or trauma when accessing medical services. The project therefore integrates empathy-based care, aiming to reduce fear, build trust, and create a safe therapeutic experience. In addition, the project promotes community awareness and professional education, encouraging better understanding of disability-specific needs among dental professionals and society in general. This contributes to long-term systemic change in how healthcare services are delivered. Through this integrated model, the project does not only provide treatment, but also builds a sustainable framework for inclusive dental care, improving health outcomes, social inclusion, and quality of life for people with disabilities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: The project The Dentist for People with Disabilities, implemented by the Drumul Independenței Association, is expected to generate significant and sustainable results in improving access to dental healthcare for people with disabilities. A primary result of the project is the increased access to free and specialized dental services for people with physical, intellectual, sensory, and multiple disabilities. By removing financial and structural barriers, the project enables beneficiaries to receive essential treatments that were previously difficult or impossible to access. Another key outcome is the improvement of oral health status among beneficiaries. Through regular consultations, preventive care, and necessary treatments, the project contributes to reducing untreated dental conditions, chronic pain, infections, and complications associated with poor oral hygiene. The project also leads to a measurable improvement in quality of life and well-being. Better oral health directly contributes to improved nutrition, communication, self-confidence, and social participation, thereby enhancing overall independence and dignity. A further important benefit is the strengthening of inclusive healthcare practices. Through trained medical staff and adapted care protocols, the project contributes to the development of a more accessible and disability-aware dental care system, with potential for replication in other healthcare settings. The initiative also generates increased awareness among healthcare professionals and the community regarding the specific needs of people with disabilities. This supports long-term attitudinal change and promotes a more inclusive approach within the healthcare sector. In addition, the project contributes to reducing social exclusion and healthcare inequalities, ensuring that people with disabilities are no longer left behind in access to essential medical services. Overall, the project delivers a sustainable and rights-based impact, aligned with the principles of equality, accessibility, and non-discrimination, as set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD).

innovations.name: Scaling Trauma-Responsive Approach in Slovak Schools
innovations.problem: Children's mental health in Slovakia is deteriorating sharply: 30% of 15-year-olds report feeling sad or depressed several times a week, and 17% have attempted self-harm or suicide (HBSC 2021/2022). At the same time, teachers feel ill-equipped to respond — over 60% report high or moderate work-related stress, and most lack the skills to work effectively with children in emotional distress or with challenging behaviour. The system's response — increasing the number of school counsellors — cannot keep pace with growing demand. What is missing is a preventive approach that equips every teacher with the understanding and tools to create safety in the classroom every day, before crisis intervention is needed.
innovations.description:
The Trauma-Responsive Approach (TRA) is a paradigm shift in how adults in schools perceive and respond to children's behaviour. Rather than sanctioning "difficult" behaviour, TRA builds adults' capacity to understand its neurological and experiential roots — and to respond with strategies that de-escalate tension and foster a sense of safety and belonging for every child.
What makes this project innovative is not TRA itself (which is internationally recognised best practice), but the train-the-trainer scaling model: expert knowledge is transferred to school specialists, who in turn coach classroom teachers, who then engage parents and the community. This peer-embedded model, co-designed with practitioners and informed by parallel experience in the Czech Republic, addresses the key barrier identified in prior pilots — that training alone is insufficient without embedded, sustained support inside the school. The project also integrates TRA into formal school documents and advocates for its inclusion in national educational policy, making the innovation systemic rather than project-bound.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
By the end of the project, the following concrete results are expected:
3 pilot schools with fully implemented TRA model, improved classroom climate and reduced challenging behaviour (measured by pre/post questionnaires and interviews)
at least 80 teachers and school specialists trained in TRA and actively applying it
approximately 800 pupils directly benefiting from TRA in the classroom
1,500 members of school communities (parents, wider staff) informed about TRA principles
100+ participants across four new piloted training programmes
a network of trained TRA ambassadors ready to support other schools without ongoing expert involvement
8 revised school policy documents (school rules and educational plans) embedding TRA principles
50+ media outputs (articles, podcasts, social media posts) raising public awareness
recommendations submitted to the Ministry of Education for TRA to be recognised as a recommended approach for inclusive education in Slovakia

innovations.name: Coruja-Academy: Digital Financial Education for the Digital Economy
innovations.problem:
Across Europe, citizens of all ages are being asked to navigate an increasingly complex digital world shaped by artificial intelligence, digital finance, online platforms and rapidly evolving technologies. However, education systems and lifelong learning programmes often struggle to provide accessible, practical and age-appropriate learning opportunities that develop the critical thinking, digital and financial skills needed to participate safely and confidently in this new environment.
The challenge is particularly significant for children, older adults, people with disabilities and communities in rural areas, who may face additional barriers to accessing high-quality educational opportunities. As digital technologies continue to transform daily life, there is a growing need for inclusive educational models that help individuals understand, question and responsibly use these technologies rather than simply consume them.
innovations.description:
Coruja-Academy has developed an innovative educational framework that combines digital financial education, critical thinking, gamification, storytelling and hands-on learning experiences to make complex concepts accessible to diverse audiences. Rather than teaching technology as an end in itself, the initiative uses frontier technologies as educational tools to help participants understand how the digital world works and how to engage with it responsibly.
A distinctive feature of the methodology is the use of blockchain as a practical example to explore transparency, security, decentralisation, trust and record-keeping. Participants experience these concepts through interactive activities, games and real-world simulations adapted to different age groups and learning needs. The same framework is successfully applied to children, young people, seniors and people with disabilities, demonstrating a high degree of adaptability and inclusion.
The initiative also promotes critical thinking about emerging technologies, digital services, artificial intelligence and online information, helping participants become informed and active citizens in the digital economy rather than passive users of technology.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Coruja-Academy has successfully implemented its educational methodology across schools, senior learning programmes and organisations supporting people with disabilities in rural Portugal.
The initiative has demonstrated that complex topics such as digital finance, online safety, blockchain, artificial intelligence and critical thinking can be transformed into accessible learning experiences for children, young people, seniors and people with disabilities. This is achieved through a combination of storytelling, gamification and hands-on activities specifically designed for different learning profiles.
One of the initiative’s most significant achievements has been the successful adaptation of the same educational framework to multiple generations and vulnerable groups, creating shared opportunities for learning, participation and digital inclusion. This approach has enabled communities that are often excluded from innovation-focused educational programmes to actively engage with the opportunities and challenges of the digital economy.
The project continues to expand its reach and is currently undergoing independent impact evaluation in collaboration with researchers from the Catholic University of Portugal, supporting the development of evidence for future replication in other European regions.

Coruja-Academy has successfully implemented its educational methodology across schools, senior learning programmes and organisations supporting people with disabilities in rural Portugal.
The initiative has demonstrated that complex topics such as digital finance, online safety, blockchain, artificial intelligence and critical thinking can be transformed into accessible learning experiences for children, young people, seniors and people with disabilities. This is achieved through a combination of storytelling, gamification and hands-on activities specifically designed for different learning profiles.
One of the initiative’s most significant achievements has been the successful adaptation of the same educational framework to multiple generations and vulnerable groups, creating shared opportunities for learning, participation and digital inclusion. This approach has enabled communities that are often excluded from innovation-focused educational programmes to actively engage with the opportunities and challenges of the digital economy.
The project continues to expand its reach and is currently undergoing independent impact evaluation in collaboration with researchers from the Catholic University of Portugal, supporting the development of evidence for future replication in other European regions.

innovations.raw_text:
Coruja-Academy: Digital Financial Education for the Digital Economy
Across Europe, citizens of all ages are being asked to navigate an increasingly complex digital world shaped by artificial intelligence, digital finance, online platforms and rapidly evolving technologies. However, education systems and lifelong learning programmes often struggle to provide accessible, practical and age-appropriate learning opportunities that develop the critical thinking, digital and financial skills needed to participate safely and confidently in this new environment.
The challenge is particularly significant for children, older adults, people with disabilities and communities in rural areas, who may face additional barriers to accessing high-quality educational opportunities. As digital technologies continue to transform daily life, there is a growing need for inclusive educational models that help individuals understand, question and responsibly use these technologies rather than simply consume them.
Coruja-Academy has developed an innovative educational framework that combines digital financial education, critical thinking, gamification, storytelling and hands-on learning experiences to make complex concepts accessible to diverse audiences. Rather than teaching technology as an end in itself, the initiative uses frontier technologies as educational tools to help participants understand how the digital world works and how to engage with it responsibly.
A distinctive feature of the methodology is the use of blockchain as a practical example to explore transparency, security, decentralisation, trust and record-keeping. Participants experience these concepts through interactive activities, games and real-world simulations adapted to different age groups and learning needs. The same framework is successfully applied to children, young people, seniors and people with disabilities, demonstrating a high degree of adaptability and inclusion.
The initiative also promotes critical thinking about emerging technologies, digital services, artificial intelligence and online information, helping participants become informed and active citizens in the digital economy rather than passive users of technology.

innovations.name: VirIAto Assist
innovations.problem: The active population faces growing pressure to adapt to AI-driven workplace transformation, yet structured, accessible training remains scarce outside major urban centres. Many professionals fear job displacement but lack the tools or spaces to engage with AI constructively. Job seekers, in particular, are at risk of being left behind in a labour market that increasingly values AI competences. Meanwhile, higher education students enter professional life without practical AI skills aligned to real workplace needs. This skills gap is especially pronounced in regional cities like Viseu, where dedicated upskilling opportunities are limited.
innovations.description: VirIAto Assist addresses this gap by delivering practical, context-adapted AI training directly within the institutions where the active population already operates — school clusters, employment centres, and universities. Rather than asking people to seek out training, the programme brings it to them. Sessions are co-designed with each partner institution to ensure immediate relevance, covering tools like generative AI assistants, prompt engineering for professional tasks, and responsible AI use. The volunteer-led, near-peer model keeps the tone accessible and non-intimidating, transforming AI from a threat into a practical ally.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Since its launch in 2026, VirIAto Assist has reached 180+ participants across 3 institutional partners in the Viseu district: a school cluster, the national employment and vocational training institute (IEFP), and a higher education institution. The programme has engaged a deliberately diverse active population — employed professionals, job seekers, and university students — demonstrating the model's adaptability across different professional contexts. All activity has been delivered at near-zero cost through volunteer commitment and institutional partnerships.
tags: Modernising labour market institutions and services
Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change
Equal access to education and training
Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: Educ'AI
innovations.problem: Students across Portugal are growing up in an AI-saturated environment without any structured preparation to understand, question or navigate it. AI literacy is largely absent from formal school curricula, leaving young people without the tools to critically engage with the technologies shaping their future. This gap is particularly acute in mid-sized regional cities like Viseu, where access to tech education initiatives is limited compared to major urban centres. Without intervention, the next generation risks becoming passive consumers of AI rather than informed, active citizens.
innovations.description: Educ'AI addresses this gap through a modular, co-designed curriculum delivered by young near-peers — volunteers aged 18–30 who bring both technical knowledge and relatable proximity to students. Sessions are adapted to each school context and cover AI concepts, real-world applications, ethical dilemmas, and digital safety. The collaborative methodology — modular, interactive, and contextualised — ensures immediate relevance for participants and allows rapid adaptation across different school levels, from primary to post-secondary. Integration into the AI for Good (ITU/UN) network connects the programme to international standards and a global community of practice.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Since its launch in 2025, Educ'AI has reached 300+ students across 4 partner institutions in the Viseu district, spanning Year 7 through to post-secondary level. The programme is actively expanding in 2026 to new schools and municipalities. All activity has been delivered at near-zero cost through volunteer commitment and institutional partnerships.
tags: Equal access to education and training

innovations.name: Vem D'AI
innovations.problem: Older adults in mid-sized Portuguese cities face significant barriers to participating in the digital transition. The rapid proliferation of AI tools — from voice assistants to generative content — has created an information gap that disproportionately affects seniors, increasing their vulnerability to disinformation, online fraud, and digital exclusion. At the same time, there is a lack of accessible, non-formal learning spaces where this population can engage with technology in a safe, supportive environment. Existing digital literacy programmes rarely address AI specifically, and even fewer are designed with and for senior communities at a local level.
innovations.description: Vem D'AI addresses this gap through an intergenerational, peer-to-peer learning model: young volunteers aged 18–30 design and facilitate sessions specifically adapted to the cognitive rhythms, life experiences, and interests of older adults. The curriculum is structured progressively — from AI fundamentals and hands-on prompt engineering to more critical topics such as deepfakes, filter bubbles, and online privacy — and is iteratively refined based on participant feedback between seasons. The model is low-cost, volunteer-driven, and inherently scalable: it requires no specialised infrastructure, relies on community partnerships, and produces replicable pedagogical materials. Its integration into the global AI for Good (ITU/UN) network gives it international visibility and a framework for cross-border transfer.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Across Seasons 1 and 2 (November 2025 – April 2026), Vem D'AI achieved the following outcomes based on 18 evaluation responses: 100% of participants reported learning something new about AI; 100% reported increased confidence in interacting with AI tools; overall satisfaction averaged 4.75 out of 5; and 100% found the practical examples helpful for understanding. Season 1 reached approximately 102 participations across 4 sessions at USAVIS; Season 2 launched in April 2026 with 24 participants in a condensed opening session. Partners include USAVIS and IPV. The project operates at zero net cost through volunteer commitment and in-kind contributions.

innovations.name: BRAVE, Empowering Girls to Shape Public Space Through Sport
innovations.problem: Girls and young women are underrepresented in both sport and public space. They are less physically active, feel less welcome in public environments, and are more likely to withdraw from sports and outdoor activities during adolescence. Although public space appears accessible to everyone, social and spatial barriers often limit the participation and visibility of girls and women.
innovations.description:
BRAVE is a capacity-building organisation that empowers girls and young women to claim, shape, and activate public space through sport and leisure activities.
To achieve this, BRAVE developed an innovative methodology that combines co-creation, sport activation, leadership development, and coaching. Through a structured trajectory, girls explore their neighbourhood, identify barriers, co-design public spaces, organise their own initiatives, and strengthen their voice as active contributors to their communities.
The methodology is built around three complementary pillars:
BRAVE Spaces – girls explore, co-create, and help redesign public spaces so they better reflect their needs and experiences.
BRAVE Actions – girls activate these spaces through sport, movement, and leisure initiatives that encourage participation and visibility.
BRAVE Voices – girls strengthen their self-confidence, leadership, and agency through coaching, enabling them to become ambassadors, role models, and co-creators of their neighbourhoods and cities.
BRAVE combines sport, placemaking, youth participation, and coaching in one integrated methodology.
Rather than seeing girls as users or beneficiaries, we position them as co-creators of public space. We do not focus solely on changing individual behaviour; we also address the social and spatial systems that create exclusion. By combining participation, activation, and empowerment, BRAVE creates lasting change for both people and places.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
BRAVE contributes to:
Increased participation in sport and physical activity among girls and young women.
Higher levels of self-confidence, leadership, ownership, and entrepreneurial skills.
Greater capacity among girls to take initiative, organise activities, and engage others.
Stronger social networks and community engagement.
Greater visibility of girls in public space.
More inclusive and gender-sensitive public spaces.
Increased awareness among local governments and organisations about gender inequalities in public space.
The methodology has already been implemented in several Belgian cities.

innovations.name: Shared Integration: Building Inclusive Communities Through Volunteering
innovations.problem:
Across Europe, many newcomers experience social isolation, loneliness and limited opportunities to build meaningful relationships in their new communities. Language courses and formal integration pathways often fail to provide the social connections needed to feel part of society.
At the same time, public debate around migration is increasingly polarised. Many people have few opportunities for direct contact with newcomers, allowing stereotypes and misconceptions to persist.
Organisations also face challenges in recruiting volunteers and often struggle to reflect the diversity of the communities they serve.
Compagnie Cordial addresses these interconnected challenges by creating meaningful encounters between newcomers and local residents through shared volunteering experiences. We tackle isolation, strengthen social cohesion and help prevent polarisation by fostering genuine human connections.
innovations.description:
The innovation lies not only in what we do, but in how we understand integration and participation.
Compagnie Cordial challenges the dominant assumption that integration is primarily the responsibility of newcomers. We shift the focus from deficits to talents, from activation to participation, and from one-sided adaptation to shared responsibility.
Our innovation combines four mutually reinforcing elements:
1. Volunteering as a lever for inclusion
We use volunteering as a powerful tool to create meaningful encounters between people who would otherwise rarely meet. By working together on concrete activities, social barriers are reduced naturally and relationships are built on shared experiences rather than differences.
2. A dual-sided transformation model
Most integration initiatives focus exclusively on newcomers. We simultaneously invest in the people who participate and the organisations that receive them. Through training, coaching and practical tools, organisations develop an inclusive reflex and learn how to create welcoming environments.
3. Community-led participation
Experienced volunteers can become ambassadors who welcome, mentor and guide new participants and partner organisations. This creates a self-reinforcing ecosystem where community members increasingly take ownership of inclusion and participation.
4. Bridging social and economic participation
Through our Work Your Magic programme, newcomers connect with HR professionals and employers through corporate volunteering. These encounters strengthen confidence, increase labour market knowledge and help employers recognise the talents and resilience of newcomers.
Together, these elements create a sustainable model that simultaneously addresses social isolation, exclusion, labour-market barriers and societal polarisation.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence:
Compagnie Cordial has evolved from a local experiment in Ghent in 2016 into one of Belgium's largest networks for inclusive volunteering:
We are now active in 7 municipalities across Flanders and Brussels.
More than 6.300 volunteers have registered since the organisation's founding.
Key results 2025
1.045 newcomers registered to do volunteer work. 60% of them started volunteer work within the same year.
343 partner organisations engaged in inclusive volunteering in 2025.
A total of 1.338 volunteers (a combination of ‘old’ and ‘newly registered’ volunteers) did volunteer work for a total of 8.885 days.
We organised 295 orientation and community activities
1177 unique volunteers attended one or more of these activities
Benefits for newcomers
Reduced social isolation and loneliness
Increased sense of belonging and wellbeing
Expanded social and professional networks
Greater confidence, civic participation and access to employment opportunities.
Benefits for organisations
More diverse and representative volunteer teams.
Stronger inclusion practices and organisational culture
Increased capacity to engage with diverse communities.
Benefits for society
Stronger social cohesion and community resilience.
Reduced prejudice and social distance.
Increased trust between different population groups
Greater resilience against social polarisation
As one volunteer described the experience: “It was medicine for the soul. For the first time since arriving in Belgium, I felt part of society again.”

Experienced volunteers can become ambassadors who welcome, mentor and guide new participants and partner organisations. This creates a self-reinforcing ecosystem where community members increasingly take ownership of inclusion and participation.
4. Bridging social and economic participation
Through our Work Your Magic programme, newcomers connect with HR professionals and employers through corporate volunteering. These encounters strengthen confidence, increase labour market knowledge and help employers recognise the talents and resilience of newcomers.
Together, these elements create a sustainable model that simultaneously addresses social isolation, exclusion, labour-market barriers and societal polarisation.
Compagnie Cordial has evolved from a local experiment in Ghent in 2016 into one of Belgium's largest networks for inclusive volunteering:
We are now active in 7 municipalities across Flanders and Brussels.
More than 6.300 volunteers have registered since the organisation's founding.
Key results 2025
1.045 newcomers registered to do volunteer work. 60% of them started volunteer work within the same year.
343 partner organisations engaged in inclusive volunteering in 2025.
A total of 1.338 volunteers (a combination of ‘old’ and ‘newly registered’ volunteers) did volunteer work for a total of 8.885 days.
We organised 295 orientation and community activities
1177 unique volunteers attended one or more of these activities
Benefits for newcomers
Reduced social isolation and loneliness
Increased sense of belonging and wellbeing
Expanded social and professional networks
Greater confidence, civic participation and access to employment opportunities.
Benefits for organisations
More diverse and representative volunteer teams.
Stronger inclusion practices and organisational culture
Increased capacity to engage with diverse communities.
Benefits for society
Stronger social cohesion and community resilience.
Reduced prejudice and social distance.
Increased trust between different population groups
Greater resilience against social polarisation
As one volunteer described the experience: “It was medicine for the soul. For the first time since arriving in Belgium, I felt part of society again.”

innovations.name: INSPIRE – an inspiring network for an inclusive labour market
innovations.problem:
People with disabilities still face significant barriers to entering the labour market today.
These barriers are:
practical (adaptation of tasks, workplace, assistive tools)
social (collaboration, communication, expectations in the workplace)
In addition, support is often fragmented across sectors (welfare, education, employment). As a result, pathways are poorly aligned and not always adapted to the individual.
Consequences:
limited access to employment
low sustainability of employment
increased risk of social exclusion
innovations.description:
INSPIRE develops an approach based on:
personalised pathways
cross-sector collaboration (welfare, education, labour market)
co-creation with multiple stakeholders
cross-border cooperation
What distinguishes INSPIRE is its methodology:
We bring together multiple perspectives: participant, job coach, expert, employer
We first analyse situations through dialogue and participatory methods
We test solutions in real-life pilot labs
We adjust based on what works and what does not
The results are consolidated in a dynamic toolbox consisting of:
methodologies (e.g. dialogue and co-creation formats)
good practices
concrete solutions (practical and social)
insights on guidance and collaboration
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
For participants:
development of skills
increased self-confidence and autonomy
progression towards employment, training or volunteering
For organisations:
improved cross-sector collaboration
increased understanding of workplace barriers
access to practical tools and methodologies
At system level:
better alignment between welfare, education and labour market
a transferable model for inclusive support
Additional result: dynamic toolbox A key deliverable is the development of a toolbox that:
evolves through different pilot labs
is based on real-life experience
can be used by other organisations
Impact measurement Impact is monitored through:
individual pathway tracking
evaluation of skills and participation
monitoring transitions (education → employment)

innovations.name: Community-based regeneration of urban deprived areas and neighborhoods
innovations.problem: Asertos addresses the multidimensional urban vulnerability affecting marginalized neighborhoods in Alicante. The core problem is the convergence of severe habitat deterioration (both in housing and public spaces) and social fragmentation, which act as critical negative determinants of physical, mental, and social health. Traditional top-down welfare models have historically failed to reverse these conditions, often worsening them by fostering a culture of chronic dependency that erodes community agency. Furthermore, these territories suffer from "unnoticed vulnerability"; institutional statistics frequently fail to capture the real depth of their exclusion, leading to systematic neglect and a lack of specialized residential and social support. This complex system of inequality results in the breakdown of social networks and the reproduction of poverty cycles, directly impacting the life expectancy and autonomy of residents.
innovations.description:
Asertos provides a paradigm shift in urban regeneration by moving from a deficit-based welfare model to a salutogenic, asset-based approach. Instead of focusing solely on what neighborhoods lack, the methodology (based on the ABCD) is designed to discover, connect, and mobilize the existing "health heritage" and local talents of the community. The operational heart of this solution is the Resource Bank, a hybrid institution where residents exchange time, skills, and materials using a social currency called "Community Assets" (AC). A key innovative mechanism is the Inmaterial Social Compensation: families receiving support for home improvements commit to "paying back" the investment by contributing 0.1 hours of community work for every euro invested. This circular economy transforms individual aid into a collective investment, turning residents from passive beneficiaries into active co-producers of their own habitat. Furthermore, the solution redefines the professional role into that of "social elevator operators". These practitioners (architects, social educators, and mediators) work through Intensive Field Monitoring (IFM), inhabiting the neighborhood to build deep relationships based on the "pace of trust". They act as facilitators ("on tap, not on top") who provide expert resources without overstepping community agency. Finally, the project ensures long-term sustainability by transitioning from temporary interventions to stable governance through the "Celestina Urbana" Multi-purpose Cooperative. This legal and relational device empowers the neighborhood to be managed as a Common Pool Resource (RUC), allowing for the autonomous management of housing, common spaces, and essential services.
The Asertos program is primarily based on the WeCo methodology and the Territoire Zéro Bidonville program. > Country: France. > Sector: Social Architecture and Urban Regeneration. > Organisation: Association Quatorze. > Project Name: Territoire Zéro Bidonville (using the WeCo methodology for slum reabsorption).
Additionally, the project is methodologically grounded in the Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) approach. > Country: United States and Ireland. > Sector: Community Development and Public Health. > Organisation: ABCD Institute (Northwestern University) and Nurture Development (Ireland). > Approach Name: Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD).
Other significant inspirations include the work of Sanctuary Housing in Scotland, which applies ABCD within social housing, and the MERGING European project (specifically the Caliu Urbà pilot in Spain).
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Asertos delivers measurable improvements in health, habitat, and community agency by shifting the focus from neighborhood deficits to local strengths. The key results and benefits are structured across three dimensions: > Collective Health and Subjective Wellbeing: The project significantly enhances the Sense of Coherence (SOC), the cognitive and emotional capacity to understand, manage, and find meaning in life's challenges. By fostering a strong Sense of Community, it reduces social isolation and improves collective resilience, providing a "health heritage" that buffers residents against structural inequality. > Physical Habitat and Living Conditions: Tangible results include 13 integral housing renovations, 67 urgent interventions to improve residential safety, and the transformation of abandoned plots into community-managed parks and gardens. Unlike traditional models, these improvements achieve 100% adherence because they are co-designed and co-produced by the residents themselves. > Mobilization of Invisible Assets: The program has identified and mapped 2,467 local assets (talents, skills, and resources) that were previously unrecognized by institutional statistics. The Resource Bank has registered over 337 exchange movements, creating a circular economy of time and saberes that replaces passive dependency with active cooperation. > Empowerment and Governance: By establishing Local Operational Platforms (POL) and neighborhood assemblies, Asertos returns sovereignty to the community. A critical mass of residents (estimated at 14% of the population) acts as "positive deviants," spearheading a sustainable change that bridges the gap between the neighborhood and public administration. > Socio-Economic Inclusion: Through the "learning-by-doing" approach in Formative Construction Works, the project improves the employability of residents while simultaneously rehabilitating their own habitat, turning the neighborhood into a site of active professional insertion.
The Asertos program began its pilot phase in 2017 in a single neighborhood, Barrio Cementerio, in Alicante. Following its success, the methodology was scaled up and is currently operating in five neighborhoods across the city: Cementerio/Ciudad de Asís, Carolinas, Virgen del Remedio, Colonia Requena, and Juan XXIII. Furthermore, the innovation has been adapted and replicated in other municipalities within the province of Alicante, including Mutxamel, Almoradí, and San Vicente del Raspeig. This expansion demonstrates the model's scalability and its capacity to address multidimensional urban vulnerability through localized, asset-based strategies in diverse contexts.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
Asertos delivers measurable improvements in health, habitat, and community agency by shifting the focus from neighborhood deficits to local strengths. The key results and benefits are structured across three dimensions: > Collective Health and Subjective Wellbeing: The project significantly enhances the Sense of Coherence (SOC), the cognitive and emotional capacity to understand, manage, and find meaning in life's challenges. By fostering a strong Sense of Community, it reduces social isolation and improves collective resilience, providing a "health heritage" that buffers residents against structural inequality. > Physical Habitat and Living Conditions: Tangible results include 13 integral housing renovations, 67 urgent interventions to improve residential safety, and the transformation of abandoned plots into community-managed parks and gardens. Unlike traditional models, these improvements achieve 100% adherence because they are co-designed and co-produced by the residents themselves. > Mobilization of Invisible Assets: The program has identified and mapped 2,467 local assets (talents, skills, and resources) that were previously unrecognized by institutional statistics. The Resource Bank has registered over 337 exchange movements, creating a circular economy of time and saberes that replaces passive dependency with active cooperation. > Empowerment and Governance: By establishing Local Operational Platforms (POL) and neighborhood assemblies, Asertos returns sovereignty to the community. A critical mass of residents (estimated at 14% of the population) acts as "positive deviants," spearheading a sustainable change that bridges the gap between the neighborhood and public administration. > Socio-Economic Inclusion: Through the "learning-by-doing" approach in Formative Construction Works, the project improves the employability of residents while simultaneously rehabilitating their own habitat, turning the neighborhood into a site of active professional insertion.
The Asertos program began its pilot phase in 2017 in a single neighborhood, Barrio Cementerio, in Alicante. Following its success, the methodology was scaled up and is currently operating in five neighborhoods across the city: Cementerio/Ciudad de Asís, Carolinas, Virgen del Remedio, Colonia Requena, and Juan XXIII. Furthermore, the innovation has been adapted and replicated in other municipalities within the province of Alicante, including Mutxamel, Almoradí, and San Vicente del Raspeig. This expansion demonstrates the model's scalability and its capacity to address multidimensional urban vulnerability through localized, asset-based strategies in diverse contexts.

Traditional top-down welfare models have historically failed to reverse these conditions, often worsening them by fostering a culture of chronic dependency that erodes community agency. Furthermore, these territories suffer from "unnoticed vulnerability"; institutional statistics frequently fail to capture the real depth of their exclusion, leading to systematic neglect and a lack of specialized residential and social support.
