innovations.name: Stories4wings
innovations.lead: AIFED - Association for Innovation, Training and Employment for Sustainable Development
innovations.problem: It addresses the problem of the lack of methodologies explicitly designed for prison education. With this methodology, we use the power of stories to work on pre-selected values, competencies, or skills to improve them. We solve problems of low literacy skills in a large part of the prison population.
innovations.description:
This innovative approach seeks to promote fundamental values and tools such as resilience, teamwork, the ability to cope with social exclusion, vocal training and professional acquisition, self-awareness, active citizenship, critical thinking, and digital literacy. By working on these values, it aims to facilitate the social reintegration of inmates, helping them to overcome the cultural and social barriers they face and preparing them for an active and productive life outside prison. The project responds to the need to find effective methods for educating adults in prison, a group that is often marginalised and has limited access to educational opportunities. The story-based methodology was chosen because stories have a transformative power: they can motivate, teach and change attitudes and behaviours. This approach allows inmates to reflect on their own experiences and emotions, fostering empathy and understanding, and helping them develop key skills for social reintegration.
This project based on Erasmus+ project STORIES FOR EMPOWERMENT: Storytelling can help to promote the social inclusion of adults. Educating adult learners through the use of Storytelling can help to promote the social inclusion of adults with disabilities, refugees, prisoners, addicts, and women. Storytelling is a non-formal educational method based on narrating a series of stories to each group to stimulate reflection, self-recognition, and personal development. Listening to stories provokes greater brain activation compared to other reading methods, which fosters a deeper connection with the listener’s personal experiences.
The Stories for Empowerment project has been designed to foster the personal development of participants and contribute to their social inclusion and active citizenship, thus justifying its implementation.
The main objectives of the project are:
To support and enhance the work of adult educators working with marginalized adults
To activate empowerment processes in the target groups
To build a shared European methodology for working with the Storytelling method
To provide operational working tools
To get to know European cultures through traditional Storytelling
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: AIFED - Association for Innovation, Training and Employment for Sustainable Development
innovations.evidence: 1. Methodology (Selecting and Analyzing Values, Skills and Competences) The Methodology for applying characteristics such as values, competences and skills is created as a short introduction for all target groups covered by the project: educators and trainers in adult prisons, to understand the core importance of storytelling and story-based methodology in education. It has been created to better understand the Manual (Selecting and Analyzing Values, Skills and Competences. 2. Manual This Manual presents a structured, story-based methodology to support adult education for adult learners in correctional facilities, fostering critical values, skills, and competencies essential for inmates’ personal growth and social reintegration. Through carefully selected values/skills and competences, the approach enhances reflection, provides empathy, and draws inmates into an active learning experience. We have selected the most essential values, skills, and competences, such as resilience, teamworking, ability to cope with social exclusion, vocational skill development, self-awareness, active citizenship, critical thinking, and technology literacy. For each value, skill, and competence, the Manual explores the consequences of applying it and not applying it. The Manual discusses the impact of these values, skills, and competences on inmates both during their time in prison and after their release. For each of the values/skills/competences covered in the different stories, we aim to achieve a specific impact, all in accordance with the objectives of our project. 3   A moodle with ressources for educator in prison.

innovations.name: Educational and Social Reintegration of Sick Children: Scalable Peer Mentoring
innovations.lead: HospiEdu Foundation for Supporting Sick Children’s Learning
innovations.problem: Every year, thousands of Hungarian students miss school for months or even years due to severe medical or mental health conditions. While 20% of the 1.3 million school-age population (approx. 260,000 children) report health issues hindering daily tasks (ELTE - HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children) - National Research, Development and Innovation Office, 2022), according to the WHO, every 7th student struggles with mental health problems. A critical systemic challenge is that the educational rehabilitation process is fragmented, taking place across three distinct sectors (healthcare, education, and social services) and across three different locations (hospital, home, and school). Due to this institutional divide, affected children frequently fall through the cracks of the public support systems. Left outside the radar of care, these vulnerable students are forced to struggle entirely alone with their curriculum and school reintegration while simultaneously coping with the severe difficulties of their recovery process. Furthermore, this isolating ordeal deeply impacts not only the individual children but also their families and entire school communities, underscoring an urgent, systemic need for structured intervention. This problem aligns directly with the core challenges addressed by the European Child Guarantee.
innovations.description: The HospiEdu Foundation program introduces a unique, nationwide, scalable peer-to-peer mentoring framework organized around a well-structured Theory of Change (Social Impact Chain). Instead of relying solely on professional teachers, the program taps into an underutilized social asset: high school and university students. The innovation consists of three interconnected pillars operating on a national scale: Structured Volunteer Training & Academic Integration: Volunteers undergo rigorous pedagogical, psychological, and communication preparation. This is integrated into higher education through accredited, credit-bearing "HospiEdu courses" at major universities, and aligned with mandatory high school community service (IKSZ). Personalized Peer Mentoring: The matchmaking system delivers direct services through home-based online, personalized face-to-face, and hospital-based study room (tanulószoba) education. Beyond somatic illnesses, the program heavily focuses on supporting youth struggling with mental health disorders, preventing them from dropping out, and facilitating proper communication. Extended Focus on Mental Health & Quality Assurance: To guarantee a safe connection between the supported children and the volunteers, and to foster psychological resilience, a rigorous, professionally grounded monitoring system has been implemented. This features mandatory digital logbooks (e-napló) and compulsory case discussion/supervision sessions. By shifting the focus from passive care to active community integration, the solution relieves pressure on both parents and the public school system.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: HospiEdu Foundation for Supporting Sick Children’s Learning
innovations.evidence:
Since its inception in 2014, the program has achieved significant systemic and individual results: - Over 2,200 hospitalized or recovering children supported nationwide, preventing academic regression, keeping them connected to their communities, and securing their successful school reintegration and long-term social re-inclusion. - More than 2,600 high school and university students mobilized and trained as active citizens. While supporting sick children, these peer mentors undergo profound personal development, showing measurable growth in empathy, cooperative skills, creativity, and communication competencies. - Systemic Educator Empowerment: Since 2024, through specialized staff workshops, the program has trained nearly 1,000 educators across 42 educational institutions nationwide, equipping them with practical tools for the pedagogical support and integration of youth struggling with mental health disorders. - Measurable psychological benefits: Evaluation data shows a significant drop in anxiety levels and an increase in motivation to recover among the participating children, alongside heightened social competence and enhanced future employability among the volunteers.
The innovation has been successfully scaled up nationally and is currently being replicated and adapted internationally: 1. National Scaling-up: In Hungary, the model has expanded into a nationwide ecosystem, supporting 2,200+ children and training 2,600+ volunteers by integrating into the national high school community service (IKSZ) and major university credit systems. 2. International Replication & Adaptation: One of our core professional methodological books has been translated into English and is fully accessible to members of the European Hospital Teachers network (HOPE - hospitalteachers.eu) for international use. Furthermore, a Belgian organization specializing in supporting children with Special Educational Needs (SEN) is currently translating into French.

innovations.name: Academia Geração +
innovations.lead: Innovate Autism — Association for Citizenship and Inclusion
innovations.problem: A population on the autism spectrum faces daily challenges that go far beyond the clinical dimension of their condition. Despite their potential, skills, and genuine desire to contribute to society, autistic people encounter structural and attitudinal barriers that make access to the labour market extremely difficult, often leaving them in prolonged situations of unemployment, social isolation, and economic dependence. In Portugal, employment rates among people with disabilities remain significantly below the national average, and autism presents particular challenges in this regard. Many autistic young people complete their education or vocational training without having access to adequate support for the transition to the world of work. The end of the school pathway frequently represents a rupture point, after which there is little or no structured support to help them take the next step towards professional integration. On the side of employers, there is still considerable lack of awareness and knowledge about autism, what it means in practice, and how to create inclusive working conditions that allow autistic people to perform at their best. Many companies are willing to promote inclusion but lack the tools, training, and guidance to do so effectively and sustainably. This gap between intention and practice results in missed opportunities on both sides — for the young person seeking employment and for the organisation that could benefit from their unique skills and perspective. The challenges faced by autistic young people in accessing employment are also compounded by difficulties in navigating social and communicative aspects of the recruitment process, such as interviews, networking, and understanding unwritten workplace norms. These are areas where, without targeted support, even highly capable individuals may struggle, not because of a lack of competence, but because the process itself is not designed with neurodiversity in mind. Furthermore, not all autistic people are suited to traditional employment environments. For some, self-employment and entrepreneurship represent more appropriate and sustainable pathways, yet access to training and support in these areas is equally scarce. innovations.name: Energies with the South
innovations.problem: Southern Italy faces a severe socio-demographic crisis characterized by high youth unemployment, widespread inactivity among young people, and significant population decline. NEET rates remain among the highest in Europe, reaching 40.2% in Catania, 38.2% in Naples, 27.2% in Calabria, and 22.2% in Apulia. At the same time, youth unemployment exceeds 30% in several areas and contributes to the continuous outmigration of young people, undermining the long-term social and economic sustainability of local communities. These challenges are driven by multiple structural factors, including high school dropout rates, low qualification levels, limited career guidance services, and a fragile economic fabric unable to fully absorb local talent. Despite the region’s strong potential in the green transition - with Apulia generating over half of its electricity from renewable sources, Sicily hosting more than 23,000 photovoltaic plants, and Calabria covering over 50% of its energy consumption through renewables - a significant skills mismatch persists. Many companies struggle to recruit qualified technical and green professionals, while thousands of young people remain excluded from education, training, and employment opportunities. The problem is further exacerbated by insufficient local support services, inadequate training infrastructures, and weak connections between education providers, employers, and employment services. As a result, Southern Italy faces the paradox of growing demand for green skills alongside a large pool of underutilized human capital. Energies with the South addresses this gap by proposing integrated and place-based solutions capable of connecting vulnerable young people with emerging labour market opportunities, strengthening territorial ecosystems, and promoting a just and inclusive green transition.
innovations.description:
The project leverages the experience and evidence generated by the “Green Skills Academy” pilot implemented in Sicily and Apulia in 2024-2025. The pilot successfully validated a model combining empowerment, green skills training, and job placement, providing a tested methodology that can now be scaled and adapted across additional regions, contexts and organizations.
Energies with the South introduces an innovative social innovation model that addresses youth unemployment, skills mismatch, and demographic decline through an integrated, ecosystem-based approach. Rather than focusing solely on training or employment services, the project combines personalized coaching, empowerment, technical education, stakeholder engagement, and community activation within a single framework. The project’s innovation lies in its holistic methodology. Participants receive individualized support throughout the entire journey - from outreach and engagement to training, mentoring, placement, and long-term empowerment. Technical training for green jobs is complemented by soft skills development, personal growth, and self-determination pathways, ensuring that beneficiaries are equipped not only with professional competencies but also with the confidence and agency needed to build sustainable futures. A second innovative element is a cross-sector partnership model that mobilizes actors from education, employment, business, civil society, and public institutions to co-create solutions for youth inclusion and the green transition. Through this collaborative ecosystem, the project strengthens local capacities, aligns training with labour market needs, and creates direct pathways into employment opportunities linked to the green transition. A distinctive feature of Energies with the South is the creation of territorial Coalitions: innovative multi-stakeholder alliances, involving organizations of different nature and dimension, which act as local innovation platforms that mobilize resources, foster collaboration, strengthen community ownership, and support the co-design of solutions for employment, entrepreneurship, and sustainable development. Moreover, the project aims to promote a long-term systemic change by supporting youth entrepreneurship in the green economy and facilitating dialogue among civil society, businesses, and institutions to co-design policies and strategies for a just transition. This approach transforms isolated interventions into a sustainable territorial ecosystem capable of generating lasting social and economic impact across Southern Italy. Finally, the project's methodology responds to European policy priorities, such as the European Green Deal, the Just Transition Mechanism, and the European Pillar of Social Rights and the training is also based on the reference framework of the GreenComp, by demonstrating how social cohesion and ecological transition can be pursued simultaneously, not as competing agendas. At the territorial level, this translates into a model that strengthens community resilience by reconnecting young people to their local economies rather than allowing demographic decline to continue unchallenged.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Energies with the South will create tangible and long-lasting benefits for both young people and local territories by transforming vulnerable NEETs into active participants in Southern Italy’s green transition. Over three years, the project will engage 300 NEETs across Sicily, Apulia, Calabria, and Campania. Through a combination of personalized support, empowerment activities, technical training, and employment services, participants will develop the skills, confidence, and professional networks needed to access quality employment opportunities in the renewable energy and sustainability sectors. A key result of the project is the integration of soft skills development and green technical competencies. Participants will strengthen essential transversal skills such as teamwork, communication, problem-solving, leadership, self-efficacy, and time management, while simultaneously acquiring industry-relevant knowledge linked to renewable energy, sustainability, and the green economy. This dual approach addresses one of the main barriers to youth employability: the gap between technical qualifications and personal readiness for work. The project will also generate direct employment outcomes through internships, work-based learning opportunities, and job placement activities developed in partnership with companies operating in the renewable energy sector. By aligning training pathways with real labour market needs, the initiative contributes to reducing the skills mismatch currently affecting Southern Italy’s green economy. Beyond individual benefits, Energies with the South will strengthen local ecosystems for inclusive growth. Through multi-stakeholder coalitions, the project will create sustainable territorial networks capable of supporting youth employment beyond the project duration. The project's most significant contribution is the validation and scaling of a replicable social innovation model that aligns youth empowerment, green skills, employability, and community engagement within a single framework - demonstrating that a stronger, fairer, and more sustainable South is both achievable and transferable to other European cohesion regions. By connecting young people with emerging opportunities in renewable energy and sustainability, the project contributes to a more inclusive, resilient, and just transition while helping Southern Italy become a place where young people can choose to stay, return, and thrive.

innovations.name: NoRo Centre for Rare Diseases
innovations.problem: In Romania, approximately 1.3 million people are affected by rare diseases but 90% of patients do not receive the correct diagnosis or adequate treatment and medical care. The problem is less pronounced but still present at EU level, where 40% of patients with a rare disease receive an incorrect diagnosis . Although declared in Romania's National Health Strategy in 2014 as a national priority, rare diseases are often not adequately addressed by the national health system due to their small and disconnected patient populations, the lack of knowledge of doctors on rare diseases and the lack of diagnosis centres. This leads to fragmented medical and care services for patients with rare diseases and their families.
innovations.description:
The Pilot Reference Centre for Rare Diseases (NoRo) was launched in June 2011. It is innovative in its holistic and centralised approach to rare disease care, providing a one-stop-shop for people living with a rare disease. Patients at the NoRo have a designated case manager who provides them with guidance and counselling through the different services available to them. Set up by the Romanian Prader Willi Association (RPWA), in partnership with the leading Norwegian Frambu Resource Centre for Rare Disorders and funded by the EEA and Norway Grants, the centre combines medical, social and educational services for patients and their families. The NoRo was also supported through the INNOVCare project which ran until 2018.
The NoRo works to increase awareness of rare diseases in the medical and wider community. It brings together 50 pro-bono doctors that work collaboratively on an information website about rare diseases, a national online map of services and guidelines for patients and professionals. The doctors also respond directly to patients' questions via the helpline or during NoRo workshops. The NoRo has trained almost 500 health specialists and doctors via online and offline courses and works with schools to organise role-playing sessions and debates in order to raise awareness of these diseases amongst teachers and pupils. Part of this work is the Trial for Flight programme aimed at providing young people with rare diseases with the necessary skills to become autonomous and fully integrated in their communities.
The NoRo also runs a registry for rare disease patients in Romania. This allows efficient planning and allocation of resources for the centre and supports the monitoring of the impact of rare diseases and the situation of patients in Romania.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The NoRo is unique in Romania and currently offers services to over 10% of patients diagnosed with rare diseases in the country. Over the past 6 years, the centre’s doctors undertook over 2 200 consultations. innovations.name: Art at the Heart of the Village
innovations.problem: Romania is experiencing a continuous decline in theatre attendance, with cultural consumption studies (2018, 2019, 2022) showing a decrease from 37% of respondents attending theatre at least once a year in 2014, to 27% in 2019, and only 20% in 2022 (excluding pandemic years). One of the main causes is limited access to cultural infrastructure, particularly in rural areas. Studies indicate that in 60% of cases, people perceive there is no access to theatre in their communities, while 70% of cultural audiences come from urban environments. "Art at the Heart of the Village" addresses this cultural inequality by bringing professional theatre and cultural education directly into rural communities. Romania’s rural population represents 87.5% of the territory and 45% of its population, yet remains significantly underserved in terms of cultural access. The project responds to this imbalance by developing new audiences, especially among young people in rural areas, supporting both cultural inclusion and long-term audience formation. In addition to rural outreach, the project tackles another gap in the Romanian theatre sector: the limited number of international collaborations. To strengthen artistic exchange, the project includes an intensive theatre workshop led by Norwegian artists Tor Arne Ursin and Anne-Sophie Erichsen, working with twelce experienced actors from the association’s core artistic team. Ursin, co-founder of Grenland Friteater and collaborator of major figures such as Eugenio Barba, Ryszard Cieślak, and Mike Pearson, and Erichsen, a director shaped by mentors such as Elsa Kvamme and Ingemar Lindh, bring direct knowledge of European experimental theatre traditions. Their workshop enables actors to translate theoretical knowledge into embodied practice, strengthening physical training, improvisation, and performance methods. This exchange is expected to significantly enhance the artistic quality of future productions while fostering stronger international connections and innovation within Romanian theatre practice.
innovations.description: The project introduces an integrated model that combines rural touring theatre, in-school arts education, and international artistic exchange within a single framework. By transforming non-traditional rural spaces, such as schools and community areas, into performance venues, it removes physical and cultural barriers to theatre access. The inclusion of interactive workshops for children and youth, alongside professional performances and advanced actor training with international practitioners, creates a multi-level cultural intervention that addresses both audience development and artistic capacity-building simultaneously.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Through its touring theatre model and integrated educational workshops, Cultură’n Șură delivered cultural programmes in over 100 localities nationwide, presenting more than 200 performances in rural areas.
The project increased access to high-quality cultural experiences for over 2,000 rural spectators and provided hands-on theatre education for more than 250 children and young people. It strengthened the creative and technical skills of participating actors through international training, improving their artistic practice and future output. Communities benefited from increased cultural participation, improved social cohesion, and exposure to contemporary performing arts. The project also contributed to long-term audience development in underserved rural areas and fostered greater confidence and creativity among young participants.

innovations.name: Change the World
innovations.problem: "Change the World" aims to bridge the soft skills gap in formal school curricula and address the low levels of civic participation among children. In Portugal, civic participation and engagement among children and young people are weak. According to a 2023 study by the Ministry of National Defence based on National Defence Day surveys (covering approximately 135,000 young people), only 1.4% of participants chose "participation and citizenship" as a topic of interest, making it the least selected out of 16 possible themes. We know that our world is increasingly affected by severe social and environmental challenges, such as wars, conflicts, climate change, and social and educational inequalities, among others. It is urgent that everyone possesses the necessary skills to identify these problems and conceive creative, effective solutions to resolve them. This problem is particularly relevant because without generations prepared to tackle social challenges, we will not have resilient and socially responsible citizens. Furthermore, the labour market is transforming rapidly, demanding the continuous development of skills and knowledge with practical application throughout personal and professional life. In this context, entrepreneurship plays a fundamental role in fostering creativity, adaptability, and complex problem-solving abilities. Children are the citizens of tomorrow and will have to deal with the social and environmental challenges of their communities and the world. Therefore, it is imperative to stimulate children to think differently to find alternative - and, above all, creative - solutions to the challenges faced by society. With this purpose in mind, "Change the World" was born. It is an educational project that aims to empower younger generations (children in the 1st and 2nd cycles of basic education, aged 6 to 12) in social innovation and entrepreneurship, turning them into empowered, transformative agents of the world they live in.
innovations.description: “Change the World” features the following innovative elements: - The intervention methodology is centred on children's ideas and voices, making them the protagonists of the entire learning process. The project applies a differentiating approach by exploring social entrepreneurship through creative and participatory activities that encourage children to identify social and environmental problems, reflect on their causes, and imagine innovative solutions. To achieve this, it utilizes the children’s book "Quando for grande quero mudar o mundo!" ("When I Grow Up, I Want to Change the World!"), developed by the IRIS team, which guides children in discovering their creative and entrepreneurial potential. Focusing on social innovation and entrepreneurship, this educational and guided methodology promotes the development of essential transversal skills for children’s personal growth and future professional lives, making them more aware of the world around them and their role in society. - Activities can be carried out at each child's individual pace using intuitive and appealing materials. These resources facilitate the learning of complex concepts in a simple, playful manner, using child-friendly language.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Since 2021, “Change the World” has been tested and validated with 9.022 children, 246 schools, and 713 educators. We also have more than 270 ideas stored in our social innovation idea bank, resulting from the annual "Idea Competition" initiative. A recent implementation in 9 schools within the Porto Metropolitan Area between September 2025 and January 2026, involving 558 children and 4 educational technicians, yielded the following results: - 69% of the children considered that they had learned a lot about social innovation (a data point corroborated by the educational technicians) - 80% now know what social entrepreneurs are - 90% of the children generated a social innovation idea, and 94% wished to see their idea put into practice. From the perspective of the educators, after completing the programme, the children demonstrated: - Increased interest in resolving the social and environmental problems surrounding them - Greater awareness of concepts related to social innovation - Enhanced creativity and initiative in problem-solving - Heightened sensitivity toward social and environmental challenges - Increased attentiveness to the reality surrounding them.

innovations.name: NEW ENERGY TO CARE
innovations.problem: Elder care homes face growing pressure from staff shortages, rising workloads, and limited time for meaningful human interaction. Many older adults experience loneliness, social isolation, and a lack of stimulating activities, which negatively impact wellbeing and quality of life. At the same time, many young people struggle to gain their first work experience and have limited opportunities to contribute to their communities. Current care and workforce models do not effectively connect these unmet needs and untapped resources.
innovations.description: New Care to Elder Care introduces an innovative intergenerational model that connects young people with elder care homes through flexible, meaningful support tasks. Using a purpose-built mobile platform, care homes can quickly access motivated young people to assist with social, recreational, and everyday support activities. The model creates valuable human connections, reduces loneliness, supports care staff, and provides young people with practical experience and pathways into working life. By combining a new resourcing model with digital technology, the project creates a scalable and sustainable approach to strengthening wellbeing in elder care communities.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
For older adults

More meaningful social interaction and activities
Improved wellbeing, engagement, and quality of life
Greater connection to the local community and younger generations
For care homes
Additional support for non-medical tasks and activities
More time for professional staff to focus on care priorities
Improved atmosphere and resident satisfaction
A flexible and cost-effective way to access extra help For young people
Valuable first work experiences and references
Development of practical, social, and communication skills
Increased confidence, purpose, and community engagement
Greater interest in care and social sector careers For society
Stronger intergenerational connections
New pathways into suitable work for young people
Better use of local community resources
A scalable and sustainable model that can be replicated across care settings
Over 20 pilots, in both elder and disabled care units

innovations.name: UPFARM: Unlocking the Potential of social FARMing for inclusive, sustainable, and regenerative jobs against long-term unemployment
innovations.problem: Long-term unemployment
innovations.description:
UPFARM builds on the long-standing experience of social farming in Italy, and particularly in the Tuscany Region, where social cooperatives, farms, municipalities, health and social services have developed inclusive employment pathways for vulnerable groups through agricultural activities. Rather than replicating a single project, UPFARM draws inspiration from a wide range of existing social farming practices and territorial networks that have demonstrated the potential of agriculture to promote social inclusion, skills development, and labour market integration. The project builds on these experiences and seeks to strengthen, systematise, and scale them through new tools, governance models, and multi-stakeholder partnerships.
UPFARM moves beyond viewing social farming as a collection of isolated initiatives and instead treats it as a territorial ecosystem for labour inclusion. Its innovation lies in combining social farming, employment services, social and health services, municipalities, and third-sector organizations within a shared governance framework aimed at supporting long-term unemployed people. Rather than focusing solely on job placements, UPFARM develops and tests new tools, integrated assessment and matching methods, and collaborative governance models that can be embedded into local and regional policies. Through four Living Labs, the project creates real-world environments where stakeholders co-design solutions, strengthen cooperation, and experiment with new inclusion pathways. A further innovative aspect is the project's scaling approach: UPFARM is not only generating local results but also building the conditions for social farming to become a structured and transferable component of Tuscany’s employment and social inclusion system. By connecting local experimentation, regional policy development, and European learning, the project seeks to create lasting systemic change rather than temporary interventions.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence: Although UPFARM is still ongoing, the project has already generated important results. In the frontrunner territories, it has successfully mobilised and engaged a broad network of stakeholders, including municipalities, social and health services, public employment services, social farming enterprises, social cooperatives, and third-sector organisations. This has strengthened local collaboration and created new opportunities for integrated support pathways for long-term unemployed people. The project is also delivering its first job placements, translating the co-designed approaches into concrete employment opportunities. Beyond these initial outcomes, UPFARM is helping to build stronger local alliances, shared methodologies, and a common vision for using social farming as a tool for social and labour inclusion, laying the foundations for longer-term systemic impact and future scaling across Tuscany.

innovations.name: Empowering Communities Through Financial Literacy Adventures
innovations.problem: Despite its impact on quality of life, social mobility and wellbeing, financial literacy remains inaccessible to many people. Children and young people often leave education without the skills needed to manage money, understand financial products or make informed financial decisions. At the same time, many adults face increasing financial complexity, rising living costs and economic uncertainty without adequate support or practical financial education. The consequences extend beyond personal finances. Low levels of financial literacy contribute to financial vulnerability, over-indebtedness, stress, reduced economic participation and social exclusion. These challenges disproportionately affect vulnerable groups, including low-income families, unemployed individuals, young adults entering the workforce and people with limited access to educational opportunities. Traditional approaches to financial education are frequently perceived as complex, theoretical or inaccessible, creating barriers to engagement and limiting their effectiveness among those who could benefit most. O Secretário was created to address this gap by making financial literacy accessible, engaging and relevant to everyday life. Through innovative and inclusive learning experiences, the initiative helps individuals and communities develop the knowledge, confidence and decision-making skills needed to improve their financial wellbeing and strengthen their long-term social and economic resilience.
innovations.description: O Secretário reimagines financial literacy as an engaging, inclusive and participatory experience rather than a traditional educational programme. The initiative combines games, storytelling, experiential learning and real-life decision-making challenges to create meaningful learning experiences that are accessible to people of all ages and backgrounds. By transforming complex financial concepts into interactive adventures, participants learn by doing, exploring and reflecting on situations that mirror everyday life. The innovation lies not only in the methodology, but also in its ability to reach audiences that are often excluded from conventional financial education. Through immersive activities, educational games, community events, workshops and freely accessible resources, O Secretário removes barriers to participation and makes financial learning approachable, enjoyable and relevant. The model is designed to be flexible and adaptable across different settings, including schools, municipalities, companies, community organisations and social inclusion programmes. It can be tailored to local needs and cultural contexts while maintaining a consistent focus on financial wellbeing, empowerment and inclusion. By combining education, play and social innovation, O Secretário creates a scalable and transferable approach that helps individuals build confidence, strengthen decision-making skills and improve their long-term financial resilience. Rather than simply teaching financial concepts, it empowers people to navigate real-life challenges and make informed choices that positively impact their lives and communities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Since its creation, O Secretário has engaged thousands of participants through workshops, educational games, community events, school activities, corporate programmes and freely accessible learning resources. The initiative has demonstrated that financial literacy can become more accessible and impactful when delivered through play, storytelling and experiential learning. Participants report increased confidence in managing everyday financial decisions, a better understanding of financial concepts and greater engagement compared to traditional learning approaches. Key benefits include: - Improved financial knowledge, confidence and decision-making skills; - Increased access to financial education for children, families, workers and vulnerable groups; - Greater engagement and participation through interactive and inclusive learning methodologies; - Enhanced financial wellbeing and resilience, helping individuals better navigate financial challenges; - Strengthened collaboration between schools, municipalities, companies, NGOs and community organisations; Creation of innovative educational resources that remain freely accessible to wider audiences. Beyond individual outcomes, O Secretário contributes to broader social impact by promoting financial inclusion, reducing barriers to financial education and supporting more informed, resilient and empowered communities. The project's innovative approach has also gained national and international recognition, demonstrating its potential for replication, adaptation and scaling across different communities and contexts. (MAIAwards 2026). It is also part of local group from UrbACT Human Power Hub Europe. Since 2022, the initiative has engaged over 12500 participants, collaborated with 7 municipalities, and more than 30 entities - a flock of oddie birds from schools and organisations, while creating more than 11 freely accessible educational resources and 3 collaborative products.
O Secretário has been progressively scaled up from a local pilot initiative into a multi-context social innovation programme with increasing geographic and sectoral reach.
The methodology has been replicated and adapted across 7 municipalities in Portugal, where it has been implemented in schools, community programmes, companies and social inclusion initiatives. In these contexts, the approach was tailored to different age groups and audiences, including children, young people, families and vulnerable communities (such as people with disabilities, victims of domestic violence, unemployed, at prision), while maintaining the core principles of play-based and experiential financial education.
In addition to municipal-scale implementation, the initiative has been scaled across schools, NGOs and community organisations, expanding its reach beyond formal education into non-formal and informal learning environments. It has also been applied in corporate and organisational settings, supporting employee financial wellbeing and broader social responsibility objectives.
Through the growing ecosystem of the Human Power Hub, Human Power Hub Europe, and international integration in networks such as The Civics Innovation Hub, the model is currently positioned for further adaptation and cross-border replication, with interest in translating and localising the methodology for other European contexts.
This scaling process has been supported by freely accessible resources and collaborative co-creation, enabling different stakeholders to access but also to implement and adapt the innovation with minimal barriers while preserving its impact and identity.

innovations.name: REThink for mental health of the youths in Romania
innovations.problem: 1 in 3 students globally reports being bullied monthly (UNESCO, 2019). Bullying and cyberbullying are widespread among Romanian youth as well, with 82% of students reporting that they have witnessed bullying and 27% admitting to bullying others(Save the Children, 2022). These experiences are linked to increased anxiety, depression, emotional distress, and poor wellbeing. Despite the scale of the problem, schools have limited capacity to provide evidence-based prevention and early intervention, often relying on a single counselor for approx. 800 students on average.
innovations.description: REThink uses therapeutic games grounded in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and REBT to train emotion recognition, relaxation, mindfulness, rational thinking, problem solving, attention to positive stimuli, compassion, and self-compassion. The project uses two age-adapted versions: REThink Game for children and adolescents and REThink Life for young adults/ university students. The intervention is also supported by MoodWheel, another one of our apps, a digital wellbeing monitoring tool that helps identify emotional needs, bullying experiences, and risk factors in real time. The game-based assessment system, in our previous RCTs, predicted hyperactivity levels, emotional problems, and the frequency of prosocial behaviors in children and adolescents, as well as rational and irrational thoughts, stress, anxiety, and depression in adults. Game scores were associated with emotion regulation abilities with regard to mindfulness and acceptance levels, putting into perspective, rumination, and attention to positive and negative stimuli.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
REThink has demonstrated strong results across multiple randomized controlled trials involving children, adolescents, and young adults. Studies conducted by David et al. (2019), David and Fodor (2023a, 2023b), and subsequent REThink Life trials found significant improvements in emotional wellbeing, emotional awareness, emotional control, focused attention, resilience, and prosocial behaviors, alongside reductions in emotional distress, depression, anxiety, irrational beliefs, rumination, catastrophizing, and other mental health difficulties. The benefits extend beyond individual participants. For children, adolescents, and university students, REThink provides practical, evidence-based skills for managing emotions, coping with bullying and adversity, and building resilience, compassion, and self-compassion. For schools and universities, it offers a scalable and cost-effective prevention tool that can strengthen student wellbeing, support safer and more inclusive learning environments, and complement existing counseling services. For teachers, counselors, and wellbeing ambassadors, REThink provides structured resources that facilitate early identification of emotional difficulties and support the delivery of evidence-based interventions. Parents benefit from greater access to mental health prevention tools and increased opportunities to support their children's emotional development. At community and societal level, REThink contributes to reducing the burden associated with bullying, cyberbullying, emotional distress, and untreated mental health problems, while promoting mental health literacy, social inclusion, help-seeking behaviors, and evidence-based prevention practices. By combining validated therapeutic games, digital wellbeing monitoring, and implementation through educational institutions, REThink creates a sustainable model that can improve youth mental health outcomes at scale and strengthen the capacity of schools, families, and communities to support young people's wellbeing. (Source evidence: David, Cardoș & Matu, 2019; David & Fodor, 2023a; David & Fodor, 2023b; Iuga, Tomoiagă & David, 2023; Tomoiagă & David, 2023).
The REThink innovation has been implemented in multiple schools and educational settings across different regions of Romania, including both urban and rural communities. The intervention was delivered by different teachers, school counselors, psychologists, and facilitators, demonstrating its transferability across contexts while maintaining its core evidence-based approach. The innovation has also been continuously adapted based on feedback collected from students, educators, and implementation partners. Particular attention was given to the experiences and needs of children from rural and underserved areas, resulting in refinements to the content, implementation process, engagement strategies, and accessibility of the intervention. These adaptations have helped ensure that REThink remains relevant, acceptable, and effective for diverse groups of young people.

innovations.name: SEQ Elevate: Skills for the Future
innovations.problem: While the European Pillar of Social Rights strives for inclusive education and training, young people from marginalized groups face significant challenges acquiring competitive labor market skills. This limits their job opportunities plus exacerbates existing inequalities in society. Existing training programs typically prioritize intellectual skills, ignoring the critical social and emotional skills essential for job success in the post-COVID era. innovations.name: Glasses for the Blind - National Roadshow
innovations.problem: Romania has an estimated 80,000 people with visual impairments, including around 30,000 blind people. Yet access to modern assistive mobility technology remains limited, especially outside major cities. For most blind people, mobility still depends on the same traditional options: the white cane, guide dogs (Romania has 21), or support from family, friends, and caregivers. These tools are valuable, but they do not fully solve the need for independent, confident, and scalable mobility. Guide dogs are extremely limited, while advanced assistive technologies are often difficult to access, test, or trust without direct experience. The problem is not only technological. It is also geographic, social, and emotional. Innovation often stays in labs, conferences, hospitals, or capital cities, far from the communities it is meant to serve. This creates distance, hesitation, and unequal access to solutions that could improve daily life. The .lumen Glasses for the Blind National Roadshow addressed this gap by bringing the technology directly to blind and visually impaired people across Romania. By 15 May, the team had reached 40 cities, delivered 623 live demos, and spent 51 demo days in direct contact with the community. Through hands-on testing, participants could experience the .lumen Glasses for themselves, ask questions, express concerns, and form their own opinion. The roadshow helped make advanced mobility technology more accessible, while paving the way for greater openness, confidence, and future adoption through partnerships, public programs, and reimbursement pathways.
innovations.description: The innovative solution was twofold: a breakthrough assistive mobility device and a community-first way of bringing it to the people who need it most. The .lumen Glasses for the Blind are designed to replicate key guide dog functions through technology. Using AI, computer vision, sensors, haptic guidance, and audio feedback, the glasses help blind users understand their surroundings, avoid obstacles, and follow safer paths with greater confidence. Instead of only detecting what is around the user, the system actively guides them through directional feedback. But innovation also means access. The National Roadshow turned this technology into a direct, hands-on experience for the blind and visually impaired community across Romania. Rather than keeping the product in labs, conferences, or institutional meetings, .lumen brought it closer to people’s homes, local associations, families, and support networks.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence: By 15 May, the .lumen Glasses for the Blind National Roadshow had delivered clear, measurable results: 40 Romanian cities reached 623 live demos delivered 51 demo days completed 169 person-days invested by the .lumen team Direct engagement with blind and visually impaired people, families, local associations, public representatives, and accessibility stakeholders. The main benefit was access. The roadshow brought advanced assistive mobility technology closer to communities that rarely get the chance to experience it first-hand, especially outside major urban innovation hubs. For blind and visually impaired participants, the demos created a real opportunity to test the .lumen Glasses, understand how the technology works, ask questions, and build confidence through direct experience rather than promises. The project also created stronger bridges with local communities, associations, and institutional stakeholders, paving the way for future partnerships, public accessibility programs, and reimbursement pathways. Most importantly, the roadshow helped open a wider conversation about mobility, independence, and dignity for Romania’s estimated 80,000 visually impaired people. It showed that innovation becomes meaningful when it reaches people where they are.

innovations.name: Ordinary Needs for EXTRAORDINARY Children
innovations.problem: Romanian education recognises only one form of success: high grades. Children from vulnerable backgrounds, who grew up too fast, cared for siblings, survived hardship, develop remarkable skills in adaptability, empathy, and resilience that school fails to see or value. The result: disengagement, absenteeism, dropout. These children are not underperformers. They are simply unseen.
innovations.description:
Narada flipped the question: instead of starting from what these children don't know, it started from what they do. Grounded in Hidden Talents in Harsh Environments research and SBC methodology used by UNICEF and WHO, the programme builds a school ecosystem where practical talent becomes the engine of learning. Teachers are trained as mentors, not evaluators. EXTRA Labs are safe spaces for exploration. Projects are real, communities are involved. This is not a one-off intervention, it is a scalable, measurable shift in mindset.
The project is grounded in the academic study Hidden Talents in Harsh Environments (Ellis et al., 2020), published in the journal Development and Psychopathology (Cambridge University Press). The study was conducted by an interdisciplinary team of researchers from the USA and the Netherlands, Bruce J. Ellis (University of Utah), Laura S. Abrams (UCLA), Ann S. Masten (University of Minnesota), Robert J. Sternberg (Cornell University), Nim Tottenham (Columbia University), and Willem E. Frankenhuis (Radboud University) and proposes that, although early adversity can undermine development, children growing up in harsh environments develop intact, or even enhanced, cognitive and social skills as adaptive responses to their environments. Asociația Narada used this theoretical framework as the research foundation for the project Ordinary Needs for EXTRAORDINARY Children, developing on this basis an original methodology adapted to the Romanian educational context.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The programme delivered measurable results across all levels. 140 students directly involved, 6,500 indirect beneficiaries. 93% of students expressed their talent for the first time. 90% want to continue after the pilot. Nearly half now describe themselves as "more courageous, open, and self-confident" compared to the start. Absenteeism dropped significantly; motivation and sense of belonging increased for over 70% of participants. The 20 trained mentor-teachers grew their capacity to identify hidden talents from 72% to 90%. The number of those who feel they genuinely support students' development doubled. 10 real community projects completed: a published book, theatre plays, podcasts, murals, an entrepreneurial fair generating 16,000 RON. 10 EXTRA Labs equipped and permanently retained by schools. 8 out of 10 schools have concrete continuity plans. Media value generated: €250,000, reaching 1.83 million people.
Adaptation: Implementation was tailored to each of the 10 participating schools, taking into account the specificities of the local community, as well as the needs and talents of the students involved. The type of project developed by each school was chosen based on the children's interests, without imposing a standard model. The personal plans of scholarship-supported students were adjusted along the way, wherever the team identified a need for additional support. An organic component of the adaptation process was the Recognition and Validation Gala, which fostered a sense of belonging among all participating students across all schools, strengthening motivation for continued engagement.
Scale-up: The project did not undergo a formal scale-up process; however, scaling occurred naturally: 7 out of 10 participating schools found their own resources and continued the activities in the following school year, the school magazine, the community fair, the podcast, creative writing workshops, painting and hand-made craft workshops, and the theatre troupe attracting additional students eager to get involved.
Replication: We have no information indicating that other schools have independently adopted the model. However, we have published all resources necessary for replication: the research report, the good practices guide, and a publicly accessible toolkit. As a result of the project's impact, we are currently co-developing with the Institute for Research on Quality of Life (ICCV) at the Romanian Academy the first standardized instrument for measuring critical thinking, self-regulation, and self-discipline in school-age children, competencies essential for navigating an unpredictable future, yet systematically overlooked by traditional education.

The personal plans of scholarship-supported students were adjusted along the way, wherever the team identified a need for additional support. An organic component of the adaptation process was the Recognition and Validation Gala, which fostered a sense of belonging among all participating students across all schools, strengthening motivation for continued engagement.
Scale-up: The project did not undergo a formal scale-up process; however, scaling occurred naturally: 7 out of 10 participating schools found their own resources and continued the activities in the following school year, the school magazine, the community fair, the podcast, creative writing workshops, painting and hand-made craft workshops, and the theatre troupe attracting additional students eager to get involved.
Replication: We have no information indicating that other schools have independently adopted the model. However, we have published all resources necessary for replication: the research report, the good practices guide, and a publicly accessible toolkit. As a result of the project's impact, we are currently co-developing with the Institute for Research on Quality of Life (ICCV) at the Romanian Academy the first standardized instrument for measuring critical thinking, self-regulation, and self-discipline in school-age children, competencies essential for navigating an unpredictable future, yet systematically overlooked by traditional education.

innovations.name: The Blitzjob Method
innovations.problem:
Many young people are not reached effectively by conventional counselling, formal participation formats, application-based programmes or labour-market measures. They may face poverty, school absenteeism or disengagement, psychosocial stress, migration or refugee experiences, insecure housing, discrimination, weak institutional trust or uncertain educational and professional perspectives.
Almost 40% of young people in Berlin drop out of their vocational training programme. In certain districts of Berlin, up to 20% are neither in school, training nor employment. As in numerous other regions in Europe, the gap between formal training and real work is simply too wide, filled with anxiety and institutional distrust.
What is missing is a safe, concrete and low-threshold opportunity to act, to be useful, to receive respectful feedback and to reflect on one’s own abilities in a real social context.
innovations.description:
To bridge this gap, we developed the Blitzjob method. The first idea emerged more than 20 years ago and won the Innovation Prize of the Youth and Family Foundation of the State of Berlin.
Within a ten-year period of piloting practice and exchanging knowledge in circles of community psychology, public health and trauma research, we assembled the systematic setup that could transform short, everyday tasks into low-threshold experiences of inclusion, learning, usefulness, pride and employability.
We achieved a legal settlement with the German authority responsible for monitoring employment subject to social security contributions, so that Blitzjobs could run in all sectors and yet, for participating young people, be situated outside the primary labour market.
We modelled data for years in order to build custom-made software to register constructive growth among young people with few formal qualifications. We conducted stakeholder analysis in order to realise the switching of roles and set up a gamification foundation capable of anticipating the needs and capabilities of young people long before problem-solving became a stand-alone quality.
We formed the Blitzjob Method to include core game rules such as the use of alias names for participating young people, all designed to help stakeholders set aside discrimination, selection pressure and performance ideals.
We also set up a training programme for professional coaches to conduct personalised matching and guide participatory feedback.
Young people receive individual assignment offers through a coach and can say yes or no without pressure or sanction. Assignment hosts do not recruit, select or pay young people directly. Each assignment is prepared, matched, insured, documented and reflected upon by Caiju.
The method uses social-artistic gamification: roles, rules, names, feedback, points and reflection create a “real-life role play” that makes participation safer, more understandable and more motivating. At Caiju, we also describe the deeper approach as psychosocial mainstreaming: protective and reflective principles from psychosocial work are embedded into ordinary civic, social, educational and work-related settings.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Since 2010, Blitzjobs in Berlin has enabled 850 young people between 13 and 25 years old to complete over 8,500 short everyday tasks across more than 300 placement sites, with 72% reporting significantly boosted self-confidence and vocational readiness. In 4,800 assignments, participating young people, alone or in small teams, have earned over €160,000 in allowances for 26,700 hours of diverse tasks.
The main benefit and motive for participating young people, however, is not the payment of allowances. Beyond practical exercises, Blitzjobs facilitates experiences of usefulness, social contact, responsibility, respectful feedback and orientation, all of which add up to systematically empowered social inclusion.
We regard completed Blitzjobs as “memory pearls”: small, comprehensible experiences that young people can draw on in their capacity-building and in moments of uncertainty, transition or crisis.
The “memory pearl” concept provided the argument for the short duration of each Blitzjob. A Blitzjob lasts no longer than a few hours on one day. It is enacted through an encounter and cooperation between a Blitzjobbee and, for them to begin with, a stranger. It is rounded off with a reflection session lasting a few minutes and finally confirmed by the allowance earned, which is not paid out until the beginning of the following month. This small rule leads half of the Blitzjobbees to open their first bank account, a crucial requirement for saving money and gaining social capacity.
The Blitzjob methodology derives from the notion of acupunctural intervention in urban architecture as well as from trauma treatment, nurturing the constitution of actionable knowledge within the uneasiness of psychosocial stress. The model also benefits hosts, neighbourhoods and local institutions by turning everyday tasks and needs into inclusive learning opportunities.
You may simply need some help, and without needing the slightest spirit of philanthropy, you end up giving space and opportunity to marginalised youth. The thousands of individual cases, with only around 0.1% of Blitzjobs failing in conflict, show the tremendous urge not only among young people but also among labour-market and civil-society actors to take part in meaningful tasks that are rewarding for others.

innovations.name: Saving food, Feeding the People
innovations.problem: Food waste and poverty are two big challenges in Romania. According to recent Eurostat estimates, Romania generates approximately 3.45 million tonnes of food waste were generated (2022), and around 188 kg of food is wasted per person each year (2026). At the same time, Romania continues to face some of the highest poverty and social exclusion rates in the European Union. According to Eurostat, 27.9% of Romania's population was at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024, the second-highest rate in the EU. Furthermore, 33.8% of children in Romania were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, highlighting the vulnerability of many households and communities. At the same time, nonprofit organizations supporting vulnerable groups often operate with limited resources and struggle to meet growing needs. The lack of efficient mechanisms for redirecting surplus food results in unnecessary environmental impacts, including wasted natural resources and greenhouse gas emissions associated with food production and disposal. The Regional Food Bank Cluj addresses this gap by creating a structured and reliable system that recovers surplus food and redistributes it to people in need through accredited partner organizations.
innovations.description:
The Regional Food Bank Cluj operates within the established food banking model developed and promoted internationally by the European Food Banks Federation (FEBA), which brings together food banks across Europe and supports the exchange of best practices, operational standards, and food recovery solutions. This model has demonstrated its effectiveness in simultaneously reducing food waste and supporting people experiencing food insecurity. At the national level, the initiative is part of the network coordinated by the Romanian Federation of Food Banks (FBAR), which supports the development and strengthening of food banking activities throughout Romania. The Regional Food Bank Cluj is one of the nine regional food banks that form the Romanian food bank network, working together to recover surplus food from companies and redistribute it through nonprofit partner organizations to vulnerable communities. Therefore, the project is based on a proven and widely recognized approach implemented by food banks across Europe and adapted to the Romanian context through the coordinated efforts of FBAR and its member food banks. This established model provides the operational framework, partnerships, and quality standards that guide the activities of the Regional Food Bank Cluj.
The Cluj Regional Food Bank offers an integrated solution that transforms food surplus into social value. Rather than treating food waste and food insecurity as separate issues, the organization addresses both simultaneously through a collaborative, multi-stakeholder model. The initiative creates a bridge between food donors and charitable organizations, ensuring that surplus food is safely collected, stored, and redistributed according to established quality and food safety standards. This approach allows companies to reduce waste while supporting local communities and advancing their sustainability commitments. The model is further strengthened through partnerships with schools, universities, local authorities, and civil society organizations, creating a broader culture of responsible consumption, environmental stewardship, and social solidarity.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
- Recovery and redistribution of significant quantities of surplus food that would otherwise become waste. (since our establishment in 2018, we have collected 6.520 tons of food) - Improved access to food for vulnerable individuals and families through a network of partner nonprofit organizations (currently a number of 142). - Reduction of environmental impacts associated with food waste, including unnecessary use of resources and greenhouse gas emissions. - Strengthened cooperation between businesses, nonprofit organizations, educational institutions, and public authorities. - Increased awareness of food waste prevention, responsible consumption, and food donation among community members. - Enhanced capacity of local charities and social service organizations to support their beneficiaries. - Promotion of social inclusion and community solidarity through collaborative action.
The food banking model has been successfully replicated and scaled across Europe and globally. Food banks operate in numerous countries, adapting the model to local legal, economic, and social contexts while maintaining the core principle of recovering surplus food and redistributing it to people in need. In Romania, the model has been adapted and expanded through the network of the Romanian Federation of Food Banks (FBAR), which currently brings together nine regional food banks serving communities across the country. Through this coordinated network, food recovery and redistribution activities have been scaled to reach thousands of beneficiaries through partnerships with food donors, nonprofit organizations, and public institutions. The Regional Food Bank Cluj represents the implementation of this proven model at the regional level, adapting it to the specific needs of the region while contributing to the national effort to reduce food waste and strengthen food assistance for vulnerable populations.

innovations.name: LAMPA Conversation Festival
innovations.lead: DOTS Foundation for an Open Society
innovations.problem: The main mission is to foster a culture of democracy within Latvian society by providing a horizontal platform for civic (and civil!) discussions, where everyone is equal regardless of their social status; strengthening civic skills such as organisational, public speaking, facilitation, collaboration, etc; and by relentlessly emphasising the importance of respectful (civil) communication in our public, professional, and private lives. Democracy is a multitude of voices and an ongoing conversation – and LAMPA both embodies and enables it.
innovations.description:
The LAMPA Conversation Festival was inspired by and modeled on democracy festivals organised in other Baltic-Nordic countries, namely the Danish Folkemoedet on the island of Bornholm and the Estonian Arvamusfestival in the small town of Paide.
In the context of Latvia, innovation in the practice consists of its collaborative design (290 organisations pool their resources) and ability to reach out to diverse societal groups. At present, it is no way a small thing. 1.Ideological diversity has been a core feature of the festival: liberals and conservatives, urban dwellers and countryside folks, civil society and businesses, farmers and eco-activists, decision-makers, and individuals of various ages, gender, languages, beliefs, interests, and moral foundations. No moral judgment, everyone is welcome to attend and co-create. 2.LAMPA has become a playground for ordinary citizens to hone their civic skills in public speaking, facilitating, moderating, and organising discussions of all types. 3.We humanise politics and politicians. At the Politicians’ Roast comedians roast politicians, who later strike back and roast themselves and comedians. At the Politicians’ Disco, politicians become DJs and convey their messages through music. 4.LAMPA has become a go-to summer festival for young people. Its audience is relatively young: up to half of attendees are under 30 years old, and nearly 30% are under 20. The festival’s communication, design, and very much its format has managed to appeal to younger audiences. LAMPA is stylish, enjoyable, and free to attend. And, of course, it has a festival tent city, just like other festivals do.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: DOTS Foundation for an Open Society
innovations.evidence:
Impact spreads like ripples in water. However, data confirm that the LAMPA festival: 1. Mitigates the risk of societal polarisation: visitors meet and hear people they wouldn’t have otherwise encountered (85% in 2025), experience civil discussions among people with different views (90% in 2025). Organisations reach new audiences. 2. Builds social capital and fosters cooperation: for visitors LAMPA is a place for meeting and networking, where they could reconnect with long-unseen acquaintances, make new contacts, and find like-minded people (71% in 2025). Organisations find synergies and build partnerships. In 2025, 80% of event organisers stated that participation in LAMPA motivated them to collaborate better with others, including cross-sector collaboration. 3. Develops an informed society: visitors gain new knowledge, broaden their perspective, and learn more about topics they don’t usually think about in daily life (89% in 2025). Moreover, LAMPA has also become a training ground for people and organisations to hone their skills in public speaking, holding difficult conversations, moderating discussions, and organising public events. 4. Infuses positive emotions and optimism about Latvia’s society and its future. In 2025, the second most frequently mentioned benefit cited by visitors were positive emotions, time well spent, and increased optimism. In the open-ended questions, people described the joy and positive emotions they had experienced, praised the friendly and engaged audience, and mentioned the boost of optimism about Latvia’s future. 76% of visitors agreed that at LAMPA, their optimism about Latvian society and its future grew. Besides, LAMPA also provides motivation for the festival’s co-creator community and event organisers to further improve their work — 84% of them agreed with this statement Emotions play a significant role in public life, and it is of vital importance to steer joy, excitement, curiosity, connectedness, acceptance, and inspiration as an antidote to fear, anger, anxiety, resentment, and exclusion.
LAMPA has inspired the creation of several other democracy festivals: discussion festival “Būtent!” (Vilnius, Lithuania), Odunpazarı Listening, Dialogue, Solidarity (3D) Youth Festival (Eskişehir, Tukey – no longer organised), and upcoming Ukrainian democracy festival called “Ganok!” (August 8-9, 2026 in Poltava, Ukraine).
Over the years, LAMPA has grown from 3,300 to over 25,000 visitors, from 50 to 365 events, from several dozen to 290 content partners (event organisers). Its brand awareness among Latvian society has grown to 83% (Norstat Omnibus survey, November 2025). And for mainstreaming and achieving a lasting impact, scale does matter.
authors: DOTS Foundation for an Open Society

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
Impact spreads like ripples in water. However, data confirm that the LAMPA festival: 1. Mitigates the risk of societal polarisation: visitors meet and hear people they wouldn’t have otherwise encountered (85% in 2025), experience civil discussions among people with different views (90% in 2025). Organisations reach new audiences. 2. Builds social capital and fosters cooperation: for visitors LAMPA is a place for meeting and networking, where they could reconnect with long-unseen acquaintances, make new contacts, and find like-minded people (71% in 2025). Organisations find synergies and build partnerships.
