innovations.name: Talento Experto +45
innovations.problem:
The initiative addresses a structural and rapidly growing labour market challenge: the increasing exclusion of workers aged 45 and above from employment opportunities. In Madrid, the unemployment rate for this group stands at 14%, significantly higher than the regional average of 9%, reflecting systemic barriers rather than cyclical trends.
Spain is currently undergoing two major demographic trends: increasing life expectancy and declining birth rates. This is leading to a gradual ageing of the working population, making the exclusion of people over 45 from the labour market even more unsustainable. Fully integrating them into the workforce is not only a matter of social justice, but also a strategic necessity to ensure the sustainability of employment, innovation, and social cohesion. Generation analyses and publishes regular reports on access to employment for people aged 45 and above. In our research, conducted in collaboration with the OECD and presented in the report The Mid-Career Opportunity, we note that this population faces a combination of structural disadvantages. Many individuals have extensive professional experience but struggle to reposition themselves in a labour market that increasingly demands digital skills, new job search strategies, and familiarity with evolving recruitment practices. Limited digital literacy often restricts their ability to access online job platforms, complete administrative processes, or participate effectively in standardised hiring processes. At the same time, financial pressures and the need for income can discourage participation in longer training programmes, while reduced access to professional networks limits exposure to new job opportunities. The challenge is especially pronounced among the long-term unemployed, for whom barriers tend to be more complex and cumulative. Generation’s qualitative insights indicate that a significant share face structural constraints that go beyond employability alone, including prolonged detachment from the labour market, loss of confidence and self-esteem, age-related bias in recruitment processes, and weaker access to formal career support systems. In addition, some individuals rely on informal or unstable income sources, while others face administrative or eligibility barriers linked to employment services. Together, these factors reduce both their immediate availability for work and their ability to re-engage effectively with traditional activation programmes, while their general wellbeing is severely affected. At the same time, traditional employability interventions often fail to engage this group effectively. Many participants prioritise immediate access to employment over reskilling, leading to low participation in conventional training bootcamps. This mismatch between programme design and participant needs creates a persistent gap in service provision, leaving a large pool of experienced workers underutilised.
innovations.description: “Talento Experto +45” responds to this challenge by redesigning the employability model to reflect the realities, motivations, and constraints of +45 workers. Rather than centring on long training cycles, the programme prioritises rapid reintegration into the labour market through a holistic and highly structured approach. The intervention is organised around three integrated processes: mobilisation, orientation, and placement. Mobilisation combines digital campaigns with offline outreach, including job fairs, partnerships with social organisations, and direct referrals, ensuring accessibility for individuals with limited digital skills. Orientation is delivered through seven tailored pathways depending on the participant profile and needs (e.g., entrepreneurship), each combining group sessions and individual coaching, to help participants update their professional profiles, strengthen their job search strategies, and regain confidence. Placement is embedded throughout the programme, with active labour intermediation, employer engagement, and targeted hiring events designed to accelerate recruitment. The seven itineraries follow a no-one-left-behind approach, supporting people facing barriers to employment before they enter a full education-to-employment program. Based on each participant’s interests, experience, and skill levels, we offer seven tailored pathways: 1. Entrepreneurship. For participants with strong sector experience who want to pursue self-employment, supported by a specialized mentor. 2. Soft Skills. For participants with technical skills who need to strengthen workplace skills such as communication, teamwork, and adaptability. 3. General Technical Skills. Focused on core employability skills, including digital, green, communication, and workplace safety skills. 4. Generation Bootcamp. The main pathway for participants needing both technical and soft skills training to access specific job opportunities. 5. Upskilling. For participants ready to work but needing additional soft or technical skills to improve employability. 6. Professional Competency Accreditation. Supports participants in certifying prior professional experience to improve job prospects. 7. Employment Mediation. For job-ready participants needing support with CVs, interviews, networking, and job matching. Access is limited to participants assessed as employment-ready. A defining feature of the model is its strong employer orientation. Participants engage with employers through interviews and hiring events early in the process, allowing for faster alignment between talent supply and demand. At the same time, the programme places significant emphasis on soft skills and professional repositioning, recognising that many participants already possess relevant experience but require support in translating it into current labour market opportunities. Notably, a significant share of placements has been achieved through pathways focused primarily on guidance and soft skills rather than technical reskilling, highlighting the effectiveness of this approach. The delivery model is also adapted to overcome access barriers. Low digital literacy is addressed through simplified tools, avoidance of fully digital processes (e.g. QR-based systems), and on-site support for documentation and applications. This ensures inclusivity and prevents the exclusion of those most in need of support. In addition, the programme is embedded within a broader public-private ecosystem, bringing together the Madrid Employment Agency, employers, social organisations such as Cáritas and the Red Cross, and training providers. This collaborative model enables both operational efficiency and systemic impact, positioning the initiative as more than a standalone programme. Lastly, the initiative brings an innovative approach to the social sector through its ability to measure the real progress of beneficiaries, supported by advanced digital tools such as Salesforce and Power BI, which enable
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project has achieved strong and measurable outcomes, meeting or exceeding most of its core performance indicators well ahead of completion. By May 2026, more than 550 participants had been mobilised, with over 500 beneficiaries actively engaged in labour intermediation processes, surpassing initial expectations in this area. In terms of employment outcomes, the programme achieved its target of 210 job placements before the end of the implementation period, representing a placement rate of approximately 50–52%. By the end of the programme in July 2026, we expect to place nearly 300 participants. These results are further strengthened by a 65% job retention rate three months after placement, demonstrating that employment outcomes are both fast and sustainable. The profile of participants in the project shows a clear concentration in older age groups, with 54% aged between 51 and 60, 26% between 45 and 50, and 20% over 60. Most had been unemployed for between 6 and 12 months (81%), while 19% had been out of work for more than a year, highlighting a situation of sustained labour vulnerability. There is also a strong female representation (62%), compared to 38% men, pointing to a feminisation of unemployment within this age group. In terms of educational background, the group is heterogeneous: 45% hold a university degree, 25% have vocational training, 21% have completed upper secondary or compulsory education, and 9% have primary education only. This diversity has required the design of tailored pathways adapted to very different career trajectories, ranging from highly qualified individuals to others with profiles more oriented towards operational roles. Beyond quantitative metrics, the initiative has generated significant system-level benefits. The collaboration has led to a 15% increase in social partners and strengthened relationships with employers and public institutions, expanding the network available to support future participants.  It has also contributed to increased visibility and influence, with over 20 invitations to conferences and public events, multiple media appearances, and a 26% growth in social media reach. The programme has also received notable recognition, including the Vanguardists Award 2025 in the Cultural Management and Talent category and a second prize at the VI Generacción Awards, highlighting both its social impact and its contribution to promoting generational diversity in the labour market. At the individual level, the benefits are equally significant. Many participants joined feeling disconnected from the labour market, lacking recent training, or with low levels of digital skills. They now report increased confidence, clearer professional direction, and improved ability to navigate job search processes. Testimonials illustrate the transformative impact of the programme, from individuals re-entering the workforce after closing family businesses to migrants over 60 successfully integrating into the Spanish labour market and regaining economic independence. The story of Nuria Romero, for example, illustrates this process of personal and professional transformation. After spending her entire working life self-employed in a family kiosk, Nuria did not know how to navigate the labour market, prepare a CV, or face a job interview, which caused her insecurity and a lack of confidence. After completing the programme, she successfully reoriented her career and secured a position as an administrative assistant in a company. “Thanks to Fundación Generation Spain, I have learned how to navigate the labour market and had my first interview with a company at the age of 46, where I was selected. This experience has restored my confidence and given me clarity about my professional goals,” she explains. Finally, in line with our commitment to social innovation and the lessons learned from working closely with over 45 people, we recognise that today’s labour market has become a highly competitive “red ocean”:

innovations.name: Microplastic Detectives — Strengthening Young Minds Through Water
innovations.problem: Two crises meet in young people. First, a mental-health crisis: 75% of young people perceive the future as threatening (Lancet Planetary Health, 2021). Constant exposure to environmental bad news produces eco-anxiety, powerlessness and resignation — yet almost no programs combine environmental education with movement, nature and psychological support. Second, an environmental crisis that feels abstract and hopeless: microplastic spreads invisibly and originates on land, in rivers and wastewater, long before it reaches the ocean. Existing treatment plants reach their limits and let microplastics pass; there are no binding limit values yet, so action stalls. Disadvantaged students are hit hardest: fewer resources to process anxiety, fewer chances to experience science first-hand, and the persistent feeling “I am too small to change anything.” Microplastic Detectives addresses exactly this intersection — turning a paralyzing problem into a hands-on path to agency.

innovations.name: SUPPORT: Supported Employment for Reducing Long-Term Unemployment among Persons with Disabilities
innovations.lead: European Association of Service providers for Persons with Disabilities (EASPD)
innovations.problem: The persistent issue of long-term unemployment among persons with disabilities in the open labour market.
innovations.description: SUPPORT will enhance the employability & integration of long-term unemployed persons with disabilities (PwD) and mental health challenges in the open labour market (OLM) by expanding Supported Employment (SE) practices from AT & BE, which have been proven effective in specific contexts and are scalable across different regions. Rather than replicating existing practices, SUPPORT introduces a socially innovative approach that redefines how employment is structured by involving Service Providers for PwD and promoting collaboration with OLM actors. Sustainable employment will be achieved through comprehensive job coaching across 8 European regions, supporting both employees and employers. Focusing on workplace integration via the place-then-train approach, the project will shift from traditional employment models to more inclusive practices that consider the diverse needs of persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups and the requirements of the OLM. In pilot regions where such practices are lacking or underdeveloped, SUPPORT will implement innovative SE models to foster inclusive employment and promote economic autonomy for marginalised workers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.beneficiaries: European Association of Service providers for Persons with Disabilities (EASPD)
innovations.evidence: - Development of country adaptation plans to implement Supported Employment practices effectively - Development of a comprehensive training material tailored for employers, employment services, and service providers to implement the Supported Employment model successfully - National Capacity Building sessions in 8 countries (AT, BE, CRO, GR, IT, ES, RO, NO) with the involvement of employers, employment services, and service providers - Employment of 130 long-term unemployed individuals through supported placements on the open labor market in the 8 participating countries
authors: European Association of Service providers for Persons with Disabilities (EASPD)

innovations.name: Silver Volunteering for Active Ageing
innovations.problem: The project addresses the critical social challenges faced by individuals over the age of 60 who have completed their professional careers. The core problems identified include: - Social Isolation and Loneliness: Many seniors experience profound loneliness and social exclusion following retirement. This transition often leads to a loss of social networks and emotional distress related to feelings of "loss". - Lack of Self-Realization and Low Self-Esteem: Retirees frequently face a lack of purpose and opportunities for self-realization. This demographic often struggles with low self-esteem as they transition from being active professionals to a less defined social role. - Barriers to Meaningful Engagement: While many seniors have a strong desire to remain active and useful to society, they face significant difficulties in finding organizations that can effectively utilize their specific life experiences and skills. - Systemic Gaps in Senior Coordination: There is a lack of a structured coordination system to facilitate senior volunteering. - This prevents seniors from effectively participating in civic and democratic life, which is essential for healthy and active aging. By addressing these issues, the project seeks to transform the perception of aging from a period of withdrawal to one of active, value-driven contribution to society.
innovations.description: The project "Seniors World: Silver Volunteering for Active Ageing" introduces a structured, multi-dimensional approach to active aging by bridging the gap between retirees' wealth of experience and the needs of the community. The innovation lies in the following components: - Dedicated Coordination System: The project establishes a specialized coordination framework specifically designed for senior volunteers. - Unlike general volunteering platforms, this system focuses on matching individuals over 60 with roles that align with their specific life experiences and professional backgrounds. - Strategic Networking and Database Development: A core innovation is the proactive creation of a verified database of "senior-friendly" host organizations, including NGOs, public institutions, and private companies. - This ensures that seniors are placed in environments that are prepared to value and utilize their unique skills. - Integrated Educational and Civic Empowerment: The solution goes beyond simple placement by integrating educational modules. - Volunteers participate in specialized training and lectures on democratic values, the future of the European Union, and the ethics of solidarity, ensuring that their service is both personally enriching and civically impactful. This serves to challenge ageist stereotypes and provide a "proof of concept" that encourages a broader societal shift toward valuing senior contributions. Regional Pilot Model: By focusing on three major hubs (Vilnius, Kaunas, and Klaipėda) and targeting a specific pilot group of 38 volunteers, the project created a scalable model for active aging that can be replicated across other regions. The project began as a pilot project titled “Expanding Opportunities for Volunteer Work Among Older Adults”; Focusing on three main centers (Vilnius, Kaunas, and Klaipėda) and targeting a specific pilot group of 30 volunteers, the project developed a model for active aging that can be adapted to other regions. The project is currently being continued and expanded in other regions.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project is designed to deliver specific, measurable outputs that create a foundation for senior engagement: Activation of Senior Volunteers : A primary result was the direct engagement of 38 senior volunteers (aged 60+). Volunteering Coordination System „Volunteering Journey“ : The development of a formal system to coordinate senior activities, ensuring that the process of matching volunteers with organizations is structured and sustainable. Creation of a Dynamic Database : A central database for volunteering opportunities will be established and continuously updated to provide long-term access for seniors seeking roles. Comprehensive Training Program : Implementation of specialized educational sessions, including training on democratic values, solidarity in volunteering, and the future of the European Union, led by expert lecturers. Broad Public Awareness : Success stories and project initiatives are being promoted through major national media outlets (such as 15min, LRT, Delfi, and TV3) to reach a wide audience and shift public perception. The project yields significant benefits at both the individual and societal levels: Promoting Healthy and Active Aging : By engaging in meaningful work, seniors find ways to age actively, which research suggests can have a "rejuvenating" effect on mental health and brain function,. Mitigation of Social Exclusion : The project directly combats the loneliness, social isolation, and emotional distress often associated with retirement and the loss of professional roles,. Enhanced Self-Esteem and Self-Realization: Seniors gain a renewed sense of purpose and self-worth by applying their lifelong skills and "life experience" to benefit society,. Civic and Democratic Empowerment: Participation in training and volunteering strengthens the civic and democratic engagement of older citizens, ensuring they remain active voices in the community,. Intergenerational Solidarity: The project fosters a culture of solidarity and shared values, bridging the gap between generations and utilizing the untapped potential of the senior population for the public good.

innovations.name: Social X – micro-incubator for social innovation
innovations.problem: Sweden has a growing number of so-called micro-innovators — individuals, social entrepreneurs, and small civil society actors with creative solutions to societal challenges in areas such as inclusion, health, integration, and education. Despite this, the innovation support system is designed for growth-oriented tech companies, which systematically excludes these actors from support and funding.
innovations.description: The Innovative Solution: A Micro-Incubator Model for Social Innovation Social X introduces a structured programme that combines proven incubation methodology with the specific logic of social innovation — something that doesn't currently exist in Sweden's innovation support landscape. The key innovations are: 1 . Full journey from idea to validated prototype Most existing support stops at business plans or concept development. Social X takes innovators all the way through to a prototype tested against real end-users and public sector stakeholders. 2. Adapted business development for social value Rather than pushing micro-innovators to "be more commercial" or "scale faster" — advice that can be harmful to social innovations — the programme offers coaching specifically designed for social business models that balance societal impact with economic viability. 3. Built-in horizontal inclusion Gender equality, accessibility, and non-discrimination are embedded from the start in selection, methods, and delivery — not treated as add-ons. In essence, Social X fills the gap between general business support and advanced incubation, creating a bridge into the innovation system for those who have previously been locked out of it.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Goal 1 — Strengthen individual micro-innovators At least 30 participants in the Formation phase At least 10 progressing into the Incubation phase 75% of participants report increased competence and confidence in their innovation ability Minimum 50% women among all participants Minimum 20% participants with a foreign background Goal 2 — Develop and validate social innovation prototypes At least 10 prototypes (products, services, or models) developed and exposed to potential end-users At least 15 organisations (public, private, or civil society) actively participating in validation activities At least 4 innovations assessed as having real potential for implementation or further development after the programme ends Key Benefits At the individual level, micro-innovators gain structured coaching, business development support, network access, and a credible pathway from idea to validated prototype — building competence, confidence, and routes toward self-employment or employment. At the organisational level, public sector bodies, civil society, and businesses gain access to creative, cost-effective solutions tailored to real needs, and develop new ways of collaborating with innovators who are closest to the problems they face.

innovations.name: Creators for Change
innovations.problem: Many young people have ideas, energy and a desire to contribute to their communities, but they are rarely involved in shaping the educational opportunities available to them. Educational activities are often designed for young people rather than with them. This challenge is particularly visible in rural and small urban communities, where access to educational opportunities, non-formal learning experiences and youth participation initiatives can be limited. Young people in these communities often have fewer opportunities to develop leadership skills, test ideas, participate in decision-making processes or connect with wider national and international networks. As a result, many young people remain consumers of educational experiences rather than active contributors. Schools, libraries and community organisations also miss valuable opportunities to benefit from young people's perspectives, creativity and understanding of the realities their generation faces. Creators for Change was developed to address this gap by creating a structured pathway through which young people can move from participation to co-creation and from beneficiaries of education to creators of educational opportunities for others.
innovations.description: Creators for Change is built around a simple idea: young people should not only participate in education but also help create it. The programme offers a structured two-year pathway that helps young people become creators of educational opportunities for their communities. Participants gradually move from exploring community needs to designing, delivering and improving educational activities for others. The model is organised around four stages: 1. Orientation Participants join a cohort-specific bootcamp to explore the needs of their schools, libraries, and communities. They reflect on their interests, define personal goals and learn the foundations of teamwork, communication, leadership and educational facilitation. From the beginning, they are encouraged to contribute their own ideas and perspectives on education. 2. Calibration Participants learn how to transform ideas into educational resources and communication materials. They take part in creative challenges and develop videos, visual materials, campaigns and learning activities based on topics relevant to young people. During this stage, they strengthen their digital, creative and communication skills while learning how to make complex topics accessible to others. 3. Activation Participants implement what they have created by facilitating workshops and educational activities in schools, libraries and community spaces. They work directly with students, teachers and librarians, putting their ideas into practice and expanding access to educational opportunities, particularly in rural and small urban communities. 4. Consolidation Participants continue developing their skills and take on more active roles within the programme. They can support new cohorts, test new educational formats, contribute to programme development and access national and international learning opportunities. This stage helps them strengthen their confidence, leadership skills and long-term engagement in their communities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
During its first two years of implementation, Creators for Change has engaged 165 young participants and 20 teachers and librarians through 11 training bootcamps.
More than 130 participants have transitioned from beneficiaries of educational activities to creators of educational resources and workshop facilitators. Over 70 participants have taken leadership roles and contributed to the development of new educational formats.
Participants have organised 289 workshops reaching 6,291 children and young people in their communities. The programme has reached 24 communities across Romania, with a strong focus on rural and small urban areas.
Creators have also developed 11 educational communication campaigns and produced 462 short videos, generating more than 1.1 million organic views. These activities helped young people strengthen communication, facilitation, leadership, digital and creative skills while making complex topics more accessible to their peers.
The programme has strengthened collaboration between young people, schools, libraries and community organisations. In 82.7% of participating communities, creators became active partners with local educational institutions and implemented multiple activities alongside teachers and librarians.
Additionally, 45 young women from the programme have participated in international projects, exchanges and events in cities such as Berlin, Brussels, Strasbourg, Paris, Athens, Bangkok and Yerevan, gaining access to learning and representation opportunities that are often less accessible to young people from rural and small urban communities.

innovations.name: ALL.D: enrichment, transfer and scale up of an Innovative Labour Insertion Model
innovations.problem: People with intellectual disabilities, autism spectrum disorder and mental health conditions face significantly higher risks of long-term unemployment, social exclusion and poverty. Existing employment services are often fragmented and insufficiently adapted to their specific support needs. In addition, employers frequently lack the knowledge, confidence and tools required to recruit and retain these groups successfully. ALL.D addresses the need for more integrated, personalised and transferable labour insertion approaches capable of generating sustainable employment outcomes across different European contexts.
innovations.description: The project is explicitly based on the existing Labour Insertion Model already developed and implemented by LaFACT/FUPAR and aims to enrich, transfer and scale it up. ALL.D improves and systematises LaFACT's Labour Insertion Model and transfers it to organisations in Greece, Italy and Romania through a structured process of adaptation, testing and mutual learning. The innovation combines: - A person-centred labour insertion methodology (LaFACT Labour Insertion Model). - Cross-sector collaboration through local alliances and a quadruple helix approach. - Capacity building for employment and social inclusion stakeholders. - Long-term support before, during and after employment. - An open-access AI-powered interactive platform that generates customised labour insertion action plans and facilitates knowledge sharing across Europe.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Expected results include: - Improved employability and employment outcomes for long-term unemployed people with disabilities and mental health conditions. - A validated and transferable Labour Insertion Model adapted to four European countries. - Strengthened cooperation between social organisations, employers, academia and public authorities. - Increased capacity of local stakeholders to support inclusive employment. - Creation of an open-access digital platform supporting labour insertion services. - A scalable model capable of replication in other European regions and countries.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: My Voice
innovations.problem: In a democracy, the average citizen has formal rights to influence decisions but rarely a real, practical channel to use them. Between elections every four years, people are left to participate passively or cynically while power concentrates in ever fewer hands – a gap that is widening as authoritarian and populist tendencies rise across Europe and trust in institutions falls. Referendums, the one direct tool available in Latvia, are rare, slow and expensive. Citizens want to solve concrete, everyday problems affecting their quality of life and public services, but individual concerns seldom translate into action, and those least connected to power are the least heard of all. There has been no everyday instrument to turn one person's idea into collective influence on the law before ManaBalss (MyVoice).
innovations.description: Before ManaBalss (MyVoice), there was no everyday instrument to turn one person's idea into collective influence on the law. Our innovation is not the website but the binding bridge behind it: a legislated guarantee that any initiative reaching 10,000 signatures (0.5% of the population) must be formally reviewed by parliament. Unlike ordinary petition sites that collect signatures and hope someone listens, ManaBalss is wired directly into the lawmaking process – every qualifying idea is fact-checked, made legally sound, and then genuinely considered by elected officials. Just as important, it activates the large, normally passive majority: citizens willing to give just two minutes become a real political force, regardless of wealth, status or connections. The result is a fast, trusted, everyday alternative to referendums – and in moments of crisis, a democratic "first-aid kit".
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: In nearly 15 years ManaBalss has become an integral part of Latvian democracy. 118 citizen initiatives have won support in parliament and changed the laws – one of them the Constitution, the only known citizen-initiated constitutional change made through digital democracy anywhere in the world. Around one-third of Latvia's population are platform users and over two-thirds are readers – both world records for civic engagement. Collective submissions have featured constantly on parliament's agenda for 15 years, and the estimated fiscal impact of these initiatives on the state budget runs into the €100–200 million range. The work has been recognised with the European Parliament Citizens' Prize.

innovations.name: PATHS
innovations.problem: In the Danube Region, the project addresses the critical lack of opportunities for informed career choices and widely available guidance services, particularly for children in disadvantaged rural areas and families with low educational attainment, which highlights severe inequalities in equity and opportunity. Because existing career awareness initiatives are merely ad hoc, limited, and confined to institutional classroom settings, young people lack a holistic approach to career guidance, significantly increasing student dropout rates across secondary, higher, vocational, and adult education. Consequently, these disadvantaged rural areas suffer from a severe "brain drain" driven by the outward migration of youth and highly educated individuals, leading to an aging resident population and the rapid depopulation of the countryside. This ongoing demographic crisis not only undermines the well-being and living standards of local youth—especially NEETs—but also poses a direct threat to the overall social and economic sustainability of these rural settlements within the Danube region.
innovations.description: To address these challenges in the Danube Region, the project's innovative solution is the establishment of a municipal-level Life Path Support Service (LPSS) that operates independently of traditional education and training institutions with the help of trained local mentors. This social innovation directly links the local settlement environment with career orientation to expand available services right where young people live, compensating for the lack of capacity and resources within schools and rural settlements. The solution relies on building and maintaining cross-sectoral cooperation by utilizing local community spaces to create more attractive, liveable environments that counteract the brain drain. Specifically, it provides rural youth with localized, innovative, and self-awareness-based career guidance services, which are followed by an individual development process where young people can test their knowledge and skills through short-term work placements in real workplace environments.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The key results and benefits of the project include the establishment of an independent, municipal-level Life Path Support Service (LPSS) that provides rural youth with full access to innovative, self-awareness-based career guidance directly in their own localities. Through this service, young people gain the opportunity to participate in "I own the path!" camps and specialized individual development processes, allowing them to test their knowledge and skills through short-term work placements in real workplace environments. This directly improves their labor market situation, enhances their well-being, and strengthens the retention capacity of rural areas to counteract brain drain and depopulation. Additionally, the project delivers a jointly developed, two-component model tested across multiple partner countries, expanding local professional capacities by training a diverse network of mentors (including teachers, social workers, and SME professionals) who are qualified to run the LPSS and supervise youth placements. Finally, the project benefits the region by fostering long-term cross-sectoral cooperation and creating a dedicated Danube Region LPSS Strategy, Action Plan, and Network to ensure continuous knowledge exchange and sustained career support after the project's closure.
tags: Equal access to education and training
Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: Kalletal Medical Care Center
innovations.problem:
Kalletal is a rural municipality in the far northeast of North Rhine-Westphalia. Spread across 16 settlements , Kalletal is home to just over 13,000 people. Like many rural municipalities, Kalletal faces increasing challenges in ensuring local healthcare provision. Demographic change exacerbates the situation: the average age of practising physicians in Kalletal is rising while the need for care in an ageing population is increasing.
The healthcare situation was described as alarming. There is an acute shortage of family physicians ( target: 8.2 general practitioner positions; actual: 5.25 ). Some practices have closed and further closures are expected. Specialist care is often unavailable or difficult to reach, and solo-practice structures are unattractive to young doctors. There is also a shortage of other health professionals (e.g., therapists, midwives, nursing staff). In addition, generally low health literacy among the population further strains the healthcare system.
To address these challenges and develop sustainable solutions, the municipality applied to participate in the pilot project “Municipal Development Advisory Boards – Shaping the Future Together Locally” (Berlin Governance Platform; January 2022–December 2023 ; funded by the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) ). The goal was to develop broadly supported recommendations for the municipal council on how to improve and secure healthcare in Kalletal for the future through a moderated, multi-stakeholder dialogue.
innovations.description:
The social innovation of MVZ Kalletal lies in combining structured citizen participation and cross-sector consensus-building with a concrete institutional solution to secure rural healthcare. Instead of isolated measures, the municipality used a Municipal Development Advisory Board (KEB) to jointly analyse needs, define objectives, and develop implementable measures that were then translated into the creation of a medical care centre (MVZ).
Participatory model (Municipal Development Advisory Board)

innovations.name: A loaf of bread a day for a poor elderly person
innovations.problem:
Many elderly people live in extreme poverty, without enough food, family support, or resources for a decent life. Low income, isolation, and lack of daily help expose them to hunger, illness, and social neglect. The project addresses this problem by providing a daily loaf of bread and constant support for vulnerable seniors.
In many communities in Romania, a significant number of elderly people live in extreme poverty, social isolation, and without family support. Many of them survive on very low incomes that are not sufficient for daily food, medication, or basic utilities. Without a support network, these individuals face high risks of hunger, illness, and social exclusion.
Our project directly addresses this issue by ensuring daily food support and maintaining a constant connection with beneficiaries.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
• Ensuring daily food for elderly people living in extreme poverty. • Reducing the risk of hunger, isolation, and social neglect among vulnerable seniors. • Increasing community involvement through volunteering and regular donations. • Improving the living conditions and dignity of beneficiaries. • Creating a local support network between the NGO, volunteers, donors, and partners. • Providing emotional support and human contact for lonely elderly people. • Developing a fast, transparent, and easily replicable support model for other communities.
• Over 300 beneficiaries supported since the launch of the project.
• 7 active volunteers involved in case identification, distribution of aid, and monitoring.
• 1 partner bakery involved in supporting the project.
• 4 local partners involved, including churches and local authorities.
• 2 households repaired or improved to ensure decent living conditions.
• Approximately 20 people received additional forms of support (food, firewood, clothing, medication, and other assistance).
The local network consists of volunteers, donors, local partners, and community institutions working together to identify and support vulnerable cases.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

• direct identification of beneficiaries through constant human contact;
• extending support beyond food, based on real needs observed in the field.

innovations.name: Tura de duminică
innovations.problem: Loneliness, mental health & sedentary lifestyle: - 1 in 6 people feel lonely - People with social connections are half as likely to experience anxiety or depression as those who are lonely - One-third of the global population aged 15 years and older engages in insufficient physical activities, which affects health
innovations.description: In a world where we forgot to move and meet new people, the innovative solution Tura discovered is returning to one of the first principles: walk more along other people. Tura de Duminică sets itself apart from other sports initiatives — and as one of its close community members put it: 'In a typical running group, 85% is about sport and only 15% about socializing and connection. At Tura de Duminică, it's exactly the other way around.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
People found a new habbit that helps both their mental health & their physical health. They feel less lonely and more active. It started with one park. Now it takes place in 5 parks in Bucharest and in 6 other cities in Romania. Simultaneously.
In the first year, we grew organically: from 3 people in Herăstrău to 1,000+ participants across 10 cities, supported by 15+ volunteers

innovations.name: Job-In
innovations.lead: FAB - Association for the Promotion of Work and Employment
innovations.problem: Job-In addresses the growing challenge of young people aged 18–24 who are not in employment, education, or training (NEETs) and who remain disconnected from existing labour market, educational, and social support systems. Many of these young people face multiple and interconnected barriers, including mental health challenges, social isolation, unstable living conditions, low educational attainment, lack of daily structure, substance abuse issues, and repeated experiences of failure or exclusion. Traditional support programmes often require a level of self-organisation, motivation, and institutional engagement that many of these young people are not yet able to demonstrate. As a result, they frequently disengage from available services and become increasingly isolated from society and the labour market. In Wiener Neustadt, stakeholders have identified a significant gap in low-threshold, flexible, and relationship-based support services for young adults who are difficult to reach and who require intensive trust-building and individualized guidance before they can successfully engage in education, training, or employment pathways. Job-In addresses this gap by providing outreach-based engagement, a safe and accessible community space, psychosocial support, practical skills development, and individualized coaching. The project creates opportunities for participation, empowerment, and gradual reintegration, enabling young people to overcome barriers, strengthen their resilience, and reconnect with education, training, employment, and social participation.
innovations.description: Job-In introduces a comprehensive social innovation model for engaging and supporting hard-to-reach NEET young people (18–24 years) who are disconnected from education, employment, and existing support systems. The project combines multiple innovative approaches into an integrated, low-threshold support model specifically designed around the realities, needs, and aspirations of vulnerable young people. One of the project’s core innovations is the combination of Digital Streetwork and traditional outreach youth work. Project staff actively engage with young people both in public spaces and through digital channels such as Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, and other online communities. This hybrid outreach approach enables the project to reach highly disengaged and “invisible” young people who rarely interact with conventional support services, creating new pathways for trust-building and early intervention. Another key innovation is the establishment of a permanently accessible “Open Space” community hub that operates without mandatory participation, formal admission procedures, or predefined attendance requirements. Young people can enter, leave, and engage at their own pace, creating a safe environment that prioritises trust, voluntary participation, and relationship-building over compliance and performance. The project follows a strong co-creation and participatory approach. Young people are not treated as passive beneficiaries but as active partners in shaping the project. Participants contribute to designing activities, defining priorities, shaping the physical environment, developing project rules, selecting equipment and learning opportunities, participating in outreach activities, and influencing their own individual support pathways. This approach strengthens empowerment, self-efficacy, ownership, and long-term engagement. Job-In further introduces an integrated “one-stop-shop” support model that combines outreach work, psychosocial support, individual coaching, skills development, career guidance, digital learning, community participation, and transition management within a single coordinated structure. By bringing multiple support functions together, the project reduces fragmentation, lowers access barriers, and ensures continuity of support. A further innovative element is the implementation of a flexible and non-linear support pathway based on the phases “Drop-In”, “Build-Up”, and “Step-Out”. Unlike traditional programmes that follow fixed progression models, participants move through these phases at their own pace. The model explicitly allows for setbacks, re-engagement, and varying levels of participation while maintaining continuous access to support services. The project also applies innovative learning methodologies based on experiential learning, practical activities, and participant interests rather than traditional classroom-based approaches. Activities include peer-to-peer learning, DIY workshops, creative media production, digital content creation, autonomy labs, pop-up working groups, action weeks, community projects, and real-life learning experiences that generate tangible outcomes and visible achievements. Peer involvement is another central innovation. Young people are encouraged to act as ambassadors, multipliers, workshop facilitators, and outreach supporters both online and offline. This peer-led approach creates authentic access points, increases trust among participants, and strengthens social inclusion. The project additionally integrates digital learning opportunities covering career orientation, digital skills, AI literacy, media competence, language learning, and occupation-specific modules. These flexible learning formats enable participants to acquire relevant competences at their own pace and according to their individual interests and goals. Job-In also strengthens innovation at system level by connecting labour market services, youth support organisations, educational institutions, health se
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: FAB - Association for the Promotion of Work and Employment
innovations.evidence: Job-In creates tangible and sustainable outcomes for people facing barriers to social participation, education and employment. Through low-threshold access, participatory approaches and continuous relationship-building, the project supports individuals in developing confidence, skills and realistic pathways towards inclusion and labour market integration. A recent success story illustrates the project's impact: A young refugee from Ukraine joined Job-In through the open space programme and aspired to start an apprenticeship with the Austrian Federal Railways (ÖBB). Through personalised support, including career guidance, application preparation, interview training and participation in low-threshold daily activities, he strengthened his language skills, self-confidence and understanding of the Austrian labour market. As a result, he successfully completed the recruitment process and received an apprenticeship offer from ÖBB starting in September 2026. As part of Job-In's follow-up support, he remains in regular contact with the project team and continues to share his positive progress and experiences. This example demonstrates how Job-In's holistic, participatory and flexible approach helps people overcome complex barriers, strengthen their self-efficacy and successfully transition into education, training or employment. Key benefits include increased social inclusion, improved employability, stronger participation in community life and sustainable integration into education and the labour market. Beyond individual outcomes, Job-In also strengthens cooperation between support services, employers and local stakeholders, creating more effective pathways for people who are often underserved by conventional support systems.

Job-In
Job-In addresses the growing challenge of young people aged 18–24 who are not in employment, education, or training (NEETs) and who remain disconnected from existing labour market, educational, and social support systems. Many of these young people face multiple and interconnected barriers, including mental health challenges, social isolation, unstable living conditions, low educational attainment, lack of daily structure, substance abuse issues, and repeated experiences of failure or exclusion. Traditional support programmes often require a level of self-organisation, motivation, and institutional engagement that many of these young people are not yet able to demonstrate. As a result, they frequently disengage from available services and become increasingly isolated from society and the labour market. In Wiener Neustadt, stakeholders have identified a significant gap in low-threshold, flexible, and relationship-based support services for young adults who are difficult to reach and who require intensive trust-building and individualized guidance before they can successfully engage in education, training, or employment pathways. Job-In addresses this gap by providing outreach-based engagement, a safe and accessible community space, psychosocial support, practical skills development, and individualized coaching. The project creates opportunities for participation, empowerment, and gradual reintegration, enabling young people to overcome barriers, strengthen their resilience, and reconnect with education, training, employment, and social participation.
Job-In introduces a comprehensive social innovation model for engaging and supporting hard-to-reach NEET young people (18–24 years) who are disconnected from education, employment, and existing support systems. The project combines multiple innovative approaches into an integrated, low-threshold support model specifically designed around the realities, needs, and aspirations of vulnerable young people. One of the project’s core innovations is the combination of Digital Streetwork and traditional outreach youth work. Project staff actively engage with young people both in public spaces and through digital channels such as Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, and other online communities. This hybrid outreach approach enables the project to reach highly disengaged and “invisible” young people who rarely interact with conventional support services, creating new pathways for trust-building and early intervention. Another key innovation is the establishment of a permanently accessible “Open Space” community hub that operates without mandatory participation, formal admission procedures, or predefined attendance requirements. Young people can enter, leave, and engage at their own pace, creating a safe environment that prioritises trust, voluntary participation, and relationship-building over compliance and performance. The project follows a strong co-creation and participatory approach. Young people are not treated as passive beneficiaries but as active partners in shaping the project. Participants contribute to designing activities, defining priorities, shaping the physical environment, developing project rules, selecting equipment and learning opportunities, participating in outreach activities, and influencing their own individual support pathways. This approach strengthens empowerment, self-efficacy, ownership, and long-term engagement. Job-In further introduces an integrated “one-stop-shop” support model that combines outreach work, psychosocial support, individual coaching, skills development, career guidance, digital learning, community participation, and transition management within a single coordinated structure. By bringing multiple support functions together, the project reduces fragmentation, lowers access barriers, and ensures continuity of support. A further innovative element is the implementation of a flexible and non-linear support pathway based on the phases “Drop-In”, “Build-Up”, and “Step-Out”. Unlike traditional programmes that follow fixed progression models, participants move through these phases at their own pace. The model explicitly allows for setbacks, re-engagement, and varying levels of participation while maintaining continuous access to support services. The project also applies innovative learning methodologies based on experiential learning, practical activities, and participant interests rather than traditional classroom-based approaches. Activities include peer-to-peer learning, DIY workshops, creative media production, digital content creation, autonomy labs, pop-up working groups, action weeks, community projects, and real-life learning experiences that generate tangible outcomes and visible achievements. Peer involvement is another central innovation. Young people are encouraged to act as ambassadors, multipliers, workshop facilitators, and outreach supporters both online and offline. This peer-led approach creates authentic access points, increases trust among participants, and strengthens social inclusion. The project additionally integrates digital learning opportunities covering career orientation, digital skills, AI literacy, media competence, language learning, and occupation-specific modules. These flexible learning formats enable participants to acquire relevant competences at their own pace and according to their individual interests and goals. Job-In creates tangible and sustainable outcomes for people facing barriers to social participation, education and employment. Through low-threshold access, participatory approaches and continuous relationship-building, the project supports individuals in developing confidence, skills and realistic pathways towards inclusion and labour market integration. A recent success story illustrates the project's impact: A young refugee from Ukraine joined Job-In through the open space programme and aspired to start an apprenticeship with the Austrian Federal Railways (ÖBB). innovations.name: Rugby for all
innovations.problem:
This situation contributes to broader issues such as social exclusion, low levels of youth engagement, limited development of life skills, and reduced opportunities for personal and community development. At the same time, access to structured, inclusive sport programs is uneven, with insufficient integration between schools, local authorities, and community organisations.
Additionally, the Romanian sport system is characterised by limited investment in grassroots initiatives and weak collaboration across sectors, which reduces its capacity to deliver social impact.
As a result, many young people lack:
access to inclusive and affordable sport opportunities
opportunities to develop key transversal skills (teamwork, leadership, resilience)
structured environments that support both physical activity and social inclusion
The problem is further compounded by the lack of sustainable models that combine sport, education, and community development through effective partnerships between public institutions, private actors, and civil society.
innovations.description:
Rugby for All introduces an innovative, sport-based social intervention model that integrates physical activity with non-formal education, community engagement, and cross-sector collaboration. Instead of focusing solely on sport participation, the initiative uses rugby as a structured tool to develop life skills, promote social inclusion, and activate local communities.
The innovation lies in combining three dimensions into a single, coherent model:
Sport as a vehicle for social change Rugby is used intentionally to develop transversal skills such as teamwork, discipline, leadership, resilience, and respect, supporting participants beyond physical activity.
Integrated public-private partnership approach (PPP) The initiative brings together schools, local authorities, NGOs, and private partners in a collaborative framework, enabling resource sharing, joint planning, and increased impact in contexts with limited public investment.
Structured and replicable methodology The project is designed as a repeatable model that combines training sessions, mentorship, and community-based activities, allowing it to be adapted and implemented in different regions and contexts.
In addition, Rugby for All shifts the focus from performance-driven sport systems to grassroots participation and inclusive access , addressing gaps in traditional sport development models. It creates pathways for engagement not only in sport, but also in education, volunteering, and community involvement.
By bridging sport, education, and social inclusion through a partnership-based model, the initiative offers a scalable solution for tackling youth disengagement and limited access to opportunities , particularly in underserved communities.

innovations.name: METAVERSING
innovations.lead: AIFED - Association for Innovation, Training and Employment for Sustainable Development
innovations.problem: Young people today are experiencing rapid digital transformation, yet they lack the skills, protections, and opportunities to participate safely, critically, and democratically in spaces such as the Metaverse. Many, especially vulnerable young people, face exclusion, misinformation, limited civic engagement, and unequal access to digital tools. The project addresses these gaps by promoting EU values, critical thinking inclusion, digital literacy, and active citizenship in both virtual and real environments.
innovations.description: METAVERSING introduces an innovative methodology that employs the Metaverse as a safe, inclusive, and value‑driven learning space where young people can build digital skills and explore EU values, policies, and priorities while being active participants. The combination of immersive virtual activities with non‑formal education and face‑to‑face youth work bridges digital gaps, empowers vulnerable groups, and equips youth workers with new tools to engage, educate, and connect young people across Europe.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: AIFED - Association for Innovation, Training and Employment for Sustainable Development
innovations.evidence:
The project creates innovative metaverse‑based learning spaces and combines them with non‑formal education to strengthen youth participation, digital skills, and inclusion. It equips young people and youth workers with the tools to navigate virtual environments safely and democratically, promotes EU values and human rights online, and builds a strong transnational network that supports long‑term civic engagement and digital transformation. The result is a more empowered, connected, and digitally competent generation capable of shaping both virtual and real‑world communities.
The project has also been developed in the border countries (Albania, Kosovo,, as well as countries belonging to the neighborhood countries of the EU being adapted for Morocco and Brazil. Moreover, the project has been carried out in other countries that do not belong to the network.

innovations.name: We grow through agricultural education
innovations.lead: Civitas Foundation for the Civil Society
innovations.problem: Romania is both the European Union country with the highest proportion of its population working in agriculture (over 20%) and among the European countries with the oldest farmers. Only 3% of farmers were under 35 in 2016, and the share of young farmers has been in permanent decline since 2010. The number of young farmers with formal training in the field is far below the EU average. According to the SWOT analysis carried out by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development, almost 97% of farmers have only practical experience, and even among young managers of agricultural holdings (under 35), an overwhelming 89.6% have only “the school of life” in agriculture. This translates into agricultural labor productivity four times lower than the EU average. In addition, only about 3,400 agricultural high school students in Romania participated in internships with private companies during 2020–2022, a small number compared to a total of roughly 16,000 students. The development of the professional and technical education (PTE) and dual education systems cannot be achieved without strengthening partnerships with economic agents
innovations.description:
In response to the challenges identified above, the consortium has focused its efforts on several core pillars of agricultural education in Romania. The proposed solution is an integrated set of activities designed to strengthen work-based learning (WBL) and to build a sustainable community of teachers: • Grant competitions – both for experienced high schools (with an integrated dimension of WBL activities and the sharing of experience) and for those with fewer than 5 grants in the program. • 4 regional meetings – to promote good WBL practices and facilitate the exchange of experience between high schools. • Performance evaluation instrument – developed, tested, and applied to all high schools implementing WBL activities. • Documenting good practices through at least 3 case studies. • Practicum training courses – to develop the skills of new teachers in organizing quality practicum programs. • Online community meetings – held every 3 months starting in the second year. • WBL exchange experiences – a new and innovative intervention through which a high school may apply only once to address its needs in knowledge, network, or training (e.g., exchanges with similar high schools, universities, or local entrepreneurs). • Summer school for teachers
The central sustainability element is the development of a community of practice among agricultural high school teachers, intended to become a common voice for agricultural education.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Civitas Foundation for the Civil Society
innovations.evidence: The key results are: • 180 students gain relevant skills and abilities by participating in internships. • 15 practicum programs implemented by high schools. • 45 practicum partnerships established between high schools and local agribusinesses. • 300 students increase their perception and motivation regarding their future career in agriculture by participating in study visits. • 1 evaluation instrument developed, tested, and applied across all 15 practicum projects. • 3 best-practice case studies promoting WBL activities among agricultural high schools. • 40 teachers develop their knowledge and skills to implement practicum activities. • 30 high schools improve their WBL practices by benefiting from the 30 WBL exchange experiences. • At least 80 teachers from 4 different regions interact on WBL topics during the 4 regional meetings. • 7 online community meetings with approximately 210 participating teachers (~30 per meeting). • 1 summer school organized by Civitas for 40 teachers Beyond these results, the program brings broader benefits: the involvement of agribusinesses (around 24 practicum partnership agreements), indirect benefits for students’ families and the communities around the high schools, and an improved public image of agricultural high schools in Romania. The figures above highlight our most recent three-year cycle; however, they are part of a 12-year legacy of spectacular results and transformative change in the sector.

innovations.name: Bridging the Skills Gap
innovations.problem: Refugees, migrants and asylum seekers in Greece often face multiple barriers to labour market integration, including limited access to targeted skills training, insufficient knowledge of local employment pathways, language and digital gaps, lack of professional networks, and difficulty connecting with employers. At the same time, several sectors of the Greek economy face persistent skills shortages and need practical mechanisms to identify, prepare and recruit motivated workers. Bridging the Skills Gap addresses this mismatch by creating a structured pathway from skills development to employability and job placement. The project responds both to the exclusion of vulnerable populations from decent work opportunities and to the needs of employers for trained, supported and job-ready candidates.
innovations.description:
Bridging the Skills Gap is innovative because it does not treat labour market integration as a sequence of fragmented services, but as a complete pathway from skills identification to training, employability support, employer engagement and job placement. The project combines vocational training, social and digital skills development, tailored career support, private sector partnerships and artificial intelligence tools into one integrated model that responds simultaneously to the needs of vulnerable people and the needs of employers. Its distinctive added value lies in connecting inclusion with real labour market demand. Refugees, migrants and asylum seekers are not approached only as beneficiaries of support, but as potential workers whose skills, aspirations and professional growth can contribute to the Greek economy.
Through mobile training missions, the project brings services closer to communities in remote areas of the mainland and islands, including Open Accommodation Sites, Reception and Identification Centres, and Community Hubs. An important innovation of the project is the launch of a unique training programme in the shipbuilding industry, offering tailor-made courses delivered directly in shipyards across the Ship Repair and Shipbuilding Zone, responding to the sector’s specific and growing skills needs.
The use of artificial intelligence to strengthen employability further enhances the model by supporting more targeted matching, personalised guidance and scalable service delivery. This makes the project more than a training intervention: it is a practical, data-informed and employer-facing integration model that can be adapted, replicated and scaled in other regions and European contexts.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence: Bridging the Skills Gap is expected to generate measurable benefits for both vulnerable communities and the Greek labour market. The project will provide social and digital skills training to 400 participants, European Way of Life workshops to 250 participants, introductory vocational courses across multiple sectors to 550 participants, and certified vocational training programmes to 350 participants in high-demand sectors such as industrial automation, professional truck driving, shipbuilding, hospitality and catering (HoReCa), among others. In addition, 2,100 refugees, migrants, and asylum seekers will receive tailored employability services to support their integration into the labour market. The project will also strengthen collaboration with employers by engaging 325 companies through Odyssea’s employer network and organising three job fairs, each expected to attract more than 500 visitors. Beyond these quantitative targets, the project strengthens participants’ confidence, employability profiles and access to decent work. It also benefits employers by connecting them with trained and motivated candidates in sectors facing skills shortages. At system level, the project contributes to a more inclusive and protective integration environment, supports early social and economic participation, and offers a scalable model for linking skills development, career guidance, private sector engagement and job placement.

Bridging the Skills Gap
Refugees, migrants and asylum seekers in Greece often face multiple barriers to labour market integration, including limited access to targeted skills training, insufficient knowledge of local employment pathways, language and digital gaps, lack of professional networks, and difficulty connecting with employers. At the same time, several sectors of the Greek economy face persistent skills shortages and need practical mechanisms to identify, prepare and recruit motivated workers. Bridging the Skills Gap addresses this mismatch by creating a structured pathway from skills development to employability and job placement. The project responds both to the exclusion of vulnerable populations from decent work opportunities and to the needs of employers for trained, supported and job-ready candidates.
Bridging the Skills Gap is innovative because it does not treat labour market integration as a sequence of fragmented services, but as a complete pathway from skills identification to training, employability support, employer engagement and job placement. The project combines vocational training, social and digital skills development, tailored career support, private sector partnerships and artificial intelligence tools into one integrated model that responds simultaneously to the needs of vulnerable people and the needs of employers. Its distinctive added value lies in connecting inclusion with real labour market demand. Refugees, migrants and asylum seekers are not approached only as beneficiaries of support, but as potential workers whose skills, aspirations and professional growth can contribute to the Greek economy.
Through mobile training missions, the project brings services closer to communities in remote areas of the mainland and islands, including Open Accommodation Sites, Reception and Identification Centres, and Community Hubs. An important innovation of the project is the launch of a unique training programme in the shipbuilding industry, offering tailor-made courses delivered directly in shipyards across the Ship Repair and Shipbuilding Zone, responding to the sector’s specific and growing skills needs.
The use of artificial intelligence to strengthen employability further enhances the model by supporting more targeted matching, personalised guidance and scalable service delivery. This makes the project more than a training intervention: it is a practical, data-informed and employer-facing integration model that can be adapted, replicated and scaled in other regions and European contexts.
Bridging the Skills Gap is expected to generate measurable benefits for both vulnerable communities and the Greek labour market. The project will provide social and digital skills training to 400 participants, European Way of Life workshops to 250 participants, introductory vocational courses across multiple sectors to 550 participants, and certified vocational training programmes to 350 participants in high-demand sectors such as industrial automation, professional truck driving, shipbuilding, hospitality and catering (HoReCa), among others. innovations.name: Pathways to employment through social farming placements
innovations.problem: These social farms provide an ideal local, community based space where people are supported in a very natural ways by the farmer. Ther area lot of different activities and aspect to the fam which is also a live "workplace" that allow people to become comfortable and to develop, confidence, skills, interests and capacity. This type of support is particularly important for those who are more marginalised and more distant from the labour market.
innovations.description:
This initiative allowed the WorkAbility Leitrim Employment Specialist to develop a very flexible and focused plan in collaboration with the person to help them to address challenges and barriers in their journey to employment. The social farm provided the space, the activities, interests etc and the social farmer was the person in the community who provided the support to the person to help them to work through their challenges and to achieve the goals in their plan. The social farm has a natural way of connecting people with others, with a wide variety of activities, tasks and learning experiences and also of providing many different opportunities such as animal care, horticulture, workshop skills, project planning, team work and communications.
Social farming / care farming is taking place in numerous other countries in different arrangements. We are not aware that these initiatives partner or collaborate with inclusive employment approaches such as WorkAbility Leitrim and to add value to the ESF funded initiative.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: These people were supported to experience an active workplace environment at their own pace, and to participate in a live work environment. This helped them to build and establish work routines, build their capacity and confidence, take and follow instructions. At its core, this initiative delivers supported employment which focuses on aiding individuals with disabilities, (or other challenges) in finding and maintaining employment. This approach allows for tailoring support to meet the unique needs of each person, ensuring they can progress and thrive in the workplace.
