innovations.name: Kidibot
innovations.problem: - Children nowadays they don't read books anymore, - Their attention span decreased due short format content, video and other cheap dopamine solutions - The percentage of children that would fail the Marshmallow Test is higher than ever (instant gratification is something that the whole society pushes for) - Huge negative social pressure to give in to the low quality dopamine - The teachers have very few means to motivate the children to learn - 42% functional illiteracy at PISA tests in Romania (highest in EU)
innovations.description: Kidibot solves this crisis by fighting fire with fire, using the exact mechanics that make video games addictive—gamification, behavioral economics, and peer group dynamics—but directing them toward a noble cause: reading, learning and doing good deeds. Instead of fighting technology, Kidibot leverages it to make physical books exciting again. Our core innovation lies in shifting the narrative from a solo, adult-enforced chore to a collective, kid-driven mission through three main pillars: -   Positive Peer Pressure & Team Dynamics: Instead of playing alone, children form alliances with their real-life classmates. To elevate their class in the global rankings and defeat the "Crocobets" (the anti-reading cosmic villains), every single student must contribute. This completely flips the classroom subculture: being smart and well-read becomes the ultimate status symbol, prompting top readers to naturally mentor and encourage struggling classmates. -   A Rewarding Gamification Loop: Students read physical books of their choice, then log onto Kidibot to solve quick, validation quizzes that prove comprehension. Passing a quiz awards them points, badges, and virtual currency to upgrade their avatars and help their team win battles. This provides the instant gratification and dopamine release children crave, successfully replacing the habit of endless scrolling with a structured, productive feedback loop. We became an Youtube of quizzes. Over 14k quizzes generated by children and teachers! -    Empowering the Educational Ecosystem: Kidibot acts as a force multiplier for teachers and parents. It gives educators a powerful, effortless tool to track reading progress in real-time and foster healthy classroom cohesion, transforming the act of learning into an engaging adventure that easily competes with low-quality digital entertainment.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Kidibot has successfully transformed the educational landscape by demonstrating measurable, wide-scale impact and fostering a powerful ecosystem of reading. Our key achievements include: - Massive Student Engagement: Over 100,000 children have been empowered by the platform, successfully shifting their screen time toward productive reading habits and significantly improving their literacy and comprehension skills. -  Strong Educator Alignment: More than 9,000 teachers actively utilize Kidibot as a crucial pedagogical tool, leveraging the platform to motivate entire classrooms, track progress effortlessly, and foster collaboration among students. - Active Parent Community: Over 36,000 parents are integrated into the ecosystem, allowing them to support their children's educational journeys and constructively manage their digital consumption. - Widespread High-Level Recognition: The platform’s innovative approach and social value have been validated by 32 prestigious awards received at national, European, and global levels, cementing Kidibot's position as a leading solution in educational innovation and social impact.
Initially, we launched it in Romania. After that we launched it in Moldova (same language), USA, UK, Italy, Spain. We could not handled with the existing financing so many countries, so we scaled back to Romania, Moldova and USA. Kidibot Romania has many features (quizzes, courses, battles, micro-courses, good deeds, blog). Kidibot Moldova also has most of the features. Kidibot USA has the lowest number of features and the least focus, unfortunately (now is drifting)

innovations.name: Omama
innovations.problem: Slovakia has a Roma community of around 500 000 people, making up 9% of the country’s population. A high percentage of Roma reside in housing that is sub-standard when compared with that of the majority of the population. Roma settlements are characterised by a substantial lack of basic infrastructure, safe water, electricity, roads, and safety procedures. Children growing up in such settlements often face a lack of stimulation at a formative age, which contributes to low educational performance and later to unemployment. Many Roma parents are not aware of the importance of early years interventions in breaking this vicious cycle of social exclusion.
innovations.description:
The Omama project is the first project in Slovakia that aims to improve the psycho-social development of children living in poverty by focusing on intervention in the first three years of children’s lives.
The idea of helping children in poverty was inspired by an early years intervention project implemented in Jamaica , which demonstrated the long-term gains and positive impact of early years interventions. Launched in 2018 by the NGO ‘Way Out’ ( Cesta Von ), Omama works with local social workers and professionals that work with poverty-afflicted communities to identify Roma women that can be trained and employed as ‘Omamas’. Each Omama identifies up to 15 children in families living in her community and provides them with weekly, one-hour individual sessions. The sessions take place in the presence of the mothers of the children and focus on cognitive stimulation and interactive play. They aim to improve communication between parents and children, as well as teach parents different stimulation methods that they can practise in their everyday life. Sessions are highly structured and repetitive, so that children can anticipate the activities based on the previous session. This allows them to learn in an organised way and provides them with security and predictability.
To become an Omama, women must have experience with young children and receive training in early intervention techniques to stimulate the cognitive and psycho-social development of children aged 0–3 years. Each Omama has a personal mentor who meets them regularly and guides them in their work. Omamas carry out three individual sessions per day as part of their part-time contract. If needed, Omamas can provide further assistance to children during the transition into formal pre-school education. Currently, a few Omamas are employed full-time, which means they work with 26 children, including children aged 4–5, and run pre-school clubs with them to provide continual education before they start school.
The project closely collaborates with Play Wisely , a programme developed in the USA that focuses on children’s brain development. Play Wisely trains Omamas in how to use cognitive tools, such as playing cards, to stimulate a child’s perception, attention, memory, and language development. The project also collaborates with Slovakia’s largest online bookstore, martinus.sk , which provides Omamas with a set of children’s books tailored to a specific age group, free of charge. Many of the families speak the Roma language at home and, through sessions and books, Omamas increase children’s exposure to the Slovak language, which is used in schools, thereby supporting future integration. The project also runs monthly parental clubs, during which experts talk to parents about topics such as breastfeeding, financial problems, or dental hygiene for young children.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The team has grown from 5 to 16 Omamas, covering 11 locations and able to deliver sessions for approximately 280 children. The estimated cost per child, for three years of interventions, is around EUR 3 000. The impact is expected to bring 10 times more value (around EUR 30 000) than the initial cost, as early interventions can increase employment opportunities for the affected individuals later in life and contribute to breaking the cycle of poverty for future generations . While it is too early to gather results for this specific project, the findings from the evaluation of the programme in Jamaica are promising. 20 years after the intervention ended, children who received early stimulation earned, on average, 25% more in adulthood compared to stunted children without this stimulation. The early stimulation intervention enabled the stunted group of children to earn, on average, the same level of earnings as the non-stunted group .
Collaboration with Accenture resulted in the development of an app to track the profile of every participating child and evaluate the project’s impact on an ongoing basis. Omamas are trained to use the app, which increases their IT skills and employability. The Research Institute for Child Psychology and Patho-psychology ( Výskumný ústav detskej psychológie a patopsychológie ) is planning an impact evaluation of the project. Additionally, Oxford University will train a team of Slovak experts to use the Inter-NDA neuro-developmental assessment app to evaluate the impact of the project.

innovations.name: Ballyhoura Breakthrough
innovations.problem: Traditional social inclusion programmes can be overly siloed, target-driven and focused primarily on labour market activation, making it difficult for people experiencing complex and intergenerational disadvantage to engage fully with supports. Individuals and families often face multiple interconnected challenges including housing insecurity, poor wellbeing, low confidence, social isolation, family pressures and difficulty navigating fragmented services. innovations.name: Salinaria – Community Wellbeing and Salt Therapy Center
innovations.problem: Families and children in small towns often have limited access to affordable wellbeing and preventive health services, as well as to safe and inclusive community spaces focused on relaxation, prevention and quality time together. In Salonta and nearby communities, air pollution, seasonal respiratory discomfort, stress and limited opportunities for healthy community interaction affect both children and adults. At the same time, there are few accessible local spaces dedicated to wellbeing, emotional balance and family-oriented activities.
innovations.description: Salinaria offers an innovative community-based approach that combines modern halotherapy technology, wellbeing, social inclusion and educational activities for children within a calm and accessible environment designed for families and local communities. Unlike traditional wellbeing services focused only on therapy, Salinaria integrates prevention, emotional wellbeing, community interaction and social economy principles into one local initiative. The project creates a welcoming space where children, parents and grandparents can relax, reconnect and participate in creative and community-oriented activities together. A unique element of the project is SARI, the friendly crystal mascot of Salinaria, developed to support children’s emotional wellbeing through stories, educational coloring sheets and interactive activities that encourage creativity, calmness and positive social interaction. Each educational activity also promotes environmental awareness, inclusion of children with disabilities, empathy, community involvement and respect for diversity in a friendly and accessible way.

innovations.name: LuckyWay – Community-Powered Debt Relief
innovations.problem: Across Europe, millions of people experience financial stress, debt overload, and social exclusion caused by rising living costs, consumer loans, and limited access to supportive financial recovery mechanisms. Debt problems negatively affect mental health, family stability, employment, and social participation. Traditional solutions such as refinancing or charity often remain inaccessible, temporary, or stigmatizing. LuckyWay addresses the growing need for a community-based, preventive, and socially inclusive support system that helps people regain financial stability before they fall into deeper crisis.
innovations.description:
LuckyWay is a social innovation platform based on collective community support. Participants voluntarily contribute small monthly amounts into a transparent community fund. Through a fair and regulated selection process, the platform helps selected members reduce or fully eliminate debt burdens. Unlike traditional financial services, LuckyWay does not provide loans, investments, or gambling activities. Instead, it combines digital community participation, social solidarity, and financial relief into one scalable ecosystem. The model promotes mutual support, social trust, financial resilience, and community empowerment through accessible micro-contributions.
LuckyWay MTÜ (Estonia, social innovation / community support sector) was inspired by community-based mutual aid and solidarity models where people contribute small regular amounts to help members facing financial hardship. The project adapts this approach to the growing problem of household debt and financial stress by creating a transparent community support system that helps participants reduce debt burdens and regain financial stability.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project aims to reduce financial stress and social exclusion among vulnerable and financially burdened individuals. Expected outcomes include improved mental well-being, increased social stability, reduced debt pressure, and stronger community engagement. The initiative may also indirectly decrease pressure on social welfare systems and improve economic participation by enabling people to recover financially faster. LuckyWay creates a positive social impact by transforming small individual contributions into meaningful collective support while strengthening solidarity and civic participation.

innovations.name: Sli WorkAbility
innovations.problem: People with disabilities in rural areas such as Donegal face persistent barriers to meaningful employment, including limited local opportunities, a lack of inclusive employers, and inadequate access to tailored training and support. These barriers disproportionately affect people with additional or multiple support needs, resulting in economic exclusion, reduced independence and social isolation. While inclusion is widely discussed in policy and practice, there are few visible, practical examples of inclusive employment in rural communities. As a result, less than 30% of people with disabilities in Donegal are in paid employment, significantly lower than the national average of 49%. Employers often lack the confidence, skills and real‑world models needed to implement inclusive practices successfully, leading to missed opportunities for both individuals and organisations. This has been compounded by a ‘placement for clicks’ culture of unpaid work experience that is profiled on social media as a quid pro quo for participation, which has effectively reduced the pressure on employers to create paid roles for people with disabilities. Real progress requires supported employment pathways demonstrating effective inclusion in rural social enterprises – if you can’t see it, you can’t be it.
innovations.description: Sli WorkAbility addresses the gap between aspiration and action by responding to the need for supported, structured employment pathways that provide real jobs, recognised skills and visible role models. Spraoi agus Sport is a thriving and diverse Social Enterprise, operating a commercial Garden Centre, Pre & After School Childcare, A Circular Economy Hub and a Digital Creative Lab as income generating projects. In additon to this, we deliver Inishowen's WorkAbility Programme - a Govt supported intervention to bring people with disabilities closer to employment by providing training, soft supports and mentoring to people with disabilities, and support and encouragement to employers around inclusive employment within their businesses. This dynamic places us in a unique position to provide diverse opportunities for Inclusive Employment across four distinct workstreams and then provide practical leadership, role modelling and exemplars to other employers around inclusive employment. We   are positioned to 'walk the talk' and engage employers with confidence and knowledge that we are not asking them to do anything that we do not already do ourselves. We become the powerful advocates for inclusive employment as a commercial peer of our local business leaders, not as a lobby group or disability rights organisation - although we are also these things. The innovation lies in our success a profitable Social Enterprise and significant local employer, and in the diversity of job roles and pathways that we are able to offer to participants, across four diverse workstreams which offer wider interest and access to our client group, and wider value to Spraoi. We then seek to exploit our profile and standing as a multi-award-winning Social Enterprise to amplify our message and experience around Inclusive employment, and that is also part of what underlies this application. We seek to platform the work of people with disabilities at every opportunity. By embedding inclusive employment opportunities within Spraoi, the project aims to demonstrate what positive, inclusive employment can look like in practice.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The project was initiated in 2025 and is embedding now, with more than 20 jobseekers with disabilities engaged per week across Spraoi's activities and we intend to begin a programme of paid apprenticeships within Spraoi by September of this year, to develop a series of shareable case-studies for others to follow.

innovations.name: The Air in Our School
innovations.problem:
Many schools lack accessible tools and awareness regarding indoor air quality, even though poor ventilation and air pollution can affect students’ health, concentration and learning performance. The project addresses the need for healthier learning environments, environmental education and community involvement by using citizen science and low-cost open-source technologies to help schools better understand and improve the air children breathe every day.
Air quality in schools is a significant public health and educational issue across Europe and Romania alike. Children spend between 700 and 900 hours per year in classrooms, and prolonged exposure to pollutants such as PM2.5, CO₂, volatile organic compounds (TVOC), noise, or inadequate temperatures can directly affect their health, concentration, and academic performance. The European SINPHONIE project, conducted across 25 countries, found that many schools struggle with insufficient ventilation and elevated indoor pollutant levels — contributing to reduced concentration, headaches, fatigue, respiratory symptoms, increased absenteeism, and worsening of asthma and allergies. The World Health Organization sets strict limits for fine particulate matter exposure (maximum 5 µg/m³ annual average and 15 µg/m³ over 24 hours) and flags ambient noise as one of the most significant environmental health risks in European urban settings, affecting children's sleep, stress levels, and learning capacity.
In Romania, indoor air quality is frequently overlooked, despite evidence suggesting that indoor pollution can exceed outdoor levels for much of the year. Over 200 open-source environmental sensors were installed across Romanian schools in previous endeavours, and hundreds of students and teachers participated in citizen science activities. Monitoring revealed frequent exceedances of recommended CO₂ and fine particle thresholds during class hours. Participants consistently reported sensations of heavy, stale air, fatigue after prolonged periods without ventilation, and a lack of accessible tools or information to understand what they were breathing. The project responds to a concrete community need: real-time environmental data, practical health education, and meaningful student involvement in understanding and improving the spaces where they learn.
innovations.description:
The project uses citizen science, low-cost open-source air quality sensors and hands-on STEM education to transform schools into active environmental learning spaces. Instead of relying only on theoretical education, students and teachers participate directly in real-time environmental monitoring, data analysis and practical workshops, creating a scalable and community-driven model for healthier and more sustainable schools.
The project was inspired by international citizen science and open-source environmental monitoring initiatives focused on air quality, environmental education and community engagement. It also follows approaches used by global open-data and DIY sensor communities that promote low-cost technologies, participatory science and healthier learning environments through real-time environmental monitoring and STEM education activities.
The innovation was adapted and implemented in multiple schools and educational activities in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, where students and teachers participated in citizen science workshops, air quality monitoring and STEM education activities. The project expanded from pilot monitoring activities to broader community engagement initiatives involving real-time environmental dashboards, classroom monitoring systems and hands-on educational workshops focused on indoor air quality, sustainability and environmental awareness.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Increased awareness about indoor air quality, ventilation and environmental health in schools Direct involvement of students and teachers in citizen science and STEM activities Installation of real-time air quality monitoring systems in educational spaces Development of practical digital, environmental and technical skills among students Promotion of healthier and more sustainable learning environments Creation of a scalable and replicable model for schools and local communities Strengthened community engagement through open data and environmental education initiatives
Implemented across 4 schools in Cluj-Napoca, the project combined participatory monitoring infrastructure with hands-on environmental education. Air quality sensors were installed in classrooms, laboratories, common areas, and outdoor school zones, measuring PM2.5, PM10, CO₂, temperature, humidity, and volatile organic compounds (TVOC) in real time. All data was made publicly accessible through an online platform at cluj-napoca.pulse.eco. Over 400 students participated directly in workshops and practical demonstrations, while dozens of teachers were trained in data monitoring and interpretation — learning to read live dashboards, understand what the numbers mean, and explain the health implications to their students.
Monitoring revealed frequent CO₂ spikes during class hours, significant differences between well-ventilated and poorly ventilated classrooms, and episodic increases in fine particulate matter near heavy traffic or at specific times of day. These findings had a direct behavioural impact: classrooms were aired out more frequently, conversations about ventilation and indoor comfort became routine, and awareness of air quality as a factor in health and academic performance grew measurably. Beyond the schools themselves, the project helped build a more environmentally engaged local community — involving parents, encouraging interdisciplinary use of real data in lessons, and sparking student interest in IoT technology and environmental monitoring. Students were not passive beneficiaries: they collected the data, interpreted it, and communicated it. That shift — from recipient to actor — is arguably the project's most durable result.

The project addresses the need for healthier learning environments, environmental education and community involvement by using citizen science and low-cost open-source technologies to help schools better understand and improve the air children breathe every day.
Air quality in schools is a significant public health and educational issue across Europe and Romania alike. Children spend between 700 and 900 hours per year in classrooms, and prolonged exposure to pollutants such as PM2.5, CO₂, volatile organic compounds (TVOC), noise, or inadequate temperatures can directly affect their health, concentration, and academic performance. The European SINPHONIE project, conducted across 25 countries, found that many schools struggle with insufficient ventilation and elevated indoor pollutant levels — contributing to reduced concentration, headaches, fatigue, respiratory symptoms, increased absenteeism, and worsening of asthma and allergies. The World Health Organization sets strict limits for fine particulate matter exposure (maximum 5 µg/m³ annual average and 15 µg/m³ over 24 hours) and flags ambient noise as one of the most significant environmental health risks in European urban settings, affecting children's sleep, stress levels, and learning capacity.
In Romania, indoor air quality is frequently overlooked, despite evidence suggesting that indoor pollution can exceed outdoor levels for much of the year. Over 200 open-source environmental sensors were installed across Romanian schools in previous endeavours, and hundreds of students and teachers participated in citizen science activities. Monitoring revealed frequent exceedances of recommended CO₂ and fine particle thresholds during class hours. Participants consistently reported sensations of heavy, stale air, fatigue after prolonged periods without ventilation, and a lack of accessible tools or information to understand what they were breathing. The project responds to a concrete community need: real-time environmental data, practical health education, and meaningful student involvement in understanding and improving the spaces where they learn.
The project uses citizen science, low-cost open-source air quality sensors and hands-on STEM education to transform schools into active environmental learning spaces. Instead of relying only on theoretical education, students and teachers participate directly in real-time environmental monitoring, data analysis and practical workshops, creating a scalable and community-driven model for healthier and more sustainable schools.
The project was inspired by international citizen science and open-source environmental monitoring initiatives focused on air quality, environmental education and community engagement. It also follows approaches used by global open-data and DIY sensor communities that promote low-cost technologies, participatory science and healthier learning environments through real-time environmental monitoring and STEM education activities.
The innovation was adapted and implemented in multiple schools and educational activities in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, where students and teachers participated in citizen science workshops, air quality monitoring and STEM education activities. The project expanded from pilot monitoring activities to broader community engagement initiatives involving real-time environmental dashboards, classroom monitoring systems and hands-on educational workshops focused on indoor air quality, sustainability and environmental awareness.
Increased awareness about indoor air quality, ventilation and environmental health in schools Direct involvement of students and teachers in citizen science and STEM activities Installation of real-time air quality monitoring systems in educational spaces Development of practical digital, environmental and technical skills among students Promotion of healthier and more sustainable learning environments Creation of a scalable and replicable model for schools and local communities Strengthened community engagement through open data and environmental education initiatives
Implemented across 4 schools in Cluj-Napoca, the project combined participatory monitoring infrastructure with hands-on environmental education. Air quality sensors were installed in classrooms, laboratories, common areas, and outdoor school zones, measuring PM2.5, PM10, CO₂, temperature, humidity, and volatile organic compounds (TVOC) in real time. All data was made publicly accessible through an online platform at cluj-napoca.pulse.eco. Over 400 students participated directly in workshops and practical demonstrations, while dozens of teachers were trained in data monitoring and interpretation — learning to read live dashboards, understand what the numbers mean, and explain the health implications to their students.
Monitoring revealed frequent CO₂ spikes during class hours, significant differences between well-ventilated and poorly ventilated classrooms, and episodic increases in fine particulate matter near heavy traffic or at specific times of day. These findings had a direct behavioural impact: classrooms were aired out more frequently, conversations about ventilation and indoor comfort became routine, and awareness of air quality as a factor in health and academic performance grew measurably. Beyond the schools themselves, the project helped build a more environmentally engaged local community — involving parents, encouraging interdisciplinary use of real data in lessons, and sparking student interest in IoT technology and environmental monitoring. Students were not passive beneficiaries: they collected the data, interpreted it, and communicated it. That shift — from recipient to actor — is arguably the project's most durable result.

innovations.name: Together Academy
innovations.problem: In Ireland, approximately 90% of adults with Down syndrome are unemployed or underemployed. Upon leaving school, many face a "digital cliff," where structured support completely disappears, leading to social isolation and a loss of purpose. Standard employment models rarely accommodate the specific learning paces or workplace adjustments required by neurodivergent individuals, leaving a massive pool of eager, capable talent completely untapped.
innovations.description:
Together Academy disrupts traditional charity models by operating as a commercially viable social enterprise hybrid. Rather than keeping training behind closed doors, its innovation lies in its highly visible, public-facing "living classrooms"—specifically the landmark partnership with commercial brand Happy Out. By integrating rigorous, customized vocational training directly with a live, high-volume retail environment, the project shifts the narrative from "charity" to "capability." It utilizes specialized visual aids, digital learning tools, and job-carving techniques that rethink how hospitality roles are structured.
Phase 1: The Genesis The project began as a localized proof-of-concept at Wanderers Rugby Club, featuring just one training café and one foundational classroom programme. This initial phase proved that tailored, hands-on hospitality training could successfully build workplace confidence in adults with Down syndrome. Phase 2: Commercial Integration To test students in a high-volume market, the academy scaled up by partnering with popular specialty coffee brand, Happy Out. This led to their landmark flagship café at the Dún Laoghaire Baths, proving that graduates could thrive in competitive, fast-paced commercial environments. Phase 3: Modern Enterprise Ecosystem Backed by the WorkAbility Programme (co-funded by the Department of Social Protection and the EU), the project expanded into a comprehensive, multi-site network: Three Locations: The café network grew to three, adding a corporate staff café at SMBC Aviation Capital HQ alongside the Wanderers and Dún Laoghaire locations. Expanded Curricula: The single programme evolved into two distinct pathways—a 2-year accredited Employability Skills Programme and an intensive, 9-month Vocational Training Programme geared toward immediate workplace readiness. Supported Employment: The academy launched a dedicated Employment Service, shifting focus from just training students to actively placing them in the wider workforce with the help of dedicated job coaches.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: Hands-on Skill Development: Students gain accredited, real-world experience in high-demand hospitality and retail roles. Supported Employment: The dedicated Supported Employment Service matches graduates with inclusive employers, providing job coaches and diversity training to ensure long-term, independent career success. Visible Inclusion: By placing young adults at the forefront of popular local cafés, the project directly challenges societal stereotypes and fosters authentic community integration.

innovations.name: Education - Back to the roots
innovations.problem:
1. Youth NEET rate: Romania faces one of the most pressing youth employment challenges in the EU, with a NEET rate of 19–19.4% -  meaning roughly one in five young people is currently neither in education, employment, nor training. This alarming statistic underscores the urgent need for early educational intervention. "Back to the Roots" addresses this directly by exposing children and adolescents from diverse socioeconomic backgrounds to the full spectrum of professional pathways available to them, while reinforcing a clear message: completing each stage of formal education -  middle school, high school, and university - is a concrete and achievable stepping stone toward a fulfilling career.
2. Youth disengagement and lack of motivation Beyond statistics, practitioners working with young people in Romania increasingly encounter a widespread crisis of motivation, driven largely by a perceived absence of future prospects. When young people cannot see a realistic path forward, ambition stalls. "Back to the Roots" responds to this challenge through a structured professional orientation program that brings living proof back into the classroom: alumni who were educated in the same schools, from the same communities, and who have gone on to build meaningful careers. Their stories serve as tangible evidence that regardless of where one starts, persistence and hard work can translate into genuine success.
innovations.description:
Learning by doing State of the art practical exercises (smart homes functionalities)
While inspirational visits and career talks in schools are not a new concept, what is consistently missing is structure, planning, and follow-through. Many similar initiatives exist in fragmented form — one-off events with little coordination and no sustainable methodology behind them. This is precisely the gap "Back to the Roots" fills.
The program is built on a dual-input planning model: activities are designed by actively listening to young people's expressed interests and preferences, ensuring relevance and engagement, while simultaneously promoting a core set of high-impact professions — engineer, economist, physician, lawyer, HR specialist — that offer strong long-term prospects and are currently underrepresented in students' career awareness.
This combination of responsiveness to youth feedback and deliberate professional promotion is what distinguishes the initiative from ad-hoc school events. The result is a coherent, replicable program architecture that delivers consistently, rather than a one-time motivational moment that fades without lasting impact.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
A generation with a better orientation regarding the career steps, youngsters with audible voices (trust increased), improved the communication
Results to date
Since October 2025, the program has reached over 500 young people across Alba County through both group and individual professional orientation sessions, operating across two cities and one commune. Six formal collaboration agreements have been established with local institutions — one high school, two middle schools, two day centers, and one permanent care center — and more than 14 sessions have been delivered to date.
Observed impact
The response from young participants has been notably positive. Engagement levels are visibly higher in one-on-one sessions with field experts aligned to each student's area of interest, and a clear pattern has emerged in group settings as well: by the second meeting, participants are markedly more open, relaxed, and willing to engage in dialogue. This progression reinforces a key design insight — the presence of a consistent facilitator across all sessions acts as a trust anchor that enables richer, more authentic conversations. This role is fulfilled by the association's president, who attends every session and serves as the connective thread holding the program's relational dynamic together.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: Sew for Inclusion
innovations.problem:
The project addresses the deep social exclusion and discrimination faced by Roma communities living in segregated conditions in Șumuleu 33, Miercurea Ciuc, where 72 families — nearly 500 people — live in extreme poverty and isolation. Many families lack access to stable housing, quality education, healthcare, and employment opportunities, while children often grow up without opportunities for social participation, vocational development, or self-confidence. Roma women in particular face significant barriers to employment and economic independence. At the same time, there is a growing need for adaptive and dignified care products for elderly people and individuals with reduced mobility. Through our community-based sewing workshop, vocational training activities, and the development of Oldy adaptive pajamas, the project creates employment, practical learning opportunities, social inclusion, and dignified care solutions while challenging stereotypes and reducing inequalities.
In the context of an aging population and the rapid growth in the number of people receiving home care, there is an increasing need for specialized medical textile products that are accessible and easy to use. Oldy addresses this challenge through a design adapted for bedridden individuals: faster dressing and undressing (opens on one side), reduced pain during handling (the patient does not need to be lifted when changing the pajamas — only turned on their side), easy access for medical care and hygiene, reduced workload for caregivers, and improved patient comfort and dignity.
The Oldy adaptive pajama responds to a real and growing problem in Romania's healthcare and home care system: the large number of bedridden individuals who are dependent on daily care and for whom changing clothes is difficult, painful, and time-consuming — both for the patient and for family members or medical staff.
According to statistics published by the National Health Insurance House, in 2025 between 9,000 and over 10,000 immobilized or severely mobility-impaired individuals received home medical care services on a quarterly basis. In Q3 2025, the National Health Insurance House reported 10,078 beneficiaries of home medical care services and over 1,063,660 medical services performed at home.
innovations.description:
Our innovative solution is a community-based sewing workshop that combines employment, vocational education, and social entrepreneurship in one integrated model. The workshop employs women from the segregated Roma settlement of Șumuleu 33 while also providing regular small-group sewing sessions where children and young people learn practical skills directly through hands-on experience. Volunteers, seamstresses, and community members work together in the same space, creating an environment where learning, mentoring, and income generation happen simultaneously. The workshop operates both as a social support space and as a small-scale production unit. Participants gradually move from simple creative activities to producing real products, including handmade bags, decorations, and Oldy adaptive pajamas designed for people with reduced mobility. This practical learning model helps children and young people build confidence, responsibility, teamwork, and vocational skills while seeing tangible results from their work. What makes the initiative innovative is the way it connects social inclusion with economic sustainability. Instead of offering short-term aid, the project creates a long-term community-driven system where marginalized people actively participate in production, learning, and decision-making. The sewing workshop not only generates employment and income opportunities but also challenges stereotypes, strengthens dignity, and creates direct connections between vulnerable communities and wider society.
The innovation behind the Oldy pajama stems from a direct personal experience. The idea emerged during a period when the founder's father was seriously ill and bedridden, and the family faced daily challenges around changing clothes, providing care, and preserving the patient's dignity. The products available on the market at the time were either standard pajamas — difficult to use for immobilized individuals — or highly technical medical garments that were uncomfortable and impersonal in appearance, closer to hospital wear than to clothing.
Oldy proposes a new approach: a medically adapted pajama that retains the look, comfort, and emotional warmth of a normal home garment. The innovation lies in combining medical functionality with a humane and dignified product design.
The pajama is specifically designed for: bedridden individuals, elderly people dependent on care, oncology patients, and people with disabilities or neurodegenerative conditions.
Compared to existing products on the market, Oldy stands out through: an opening system designed for quick changes without excessive lifting of the patient; easy access for hygiene, diaper changes, IV lines, and medical care; reduced pain and minimized physical handling; soft, comfortable materials closer to everyday clothing than to medical equipment; and a discreet, dignified design that reduces the feeling of being a "patient."
The social dimension is also part of the innovation. The pajamas are being developed within a future social economy structure, where vulnerable individuals and women from marginalized communities can learn tailoring and gain access to stable income and employment. In this way, Oldy generates both medical and human impact, as well as local social and economic impact.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The project has created a safe, supportive, and inclusive space where Roma women, children, and young people can learn, work, and build confidence together. Two women are already employed in the sewing workshop on a long-term basis, while children regularly participate in practical sewing activities that help them develop vocational skills, creativity, responsibility, and self-esteem. The workshop has also strengthened community trust and participation by creating positive daily routines, mentoring relationships, and opportunities for social inclusion. Participants experience success through producing real products and contributing to meaningful work, which helps reduce feelings of exclusion and hopelessness. At the same time, the initiative generates sustainable income through the production and sale of Oldy adaptive pajamas and handmade products, supporting both the long-term operation of the workshop and future employment opportunities within the community.
In total, nearly 100 children participated in activities led by seven volunteers. We organize 2–5 activities per week depending on the volunteers' schedules, in groups of 3 to 12 children.
To date, we have sold 80 pajamas. 50 units are currently stocked in nearby stores, in Cluj-Napoca and Târgu Mureș. We have 200 units in stock and a production capacity of 200–300 units per month.
Our other products (some made together with the children) include: wallets in three sizes, pencil cases, hair accessories, hair ties, decorations, the Pinduriq doll, tote bags and handbags — all made through recycling and reuse of materials. We sell these products at fairs. We have participated in the Christmas Fair, the March 8th Fair, and the Whitsun Fair. Young people from the community help us at these events, and our goal is to gradually teach them and delegate this responsibility to them.
The estimated turnover for 2026 is €50,000. The project is becoming self-sustaining through: direct sales (webshop: https://prgz15-wh.myshopify.com/ ), partnerships with NGOs and medical institutions, social fairs and recurring orders, and reinvestment of profits into the workshop and salaries.
To date, we have personally presented the pijama at county hospitals in Harghita, Covasna, Mureș, Brașov, Cluj, and several local hospitals, at the Social Enterprises Fair in Sibiu, and at the Social Business Conference in Lugano, Switzerland. We work with volunteers supporting the marketing of the Oldy pajama, and our partners include NGOs such as Social Business Earth (Switzerland), Atelierul de Pânză (Bucharest), and several local organizations.

Sew for Inclusion
The project addresses the deep social exclusion and discrimination faced by Roma communities living in segregated conditions in Șumuleu 33, Miercurea Ciuc, where 72 families — nearly 500 people — live in extreme poverty and isolation. Many families lack access to stable housing, quality education, healthcare, and employment opportunities, while children often grow up without opportunities for social participation, vocational development, or self-confidence. Roma women in particular face significant barriers to employment and economic independence. At the same time, there is a growing need for adaptive and dignified care products for elderly people and individuals with reduced mobility. Through our community-based sewing workshop, vocational training activities, and the development of Oldy adaptive pajamas, the project creates employment, practical learning opportunities, social inclusion, and dignified care solutions while challenging stereotypes and reducing inequalities.
In the context of an aging population and the rapid growth in the number of people receiving home care, there is an increasing need for specialized medical textile products that are accessible and easy to use. Oldy addresses this challenge through a design adapted for bedridden individuals: faster dressing and undressing (opens on one side), reduced pain during handling (the patient does not need to be lifted when changing the pajamas — only turned on their side), easy access for medical care and hygiene, reduced workload for caregivers, and improved patient comfort and dignity.
The Oldy adaptive pajama responds to a real and growing problem in Romania's healthcare and home care system: the large number of bedridden individuals who are dependent on daily care and for whom changing clothes is difficult, painful, and time-consuming — both for the patient and for family members or medical staff.
According to statistics published by the National Health Insurance House, in 2025 between 9,000 and over 10,000 immobilized or severely mobility-impaired individuals received home medical care services on a quarterly basis. In Q3 2025, the National Health Insurance House reported 10,078 beneficiaries of home medical care services and over 1,063,660 medical services performed at home.

Instead of offering short-term aid, the project creates a long-term community-driven system where marginalized people actively participate in production, learning, and decision-making. The sewing workshop not only generates employment and income opportunities but also challenges stereotypes, strengthens dignity, and creates direct connections between vulnerable communities and wider society.
The innovation behind the Oldy pajama stems from a direct personal experience. The idea emerged during a period when the founder's father was seriously ill and bedridden, and the family faced daily challenges around changing clothes, providing care, and preserving the patient's dignity. innovations.name: Virtual Empowerment
innovations.problem: Barriers to independence for vulnerable groups: • Neurodivergent individuals, wheelchair users, and those with acquired brain injuries often struggle with social interactions, procedural memory and executive functions, making everyday tasks (e.g., using public transport, grocery shopping or responding to emergencies) overwhelming. • High societal costs: Dependence on specialized transport, one-on-one support or delayed integration into society places a financial and organizational burden on municipalities, schools, and caregivers. • Lack of accessible training: Traditional methods (e.g. role-playing or real-life practice) are often stressful, inconsistent or impractical for these groups, leading to low confidence and slow progress.
innovations.description: Virtual Empowerment uses VR as a safe, scalable and engaging tool to teach practical skills through: • Immersive learning: Users practice in risk-free, repeatable environments (e.g. planning routes, interacting with bus drivers, handling train delays, or correcting station exits). • Tailored scenarios: Training adapts to user-specific challenges (e.g. autism, mobility limitations) and local contexts. • Privacy-first design: Standalone VR headsets eliminate cloud storage, fully aligning with data protection requirements. • Proven results: Modules like Virtual Public Transport deployed at 50 special needs schools show measurable gains in confidence and independence.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Measurable outcomes: • 3,000 youth trained in Virtual Public Transport, with 25% earlier transition from student transport to public transport. • Reduced societal costs: Less reliance on specialized services (e.g. student transport, constant supervision). • Scalability: Ready for international expansion (e.g. via partnerships with software, education or impact organizations abroad). • Broad applicability: Suitable for elderly, MBO youth, newcomers and other groups needing life skills training.Social benefits: • Empowerment: Users gain confidence and autonomy in daily life. • Inclusion: Bridges gaps for hard-to-reach youth and marginalized groups.

innovations.name: zeit*raum*schaffen
innovations.problem:
The planning phase confirmed that existing services in Salzburg have limited reach when it comes to young adults up to the age of 30 who find themselves in precarious circumstances, like:
psychological stress such as anxiety, social insecurity and worries about the future
loneliness and a lack of social belonging
experiences of discrimination on the grounds of gender, sexual orientation, background or health status
precarious housing situations
financial pressures
difficulties in finding work or training
In addition to these challenges, there is a desire for a safe, consumption-free space where people can interact without feeling pressured to perform. Equally clear is the need for a voice and the opportunity to actively shape their own lives. It is evident that these challenges rarely occur in isolation. Rather, they stem from complex life situations in which issues of identity, relationships, economic stability, and career direction are closely intertwined. The target group consists of young adults from multiply marginalized communities experiencing intersectional discrimination and compound burdens across economic, social, and psychological dimensions. Persistent loneliness often exacerbates their vulnerability, creating barriers to accessing traditional support systems. Their needs include safe, trust-based spaces that foster genuine connection, holistic support addressing these overlapping challenges, and empowering structures that enable stabilization and pathways to social and professional inclusion.
The project therefore does not respond with an isolated measure, but rather by creating a structured framework that allows for time, space, and participation.
innovations.description: We transform time from pressure into a resource, space from institutional barriers into safe havens, and participation from mere attendance into active co-creation by the target group. The project’s unique participation success stems from the active self-representation of our multiply marginalized target group, who co-decide on key aspects and shape the initiative from within and during the conceptual phase, the target group was already actively involved. Participatory co-created offer, funded conceptual phase with target group involvement. Guided by the central question "How do I want to live, work and love?", we apply a participatory approach from concept development, consistently involve target groups, foster cooperation and networking, provide scientific accompaniment, and are supported by the National Competence Centre for Social Innovation "SI plus".
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: For the project’s success, it is crucial to address participants’ multiple burdens and intersectional contexts, systematically dismantle project-internal structural barriers, and create a participatory, holistic program with trust-based spaces for encounter and exchange—delivering stabilization of life circumstances and, ideally, professional and social inclusion. Key results include a proven co-creation model, scientific evidence of effectiveness, and a scalable framework, with impact across timeframes: short-term support (e.g., daily routine structuring), medium-term access improvements (e.g., through person-centered case management on all relevant life topics), and long-term sustainable self-representation structures extending beyond the project. Benefits range from participant empowerment and reduced loneliness to improved social work practices and more inclusive systems.

innovations.name: Impact Makers Support for Microinnovators
innovations.problem: Many social entrepreneurs are excluded from traditional innovation and business support systems because their organisations and business models do not fit conventional structures focused on profit-driven companies. As a result, important social innovations are never tested or developed, despite their potential to address major societal challenges such as exclusion, unemployment, integration and mental wellbeing. Women, migrants and people with backgrounds in civil society are particularly underrepresented in mainstream innovation systems and often lack access to networks, financing and tailored support.
innovations.description:
The project creates an inclusive support model specifically adapted for early-stage social entrepreneurs and grassroots innovators. Instead of expecting social innovators to adapt to traditional business systems, the programme redesigns support structures around their actual needs and realities. The model combines mentorship, peer learning, ecosystem navigation, social impact measurement, business development and financing preparedness into one integrated process. The project also strengthens collaboration between civil society organisations, cooperative actors and innovation ecosystems.
The project builds on experiences and insights from several earlier initiatives supporting social innovation and impact-driven entrepreneurship in Sweden.
Key sources of inspiration include: - Zebra Impact Ventures / Zebra Impact Academy (Sweden), supporting impact-oriented entrepreneurs and ecosystem collaboration, - Coompanion’s long-standing work supporting cooperative and social enterprises across Sweden, - Mikrofonden’s experience from over 170 social investment initiatives and financial support structures for social enterprises, - and grassroots innovation approaches developed within civil society and community-led entrepreneurship initiatives.
The project also builds on findings from the Swedish pre-study “Ökad investeringsmognad i sociala företag” carried out by Mikrofonden, Founders Loft and Coompanion, which identified major gaps in existing innovation support systems for early-stage social innovators and microinnovators.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The project increases access to innovation support for underrepresented groups and strengthens the capacity of social entrepreneurs to develop sustainable solutions to societal challenges. Expected results include: - increased entrepreneurial confidence and skills among participants, - stronger collaboration between civil society and innovation ecosystems, - more tested and validated social innovation ideas, - increased understanding of social impact measurement, - and improved access to networks, financing and long-term support structures. The project also aims to develop a scalable methodology that can inspire similar initiatives nationally and internationally.

innovations.name: Konfliktsimulator
innovations.problem: Conflicts are a persistent and growing challenge in schools and youth settings. According to a 2024 German nationwide survey among 1,311 school principals (forsa/VBE), 60% report that violence at their school has increased over the past five years. 65% of schools have experienced verbal or psychological abuse directed at teachers, 36% digital violence, and 35% physical attacks. Nearly every second teacher reports problems with violence among students. Yet despite this reality, the vast majority of educators receive little to no practical training in conflict management. Initial teacher training and continuing professional development overwhelmingly rely on theoretical, lecture-based formats with little or no space for practice, reflection, or repetition. Our own needs assessment (2025, n=79) confirmed this: while almost all respondents reported dealing with conflicts regularly, the foundational thesis was validated: systematic training in evidence-based conflict methods is largely absent. The consequences are significant. Unresolved conflicts escalate, create lasting harm for young people, increase teacher burnout, and undermine the social cohesion of school communities. Cyberbullying, exclusion, discrimination, and escalating confrontations between students have become everyday realities that educators feel ill-equipped to handle. The core problem is not a lack of willingness, it is a lack of accessible, effective, practice-oriented training. Existing offers are too infrequent, too abstract, and too disconnected from real-life situations to produce lasting behavioral change. What is needed is a scalable solution that allows educators to practice conflict skills repeatedly, in realistic scenarios, with immediate feedback and without requiring them to leave their professional context.
innovations.description: The Konfliktsimulator is a AI-powered training platform that enables educators to practice conflict management in immersive, repeatable simulations and is available via VR headset or standard web browser, requiring no specialist hardware or dedicated training time. The core innovation lies in combining four elements that have never before been brought together in conflict training for educators: 1. Realistic, AI-driven conflict scenarios. Users enter an interactive virtual environment and engage in real-time dialogue with adaptive AI characters. These characters respond dynamically to the user's conversational choices, mirroring the unpredictability of real-life conflicts. No two sessions play out the same way. 2. Evidence-based micro-methods. Rather than teaching abstract theory, the Konfliktsimulator trains small, concrete, immediately applicable intervention techniques, such as active listening, mirroring, and solution-focused questioning. Users discover and practice these methods step by step through a gamified learning journey, building a practical toolkit for their professional daily life. 3. An AI personal coach. After each session, an AI-powered coach delivers individualized feedback: what worked, what was missed, and what to try differently. This after-action review makes learning progress visible and motivates continued practice; a feature entirely absent from conventional training formats. 4. Dual accessibility. The training runs both on VR headsets for full immersion and on any standard internet browser, removing barriers of cost, infrastructure, and geography. Sessions last 15–20 minutes, fitting into the professional routine without requiring leave or travel. The approach draws on the logic of flight simulators: high-stakes skills are best learned through repeated, consequence-free practice in realistic conditions. Applied to social and communicative competences, this represents a genuine methodological innovation for the field of civic education and conflict transformation. The Konfliktsimulator is co-developed with its target groups through needs assessments, focus groups, and iterative testing cycles, ensuring that scenarios reflect real professional challenges. It is scientifically accompanied by Ostfalia University of Applied Sciences, with impact measured through a pre-post evaluation design.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: The Konfliktsimulator produces results and benefits on three interconnected levels: for individual practitioners, for the institutions they work in, and for society at large. Benefits for individual practitioners After engaging with the Konfliktsimulator, educators gain a measurable increase in conflict competence. Specifically, users are expected to: know and be able to name more evidence-based conflict methods than before; apply a broader and more varied range of micro-methods in simulated conflict situations; and feel more confident and capable of handling conflicts constructively in their professional daily life. innovations.name: HOLÍSTICA: Women transforming vulnerability into community leadership
innovations.problem: Many women affected by poverty, migration, gender-based violence and social exclusion remain trapped in long-term dependency, unemployment and informal survival economies. Traditional assistance models often fail to generate sustainable autonomy, leadership opportunities or long-term social integration. In vulnerable territories, especially those affected by structural inequality or humanitarian crises such as the Amizmiz earthquake area in Morocco, women face additional barriers: lack of access to employment, limited education opportunities, social isolation, economic dependency, and weak community support systems. These conditions increase the risk of chronic exclusion and intergenerational poverty.
innovations.description: Holística introduces an innovative cooperative and community-based empowerment model that transforms vulnerable women from passive beneficiaries into active leaders, workers and decision-makers. The innovation lies in: combining social inclusion with economic participation, building women-led cooperative structures, integrating psychosocial support with employability, creating collective economic opportunities, and adapting the methodology across different countries and cultural contexts. Unlike traditional assistance programmes, Holística focuses on ownership, participation and long-term resilience. Women are not only supported — they actively shape the project, participate in decision-making processes and contribute to community development. The project also creates a transnational bridge between Andalusia and Morocco, facilitating shared learning, intercultural cooperation and transferable social innovation practices. The methodology has been adapted and implemented in Andalusia (Spain) and Morocco, responding to different cultural, territorial and social realities.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: -Women in situations of extreme vulnerability increased economic autonomy. -Participants transitioned from welfare dependency to active participation in cooperative economic activities. -Strengthening of women’s leadership and decision-making capacities. -Improved employability, self-confidence and community participation. -Creation of sustainable local support networks. -Development of community resilience in vulnerable territories. -Implementation of the model in both Spain and Morocco. -Increased social inclusion and reduction of isolation among participants. -Promotion of social cohesion through community-based economic participation.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: SYNCLUSIVE
innovations.problem: Older adults, particularly women over 50, face significant barriers to employment in Bulgaria, including outdated skills, digital exclusion, low confidence, age discrimination, and limited access to quality reskilling opportunities. Labour market services often lack integrated and personalised support for this target group.
innovations.description: SYNCLUSIVE applies a Living Lab methodology that combines research, co-creation, training, psychological support, and employer engagement in one integrated ecosystem. The Sofia pilot develops personalised pathways for participants through digital and green skills courses, mentoring, peer support, and collaboration between public institutions, NGOs, businesses, and researchers.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization
innovations.evidence: Over 100 participants completed training programmes in digital, green, and personal skills; Improved employability, confidence, and digital literacy among people aged 50+; Over 15% of participants successfully transitioned into new employment opportunities; Over 85% improved their self-efficacy; Strengthened cooperation between municipalities, employers, NGOs, and researchers; Increased awareness of inclusive employment practices and lifelong learning.

innovations.name: Young People Who Do Not Give Up
innovations.problem: The Barriera di Milano and Aurora districts of Turin are multicultural urban areas characterised by high youth unemployment, school dropout rates, social exclusion, economic fragility and negative stereotypes. Many young people, especially migrants, asylum seekers and disadvantaged youth, experience limited access to cultural opportunities, social participation and positive self-representation. These neighbourhoods are often described only through narratives linked to insecurity and marginalisation, while the creative energies and positive experiences of local communities remain invisible. The project addresses: -Social exclusion and isolation among vulnerable youth; -Lack of access to cultural and digital participation; -Weak community cohesion between generations and cultures; -Negative public narratives about multicultural neighbourhoods; -Limited opportunities for youth empowerment and active citizenship.
innovations.description:
The project introduces an innovative model of community storytelling combining social innovation, digital participation and intercultural creativity. Its core innovation is the creation of a permanent Podcast Hub as an open social and multimedia laboratory where young people become storytellers, podcasters, musicians, photographers and community communicators. The initiative combines: -Participatory podcasting and digital storytelling; -Urban music and creative expression; -Peer-to-peer learning and youth-led communication; -Intercultural and intergenerational collaboration; -Community events and artistic interventions in public spaces.
Rather than treating young people as passive beneficiaries, the project positions them as active creators of social narratives and cultural change. The use of podcasts, social media storytelling, rap music and multimedia communication makes the approach highly accessible to younger generations and replicable in other urban contexts.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Expected results include: -Direct involvement of more than 300 young people; -Creation of at least 20 multimedia productions including podcasts, videos and digital stories; -More than 400 hours of educational and creative workshops; -Increased self-confidence and sense of belonging among participants; -Strengthened intercultural dialogue and social cohesion; -Improved digital, communication and teamwork skills; -Increased participation of vulnerable youth in community life; -Creation of a permanent cultural and educational Podcast Hub. The project contributes to social inclusion, active citizenship and positive territorial regeneration through culture and creativity.

innovations.name: ECSILI - Empowering Communities: A Local Action Plan for Social Inclusion and Labour Integration of Refugees
innovations.problem: Social and Labour Market inclusion of Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw and Arad, lack of integrated support system among local resources, lack of personalised counselling programmes for Ukrainian refugees. As the war in Ukraine persists, the social inclusion of Ukrainian refugees within their host communities in Europe has become an increasingly urgent issue. Despite institutional efforts, language barriers, inability to access public services and skills mismatch are the most significant causes of their inactivity and social exclusion.
innovations.description: ECSILI introduces a new model of inclusion support based on collaboration among social services, local employment services and third sector organisations. The model created new procedures, roles and responsibilities for collaboration, aiming for the creation of an integrated support system rooted in the community resources, allowing the provision of comprehensive support to Ukrainian refugees seeking stability in their new community. Additionally, the new system is rooted in individualised counselling for each Ukrainian refugee participating in the project. Through assignment of a case manager and the co-creation of an Individualised Action Plan with the refugees, each person is provided with personalised counselling and accompanied through the achievement of their inclusion goals. Finally, to strengthen the employment support dimension of the project, a Digital Skills profiling tool has been introduced for skills-career path matchmaking, allowing participants to evaluate opportunities beyond their educational qualifications. This is particularly useful for Ukrainian refugees as recognition of foreign diplomas is one of the main hurdles to finding a suitable job.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: In an effort to monitor the ongoing implementation, the project consortium has conducted interviews with local staff members and Ukrainian refugees participating in the programme. The model has been praised for having created a clear, direct line of communication and collaboration between social services and employment services, previously working in silos, as well as with third sector organisations with strong ties with the Ukrainian community. Additionally, some Ukrainian refugees interviewed praised the initiative of individualised counselling, opening new possibilities for integration and supporting them with stressful bureaucratic endeavours.

In an effort to monitor the ongoing implementation, the project consortium has conducted interviews with local staff members and Ukrainian refugees participating in the programme. The model has been praised for having created a clear, direct line of communication and collaboration between social services and employment services, previously working in silos, as well as with third sector organisations with strong ties with the Ukrainian community. innovations.name: Local Education Hubs
innovations.lead: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises
innovations.problem:
The Territorial Educational Hubs operate within a local context characterised by a high degree of fragmentation in social, educational and community services, and aim to foster collaboration that supports the educational pathway both within and outside schools.
In particular, the Educational Hubs aim to streamline public interventions in the field of youth policies, starting with those that intersect with the educational policies of the Autonomous Province of Bolzano, promoting an approach based on the creation of Educating Communities as spaces of autonomy and empowerment for the whole community, starting with the youngest members.
innovations.description: The project aims to facilitate and support public-private network relationships with a view to establishing Educational Hubs through participatory practices and tools. The approach tested combines the methodology of co-planning and co-design with collaborative tools designed to strengthen internal network relationships and ensure greater synergy even in the phases following the project itself.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises
innovations.evidence:
For the Autonomous Province of Bolzano, the Educational Hubs represent a pilot scheme that has activated local networks comprising schools and third sector organisations active in the development of youth policies, with the aim of broadening the scope of educational intervention, based on principles of continuity and shared responsibility, through the adoption of protocols and specific projects tailored to the needs emerging in each local area.
This pilot scheme has enabled the development of new methodologies (for example, regarding the presence of staff in school premises and during school hours; regarding practices for engaging with and meeting young people; regarding protocols for managing suspensions from educational activities) co-decided by the planning network through a different collaborative approach to planning.
authors: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises

innovations.name: SEA plattform for Micro Innovation
innovations.problem:
The current innovation system is fragmented and creates structural barriers for individual micro-innovators by demanding significant financial resources and established organizational capacity. This leads to several issues:
Structural Discrimination: A one-sided focus on venture capital-driven growth companies favors specific sectors (technology, life science) and groups (99% of capital goes to companies run by men).
Systemic Gaps: Support systems like science parks and incubators are mostly directed at growth companies, excluding social innovators who may belong to underrepresented groups or start businesses as a solution to exclusion.
Three-Level Challenges:
Structural: Skewed allocation of capital and lack of financial support for social innovations.
Organizational: A lack of platforms that align advice with financing.
Individual: Innovators often do not see themselves as entrepreneurs and may lack knowledge about innovation processes or lack a professional context.
innovations.description:
he project introduces a unique support structure by employing six micro-innovators (equal gender distribution) in part-time positions (25%) for 12 months. This approach provides:
Financial and Professional Prerequisities: Time and funding to complete a structured innovation process.
The SEA Innovation Process: A guided path including idea development, potential analysis, creation of sustainable business plans, and prototype testing.
Organizational Development: A specific phase for establishing organizational and financing models to ensure the innovations become viable long-term businesses or services.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The project is designed to deliver several measurable outcomes:
Tangible Innovations: The delivery of at least three prototypes (products, models, or services) addressing social needs.
Capacity Building: Six micro-innovators will have completed the full innovation process, gaining competence in business development and marketing.
Societal Impact: By preventing promising solutions from being shelved, the project increases the degree of innovation in the social sector and addresses economic inequality
