innovations.name: Leaders Gang
innovations.problem: The social problem addressed is the lack of, or barriers to, social mobility among young adults from vulnerable backgrounds. Our aim is to increase these young people’s employability and improve their transition into the labour market. Based on a study conducted for Edulog and presented in November 2021 on access to higher education and the transition to the labour market, it is possible to identify more precise data regarding the Portuguese context: First, access to higher education is not, in itself, a guarantee of equal opportunities or employability. Professor Alberto Amaral, one of Portugal’s leading experts in higher education, highlights, based on the study, that inequality in access to higher education persists in access to employment. He further emphasises that students from disadvantaged backgrounds “face a higher risk of unemployment”. Second, transversal skills are less developed in more disadvantaged contexts and play a significant role in young people’s employability. The study discusses the correlation between vulnerable socio-economic backgrounds and lower development of transversal skills, with a negative impact on the employability of recent graduates. Third, support networks and role models are important for young people’s employability and career development. In the academic debate on the leadership potential of young adults, several points help to contextualise this social problem. The first is that young people from disadvantaged backgrounds are less likely to take on leadership positions, as they also have less access to resources that enable professional development (Komives & Dugan, 2014). It would be highly desirable to see leaders from disadvantaged backgrounds in prominent positions, as this helps to show young people from vulnerable contexts that such roles are within their reach. This applies not only to leadership, but to any highly sought-after profession in our society. The second point relates to the importance of developing young people’s confidence and decision-making capacity (Kress, 2006). Confidence and the ability to make decisions are essential for navigating a labour market that is changing at an increasingly rapid pace and that, since 2008, has already experienced a third major economic shock (the financial crisis, the pandemic, and the war in Ukraine combined with strong inflationary pressure, including rising interest rates). This group is largely neglected or off the radar. From the very first contact, we identified a feeling of complete surprise; they did not expect to be recognised. During the first face-to-face training session, participants asked why the focus was on overcoming adversity rather than on achieving the highest grades. We explained that high-achieving students are already identified and have greater access to scholarships and support programmes. In 2023, we contacted more than 125 young people aged 20 to 21, and the response was consistent: they were astonished. On the employer side, more than twenty companies were contacted, and all highlighted the importance of this programme for the country and for their recruitment needs.
innovations.description: Leaders Gang provides an innovative, evidence-based solution that combines data-driven identification, real-world skills development, and peer-led impact to overcome barriers to social mobility. Its first innovation lies in how beneficiaries are identified. In partnership with public education authorities, the programme uses objective education data to identify young adults who demonstrated exceptional academic progress during secondary education despite socio-economic disadvantage. This approach moves beyond traditional merit-based or deficit-based selection models, ensuring fairness, precision, and transparency. The second innovation lies in the methodology. Instead of relying solely on classroom-based training, participants develop employability and leadership skills by facilitating workshops for younger students. This learning-by-teaching model positions beneficiaries as active contributors rather than passive recipients, strengthening autonomy, confidence and responsibility while generating immediate social value. The programme integrates structured mentoring, individual tutoring and reflective practice, ensuring that skills development is intentional, supported and measurable. Participants receive continuous feedback and are encouraged to adapt their learning paths, reinforcing ownership and self-determination. A third innovation is the strong multiplier effect embedded in the design. Each participant supports multiple secondary school students, often in their former schools, becoming realistic and relatable role models. This reinforces social cohesion, strengthens local trust and helps reduce territorial inequalities. Finally, Leaders Gang stands out for its rigorous approach to impact measurement. The programme has undergone external evaluation, including a randomised control trial, establishing a causal link between participation and improvements in key 21st-century skills. sections.question: Problem
sections.answer: The social problem addressed is the lack of, or barriers to, social mobility among young adults from vulnerable backgrounds. Our aim is to increase these young people’s employability and improve their transition into the labour market. Based on a study conducted for Edulog and presented in November 2021 on access to higher education and the transition to the labour market, it is possible to identify more precise data regarding the Portuguese context: First, access to higher education is not, in itself, a guarantee of equal opportunities or employability. Professor Alberto Amaral, one of Portugal’s leading experts in higher education, highlights, based on the study, that inequality in access to higher education persists in access to employment. He further emphasises that students from disadvantaged backgrounds “face a higher risk of unemployment”. Second, transversal skills are less developed in more disadvantaged contexts and play a significant role in young people’s employability. The study discusses the correlation between vulnerable socio-economic backgrounds and lower development of transversal skills, with a negative impact on the employability of recent graduates. Third, support networks and role models are important for young people’s employability and career development. In the academic debate on the leadership potential of young adults, several points help to contextualise this social problem. The first is that young people from disadvantaged backgrounds are less likely to take on leadership positions, as they also have less access to resources that enable professional development (Komives & Dugan, 2014). It would be highly desirable to see leaders from disadvantaged backgrounds in prominent positions, as this helps to show young people from vulnerable contexts that such roles are within their reach. This applies not only to leadership, but to any highly sought-after profession in our society. The second point relates to the importance of developing young people’s confidence and decision-making capacity (Kress, 2006). Confidence and the ability to make decisions are essential for navigating a labour market that is changing at an increasingly rapid pace and that, since 2008, has already experienced a third major economic shock (the financial crisis, the pandemic, and the war in Ukraine combined with strong inflationary pressure, including rising interest rates). This group is largely neglected or off the radar. From the very first contact, we identified a feeling of complete surprise; they did not expect to be recognised. During the first face-to-face training session, participants asked why the focus was on overcoming adversity rather than on achieving the highest grades. We explained that high-achieving students are already identified and have greater access to scholarships and support programmes. In 2023, we contacted more than 125 young people aged 20 to 21, and the response was consistent: they were astonished. On the employer side, more than twenty companies were contacted, and all highlighted the importance of this programme for the country and for their recruitment needs.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer: Leaders Gang provides an innovative, evidence-based solution that combines data-driven identification, real-world skills development, and peer-led impact to overcome barriers to social mobility. Its first innovation lies in how beneficiaries are identified. In partnership with public education authorities, the programme uses objective education data to identify young adults who demonstrated exceptional academic progress during secondary education despite socio-economic disadvantage. This approach moves beyond traditional merit-based or deficit-based selection models, ensuring fairness, precision, and transparency. The second innovation lies in the methodology. Instead of relying solely on classroom-based training, participants develop employability and leadership skills by facilitating workshops for younger students. This learning-by-teaching model positions beneficiaries as active contributors rather than passive recipients, strengthening autonomy, confidence and responsibility while generating immediate social value. The programme integrates structured mentoring, individual tutoring and reflective practice, ensuring that skills development is intentional, supported and measurable. Participants receive continuous feedback and are encouraged to adapt their learning paths, reinforcing ownership and self-determination. A third innovation is the strong multiplier effect embedded in the design. Each participant supports multiple secondary school students, often in their former schools, becoming realistic and relatable role models. This reinforces social cohesion, strengthens local trust and helps reduce territorial inequalities. Finally, Leaders Gang stands out for its rigorous approach to impact measurement. The programme has undergone external evaluation, including a randomised control trial, establishing a causal link between participation and improvements in key 21st-century skills. Ongoing assessment uses validated tools to measure a broad set of cognitive, social and emotional competencies. Together, these elements form a scalable and replicable model that connects education, employment and social cohesion through collaboration between public institutions, civil society, companies and young people.

innovations.name: U-PLAYS - Ukrainian Participation in Language, Athletics, and Youth Support
innovations.problem: U-PLAYS addresses the social exclusion of Ukrainian youth displaced by the war, who face barriers to integration due to limited language skills, reduced employability, and restricted access to inclusive community activities.
innovations.description:
U-PLAYS introduces an integrated, user-centered model that combines sport, language learning, and employment training into a single, coordinated pathway for youth integration. By delivering activities simultaneously across countries and actively involving participants in co-design, it ensures relevance, motivation, and measurable impact.
This initiative is born from a successful implementation of the project in the local context in Latvia and will now see its first scalability to a European context.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence: Key activities include (in each country respectively) 50 sports sessions to improve fitness and teamwork, 50 German, Latvian and Slovakian language classes to boost language proficiency, and 50 employment workshops to equip participants with job readiness skills. Implemented by professional trainers and language instructors, the project activities will be held conducted simultaneously in Austria, Latvia and Slovakia. Expected outcomes include improved physical fitness, better language skills, and increased employment prospects for participants. U-PLAYS adopts a user-centered approach, involving participants in planning and execution to meet their needs. The project aims for sustainable impact, creating a scalable model transferable to other EU contexts.

innovations.name: Harnessing the power of physical activity to sustainably recover from depression
innovations.problem:
It is estimated that 1 in 5 people in France will experience mental health issues at some point in their lives.
12.5% of French people aged 18-85 faced depression each year in 2021, a steep increase from 2017 figures (+3.7 pt). Depression disproportionately affects the most vulnerable members of society, namely women (15.6%), young adults (20.8%), unemployed individuals (22%) and people in precarious economic situations (18.8%). It not only reflects but also exacerbates pre-existing social disparities. (Source : Baromètre santé France 2021)
Beyond its emotional and psychological toll, depression significantly impacts daily functioning, overall well-being, and physical health. It often coexists with or worsens other chronic conditions such as cardiovascular diseases and diabetes, and is frequently linked to social isolation and sedentary lifestyles. People living with depression tend to get trapped in a vicious cycle by adopting unhealthy habits (poor diet, lack of exercise, alcohol and/or substance addiction, etc.) which in turn worsen further the depressive symptoms.
Today, mental health related costs are the leading source of expenditure for the French health insurance system (€23 billion in direct costs annually), and the leading cause of long-term sick leave.
Our project aligns with national priorities, as mental health has been named the “Grande Cause nationale” (National Cause) for 2025/26 in France, underlining the urgent need for innovative, preventive, and community-based responses to the country’s growing mental health crisis.
innovations.description:
Je Bouge Pour Mon Moral (JBPMM) offers an innovative and complementary response to traditional mental health care by combining adapted physical activity with peer-to-peer social support. Free and accessible to all, the programme helps break social isolation and empowers participants to take an active role in their recovery.
The programme is delivered in cohorts of 10 to 12 participants, fostering group dynamics, mutual support and lasting social bonds. From enrolment, each participant benefits from individualised support, provided by a participant coordinator and a qualified Adapted Physical Activity trainer (APA), including an initial assessment to identify motivations, barriers and specific needs.
The core of the programme consists of 12 weeks of supervised physical activity, focused on Nordic walking—an accessible, nature-based activity with proven benefits for depression. Support is progressive: two supervised sessions per week for six weeks, followed by one supervised session and one autonomous group session during the remaining six weeks, complemented by collective workshops to build a personalised physical activity continuation plan.
Beyond the initial programme, JBPMM provides 12 months of post-programme support to ensure long-term impact. Participants join a local alumni community that encourages ongoing practice and social connection. Monthly group walks are organised by the APA trainer, and participants are signposted towards local sports clubs and associations to embed their practice within the local ecosystem.
JBPMM addresses an unmet need in mental health care. While sports clubs, coaches and Sport-Health centres contribute to health promotion, what they offer often fails to meet the specific needs of people experiencing persistent mental health challenges. Many are undiagnosed or socially isolated, lack motivation and self-confidence, and require structured, evidence-based programmes proven to reduce depressive symptoms.
JBPMM’s innovation lies in:
- identifying and engaging underserved individuals, notably through social media outreach;
- delivering a programme grounded in scientific recommendations for depression treatment;
- adopting a holistic approach that addresses physical, emotional and social dimensions of recovery.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
This project aims to create sustainable and measurable improvements in mental health and overall well-being among adults living with depression and related conditions. It is designed to achieve the following tangible outcomes. In 2025, we measured the following impact:
- 50% reduction in depressive symptoms, as measured by scientific tools (PHQ-9, QIDS, BDI II), with sustained benefits 3 months post-program
- 17% increase in self-esteem, as participants experience personal achievements relying on their own resources (rather than medication), as measured with the Rosenberg self-esteem scale
Enhanced social inclusion, through group sessions that foster connection and a sense of belonging Improved physical health through the resumption of regular physical activity, leading to reduced symptoms of chronic conditions often associated with sedentary lifestyles.
Previous iterations of the program have already shown strong results in terms of improved mental well-being, increased self-esteem, and regular engagement in physical activity among participants - even 6 months after completion of the program.
In the Grand Est region, the programme expanded from 1 to 10 cities between 2022 and 2026. Building on this momentum, JBPMM is now initiating its scale-up in three new regions in France: Hauts-de-France, Nouvelle- Aquitaine and Occitanie. The overarching objective is to reach national coverage by 2030, by launching the JBPMM program in two more regions each year until then.

innovations.name: Performing Arts Festival - "Connectivity Technique"
innovations.problem: The numbers of young people who are NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) is rising. Many of these suffer from mental health problems such as lack of confidence, low self-esteem, poor communication skills and a lack of creativity. The challenge is to transform these young people  from "idle resources" to creative professionals through involvement in the different performing arts sectors managed by Dynamic Lab: Artistic and Performance Sector: NEETs can be included in professional training courses to become performers or choreographers, learning innovative contemporary and aerial dance techniques. Dynamic Lab has solid experience in turning passion into a career, thanks to international scholarships and collaborations Management and Production Sector: Under the guidance of experts in Executive Events Management: Young people can acquire skills in Euro-planning, Marketing and event management. This sector offers NEETs practical training on how to manage the financial feasibility and logistics of a festival. Communication and Digital Sector: Thanks to Dynamic Lab's experience in Web Marketing and the creation of digital content, young people can be employed as Content Creators or Social Media Managers for sustainable tourism and the arts, enhancing their natural digital predisposition. The added value of Dynamic Lab lies in the ability to offer NEETs not just a "school", but a "Creative Space"
innovations.description:
At the Largo San Francesco 8/a location, the model has been expanded by integrating the "Creative & Cultural HUB". Here innovation has translated into the coordination of the board of the Culture Council (2021), transforming the residence into a strategic consultancy body for local cultural policies. At the headquarters in Via Principe Amedeo 106-110, the festival has adapted its offer by focusing on the production and organization of Theater and Dance courses specific to the province. Here the "Connectivity Technique" is actively applied, creating a center of attraction for emerging artists from the south-east of Bari. The adaptation of the model allowed Dynamic Lab to become the only winner of the Cross Border Open Innovation in the Performing Arts sector for the reference area.
Connectivity Technique: The use of a proprietary methodology based on improvisation and sensory perception to create a fluid fusion between contemporary dance, hip hop and aerial dance. Integrated Multidisciplinary Hub: The transformation of physical space into a permanent laboratory that integrates artistic production, professional training and strategic consultancy for the creative industries. Digital & Green Transition: The adoption of protocols for the "zero waste" management of events and the use of digital technologies for audience development and territorial marketing.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: Employability of NEETs: Transformation of inactive young people into qualified professionals in the fields of arts management, and in the production of dance and theater festivals for social inclusion. innovations.name: Mobile Centres delivering integrated support in rural and underserved areas
innovations.problem:
Ukrainian refugees living in rural and underserved areas face compounded barriers to integration due to the absence or limited availability of essential services. Unlike urban settings, these areas often lack regular access to language courses, employment guidance, psychosocial support, childcare options, and community based integration activities. Geographic isolation, limited public transport, and fragmented local infrastructures further restrict participation in available support mechanisms.
Evidence from the project’s Needs Assessment indicates that refugees residing outside urban centres are significantly less likely to engage in learning or employment related activities, despite clear motivation to do so. The lack of nearby services increases social isolation, delays labour market integration, and exacerbates psycho emotional strain, particularly among women, caregivers, older persons, and individuals with reduced mobility. Fixed service provision models alone are insufficient to ensure equitable access across diverse territorial contexts.
innovations.description:
The Mobile Centres introduce a flexible, outreach based service delivery model designed to bring integrated support directly to rural and underserved areas where services are limited or unavailable. Rather than requiring refugees to travel long distances to access assistance, the Mobile Centres adapt the integrated hub model to local contexts by delivering services within accessible community spaces.
Mobile Centres operate through temporary setups in locations such as community halls, schools, municipal buildings, libraries, and other locally available venues. Trained facilitators and practitioners provide coordinated activities including language learning sessions, employment related guidance, psychosocial support, and community engagement initiatives. The services are delivered in a structured yet adaptable format, allowing responsiveness to local needs while maintaining consistent quality standards.
The innovation lies in combining mobility with integration. Mobile Centres are not isolated outreach actions but function as part of a coordinated ecosystem aligned with a clear Theory of Change and a structured Pilot Roll Out Plan. This ensures continuity between mobile and fixed services, effective referral pathways, and ongoing learning and adaptation.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
For beneficiaries, the Mobile Centres significantly reduce geographical and logistical barriers to participation. Refugees gain access to learning and support opportunities close to where they live, lowering travel costs and time constraints while increasing sustained engagement. This contributes to improved language acquisition, greater confidence in navigating local systems, and enhanced psychosocial wellbeing.
For local communities, the Mobile Centres strengthen outreach capacity and foster inclusive local responses. By collaborating with municipalities, civil society organisations, and community actors, the model improves coordination, visibility, and trust in integration initiatives, even in areas with limited infrastructure.
At system level, the Mobile Centres demonstrate how flexible delivery mechanisms can complement fixed service provision. The approach provides a practical solution for regions where establishing permanent hubs is not feasible, while remaining aligned with broader integration strategies and policy objectives.

innovations.name: eDU Hubs and Mobile Centres, an integrated community based model for the long term integration of Ukrainian refugees
innovations.problem:
The eDU Hubs and Mobile Centres project addresses the structural gap between emergency humanitarian assistance and sustainable, long term integration of Ukrainian refugees within European host societies. While immediate responses have ensured safety and access to basic services, many refugees continue to face persistent barriers to social, economic, and psychosocial inclusion.
Evidence gathered through a cross country Needs Assessment conducted in Germany, Romania, and Slovakia shows that language barriers significantly limit access to employment, education, and public services. Despite high levels of educational attainment, many refugees experience unemployment or underemployment due to non recognition of qualifications, lack of local experience, and limited access to tailored employment pathways. In parallel, prolonged displacement has generated psycho emotional strain, while access to psychological support remains fragmented and poorly understood.
Service provision is often sector based and geographically uneven, particularly disadvantaging refugees living in rural or semi rural areas. Uncertainty regarding future legal status and settlement prospects further reinforces the need for coherent, long term integration pathways. The absence of holistic, coordinated, and locally anchored models represents a critical barrier to durable inclusion.
innovations.description:
The eDU Hubs and Mobile Centres model introduces an integrated, community based approach to refugee integration that combines fixed hubs with mobile service delivery. The innovation lies in the coordination of multiple support dimensions into a single, accessible ecosystem rather than in the creation of isolated services.
Fixed eDU Hubs serve as trusted entry points within local communities, while Mobile Centres extend outreach to underserved and rural areas. Through this dual structure, the model ensures continuity of support regardless of geographical context. Services include language learning, employment guidance, psychosocial support, childcare facilitation, and community engagement, designed to function as interdependent components rather than standalone interventions.
The model is grounded in a Theory of Change that links identified needs to expected outcomes at individual, community, and system level. It was refined through a participatory process involving refugees, practitioners, and cross sector stakeholders. Collaborative innovation labs and stakeholder mapping exercises further strengthened local ownership and alignment with existing ecosystems.
A Pilot Roll Out Plan guides the phased implementation of the model, allowing for testing, adaptation, and learning in real life contexts. Continuous monitoring and feedback loops are embedded to ensure responsiveness to contextual differences across countries and communities.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
At beneficiary level, the model improves access to coordinated integration pathways, reducing fragmentation and lowering barriers to participation. Refugees benefit from personalised support that strengthens employability, social participation, and psychosocial wellbeing.
At community level, the project enhances cooperation between civil society organisations, public authorities, employers, and educational actors. This contributes to improved service coordination, increased intercultural interaction, and stronger social cohesion.
At system level, the project generates transferable knowledge on integrated integration models. The Needs Assessment findings, refined intervention logic, and pilot learning support evidence based planning and inform policy relevant discussions.
The project engages approximately 6,000 Ukrainian refugees and host community members, with at least 1,500 individuals expected to experience substantive improvements in their social, economic, or psychosocial situation. Additional benefits include strengthened professional capacity among practitioners and wide indirect reach through communication and dissemination activities.

innovations.name: Crowdbuilding
innovations.problem:
The Netherlands is in a housing crisis. Housing construction needs to be radically transformed: more sustainable, more social, and more affordable. Collective self-build offers people the opportunity to create their own living environment together with others, with more say in the design, construction, and ultimate use. There are also advantages for municipalities, as it means greater support, participation, social innovation, and social cohesion. Building and living together creates resilient residential communities that contribute to the local community by caring for each other and their surroundings. What if 10% of the homes that need to be built, could be realized this way?
To get started, a potential builder needs connections. This allows them to learn, find the right professionals, and connect with others so they can launch initiatives together with other co-builders.  Municipalities also face challenges. How do you, as a municipality, inform your residents and ensure that initiatives meet the right requirements? How do you allocate plots and manage projects efficiently?
innovations.description:
For residents , CrowdBuilding is the ideal starting point for building and living together. At Crowdbuilding.com, everyone dreaming of shared housing can find information and inspiration, start or join a group, connect with each other, register for plots, and much more. Together, we are building a fair and sustainable housing system where collective self-build is a viable option.
Construction groups, housing cooperatives, and self-builders are essential for good professional support. That's why CrowdBuilding is building a national network of partners who can offer quality, experience, and reliability. With a network of dedicated process facilitators, creative architects, smart consultants, and expert contractors , we can tackle the housing crisis in the Netherlands in an innovative and high-quality way.
As an expert in collective housing, CrowdBuilding is also the ideal partner for municipalities in facilitating collective self-build. With relevant knowledge and a unique platform, CrowdBuilding helps municipalities support residents in every phase of their housing dream, from orientation to realization. CrowdBuilding is here to help municipalities facilitate collective self-build as part of their housing policy. Through a customized municipal page on the platform, we facilitate the entire process in a clear and concise manner, from inventorying and registering interested groups to selecting and allocating plots.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
In the last two years multiple housing projects have been built, others are still in the proces of planning or building; projects vary from eco-villages, tiny houses and redesigning old officebuildings into compact cityhouses for the elderly or the young.
Already two provinces and three municipalities are working as partners and the movement is rapidly expanding.
Eighty partners (procesmanagers, acrhitects, builders) take part in the expert network.
The online platform offers education through e-learnings, events and storytelling, tools (step-by-step planning) and matchmaking where residents can find an existing cooperation, start a cooperation and find available plots for self-building.

innovations.name: Volunteers Everywhere
innovations.problem: Many refugees from Ukraine face social isolation, language and cultural barriers, and lack access to community-based support. At the same time, volunteer engagement is fragmented and lacks common standards, tools, and coordination.
innovations.description:
VolEVer uses a mobile app and shared standards to organise volunteer–refugee matching in a clear and safe way, making it easier to expand the model to new places without losing quality.
The project builds on OPU’s previous digital volunteer registry (idobrovolnik.cz), but has been significantly adapted to introduce a mobile app, unified training, and cross-border coordination.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Key results include a mobile app that safely matches volunteers with refugees, a shared methodology and training package, and improved coordination across countries. Benefits include more accessible support for refugees, better-prepared volunteers, higher programme quality, and easier scaling of community-based activities.

innovations.name: SkillsPath - SKILLs and Innovation for Youth Employment PATHways
innovations.lead: International Rescue Committee IRC Deutschland gGmbH
innovations.problem:
Europe’s work landscape is rapidly changing due to digitalisation, decarbonisation, demographic shifts, and migration. innovations.name: Women and Community Resilience through Inclusive Skills Development
innovations.problem: Vulnerable women, displaced families and marginalised communities face long-term unemployment, social exclusion, limited access to training, and psychosocial stress. Traditional services often fail to reach them due to language barriers, low digital literacy, stigma and lack of community-based delivery models.
innovations.description:
The project introduces a community-embedded, low-threshold training model that integrates employability skills, life skills and psychosocial support. It uses peer learning, volunteer professionals, culturally adapted content and safe community spaces to remove access barriers and create sustainable social inclusion pathways.
The innovation has been adapted and implemented in different local contexts, including community-based initiatives in the Netherlands and preparatory implementation in Middle Eastern contexts addressing displacement-affected communities. While maintaining the core model of inclusive, low-threshold skills development combined with psychosocial and social inclusion support, the project has been locally adapted to respond to language, cultural and socio-economic needs of each target group. Adaptations include culturally tailored training content, flexible delivery formats for low digital literacy communities, and integration with local volunteer networks and social service providers. This demonstrates the model’s strong transferability and potential for further replication and scaling across Europe and neighbouring regions.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Over the past period, our volunteers have already provided hairdressing training to around 30 women through informal community sessions. These activities focused not only on practical hairdressing skills, but also on confidence, social connection and feeling more at home in Dutch society.
In addition, Stichting DOING organised several integration and employability workshops under the initiative “Bridging Cultures Together: A Collaborative Integration Project”, in cooperation with Maat for Peace, Development and Human Rights. Through these workshops we supported refugees with understanding Dutch society and work culture, developing employability skills, overcoming common barriers, and strengthening intercultural understanding with local community members.
Based on this existing grassroots experience, we are now professionalising and scaling this model into the structured POWERWOMEN Eindhoven programme, with certified hairdressing training, internships and direct pathways to work and self-employment.
tags: Equal access to education and training

innovations.name: The Room for Mental Power
innovations.problem: Young adults in the Netherlands face growing mental health challenges, with around one in three experiencing psychological problems, while existing support is often fragmented, difficult to access and poorly aligned with their daily lives. Help frequently arrives late, focuses mainly on symptoms rather than underlying causes and is limited by rigid rules, siloed funding and lack of regional coordination. Many promising local initiatives struggle to scale or sustain their work because they run up against institutional barriers and short-term project financing. As a result, young adults aged 16–35 risk not receiving timely, appropriate and affordable support to stay mentally healthy, recover and participate fully in society.
innovations.description: Ruimte voor Geestkracht is a long-term national programme of FNO that works for ten years with young adults, regional networks and national stakeholders to create a society in which young adults have space to be and remain mentally healthy. The programme combines regional collaboration in five areas with strong youth participation, ensuring that young adults do not just give feedback but actively co-decide on priorities and solutions. Through Team Geestkracht, a dedicated youth panel, young adults advise, set agendas and support regions in organising meaningful youth involvement. Ruimte voor Geestkracht focuses on reshaping rules, systems and financial flows, looking beyond healthcare alone to address root causes of mental health problems and build sustainable, integrated support structures.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Ruimte voor Geestkracht strengthens regional networks that work on mental health in ways that genuinely fit young people’s lives, improving the quality, accessibility and affordability of support for those who need it. Young adults become co-owners of the programme, ensuring that their perspectives shape decisions, interventions and long-term system change rather than being treated as an afterthought. Valuable local initiatives gain support to overcome barriers such as fragmented rules or insecure funding, increasing their capacity to continue and grow. By targeting underlying causes and focusing on durable collaboration, the programme contributes to more resilient young adults and a more coherent mental health ecosystem.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Prins Heerlijk
innovations.problem: Prins Heerlijk responds to the limited labour market perspectives of young people with serious learning difficulties or a disability, who often leave school without a qualification and struggle to find and keep meaningful work. Many of them experience low self-confidence, social isolation and a lack of opportunities to develop practical skills in real work environments. At the same time, employers in horeca, retail and care face shortages of motivated, well-prepared staff, while social support systems are not always equipped to provide integrated learning, work and living trajectories. This situation risks long-term dependence on benefits and reduced participation in society for these young people.
innovations.description: Prins Heerlijk is a social enterprise that combines education, work-based learning and tailored support in its own training companies in hospitality and retail, complemented by placements with partner employers in care and service sectors. Young people aged roughly 16–27 learn a profession while working in real restaurants, shops and service locations, supported by professional coaches who focus on development, autonomy, responsibility and wellbeing at the individual’s own pace. In cooperation with VET providers such as De Rooi Pannen and ROC Tilburg, participants can obtain an MBO diploma, increasing their chances of sustainable employment. For those who need more intensive support, Prins Heerlijk offers additional guidance and the option of assisted living in its own housing facilities, ensuring an integrated trajectory from learning to living and working.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Prins Heerlijk enables young people with learning difficulties or a disability to grow into confident service staff in hospitality, retail and care, often obtaining recognised qualifications and securing lasting jobs. Participants report increased self-esteem, independence and pride in their work, while families and professionals observe greater social participation and stability. Employers gain motivated, well-prepared employees and benefit from ongoing collaboration with a specialised partner that understands both educational and workplace requirements. The organisation has received several awards for its socially responsible entrepreneurship and innovative education-in-enterprise model, underlining the broader societal added value of this approach.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Herenboeren
innovations.problem: In many Dutch regions, citizens feel disconnected from how their food is produced and how nearby land is managed. Industrial food chains often prioritise efficiency over soil health, animal welfare and biodiversity, while leaving consumers with little influence over production choices. Households seeking seasonal, local food with a smaller ecological footprint frequently lack accessible, affordable options. At the same time, there are few inclusive community spaces where residents can learn about sustainable agriculture, meet farmers and involve children in nature-based activities. Farmers themselves face pressure to remain economically viable while transitioning to more sustainable practices. These challenges point to the need for collaborative models that share risks, responsibilities and benefits between citizens and farmers, and that restore a direct relationship with the land.
innovations.description: Herenboeren introduces a cooperative, citizen-owned farm model in which around 250 households jointly establish and govern their own “Herenboerderij”. Each household makes a one-off investment of approximately €2,000–€2,500 and pays a monthly fee of about €45–€80 per person, depending on location and meat consumption. In return, members receive a weekly share of seasonal vegetables, fruit, eggs and, for those who wish, occasional meat from their own farm. Professional farmers are employed as agrarian managers with a stable income, ensuring high-quality, nature-driven production. Members can voluntarily help on the land or join working groups, strengthening skills and shared ownership. This model reconnects people with food production while creating a transparent, fair and resilient local food system.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: There are already 23 operational Herenboerderijen across the Netherlands, with dozens more in development and more than 9,000 citizens involved as cooperative members. Participating households regain control over their food supply and enjoy fresh, seasonal produce grown on land close to home. Nature-driven farming practices improve soil health, support biodiversity and ensure better living conditions for animals, contributing to a more future-proof food system. The farms function as lively community hubs, hosting open days, guided tours and activities for children such as treasure hunts, creative workshops and cooking with young chefs. Social events, including picnics and thematic workshops, encourage interaction between members and farmers, fostering stronger community ties and a shared sense of responsibility for the local environment.
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

Each household makes a one-off investment of approximately €2,000–€2,500 and pays a monthly fee of about €45–€80 per person, depending on location and meat consumption. In return, members receive a weekly share of seasonal vegetables, fruit, eggs and, for those who wish, occasional meat from their own farm. Professional farmers are employed as agrarian managers with a stable income, ensuring high-quality, nature-driven production. Members can voluntarily help on the land or join working groups, strengthening skills and shared ownership. This model reconnects people with food production while creating a transparent, fair and resilient local food system.
There are already 23 operational Herenboerderijen across the Netherlands, with dozens more in development and more than 9,000 citizens involved as cooperative members. Participating households regain control over their food supply and enjoy fresh, seasonal produce grown on land close to home. Nature-driven farming practices improve soil health, support biodiversity and ensure better living conditions for animals, contributing to a more future-proof food system. The farms function as lively community hubs, hosting open days, guided tours and activities for children such as treasure hunts, creative workshops and cooking with young chefs. Social events, including picnics and thematic workshops, encourage interaction between members and farmers, fostering stronger community ties and a shared sense of responsibility for the local environment.

innovations.name: Stadskamer Achterhoek
innovations.problem: Many people in the Achterhoek experience “colour loss” in their lives after disruptive events such as mental health challenges, social isolation, or other life crises. Traditional care systems often focus on diagnoses and protocols rather than on people’s own pace, strengths, and recovery journeys, which can make support feel conditional and distant. Long waiting lists in mental health care further delay access to meaningful activities and peer connection, deepening loneliness and passivity. There is a clear need for accessible, non-stigmatising environments where people of all ages can participate, recover socially, and regain a sense of belonging without having to fit rigid care-system prerequisites.
innovations.description: Stadskamer creates welcoming, recovery-oriented spaces across thirteen lively support points in the Achterhoek where everyone is invited to “just be”, participate, and work on personal recovery. The organisation uses the “Route van de Vraag” to start from each participant’s own question, wishes, and rhythm, instead of predefined trajectories. A broad “waaier van mogelijkheden” of activities—developed directly from participants’ needs—offers accessible recovery pathways that quickly connect people to suitable programmes. People can join as participants, volunteers, team members, local entrepreneurs, or care initiatives, making Stadskamer both a community hub and a driver of more human-centred care.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Stadskamer has grown into thirteen vibrant local hubs where young and old can participate, feel welcome, and work on recovery in their own way. This low-threshold offer enables people to quickly access meaningful activities and peer support, contributing to shorter mental health care waiting times. Participants regain confidence, structure, and social connections, which brings “more colour” back into their lives. At the same time, the initiative mobilises volunteers, professionals, and local partners around positive health, shared recovery, and social inclusion, strengthening the wider community fabric.

innovations.name: Sociëteit Tof
innovations.problem: Seniors with prior high socio-economic status, broad education, or cultural interests often experience memory issues or isolation, feeling out of place in standard day care settings. These individuals, living independently, require active daily structure to maintain skills, prevent decline, and relieve family caregivers, yet conventional programs fail to match their backgrounds, leading to disengagement and lost societal contributions. This gap distances them from meaningful participation, exacerbating vulnerability in later life.
innovations.description: Sociëteit Tof, hosted by Proteion in Roermond's Retroscoop, provides specialized day activities from Monday to Friday for self-reliant seniors with distinguished backgrounds. Tailored to education, career history, and interests, offerings include discussions, (art) painting, reading, classical music, chess, lectures, museum visits, and library trips, led by facilitators ensuring inclusive dialogue. A shared warm lunch enhances community, offering an upscale alternative to regular day care while supporting skill preservation.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Participants feel valued and heard, engaging in stimulating conversations that boost confidence and role fulfillment. Families gain respite as seniors maintain autonomy through culturally resonant activities that sustain cognitive and social skills. The model promotes well-being for educated elderly, fostering connections and purpose without stigmatizing care environments.

innovations.name: Dynamisch Op Weg
innovations.problem: Many people in the Netherlands face significant barriers to entering or returning to the labour market, including limited work experience, uncertainty about their abilities, and a lack of supportive, low-threshold opportunities to start. Standard recruitment and employment pathways often demand immediate productivity and full clarity about job fit, which can deter those who are unsure, anxious, or have been out of work for longer periods. As a result, people who could thrive with the right guidance and gradual onboarding remain side-lined, missing chances to develop skills, confidence, and sustainable work perspectives.
innovations.description: Dynamisch op Weg tackles these barriers by offering a highly accessible entry route into work, where people can quickly sign up and even test a working day before committing. This trial option lowers psychological and practical thresholds, allowing candidates to explore whether the work suits their interests, capacities, and personal situation. The organisation positions itself as a supportive team environment, signalling that newcomers “fit perfectly” and will not be left alone in figuring things out. This client-friendly, stepwise approach makes work-based learning and reintegration more attractive and realistic for those who need security and experimentation before taking the next step.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence:
By enabling people to try out a working day, Dynamisch op Weg helps participants make informed choices about their future job, reducing mismatches and early drop-out. Candidates gain a concrete, experience-based understanding of tasks, team culture, and expectations, which builds confidence and motivation. The organisation simultaneously identifies who is likely to succeed with further support, increasing the effectiveness of its onboarding and guidance. This mutual clarity benefits both participants and the employer, fostering more sustainable placements and better prospects for continued participation in the labour market.
The biggest gain is for the well-being of the young people themselves, the social benefits of the project seem to be great. The Work and Health research group of HAN University of Applied Sciences (HAN) has started an impact calculation.
70% of participants found a job after completing the program.
20% continue to a BBL training program at InfraVak.
90% of the participants come to work on a trial basis for a week.

innovations.name: Campus Woudhuis
innovations.problem: Many people who receive care or guidance from institutions struggle to find or keep regular paid work, despite having talents and motivation to contribute. They are often seen primarily as “clients” instead of colleagues, which limits their opportunities for development, autonomy, and participation in society. At the same time, employers experience a gap between their ambition for social responsibility and concrete ways to involve people with support needs in their teams. This leads to underused labour potential, persistent exclusion from the labour market, and a missed opportunity to build more diverse, socially cohesive workplaces in and around Apeldoorn.
innovations.description: Campus Woudhuis operates as a green work–learn company and living lab for inclusive entrepreneurship on the Woudhuis estate near Apeldoorn. The campus offers practical work in nature management, hospitality, activities on the estate, and projects with nearby employers (“common grounds”), combined with coaching and learning trajectories. People who find it difficult to access regular work are hired through open hiring: everyone who can and wants to contribute is welcome, without heavy selection procedures or stigmatising labels. Partners IVN, Natuurmonumenten, ’s Heeren Loo and De Onderwijsspecialisten jointly run the cooperative estate and knowledge centre, connecting care, education, nature organisations and employers around one inclusive workplace.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: On Campus Woudhuis, around 35 people with very diverse backgrounds work together on meaningful tasks, ranging from nature management and hospitality to research and learning projects. Participants “bloom” by doing what they enjoy, discovering talents, gaining work experience, and increasingly co-deciding on the future of the campus. The environment deliberately avoids the word “client”, which strengthens equality, pride, and ownership among workers. Employers on and around the estate benefit from motivated staff, higher job satisfaction in teams, and a more diverse workforce that reduces the need for traditional day-care arrangements. Through its knowledge platform with partners such as Movisie, universities of applied sciences and WUR, the campus also generates insights for broader practice and policy on inclusive work.

innovations.name: Buurtbaan
innovations.problem: In Amsterdam's diverse neighborhoods like West and Zuidoost, sleutelpersonen—local key figures with deep community ties—lack formal recognition and paid opportunities despite their vital role in fostering connections and inspiration. These individuals, often distant from the labor market due to limited formal qualifications, face barriers to sustainable employment, hindering neighborhood resilience and bottom-up development. Traditional structures overlook their experiential knowledge, resulting in fragmented community building and missed chances for in-streaming talent into professional roles.
innovations.description: Buurtbaan transforms voluntary sleutelpersonen into paid community builders through a 2-year program of 25 jobs, providing coaching, training, and recognition aligned with municipal regulations since 2021. Launched in Amsterdam West in 2017, it emphasizes neighborhood strengthening from within—reaching and inspiring residents without relegating participants to assistant tasks. Flexible models like subsidies atop benefits, ZZP entrepreneurship, or full buurtwerker roles empower participants to lead with their strengths, fostering peer-to-peer training and ambassadorship for scalability.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence: Participants gain profound recognition, perspective, and career advancement, with many aspiring to become ambassadors and trainers for future buurtbaners. Neighborhoods benefit from sustainable "layer-upon-layer" strengthening, enhancing connections between residents and organizations while promoting in- and through-flow of local talent. Shared intervision reveals broad support for the model, delivering dual impact: personal development for sleutelpersonen and resilient, resident-led community building.

innovations.name: NO-STRESS
innovations.problem: In 2019, there were over 3 million accidents at work, often due to accidental events and human error. Psychologists attribute the causes of these phenomena to stress and fatigue, which manifest themselves both mentally and physically and derive from productive tasks and work environments. Even when stress does not cause accidents, it can still have repercussions on workers' health and social lives. In the literature, the physical, physiological and psychological aspects of stress have already been studied through the analysis of biometric data, but they have never been integrated with neurophysiological and psychological data. The NO-STRESS Manufacturing project, therefore, aimed to develop an integrated system of technologies aimed at analysing and understanding the main causes of stress for workers on production lines from multiple perspectives to collect reliable and accurate human-centred evidence.
innovations.description: The NO-STRESS Manufacturing project has proposed a system that integrates different and complementary technologies, such as exoskeletons, voice assistance and non-invasive biomedical devices. This solution allows real-time monitoring of data relating to physical effort, psychological workload, through the verbal administration of questionnaires, and the physiological parameters of workers in real industrial contexts. The combination of these data is essential for analysing the causes of work-related stress and mitigating its intensity, providing reliable evidence for redesigning the work environment in order to improve the well-being of workers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
The NO-STRESS Manufacturing project merged already tested technologies for biometric measures with already commercialised tools for physical and vocal assistance aimed at studying cognitive load and stress in workplaces. This implies developing a platform-based monitoring system with tools aimed at workers’ well-being. Over time, the technology integration performed by this project would imply personalising types of workers and tasks, up to aiding the design of collaborative or digital technologies in Manufacturing. Companies will get healthier working contexts, increased workers’ well-being, risen production efficiency and fewer human errors, absences and/or downtime. They will be able, over time, to link their safety procedures, risk or efficiency assessments to the factors that affect workers’ load and performance.
Universities and research centres will gain a data source to advance their research in work-related stress, in the manufacturing sector and beyond.

innovations.name: Wender – Empowering vulnerable people through shelter and reintegration
innovations.problem: Many individuals in the Netherlands, including youth, elderly, women, men, and families, face severe barriers to stable living and employment. Issues such as homelessness, addiction, mental health challenges, debts, and domestic violence create complex, intertwined problems that distance people from the labor market. Traditional support systems often fail to provide the integrated shelter, housing assistance, and ambulatory care needed to restore self-reliance, leaving vulnerable groups trapped in cycles of instability without pathways to sustainable jobs or training.​
innovations.description:
Wender, as a unified organization, started operating under its current name in 2021. It emerged from the collaboration between Het Kopland and Zienn, with the name change announced in April 2021 and full legal merger completed by January 2023. The foundational work traces back further through its predecessor organizations.
Wender addresses these challenges through a client-centered approach that combines safe shelter, housing support, and personalized guidance to empower individuals toward autonomy. Operating in Friesland, Groningen, and Drenthe, the organization fosters resilience by helping clients regain control over their lives, tackling root causes like addiction and debt holistically. This method emphasizes collaboration with partners and networks, including Valente and regional chains for domestic violence and youth homelessness, to deliver tailored interventions beyond conventional frameworks.​
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Wender's interventions enable clients to achieve a "positive turning point," securing safe, independent living and enhanced self-sufficiency. By strengthening personal agency, the approach supports long-term stability for those with multifaceted issues, reducing reliance on emergency services. Clients gain practical skills for daily life management, while partnerships amplify societal benefits, creating stronger community outcomes through bundled efforts with local organizations.​

innovations.name: Butterfly Effect
innovations.problem: Social isolation and fragmented community ties plague care locations in the Netherlands, where shortages of volunteers and housing exacerbate disconnection between residents with and without care needs. Traditional models struggle to integrate diverse talents, leaving gaps in mutual support and equal participation. This hinders well-being, safety, and natural human connections, particularly amid volunteer deficits and housing pressures, distancing vulnerable groups from active societal roles.
innovations.description: Butterfly Effect deploys dedicated neighborhood connectors—local volunteers—who actively link residents, harnessing individual talents to build inclusive, buzzing communities. Collaborating with housing corporations and care organizations, it creates spaces where everyone contributes equally, blending care with everyday life. This social enterprise model promotes sustainable volunteer engagement, turning care sites into dynamic hubs of connection and shared responsibility.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Neighborhood connectors enhance resident well-being, safety, and belonging, as participants report stronger community bonds and genuine contributions to neighbors' lives. Testimonials highlight improved cohesion, with care woven into daily interactions, addressing volunteer shortages effectively. The approach yields societal gains through empowered locals driving vitality, proving scalable for broader social impact.

innovations.name: Broodje Aap & Linke Soep
innovations.problem: Newcomers and status holders in Tilburg face significant hurdles integrating into Dutch society, including language barriers, limited social networks, and distance from the labor market. Many struggle with practical participation, lacking opportunities to practice Dutch, gain work experience, or build connections essential for employment. Traditional integration paths often overlook hands-on, community-based approaches, leaving refugees and migrants with migration backgrounds isolated and without pathways to sustainable jobs or volunteering.
innovations.description: Broodje Aap & Linke Soep creates an intercultural kitchen in Tilburg-West as a meeting place where newcomers cook lunches and catering alongside locals and volunteers. Programs like "Meedoen in de taalrijke keuken" and "Leren en werken in de horeca" offer language practice, horeca training, excursions, stages, and future planning, fostering societal participation. This social enterprise promotes cultural exchange and zero-waste principles through collaborative meal preparation and delivery.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence: Participants gain confidence, Dutch proficiency, horeca work experience, and new social networks, enabling steps toward paid work or volunteering. The initiative facilitates hundreds of global encounters via Tilburg4Global Goals, strengthens community ties in Tilburg-West with partners like De Reinevaer, and supports status holder inburgering as a Menss-partner. Intercultural meals enhance mutual understanding and practical societal inclusion.

innovations.name: Bovengrondse Vakschool
innovations.problem: In Heerlen-Noord, residents face significant barriers to employment, education, and well-being, with limited opportunities exacerbating social exclusion and economic stagnation. People distant from the labor market—such as long-term unemployed, single parents, and those needing skill development—struggle amid fragmented support systems that fail to connect training with real job needs. Traditional approaches often overlook personal growth, basic worker skills like punctuality and teamwork, and community integration, leaving individuals without sustainable pathways to work and trapping the region in cycles of low cohesion.
innovations.description: The Bovengrondse Vakschool creates a collaborative platform uniting employers, education, government, and civil society to tailor training to candidates' strengths and employers' basic requirements. Offering practical programs in nine work spheres across vakwerk (green, technical, construction), dienstwerk (logistics, ICT, hospitality), and zorgwerk (horeca, cleaning, care), it emphasizes personal development alongside vocational skills. Community initiatives like bike repair donations via Stichting Leergeld and ANWB, plus intergenerational activities such as the naaiclub, build social bonds while aligning with circular reuse principles through repair and upcycling projects.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.evidence: Participants gain employability, confidence, and social connections, as seen in stories like Dieudonnee Gans, who transitioned from isolation to bike repair work and aspirations in technical roles. The school boosts local cohesion via green maintenance, bike donations to underprivileged children, and community events reducing loneliness. Employers benefit from pre-vetted talent, while the region sees economic uplift through sustained job placements and strengthened networks, creating meaningful work that values personal growth over perfect vacancy matches.

innovations.name: Boefjes en Barista’s
innovations.problem:
Across Europe, both older adults and young parents often experience major life transitions that affect their social networks. Although their circumstances differ, both groups may find that the social connections that once supported them no longer fully match their needs.
At the same time, natural meeting places are disappearing from neighbourhoods and generations increasingly live separate lives. As a result, many people lack opportunities to build new relationships, experience belonging and find informal support within their community. In essence, many people no longer have the “village” they need. Rather than focusing solely on reducing loneliness, Boefjes en Barista’s creates the conditions in which social connectedness can grow.
innovations.description:
Boefjes en Barista’s is a community-based social intervention that transforms care homes into vibrant neighbourhood community spaces where older adults, parents and young children (0-4 years) meet, connect and become part of each other's lives.
“Boefjes” is a Dutch affectionate term for someone who is playful, curious and young at heart. In Boefjes en Barista’s, the “Boefjes” are not only the children. We believe that nobody is ever too old to play. Through play, laughter and shared experiences, older adults and young children bring out the playful side in one another and discover that the child within us never truly disappears. The “Barista’s” represent the welcoming coffee bar at the heart of the intervention. Together, playfulness and hospitality create a warm environment where meaningful relationships and a sense of belonging can grow across generations.
A “Bakkie” is a Dutch informal word for a cup of coffee or tea. At Boefjes en Barista’s, however, a “Bakkie Geluk” (“a cup of happiness”) is about much more than a drink. The coffee bar is a central part of the methodology and serves as a tool for hospitality, equality and connection. Participants are welcomed, served and invited to slow down, relax and spend time together. Around a Bakkie Geluk, conversations start, friendships grow and new relationships are formed. The term symbolises the many small moments of joy, attention and belonging that emerge when people of different generations come together. In this sense, participants do not simply receive a cup of coffee; they receive a moment of connection.
Inspired by the belief that “it takes a village to raise a child” and “it takes a village to grow old happily”, the intervention creates welcoming intergenerational communities where people build meaningful relationships and experience a sense of belonging. What makes the intervention unique is that it creates one change pathway for two target groups. Older adults and young parents are not brought together as helpers and recipients of support. Instead, both groups participate as equal members of the same community. Both are looking for connection, meaningful relationships and a sense of belonging during a life stage in which their social networks are changing. The methodology is built around eight core principles: intergenerational contact, connective play, a welcoming coffee bar, equal encounters, reciprocity, active community connectors, weekly structure and community building. Together, these principles create the conditions in which social connectedness can grow naturally.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Boefjes en Barista’s strengthens social connectedness by helping participants build new relationships, expand their social networks and experience a stronger sense of belonging. Participants get to know one another through repeated encounters, develop meaningful relationships and increasingly become part of a community in which they feel welcome, valued and recognised. The intervention also encourages reciprocity: participants both give and receive support, attention and friendship. Over time, informal support networks emerge naturally. Participants continue to meet outside the gatherings, help one another with practical or social needs and contribute to a more caring neighbourhood. Beyond individual outcomes, the intervention strengthens community cohesion by reconnecting generations and creating places where people know, trust and support one another.
The methodology has also proven valuable in dementia-friendly settings, where the emphasis on equal encounters, social participation and meaningful roles supports inclusion and wellbeing for people living with dementia.
Since its launch in 2018, Boefjes en Barista’s has been implemented at multiple locations in the city of ’s-Hertogenbosch and, since 2023, at several locations in Eindhoven. The intervention consistently demonstrates that regular intergenerational encounters can strengthen social connectedness, create a sense of belonging and contribute to more caring communities.
The example below illustrates the impact that can be achieved at a single location. In 2025, one location organised 98 weekly Boefjes en Barista’s gatherings in a care home community space. Together, these activities attracted 3,161 participant visits, including 943 care home residents, 401 older adults from the neighbourhood, 841 parents and 965 young children.
Throughout the year, participants shared 4,370 “Bakkies Geluk” (cups of happiness), played 294 games together, sang 588 songs, exchanged 490 hugs and shared 1,952 “Boefjes high-fives”. These moments may seem small, but together they create the welcoming atmosphere and repeated encounters that allow relationships to develop over time.
The impact is reflected not only in participation levels, but also in participants’ experiences. Older adults rated the programme 4.5 out of 5 on average. Nearly 90% indicated they would miss Boefjes en Barista’s if it were no longer available. Many described it as one of the highlights of their week and valued the regular contact with young children and families.Parents rated the programme 9.3 out of 10 on average. Almost all participants indicated they would miss the programme if it disappeared, while 75% gave a Net Promoter Score of 9 or 10 and actively recommended it to others. What stands out is that participants do not only come for the activities themselves. Older adults value the opportunity to remain connected to community life, while parents appreciate both the welcoming atmosphere and the opportunity to contribute to the wellbeing of others. Many parents initially attend because their child can play and because they are looking for a place to get out of the house, but continue coming because they feel welcome, connected and able to make a positive difference in the lives of others. This reflects one of the intervention’s core principles: reciprocity. Participants are not passive recipients of support but active contributors to a community in which everyone can give and receive attention, friendship and practical support. Over time, meaningful relationships and informal support networks emerge both within and beyond the weekly gatherings.

Since its launch in 2018, Boefjes en Barista’s has been implemented at multiple locations in the city of ’s-Hertogenbosch and, since 2023, at several locations in Eindhoven. The intervention consistently demonstrates that regular intergenerational encounters can strengthen social connectedness, create a sense of belonging and contribute to more caring communities.
The example below illustrates the impact that can be achieved at a single location. In 2025, one location organised 98 weekly Boefjes en Barista’s gatherings in a care home community space. Together, these activities attracted 3,161 participant visits, including 943 care home residents, 401 older adults from the neighbourhood, 841 parents and 965 young children.
Throughout the year, participants shared 4,370 “Bakkies Geluk” (cups of happiness), played 294 games together, sang 588 songs, exchanged 490 hugs and shared 1,952 “Boefjes high-fives”. These moments may seem small, but together they create the welcoming atmosphere and repeated encounters that allow relationships to develop over time.
The impact is reflected not only in participation levels, but also in participants’ experiences. Older adults rated the programme 4.5 out of 5 on average. Nearly 90% indicated they would miss Boefjes en Barista’s if it were no longer available. Many described it as one of the highlights of their week and valued the regular contact with young children and families.Parents rated the programme 9.3 out of 10 on average. Almost all participants indicated they would miss the programme if it disappeared, while 75% gave a Net Promoter Score of 9 or 10 and actively recommended it to others. What stands out is that participants do not only come for the activities themselves. Older adults value the opportunity to remain connected to community life, while parents appreciate both the welcoming atmosphere and the opportunity to contribute to the wellbeing of others. Many parents initially attend because their child can play and because they are looking for a place to get out of the house, but continue coming because they feel welcome, connected and able to make a positive difference in the lives of others. This reflects one of the intervention’s core principles: reciprocity. Participants are not passive recipients of support but active contributors to a community in which everyone can give and receive attention, friendship and practical support. Over time, meaningful relationships and informal support networks emerge both within and beyond the weekly gatherings.

innovations.problem: Blind and visually impaired individuals faced significant barriers when accessing goods, services, and digital information. innovations.name: Elliz in Company
innovations.problem: Elliz in Company aims to guide individuals to participation by creating a safe and welcoming environment first. We help people regain confidence, discover talents, and develop new skills at their own pace. Our ultimate goal is to empower them to become self-reliant and find meaningful work that suits their abilities and aspirations. It’s not just about making products—it’s about helping people grow and reclaim their place in society.
innovations.description:
Elliz in Company is innovative because it transforms traditional reintegration into a human-centered, empowering experience.
Peer contact as a foundation : Elliz creates a warm, informal environment where participants connect at eye level. The “coffeetable” culture and collaborative workshops foster trust, mutual learning, and solidarity—people learn from and support each other instead of being treated as cases.
Freedom and autonomy : Participants set their own pace and choose activities that match their interests and talents, from textile crafts to technical work. This freedom builds confidence and ownership, making reintegration a personal journey rather than a rigid program.
Focus on well-being and meaningful work : Elliz prioritizes emotional safety and personal growth before productivity. Through the process of “ontdooien, ontplooien, zelf rooien,” individuals regain self-worth and move toward work that suits their abilities and aspirations.
Combining craftmanship with social impact : Elliz in Company creates unique, handcrafted products with a story. From memory blankets and comfort toys made from cherished fabrics to sustainable bags, accessories, and decorative items; every piece reflects creativity and care. We also restore bicycles and craft personalized items using laser technology. All products are made from recycled or repurposed materials.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Elliz in Company has supported hundreds of individuals in regaining confidence, discovering talents, and moving toward meaningful work. Participants report improved well-being, stronger social connections, and reduced isolation. Our approach leads to measurable outcomes: increased self-reliance and successful transitions to employment or education. Society benefits through reduced stigma and greater participation.
