innovations.name: Binnenwerk
innovations.problem:
Standard jobs may not always fit these employees, for example because they are deemed to be too slow for the regular workpace or need extra instruction. Given the situation these employees are in, they also have specific needs from an employer.
Employers aren’t always equipped to provide this and may lack an incentive to put in the hard work, when there are other potential future employees available without such needs.
innovations.description:
Binnenwerk collaborates with national and local governmental organisations to create sustainable, stable jobs for the target group. New jobs are created around work that needs to be done and the threshold to take up one of these jobs is lowered.
During their employment, Binnenwerk invests in the learning and long term development of their employees. They do so via trainings, coaching and support to get the appropriate licensings. And Binnenwerk offers clear answers to help the employees navigate in the complex situation they are (regarding regulations and labour laws). Thus helping them make choices and oversee consequences.
Employees can get a contract for indefinitely or could continue to another job if that is a better fit.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Sylvo Thijsen, director of Staatsbosbeheer (one of the main partners) "Research shows that Binnenwerkers are happy with their jobs; they do meaningful work, feel valued, and are simultaneously working on their own personal development." Over 1,000 jobs have now been created in archive work, property-related tasks, clearing personnel files, or forest and nature management.

innovations.name: The Day Centre for the Elderly in Novska
innovations.lead: Development Agency of the City of Novska – NORA
innovations.problem: The project addresses the growing challenges of population ageing, social isolation, and limited access to community-based care services for older people in the Novska region. Many elderly individuals face the risk of institutionalisation due to insufficient support in the community, lack of organised daily activities, and inadequate social and psychosocial assistance, which negatively affects their well-being and quality of life.
innovations.description: The project introduces a community-based care model that allows older people to remain in their own homes while accessing comprehensive, organised support through a day centre. By combining personalised psychosocial assistance, structured activities, medical supervision, meals, and safe transport, the centre offers an integrated alternative to institutional care, reducing isolation and promoting active, dignified ageing within the local community.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: Development Agency of the City of Novska – NORA
innovations.evidence: The project established a fully equipped Day Centre providing half-day and full-day services to 20 regular users and reaching more than 70 older persons through additional activities. It improved access to community-based care, reduced social isolation, and prevented unnecessary institutionalisation. Users benefit from personalised support, social and cultural activities, medical supervision, nutritious meals, and safe transportation. The centre also created new jobs, strengthened local cooperation among social services, and contributed to a more inclusive and resilient community. Overall, the project significantly enhanced the quality of life and social participation of older residents in Novska.
authors: Development Agency of the City of Novska – NORA
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: proBUDI VJEŠTinu
innovations.problem: Before the project “proBUDI VJEŠTinu”, the local community in Novska faced several interconnected challenges: a lack of social enterprises and limited opportunities for sustainable job creation, particularly for vulnerable groups; a high volume of bulky waste such as old furniture and textile products ending up in landfills; and very few services focused on repair, reuse, and upcycling of materials. This resulted in missed opportunities for circular economy development, environmental protection, and community-based skill-building. There was also no structured mechanism for reinvesting economic activity into the local community. The project addressed these issues by establishing the first social enterprise in Novska dedicated to reuse and repair of wooden and textile products, creating social, environmental, and economic value for the area.
innovations.description: The project “proBUDI VJEŠTinu” introduced an innovative, community-based circular economy model by establishing the first social enterprise in Novska focused on the reuse, repair, and upcycling of wooden and textile products. The solution combines environmental impact with social entrepreneurship: discarded furniture and materials are transformed into functional, renewed products, reducing waste and promoting sustainable consumption. At the same time, the enterprise provides practical skill-building, new service opportunities (repairs, furniture assembly, custom wooden items), and reinvests generated profit into community development. This integrated model blending reuse practices, local craftsmanship, social enterprise governance, and reinvestment of profits for community benefit, represents a new approach within the local context and strengthens the foundations for long-term social and environmental sustainability.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The project established the first social enterprise in Novska focused on reuse, repair, and upcycling of wooden and textile products, reducing bulky waste and extending product life. It created new local service opportunities and practical skill-building in carpentry and circular economy practices. The enterprise reinvests its profit into community development, strengthening local sustainability. Overall, the project delivered environmental benefits, promoted social entrepreneurship, and increased access to affordable repair and upcycling services for citizens.

innovations.name: Gardener's Stitch
innovations.problem: This project addresses several interrelated issues: excessive consumerism in the apparel sector, the lack of functionality in clothing designed for specific activities (gardening), and the lack of community empowerment in sustainable fashion. The project solves this by offering transformable and sustainable apparel that performs multiple functions at once (reducing the need to buy more), and through the educational program "Gardener's Stitch", which teaches community members to create the garments themselves from old fabrics, thus promoting the circular economy and reducing waste.
innovations.description:
The innovation of this project lies in the combination of three elements: -Design Innovation: The creation of transformable gardener's apparel with adjustable and detachable details, which reduces the need for excessive consumption. -Educational Innovation: The "Gardener's Stitch" training teaches community members to create the functional garments themselves from old fabrics/scraps, directly fostering the circular economy. -Social Model: The successful integration of creativity, sustainability, and community empowerment through social entrepreneurship principles.
The project was inspired by the opportunity to participate in the "Dizaino sparnai" (Design Wings) project and to have the chance to collaborate with experienced mentors and young designers.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Key Results: -Transformable Collection: Creation of a functional, sustainable gardener's apparel design (with adjustable and detachable details) that allows the garments to be worn in multiple ways. -Educational Platform: Development of the "Gardener's Stitch" training and sewing instructions/video tutorials, focused on making clothes from old fabrics. Key Benefits: -Sustainability and Circular Economy: Significantly reduced excessive consumerism through versatile design and promotion of fabric reuse (zero waste principle). -Community Empowerment: Women acquire practical sewing skills and creativity, while fostering a stronger sense of community through shared, creative activity.

innovations.name: Platforma de mediu pentru București
innovations.problem: Bucharest faces increasingly severe environmental challenges that directly affect the quality of life of its residents. Air pollution, inadequate waste management, dirty streets, outdated public transport, heavy traffic, and sidewalks occupied by cars contribute to a deteriorating urban environment and recurring social tensions. The core issue is the absence of a long-term, structural, and collaborative approach capable of generating sustainable solutions. Fragmented efforts and limited coordination hinder progress toward cleaner air, better mobility, and improved urban infrastructure. A neutral space that enables cooperation among civil society, public institutions, companies, and citizens is essential to address these complex environmental problems. Platforma de mediu pentru București responds to this need by facilitating collaboration around shared environmental priorities and collective impact.
innovations.description: Platforma de mediu pentru București is a neutral collaborative space where civil society, academia, public authorities, and companies work together to address the environmental issues of the capital city. Initiated by Fundația Comunitară București and ING Bank Romania, it supports the development of projects that identify and address environmental issues and opportunities within Bucharest’s communities. Fundația Comunitară București attracts private funding (from companies that pool their resources to increase community impact) and co-finances environmental initiatives in the form of grants awarded to NGOs and civic groups selected through periodic project calls (funding rounds). In each funding round, a number of projects are selected to receive support for a period of 3–4 years, depending on project results and on the platform’s ability to attract new sources of funding.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: By 2025, Fundația Comunitară București aims to build a community that can generate collective impact in addressing the complex environmental challenges of the capital, challenges that no single actor can resolve independently. As a facilitator, it provides a neutral collaborative space where community members can develop project ideas and advocacy initiatives. Through previous funding rounds, a total of 14,882,484 lei, including 2,521,250 lei supported through the În ZONA TA initiative, has been invested in the implementation of 58 environmental projects in Bucharest and Ilfov between 2021 and 2025. These investments have strengthened local capacity, encouraged long-term engagement, and contributed to more coordinated solutions for air quality, waste management, mobility and urban green spaces. The platform has also helped build stronger connections between civic groups, public institutions, companies and residents, leading to more informed and collaborative approaches to environmental issues.

sections.question: Problem
sections.answer: Bucharest faces increasingly severe environmental challenges that directly affect the quality of life of its residents. Air pollution, inadequate waste management, dirty streets, outdated public transport, heavy traffic, and sidewalks occupied by cars contribute to a deteriorating urban environment and recurring social tensions. The core issue is the absence of a long-term, structural, and collaborative approach capable of generating sustainable solutions. Fragmented efforts and limited coordination hinder progress toward cleaner air, better mobility, and improved urban infrastructure. A neutral space that enables cooperation among civil society, public institutions, companies, and citizens is essential to address these complex environmental problems. Platforma de mediu pentru București responds to this need by facilitating collaboration around shared environmental priorities and collective impact.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer: Platforma de mediu pentru București is a neutral collaborative space where civil society, academia, public authorities, and companies work together to address the environmental issues of the capital city. Initiated by Fundația Comunitară București and ING Bank Romania, it supports the development of projects that identify and address environmental issues and opportunities within Bucharest’s communities. Fundația Comunitară București attracts private funding (from companies that pool their resources to increase community impact) and co-finances environmental initiatives in the form of grants awarded to NGOs and civic groups selected through periodic project calls (funding rounds). In each funding round, a number of projects are selected to receive support for a period of 3–4 years, depending on project results and on the platform’s ability to attract new sources of funding.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer: By 2025, Fundația Comunitară București aims to build a community that can generate collective impact in addressing the complex environmental challenges of the capital, challenges that no single actor can resolve independently. As a facilitator, it provides a neutral collaborative space where community members can develop project ideas and advocacy initiatives. Through previous funding rounds, a total of 14,882,484 lei, including 2,521,250 lei supported through the În ZONA TA initiative, has been invested in the implementation of 58 environmental projects in Bucharest and Ilfov between 2021 and 2025. These investments have strengthened local capacity, encouraged long-term engagement, and contributed to more coordinated solutions for air quality, waste management, mobility and urban green spaces. The platform has also helped build stronger connections between civic groups, public institutions, companies and residents, leading to more informed and collaborative approaches to environmental issues.

innovations.name: Vote Monitor
innovations.problem: Election observation has long relied on pen-and-paper reports, which are slow, hard to coordinate, and leave little chance for timely response. Observers might see violations on election day, but NGOs would only receive data hours or even days later (when using pen and paper)—too late to act. Even with tools like WhatsApp, information is fragmented, unstructured, and difficult to analyze. In Romania, election observation has long struggled with slow reporting methods. Observers relied on pen and paper, meaning watchdog NGOs could only issue first public statements or aggregated findings 5 to 24 hours after polling stations closed, based on mid-results we reviewed from the past decade. This delay made it impossible to react in real time to election irregularities. The Romanian case is not unique. Across Europe, democratic backsliding has become systemic. Hungary and Poland are now classified by Freedom House as “hybrid regimes,” while Georgia, Belarus, Serbia and others also face an apparent decline. Independent election observation remains one of the last defenses against this decline. With stronger tools, NGOs can react faster and help safeguard democracy before it slips further toward authoritarianism.
innovations.description: Vote Monitor replaces slow, paper-based election reporting with a fast, digital system. Observers use a simple mobile app to submit structured reports, attach photos or videos as evidence, and send updates instantly - even without internet, thanks to offline mode. NGOs receive this information in real time on a secure dashboard where all reports are automatically aggregated, visualized, and ready for analysis. This enables them to detect violations during election day, communicate directly with observers, and coordinate responses before polling stations close. By streamlining reporting, breaking language barriers with localization, and reducing delays from days to minutes, Vote Monitor turns election observation into a proactive tool that strengthens transparency and protects democratic standards. By tackling local barriers in Romania and Europe while scaling globally, the solution strengthens watchdogs as a frontline defense for democracy everywhere.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Vote Monitor, which just became WSA 2025 (World Summit Award) Winner and a Global Champion of Government and Citizenship Category, has significantly changed how election observation is carried out in practice, making it faster, more coordinated, and more actionable for NGOs and observers in the field. Instead of receiving fragmented or delayed information, NGOs now receive structured reports in real time as soon as polling stations open. This allows them to follow events as they unfold throughout election day, identify repeated issues early, and respond while voting is still ongoing.
One of the most visible changes is speed. Reporting to the public has become 80–85% faster, with NGOs now able to issue updates within roughly one hour after polling stations open, compared to 4–24 hours after polls close in the traditional model. Instead of a single end-of-day statement, NGOs can now publish 5–6 updates during election day, increasing the frequency of public information by 5–6 times.
Communication between observers and NGO headquarters has also improved significantly. The average response time dropped from around 50 minutes to 15 minutes, a 70% improvement, allowing observers to receive immediate legal or procedural guidance while still in the field.
The system also improves consistency and data quality. Reports are structured, time-stamped, and often include photo or video evidence, which allows NGOs to verify incidents quickly and escalate them when needed.
The Quick Report and flagged answers features ensure that critical violations are surfaced immediately instead of being buried in large volumes of data.
Importantly, even without internet connectivity, which is a common problem when observing in rural polling stations, 100% of observations are now recorded even in offline conditions, with data syncing once connectivity is restored, eliminating reporting gaps in rural areas.
Across 38 missions, this results in: 80–85% faster reporting to the public 5–6× more frequent updates during election day 70% faster NGO–observer communication 110,000+ violations reported by 7,500+ observers 100% data capture even without internet access Overall, Vote Monitor helps NGOs move from reactive election-day reporting to active, real-time monitoring that strengthens both electoral integrity and observer safety.

innovations.name: consolid8 Festival
innovations.problem: The sustainability and social innovation ecosystem is highly fragmented, with key actors often working in isolation. Businesses, public institutions, academic experts, innovators and community groups often operate in separate spaces, with few opportunities to exchange ideas, align priorities or explore solutions together. The ecosystem lacks a shared space where the key actors needed to create impact can work together. The festival brings business leaders, public authorities, innovators, academia and the wider community into the same place to learn from experts, find inspiration through panels and keynotes, and collaborate toward a greener and more sustainable future powered by technology, social innovation and green funds.
innovations.description: consolid8 Festival stands as a pioneering event in Eastern Europe, entirely dedicated to the realms of green technology and sustainability. It's the first event in Romania dedicated to green technologies and sustainable urban development, with a strong focus on sustainable solutions and social innovation. The festival brings together leaders from business, public administration, education, entrepreneurship and civil society who are interested in sustainability, innovation and social impact. consolid8 Festival is a unique event designed to bring together entrepreneurs, social enterprises, organisations, creators and communities interested in responsible solutions. It provides an accessible space where participants can explore approaches that address current challenges such as climate change, the transition to more sustainable business models, green cities, the digital transformation of companies through AI, and the development of community-focused social impact projects. The festival is structured around pillars such as Talks, Masterclasses, Hackathon and Experiences, turning the event into a comprehensive process that offers valuable perspectives to both communities and the business environment. By bringing together innovators, experts, companies and communities, consolid8 Festival acts as a platform for collaboration and inspiration, where innovative and sustainable initiatives gain visibility, connections and support.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: consolid8 Festival provides a comprehensive framework where participants gain access to numerous applied sessions such as keynotes, panels, masterclasses and workshops delivered by renowned international speakers. These sessions facilitate the transfer of knowledge across diverse fields to leaders from business, public administration, education, entrepreneurship and civil society, supporting the development of a more resilient, sustainable and inclusive future. The festival offers participants practical solutions and valuable perspectives drawn from the experience of professionals across various sectors, encouraging applied learning and the exchange of ideas. consolid8 Festival strengthens an active ecosystem of green solutions and social innovation, increasing the level of awareness, collaboration and visibility for local actors, the business environment and communities. The consolid8 Festival demonstrated strong community engagement and growing interest in sustainability, innovation and green solutions, bringing together hundreds of conference participants and more than 30 international experts through keynotes and panel discussions.

innovations.name: Innovative approaches to engage Ukrainian youth and host communities through civic service and social innovation
innovations.lead: Collectif pour un service civique europeen
innovations.problem: The war in Ukraine has led to the displacement of millions of people across Europe, with many young Ukrainians facing interrupted education, unemployment, social isolation and limited opportunities to participate in community life. While humanitarian assistance provides immediate support, there is a growing need for long-term solutions that promote social inclusion, personal development and active participation in host communities. Traditional volunteering programmes often struggle to engage young refugees due to administrative barriers, limited financial support and a lack of tailored pathways that recognise their specific circumstances. At the same time, local young people have limited opportunities to engage in meaningful solidarity actions alongside Ukrainian peers. INNOVolunteering addresses these challenges by creating an innovative civic volunteering pathway that combines local volunteering, international mobility, structured training and competence development, allowing Ukrainian and local young people to learn, volunteer and grow together.
innovations.description: INNOVolunteering pilots a new model of youth volunteering inspired by Civic Service principles and adapted to the realities of displaced Ukrainian youth. The methodology combines several complementary elements: - mixed volunteer groups bringing together local young people and Ukrainian refugees in equal conditions; six-month volunteering pathways based on personalised learning objectives and mentoring; - financial support through monthly stipends and accommodation to remove participation barriers; host organisations selected jointly with municipalities to ensure that volunteering activities respond to real local community needs; - a structured training programme combining online learning modules and face-to-face workshops on civic engagement, inclusion, intercultural dialogue, humanitarian support, communication and employability; - continuous mentoring by youth workers and project coordinators; - transnational exchanges and study visits enabling volunteers from different countries to exchange practices and jointly design future community actions; - competence recognition through self-assessment, learning follow-up and personal development planning. The innovation does not consist only in volunteering itself but in creating an integrated pathway linking social inclusion, non-formal education, civic participation and employability within a single coordinated programme. Key results and benefits: The project is currently being implemented in France, Czechia and Poland through partnerships between civil society organisations and municipalities.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.beneficiaries: Collectif pour un service civique europeen
innovations.evidence: xpected results include: 1. engagement of more than 100 young volunteers, including Ukrainian refugees and local participants; development of sustainable volunteering pathways lasting six months; 2. creation of mixed local and international volunteer teams supporting community initiatives; 3. strengthened social inclusion, language skills, confidence and employability of participating young people; 4. strengthened cooperation between municipalities, NGOs and youth organisations; development of reusable training modules, implementation guidelines and operational tools that can be transferred to future volunteering programmes; 5. evidence and recommendations supporting the integration of civic volunteering into local and regional public policies. Beyond the direct impact on participants, the project demonstrates how volunteering can become an innovative social inclusion mechanism for displaced populations while strengthening community resilience.
authors: Collectif pour un service civique europeen

innovations.name: IT.A.CÀ Festival del Turismo Responsabile
innovations.problem: Many destinations struggle with the negative effects of mass tourism: pressure on the environment, loss of local identity, exclusion of vulnerable groups and little involvement of communities in decision-making. Travel often becomes a product to consume quickly, rather than a meaningful encounter with a place and its people. IT.A.CÀ responds to this by promoting a slower, fairer and more respectful way of travelling that benefits both visitors and residents.
innovations.description: The festival’s innovation lies in its bottom-up approach. IT.A.CÀ is not a fixed format: each territory shapes the programme according to its own story, resources and priorities. Everything, from the themes to the activities, is co-designed with local actors. The festival also encourages “slow mobility” (walking, cycling), accessible routes, community storytelling and events that highlight the social and cultural fabric of each area. It is an open, flexible model that communities can adopt and make their own.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: -Thousands of participants join every year across multiple Italian regions. - Hundreds of events help people rediscover local areas in sustainable and inclusive ways. - Over 700 organisations have been involved since 2009, strengthening collaboration between citizens, associations, institutions and tourism operators. -The festival raises awareness about responsible travel, supports local cultural initiatives and creates spaces for dialogue on sustainability, migration and global citizenship. -IT.A.CÀ has been recognised nationally and internationally for its innovative approach to tourism.

innovations.name: Housing Thessaloniki: From identifying vacant housing stock to creating a model of social housing for Greece
innovations.lead: Major Development Agency of Thessaloniki, Social Rental Agency (SRA)
innovations.problem: Greece demonstrates one of the most acute housing crises exacerbated by the fact that it is also the sole EU member state with 0% social housing stock. Greece faces one of the most serious housing affordability crises in Europe. Stagnant incomes, rising ownership changes, and sharp increases in sale and rental prices (65% for rent from 2016–2023; 10% per year for sales over the past decade) have heightened housing insecurity for more people. The dominant housing interventions to date have been primarily based on market solutions with little investment in creating public social infrastructure to combat housing exclusion (subsidized loans, incentives for property owners without social conditionalities etc.). In addition, according to research conducted by the SRA, the problem in relation to the brick-and-mortar aspect relates not to the necessity for new construction but the sheer amount of vacancies in Thessaloniki. In the metropolitan area vacant properties which had former residential use are 35,000 and in the central municipality more than 16,500 homes remain empty, with an 8% increase in the last 5 years in the number of vacancies. This phenomenon, in addition to leaving a significant number of homes outside of the residential rental sector also impacts energy efficiency targets since these units dispersed across condominiums create “energy gaps” in the urban fabric.
innovations.description:
The innovation of this project lies at many levels. Social Housing models have appeared in many cities throughout Europe. But few can compete with the labyrinthian trajectory that Housing Thessaloniki had to disentangle. The number of uncommon synergies achieved at multiple levels surpasses imagination.   Sharing data between Thessaloniki municipalities, connecting homeless challenges with environmental national obligations, shifting perceptions toward re-using vacant properties, having to pass new regulations to establish necessary legal management bodies and offering a portfolio approach to addressing homelessness, are only some of the tips of the icebergs below!
This project was inspired by the social rental agency models in Belgium, Poland and Hungary, as well as innovative housing modules implemented in Spain (La Borda) and Belgium (CALICO), along with the Housing First approaches used in Ghent.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: Major Development Agency of Thessaloniki, Social Rental Agency (SRA)
innovations.evidence: - Renovation and energy upscaling of 40 housing units across the city through a single international tender (economies of scale) - Linked the housing units with national programmes combating housing exclusion whose major challenge was to find affordable housing units thus supporting optimizing results of other social programmes focusing on housing - Tested a local governance model for social housing generation and delivery - Methodology for the assessment and selection of properties - Matching system - SOPs for social monitoring and support - Standardised mechanisms for collab with Municipalities & other actors for property transfer, use and social rental - Proposals for legal changes for housing generation and delivery (with inputs from the SRA and as a result of the needs that has arisen from the implementation of the pilot project Law No. 5229/2025 of September 2025 has both introduced in legislation the concepts of social rental and social housing providers but also allows for municipalities to rent their properties at a price of their choice when these properties are rented in the framework of social rental) - Created a replicable model
authors: Major Development Agency of Thessaloniki, Social Rental Agency (SRA)

innovations.name: IKIGAI Social Hub
innovations.lead: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises
innovations.problem:
Within the Social Economy ecosystem, there is significant potential for innovation and territorial development, which risks remaining untapped due to a series of structural and cultural challenges that IKIGAI Social Hub aims to address through training and support. The main identified needs are:
Lack of specific entrepreneurial skills Many young people and social organizations have high-value social ideas but lack the skills necessary to transform them into economically sustainable projects.
Limited access to dedicated support programs Unlike traditional start-ups, social economy initiatives rarely find acceleration or incubation programs tailored to their hybrid characteristics.
Weak connection between innovation, territory, and community Innovative social solutions struggle to take root in local contexts, often due to a lack of networks, local partnerships, and spaces to engage with other ecosystem actors.
Challenges in idea validation and resource mobilization Social organizations face barriers in accessing funding, investors, and impact measurement tools, all essential elements for consolidating a business model.
innovations.description:
IKIGAI Social Hub adopts a distinctive approach to supporting start-ups and organizations in the social economy, adapting the tools and methodologies typical of the for-profit sector to the specific characteristics of the social economy. The project stands out for the following elements:
Integrated and modular pathway The program combines practical workshops, individual coaching sessions, and group activities, guiding participants from idea generation to business model validation.
Collaborative networks and co-creation The program fosters interaction between social start-ups, sector experts, investors, and local stakeholders, creating opportunities for partnerships and territorial synergies.
Personalized support and mentorship Each project receives tailored guidance from mentors with experience in the social economy and innovation, who support participants in strategic development and resource mobilization.
Integration with the entrepreneurial ecosystem IKIGAI Social Hub leverages the experience of both EURICSE and Pluriversum in accelerating traditional start-ups, adapting business innovation tools and methodologies to the social context, thereby creating a hybrid and replicable model.
Active learning approach The program encourages hands-on experimentation, rapid prototyping, and continuous feedback, allowing participants to test ideas and models in real contexts before scaling.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises
authors: EURICSE – European Research Institute on Cooperative and Social Enterprises
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Innovative Approaches to Refugee Integration: Bridging Employability and Social Inclusion through Mutual Exchange
innovations.problem:
The project responds to two intertwined needs: improving services that support the social and economic inclusion of migrants, and helping displaced people move from an initial phase of emergency towards a more stable and sustainable situation.
In both Italy and Poland, employment remains one of the central challenges. DPUs often face discrimination in the labour market, limited access to jobs due to language barriers, and difficulties securing positions that match their skills and qualifications. On top of that, the instability and temporary nature of the legal protection frameworks further undermine their prospects, creating uncertainty for DPUs and complicating the efforts of organisations supporting their social and economic inclusion.
The project also addresses the impact of the political frameworks developed in both countries over the past three years. These policies shape the conditions under which DPUs, as well as NGOs such as PAH, the Emic Foundation, and RED Nova, operate. By engaging with this context, the project seeks not only to support individuals directly, but also to strengthen the environment in which organisations work to promote inclusion.
innovations.description:
The project’s innovative solutions build on pre-planned actions by RED Nova in Italy and by PAH and the Emic Foundation in Poland. These actions are further strengthened through a needs assessment led by the OPORA Foundation and a structured mutual learning process within the consortium.
In Italy, RED Nova, which currently specialises in socio-legal assistance through its Helpline and casework on legal, mediation, and translation issues, will expand its support to include job counselling and job matching. In Poland, PAH will provide vocational training for DPUs in specific sectors such as technical professions and accountancy. With the support of Emic, participants will also access targeted job counselling and Polish language classes through a One Stop Shop (OSS), where DPUs can receive comprehensive assistance. Emic will additionally run an Entrepreneurship Academy that covers not only the practical steps of starting a business, but also protection-related issues, including rights and obligations. These interventions aim to further develop the OSS model run by Emic, making it sustainable and adaptable to more specialised needs. In Italy, RED Nova will incorporate key elements of the OSS approach into its Helpline, moving towards a more comprehensive model of social and economic inclusion.
All upscaled activities are guided by the needs assessment, which identifies concrete requirements such as language for specific professional purposes and greater awareness of employment-related rights and obligations. Mutual learning is embedded throughout the project: Emic and PAH will learn from RED Nova’s experience in setting up and managing a Helpline, including the strategy and operations this entails, while RED Nova will draw on Emic’s expertise in job counselling to strengthen its employability support.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence:
Needs-based, integrated support package in Poland
A comprehensive needs assessment confirms the importance of making the labour market more accessible for DPUs in Poland, with particular attention to language barriers. In response, PAH and the Emic Foundation will offer an integrated package combining vocational courses, targeted job counselling, and Polish language classes tailored to specific professional fields.
Adaptation of RED Nova’s Helpline into an OSS-like service in Italy
RED Nova will adapt its existing Helpline into a more holistic, OSS-like service delivered by phone. In addition to ongoing socio-legal and mediation casework, the Helpline will gradually integrate employability support, guided by the needs assessment findings and the consortium’s mutual learning process.
Direct and long-term impact on beneficiaries and service providers
During the project, beneficiaries will test and benefit from the enhanced services, improving their chances of social and economic inclusion. In the longer term, the strengthened models in Poland and Italy are expected to continue beyond the project period, with the potential to be adapted and replicated by other actors.
Tested model and Best Practice Toolbox
The integrated support model will be tested, evaluated, and documented. The results will be compiled into a freely accessible online Best Practice Toolbox, enabling other organisations and stakeholders to draw on the project’s methods, tools, and lessons learned.

innovations.name: Centrul Cultural Plai - AMBASADA
innovations.problem: Ambasada addresses the lack of accessible spaces and resources for collaboration within the creative and non-profit sectors. In Romania, independent artists, social entrepreneurs, and NGOs often struggle to find affordable venues, professional support, and cross-sector connections needed to develop impactful initiatives. At the same time, there is limited interaction between cultural actors, businesses, and local communities, which weakens social cohesion and innovation potential. Ambasada responds to these gaps by offering a shared, inclusive space that facilitates collaboration, education, and community engagement, turning cultural and social creativity into sustainable impact.
innovations.description: Ambasada is a social enterprise in Romania developed with the aim of incubating and increasing the impact of the local, national and international doers. Since 2015, Ambasada has offered a meeting place for non-governmental organisations, freelancers, artists, musicians, social and creative entrepreneurs. It consists of a bistro, co-working space, meeting rooms, performance and rehearsal spaces, and an event hall accommodating between 100 and 300 people. It offers free facilities and services for the creative and non-profit sectors, supported by income from the bistro and related commercial activities. In 2020, as part of the Cultural and Creative Spaces and Cities project, AMBASADA launched a community garden in the Azur yard. Responding to feedback from its active community, it later transformed this space into a hybrid work and meeting area.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
At Ambasada, a free community space was established to bring together creative professionals and encourage dialogue between artists and cultural actors. Among its key results and benefits are the creation of a supportive environment for collaboration, the strengthening of local creative networks, and the promotion of cultural exchange. In addition, Ambasada carries out educational and inclusion activities for disadvantaged youth, providing opportunities for learning, creative expression, and social participation through culture. This holistic approach has positioned Ambasada as both a cultural hub and a catalyst for community development.
Within the European Trans Europe Halles network, AMBASADA has inspired, at the international level, models for supporting non-profit communities built around cultural centres operating in repurposed spaces.

innovations.name: UrbanDig Adrianio
innovations.problem:
UrbanDig Adrianio addresses the invisibility and under-appreciation of the Hadrian’s Aqueduct as a cultural and environmental resource, the lack of citizen awareness and engagement with this shared heritage, and the resulting weak connections between the neighborhoods it links.
The project responds to limited community participation in shaping local urban development, the absence of creative and educational tools that connect people to water heritage, and the fragmentation between cultural, environmental, and planning sectors that prevents integrated and sustainable approaches to urban resilience.
innovations.description:
UrbanDig Adrianio introduces an innovative, cross-disciplinary model that transforms an invisible piece of ancient infrastructure—the Hadrian’s Aqueduct—into a catalyst for cultural activation, environmental awareness, and community-led urban development.
By blending artistic research, participatory performance, place-based education, sensory mapping, and neighborhood co-design, the project creates new ways for citizens to engage with hidden heritage and to envision sustainable futures for their public spaces.
Its approach breaks down silos between culture, water management, education, and urban planning, offering a replicable methodology that uses storytelling, creativity, and collective action to strengthen social cohesion and support heritage-driven, climate-resilient urban regeneration.
Its main line of action has been participation in local, national, and European programmes that support art, education, research, technology, and innovation in urban contexts. These include initiatives such as Erasmus+, Urban Innovative Actions (UIA), EEA Grants, STARTS, as well as programmes of the Hellenic Ministry of Culture and municipal authorities
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
UrbanDig Adrianio delivers a set of tangible cultural, social, and environmental results: it increases public awareness of the Hadrian’s Aqueduct as both heritage and living infrastructure, strengthens connections between neighborhoods along its route, and builds new channels for citizen participation in local decision making. It generates collaborative networks between cultural actors, schools, NGOs, and public authorities, leading to more integrated approaches to urban development.
Overall, the initiative enhances community identity, activates public spaces, and provides a replicable model for heritage-driven regeneration that benefits residents, institutions, and the broader urban ecosystem through effective collaboration.
Summary of Projects around Hadrian's Aqueduct
1. Participatory design and implementation of water networks, green/blue/cultural infrastructures and a community around water and local cultural heritage in Halandri neighborhoods (EU UIA CULTURAL HIDRANT)
2. Creating and capacitating a community of active citizens and stakeholders across 7 municipalities regarding the 20km long water/cultural resource for a more resilient city (Active Citizens Fund: Walkers on Water)
3. Tools for secondary education for innovative approaches to environmental & cultural education with a focus on local development. It is performed in neighborhoods that contain heritage water lines (Erasmus+ Hadrian)
4. Artistic interventions on the invisible part of the local history bringing people from various ages, backgrounds and disciplines together to collect, map and publically present their local cultural capital (site specific UrbanDig artistic productions)
Since our very first involvement with the Hadrian Aqueduct and up to now UrbanDig Adrianio has "delivered": 3 performances, school programs for junior high school, co-creation of 3 festivals, performative guided tour, educational games, gamified dialogue tools (Demos board game), the "Walkers on Water" community engagement methodology , in-person and digital “dramatized workshops / thematic days”, sensory mapping, stakeholder mapping, digital citizen-engagement application (drop a message), support for creating the Water Solidarity Community in Halandri, transformation of a riverbank section of the Kifisos River into a cultural space.

innovations.name: PLANAVA – AI-Powered Event Planning & Accessibility Certification Platform
innovations.problem: Many cultural and educational organisations struggle to plan events efficiently and ensure full accessibility for people with disabilities, older adults, or socially excluded groups. There is no simple tool that helps organisers evaluate accessibility, meet EU guidelines, and improve inclusion. This results in uneven quality, inaccessible venues, and limited participation in cultural life.
innovations.description: PLANAVA combines AI-driven event planning tools with an automated accessibility assessment engine. The platform helps organisations design events, check compliance with accessibility standards, identify barriers, and provide a certification label. It introduces a new, scalable model for inclusive event planning, integrating digital innovation, accessibility expertise, and user-friendly guidance.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Improved accessibility and inclusion in cultural and educational events. Time savings for organisers through AI-powered planning automation. Increased participation of people with disabilities and marginalised groups. Clear, standardised accessibility certification for events and venues. Strengthened awareness of accessibility requirements in the cultural sector.

innovations.name: Buniz by OilRight – a scented candle making waste oil right
innovations.problem: Used cooking oil is a toxic waste for the environment. When it is not collected and recycled properly, it pollutes water and soil and clogs sewage systems, creating environmental damage and additional costs for public infrastructure. Despite being a common household waste, its improper disposal remains a widespread issue that requires sustainable and innovative solutions. At the same time, people with disabilities continue to face structural barriers to participating in the labour market. Many lack access to workplaces adapted to their needs, which results in limited economic opportunities and social exclusion. OilRight addresses these two problems simultaneously by transforming a harmful waste into a valuable resource while creating inclusive employment opportunities. Through its activity, the organisation aims to protect the environment and promote social inclusion by turning used cooking oil into eco-friendly, non-toxic candles and building a sustainable business model that integrates vulnerable groups into the workforce. This approach reflects a broader social innovation on the Romanian market, where environmental protection is directly connected to social impact. By turning challenges into opportunities, OilRight contributes to a cleaner environment, a fairer society, and the development of a more inclusive economy.
innovations.description:
The innovative core of OilRight is based on turning used cooking oil, a common but highly polluting waste, into a sustainable raw material for new products. Instead of relying on imported or resource-intensive materials, the organisation uses a locally available waste stream, which it collects from households, restaurants, and institutions. Through a careful filtration and processing system, the oil is transformed into a clean, stable base for eco-friendly candles, sold under the brand Buniz. What makes this solution stand out is the way it connects a clear environmental goal with social impact. The recycling process is not only an ecological intervention but also the foundation for an inclusive production model. The entire candle-making process takes place in a certified protected unit, where people with disabilities are directly involved in giving this waste a second life. By integrating oil recycling into its production and business structure, OilRight creates a model that reduces pollution, encourages responsible consumption, and supports inclusive employment. This practical and scalable approach shows how circular economy principles can be applied locally to achieve both environmental and social goals.
The project is based on an existing initiative from Slovenia, which inspired the overall concept.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: The initiative has a strong impact on three main levels: environmental, social, and economic. From an environmental perspective, OilRight reduces pollution by collecting and recycling used cooking oil that would otherwise contaminate water, soil, and sewage systems. This process encourages more sustainable consumption habits among individuals, companies, and communities. On the social side, the initiative creates adapted jobs for people with disabilities, giving them real opportunities for stable employment, skill development, and active participation in society. At the same time, it raises awareness about the importance of inclusion and shared responsibility for the environment. Economically and at the community level, OilRight demonstrates how a simple waste stream can be turned into a sustainable business model. It strengthens cooperation between citizens, companies, and institutions and offers a replicable example that can inspire similar initiatives in other regions.

innovations.name: Rock the Block
innovations.problem: Rock the Block redefines housing affordability at the local scale, by employing a series of technical-energy efficient, aesthetic, circular economy and participatory interventions and tools, in order to pilot policy solutions with local communities. It promotes community engagement, social cohesion, and local empowerment, transforming housing blocks into vibrant, inclusive spaces. The project aims to reduce urban decline, foster active citizenship, and improve residents’ quality of life through participatory affordable solutions on housing.
innovations.description: Rock the Block employs multifamily housing blocks of flats (“polykatoikia”) as the housing intervention unit for creating affordable housing solutions. The overall aim is to offer multi-level innovation solutions and thus improve housing and living conditions, by enhancing communities of mutual support, solidarity and institutional coverage. The key innovation solutions lie on the re-conceptualisation of affordability through interventions that touch upon technical, aesthetic and energy efficient aspects, and circular economy and participatory tools to engage local communities and set them in collaboration.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The establishment of the Housing Office and the Co-Living Hub, two municipal structures that are already established and will play a desicive role in the Municipality of Egaleo’s housing policy after the project ends. Both Municipal structures are expected to effect transferable impact to other European cities as well, especially the three transfer partners, i.e. the Municipalities of Paris, Napoli and Józsefváros (Budapest).
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: SEFIT | Social Ecosystems for Fair and Inclusive Transitions
innovations.problem:
The SEFIT project addresses a key systemic problem: local authorities, social innovation actors, and community stakeholders are not yet collaborating effectively enough to tackle the challenges of the green transition and the digital transition—especially for people in socio-economic disadvantage.
Imagine the problem of the green and digital transitions as a river to cross: the risk is that only a few have the boats (resources and skills) to reach the other shore. SEFIT does not just build a boat , but develops both the blueprint for building inclusive bridges (the Policy Paper and the Shared Support Guide, which teach how to create support structures and share best practices) and a targeted funding system (the Challenge Fund, which provides materials and incentives for the immediate construction of small innovative rafts where they are needed most).
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
The Social Ecosystems for Fair and Inclusive Transitions (SEFIT) project has yielded several key results and benefits, primarily focused on creating knowledge, providing financial support for innovation, and establishing frameworks for fair and inclusive implementation of the twin (green and digital) transition.
The key results and benefits include:
The primary benefit of SEFIT is its focus on driving transformative change for marginalised communities in Cork, Ireland, and Turin, Italy. The project aims to eliminate barriers and achieve an equitable and inclusive future , ensuring that green and digital change is fair for everyone .
SEFIT has produced several downloadable reports and guides, which are critical results for knowledge transfer and capacity building:
SEFIT Policy Paper: This document is a key result that shares key insights from the project on how social innovation can help shape inclusive and community-driven approaches to the green and digital transitions at local levels. A significant benefit is that it explores how municipalities can integrate social enterprise, institutional innovation, and citizen engagement into climate and digital policy frameworks.
Shared Support Guide: This guide's key result is to consolidate the key learnings developed throughout the SEFIT project into a replicable and practical tool . The benefit is the facilitation of knowledge transfer and capacity building at both national and transnational levels. It serves as a guide for various stakeholders—including municipal policymakers, private sector stakeholders, academia, and social economy actors—to develop collaborative, informed, and context-sensitive approaches to the twin transition.
Analysis and Urban Trends Report: This result is based on an in-depth analysis of documents produced by Cork and Turin. Its benefit is providing a comprehensive overview of projects active in the context of the twin transition, offering a solid basis for assessing and analysing progress and identifying areas for improvement and future opportunities .
Open Enquiries – The Report: This report presents the outcomes and insights derived from the Field Workshops held in Torino and Cork. These workshops assessed the present status of the twin transition by focusing on active projects and initiatives through direct engagement with citizens and other stakeholders.

innovations.name: EcoZani
innovations.problem: Western Macedonia (WM) has been Greece’s most significant coal region, producing 2,43% of national GDP, 45% of which has been coming from lignite industry and electricity supply. Both mining and power generation has historically been a critical source of employment in WM: in 2018, it directly employed 3,899 individuals in full-time positions and additionally 750 on 8-month contracts. Following the delignitisation goal to yield environmental benefits, the mines closure by 2028 will potentially impact approximately 16,000 jobs and another 11,000 indirectly tied to the Public Power Corporation- PPC (World Bank, 2020). Unemployment is a constant challenge for WM, recording the highest unemployment rates in the country (60% among 15-24), reaching 19,1% among the active population (ELSTAT, 2022), with a notable gender gap (34% of women unemployed). As a result of the above, the largest population decrease is recorded in WM (-10,3%, census 2021). Youth outmigration has been extensive, too: between 2009-2022 WM lost 26% of its young population. At the same time, outmigration in WM has been coupled with high numbers of NEETs (20% of youth 15-24, 14% national average) among the remaining young population. Within this context, Kozani (industrial sector accounts for 60% of GVA) the mid-sized capital city of WM, with a population of 67,224, faces multiple intertwined challenges, including economic hardship (unemployment 16,4%, ELSTAT 2022), environmental concerns, demographic shifts (3,5% population decline in 10 years). Moreover, unlike some other regions in Greece, Kozani lacks significant natural attractions or major archaeological sites to draw tourists. Despite these challenges, Kozani is striving for a "smart and alternative development" driven by innovation and investments. Moreover, the EU included Kozani in the European Mission of 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities by 2030. However, this endeavour is particularly challenging due to limited options for economic diversification. Additionally, these new development strategies remain top-down plans that have weak local grounding. Against this background, a just work transition in Kozani is closely tied to the need to transition away from lignite-based industries, while preserving the city's cultural identity and productive social capital at all ages and social groups. The youth drain, combined with prolonged structural problems, pinpoint the need for alternative employment outlets.
innovations.description: EcoZani perceives cities’ attractiveness in terms of productive social capital within the economic development triad of Talent-Technology-Tolerance. The project develops 3 T-ecosystems, to address the challenge of just work transition in the de-lignitisation era, by empowering the city’s productive social capital and preserving its socio-cultural identity. Employing the Kozani Carnival as a driver with strong bonds within generations and communities, Ecozani works towards an integrated legacy: the strategic goal is to unearth, harness and retain talent, while the tactics is to turn the event into the first Zero-waste/ Zero-emission/ Zero-exclusion (3Z) Carnival in Greece and Europe. - The Ecosystem of Talent develops a local ‘Talent Booster’ reinforcing local youth entrepreneurship by initiating a Business Youth Competition, to innovate round the 3Z transformation of Kozani’s Carnival. - The Ecosystem of Technology hosts a hands-on group of activities towards the production of new 3Z products, their application to the re-branded Carnival and the establishment of its legacy through: i) the UpCycle Creative Reuse Center and ii) the Municipal Inclusive Circu-Tech Hub in the renovated Railway Organisation Premises. - The Ecosystem of Tolerance opens EcoZani’s vision to the ‘city’. From a 3Z Carnival to a 3Z City and from 10-day to 365 use of 3Z products, includes public consultation for urban acupuncturing interventions as physical reminders of the city’s 3Z transition including upskilling/ reskilling training programmes and capacity building for unemployed people, vocational education learners and municipal administrators.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Public and Private support of youth innovation and entrepreneurship: - young people remain in Kozani, attempting to work, create, entreprendre, innovate and live in the city and its rural periphery - MoK expands its capacity to operationaly support the MICTH (incl. incubator, accelerator, fablab, coworking & community space) - young entrepreneurs and existing businesses feel supported by the local governance - young entrepreneurs and existing businesses get free support by the partneship experts on several topics of skills building (green, business, management, marketing, digital, circular, community liaison, etc.) - MoK strengthens its plans towards just work transition Activation of trans-local communities and business ecosystems: -The transition strategies get grounded to the local scale, becoming popular among local businesses and inhabitants -Local inhabitants join public consultation and participatory planning processes -Young vocational education learners, NEETs and unemployed youth get upskilled though training modules and internship in public structures and SMEs -The urban core - rural periphery relationship is being enhanced through the Business Youth Competition and the co-creation of 3Z products for agricultural purposes -People from Kozani all over the world are proud for the Carnival's re-branding as the first 3Z big event in Greece and Europe High level of innovation diffusion readiness among cities of WM and other urban contexts in Europe: -MoK is a pioneering city of WM with respect to just work transition away from lignite-based industries and preservation of its cultural identity and its productive social capital at all ages and social groups, with a special focus on youth (15-30) -MoK initiates peer-learning networks and partnerships with translocal events/festivals, with Greek and European Cities for 3Z Management of Big Events / Carnivals, with Green Transition Cities -MoK expands its capacity to transfer knowledge and heritage re-branding

innovations.name: Impact Launchpad – Social Innovation & Impact Entrepreneurship Incubation Programme
innovations.problem: Many promising social innovation ideas fail to progress due to lack of structured support, limited entrepreneurial skills, insufficient access to mentors, and weak impact validation capacities. Early-stage innovators often lack networks, resources, and market-testing environments needed to turn ideas into viable, socially beneficial ventures.
innovations.description:
The programme integrates business development with impact measurement, lean experimentation, and systems-thinking approaches. It uses a validated “Impact Pathway” methodology developed within Impact Hub Slovenia, combining mentoring, peer validation, expert clinics, and early traction testing. Participants receive tailored guidance, access to a multidisciplinary mentor pool, and connections to investors and partners.
Support is delivered through a structured incubation pathway, where each participant progresses through clearly defined stages:
Problem and solution validation (defining user needs and testing assumptions)
Prototype and MVP development (creating first functional solutions)
Market testing and early traction (engaging first users or beneficiaries)
Impact measurement and model validation (defining and testing social/environmental impact)
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Impact Launchpad is a targeted incubation programme, distinct from the broader activities of Impact Hub Slovenia, focusing specifically on early-stage social innovators progressing from idea to validated solution. Since its launch, the programme has supported 120+ innovators, primarily individuals and small teams aged 18-35, including students, early-stage entrepreneurs, and individuals from NEET or underemployed backgrounds.
Participants have worked on solutions across sectors such as:
youth employment and skills development
mental health and wellbeing
sustainable consumption and circular economy
community-based services and inclusion
digital tools for education and social impact
Participants receive:
20+ hours of mentoring and expert support per team
access to a multidisciplinary mentor pool (business, impact, legal, finance)
peer-to-peer validation sessions to test ideas in a structured environment
support in developing business models, impact frameworks, and pitch materials
As a result:
teams developed validated concepts or MVPs, tested with real users or stakeholders
several teams progressed to further incubation or acceleration programmes (e.g. Impact Next, Social Impact Award follow-up programmes)
participants increased their employment readiness and entrepreneurial capacity, with a number transitioning into self-employment or founding early-stage ventures
multiple solutions have entered pilot implementation in collaboration with NGOs, municipalities, or schools
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: AER – a zero-waste store with natural products that bring you closer to nature
innovations.problem: Modern consumption habits often generate excess waste, especially through overpackaged goods, single-use plastics, and a lack of local, sustainable alternatives. Many consumers who want to reduce their ecological footprint struggle to find practical, everyday options that align with zero-waste and ethical values. On another front, local producers and artisans often lack platforms to reach customers who care about sustainability, and community engagement and environmental education are underdeveloped in many regions. AER seeks to address these gaps by creating a retail environment where sustainable consumption is accessible and by engaging the community through education and support for local producers.
innovations.description: AER’s innovation is based on combining multiple functions under one concept: a Zero Waste retail space, an artisan bakery, a café and relaxing green space, and a hub for community education projects. This hybrid model allows people to engage in sustainable consumption, experience ethically made food, and participate in ecological awareness programs. AER offers many products in bulk so customers can bring their own containers and reduce packaging waste. The store works with local, small-scale, and artisanal suppliers who share its sustainability principles. In the bakery, AER applies zero waste practices: it bakes in moderate quantities, transforms surplus into new products, and partners with anti-waste platforms to redistribute leftovers. Packaging is compostable or reusable, and ingredients are chosen for their quality and integrity. Through community projects such as ecological education for children (“STOP Verde”), local producers’ markets (“Colțul Lokal”), and workshops, AER integrates social and environmental values into everyday life. Profits are not distributed to owners but reinvested into community and educational initiatives.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Environmental impact: • Reduction of packaging waste by offering bulk products and encouraging customers to bring their own containers. • Use of compostable or reusable packaging in the bakery and store. • Prevention of food waste through moderate production, product transformation, and partnerships with anti-waste platforms. • Promotion of sustainable consumption habits among customers. Social impact: • Creation of a community space that encourages sustainable living and environmental awareness. • Educational programs for children and adults, including ecological workshops such as “STOP Verde.” • Support for local producers and artisans through dedicated initiatives like “Colțul Lokal.” • Strong focus on community engagement and environmental education. Economic and community benefits: • Support for the local economy by prioritizing local and small-scale suppliers. • Reinvestment of profits into community and educational initiatives. • Development of a business model that links commercial activity with positive social and environmental impact.

Through community projects such as ecological education for children (“STOP Verde”), local producers’ markets (“Colțul Lokal”), and workshops, AER integrates social and environmental values into everyday life. Profits are not distributed to owners but reinvested into community and educational initiatives.
Environmental impact: • Reduction of packaging waste by offering bulk products and encouraging customers to bring their own containers. • Use of compostable or reusable packaging in the bakery and store. • Prevention of food waste through moderate production, product transformation, and partnerships with anti-waste platforms. • Promotion of sustainable consumption habits among customers. Social impact: • Creation of a community space that encourages sustainable living and environmental awareness. • Educational programs for children and adults, including ecological workshops such as “STOP Verde.” • Support for local producers and artisans through dedicated initiatives like “Colțul Lokal.” • Strong focus on community engagement and environmental education. Economic and community benefits: • Support for the local economy by prioritizing local and small-scale suppliers. • Reinvestment of profits into community and educational initiatives. • Development of a business model that links commercial activity with positive social and environmental impact.

innovations.name: Ophori – natural cosmetics and fresh skincare with a social mission
innovations.problem: The cosmetics industry often contributes to environmental degradation through the use of synthetic ingredients, excessive packaging, and a lack of transparency. These practices generate waste and pollution, putting additional pressure on natural resources and ecosystems. At the same time, people with disabilities face significant barriers to entering the labour market. Many lack access to adapted workplaces and opportunities for stable employment, which limits their economic independence and social participation. Ophori addresses both challenges through an integrated model that combines responsible cosmetic production with meaningful employment opportunities for people with disabilities.
innovations.description: The innovative approach of Ophori is based on integrating sustainable cosmetic production with social inclusion and strong social values. All products are handcrafted using carefully selected ingredients, and the composition of each product is fully transparent and publicly available. The company uses recyclable and sustainable packaging to reduce environmental impact. Production takes place in a protected unit, where people with disabilities are directly involved in all stages of the process, from preparation to packaging. By operating as a legally recognised social insertion enterprise, Ophori combines environmental responsibility with a clear social mission, demonstrating that everyday consumer products can be produced in a way that respects both nature and people.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: Ophori demonstrates how a cosmetics brand can create both social and environmental value through a clear and transparent business model. As a protected unit and social insertion enterprise, the organisation employs mainly people with disabilities, offering adapted work conditions and stable jobs. This not only provides income but also supports professional development and inclusion in the labour market. All profits are reinvested in the social mission, ensuring that economic results directly strengthen community impact. From an environmental perspective, the company reduces waste by using recyclable and sustainable packaging, integrating environmental responsibility into its production and distribution practices. Through these combined efforts, Ophori positions itself as a responsible, community-oriented business that connects economic activity with environmental care and social inclusion.

innovations.name: Community Outreach for Inclusion of Ukrainian Refugees in Bulgaria and Romania - COEXIST
innovations.problem: The war in Ukraine has forced millions of people to seek refuge across Europe, including in Bulgaria and Romania. While emergency responses have provided short-term assistance, long-term social inclusion remains a major challenge. Refugees often face language barriers, cultural differences, limited access to education and employment, and social isolation. At the same time, local communities and institutions frequently lack the knowledge, tools, and structured frameworks needed to support meaningful integration. The project addresses the need to build local capacity, foster collaboration between refugees and host societies, and create innovative, sustainable pathways for inclusion and participation.
innovations.description: COEXIST introduces a research-driven and community-based approach to refugee inclusion, combining academic expertise with grassroots action. The University of Wroclaw (Poland) plays a central role in designing and testing innovative methodologies for social inclusion, mentorship, and community engagement. These methods are grounded in evidence-based research and adapted to the specific social contexts of Bulgaria and Romania. By merging scientific analysis with local experience, the project generates practical tools and learning models that strengthen the capacity of local actors to support refugees effectively. This collaboration between academia and civil society creates a new framework for social innovation—scalable, inclusive, and transferable across Europe.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Warm Rotterdam
innovations.problem:
Rotterdam is the poorest city in the Netherlands. About 18.5 percent of Rotterdammers live below the poverty line. That is more than 87,000 Rotterdammers who can no longer provide for the basic necessities of life. In some districts of the city, a quarter to a third of the inhabitants live in poverty. One in every six children in Rotterdam grows up in a poor family.
Of these people in poverty, more than half have been living on a low income for four years or more. These people have no financial reserves. A financial setback has major consequences. Small debts grow into substantial amounts, partly due to collection costs associated with these debts
innovations.description:
In 2016, the Pauluskerk (a church) started the Warm Rotterdam program. In 2019, Warm Rotterdam became an independent foundation. We are a network organisation of experts and partners. Our experts are experts by experience. Our partners include companies, the government and civil society organisations. Together we are committed to reducing the number of Rotterdammers in poverty. We raise awareness about poverty and develop effective approaches. To this end, we mobilize and bundle the knowledge and experiences of Rotterdammers who know what it is like to live in poverty and with debts. Additionally, we put system errors on the agenda and we encourage everyone to support our goal of chasing poverty out of the city
Our experts by experience are the basis of Warm Rotterdam. We listen to them because they know how disruptive (long-term) living in poverty and debt is. They also know what would have helped them. Their knowledge and skills are the basis for 1) campaigns, 2) for putting things on the agenda for policy and administration, and 3) for stimulating companies, social organisations and residents in the city.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
We come up with concrete solutions, such as sample letters, the basic shopping list ( de basisboodschappenlijst ), the Tobia (Tijdelijke Overbruggingskrediet Burgers in Armoede ), Warm Consultation Hours and the Quality Mark Warm Collection (Keurmerk Warm Incasseren).
We make Rotterdam aware of poverty, for example through our YouTube campaigns ‘ Armoede Voor Beginners’ en ‘Rotterdam slaat terug tegen armoede’ or the '50 euro challenge' in which we challenged politicians to live on 50 euros a week.
