innovations.name: RaumBooster
innovations.problem: Many local makers, small businesses, and cultural initiatives face high barriers when trying to access or activate affordable spaces. Activation costs such as deposits, renovation, or equipment often exceed their financial capacity, while public funding requires own contributions they cannot provide. At the same time, many ground-floor spaces remain vacant. This mismatch blocks social, cultural, and economic potential at neighbourhood level.
innovations.description:
The RaumBooster introduces a cooperative matchfunding model that links community crowdfunding with public and private co-funding. It lowers entry barriers for local initiatives by rewarding civic engagement with additional grants once a defined crowdfunding threshold is reached. This hybrid mechanism mobilises new resources, activates vacant spaces, and creates a replicable model for social innovation and local economic resilience.
The model was piloted in Vienna and Graz, and later adapted in Innsbruck through the “Aufrunden bitte” mechanism. In 2025, the concept evolved into WeCreateSpace, a co-financing system that structurally links crowdfunding with public funding schemes. It is also being applied in sheBOOST to mobilise community resources for women-led local makers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The pilots in Vienna, Graz demonstrated strong leverage effects: every euro of matchfunding mobilised up to 22 euros in community contributions. Seven campaigns enabled the activation or renovation of several spaces, including cultural centres and creative hubs. The model proved that combining public, private, and civic funds increases participation, strengthens local networks, and makes urban transformation more inclusive and effective.
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Solidary Europe for Inclusive Society
innovations.lead: Faculty of Economics and Business University of Zagreb
innovations.problem: Vocational education and training (VET) schools in Croatia provide significantly fewer learning opportunities related to the European Union compared to general secondary schools. As a result, many VET students have limited knowledge about EU institutions, values, rights and opportunities for participation. Teachers and school librarians often lack the competences, tailored resources and confidence to integrate EU topics into their teaching practice, which deepens inequality in civic education and student engagement. This gap contributes to lower levels of active citizenship and social inclusion among young people in VET pathways, particularly those coming from disadvantaged regions or backgrounds. EUsolis addresses these educational disparities by equipping educators with the knowledge and tools necessary to embed EU values such as solidarity, diversity and sustainability across subjects and extracurricular activities, ensuring more equal access to citizenship education for all learners.
innovations.description: EUsolis introduced a new model of EU citizenship education in vocational schools by empowering both teachers and school librarians as co-creators of learning, rather than relying solely on traditional civics instruction. The project developed a structured modular curriculum tailored to the VET context, focusing on solidarity, diversity, youth participation and sustainable development, and demonstrated how these EU values can be meaningfully incorporated into any subject area. By using school libraries and the European Documentation Centre as active learning hubs, the project expanded access to EU knowledge beyond the classroom. Practical workshops, regional Spring and Summer Schools and open digital resources ensured that educators could immediately transfer new knowledge into school activities, creating a sustainable and scalable model for inclusive EU learning across VET systems.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Faculty of Economics and Business University of Zagreb
innovations.evidence: EUsolis successfully improved access to EU-related learning in vocational education by building the competences of teachers and school librarians across Croatia. More than 50 educators from 15 VET schools participated in specialised training and regional capacity-building events, enabling them to integrate EU values into everyday teaching and school library activities. Four thematic educational modules and a complete set of open-access learning materials were developed to support continued use after the project’s end. The project strengthened collaboration among VET schools, created new opportunities for student engagement in EU topics and increased motivation for schools to participate in European programmes. As a result, thousands of students now benefit indirectly from improved inclusion, awareness and active citizenship education. The sustainability and effectiveness of the model have been validated through its continuation in EUsolis 2.0, expanding the benefits to more schools and regions.
authors: Faculty of Economics and Business University of Zagreb
tags: Equal access to education and training
Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: JOIN-UA-EMPLOY
innovations.problem: Across the EU, displaced Ukrainians face fragmented services, language barriers, and slow recognition of skills, resulting in under-employment and prolonged welfare dependence.
innovations.description: The project introduces a portable skills profile, common referral and case-management standards, and a shared employer-engagement playbook. It integrates quick language-on-the-job modules with sector-specific matching and uses real-time feedback loops (dashboards and learning reviews) so PES teams can adjust support rapidly and consistently across countries.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Pilots are expected to shorten time-to-first job, increase the share of quality placements (stable contracts, fair wages), and raise employer satisfaction. Beneficiaries gain faster access to suitable work and progression routes; PES gain reusable tools, staff training packages, and comparative evidence on “what works,” reducing cost per successful placement.

innovations.name: ToNite
innovations.problem: City services and urban public spaces are designed mainly for daily activities, when economic businesses and public/private services provide networking points for social protection in urban areas, even more important in deprived neighbourhoods and in peripheral areas. On the other hand, according to trends in urban agglomeration and changes in urban life styles, cities are more and more lived by night,with public spaces becoming increasingly attractive for activities such as social aggregations, organisation of events, exhibitions and cultural activities. During the night, economic activities and services are reduced and the function of social protection is assigned to the public security force and, in particular, to the Local Police, whose intervention is mainly based on a traditional approach of law enforcement and control.
innovations.description:
Activating new local services able to generate social impact in the evening and night-time. 19 projects (representing 59 local organizations) were selected and financed through a Call for applications and have been working to improve the quality of life of the target areas. Projects activated cultural, socio-educational or social-health facilities, also through the functional redevelopment and re-appropriation of some public spaces just limitedly valued or used by the residents.
Urban regeneration interventions, in order to bring beauty, light points, support for socializing and improve the livability of areas with evening and night-time potential still unexpressed or perceived as dangerous. 3 urban regeneration interventions were completed and more than 7000 square meters of public spaces were regenerated.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The process of activating local communities and the strong focus on public space experienced in ToNite were the guide for developing a urban regeneration programme funded by the National Programme for Metropolitan Cities (PN Metro Plus) for around 40 million €, comprising physical interventions on public spaces and intangible actions aimed at social and cultural inclusion and the development of neighbourhood services. The urban regeneration programme operates in the same target areas as ToNite and includes a new social innovation measure called 'ImpatTO', to the value of 2.4 million €, which continues the work done by the UIA project of activating local communities and creating community spaces that offer proximity services.

Activating new local services able to generate social impact in the evening and night-time. 19 projects (representing 59 local organizations) were selected and financed through a Call for applications and have been working to improve the quality of life of the target areas. Projects activated cultural, socio-educational or social-health facilities, also through the functional redevelopment and re-appropriation of some public spaces just limitedly valued or used by the residents.
Urban regeneration interventions, in order to bring beauty, light points, support for socializing and improve the livability of areas with evening and night-time potential still unexpressed or perceived as dangerous. 3 urban regeneration interventions were completed and more than 7000 square meters of public spaces were regenerated.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer: The process of activating local communities and the strong focus on public space experienced in ToNite were the guide for developing a urban regeneration programme funded by the National Programme for Metropolitan Cities (PN Metro Plus) for around 40 million €, comprising physical interventions on public spaces and intangible actions aimed at social and cultural inclusion and the development of neighbourhood services. The urban regeneration programme operates in the same target areas as ToNite and includes a new social innovation measure called 'ImpatTO', to the value of 2.4 million €, which continues the work done by the UIA project of activating local communities and creating community spaces that offer proximity services.

innovations.raw_text:
ToNite
City services and urban public spaces are designed mainly for daily activities, when economic businesses and public/private services provide networking points for social protection in urban areas, even more important in deprived neighbourhoods and in peripheral areas. On the other hand, according to trends in urban agglomeration and changes in urban life styles, cities are more and more lived by night,with public spaces becoming increasingly attractive for activities such as social aggregations, organisation of events, exhibitions and cultural activities. During the night, economic activities and services are reduced and the function of social protection is assigned to the public security force and, in particular, to the Local Police, whose intervention is mainly based on a traditional approach of law enforcement and control.

innovations.name: Support for pre-primary education of children from marginalised Roma communites II
innovations.lead: The Office of the Government Plenipotentiary for Roma Communities
innovations.problem: The national project PRIM II addressed the low participation of children from marginalized Roma communities (MRC) in preschool education and the resulting educational disadvantages. It specifically focused on: Removing barriers preventing Roma children from attending kindergartens (social, economic, cultural, and communication barriers), Improving school readiness of children entering primary education, Creating inclusive environments in kindergartens that respond to children’s diverse social backgrounds, Strengthening cooperation between schools and families, mainly through new roles such as parental assistants, Stabilizing support professions in education and employing Roma men and women in these positions, And overall, reducing social exclusion and promoting equal educational opportunities from early childhood.
innovations.description: • A new position of parental assistant was established in kindergartens, filled by Roma men and women from the local community. These assistants effectively built a bridge between the kindergarten and families, increasing children’s attendance and parents’ trust in education. • The implemented stimulation program aimed at addressing partial developmental deficits proved effective over three school years. Only 1.45% of children entered the special education system, compared to the usual 16% in the Roma population in Slovakia. • Preferential employment of Roma in the education system has proven beneficial for all parties: it breaks down barriers among the majority population, enhances understanding of Roma socio-cultural specifics, and helps Roma gain dignified employment, often for the first time. This opportunity motivates them to pursue further education and contribute positively to their communities. • Kindergartens were better prepared for the COVID-19 pandemic, adapting to restrictions by continuing education beyond school premises. Many staff personally delivered worksheets to communities and provided strong support to parents. • Many consider the greatest success that children from Roma communities who attended at least one year of preschool and participated in stimulation activities performed well later in primary school. • By using lump-sum funding according to their specific needs, kindergartens improved material conditions for educating Roma children both during and beyond the project’s duration.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: The Office of the Government Plenipotentiary for Roma Communities
innovations.evidence:
Results of NP PRIM II: 9,048 Roma children attended at least one year of preschool. 747 project-funded staff worked in kindergartens: 311 teacher assistants, 141 specialists (mainly special educators), 140 parental assistants, and 155 inclusion coordinators. 315 Roma men and women were employed as part of inclusive teams — mainly as parental assistants (140), but also as 154 teacher assistants, 17 specialists, and 4 coordinators. 417 training events were organized for inclusion teams (methodological workshops, micro-regional meetings). 418 kindergarten staff completed a long-term educational program on innovative inclusive approaches (organized by Škola plus s.r.o., 40 groups, 80 sessions). Stimulation success rates: Children aged 3–4 years: 79.11% Children aged 5–6 years: 72.07% Only 1.45% of children were placed in the special education system (compared to the typical 6% in the Roma population), showing improved inclusion in mainstream education.
Kindergartens involved in NP PRIM II transitioned in September 2023 to a new project managed by the Ministry of Education, Science, Research and Sport of the Slovak Republic through the National Institute for Education and Youth (NIVaM) – the NP Supporting Professions 3 project. All positions were transferred to the new project, with some gradually shifting to state budget funding.
authors: The Office of the Government Plenipotentiary for Roma Communities

innovations.name: Scaling-up Integrated Services within Resilience and Innovation Facilities for Ukrainian Refugees Inclusion Project acronym: RIF4UA
innovations.lead: Terre des hommes Foundation - Aide a l'enfance dans le monde
innovations.problem: Terre des hommes conducted a comprehensive needs assessment to inform the project design, aligning the findings with existing research on refugee integration. The assessment identified the following key challenges faced by Ukrainian refugees: 1. Language and communication barriers: Limited proficiency in the local language significantly hinders access to education and employment opportunities. 2. Recognition of qualifications: Difficulties in validating Ukrainian qualifications and navigating bureaucratic procedures in both countries restrict access to the labor market. 3. Cultural adaptation: Adjusting to a new cultural and social system is challenging, particularly for young refugees who must learn and conform to local norms and practices. 4. Discrimination and prejudice: Instances of bias and social exclusion have been increasing since mid-2023, negatively affecting refugees’ morale and limiting access to employment and public services. 5. Family responsibilities: Caregiving obligations, especially for mothers, create additional barriers to entering the workforce when childcare options are limited.
innovations.description:
The innovation in this project lies in transforming existing Resilience Innovation Facilities (RIFs) from purely digital skills hubs into integrated service centers for social inclusion of refugees, with a multi-dimensional approach that links education, psychosocial support, and labor market access. By combining language learning, intercultural and psychosocial support, guidance on navigating bureaucratic systems, and labor market facilitation, the project goes beyond traditional single-focus interventions. It also includes access to preschool activities for children, enabling caregivers, particularly mothers, to engage in training or employment. This multi-dimensional methodology addresses the interconnected barriers refugees face, ranging from skills gaps and cultural adaptation to discrimination and family responsibilities, in a single, coordinated framework.
The project builds upon the successful piloting of the Resilience Innovation Facility (RIFs) approach by Terre des homme Lausanne globally, and aims to replicate and strengthen its reach and impact from learning and experiences of other partners and contexts in Romania and Hungary. The RIF approach builds upon the work of Tdh in setting up FabLabs in humanitarian contexts, including in Ukraine, Greece, Guinea, Burkina Faso and Kenya, targeting refugees and other disadvantaged groups, including with youth from the detention centre in Braila, Romania, a project supported through the European JUST programme.  Tdh piloted the RIF in Gyor Hungary from 2021 with children and youth from disadvantaged communities. Over 600 children accessed the Innovative space and over 75% of them felt empowered and self confident towards their future by attending over 200 workshops provided. The piloting of the RIF in Gyor, Hungary by Tdh showed that 85% of children and youth are reporting thinking that they can do most things if they try thanks to the activities they took part to. 78% are reporting thinking now that there are a lot of things that they do well and 82% are reporting improved knowledge on their skills, strengths and what is challenging to them. The project successfully achieved its goals of enhancing the self-confidence, social inclusion, and connectedness of participating children and youth, providing a constructive way for them to spend their free time, and promoting a sense of inclusion and empowerment. Children and youth benefited from an innovative environment for skill-building and personal growth. Similar trends were experienced from the RIFs set up in Romania.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: Terre des hommes Foundation - Aide a l'enfance dans le monde
innovations.evidence: The project is expected to generate significant results and benefits for both Ukrainian refugees and host communities in Budapest and Brașov. Participants, including youth and adults, will experience enhanced social inclusion, resilience, and self-confidence through engagement in educational, psychosocial, and intercultural activities, fostering a stronger sense of belonging. Refugees will also improve their language proficiency, vocational skills, and digital competencies, increasing employability and their ability to navigate local systems effectively. Access to employment and essential services will be facilitated through guidance on labor market integration, recognition of qualifications, and bureaucratic procedures, reducing barriers to economic and social participation. Additionally, the provision of preschool activities and childcare support will enable caregivers, particularly mothers, to engage in training or enter the workforce, strengthening family support and overall community integration. By combining these elements, the project promotes a holistic, sustainable model of inclusion, empowerment, and social cohesion that benefits both refugees and the wider local population.
authors: Terre des hommes Foundation - Aide a l'enfance dans le monde

innovations.name: Etika
innovations.problem:
Households increasingly face challenges in the liberalized energy market : rising prices, lack of transparency, and difficulty accessing renewable sources. At the same time, social inequalities persist—especially for people with disabilities who struggle to find affordable and inclusive housing. Traditional welfare systems and isolated sustainability initiatives have proved insufficient to connect environmental goals with tangible social inclusion . The key problem is how to combine the energy transition with community welfare in a fair, participatory, and economically viable way.
Etika supports projects that promote independent and inclusive living for people with disabilities. Independent living means enabling people with disabilities to decide where and with whom to live (UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities), encouraging separation from the family of origin — a transition that, for everyone, marks the passage into adult life.
Supporting people with disabilities in achieving social living is a demanding task that requires an anthropological and ethical vision , as well as specific technical, psychological, and educational expertise. Etika supports projects that bring together these two perspectives.
innovations.description:
Etika offers an integrated , cooperative response linking renewable energy and social solidarity. Created in 2016 by the Federazione Trentina della Cooperazione with Dolomiti Energia and other cooperative partners, Etika is a cooperative purchasing group that supplies 100% renewable and certified electricity and gas to families .
Each contract generates contributions to a permanent Social Fund , financing projects for inclusive housing, education, and cultural accessibility.
The model merges the Green Economy with the Social Economy, combining environmental responsibility, citizen participation, and mutualistic redistribution — transforming energy consumption into a tool for community development.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Over 71,000 contracts signed by 2024 , with a projected 80,000 by 2026.
105,937 tons of CO₂ avoided , equivalent to 5.3 million trees planted .
€4.4 million collected and €3.1 million invested in over 50 social projects supporting people with disabilities, education, and culture.
Strong partnerships across sectors (energy, finance, social inclusion, and education).
Improved consumer awareness on sustainable energy use and community welfare. The benefits are both environmental (lower emissions, efficient energy use) and social (inclusive living solutions, empowerment of vulnerable groups, participatory governance).
Etika promotes social inclusion and independent living for people with disabilities through its Social Fund , which finances innovative housing and community projects. The funds are collected from Etika’s energy users and allocated through public calls for proposals . The Scientific Committee , composed of experts, ensures transparency, quality, and impact assessment, and has developed a Cultural Manifesto and Guidelines for project design. Among Etika’s initiatives are “The Paths of Etika”, which shares stories of supported projects, and “Corpographies”, a three-year art and inclusion program created with Oriente Occidente and local cooperatives, using dance and performance to promote accessibility and cultural participation. Through these actions, Etika fosters a network of organizations and communities working together for a more inclusive society.

innovations.name: Villages Vivants
innovations.problem: In many rural areas, empty shops and closed shutters are a common sight. When a café, bakery, or grocery store closes, daily services and community life disappear with it. Yet local initiatives are flourishing. An abandoned factory can become a shared space for 50 people. A bookstore, a bike repair workshop, or a reuse center can breathe new life into rural areas. Every day, these communities are reinventing local consumption and solidarity. They respond to real local needs and focus on social impact, not profit. They are close to people, fostering connection and community. However, these initiatives often face significant challenges to settle in rural areas, such as accessing high-quality, suitable, energy-efficient premises at a fair price. Occasionally, a supportive community or a “solidarity” private owner can fill this role, but more often, project leaders have to face complex and challenging processes. They have to gett their project off the ground (legal registration, governance, economic model...) while simultaneously managing a real estate project, which demands substantial funding and technical expertise. This reality highlights the clear need—and mutual desire—for a solution to bridge this gap. Villages Vivants aims at to providing a practical, hands-on approach that enables commercial, artisanal, and community activities to take root in rural areas, transforming them into spaces that combine multiple uses and functions. These are places for social interaction and community life, fostering regional balance, celebrating local identities, and supporting greater autonomy.
innovations.description:
Villages Vivants is a rural, citizen-driven, and solidarity-focused cooperative that buys, renovates, and rents premises to host activities with social impact in rural areas. We support social and solidarity economy projects, unconventional initiatives, citizen-led dynamics, and shared spaces, helping to revitalize villages and foster community life. We also partner with local authorities and collectives with real estate projects. Through solidarity-based investments from citizens and partners, Villages Vivants can acquire new premises, strengthen its social impact, and contribute to vibrant, thriving rural communities.
This project has been developed in close collaboration with numerous local development actors and rural stakeholders, such as Terre de Liens, Habitat et Humanisme, GRAP, Ronalpia, URSCOP, Grenade...
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Villages Vivants supports initiatives led by local residents. All of these projects share a common goal: providing useful services—such as workplaces, sustainable food, personal services, access to culture, mobility, and more—while giving residents the opportunity to get involved and connected. Residents can participate as volunteers, customers, donors, investors, employees, or decision-makers in their village’s projects. By facilitating access to the premises, we make it easier for these initiatives to get off the ground and help ensure their long-term sustainability.

innovations.name: YoU Decide - Supporting Displaced Youth of Ukraine in Making Informed Decisions
innovations.problem: The project addresses the risks faced by displaced Ukrainian youth during their transition into adulthood, including limited access to reliable information, fragmented support systems, and heightened vulnerability to exploitation and exclusion. By understanding their specific needs and tailoring solutions through safe digital tools, dialogue with local stakeholders, and awareness raising, the project seeks to close critical gaps in integration and ensure that young people can access the rights and opportunities essential for their well-being and future.
innovations.description: The You Decide project introduces a digital “one-stop shop” app that provides displaced youth with safe, localised, and multilingual access to services and support systems in their place of residence. What makes this approach innovative is its participatory design: Ukrainian youth are directly engaged in co-developing project tools, ensuring that the solutions are relevant, user-friendly, and truly meet the needs of the target group. This combination of technology and youth-led design bridges existing gaps in information access and integration support.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: 1) Development of a multilingual digital app providing displaced youth with safe, localised access to information on available services tailored to their needs (education, employment, health, and social services). 2)Mapping of at least 145 services a across three capital regions of Prague, Warsaw and Budapest to improve coordination and reduce service gaps. 3) Establishment of Local Youth Integration Hubs, fostering dialogue and cooperation between young people, service providers, and authorities. 4) Increased awareness among youth of their rights and available support, reducing risks of exploitation, trafficking, and exclusion. 5) Policy recommendations and best practices disseminated at national and EU levels, strengthening long-term integration frameworks. 6) Empowerment of displaced Ukrainian youth through participation in co-design, ensuring that solutions are relevant, trusted, and sustainable.
tags: Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Hero’s Journey
innovations.problem: Since 2024, Lithuania has implemented inclusive education, where children with Special Educational Needs (SEN) attend mainstream schools. However, existing teaching tools are not adapted to universal design principles. Teachers lack accessible visual, non-verbal, or SEN-specific tools, which results in exclusion, bullying, and difficulties for children to reach their potential. We aim to make easier life for educators. To offer the tool kit to make them the biggest concentration being with kids during the lessons, and to have plan for running it.
innovations.description: The project introduces an innovative universal design of educational materials, integrating neuropsychology and emotional self-regulation insights. The solution includes methodological material, reflection and situation cards, posters for self-reflection and self-regulation skills, a guide, and lesson plans. These resources are visually appealing, playful, and practical, ensuring inclusivity and emotional development in schools, day care centers, and homes.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Increased inclusion of children with SEN in group activities. Reduction of bullying in participating groups. Strengthened resilience for socially excluded children (e.g., from disadvantaged backgrounds). Impact on at least 1,500 children in Lithuania within the first year (including 50 with SEN, 500 from vulnerable families, and 700 from rural areas). Tools will support teachers and parents, foster empathy, cooperation, and problem-solving skills.
Already piloted in over 120 Lithuanian classrooms with previous methodology. Planned piloting in 12 schools and day centers within the year (pilot stage). Expansion to 100 more schools/day centers after the pilot. International partnerships in Ukraine (school network, supporting post-war education) and Sweden. Collaboration with global partners such as Think Equal and Gemmes ensures adaptation and use in international contexts.
tags: Equal access to education and training
Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: TechCheck & Cite
innovations.problem: When a student submits their final thesis for technical review, feedback can take days or even weeks. Faculty staff spends approximately 24 thousand hours annually to manually check theses formatting and citations. During peak submission periods, this workload becomes unmanageable. High resubmission rates lead to graduation delays, as each rejected thesis requires another round of manual review, creating a cascade of inefficiency. Manual checking is also inconsistent, as some errors are caught while others slip through, leaving students with a perception of arbitrariness in the process, and the faculty with the perception of rules inconsistencies. Additionally, students struggle with formatting source citations correctly and adhering to diverse referencing standards, which is an essential skill, but also a bottleneck of academic writing. Cite directly addresses this problem by automatically citing research papers according to faculty- and journal-specific styles and rules. The algorithm can also verify citations against a newly specified custom set of rules, reducing mistakes and supporting consistent, accurate academic writing and literacy.
innovations.description: TechCheck & Cite offer a joint solution that redefines how academic writing and digital literacy are supported. While many tools focus on literature reviews (fostering academic indecency), mere reference management or plagiarism detection, none address the technical dimensions of academic writing: technical editing, formatting, structure, presentation and citations all at once. TechCheck combines educational guidance with automated technical checks, ensuring documents consistently meet institutional standards. Within this ecosystem, Cite functions both as a dedicated module as well as a standalone solution powered by a custom-built citation algorithm based on over 100 hours of researching academic writing rules of all Slovenian faculties and major internationally used citation and referencing styles. This foundation enables automated, accurate verification of citations and references — integrated seamlessly into TechCheck. Together, they deliver a holistic platform for academic and digital literacy, guiding users toward precise, professional and credible academic outputs.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: TechCheck saves faculty staff significant chunks of time by automating technical reviews, ensuring that submissions consistently follow formatting and structural requirements. For students and researchers, it provides interactive, real-time feedback, building both digital literacy and academic writing skills. By detecting and correcting errors early, TechCheck reduces the number of resubmissions, helping prevent delays in graduation or publication. With the integration of Cite, users also benefit from automated source referencing and citation-checking that guarantees compliance with faculty-specific and international referencing standards. This not only improves the quality and credibility of academic work but also reduces the burden on supervisors and editors. The platform is designed to integrate seamlessly with existing learning management systems used by universities and scientific journalis, making it accessible across disciplines and academic levels and ensuring broad impact for institutions and individuals alike.

Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: SciComic
innovations.problem: On one hand, one in seven people have some kind of learning difficulties such as dyslexia, ADHD or dyspraxia. These challenges do not reflect intelligence, but rather the need for alternative learning methods. Because of this, two-thirds of such students never obtain a university degree, as highly specialised language makes traditional academic texts often inaccessible. Current adaptations in educational systems are limited and mostly targeted at primary and secondary schools, leaving university students without sufficient support. Students often resort to time-consuming methods such as animated educational videos or expensive private tutoring, which are unsustainable solutions in the long run. On the other hand, researchers spend years producing valuable papers that are read by only a handful of people, meaning their work does not reach its full impact potential. This double-sided problem — inaccessible learning for students and limited dissemination for researchers — creates barriers to equal education, contributes to low study completion rates, and hinders the broader use and sharing of scientific knowledge.
innovations.description: SciComic is the world’s first complex-to-simple translator that utilises innovative technology to transform complex research papers into popular-science comics. By integrating multiple leading large language models with prompt engineering, keyword mapping, tailored illustrations and our own state-of-the-art fact verification loop, our web app enables students with learning difficulties to comprehend research papers quickly and effectively, while also helping researchers reach a wider audience. Unlike existing adaptations that mainly focus on intermediary switches between reading and listening, as well as unreliable generative AI tools, SciComic provides inclusive support for a broader spectrum of learning difficulties, reducing cognitive load and offering alternative learning formats. Built with scalable technologies such as Node.js, React and TypeScript, and supported by PostgreSQL and MongoDB, the app delivers results in under two minutes and requires minimal human intervention, making it both efficient and sustainable. In this way, SciComic democratises access to higher education and maximises the visibility and impact of scientific research.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: SciComic enables students with learning difficulties to comprehend research papers significantly faster, reducing study time and increasing the likelihood of completing their university degrees. Researchers benefit from greater visibility and engagement, ensuring their work reaches a wider audience. By providing an efficient, affordable, and inclusive platform, SciComic measurably improves accessibility to academic knowledge, supports educational success, and contributes to a more equitable and participatory academic environment for tens of thousands of students in the region and millions globally.

innovations.name: Enhacing Employability and Social Integration with Innovative Solutions for Displaced People from Ukraine in the Baltics
innovations.problem: Displaced individuals from Ukraine face multiple challenges as they seek stability and integration in the Baltic states. Many struggle to find employment that matches their qualifications or lack the skills required by the local labor market, creating significant employment and skills gaps. Language barriers and limited knowledge of local culture, systems, and norms further hinder integration efforts. These challenges often contribute to social exclusion, loneliness, and psychological distress, leaving many displaced persons feeling isolated from their new communities. In addition, difficulties in accessing accurate and timely information about essential services—such as healthcare, education, and legal support—create further obstacles to building a secure and independent life.

innovations.name: Support for Ukrainian children in the integration process in schools within the Slovak and Czech Republic
innovations.lead: The Center for Inclusive Education, Krajské centrum vzdělávání
innovations.problem: The project addresses the insufficient and fragmented support for Ukrainian refugee children in Slovak and Czech schools. The projects activities build progressively from direct work with Ukrainian children and parents, focusing on language, psychosocial, and career needs, to training experts, revising existing materials, and creating new teaching methods and textbooks that are lacking in both countries.
innovations.description: Early activities analyze current support systems, identify gaps, and propose sustainable recommendations. This leads to advocacy efforts, proposals for legislative changes, and public awareness-raising to ensure lasting impact.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: The Center for Inclusive Education, Krajské centrum vzdělávání
innovations.evidence:
The consortium combines governmental and non-profit partners with extensive networks, offering both grassroots flexibility and policy-level influence, and represents a model for Central and Eastern Europe, where refugee support systems are still developing despite high demand.
Key outcomes include: - a multidisciplinary support system for Ukrainian children,
- improved services in psychosocial care and language learning,
- enhanced teacher training, stronger integration outcomes, and
- effective cooperation between NGOs and government bodies. The project aims to integrate this model into Slovak and Czech national education budgets and policies for sustainable refugee support.

innovations.name: A Million Voices: Uniting Through Stories
innovations.problem:
The project addresses the psychological distress, social isolation, and lack of meaningful integration faced by Ukrainian refugees following Russia’s war of aggression. Traditional support systems often overlook emotional well-being and do not sufficiently connect refugees with host communities.
The project responds to the humanitarian crisis caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine , which has displaced millions of people into the EU. Refugees face elevated levels of psychosocial stress, trauma, social isolation, and integration barriers . While basic needs such as housing and education are addressed, mental health and social inclusion remain underserved areas .
International and European reports, including the UN’s State of Youth in Ukraine (2019) and the European Commission’s Youth Work Quality Systems (2017) , highlight significant gaps in psychosocial support and integration practices. A Million Voices addresses these by combining therapy, creativity, and social engagement, using innovative, non-formal, and culturally sensitive approaches .
innovations.description:
The project introduces a holistic and creative approach by combining art therapy (dance, music, painting, cooking) with narrative techniques (interviews, storytelling events, digital storytelling). It also integrates nature walks and multimedia to share refugee stories, making mental health support more accessible, inclusive, and community-oriented.
Types of Activities and Delivery Method Activities are professional-led, inclusive, and implemented in all three countries:
Art Therapy Programs: At least 7 workshops per country (singing, painting, gong therapy, dance therapy). Each session hosts 15–20 participants and is delivered by trained facilitators.
Community Events: Each country organises 1 cooking/dinner event , 1 outdoor movie night , 1 movie evening and 2 storytelling picnics . 1 car painting activity will be organized only in Lithuania and attended by 30 participants. These events create safe and informal spaces for integration and cultural exchange.
Murals & Opening Events: In each partner country, a large-scale mural will be co-created by refugees and local youth on a public building. Professional artists guide the process, but refugees and locals contribute to the design and painting. Once completed, each mural will be inaugurated with a public opening event , gathering at least 30 participants, community leaders, and media. The murals act as permanent, visible reminders of resilience and inclusion, anchoring the project in the urban landscape.
Story Collection & Dissemination: At least 15 interviews per country with refugees, locals, and social workers. Stories will be shared via Spotify, YouTube, QR codes on murals , and a short documentary .
Nature Walk Paths with Digital Storytelling: In each partner country, a dedicated walk path will be created where Ukrainian refugee stories are embedded into the landscape using QR codes, sound recordings, and digital platforms . This innovative method combines well-being through nature with narrative therapy, allowing both refugees and locals to experience stories in an immersive and reflective way.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Scale and Reach
450+ direct participants : 270 refugees, 135 locals, 45 professionals/social workers.
Tens of thousands indirect beneficiaries via digital storytelling, outdoor installations, documentary dissemination, and public events.
Activities take place in community centres, cultural venues, and outdoor public spaces across Lithuania, Poland, and Germany, ensuring accessibility, visibility, and long-term impact.
Key results and benefits
Improved emotional well-being of Ukrainian refugees Stronger bonds between refugees and local communities Increased public awareness through storytelling events and a documentary A replicable model of art-based refugee support Empowered participants with new creative and communicative skills

innovations.name: The Youth Activation Agency INCORPORATES European mobility
innovations.problem: Spain is one of the European countries with the highest youth unemployment rate recorded, reaching approximately 38% for those aged between 16 and 25. In the case of Asturias, in the fourth quarter of 2022, a youth unemployment rate of 47.56% was recorded, which represents a variation of 4.01 percentage points with respect to the data recorded in the previous period. The high youth unemployment rate has many negative economic and social consequences. From the social point of view, this situation of unemployment has a negative psychological impact on unemployed young people, as it lowers their self-esteem, can lead to problems of social acceptance and is a major constraint on their independence and personal development. This situation not only generates discomfort not only for the young people who suffer from it, but also for their families and the rest of society, thus becoming a problem that affects the population. On an economic level, there are also negative consequences derived from the loss of quality human capital and the loss of talent, which leads to a lack of competitiveness in the economy. In addition, the high rate causes one of the most serious problems faced by companies today, which is the talent drain, driving qualified people to look for job opportunities in other cities and even countries. This leads to serious consequences such as economic losses and reduced competitiveness of the affected sectors. At the economic level, we also find negative consequences derived from the uselessness of quality human capital and the loss of talent, which results in the lack of competitiveness of the economy. In addition, the high rate causes one of the most serious problems facing companies today, which is the talent drain, driving qualified people to look for job opportunities in other cities and even countries. This leads to serious consequences such as economic losses and reduced competitiveness of the affected sectors. For this reason, it is essential to develop programmes to adapt the professional needs of young people to the needs of companies to retain talent, thereby increasing their employability. Likewise, as formulas to solve this issue, they will carry out networking events that, together with the public-private collaboration within the framework of the project, will bring the young participants closer to the companies in the territory.
innovations.description: The main objective of this project was to improve the employability and interpersonal skills of 25 young people between 16 and 29 years old who are neither studying, nor in training, nor working, through advice and development of comprehensive training actions appropriate to their profile and interests, with special emphasis on training for employment in training actions with potential for employment generation and that allow cultural exchange and experiences in the field of the European labour market.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: The target group to which the expected results of this project were addressed was made up of young people between 16- and 29-years old living in Gijón, who were neither working nor undergoing training and who have been selected to participate in the project. This target group was benefit directly from the project because thanks to this project they got, firstly, access to both complementary and specific training that provided them with the knowledge and personal and professional skills necessary to successfully enter the labour market and, on the other hand, allowed them to experience the opportunity to live and work in another EU country, with the consequent personal and professional growth that this entails. This directly contributed to reduce one of the needs detected and which was the basis of this project, and which lay in the high rate of youth unemployment in the city of Gijón and the social, self-esteem and economic problems that this generates in the young population belonging to the target group. The activities from which the results were achieved are, mainly, the provision of complementary and specific training whose content was designed according to the needs of the current labour market and that, therefore, allowed young people to obtain a profile of interest for companies in the region. The internships abroad, which allowed them to apply in a practical way the skills and knowledge learnt and also allowed them to live a new and enriching experience and, on the other hand, it is also important to highlight the continuous monitoring tasks that the participants were be able to enjoy, which included personal coaching, labour intermediation and the monitoring, review and evaluation of the initial Work Plan established for each participant. Through the last-mentioned actions, it was possible to monitor the achievement of the objectives set and helped the beneficiaries to make the most of the opportunity they got.

innovations.problem: Vulnerable youth face multiple challenges during the transition phase from education to employment and require a range of support that goes beyond traditional interventions.   In many EU countries, as per example Spain or Greece, after many years of ESF and national funds investment in traditional vocational training and career guidance programmes, the situation for most vulnerable youth has not changed: the unemployment rates are still very high and affect the same target.  There is a critical gap between traditional interventions and vulnerable youth needs to engage with the labour market that explain this failure, among others:  - Reproducing regular mainstream education schemes, where vulnerable youth failed. - Having an established agenda that does not meet vulnerable youth individual needs. - Focusing just on facing professional challenges, forgetting the personal ones that often block vulnerable youth. - Focusing just on hard skills development or job search techniques, forgetting beneficiary’s empowerment through developing self-efficacy, emotional intelligence, soft skills and social capital. - Being delivered by professionals who are not seen by vulnerable youth as potential role models. - Not offering post-intervention support when the program is finished, whether they get a job or not.  New empowering and upskilling methodologies need to be developed, tested and assessed to support traditional interventions to address the challenge of vulnerable youth unemployment.
innovations.description: The social innovation goal is to establish mentoring as a new impactful and sustainable form of learning to empower and upskill vulnerable youth during the transition phase from education to engage with the labour market, increasing their employability and quality of life, complementing traditional vocational training and career guidance interventions, and enhancing community engagement, solidarity and helpfulness through volunteering.  The social innovation is based on Autoocupació’s successful mentoring program for underserved young entrepreneurs, scaled across Catalonia trhough public and private partnerships, across Spain trhough the Youth Business Spain network and across other EU countries through the Young entrepreneurs succeed project funded by the EEA & Norway Grants Fund for Youth Employment.  This proved mentoring methodology will be adapted to vulnerable youth needs, developing a new offer to be piloted in Catalonia and Thessaly through local public and private partnerships, assessed under a proper impact assessment framework and disseminated at EU level to facilitate its implementation in other countries, targets or contexts.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.beneficiaries: FUNDACIÓ PRIVADA PER A LA PROMOCIÓ DE L'AUTOOCUPACIÓ DE CATALUNYA, AN.KA SA - Development Agency of Karditsa,  Development Agency of Local Authorities - Private company non-profit
innovations.evidence: Ready 4 Work positions mentoring as an essential new form of learning with multiple objectives. An innovative mentoring methodology will be developed and implemented, including protocol, guidelines, and training materials (see document included as Annex). This approach will enhance the employability of young people facing vulnerability by upgrading their communication skills, capacity to access labour market opportunities, self-efficacy, and self-image. Through the facilitation of 90 mentor-mentee matches per country, the young people will have the opportunity to be guided by labour market experts in an experiential process. This voluntary knowledge transfer will complement the active engagement of the participant youth in new forms of learning, broadening their skills and knowledge base for personal and professional development. Furthermore, the improved capacity of the mentoring managers and volunteer mentors will benefit the entities involved in this project. The methodology, processes, and results of the project will be disseminated to at least 60 organisations outside the consortium, while the partners and EMN may share their know-how with organisations that are interested in this approach after the project ends. To this end, this intervention is expected to encourage cooperation between different public and private sector organisations and strengthen their partnerships.  The consortium considers the impact assessment framework as a crucial self-diagnostic and self-improvement tool, which aims to capture already from its design steps the voice of vulnerable youth, especially those currently inactive and/or long-term unemployed, i.e. those who often fly below the radar of PES, due to a perceived lack of trust towards those institutions. The end goal is to present this improved and tested impact assessment mixed methods tool, which then can be used by public and private organisations to evaluate similar interventions concerning VY based on a Theory of Change.
authors: FUNDACIÓ PRIVADA PER A LA PROMOCIÓ DE L'AUTOOCUPACIÓ DE CATALUNYA, AN.KA SA - Development Agency of Karditsa,  Development Agency of Local Authorities - Private company non-profit

innovations.name: „Culture360.ai – AI platform for CCI funding applications and business plans“
innovations.problem: Across the CCI sector, especially outside big cities, preparing grant applications and strategic documents is slow, costly and uncertain. Information on funding is fragmented across portals; formal PFSA/LKT/EU templates are complex; budget/KPI logic varies; and organisations lack in-house skills to meet compliance, language and formatting standards. Paying consultants is expensive and excludes smaller players. Generic AI assistants are not trained on Lithuanian/CCI specifics, don’t integrate cultural/funding datasets and produce outputs that require heavy manual fixing. These barriers reduce submission quality and volume, delay projects, and deepen inequalities between well-resourced institutions and small or regional creators.
innovations.description: Culture360.ai introduces a sector-specific, compliance-first approach to document creation in CCI. The platform orchestrates LT/EN language models with a rules engine that encodes PFSA/LKT/EU templates (sections, length, required annexes) and a budget/KPI builder with pre-tested formulas. Live connectors aggregate funding calls and cultural market data; users get context-aware suggestions (eligibility, evaluation criteria, indicators) inside the editor. A validator flags gaps (e.g., missing outputs, weak risk logic), while versioned exports produce submission-ready Word/PDF packages. Unlike generic AI, Culture360.ai is trained on CCI terminology and Lithuanian specifics, integrates public datasets, and enforces structure and metrics end-to end. This reduces errors and rework, standardises quality across small/regional organisations, and enables faster, fairer access to funding. The modular design (APIs, templates) makes it scalable across EU contexts while staying GDPR-compliant.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Productivity & cost: users prepare compliant applications, business plans and budgets 70–80% faster and 50–70% cheaper than hiring consultants. Volume & reach: ≥1,000 documents created and ≥500 submissions supported during the 18-month period. Quality: built-in rules/validator raise “submission-readiness” to ≥90% compliance before export, reducing rework and rejection risk. Inclusion: ≥60% of users from regions/outside big cities; ≥50% women/young creators targeted in pilots; discounted NGO licences. Capacity: ≥12 public webinars, office hours and helpdesk SLAs; reusable templates and KPI libraries. Governance & trust: GDPRcompliant EU cloud, 2FA, audit trails. Environmental co-benefits: remote-first, paper-light workflows reduce trips and printing. Sustainability: tiered SaaS revenue and API partners ensure continuity beyond grant funding.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: SoliCycle
innovations.problem: Every year large numbers of bicycles become waste while many urban residents lack affordable, reliable transport and access to job-training opportunities. Local authorities and waste centres need scalable solutions to divert bike waste from disposal, and socially vulnerable people need practical routes to employment. SoliCycle addresses both environmental (waste, loss of reusable material) and social (unemployment, skills gap, mobility access) problems.
innovations.description: SoliCycle’s innovation is an integrated, localised “repair-and-insertion” workshop model that: (1) sources large volumes of discarded bikes from déchetteries and community collections; (2) combines professional refurbishment and parts recovery with low-cost sales (often €50–€150) and community self-repair workshops; and (3) embeds a social insertion pathway by hiring trainees on supported contracts to carry out the technical refurbishment and gain job skills — creating a circular, social enterprise loop. SoliCycle was the first project of this sort in 2007, when the first workshop was opened.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
Proven diversion and reuse: in 2024 SoliCycle recovered 2,500 bicycles and sold 1,258 refurbished bikes along with 2,862 second-hand parts—preventing large volumes of bike waste and extending product lifecycles. Social impact : the workshops operate as insertion projects (e.g., ~12 people on insertion contracts in one site), providing practical training and employment pathways. Immediate social & skills impact (current staff survey):
97% of surveyed employees feel useful in their work.
100% say they do useful work.
62% say they learned to work in a team.
49% say they learned to be more professional.
21% found a solution to their housing situation.
19% received health advice.
34% say they are now better at administrative procedures.
Longer-term outcomes for former insertion employees (follow-up / survey):
25% of former insertion employees say the professional skills developed at SoliCycle were useful afterwards.
70–90% report that the relational / interpersonal skills gained at SoliCycle were useful later in their lives.
54% say SoliCycle had a positive impact on their life.
Employment status (cohort follow-up by time since SoliCycle):
6 months after: 20% in durable employment; 40% in training; 40% unemployed.
6–12 months after: 22% in durable employment; 22% in training; 44% unemployed.
12–24 months after: 53% in durable employment; 40% in training.
>24 months after: 71% in durable employment; 23% in training.
Affordable mobility : refurbished bikes are sold at low prices to improve transport access for low-income Environmental gains : reduced landfill and material waste, prolonging product life and reducing demand for new bicycle manufacturing.

innovations.name: Transformative Tourism in Practice
innovations.problem: The employment rate of people with disabilities in Hungary remains significantly below the EU average. In many cases, monotonous work takes place in segregated conditions. Hungarian society does not consider people with disabilities to be employable. Negative stereotypes and limited direct interaction contribute to their exclusion from the labour market and society. There was a need for a service model that enables inclusion through real-life, shared experiences.
innovations.description: To achieve a long-term and profound change in attitude at both the individual and community levels, positive experiences are needed for everyone involved that can override previous negative biases. To this end, the project introduced a new model of transformative tourism, where people with disabilities play an active, public-facing role in their work. The initiative combines employment creation with awareness-raising through interactive tourism packages. In addition to employing people with disabilities, it creates an interactive environment that provides all stakeholders with the opportunity for experience-based learning. Visitors pay for the programs, making the service sustainable and scalable.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence: 5 inclusive tourism packages developed Over 6,000 visitor days in 2023–2024 10 schools and 250 students involved in the pilot Active partnerships with companies and municipalities Paid employment created for people with disabilities Model included in tourism promotion platforms (e.g., pontMiskolc)

innovations.raw_text:
Transformative Tourism in Practice
The employment rate of people with disabilities in Hungary remains significantly below the EU average. In many cases, monotonous work takes place in segregated conditions. Hungarian society does not consider people with disabilities to be employable. Negative stereotypes and limited direct interaction contribute to their exclusion from the labour market and society. There was a need for a service model that enables inclusion through real-life, shared experiences.
To achieve a long-term and profound change in attitude at both the individual and community levels, positive experiences are needed for everyone involved that can override previous negative biases. To this end, the project introduced a new model of transformative tourism, where people with disabilities play an active, public-facing role in their work. The initiative combines employment creation with awareness-raising through interactive tourism packages. In addition to employing people with disabilities, it creates an interactive environment that provides all stakeholders with the opportunity for experience-based learning. Visitors pay for the programs, making the service sustainable and scalable.

innovations.name: CEGLAB – The Cegléd Volunteering Platform
innovations.problem: Despite its benefits, volunteering often lacks motivation or incentives for sustained participation. In many communities, a lack of engagement threatens the continuity of civil initiatives. Young people in particular are not easily mobilised without tangible rewards or digital solutions that match their lifestyle.
innovations.description: CEGLAB introduced a blockchain-powered digital reward system where volunteering is tracked and rewarded with CEGLAB points. These can be redeemed at participating local businesses. A circular model allows businesses to return unused points to civil or public organisations for redistribution, maintaining community flow. The system creates an ecosystem of value exchange, making volunteering more visible, traceable, and appealing.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: A functioning mobile app and blockchain-based point system were developed Multiple partners joined as volunteering hosts and point redemption partners The system successfully incentivised volunteering and strengthened local cooperation A tested model for generational engagement in local causes was established

innovations.name: CogHelp – Interactive Educational Tool for Persons with Intellectual Disabilities
innovations.problem: Traditional education methods are often ineffective for people with intellectual disabilities. Existing digital tools are rarely tailored to their needs, leading to cognitive overload (Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)) and low engagement. This limits their ability to acquire essential life and work skills. The learning abilities of people with intellectual disabilities can vary significantly; therefore, an adaptive learning system is necessary that takes individual differences into account.
innovations.description:
CogHelp was developed with a focus on the learning processes and cognitive functioning of people with intellectual disabilities in mind. The platform was designed based on the latest cognitive psychological, pedagogical, and neuropsychological research to provide users with an optimal learning environment.
The system is based on three main psychological principles: 1. Cognitive Load Theory - CLT; 2. Gamification and motivational mechanisms (Dopamine-based learning); 3. Supporting neurodiversity and adaptive learning (Personalized education).
1. Cognitive Load Theory - CLT.
The CogHelp platform reduces cognitive load through the following methods:
• Visual support ➢ Color-coded systems help you process information quickly. ➢ Simple and contrasting icons for easy visual recognition.
• Minimal text information ➢ Narrated instructions and icons instead of short, simple sentences. ➢ Text-to-Speech (TTS) function that reads instructions aloud.
• Progressive complexity ➢ Students’ progress from basic tasks to more complex tasks. ➢ AI-based difficulty level adjustment based on student performance.
2. Gamification and motivational mechanisms (Dopamine-based learning).
• Reward mechanisms ➢ Digital medals and badges that indicate achievements. ➢ Levels and challenges that increase motivation.
• Support for self-paced learning ➢ Users can progress through tasks at their own pace. ➢ AI algorithms automatically adjust challenges to performance.
• Competition and community learnings ➢ Multiplayer and cooperative learning opportunities. Students can solve tasks together. ➢ Real-time leaderboards and performance reviews. Gamification not only increases interest, but also helps develop the emotional aspects of learning, which can be particularly important for people with intellectual disabilities.
3. Supporting neurodiversity and adaptive learning (Personalized education).
• AI-powered personalized learning ➢ The system continuously analyses students' performance and makes individual suggestions for next steps. ➢ Fine-tune learning paths using Machine Learning models (scikit-learn, TensorFlow).
• Sensory support and multisensory education ➢ Providing visual, auditory, and tactile feedback. ➢ Support for touch screen interactions and haptic feedback.
• Integration of supporting technologies ➢ Text-to-Speech (TTS) ➢ Speech-to-Text (STT) ➢ Virtual mentors and chatbots: For immediate assistance.
• Optimizing learning pace ➢ If a user makes too many mistakes in a module, the system automatically suggests a simpler version. ➢ More complex, multi-step tasks are available for fast-progressing students.
Psychologically based interaction models
The system's user interactions were designed based on cognitive and behavioral psychology models
Psychological principle: Selective attention, Implicit learning, Behavioral conditioning, Social learning
Application in CogHelp  Highlighted visual elements and minimal distractions, Repetition mechanisms embedded in exercises, Reward system for correct answers, Collaborative tasks.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
-34% increase in task completion without assistance
-Accuracy improved from 65% to 87%
-Learning sessions became 40% more time-efficient, after the introduction of individual learning paths, the average task completion time decreased from 12 minutes to 7 minutes, indicating faster understanding and more efficient information processing.
-Daily usage nearly doubled from 20 to 45 minutes
-Significant improvement in users’ decision-making and cognitive autonomy
-Tasks can be completed an average of 25% faster
-The average learning time was reduced by 30% because the tasks were more accurately tailored to the users' abilities

innovations.name: Community Coaching – Methodological Development for Disadvantaged Neighbourhoods
innovations.problem: Over one million people in Hungary live in deep poverty, often in segregated areas with limited infrastructure. Traditional integration efforts have yielded limited success due to weak adaptation of international methods and lack of documentation of local good practices. Disempowered communities struggle to initiate change from within.
innovations.description: Community coaching provides a structured yet flexible framework for empowering local residents. The method includes stages of visioning, need assessment, strategic planning, action, reflection, and sustainability. It builds leadership, strengthens local networks, and enhances cooperation between communities and professionals. University students and researchers supported implementation, reinforcing the practice-research link.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: Community Coaching Handbook published with practical examples 30-hour university course curriculum developed Local self-help association established and functioning independently Increased leadership and advocacy skills among residents Successful community actions (clean-ups, infrastructure improvements) Method made available for other disadvantaged areas and practitioners

innovations.name: Be the Queen of Numbers! – Drama-based Confidence Building in Mathematics for Girls
innovations.problem: Between the ages of 8 and 12, many girls experience a significant drop in mathematical confidence and interest—not due to ability, but because of social and cultural influences that create a negative self-image. This reduces the number of girls pursuing STEM-related education and careers later in life.
innovations.description: The project uses drama pedagogy to counteract cultural disconnection from mathematics. It creates an engaging, story-driven environment where girls act as advisors to a fictional princess, solving math-related challenges. This creative approach strengthens self-awareness, logical thinking, and collaboration—key factors in long-term engagement with STEM.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Drama-based methodology developed and piloted in schools Positive feedback from both teachers and participants Increased mathematical confidence and motivation among girls Strengthened group dynamics and collaborative learning Created a replicable script and structure for future workshops

innovations.name: SkillJump – Applying Competency-Based Knowledge in the SME Sector
innovations.problem: Rapid technological change, particularly the rise of artificial intelligence, is disrupting traditional job structures. SMEs often lack the tools to assess and develop employees based on future-proof skills. There is a need for competency-based recruitment and workforce planning solutions that are practical and scalable.
innovations.description: SkillJump offers SME-friendly tools to assess and improve both employee and leadership competencies. It includes a detailed feedback system, competency definitions for HR decision-making, and a conceptual framework for a digital platform where skills can be matched to tasks and projects. The solution promotes efficiency, self-awareness, and strategic workforce development.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Two competency tests developed and validated (for employees and leaders) Structured feedback and development recommendations provided Use cases confirmed for hiring, talent management, and job satisfaction improvement SME leaders supported in developing conscious leadership skills Conceptualised a future AI-supported “competency marketplace"
tags: Modernising labour market institutions and services

innovations.name: Stress Relief and Mental Vitality – A Therapeutic Yoga-Based Training for Holistic Well-being
innovations.problem: Growing mental overload, emotional stress, and value disorientation in society have led to rising rates of anxiety, depression, and burnout. Traditional solutions often lack integration of body-mind approaches. There is a need for holistic, evidence-based practices that enhance resilience and promote sustainable well-being.
innovations.description: The training combines yoga therapy, cognitive restructuring, and traditional wellness systems (Ayurveda, meditation) in a structured and repeatable programme. It is grounded in scientific validation using nine standardised psychological scales measuring 23 indicators. Participants showed significant improvements in areas like insomnia, self-worth, hopelessness, anxiety, and social functioning.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Training delivered through 6–10 structured group sessions Home-based practice model developed 90% of participants reported significant improvement in multiple mental health domains Normalisation of clinical-level values in anxiety, depression, and sleep disorders Published evaluation using nine validated psychological assessments
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

Participants showed significant improvements in areas like insomnia, self-worth, hopelessness, anxiety, and social functioning.

innovations.problem: Lack of cooperation among local organisations often leads to fragmented services, inefficiencies, and limited access for residents. Even organisations under the same ownership or sector frequently do not engage in joint planning. Larger towns face particular challenges due to the number of actors and lack of coordination mechanisms.

The method helped identify short- and long-term development opportunities and inspired follow-up initiatives such as a sports guide and public fair.

innovations.name: Felirom.hu – Smart Notebook and Web Application for Small-scale Farmers
innovations.problem: Small producers face major challenges in managing mandatory records related to production, processing, packaging, and sales. Traditional tools are inefficient and error-prone, making compliance and business optimisation difficult.
innovations.description:
Felirom.hu is a cloud-based web application designed by and for small-scale producers. It simplifies daily tasks through modular data entry, improves transparency and traceability, and enables better production planning. Continuous user testing ensured the system aligns with real needs.
The innovation of Felirom.hu goes significantly beyond technological solutions available on the commercial market. Its uniqueness primarily lies in the participatory action research methodology employed in its creation. Unlike standard commercial apps—which are typically designed for larger-scale agricultural producers, require high-level digital literacy, and involve considerable expenses—our application was co-designed directly with small-scale producers through intensive, bottom-up engagement processes within an EIP-AGRI operational group.
This participatory approach allowed us to specifically tailor the application to the real-world needs, capacities, and technological comfort level of these small producers. Thus, Felirom.hu uniquely addresses their everyday operational challenges, such as streamlined data collection, simplified administrative tasks, and easier compliance with mandatory requirements, all without imposing high financial or technological barriers.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Easy-to-use admin platform for small producers Improved regulatory compliance and risk reduction Better forecasting of production peaks Enhanced planning of supplies and packaging Built-in adaptability for future features and integration
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change
