innovations.name: Digital Works for Youth
innovations.problem: Young people in Latvia and Romania, especially NEETs, face persistent barriers to employment, including low self-confidence, limited digital skills, and a lack of access to supportive networks and opportunities. Traditional employment services often fail to engage these youth or offer tailored, practical solutions. There is a growing need for innovative, inclusive approaches that combine mentoring, skills training, and employer engagement to bridge the gap between young people and the labour market, particularly in underserved regions and among vulnerable groups.
innovations.description:
Digital Works for Youth introduces a compact, practice-based model tailored to NEET youth, offering digital skills training, personalised mentoring, and job speed-dating events. The innovation lies in combining these elements into a three-phase learning and employment cycle that is accessible, engaging, and replicable. The methodology builds on the successful “Go Remote” project but adapts it with a clearer national focus, improved profiling tools, and stronger links to real employers. The project also includes face-to-face activities, especially an international bootcamp in Poland, which brings together NEET youth from both countries for intensive peer learning, confidence-building, and networking. This approach bridges the gap between education and work, using digital tools to reach and activate youth, helping them truly realise their potential.
This project builds on two successful initiatives: the “Go Remote” project (Latvia, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia), led by Visas Iespējas, and the SEPAL project (Romania and other EU countries), implemented by Bucovina Institute. Go Remote focused on tackling youth unemployment through digital mentoring, remote job training, and online job speed-dating, reaching over 6,000 young people, including NEETs. SEPAL offered a personalised, inclusive approach to working with disadvantaged NEET youth, emphasising one-on-one support, in-person guidance, and reintegration into the labour market. Digital Works for Youth combines the digital outreach and innovation of Go Remote with the deep personalisation and tailored support methods of SEPAL.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Digital Works for Youth will empower 600 vulnerable young people (aged 18–30) in Latvia and Romania, especially NEETs, through a structured model of mentoring, training, and job speed-dating events. Key results include: Mentoring for at least 240 participants, focused on personalised guidance and support. Digital skills training for at least 360 participants, improving confidence and employability. Job speed-dating events for at least 400 participants, directly connecting youth with employers. At least 120 participants expected to enter employment. Two full cycles of activities implemented in both countries, each lasting 9–11 months. Enhanced youth engagement through in-person meet-ups and international bootcamps, improving peer support and learning. The project uniquely combines scalable digital outreach with personal, local-level support - drawing from the best practices of Go Remote and SEPAL - and aims to create a replicable model that can be scaled nationally and internationally in future.

innovations.name: WeCan
innovations.problem: In 2020, Ireland's employment rate for people with disabilities was significantly lower than the EU average. While the EU average was 51.3%, Ireland's was just 32.6%. This puts Ireland at the bottom of the list for disability employment in the EU. The employment rate for people with intellectual disabilities in Ireland is even lower, at 17%.
innovations.description: • Innovation not only in what WeCan does, but in how it does it. Created a circular model that supports people, the planet and the local community. • Combines inclusive employment with sustainability – creating shared value across multiple sectors. • Aligns social inclusion and environmental action, showing people with Intellectual Disabilities can be key agents of climate action. • Builds multi-stakeholder cooperation – turns a small environmental action into a broad social movement.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
• Paid, meaningful employment for people with intellectual disabilities  – currently 3 people with intellectual disabilities are employed by WeCan working a combined total of 30 hours with ambition to scale. • 1000 cans and plastic bottles are returned weekly from 85 Businesses in Kilkenny City and County. • This results in a reduction of approximately 500kg of CO2 emissions each week. Outcomes and Results
Since its launch in March 2024, WeCan has delivered remarkable, measurable impact:
234,000+ bottles and cans collected turning everyday recycling into purposeful action
7,000+ bottles and cans collected weekly from over 80 local businesses
500+ kilograms of CO₂ emissions saved every week which is a significant contribution to climate action
85 passionate supporters and volunteers from CluneTech and SOS Kilkenny keeping the initiative thriving
31,000 people reached through social media alone
Celebrated Locally and Nationally

innovations.name: RECIK Compass Program
innovations.problem: The competitiveness of the economy depends primarily on whether it has an adequate workforce or not. In addition to professional knowledge, it is increasingly important that the competencies of employees meet the expectations of employers, which is even more important in jobs that do not require professional training, as this is a basic condition for their employability. In this way, the development of competencies becomes an important tool for social integration. Currently, Hungary does not have a standardized competency nomenclature that defines the competencies related to different occupations. A system of competency expectations has not been established on the basis of which the required competencies can be defined for different levels of training and jobs. There are no appropriate measurement tools or methods for a significant part of the competencies. The socio-economic significance of the program is to overcome structural labor shortages, align supply and demand, and meet labor market needs in order to ensure that companies have access to a workforce with appropriate competencies and qualifications. Decrease labor shortages in manufacturing and assembly plants, supporting selection and integration, and reducing turnover rates. Furthermore, unemployment among job seekers with fewer opportunities in Northern Hungary should decrease, while employment should increase, which would lead to securing the human resources of businesses operating in the region and increasing the competitiveness of the economy. As a result of the process, the goal is to create a development and support system based on real labor market needs, sustainably improving the employment indicators of the region, which also contributes to improving the employability of low-skilled, disadvantaged job seekers and developing their adaptability in order to meet the requirements imposed on employees by "Industry 4.0". We intend to fill vacant positions with domestic workers by developing the locally available labor pool.
innovations.description: The novelty of the ReCIK Compass Program is that it does not determine individuals' employment abilities using paper-based, self-answered tests and questionnaires, but rather it objectively assesses various competencies during task performance, simulated work, and activities. As a result, both a suitable job roles and development plans can be determined in a targeted manner. By exploring strengths, they receive positive feedback, which strengthens their self-esteem and self-knowledge. By identifying areas for development, training and mentoring increase their adaptability and better meet employer expectations. Our complex method contributes to the spread of the method when employers hire workers based on competencies and abilities, and to overcoming prejudices. Further novelties: • The complexity of the development process: measurement-development-feedback-mentoring support. • The measurement covers a wide range of skills and competencies. • A complex measurement and development process that is able to measure the competence deficits of the target group and effectively develop their abilities and skills in a short time. • Competency-based labor market consulting and mentoring support. • A physical measuring instrument that is suitable for objectively measuring a significant range of abilities and skills. • So far, relatively few professionals have recognized the importance of developing the target group from their basic skills not only with training methods and tests, but also with experience-based tools and software that evaluates these and processes the data.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence: The project involved 105 low-skilled individuals with fewer opportunities, all of whom live in disadvantaged settlements. During the project, 315 measurements were carried out with the target group included in the program: initial, intermediate, and one-year follow-up measurements. During the program, 180 hours (6 groups x 30 hours) of training developing employment competencies were implemented, as well as a total of more than 3,000 support sessions (approx. 30 sessions / person), which included community programs in addition to individual mentoring and counseling. A key result of the pilot project is that 75% of the measured employment competencies improved thanks to the training. Working memory, visual error detection, eye-hand coordination, load capacity, manual dexterity and quick reaction developed the most. As a result of mentoring support, significant qualitative changes occurred among soft indicators: • In addition to the development of employment skills and abilities, self-image was formed, self-confidence and self-esteem improved, • Their network of contacts has expanded, cooperation and problem-solving skills have improved, • Increased activity and motivation levels, • The autonomy of the participants became stronger, their degree of vulnerability was reduced, • As a result of labor market integration and employment, the quality of life has improved and the degree of social integration has increased as-well. Labor market integration was not a direct objective of the project, but its main results were noticeable in the field of employment. At the beginning of the project, 61% of the 105 people involved were unemployed and only 4 had work experience in the private sector. During the duration of the project, their number increased by five times, meaning 22 people (21%) were employed in the private sector. Overall, the number of unemployed people in the disadvantaged target group decreased from 64 to 34.

innovations.name: WorkPilots Path to Work
innovations.problem: Huge amount of people (young, refugees, disabled..) are excluded or struggle to get into working life which causes both personal and societal challenges. Traditional jobs and recruitment processes rarely work for them, leaving them as lost talents. There is a gap between training and finding suitable work, just building skills is not enough.
innovations.description:
WorkPilots is a mobile job and task matching service that provides easy and fast connections for any work opportunities, focusing on low-barrier options and empowering untapped talent. It is transforming the way to support underserved individuals towards a suitable working life beyond high-barrier jobs, recruitment processes and job interventions. Platform enables fast matching and efficent managing of various tasks, ranging from short one-hour tasks to exploring diverse career options with ABC‐path. Starting with simple, short-term tasks (Any Tasks), then progressing to more complex assignments (Better Tasks), and finally leading to sustainable suitable work (Career). It is adopted to customers own brand, needs and users – so they decide how and who uses the platform and how to integrate with their own support work.
The project has been adapted from Kenya - Ajira Digital program.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: We have now successfully created 20 platforms which are targeted to some underserved people. In total we have facilitated over 45,000 job opportunities. Over 7000 have got their very first experience and we have hundreds of touching stories how the model and experiences have helped both sides.

innovations.name: Etiaiset
innovations.problem: Many older adults, especially those who are homebound, face limited access to social interaction, cultural engagement, and meaningful activities. Physical limitations, long distances, or lack of transport can prevent them from participating in community events, leading to isolation, decreased well-being, and reduced functional capacity. At the same time, it can be difficult for volunteers to engage in home-based support, as in-person visits require time, travel, and coordination. These barriers limit both participation and the potential for community support.
innovations.description:
The multi-stakeholder model - Etiaiset - offers a solution by co-developing digital group activities that bring connection, creativity, and stimulation directly into older adults’ homes. The model brings together welfare area professionals, municipal services, cultural organizations, NGOs, volunteers, and technology experts. Each contributes to creating content that is accessible, meaningful, and easy to use. This approach not only supports aging in place and reduces loneliness but also enables remote volunteering, making it easier for individuals to contribute from wherever they are. Through user-centered service design, shared experimentation, and practical implementation, the model promotes inclusive and scalable well-being services for older adults.
The content of the Etiäiset sessions is co-created with a wide range of actors and varies between cultural, physical, and social themes. Examples include:
Art and Creativity : Kaakon Taide has organized remote painting and drawing sessions, supported by pre-recorded instructional videos. They have independently funded and delivered art materials to participants so they can actively join from home.
Physical Exercise : Several municipal sports departments have provided live virtual group exercise classes tailored for older adults.
Social Engagement : Volunteers and NGO representatives have hosted remote conversation circles, and Heikintalo staff organized an interactive knowledge quiz session.
This has been just the start as we have experimented the idea. In addition, we have created eight distinct elderly customer personas to guide future service design. These personas represent different interest profiles and functional capacities, helping tailor content to serve a wide range of needs and preferences:
Interested in Physical Activity – Pirkko, 82 Former caregiver, enjoys exercise but is hesitant to go out. Lives alone, moderate capacity. Limitation : Spouse has memory disorder, self-initiative decreased.
Bench Sports Enthusiasts – Pertti, 85 Sports fan and former athlete. Limitation : Uses a wheelchair.
Nature Lovers – Inkeri, 68 Widow and nature enthusiast. Limitation : Early-stage memory disorder.
Handicraft Enthusiasts – Liisa, 75 Knits and enjoys crafts. Limitation : Mobility issues, prefers to stay home.
Interested in Culture and the Arts – Eelis, 75 Sociable and art-oriented. Limitation : Relatives limit outings due to past substance use.
Interested in Music and Singing – Martta, 81 Former choir member, misses singing and friends. Limitation : Cannot move independently.
Interested in Travel, Food, and Languages – Siiri, 79 Well-traveled and culturally curious. Limitation : Uses a wheelchair.
No Clear Interest Type – Juhani, 85 Has no previous hobbies, seeks social contact. Limitation : Hearing loss and difficulties managing daily life.
These personas support user-centered content planning and allow for targeted and meaningful remote group activities that resonate with real-life needs and preferences of the elderly. We can see a great variety of content creation possibilities. We have even envisioned a virtual baking hour focusing on traditional Sourt-Carelian pastry baking traditions.
Business Model The Etiäiset model currently operates on a non-commercial basis:
It is integrated into the digital service infrastructure of home care clients, meaning that participants are already using remote care systems.
Participation in this pilot phase is is free for elderly clients. Activities are facilitated by volunteers, municipal staff, and NGO members, without financial compensation at this stage. These remote activities are for them a novel part or their basic activity and helps them modernize their services with the help of our platform.
The model is built on multi-sector cooperation and leverages existing resources, such as municipal video conferencing platforms and cultural organizations' content.
In the future, the model could evolve into a hybrid business model where municipa
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
The multi-stakeholder model has led to concrete outcomes and clear benefits for both older adults and participating organizations: Results The Etiäiset model has produced concrete outcomes:
The model has been successfully piloted and is now transitioning to permanent use within the South Karelia welfare area.
A total of 19 named participants have taken part across multiple groups (before the summer break).
Sessions have included cultural, physical, and social activities co-created with professionals and volunteers.
Technical and social feasibility has been demonstrated through real-world use.
A practical handbook has been created to support consistency in implementation and provide guidance to facilitators. Key Benefits - Easy to join: Sessions require no travel, and participation happens comfortably from home. - Inclusive and accessible: Suitable for older adults with limited mobility or cognitive decline. - Social engagement: Reduces loneliness and fosters a sense of belonging. - Routine and rhythm: Regular sessions bring structure and anticipation to the week. - Creative stimulation: Activities support emotional well-being, self-expression, and memory. - New role for volunteers: Enables meaningful contribution without in-home visits. - Cross-sector collaboration: Strengthens partnerships between welfare, culture, municipalities, and civic society. - Scalable and replicable: The model can be adopted by other welfare regions. This model shows how meaningful digital interaction can become a lasting part of elder care and community support.
User Feedback
Verbal feedback from participants and facilitators has been highly positive.
Clients have appreciated the ease of access, meaningful content, and the opportunity to engage socially without leaving home.
Although no formal user survey has yet been conducted, the anecdotal evidence indicates strong acceptance and value among users.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
The multi-stakeholder model has led to concrete outcomes and clear benefits for both older adults and participating organizations: Results The Etiäiset model has produced concrete outcomes:
The model has been successfully piloted and is now transitioning to permanent use within the South Karelia welfare area.
A total of 19 named participants have taken part across multiple groups (before the summer break).
Sessions have included cultural, physical, and social activities co-created with professionals and volunteers.
Technical and social feasibility has been demonstrated through real-world use.
A practical handbook has been created to support consistency in implementation and provide guidance to facilitators. Key Benefits - Easy to join: Sessions require no travel, and participation happens comfortably from home. - Inclusive and accessible: Suitable for older adults with limited mobility or cognitive decline. - Social engagement: Reduces loneliness and fosters a sense of belonging. - Routine and rhythm: Regular sessions bring structure and anticipation to the week. - Creative stimulation: Activities support emotional well-being, self-expression, and memory. - New role for volunteers: Enables meaningful contribution without in-home visits. - Cross-sector collaboration: Strengthens partnerships between welfare, culture, municipalities, and civic society. - Scalable and replicable: The model can be adopted by other welfare regions. This model shows how meaningful digital interaction can become a lasting part of elder care and community support.
User Feedback
Verbal feedback from participants and facilitators has been highly positive.
Clients have appreciated the ease of access, meaningful content, and the opportunity to engage socially without leaving home.
Although no formal user survey has yet been conducted, the anecdotal evidence indicates strong acceptance and value among users.

Many older adults, especially those who are homebound, face limited access to social interaction, cultural engagement, and meaningful activities. Physical limitations, long distances, or lack of transport can prevent them from participating in community events, leading to isolation, decreased well-being, and reduced functional capacity. At the same time, it can be difficult for volunteers to engage in home-based support, as in-person visits require time, travel, and coordination. These barriers limit both participation and the potential for community support.
The multi-stakeholder model - Etiaiset - offers a solution by co-developing digital group activities that bring connection, creativity, and stimulation directly into older adults’ homes. The model brings together welfare area professionals, municipal services, cultural organizations, NGOs, volunteers, and technology experts. Each contributes to creating content that is accessible, meaningful, and easy to use. This approach not only supports aging in place and reduces loneliness but also enables remote volunteering, making it easier for individuals to contribute from wherever they are. Through user-centered service design, shared experimentation, and practical implementation, the model promotes inclusive and scalable well-being services for older adults.

innovations.name: Fator C’Idade – Senior Entrepreneurship and Impact Incubator
innovations.lead: IPN Incubator - Association for the Development of Incubation Activities for Ideas and Businesses
innovations.problem: While one might assume that certain human inequality factors—such as skin colour, religious belief, gender or sexual orientation—are the most discriminatory in terms of access to the labour market, it is actually age that weighs heaviest during recruitment, particularly when an employer must choose between two candidates for the same position (Special Eurobarometer 493: Discrimination in the EU (2019)). The term ageism thus refers to the typically negative discrimination against older individuals, often based on subjective criteria (such as perceived productivity), which is rarely questioned either socially or culturally (Rosa, 2020). Among the stereotypes associated with older workers are lower flexibility and motivation, outdated skills, and reduced functional health—despite inconclusive scientific evidence regarding any direct correlation between age and productivity at work (Chiu et al., 2001). Specifically in relation to entrepreneurship, various studies show that greater openness and acceptance of older individuals has a positive effect on entrepreneurial activity, while ageism has the opposite effect (Weber & Schaper, 2004; Zhang, 2008). Conversely, overcoming such cultural barriers can enable older adults to pursue entrepreneurial ventures (Kautonen et al., 2011). In fact, some empirical studies suggest that the likelihood of self-employment increases with age (Blanchflower, 2004; van Solinge, 2014).
innovations.description:
Entrepreneurship has increasingly been seen as a viable option to mitigate the challenges outlined above, offering an alternative for keeping older individuals active and employed for longer, with highest motivational levels. Several arguments support this view: i) The need to ensure the sustainability of social security systems, as self-employed individuals, on average, remain in the labour market longer than salaried employees (Zhang, 2008; Zissimopoulos & Karoly, 2007); ii) As physically demanding jobs become less common in deindustrialised economies, human capital and innovation play a greater role in driving economic growth, making older adults' accumulated knowledge, professional networks, and maturity a relative advantage over younger generations; iii) Improved health conditions and increased life expectancy allow older people to become entrepreneurs for a significant period, helping to reduce the boredom and loneliness often associated with retirement; iv) With an ageing population, promoting successful entrepreneurship can help dismantle discriminatory stereotypes and improve the public image of older people; v) Technological advances can help bridge distances and overcome some of the physical limitations that older people may face; vi) Entrepreneurship can offer them greater freedom, autonomy, flexibility, and higher levels of job satisfaction; vii) Last but not least, entrepreneurship is often a response to the need for additional income, especially during times when government pensions are reduced. Besides this scientific evidence, but mostly based on our practical experience of several editions of implementing capacitation programs for 50+ citizens, we believe entrepreneurship can be part of the solution to the societal challenges mentioned. In particular, later-life entrepreneurship can help more experienced individuals regain control of their lives, rejecting the devaluation often imposed by others. Currently, there are only around 50 senior entrepreneurship support initiatives worldwide. NONE OF THEM IS AN INCUBATOR. UNTIL NOW. Fator C’Idade SENIOR AND IMPACT ENTREPRENEURSHIP IN COIMBRA We propose the creation of an incubator based in Coimbra to: • support the development of business ideas led by people over 50; • encourage social and civic initiatives that promote active and healthy ageing; • and consolidate businesses focused on the longevity economy, through the development of products and services for older people.
IPN was a member of the European consortium Silver Starters, which aimed to promote senior entrepreneurship. After this consortium, IPN was later the organiser of the first edition of the Empreendedorismo 5.0 programme, delivered entirely online due to the Covid-19 pandemic, with excellent results and a final Demo Day featuring video pitch presentations. Given this accumulated experience, IPN has developed unique applied knowledge in implementing this type of initiatives in Portugal for over 50's.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: IPN Incubator - Association for the Development of Incubation Activities for Ideas and Businesses
innovations.evidence: Our three-year roadmap includes acceleration events, capacitation and incubation programmes, mentoring, networking, and support in accessing funding. It aims to engage at least 240 participants, amplifying both social and economic value through their joint impact. In the Coimbra region—and indeed across the country—there is currently no Senior and Impact Incubator in operation, making Fator C’Idade a truly pioneering project with significant transformative potential. In fact, there are only around 50 active initiatives supporting senior entrepreneurship worldwide (Matos, C. S. & Amaral, M. (2019). "Chapter 2: Senior entrepreneurship: global mapping of supporting initiatives and programmes", in Handbook of Research on Entrepreneurship and Aging, Edward Elgar Publishing), despite the well-documented benefits of having citizens motivated to work in areas they enjoy for longer. Most of these initiatives offer only informational and consultancy services or deliver training programmes on a project basis, often lacking an integrated or sustainable model. As such, the Fator C’Idade – Senior and Impact Entrepreneurship project is not only a national first, but also a pioneer in the international context.

innovations.name: Examining entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial attitudes among students in higher education institutions
innovations.problem: Among the fields of study in higher education, economics is still the most popular among boys today. European Union statistics show that even among recent graduates in economics, the propensity to become entrepreneurs is extremely low, regardless of whether the theoretical and practical knowledge acquired during the training provides the right skills to start and successfully run a business.  At the same time, it is very important to increase the number of self-employed and non-self-employed people in the EU, including in our country, thus reducing the risks in a possible recessionary economic environment.
innovations.description: The aim of the research is to identify the traits, entrepreneurial competences, entrepreneurial attitudes, entrepreneurial motivations, entrepreneurial behaviours, entrepreneurial characteristics that determine who becomes a successful entrepreneur throughout life, or who fails at the early stages of entrepreneurial life. It is clear that the existence of success factors is important, but it is also necessary to clarify in which combination and with which emphasis these entrepreneurial traits ensure that an individual becomes a successful entrepreneur. This research attempts to examine these in a complex way.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence: Through the identification of certain elements of entrepreneurial attitudes and entrepreneurial propensity, the establishment and successful operation of enterprises among students of higher education institutions can be increased through targeted programmes, thus increasing the proportion of self-employed in the national economy, and also helping social inclusion, supporting the stratification of the population by becoming employed, and reducing social and income disparities.

innovations.name: Territoires zéro chômeur de longue durée (Long term unemployed territories)
innovations.lead: Territoires zéro chômeur de longue durée (Long term unemployed territories)
innovations.problem:
The main objective of the project is to make the right to employment accessible as stated in the preamble of the French Constitution: Everyone has the duty to work and the right to get a job. This right, which also exists in the constitutions of various countries in Europe and around the world, is not yet a reality for everyone.
Despite the numerous attempts that have emerged and the various public services that have been established, long-term unemployment in France affects more than 2 million people and around 34.3 million people in OECD countries.
Our society creates  exclusion when people want to work but cannot access a job that matches their skills and abilities. That is why the entire society, just like the State, must take part in developing solutions to effectively combat unemployment deprivation because "unemployment is a trial, not only because of the precarious situation it entails, but also because it is a factor of exclusion [...] it isolates us, depriving us of the right to participate in social life." (Parrique, Timothée, Ralentir ou périr, l’économie de la décroissance, seuil, 2022,p.136.)
innovations.description:
To try to provide a solution in France that could be replicated in other geographical areas, a starting point is therefore the notion of employment deprivation. Unlike administrative categories that designate unemployed individuals, it "allows for great flexibility in hiring and can thus take into account the multifaceted aspects of professional precariousness" (DARES, p.21) and consequently find a solution suitable for those farthest from employment.
Information through door-to-door outreach, at the foot of buildings, at school exits, within associations, or even at bus stops are some of the strategies implemented by project teams with the aim of reaching out to those furthest from employment and reducing non-take-up. This information dynamic is accompanied by the integration of willing individuals from the creation, implementation, and development of the project. Together, people deprived of employment (PDE), economic partners, employment services, residents, local elected officials, among other members of the Local Committee for Employment (LCE) , work jointly to identify the needs of the territory and the skills of the PDE. This process leads, on the one hand, to the identification of jobs that are accessible and suitable for the willing PDE, and on the other hand, to the identification of useful work that will transform into economic opportunities with a view to creating the Company for employment purposes (CEP) . The forms of involvement planned in the project and the dynamics of cooperation engaged thus seem to constitute a true enactment of deliberative liberalism, which aims to re-embed the economy in democracy by restoring self-confidence and trust in others, while giving people a new place in the system of relationships.
It is not about identifying previous work experiences or degrees to force people into the job market at any cost, but about highlighting their skills, what they wish to do, what they know how to do, and what they want to learn, with the aim of finding a solution that meets their personal needs (health, family, mobility, etc.) and employment needs, either through partners in the social and solidarity economy or through the traditional economy. If the solution is not found in the proposals made through local partners, PDE are offered a job in a CEP.
The CEP's establishes an exceptionally inclusive and demanding employment framework: no selection hiring, permanent contracts, chosen time, with an adaptation of the workload to the abilities and constraints of the employees to make employment accessible.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: Territoires zéro chômeur de longue durée (Long term unemployed territories)
innovations.evidence:
Since the beginning of the experimentation, around 7725 people have exited unemployment, thanks to territorial cooperation, the economic partners of the region, and the 93 Companies for employment Purposes (CEP) created in 85 territories in France to date within the project. 58% women – 42% men ; Average age 47 years  (2024) ; 23% of them are people with disabilities
Have a job help people to get back to the public sphere,  place common to all , get back to the school to pick up their children, they’re perceive otherwise by society and theirs families. (Dignity, participation in local life, citizenship)
They have a job that make sense because it respond to societal and global challenges : ecological transition, local development, Social cohesion.
Faced with the constraints of the current economic model and the organization of work, this logic of inversion rooted in territorial cooperation can also contribute to a redefinition of prosperity through practices that promote emancipation , thus offering bottom-up solutions that can contribute to a different way of thinking and conducting public policy adapted to the territories, three out of four of which have a poverty rate among households higher than the French national average . (DARES, 2024,p.34)
Access to a suitable job, with a permanent contract, on a chosen schedule, based on the voluntary participation of individuals, their wishes, and their skills, reduces poverty and precariousness . Permanent contract and flexible working time means projects, family vacations, better material living conditions , higher income, better health.
The ecological transition is the field generating the most additional jobs within the experimentation, representing 36% of the share of activities created (in FTE) and 32% of the gross margin generated within the CEP. These jobs fall within the three domains and the seven pillars which make up the circular economy:  extraction/exploitation and sustainable purchasing, eco-design, industrial and territorial ecology, functional economy, responsible consumption, extending the duration of use, and waste recycling.

sections.question: Problem
sections.answer:
The main objective of the project is to make the right to employment accessible as stated in the preamble of the French Constitution: Everyone has the duty to work and the right to get a job. This right, which also exists in the constitutions of various countries in Europe and around the world, is not yet a reality for everyone.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:

innovations.name: Move On with ALMA
innovations.lead: Executive Unit ESPA of the Ministry of Labour and Social Security
innovations.problem: The pilot addressed the problem of high unemployment rate in young NEETs, especially the vulnerable young.  Young people who come from a disadvantaged social background on the verge of poverty experience low self-esteem, lack confidence and are usually disorientated, have no sense of purpose or belonging, leading them to gradual inactivity and social exclusion.
innovations.description: It is the first time in Greece, a European mobility project targets disadvantaged young NEETs and adopts innovative ways for reaching out to people who are not seen or heard in the community inspiring them to reset their goals and restore their hopes for a better future. It is also implemented in a region on the border with ethnic minorities and has a very sensitive geopolitical significance for both Greece and Europe. It is the first time that underprivileged young people can live and work as European citizens in another member state giving them a sense of achievement, boosting their self-esteem and confidence, and motivating them to reengage in the labour market, society and community.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: Executive Unit ESPA of the Ministry of Labour and Social Security
innovations.evidence:
Disadvantaged and deprived young NEETs enhanced their self esteem and self empowerment, upgraded their employability, improved their prospects for re-entering education/training and/or the labour market, increased their trust in the European idea. They believed that they actually deserved to pursue their dreams, set new goals and be active in the community again. The participants in the pilot found work in Germany, got a job back in Greece, entered training while others followed further counseling seeking more support for reengaging in the labour market and society. The ALMA pilot brought a change in their lives and made them "move on" with new aspirations.
The participants
The Greek ALMA pilot project “ Move On with ALMA ” involved the participation of thirty (30) young vulnerable NEETs with significant results on soft and hard skills outcomes. Twenty-three (23) were young women and seven (7) young men in two (2) groups (13 people in the 1st group and 17 in the 2nd group) with different levels of vulnerability and from the region of Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, a region of sensitive geopolitical position at the north-eastern border of Greece were reached out.
The main reasons for their participation in the Programme were multiple:
73 %, for the opportunity to work abroad and the familiarity with a different working environment;
55 % for the opportunity to enhance knowledge and skills;
35 % for the opportunity to gain professional experience,
27 % for the opportunity to strengthen the profile.
The young vulnerable NEETs enrolled, came from a disadvantaged socioeconomic background, struggling with health, personal or family issues, with low self-esteem lacking confidence and a sense of belonging. They all attended initial sessions for their preparation for the mobility stage engaging them in a wide array of activities. However, the total number of participants who finally participated in mobility and moved to Berlin in Germany to be placed in a supervised job position were seventeen (17). The 1st group involved 10 people, while the 2nd group 7 people. The others who did not follow, either had to withdraw due to health problems, or found work.
Results and impact -  evaluation of the pilot’s added value and innovation
The findings of the pilot’s external evaluation highlighted the benefits the participants received as follows:
Professional development : Gaining work experience abroad increased opportunities to enter the labour market (out of 17 participants, 7 found a job and 3 joined training programmes for further upskilling).
Personal empowerment : Adapting to a new environment developed skills of autonomy and resilience.
Social inclusion & cooperation : The ability to socialize in a multicultural environment and new acquaintances.
Acquiring communication skills in a foreign language : All participants improved their German skills for everyday use, although in some cases communicating in a foreign language was a challenge.
Additionally, the participants benefited significantly from transnational mobility , considering the experience of living abroad to be particularly beneficial and gaining work experience in a European country. They found the experience gained from the supervised job abroad particularly useful. They built up their self-confidence and self-esteem as a result of living and gaining work experienceabroad and developed their social skills by getting to know others . They improved their job-search skills , some found work in Germany, others back in Greece and others entered a training program.
In fact, the acquisition of new knowledge, skills and competences from the supervised acquisition of professional experience in Germany, as well as the strengthening of job-search skills, were achieved, as 72% of participants said that they improved their job-search skills after participating in the Programme, together with skills to apply for and use job search channels. 64% said that their openness and self-confidence had

innovations.name: Improving the competencies of young people in Lithuania and Spain
innovations.problem:
This initiative was implemented in collaboration with the Baltic Institute of Technology. The project is aimed at young people facing fewer opportunities – those who are not in employment, education, or training, or who are experiencing social exclusion.
More than just work experience.
This project aimed not only to provide international work experience, but also to offer something deeper – motivation, self-confidence, and a sense of direction in life. All participants were NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), lacking practical experience, professional direction, and self-confidence. Participants travelled abroad where they didn’t just study or work – they also experienced everyday life in a different culture, faced challenges, solved real problems, and in doing so, grew as individuals and strengthened their identity.
innovations.description:
The project was implemented by the Baltic Institute of Technology (BIT), in partnership with the Spanish partners Arrabal and ADC*E. It consisted of three structured phases:
Participants took part in ICT training (graphic design, no-code platforms, RPA tools), Spanish language lessons, and soft skills development.
Three experienced mentors supported each group with career coaching, motivation building, and setting personal goals.
Each participant created a CV and attended preparatory sessions to align expectations with real work settings.
Participants completed internships in Málaga (30) and Barcelona (3), hosted by Arrabal and ADC*E.
They engaged in real work environments in the ICT, creative industries, Artificial Intelligence sectors.
Mentoring and cultural integration activities supported reflection and adaptation.
Participants received individual job coaching, CV refinement support, and assistance with employment or further training. An HR professional was involved to provide hands-on guidance.
Participant Profile and Selection Process
Participants were selected through an open call, which was promoted via the Baltic Institute of Technology's Facebook page and at the Vilnius College of Design. The selection process included motivation interviews, eligibility assessments, and an evaluation of participants' readiness to commit to all phases of the project.
The project targeted young people facing fewer opportunities, especially those:
From low-income backgrounds,
With limited or no formal work experience,
With digital or creative potential but lacking opportunities to apply their skills in practice,
Showing motivation to grow, but lacking the tools, support system, or environment to do so.
A total of 33 participants were selected – 19 men and 14 women, representing 16 different municipalities across Lithuania, including both large cities and small towns. Their educational backgrounds ranged from secondary to post-secondary education, and many had informal or self-taught IT and creative skills (such as programming, graphic design, or digital tools).
All selected participants successfully completed the preparation phase and continued to the mobility phase abroad.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
A total of 33 young people under the age of 29 took part in the project—19 men and 14 women. As a result, 33 out of 33 participants have successfully reintegrated—either by entering employment or resuming their studies.
Social Integration was also a key component. Young people established new contacts.

All selected participants successfully completed the preparation phase and continued to the mobility phase abroad.
A total of 33 young people under the age of 29 took part in the project—19 men and 14 women. As a result, 33 out of 33 participants have successfully reintegrated—either by entering employment or resuming their studies.
Social Integration was also a key component. Young people established new contacts.

innovations.name: Futuro Direzione Sud
innovations.problem: Futuro Direzione Sud plays a crucial role in mitigating two challenges facing southern Italy: youth depopulation, with the dramatic consequence of brain drain leaving a territory deprived of its potential for innovation, and high school dropout rate, in Sicily of 25.2%, supporting young people in choosing their future and motivating them not to lose hope in the future of the South. In fact, this program catalyses processes of change on various interconnected levels by initiating a reconfiguration of the territorial imaginary by activating in young people a new narrative of the South as a space of opportunity and innovation. It also develops territorial capacity building by strengthening the connections between the educational system and the local socio-economic fabric, creating enabling conditions for vocational and training paths rooted in the territory.
innovations.description: Futuro Direzione Sud offers significant added value through its innovative and interactive orientation methodology based on a peer-to-peer approach. In contrast to traditional face-to-face approaches, the project is based on an engaging combination of working tables and practical workshops. This methodology allows students to actively participate and acquire practical skills through direct and collaborative experiences. The interactive approach fosters deeper and more applied learning, developing practical and soft skills that are essential for professional and academic success. In addition, the project is distinguished by the choice to move the school from a traditional setting to an environment of innovation and avant-garde. Instead of just conventional company visits, students explore cutting-edge locations that represent the future of the industry. This exposure to a dynamic and futuristic context stimulates the interest and curiosity of students and also prepares them to confront the realities and challenges of emerging sectors: being immersed in an innovative environment can help them better understand future professional opportunities and visualise how their skills can be applied in high-tech and innovative contexts.

innovations.name: THRIVE - Upskilling Program for Women*
innovations.problem: The THRIVE program exists at the intersection of two critical challenges: the urgent need for economic integration pathways for refugee women, and the growing demand for data and AI talent across Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Since 2015, the popular image of a refugee in Europe is most commonly young men, but almost 40% of refugees are women. However, only 25% of these women are employed after five years. Many factors such as childcare responsibilities, not knowing the host country's language, and unfamiliar forms of bureaucracy can make settling in for women extremely difficult. In addition, many women do not have the formal qualifications required to work in the host country. Little formal work experience, difficulties with the recognition of previous qualifications, and a lack of professional networks prevent women from building a self-determined future. Moreover, according to the MINT Herbstreport 2023, the demand for digital skills in the DACH region is accelerating. AI specialist roles have grown by over 50% since 2019, yet small and mid-sized enterprises struggle to fill vacancies. This talent gap presents a unique opportunity — one that THRIVE is designed to meet. Refugee women remain underrepresented in the digital workforce, despite being highly educated., 75% of the 250 women participating in the current iteration of the program hold at least a Bachelor's degree and brought professional experience from their countries of origin. While 60% of the participants are actively looking for jobs in the tech industry, they face systemic barriers in entering the DACH labor market. More than half of the 20% of learners who are currently employed reported feeling underemployed, that their role does not match their skills and experience.
innovations.description: Kiron’s THRIVE program has been designed to empower refugee and migrant women* to (re)enter the labor market through a comprehensive upskilling program – specifically preparing participants for a career working in the tech sector. An innovative combination of language learning for workplace communication, live workshops to foster transferable skills, small group tutoring and 1:1 career coaching with professionals complements the self-paced elements of the program – facilitating opportunities for individualized guidance and job-specific knowledge. This program not only prepares participants for the demands of the modern workplace, but also introduces them to a supportive professional network through strategic partnerships, headed by FactSet, which culminates in a dynamic networking event held in Frankfurt. Its combination of flexible, low-threshold online courses, that allow participants to study alongside their other responsibilities, and regular live sessions and community-building and support structures makes THRIVE an accessible and achievable upskilling opportunity for refugee and migrant women* looking to enter the tech sector.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence:
456 women* from more than 20 countries participated in the pilot round of the THRIVE program. 22 graduates found paid employment and 18 were awarded scholarships to continue their studies. 86% of participants reported feeling more confident applying for jobs after completing the program and 80% said they had significantly improved their language skills. The current iteration of THRIVE, which will conclude later in 2025, received 1,500 applications with 250 women* ultimately selected to participate. The program is on course to achieve its targets of a 70% retention rate after 90 days and a 55% completion rate. Of the 250 participants, 12% are expected to find jobs or internships upon graduating. So far, learners are responding particularly well to the tutoring component of the program, with sessions achieving a high turnout and active participation. THRIVE alumni have reported that they leave the program with new skills and improved knowledge of the DACH labor market and how to successfully apply for jobs. They feel more hopeful about their employment prospects and are grateful for the guidance and support of Kiron’s Student Support Team and the volunteers from our corporate partners who host coaching sessions and workshops. Many participants cite the networking opportunities, both with other women* on the program and tech professionals, as a valuable resource for their career development.
After consulting with partners on the ground and conducting a needs analysis, Kiron adapted the THRIVE concept for the Afghan context in order to provide synchronous and asynchronous online courses, coaching, and networking opportunities for women in Afghanistan. Kiron implements this program in collaboration with The Liaison Office, based in Kabul. THRIVE Afghanistan focuses on trainings in e-commerce and digital marketing in order to upskill women for the local, regional and international labor markets. The program provides a vital opportunity for Afghan women to continue their education and build resilience and independence. The chance to study alongside and network with other women has proven to be particularly valuable for the Afghan participants.

innovations.name: FUNDS 2
innovations.problem:
Strong barriers to funding in the social enterprise market exist: difficult involvement of institutional investors in pre-seed & seed investments, high transaction costs, incentives for funds to give larger tickets to fewer companies, lack of impact-related knowledge and expertise from investors.
For instance, investing in social enterprises and impact projects in the seed stage is highly complex and requires strong involvement of investors and high transaction costs and for 3 main reasons:
- Seed investment implies lower tickets but the time spent by the investment teams to structure each deal remains equivalent to larger investment tickets ;
- Founding teams behind impact project are usually less knowledgeable about investment processes, meaning they need to be supported thoroughly and throughout the investment process ;
- Impact assessment requires a strong involvement from the investors during the whole investment process.
We identified a consensus on the need for seed impact financing and its insufficient coverage, with an order of magnitude of several tens of millions of euros missing per year for impact companies in the seed phase only in France. Several factors play a role in the access to funding: geographical location of the projects, their development potential, the type of impact sought, the form of innovation on which the project is based, the legal form of the project but also the type of customers and end users (BtoC, BtoB, BtoBtoC, etc.), the sectors of activity, or the type of solution developed (digital, hardware or both). Innovative commercial companies with very high development potential tend to align with the logic of successive capital raisings at the detriment of others.
More specifically regarding Business Angels involvement, we found out that access to financing remains difficult for young impact projects in France, despite strong availability of capital, popularization of impact investment and societal trends that are favorable to their emergence and their development, and that Business Angels have a key role to play : founding teams behind impact project are usually less knowledgeable about investment processes, which tends to lengthen the investment processes & requires additional support from investment teams. Impact assessment requires a stronger involvement from the investors with many more criteria to analyze. Therefore, funds alone  struggle in the impact pre-seed stage and can greatly benefit from associating with Business Angels who have much more time to allocate to support the startups as board members and/or operating partners.
On the other hand, angel investors pursue human and entrepreneurial adventure through their investments, have a low aversion to risk but a relatively small investment capability and quite often no follow-on capability (contrary to investment funds). A distinctive characteristic lies in the fact that they offer unpaid support to the investees, put their expertise and network at the service of the company, and build a working and trusting relationship with the founders. In addition, the strong involvement of angels as volunteers allows to overcome transaction cost challenges associated with detailed impact assessments and deal structuring.
innovations.description:
The theoretical financing chain starts with grants and love money, then business angels and finally multiple investment rounds from VCs (venture capital funds). However this model has its own flaws and in difficult financing markets (such as 2023, 2024 or 2025), it is not robust as startups need to convince for each round a new type of investor with diverging interests between the founders, the past investors and the new investors.
Therefore, we want to mix BA and VC investments to support social enterprises and impact startups.
Funds alone struggle in the impact pre-seed and seed stages and would benefit from associating with Business Angels, each of them bringing free sectoral expertise and know-how and unpaid support to the projects they invest in, which cannot be provided by funds. Greater collaboration between angel investors and funds would therefore be desirable insofar as it meets a need and provides better support to entrepreneurs while bridging what is commonly referred to as the valley of death.
Our aim is to provide investments towards social enterprises and impact projects from both Business Angels and Investment funds while lowering the high transaction costs by relying on pro bono work by angel investors in every step of the investment process. The association of angel investors and funds facilitates the involvement of Business Angels and allows the pulling of the best from both worlds: expertise & support from angel investors to investees and professionalism, follow on capacity & support functions from funds.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
As of june 2025, Impact Business Angels and Groupe SOS Participations supported 22 social enteprises with a total of ca. € 3.5 M invested. PULSE's teams led capitalization works allowing the initiative to be replicated EU-wide. Regarding the promotion of impact investment and co-investment schemes between BA and VCs, the consortium conducted various communication activities, participated to various events and organized a series of webinars. We also launched our VC micro fund / investment vehicle, named "Impact Seed Ventures", which aims to Support and assist ambitious, impact-driven projects from the seed stage onwards, with the aim of creating a more inclusive and sustainable society. The sectoral focus will be on i) transition and sobriety ; ii) social cohesion iii) Sustainable consumption with a transversal focus on: i) economic performance; ii) impact and iii) social coherence.
Under the EPSI - Empowering Partnerships for Social Impact in Bulgaria project, we act as mentors and knowledge transfer partners contributing to the activities  and developing financial instrument and more specifically helping the set up of an impact investment community led by Business Angels.

We also launched our VC micro fund / investment vehicle, named "Impact Seed Ventures", which aims to Support and assist ambitious, impact-driven projects from the seed stage onwards, with the aim of creating a more inclusive and sustainable society. The sectoral focus will be on i) transition and sobriety ; ii) social cohesion iii) Sustainable consumption with a transversal focus on: i) economic performance; ii) impact and iii) social coherence.
Under the EPSI - Empowering Partnerships for Social Impact in Bulgaria project, we act as mentors and knowledge transfer partners contributing to the activities  and developing financial instrument and more specifically helping the set up of an impact investment community led by Business Angels.

innovations.name: ALMA from one Eu2Eu
innovations.problem: Despite numerous national and EU-level efforts, many NEETs remain disconnected from education and the labor market. In France, although a strong support system exists, the most fragile youth—those with psychological issues, long-term unemployment, or a migrant background—are still at risk of exclusion. Traditional local programs are not always sufficient. These young people need new opportunities, structured support, and a sense of purpose. The challenge is not only professional but personal and social: helping them regain confidence, autonomy, and the motivation to reintegrate into society. In addition, there are currently not work related experience offered to Youth in Romania, Bulgaria and Poland, where even (unpaid) internship are scarce, and there is no system similar to French national Civic Service. We aimed through the French experience, undertaken with locals, to disseminate also good practices locally.
innovations.description:
ALMA France FROM1EU2EU offers a dual innovation: - mixing ALMA and EU mobility with the civic service model and volunteering. Strategic use of France’s Civic Service ecosystem: Many ALMA participants are former Civic Service volunteers, already equipped with basic training, teamwork skills, and a sense of civic engagement—making them ideal candidates for EU mobility when accompanied with tailored mentoring. The partnership model is also key: all hosting organizations were ESC/Erasmus+ certified, ensuring high quality and compliance. Detailed partnership contracts established expectations, ensured flexibility, and protected the needs and rights of vulnerable participants. - Transnational engagement with public benefit: Rather than placing participants in private sector internships, ALMA France focused on volunteering and public interest missions abroad. These created real, visible impact in host communities and raised awareness and support for the program. Some local governments (e.g., Kielce in Poland) have since shown interest in launching their own ALMA initiatives or create local volunteering systems, helping reach out disadvantaged local Youth in similar manner. Youth were also systematically in very high level events, to help disseminate their experience to national level, such as 3 Embassy's events, the International Direct Democracy Forum, Karpacz Economic Forum (biggest of Central Europe), 2024 Paris Olympics, the Fall of Berlin Wall Berlin Conference and the first Weimar Triangle event post renewal of relations between Poland, Germany and France.
This project is inspired by French national civic service and the systematised use of volunteering as a tool of insertion. It is also largely I spired form our global action through European Civic Service where we intertwined insertion and EU mobility and make EU instruments such as EU Solidarity Corps articulate themes elves with national volunteering frames.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Out of 30 NEETs Youth, over 20 were faced with serious challenges (psychiatric, migrant background, etc). 28 are inserted by the end of project, including 2 declared permanently disabled. 2/3 of the 26 remaining are now in jobs, with average income over French average. Post project, Poland created the basis for a national volunteering law, Romania study it, and Bulgaria has nominated a national coordinator on the matter. ALMA as a EU pilot is implemented now at regional level, in two of the territories of our project. All participants report higher self confidence, positive discovery of Europe and higher feeling of European belonging. A network of cooperation EU structure was also established leading to a polish led other ALMA project during Paris 2024 Olympics and in Germany.
This project led Kielce region to enter ALMA EU pilot to replicate it. In addition we ourselves implemented similar action within a Polish led other ALMA project (New Horizon) during Paris 2024 Olympics and later on in border regions of France and Germany.

innovations.name: Knockanrawley Workability Project
innovations.problem: The project addresses the disadvantage experienced by people with additional needs. This cover a social and economic disadvantage. We work with young people from the age of 16. We are partnered with 4 Rehab Care centres, Irish Wheelchair Association, Moore Haven Centre, and Scoil Chormaic Special Needs School.  Most of our participants are on level 1/2 on the framework; however they have many qualities on a practical level, and with support, we feel they can progress on the pathway to employment. For some participants, this could be a 20-hour job, while for others it may be a 4-hour job.
innovations.description:
Through the Workability project people with additional needs are provided with the support and opportunity to increase their participation in education,training and employment. This is achieved   through a suite of person centred supports to realise the full potential of the individual.
The project was originally established in 2019 and called The Ability Project.There was 57 projects across the country.The remit of the project from the onset was to support people with additional needs into education,training or employment while providing them with the same opportunities as their peers.This provides a fairer and more inclusive society.The project collaborates with individuals with additional needs and the mental health sector.Knockanrawley Resource Centre has housed and facilitated  The Ability Project from the onset and now operates the Workability Project.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
Promotes positive pathways into education, training, and employment for participants. Provides individuals with additional needs the opportunity to gain confidence and self-belief to progress to be work-ready and move closer to the labour market. It creates an awareness for employers and encourages them to provide opportunities. WorkAbility Programme aims to ensure that people with additional needs are fully supported to find and maintain employment. Organisations which employ programme participants are supported to ensure that their employment is successful.
This initiative has improved the soft skills of our participants, built confidence, provided immense responsibility, job satisfaction, built rapport with students and staff (at collection times) increased training opportunities as each participant had to complete Fresh Today compulsory training before starting and are now more work ready. The school kitchen has now become a social hub and a hive of activity.
We feel this initiative has provided our participants with that first step on their pathway to employment in a very supportive and meaningful way.
The government intend to provide the hot lunches to 900 schools in Ireland and if other Workability projects or disability services took on the initiative like we did it could provide similar opportunities and eventually employment reducing the percentage of people with additional needs unemployed.

innovations.name: Personaliza. Tailored Employment Solution to Eradicate Homelessness
innovations.problem: Employment is recognised in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and our Constitution. The 2030 Agenda dedicates an SDG to economic growth and decent work. The relevance of the employment dimension to the risk of exclusion is evident, and comprehensive actions are necessary to optimise results. The European Pillar of Social Rights (ESPR) and its Action Plan seek to substantially improve the lives of citizens by "leaving no one behind." One of these actions has facilitated the creation of the European Platform on Combating Homelessness (EPOCH), to which the 27 Member States have signed up to end homelessness by 2030. One of the recommendations put forward for this purpose is using European funds by States to support measures aimed at inclusive policies to combat homelessness, as proposed in the draft. In the fifth European study on residential exclusion, FEANTSA and the Abbe Pierre Foundation estimate that 700,000 people in Europe are living on the streets or are housed in temporary emergency collective accommodation. These figures represent a 70% increase over the last 10 years. According to data from the INE survey on homelessness in Spain, there are an estimated 28,552 homeless people. Homelessness has increased by 24.5% compared to the 2012 survey data. Female homelessness has risen to 23.3% compared to 19.7% in 2012. Homelessness is also becoming chronic. Forty per cent of homeless people have been homeless for more than three years, and 63% of women have been homeless for more than a year. Regarding employment, only 5.4% of people experiencing homelessness have access to work. Looking at the data on excluded groups commonly served by the ESF, such as those with disabilities, where 26.9% are employed, or mental disabilities, with an employment rate of 17.7% (2021, source: National Statistics Institute, from now on INE), we can see that people experiencing homelessness are still far behind in terms of percentage access to employment, with a need for personalised support management to achieve this and thus overcome the number of additional barriers they must face, such as lack of housing, long periods of unemployment, low levels of training (12.4% of women have university degrees, compared to 7.7% of men), low qualifications, low levels of digital skills, deterioration of personal skills or competencies, complex social and family environments, physical and mental health problems, addictions, administrative difficulties in accessing social protection resources and benefits. The very low percentage of homeless people with jobs (10.5% of women have jobs compared to 3.9% of men) also highlights the ineffectiveness of traditional pathways. Currently, we have identified that there are few socio-labor activation and integration programs specifically aimed at serving people experiencing homelessness in Spain and Europe. HOGAR SÍ presents this project aimed at a group severely excluded from the labour market, for whom traditional approaches fail to achieve the desired results. One-size-fits-all solutions are often ineffective for people with greater support needs. This project allows us to scale and consolidate, for the first time with European Social Fund funding, a project already demonstrating results on a smaller scale. This project thus responds to the common challenge of the European Union Member States to offer an effective and efficient solution that can contribute to preventing and reducing the problem of homelessness in Spain and, at the same time, serve as an example or inspiration for similar initiatives both nationally and in other countries.
innovations.description:
We are a real solution to a current, unsolved problem. We have been able to test a practice and evaluate its impact. Incorporates modern methodologies that optimise processes and generate greater impact It has an inclusive approach and promotes job opportunities for the most vulnerable people, adapting to their needs while working from the people's strengths and vocations. It is a sustainable intervention model based on people achieving stable employment and creating a social impact. It's a replicable and scalable model. We're ready to showcase and share it with others. It promotes social participation, involving other stakeholders, from businesses to the community. Individuals will participate fully and actively in their change process. It deploys a support system that promotes flexible, professional training and development tailored to the labour market's demands and the participants' needs. It has an impact measurement system with clear indicators based on achieving employment and improving people's quality of life.
AT THE EXTERNAL LEVEL. Beyond the Employment Program developed by HOGAR SÍ in the field of Personalised Employment, it is necessary to analyse existing developments in this area to leverage lessons learned, establish improvements and understand the strategies currently being implemented. For the design of our methodological framework, we based ourselves on two methodologies aimed at the personalisation of employment: The Personalised Employment model by Beth Keeton, a North American expert in the same and promoter of its implementation in Spain through Plena inclusión oriented towards a model of support for access to the labour market for people with intellectual disabilities, and the IPS Methodology (Individual Placement and Support), which seeks the socio-labour integration of people with severe mental disorders by promoting insertions in competitive positions and with 8 principles focused on the integration of services, individualisation throughout the process, relationships and synergies with companies, and decisions centred on personal preferences. Based on this latter methodology, an inspiring experience for our model and methodological design was the "Working First 13" program, developed in Marseille. It utilises far-reaching innovative practices such as Place-Train (place and then train), mental health recovery through the development of a person's strengths, interests, and professional preferences; the integration of health, social, professional, and business services; interventions within the individual's context; and unlimited durations. INTERNALLY. In our desire for HOGAR SÍ to be committed to implementing personalised employment solutions adapted to the heterogeneous situations of homeless people, in 2019 we participated in the " B- Value, innovation for third sector entities" program promoted by the Banco Sabadell Foundation and Ship2B, to professionalise the value proposition and make self-sustaining projects of non-profit social entities throughout Spain. Being one of the finalist entities and receiving funding and informational support through an AfterShare campaign, we designed a novel care methodology based on the personalisation of employment as a key factor in getting out of homelessness. In 2020, we implemented this methodology through the "Employ with Impact" project, testing a personalised employment solution. Support for realising the right to housing and employment is integrated into a single process tailored to each individual and company and open-ended in time. This ensures that this right is maintained and generates autonomous processes that allow individuals to escape the homelessness they were experiencing. In addition to this experience, in 2021, we carried out the Personalised Employment Solutions project promoted by HOGAR SÍ and Plena Inclusión with the support of the La Caixa Foundation.
