innovations.target_group: Homeless persons
innovations.evidence: We have identified different results and benefits by focusing on the various levels of impact that the project will have: Impact on beneficiaries: the Program's objective is to facilitate participants' entry into employment and stabilisation in the labour market, as well as to promote processes of autonomy that allow them to leave the specialised support system and make decisions about their own lives. 98% of the total number of people served will be unemployed, 58% of whom will be long-term unemployed. 30% will have a recognised disability, and only 2% will be employed. Regarding the impact on direct participants: 81.4% of people gain work experience for integration throughout their journey; 2 out of 3 people who are integrated have adequate skills; 53.5% who improve their digital skills obtain employment; 94% of people express job satisfaction; The average income of those targeted upon entry is €178.18, while upon exit it rises to €960.44, practically approaching the €1,080 minimum wage; 9 out of 10 people who complete their work plan do so with a salary; 54% access standard housing outside the care network; 63% of people manage to keep their jobs six months after completing the intervention. Expected results concerning the investment made. It is expected to serve 292 people simultaneously annually in five autonomous communities. The predicted employment incorporation rate is 30% of the total number of people served. All people are referred to and access local resources within the care network. There will be a shift in income sources, with more than 50% of people expected to receive benefits upon entry, compared to 4% upon exit. It is estimated that around 170 people served will achieve complete independence, leaving the care system. Impact on disadvantaged groups. The 2022 INE homeless survey indicates that only 5% of people experiencing homelessness are employed, compared to the 30% target Personaliza seeks to achieve. 56% of the intervention population will go from living on the streets or in shelters and not having a job to having a residential improvement, addressing an unmet need. Expected impact on the environment. we have ensured that more than 90 companies are offering tailored contracts annually under the personalised employment model, and we have raised awareness in 140 companies each year about assuming the assigned co-responsibility as agents of change. We have successfully conducted an average of 20 mentoring processes involving people in situations of severe exclusion and through support within the company itself, along with awareness-raising actions that foster levers toward social and labour inclusion. With Personaliza, we also aim to transfer our learnings acquired through this methodology to third-sector entities and public administration services that work with other groups through 30 annual meetings. Continue developing our volunteer plan, where we host an average of three volunteers per territory each year, bringing the reality of people in extreme social vulnerability closer to society. Impact on reducing the gender gap. According to our latest results report, 48.5% of women successfully complete their job placement program, compared to 45.3% of men. Twenty-three per cent of women in our program access job training, compared to 20.5% of men. Regarding internships in work environments, women outperform men by 5.5 points, with 56% of women trained completing internships, compared to 51.5% of men. 99.7% of the women served have applied for job offers tailored to their interests and needs, compared to 74.5% of men. Personalize is a project that incorporates innovative elements in methodology and processes, establishing a care model for people affected by homelessness that could be extended to other groups with complex labour market access needs. Personaliza. Tailored Employment Solution to Eradicate Homelessness
Employment is recognised in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and our Constitution. The 2030 Agenda dedicates an SDG to economic growth and decent work. The relevance of the employment dimension to the risk of exclusion is evident, and comprehensive actions are necessary to optimise results. The European Pillar of Social Rights (ESPR) and its Action Plan seek to substantially improve the lives of citizens by "leaving no one behind." One of these actions has facilitated the creation of the European Platform on Combating Homelessness (EPOCH), to which the 27 Member States have signed up to end homelessness by 2030. One of the recommendations put forward for this purpose is using European funds by States to support measures aimed at inclusive policies to combat homelessness, as proposed in the draft. In the fifth European study on residential exclusion, FEANTSA and the Abbe Pierre Foundation estimate that 700,000 people in Europe are living on the streets or are housed in temporary emergency collective accommodation. These figures represent a 70% increase over the last 10 years. According to data from the INE survey on homelessness in Spain, there are an estimated 28,552 homeless people. Homelessness has increased by 24.5% compared to the 2012 survey data. Female homelessness has risen to 23.3% compared to 19.7% in 2012. Homelessness is also becoming chronic. Forty per cent of homeless people have been homeless for more than three years, and 63% of women have been homeless for more than a year. Regarding employment, only 5.4% of people experiencing homelessness have access to work. Looking at the data on excluded groups commonly served by the ESF, such as those with disabilities, where 26.9% are employed, or mental disabilities, with an employment rate of 17.7% (2021, source: National Statistics Institute, from now on INE), we can see that people experiencing homelessness are still far behind in terms of percentage access to employment, with a need for personalised support management to achieve this and thus overcome the number of additional barriers they must face, such as lack of housing, long periods of unemployment, low levels of training (12.4% of women have university degrees, compared to 7.7% of men), low qualifications, low levels of digital skills, deterioration of personal skills or competencies, complex social and family environments, physical and mental health problems, addictions, administrative difficulties in accessing social protection resources and benefits. The very low percentage of homeless people with jobs (10.5% of women have jobs compared to 3.9% of men) also highlights the ineffectiveness of traditional pathways. Currently, we have identified that there are few socio-labor activation and integration programs specifically aimed at serving people experiencing homelessness in Spain and Europe. HOGAR SÍ presents this project aimed at a group severely excluded from the labour market, for whom traditional approaches fail to achieve the desired results. One-size-fits-all solutions are often ineffective for people with greater support needs. This project allows us to scale and consolidate, for the first time with European Social Fund funding, a project already demonstrating results on a smaller scale. This project thus responds to the common challenge of the European Union Member States to offer an effective and efficient solution that can contribute to preventing and reducing the problem of homelessness in Spain and, at the same time, serve as an example or inspiration for similar initiatives both nationally and in other countries.

It deploys a support system that promotes flexible, professional training and development tailored to the labour market's demands and the participants' needs. innovations.name: Social Innovation and Common goods, a path for young entrepreneurs
innovations.problem: Young people in Europe, particularly in Italy and Spain, face high youth unemployment, limited access to entrepreneurial education, and a lack of opportunities to engage in socially and environmentally responsible economic activities. Existing training and support systems often fail to integrate values such as social justice, sustainability, and community well-being, leaving a gap between young people’s aspirations and the tools available to realize them. This disconnect contributes to underutilized potential among youth and limits their role in shaping a more inclusive and sustainable economy.
innovations.description:
The project offers a unique cross-border training and mentoring pathway that blends social innovation practices with the Economy of the Common Good framework—an approach rarely integrated into youth entrepreneurship programs. It combines online learning, expert guidance, and peer collaboration to foster ethical, sustainable business development. By engaging youth in a participatory, values-based learning environment and connecting them with real-life practitioners, the project equips them with both the technical skills and the social mindset needed to launch impactful ventures that prioritize people and planet alongside profit.
This project draws inspiration from the Economy of the Common Good (ECG) movement, originating in Austria, which promotes sustainable and socially responsible business models prioritizing human dignity, ecological sustainability, and democratic participation. It also builds on successful social innovation and youth entrepreneurship initiatives from Italy and Spain. In particular, the Spanish partner, Asociación Jóvenes Solidarios Arenas de San Pedro, brings extensive experience in youth empowerment, community engagement, and implementation of international cooperation projects focused on social inclusion and sustainable development. Their activities in mentoring young entrepreneurs and organizing cross-cultural study visits significantly inform the project’s design and methodology.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing gender marginalization
innovations.evidence: 40 young participants (ages 23–27) trained in social innovation and sustainable entrepreneurship. 10 video lessons produced and made available online for wider dissemination and long-term use. 20 mentors and experts involved in delivering tailored support and real-world insights. 2 international study visits promoting cross-cultural exchange and practical learning. Increased employability and entrepreneurial readiness among youth, with a focus on ethical and community-oriented ventures. Strengthened collaboration between organizations in Italy and Spain, building a transnational ecosystem for youth empowerment and social innovation.
tags: Promoting Life long learning for all

innovations.name: Social entrepreneurship for Roma
innovations.lead: EPEKA: Scientific and Research Association for Art, Cultural and Educational Programmes and Technology
innovations.problem: The project addressed multiple interlinked challenges affecting both Roma communities and the functioning of social enterprises. Members of the Roma community, particularly the long-term unemployed and recipients of social assistance, often face social exclusion, limited access to quality education and training, and significant barriers to entering the labour market. At the same time, existing staff in social enterprises lacked sufficient training in key areas such as administration, management, and marketing, which hindered the sustainability and growth of such enterprises. There was also a lack of structured mentorship and support for Roma individuals to develop and implement business ideas, as well as a general need to raise awareness and understanding of social entrepreneurship and cooperatives. Moreover, the project aimed to counter widespread stereotypes, discrimination, and social isolation experienced by Roma individuals by fostering participation, empowerment, and visibility in economically and socially relevant roles.
innovations.description:
The project stood out for its integrated and inclusive approach to social entrepreneurship, combining capacity-building for both employed staff and members of the Roma community. Its innovation lay in offering parallel, tailored mentorship programs—one for employees of the social enterprise to strengthen managerial, administrative, and marketing competencies, and another for Roma participants focused on developing entrepreneurial skills and understanding cooperatives. By supporting Roma individuals in shaping concrete business ideas and guiding them through the process of creating business plans, the project bridged the gap between social inclusion and economic empowerment. Additionally, the project introduced social entrepreneurship not just as a skillset, but as a pathway to sustainable employment and community development, helping to reframe perceptions of Roma communities through practical engagement and public visibility. The emphasis on mentorship, fieldwork, and peer interaction outside traditional social circles further contributed to its unique and transformative impact.
The project "Social Entrepreneurship for Roma" was inspired by EPEKA’s long-standing work with Roma communities in Slovenia, particularly through initiatives like the Roma Multi-purpose Centre (VNRC Romska postaja), the Social Activation programme (SA), and the Romani Kafenava social enterprise. These projects, all based in Slovenia and led by Združenje EPEKA, provided a tested framework for combining cultural empowerment, social inclusion, and economic activation. They demonstrated the value of mentorship, community-based outreach, and entrepreneurship as effective tools for Roma inclusion, laying the groundwork for this project.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons
innovations.beneficiaries: EPEKA: Scientific and Research Association for Art, Cultural and Educational Programmes and Technology
innovations.evidence: The project brought a range of impactful results and lasting benefits. Employees of the social enterprise significantly improved their skills in areas such as administration, payroll, accounting, marketing, and management through intensive mentorship and training. At the same time, ten members of the Roma community participated in a comprehensive 225-hour programme focused on social entrepreneurship, innovation, and cooperative models. This helped them gain practical knowledge and the confidence to develop business ideas, which were further supported through guidance in drafting concrete business plans. A key achievement of the project was the successful employment of one Roma participant, representing both a personal milestone and a broader step toward inclusive employment. The initiative also generated strategic and promotional materials aimed at attracting future investment and partnerships, laying the groundwork for the continued development of socially impactful business initiatives. Beyond individual progress, the project fostered social inclusion by encouraging long-term unemployed Roma individuals and recipients of social assistance to participate in structured learning, often outside their typical social environments. This not only expanded their social networks but also helped reduce isolation. The project promoted awareness of social entrepreneurship within Roma communities through public presentations, cultural events, and field visits, actively challenging stereotypes and promoting the visibility of Roma as active, creative contributors to society. In doing so, the project strengthened both the internal capacity of the social enterprise and the broader goal of building more inclusive and sustainable communities.
authors: EPEKA: Scientific and Research Association for Art, Cultural and Educational Programmes and Technology

innovations.name: ENHANCE – ENHancing Adult learNers voiCEs
innovations.lead: European Associaton for the Education of Adults
innovations.problem: Adult learners—especially those facing gender, racial, social, and economic exclusion—are systemically excluded from influencing the very learning systems designed to support them. This results in disconnected policy, tokenistic inclusion, and missed opportunities for transformative social innovation.
innovations.description:
ENHANCE flips the system: it centers adult learners as co-creators of education. By weaving together a European matrix of critically understanding existing practices, developing participatory tools like the Learners’ Voices Roadmap, and integrating learner-led storytelling and podcasts in public life, the project shifts ALE (Adult Learning and Education) from top-down provision to collective empowerment.
The ENHANCE project draws inspiration from AONTAS’s “Community Education Network” (CEN) in Ireland, a nationally recognized approach in the adult learning and education sector. The CEN has long advocated for the inclusion of learners' voices in shaping education policy and practice, with a focus on empowering marginalized communities through learner-led consultation processes and public engagement campaigns, such as the “Learners as Leaders” initiative. This Irish model demonstrated how grassroots education can influence national strategies, serving as a foundational reference for ENHANCE’s broader European vision to systematize and scale participatory, learner-centered approaches. The approach also borrows significant elements from the works of Paulo Freire and the concept of critical pedagogy and the pedagogy of the oppressed.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities, Individuals experiencing gender marginalization, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: European Associaton for the Education of Adults
innovations.evidence: A transnational matrix of learners’ voice initiatives A Learners' Voice Roadmap and policy recommendations targeting education stakeholders and decision-makers A podcast series publicly reclaiming space for learners’ stories Increased civic and democratic participation of adult learners, particularly in relation to the 2024 EU elections Strengthened policy engagement capacities of ALE organisations and learners

By weaving together a European matrix of critically understanding existing practices, developing participatory tools like the Learners’ Voices Roadmap, and integrating learner-led storytelling and podcasts in public life, the project shifts ALE (Adult Learning and Education) from top-down provision to collective empowerment.
The ENHANCE project draws inspiration from AONTAS’s “Community Education Network” (CEN) in Ireland, a nationally recognized approach in the adult learning and education sector. The CEN has long advocated for the inclusion of learners' voices in shaping education policy and practice, with a focus on empowering marginalized communities through learner-led consultation processes and public engagement campaigns, such as the “Learners as Leaders” initiative. This Irish model demonstrated how grassroots education can influence national strategies, serving as a foundational reference for ENHANCE’s broader European vision to systematize and scale participatory, learner-centered approaches. Many new migrant communities have limited social connections and face cultural and language barriers. Partaking in sporting activities can build their sense of belonging, language skills, and inter cultural friendships. Often newcomers live in accommodation centres across the city and lack connections within the communities they reside.  In addition, we found that many  children attended school across the city and had no connection with local communities within which they were living.
By targeting the already existing sporting infrastructure, it meant that the sports clubs that agreed to come on board with our Integration though sport project were supported to actively target children and adults that were living in accommodation centres in their area and support and encourage their participation at a local level.

innovations.name: Tracking What Matters: A data framework to drive decisions and prove long-term impact
innovations.problem: Every year, billions of euros are invested in skills development across the EU, with €30–35 billion allocated to vocational training in France, ~€30 billion in Spain, ~€25 billion in Italy, and ~€42 billion in the UK. Additionally, for the 2021–2027 period, the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) has allocated €40.4 billion for skills development, with total investments in skills under EU cohesion funds reaching €67.7 billion. However, despite this massive financial commitment, there remains limited evidence on the long-term impact of VET programs. Where evidence does exist, it is often fragmented or inconclusive, making it difficult to identify what works, for whom, and under which conditions. A meta-analysis of the European Social Fund’s Youth Employment Initiative (YEI) found that while training programs showed fewer positive results than other interventions (e.g., subsidies, internships), their effectiveness increased over time. The 2023 J-PAL review of 28 randomised evaluations of TVET programs worldwide echoed this finding, noting that the long-term impact of vocational training remains unclear. This persistent gap in knowledge limits the ability of VET providers, policymakers, and funders to make data-driven decisions and optimise the return on investment of large-scale skills development efforts. Furthermore, current evaluation frameworks focus heavily on short-term indicators, such as enrolment rates, course completion rates, and immediate job placements, as seen in Cedefop’s VET indicators. In many cases, tracking stops before or immediately after graduation, meaning we often don’t know if participants secured sustained employment, experienced salary growth, or remained in their roles. This is particularly problematic when designing interventions for vulnerable populations, where understanding long-term outcomes is essential to adjust services and increase the effectiveness of public and private investment in the skilling ecosystem. Without this visibility, policymakers are left with an incomplete picture of VET’s true impact. Additionally, existing long-term impact measurement methods face key limitations. Randomised control trials (RCTs) and counterfactual impact evaluations, while considered the gold standard, are expensive, time-intensive, and ethically complex to implement at scale. Administrative data sources (e.g., employment and income records) can provide cost-effective insights but are often inaccessible or incomplete due to data privacy constraints and the need for cross-institutional partnerships. In contrast, scalable and systematic data collection through participant surveys offers a more agile and replicable approach, allowing providers to capture the “what,” “why,” and “how” behind program outcomes in real time. Finally, the growing impact of automation and AI on the labour market underscores the need for VET providers to continuously adapt and respond to evolving industry demands. The 2025 World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report found that 63% of employers identified skills gaps as a major barrier to business transformation, and 39% of current skill sets are expected to be outdated by 2030. This reality reinforces the urgency of tracking long-term VET outcomes to ensure that training remains not only effective, but also relevant and resilient in a rapidly shifting world of work.
innovations.description: Generation’s innovative solution lies in our comprehensive, multi-year learner data tracking system - one of the most extensive in the VET space globally. At the heart of our approach is a firm belief that true impact must be measured not only by how many people we serve (breadth), but also by how deeply and sustainably our programs transform lives (depth and durability). While many training providers focus on short-term outputs like graduation or initial placement, Generation systematically tracks learner outcomes for up to five years post-programme—something few, if any, VET providers do at this scale and granularity. Our data framework follows each learner across their full journey, from application to long-term career growth, capturing detailed, real-time insights across multiple dimensions: employment status, wage evolution, promotion rates, financial resilience, mental and physical well-being, sense of purpose, and learning experience. As shown in our Learner Data Map, data is collected across pre-programme, in-programme, and post-programme phases using a range of tools such as Qualtrics surveys, Salesforce, technical assessments, mentor evaluations, and alumni follow-ups. These diverse inputs feed into a sophisticated data infrastructure powering a suite of interactive dashboards that support both global monitoring and local program improvement. Specifically, our Impact Dashboard synthesises key metrics across countries and professions, measuring and comparing breadth (reach), depth (programme quality and outcomes), and durability (long-term impact) over time. The Alumni Survey Dashboard, conducted annually, allows us to track outcomes such as job retention, wage progression, promotion, and personal well-being up to five years after graduation. Additional dashboards such as the Mobilisation Dashboard, Learner Support Dashboard and Placement Dashboard provide granular insight into critical transition points and success drivers that influence outcomes. This level of durability-focused impact tracking is rare in the VET field, where most programs stop tracking outcomes at or shortly after graduation. We go further - finding answers to the questions that matter most: Did our graduates remain employed? Did their earnings increase over time? Are they thriving, not just surviving? For example, by tracking cumulative earnings and comparing them to our self-developed living wage benchmarks (used to fill in gaps in countries where public ones don’t exist), we assess long-term economic mobility grounded in real-world conditions. Maintaining this longitudinal data tracking system is challenging: it requires multi-channel follow-ups via SMS, WhatsApp, voice calls, emails, alumni events, and even interactive voice response tools. Yet we persist, because without this insight, we risk mistaking short-term outputs for real, lasting change. By investing in data collection that costs only about 1% of the overall cost per learner, we generate critical insights that improve service delivery, inform funders, and help public-private stakeholders make smarter, evidence-based decisions. In short, Generation’s innovation is not just in collecting data, but in how comprehensively and purposefully we go to understand the full trajectory of our learners’ lives, long after training ends. By embedding durability into the core of our impact model, we are helping shift the sector toward a more accountable, adaptive, and human-centred approach to VET.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
Generation’s data-driven system has led to significant results and measurable benefits at all levels of our work, enabling us to deliver higher quality training, respond quickly to emerging challenges, and enhance the overall impact of the resources we deploy. Our extensive suite of operational dashboards allows us to monitor and respond to programme performance in real time. These dashboards, covering areas such as recruitment, learner experience, instructor and mentor performance, placement rates, and alumni outcomes, are central to our ability to quickly diagnose problems and adjust our operations dynamically. If learner satisfaction drops, instructor performance varies, or placement outcomes shift, we detect it early and intervene immediately. This system enables us to deeply understand who our learners are and what barriers they face, not only through demographics but also through data on financial situation, learning access, and risk indicators. As a result, we tailor our programmes to match the specific needs of different learner profiles, improving engagement, satisfaction, and outcomes. At the learner level, this means more personalised and equitable support. At the programme level, it allows us to refine staffing, curriculum, and delivery models to match demand and improve cost-effectiveness. Our data also underpins a structured quality assurance process. From programme design to launch and evaluation, each stage includes clearly defined steps, such as learner persona development, curriculum alignment with employer needs, instructor onboarding and observation cycles, and post-programme data analysis. This ensures that every programme is launched with clear goals, real-time feedback loops, and mechanisms for continuous improvement. We prioritise data completeness and quality through dedicated systems and protocols to maximize survey response rates (e.g., through multi-channel follow-up) and protect data integrity. This gives us confidence that the insights we derive are reliable and actionable, allowing us to benchmark across countries and make informed strategic decisions. The benefits of this approach are multi-layered: - For learners, we deliver a more responsive, tailored experience that adapts to their feedback, needs, and realities; - For staff, data helps us focus our limited time and resources on the areas of greatest need and impact. In addition, we use instructor/mentor feedback and observational data to help coach and provide continuous support to staff; - For funders, especially public sector partners, we offer a high level of transparency and accountability, linking investments to real outcomes and demonstrating responsible use of public and philanthropic funds; - For society, we model how a training provider can embed accountability and quality at scale, raising standards and lifting performance across the entire VET sector.
This innovation was replicated and scaled-up in all 17 countries where Generation is operating: Australia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, France, Ghana, Hong Kong, India, Ireland, Italy, Kenya, Mexico, Singapore, Spain, Thailand, UK, USA.

innovations.name: From farm to fork: a social chain of food aid
innovations.problem: This project adresses the difficulties to access to diversified and high-quality food for the most deprived populations. Also, as part of this project, the beneficiaries have access to the "Nourishing food" training in order to learn and share practices.
innovations.description: What's new here, is that the chain of solidarity persists throughout the supply chain, and this has been our goal from the beginning. No one is left behind: from the farmers in social and professional insertion, the volunteer and the coordinators that are trained as part of this project to the beneficiaries, everyone is part of this economy and can find an essential place.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence:
At first, only few gardens and food banks were sollicited. It doubled the next year.
Today, this social chain of food aid means 420 tonnes of fruits and vegetables exchanged between 52 gardens and 38 food banks this last year. It’s 2,995 farmers involved for roughly 1,455,271 beneficiaries.

innovations.name: Driving License for Independent Living program
innovations.problem: Homelessness has increased by 70% across the EU in the past decade. It is one of the most severe forms of poverty, stemming from a complex mix of structural, institutional, and individual factors. According to the European Parliament (2020), member states should decriminalize homelessness and ensure equal access to essential public services such as healthcare, education, and social welfare. For young people, independence means learning to live responsibly and manage everyday life. This includes forming an identity, handling financial insecurity, establishing routines, and maintaining a home. Neuropsychiatric conditions, mental health challenges, or substance use issues can make these tasks more difficult. Living alone can increase feelings of loneliness, which in turn may worsen mental health and lead to social isolation. Substance use can result in unpaid rent, poor upkeep of the home, or disruptive behavior—all of which increase the risk of eviction. Irregular routines make it hard to take responsibility for daily tasks, and the lives of people experiencing homelessness or addiction are often unstable and unsafe. Financial difficulties can lead to debt, which may result in housing loss. Landlords may hesitate to rent to individuals with a history of rent arrears, disruptive behavior or criminal records, even if those issues have been resolved. Stigma and prejudice can still create significant barriers to accessing housing. Immigrants may face discrimination in the rental market, even when they are reliable and financially stable. Names, ethnic backgrounds, or religious affiliations can trigger bias. innovations.name: Holistic approach of accompanying measures and services for people living below the poverty line in West Athens within the FEAD framework.
innovations.lead: ASSOCIATION FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF WEST ATHENS
innovations.problem: West Athens is a large area with a population that faces common problems. Until now, social services have been provided at the local level by the Municipalities. In particular, poverty in West Athens is a persistent reality and ensuring basic needs such as food, shelter, education and access to health services is becoming difficult. The available resources such as FEAD would not be enough if the actions were planned separately in each Municipality and could not cover so many and different needs of the beneficiaries.
innovations.description: The way in which the social inclusion accompanying services were provided to the beneficiaries of a large area of action (West Athens - 8 Municipalities) through inter-municipal cooperation of social services. Also, the organization of the Project in stages as well as the provision of services that came to satisfy the specific and diagnosed needs of the beneficiaries themselves who chose it.
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.beneficiaries: ASSOCIATION FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF WEST ATHENS
innovations.evidence: Key Results Unified Service Delivery: Successfully coordinated 8 municipalities (covering ~500,000 residents) under a single inter-municipal strategy, avoiding fragmented efforts. Leveraged FEAD’s "Accompanying Services" (2018–2019) to maximize resource efficiency across 26,000 vulnerable families (50k+ individuals). Targeted Service Implementation Conducted needs assessments (e.g., diagnostic questionnaires) to identify gaps. Rolled out 48+ diverse services (e.g., parental counseling, art workshops, career guidance) tailored to expressed beneficiary needs. Key Benefits For Beneficiaries: Holistic Support: Addressed intertwined challenges (poverty, mental health, education) through psychosocial, nutritional, and educational services. Empowerment: Enabled vulnerable groups (e.g., parents of children with speech disorders) to access specialized support (logotherapy, bullying prevention). Social Inclusion: Creative/sports activities (art, theater, sports) fostered community integration for isolated families.
authors: ASSOCIATION FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF WEST ATHENS

The available resources such as FEAD would not be enough if the actions were planned separately in each Municipality and could not cover so many and different needs of the beneficiaries.

Empowerment: Enabled vulnerable groups (e.g., parents of children with speech disorders) to access specialized support (logotherapy, bullying prevention). Social Inclusion: Creative/sports activities (art, theater, sports) fostered community integration for isolated families.

innovations.name: The Library of Things
innovations.lead: Šiauliai County Povilas Višinskis Public Library
innovations.problem: In many communities, access to educational, creative, and sensory tools remains a privilege — limited by financial constraints, lack of space, or systemic inequality. Families with lower income, educators with scarce resources, and individuals with special needs, particularly neurodiverse children, often cannot afford items that support learning, emotional regulation, or self-expression. Essential tools such as sensory equipment, Montessori materials, or musical instruments are often out of reach for those who need them most. Moreover, many valuable items are underused or discarded due to infrequent need, contributing to waste and unsustainable consumption patterns. Public institutions rarely provide inclusive, dignified ways for people to access such tools without stigma or bureaucracy. The Library of Things addresses this gap by offering free, non-discriminatory access to a wide range of items that support personal development, education, well-being, and inclusion, while fostering a culture of sharing, mutual support, and environmental responsibility. It redefines what a public library can be — not just a place for books, but a platform for social empowerment and sustainable community life.
innovations.description:
The Library of Things reimagines the role of a public library as a socially innovative platform that offers not only access to information but also to physical resources essential for learning, creativity, and well-being. As the first initiative of its kind in Lithuania and the Baltic region, it transforms traditional library services by allowing users to borrow over 200 items — from sensory tools and educational games to musical instruments and exploration tools such as microscopes and telescopes — entirely free of charge. What makes this solution innovative is its holistic and inclusive design: 1) It directly supports neurodiverse users, families, and educators by providing access to high-quality tools that would otherwise be unaffordable. 2) It includes instructional videos and printed guides for effective use, particularly for parents of children with special needs. 3) It leverages community donations, encourages circular use of resources, and strengthens local ties through shared ownership and trust. 4) It promotes dignified borrowing without stigma, integrating sustainable practices and inclusive services into everyday life. This model is easily replicable in other regions and proves that public libraries can be active agents of social change, enabling equity, creativity, and sustainability at the community level.
The Library of Things initiative developed by Šiauliai County Povilas Višinskis Public Library (Lithuania) was inspired by the United States, one of the global pioneers of this concept. Public libraries across the U.S., such as those in Sacramento, Berkeley, and Ann Arbor, have long implemented item-lending services that go beyond books — offering tools, tech kits, instruments, and household items to promote equity, sustainability, and lifelong learning. These models demonstrated the library’s evolving role as a community empowerment hub. In recent years, similar initiatives have emerged in European countries such as the United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and the Netherlands, where Libraries of Things operate through public libraries or community-run centres. These projects share core values of resource-sharing, social inclusion, and environmental responsibility, proving adaptable to diverse social and cultural contexts. Building on these international inspirations, the Lithuanian model introduced a unique focus on neurodiversity, educational equity, and regional inclusion, making it the first of its kind in the Baltics and a replicable good practice in both library and social innovation sectors.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: Šiauliai County Povilas Višinskis Public Library
innovations.evidence:
Since its launch, the Library of Things has demonstrated a clear and growing need within the community. Over 1,300 residents have already used the service, with many items in constant circulation and waiting lists extending for several months. This sustained demand highlights not only the practical value of the collection but also its role in supporting inclusive education, creativity, and well-being. Importantly, the initiative has succeeded in engaging new user groups who do not typically visit libraries, thereby broadening cultural participation and strengthening social inclusion. It offers an accessible entry point into the library space for families, educators, and individuals with diverse needs — turning the library into a vibrant and responsive community hub. In recognition of its impact, the project was awarded the "DĖK’ui of the Year" prize at the 2024 Waste Culture Awards, organised by the Vilnius Regional Waste Management Centre. The project received over 11,000 public votes, earning the highest level of support among all nominated initiatives. The award celebrates initiatives that promote reuse practices and the sharing of sustainable ideas — confirming the Library of Things as a leading example of environmental and social innovation in the Baltic region.
The Library of Things initiative, developed and coordinated by Šiauliai County Povilas Višinskis Public Library, has already been successfully replicated in three other Lithuanian municipalities: Telšiai, Pakruojis, and Naujoji Akmenė. We led the entire implementation and mentoring process. As a result, the service now forms a geographically expanding network of socially engaged libraries, bringing access to educational and sensory items to wider and more diverse communities. This growing model strengthens interlibrary collaboration and visibility, with a clear long-term vision to scale the initiative nationally, making Library of Things services available in public libraries across all of Lithuania.

innovations.name: Mind The Gap
innovations.problem: The project has tackled the widespread social and economic exclusion of NEETs (young people not in education, employment or training) in Italy’s Campania Region. The area suffers a combination of early high school leaving, low educational outcomes, and persistent youth unemployment—conditions that leave many young people without the skills, support, or confidence to access training or work. Many NEETs face serious challenges: educational systems often fail to engage them meaningfully or provide the competencies required by today’s labour market. At the same time, material poverty, limited access to services, and a lack of motivation have deepened their sense of isolation and hopelessness. This is especially troubling given the strong demand for skilled labour in sectors like tourism and hospitality, which are central to Campania’s post-pandemic economic recovery. With the Neapolitan food culture as a global reference point, and hospitality booming beyond seasonal peaks, employers are now seeking professionals with updated international skills—from foreign language abilities to culinary techniques and customer service excellence. However, these demands often go unmet due to the gap in training and preparedness among the local workforce.
innovations.description:
The project has tackled these urgent challenges by offering vulnerable NEETs a structured, empowering pathway back into active life. Through tailored guidance, hands-on training, and a meaningful transnational mobility experience, the initiative not only has developed market-relevant skills but has also restored self-confidence, motivation, and hope. One of the project’s most innovative aspects has been the integration of the ALMA scheme into existing professional training pathways, such as those for chefs, pizza or pastry makers. This approach was complemented by additional support measures, including psychological counseling and career orientation services. These combined elements were designed to maximize the already highly positive impact of these training courses on employability and make them truly effective for the NEET target group. Furthermore, the  project has promoted effective social dialogue by actively involving FIPE (the Italian Federation of Public Establishments) that contributed by identifying key skills needed in the sector, supporting the matching between training and real labour market demands, and facilitating connections between participants and local employers—enhancing job opportunities after the mobility experience had come to an end.
In designing Mind The Gap, the partnership drew on a range of European and national initiatives that have shaped the response to the NEET phenomenon. Key among these are the Youth Guarantee, widely implemented in Campania since 2014, which highlighted both the potential and the limitations of mainstream activation programmes, and the Youth Employment Initiative, which underscored the need for targeted actions in high-unemployment regions. The ESF, particularly through the 2014–2020 Regional Operational Programme in Campania, provided valuable insights into structuring integrated, multi-level interventions for youth inclusion. Formamentis also built on its direct experience coordinating projects, such as the Erasmus+ UP-SCALE project (2020-1-IT01-KA102-008164), which supported transnational mobility for disadvantaged learners—those with disabilities, economic hardship, or special educational needs—offering tailored training and coaching for active labour market transitions. Finally, the project is grounded in the ALMA (Aim–Learn–Master–Achieve) initiative—first launched in Germany and expanded across Europe via networks like TLN Mobility. Mind the Gap builds on this model to pilot ALMA-type operations in Campania, combining personalised support with cross-border work-based learning to foster the social and professional reintegration of the most vulnerable NEETs.
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence: The project is now approaching its conclusion and has already demonstrated positive outcomes. As shown in pre-departure questionnaires and focus groups, all participants from the three training paths (kitchen, bakery, and pizza making) were highly motivated—eager to gain practical kitchen experience, improve their employability, and grow personally through an international internship. Despite their enthusiasm, students also reported some concerns. Common fears included language barriers, the pressure of meeting expectations, and the possibility of being assigned only marginal tasks. However, the post-mobility focus groups and feedback received so far have revealed overwhelmingly positive results. In particular, 100% of the participants in the kitchen path reported feeling fully integrated into their kitchen teams, taking on real responsibilities, and acquiring new culinary techniques. Beyond the technical skills, they also experienced substantial personal growth—developing teamwork, communication, stress management, and adaptability, particularly within multicultural environments. Initial obstacles were successfully overcome through observation, collaboration, and proactive learning. While data collection is still ongoing for the participants from the bakery and pizza making paths, it is worth mentioning that after returning from their international experience, participants from all paths took part in mock job interviews held at our facility. In addition to these sessions, they also received targeted input on how to build a strong and effective CV, tailored to the expectations of the hospitality sector. These activities aimed to prepare them for real-world interviews with local patisseries, pizzerias, and hotels. As a result, all participants were offered the opportunity to interview with companies in the local hospitality sector, highlighting the project’s strong impact on employability and its meaningful engagement with the local job market. The internship experience also had a transformative effect on participants’ self-perception and career outlook. Many reported increased self-confidence, clearer professional goals, and a newfound openness to pursuing international job opportunities. Among the most notable outcomes, 44% of participants have already secured employment contracts following their mobility experience, significantly exceeding initial expectations. This result reflects not only the success of the project’s design but also the participants’ capacity to convert training into real employment opportunities.

innovations.raw_text:
Mind The Gap
The project has tackled the widespread social and economic exclusion of NEETs (young people not in education, employment or training) in Italy’s Campania Region. The area suffers a combination of early high school leaving, low educational outcomes, and persistent youth unemployment—conditions that leave many young people without the skills, support, or confidence to access training or work. Many NEETs face serious challenges: educational systems often fail to engage them meaningfully or provide the competencies required by today’s labour market. At the same time, material poverty, limited access to services, and a lack of motivation have deepened their sense of isolation and hopelessness. This is especially troubling given the strong demand for skilled labour in sectors like tourism and hospitality, which are central to Campania’s post-pandemic economic recovery. With the Neapolitan food culture as a global reference point, and hospitality booming beyond seasonal peaks, employers are now seeking professionals with updated international skills—from foreign language abilities to culinary techniques and customer service excellence. However, these demands often go unmet due to the gap in training and preparedness among the local workforce.
The project has tackled these urgent challenges by offering vulnerable NEETs a structured, empowering pathway back into active life. Through tailored guidance, hands-on training, and a meaningful transnational mobility experience, the initiative not only has developed market-relevant skills but has also restored self-confidence, motivation, and hope. One of the project’s most innovative aspects has been the integration of the ALMA scheme into existing professional training pathways, such as those for chefs, pizza or pastry makers. This approach was complemented by additional support measures, including psychological counseling and career orientation services. These combined elements were designed to maximize the already highly positive impact of these training courses on employability and make them truly effective for the NEET target group. Furthermore, the  project has promoted effective social dialogue by actively involving FIPE (the Italian Federation of Public Establishments) that contributed by identifying key skills needed in the sector, supporting the matching between training and real labour market demands, and facilitating connections between participants and local employers—enhancing job opportunities after the mobility experience had come to an end.
In designing Mind The Gap, the partnership drew on a range of European and national initiatives that have shaped the response to the NEET phenomenon. Key among these are the Youth Guarantee, widely implemented in Campania since 2014, which highlighted both the potential and the limitations of mainstream activation programmes, and the Youth Employment Initiative, which underscored the need for targeted actions in high-unemployment regions. The ESF, particularly through the 2014–2020 Regional Operational Programme in Campania, provided valuable insights into structuring integrated, multi-level interventions for youth inclusion. Formamentis also built on its direct experience coordinating projects, such as the Erasmus+ UP-SCALE project (2020-1-IT01-KA102-008164), which supported transnational mobility for disadvantaged learners—those with disabilities, economic hardship, or special educational needs—offering tailored training and coaching for active labour market transitions. Finally, the project is grounded in the ALMA (Aim–Learn–Master–Achieve) initiative—first launched in Germany and expanded across Europe via networks like TLN Mobility. Mind the Gap builds on this model to pilot ALMA-type operations in Campania, combining personalised support with cross-border work-based learning to foster the social and professional reintegration of the most vulnerable NEETs.
The project is now approaching its conclusion and has already demonstrated positive outcomes. As shown in pre-departure questionnaires and focus groups, all participants from the three training paths (kitchen, bakery, and pizza making) were highly motivated—eager to gain practical kitchen experience, improve their employability, and grow personally through an international internship. Despite their enthusiasm, students also reported some concerns. Common fears included language barriers, the pressure of meeting expectations, and the possibility of being assigned only marginal tasks. However, the post-mobility focus groups and feedback received so far have revealed overwhelmingly positive results. In particular, 100% of the participants in the kitchen path reported feeling fully integrated into their kitchen teams, taking on real responsibilities, and acquiring new culinary techniques. Beyond the technical skills, they also experienced substantial personal growth—developing teamwork, communication, stress management, and adaptability, particularly within multicultural environments. Initial obstacles were successfully overcome through observation, collaboration, and proactive learning. While data collection is still ongoing for the participants from the bakery and pizza making paths, it is worth mentioning that after returning from their international experience, participants from all paths took part in mock job interviews held at our facility. In addition to these sessions, they also received targeted input on how to build a strong and effective CV, tailored to the expectations of the hospitality sector. These activities aimed to prepare them for real-world interviews with local patisseries, pizzerias, and hotels. As a result, all participants were offered the opportunity to interview with companies in the local hospitality sector, highlighting the project’s strong impact on employability and its meaningful engagement with the local job market. The internship experience also had a transformative effect on participants’ self-perception and career outlook. Many reported increased self-confidence, clearer professional goals, and a newfound openness to pursuing international job opportunities. Among the most notable outcomes, 44% of participants have already secured employment contracts following their mobility experience, significantly exceeding initial expectations. This result reflects not only the success of the project’s design but also the participants’ capacity to convert training into real employment opportunities.

innovations.name: Train the Trainers
innovations.problem: The current mental health paradigm recognizes the active role of individuals in their own recovery journey. The Recovery College serves as a model to support this approach. Well-established in the UK, the Recovery College is a learning space offering courses on mental health, enabling each person to become a "student of their own well-being." Within this framework, there is a growing need to train trainers capable of applying recovery principles across different contexts. The project aims to broaden the very concept of "trainer," by including so-called “experts by experience” — individuals who have personally faced mental health challenges — as key figures in the training process
innovations.description:
The project’s innovation lies in developing an educational approach to mental health that empowers individuals to take responsibility and play an active role in their own recovery journey. The Recovery College model places strong emphasis on the role of *peer support*—individuals who draw on their own lived experience with mental health challenges to support others facing similar situations. This peer-to-peer dynamic fosters engagement, hope, and a renewed sense of possibility, which are essential elements in the healing process.
In 2022, the Bologna Local Health Authority (Azienda USL), in collaboration with the University of Bologna, the Municipality, and the Metropolitan City, launched the project *“Perché ci vuole una città”* ("Because It Takes a City"), which led to the creation of the Bologna Recovery College. This is an innovative learning space offering co-designed mental health courses open to all citizens. The project presented here builds upon this foundation, aiming to promote the training of professionals in the recovery approach, thereby contributing to its dissemination both locally and beyond regional borders.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: Expected benefits include: the creation of a professional network able to deliver Recovery College courses consistently and effectively; the promotion of a systemic approach to well-being; the transferability of the model at both local and broader levels; and the growth of an integrated ecosystem working to support mental health across communities.

innovations.name: MY OWN-concept
innovations.problem: People with intellectual disabilities or similar support needs often face barriers to exercising their rights, making independent choices, and being recognised as experts in their own lives. Traditional support systems may limit inclusion by focusing on care rather than person wants or needs or the full scope of a person’s life. When individuals lack accessible ways to express themselves or reflect on what matters to them, they risk becoming outsiders in their own lives. There is a need for inclusive, person-centred tools that support decision-making, identity, participation, and future thinking no matter how high person´s support needs are.
innovations.description:
My Own concept is an innovative and inclusive life-planning and decision-making model co-created with people who need support. It transforms the abstract idea of self-determination and inclusion into a tangible, everyday practice through structured tools, visual elements, and inspiring methods. It is a multidimensional approach including supported decision-making, future thinking, self-directed support, and gamified reflection tools, all designed to adapt to different communication styles, life situations and levels of support need. Unlike many traditional forms or service tools, My Own is not something fixed. It is a modular and flexible set of tools that helps each person think about their own life, choices, and experiences. The ten “keys” of the concept help people and their supporters talk about important topics like voice, will, rights, goals, and community. The concept is also new in how it sees the role of professionals, family, and others. They are not there to decide for the person, but to support them by using shared language and visual tools to build understanding together. My Own combines real-life experience, systems thinking, and human rights in a way that is practical and easy to use.
In in the last couple of years, our development work has focused specifically on supported decision-making and strengthening individualized life planning. We have designed and tested concrete tools and methods that help people reflect on their lives, express their views, and make decisions that matter to them. This work has been carried out in close collaboration with people who need support, their family members, and the professionals who support them in everyday life. In our development process, we have paid special attention to the type of support each person feels they need and hope to receive. We have actively used for example principles of self-directed support (particularly inspired by the UK model) and person-centered thinking.
One of our key priorities has been to clarify complex ideas and service structures by breaking them into smaller, understandable parts, and creating accessible, visual, and practical methods that allow for real participation in decision-making. This also helps shift the focus from a service-centered model to one that is truly person-led and inclusive. My Own concept is the result of this long-term, co-creative development. It is a human rights-based, inclusive and flexible support model for enabling people to reflect on their lives, make informed decisions, and plan their future based on their own wishes, values, and needs.
We believe that the realization of self-determination and inclusion is about the whole life context, not just isolated situations. For a person to make choices and decisions, to be part of meaningful communities, or to act as an active citizen in society, they must have access to information that concerns them and matters to them, the skills to exercise their self-determination and participation in everyday life, and a sense of personal significance and belonging. This must also be considered from the perspective of support. That is why we have wanted to build the My Own concept as a diverse and holistic framework that supports different perspectives and enables individuals to grow into experts in their own lives. The My Own concept is built around ten thematic "keys", which serve as tools for both the individual and their support network. Each key opens a perspective into the person’s life, enabling reflection, communication, and future planning:
• Me, Myself and I – Focuses on identity and self-awareness. Helps individuals recognize their personality, strengths, and what makes them feel good and safe. A crucial foundation for decision-making and building confidence.
• My Voice – Encourages self-expression and makes one’s opinion heard. Supports individuals in choosing how they want to communicate and be heard, including alternative and augmentative methods.
• My Everyday Life –
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
The My Own concept leads to increased self-determination, participation, and inclusion for people with intellectual disabilities or similar support needs. It enables individuals to reflect on what matters to them, express their views, and make informed decisions. The concept improves the quality of support by providing professionals and family members with concrete tools for listening, discussing and co-planning. Key results include increased self-advocacy and inclusion and more person-centred planning of services.
My Own concept has resulted in tangible and meaningful changes on both the individual and system level.
The most important outcomes are:
• Strengthened self-determination. Individuals are supported to recognize their own values, form and express their own opinions, and make choices based on what matters to them. This builds confidence and self-advocacy.
• Increased participation and inclusion. People are more actively involved in their own lives and in their communities. The concept encourages active roles in decision-making and societal life, even in small but meaningful ways.
• Improved communication and relationships. The tools enhance mutual understanding between individuals and supporters. Difficult or abstract topics become easier to talk about, leading to more respectful, meaningful interactions.
• More personalized and goal-oriented support. When people are involved in planning and expressing their goals, services and support systems can better respond to individual expectations and needs. This leads to more effective and satisfying support.
• Greater awareness of rights and possibilities. The concept increases knowledge about rights in practical terms, and helps individuals reflect on how their rights are (or are not) being realized in daily life. It supports advocacy and empowerment.

innovations.name: AlarmAlly
innovations.lead: The Regional Centre for Social Policy in Cracow, Krakowskie Centrum Innowacyjnych Technologii INNOAGH sp. z o.o.
innovations.problem:
In many public institutions — such as universities, schools, and hospitals, as well as in hotels, shopping malls and similar places - emergency evacuation procedures, though formally established, often encounter significant challenges when put into practice. People who are excluded or need additional support are particularly vulnerable during such emergencies.
Despite the sincere efforts of public and private institutions to improve evacuation protocols and enhance safety, there is currently a lack of simple, reliable solutions available on the market. In dangerous situations Deaf individals must rely on ambient or visual signals, which are seldom paired with audible fire alarms. Some people may ignore alarms, unsure whether it’s merely a test or they may already be affected by smoke or unconscious, and therefore unable to respond.
Furthermore, Deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals, as well as those living alone and needing emergency assistance, are often left without help — even in their own homes, which should be their safest refuge.
innovations.description:
That’s where AllarmAlly steps in.
AlarmAlly is a free mobile app compatibile with both Android and IOS systems, as well as most wearable devices. Powered by artificial intelligence, the app detects the unique acoustic signature of fire alarms and immediately alerts the user through customisable vibrations and/or flashing lights. If no user response is registered, a pre-selected support person (such as a friend, parent, or safety officer) will be notified.
The app requires no additional devices - just your phone. Compared to similar features built into some phone models, AlarmAlly is more reliable - its operation has been tested under various conditions by Deaf, hard of hearing, and healthy people. The simple interface was designed in accordance with accessibility regulations, making it easy to use and intuitive.
AlarmAlly has its own landing page, where user manuals and installation instructions in Polish Sign Language are available.
The solution was developed as a micro-innovation by Marcin Kotliński, Polish innovator-programmer with funding from the ESF. The project is currently supported by the ESF+ and is moving forward through the acceleration process.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: The Regional Centre for Social Policy in Cracow, Krakowskie Centrum Innowacyjnych Technologii INNOAGH sp. z o.o.
innovations.evidence:
✅ Precise detection of fire alarm sounds using AI algorithms
✅ Customised alerts: vibrations, light signals – or both
✅ Privacy first: no data collection or storage
✅ Secure: hosted on Swiss servers, developed in Europe
✅ No ads, no distractions – completely free to use
✅ Compatible with Android, iOS & wearable devices
✅ Simple, user-tested interface
✅ Available in Polish Sign Language (PJM)
✅ Scalable internationally
authors: The Regional Centre for Social Policy in Cracow, Krakowskie Centrum Innowacyjnych Technologii INNOAGH sp. z o.o.

People who are excluded or need additional support are particularly vulnerable during such emergencies.
Despite the sincere efforts of public and private institutions to improve evacuation protocols and enhance safety, there is currently a lack of simple, reliable solutions available on the market. In dangerous situations Deaf individals must rely on ambient or visual signals, which are seldom paired with audible fire alarms. Some people may ignore alarms, unsure whether it’s merely a test or they may already be affected by smoke or unconscious, and therefore unable to respond.
Furthermore, Deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals, as well as those living alone and needing emergency assistance, are often left without help — even in their own homes, which should be their safest refuge.
That’s where AllarmAlly steps in.
AlarmAlly is a free mobile app compatibile with both Android and IOS systems, as well as most wearable devices. Powered by artificial intelligence, the app detects the unique acoustic signature of fire alarms and immediately alerts the user through customisable vibrations and/or flashing lights. If no user response is registered, a pre-selected support person (such as a friend, parent, or safety officer) will be notified.
The app requires no additional devices - just your phone. Compared to similar features built into some phone models, AlarmAlly is more reliable - its operation has been tested under various conditions by Deaf, hard of hearing, and healthy people. The simple interface was designed in accordance with accessibility regulations, making it easy to use and intuitive.
AlarmAlly has its own landing page, where user manuals and installation instructions in Polish Sign Language are available.
The solution was developed as a micro-innovation by Marcin Kotliński, Polish innovator-programmer with funding from the ESF. The project is currently supported by the ESF+ and is moving forward through the acceleration process.
✅ Precise detection of fire alarm sounds using AI algorithms
✅ Customised alerts: vibrations, light signals – or both
✅ Privacy first: no data collection or storage
✅ Secure: hosted on Swiss servers, developed in Europe
✅ No ads, no distractions – completely free to use
✅ Compatible with Android, iOS & wearable devices
✅ Simple, user-tested interface
✅ Available in Polish Sign Language (PJM)
✅ Scalable internationally

innovations.name: EDKI
innovations.lead: The Regional Centre for Social Policy in Cracow, Krakowskie Centrum Innowacyjnych Technologii INNOAGH sp. z o.o.
innovations.problem:
Children with graphomotor difficulties and spastic limbs are, in a way, excluded from artistic activities. Painting and drawing using regular crayons or writing tools is impossible for them. Observations have shown a strong need for these children to engage in painting, art, and creative activities. Artistic and manual play enriches a child's world, supporting the development of imagination, emotional expression, and fine motor skills. For children with spasticity, the main barriers are the lack of appropriate tools as well as templates—pre-prepared graphic materials that support artistic development and assist in hand therapy.
The identified problems affect not only the end users—children, but also their parents. The home environment of children with spasticity is often significantly burdened by caregiving responsibilities. One aspect of this overload is the "expansion" of the therapeutic environment into the home—specialized equipment is sometimes used at home, and exercises are carried out, which in practice means that parents must constantly remind, persuade, and monitor children during rehabilitation activities. However, children are not always cooperative or easy to communicate with. Additionally, the development of children with spasticity is often uneven, new difficulties may emerge, and previously achieved progress can regress. In this context, parents may feel fatigued by the constant need to “therapize” their children and may need some relief. A solution to this problem is the use of crayons that a child can use independently, gaining a sense of agency, while also benefiting from their therapeutic properties. Testing of the innovation has shown that EDKI are universal tool, suitable for all children with graphomotor problems.
innovations.description:
The solution was developed as a micro-innovation by Aleksandra Satława, Polish innovator-designer with funding from the ESF. The project is currently supported by the ESF+ and is moving forward through the acceleration process.
The core of the innovation is therapeutic crayons for children with graphomotor difficulties. The innovation was originally designed for children with disabilities, primarily those with hand spasticity. However, it has now become a universal, innovative tool for working with children in general.
Thanks to their special shape, the crayons stimulate and activate the hand, fingers, wrist, and elbow to extend rather than close, supporting active therapy through play. The product enables young children with hand paresis to access creative artistic activities such as writing, drawing, and coloring – which are fundamental forms of activity in the harmonious development of every child. The uniqueness of the crayons lies in their special shape, which allows drawing with an open hand by placing the crayon between the fingers.
They promote the tripod grip, are original, visually appealing, and spark curiosity. Their unusual shape, weight, and relatively high durability make them engaging for children, allowing for drawing (leaving a colorful mark) in many different ways (using various grips and angles), while also offering many possibilities for adaptation and customization. Worksheets for working with children facilitate the process of working with this tool.
An important aspect of the innovation is the ability to make the crayons at home using readily available materials, such as remnants of used crayons. The innovation includes a model design for making a silicone mold that can be printed on a 3D printer. Simply pour melted old wax crayons (made from beeswax, soy wax, or rice wax) into a mold to create fabulously colorful EDKI. A simple guide shows how to make the crayons at home.
The further development of the innovation during acceleration enabled the improvement of the production process through the design and testing of a 3D model of a cylindrical mold for crayon casting, research and testing of new materials and colors, development of EDKI brand visual identity, design of packaging adapted to children's needs, and analysis of a non-commercial implementation model through occupational therapy workshops.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.beneficiaries: The Regional Centre for Social Policy in Cracow, Krakowskie Centrum Innowacyjnych Technologii INNOAGH sp. z o.o.
innovations.evidence:
The impressions of parents and children after the EDKI testing period were overwhelmingly positive. The crayons genuinely enabled children with spasticity to draw and proved to be significantly better than traditional crayons—primarily because they were easier to use and provided a greater sense of satisfaction from drawing. Importantly, the overall positive feedback came not only from younger testers (aged 2.5–4) but also from older children (aged 9–12).
An important finding from tests conducted in therapy centers was that EDKI proved highly effective when working with children with various developmental and graphomotor difficulties. The advantages of EDKI—especially their unusual shape, weight, and relatively high durability—make the crayons intriguing to children. They allow for drawing (leaving a colorful mark) in many different ways (using various grips and angles) while also offering a wide range of adaptation and customization possibilities. According to therapists, a key advantage of EDKI is that their shape naturally positions children's fingers into a tripod grip and also helps prevent the grip from slipping. In the experts' opinion, no other crayons available on the market offer these features, and this characteristic can be very helpful in developing the habit of using the tripod (pencil) grip.
BENEFITS:
EDKI enable or make it easier for children with upper limb spasticity to draw, and they are easier to use than regular crayons.
Their main functional advantage is their thickness – they are thicker than the thickest crayons currently available on the market.
They are durable and wear down slowly.
They are safe – none of the children who tested them got hurt while using them.
They have vibrant colors and usually leave a clear mark.
They produce little mess and are easy to clean off various surfaces (such as tables, floors, or even walls painted with washable paint).
They are fairly soft, yet firm enough to maintain shape.
They are aesthetically pleasing, and their two-tone design attracts interest.

innovations.name: Cuimsiú Programme - A Workability Inclusive Pathways to Employment Programme
innovations.problem: Addressing the need for support for Neurodivergent and Disabled People seeking to enter tech employment. Our programme also addresses the need to build the capacity of employers who want to create more inclusive workplaces.
innovations.description: The Cuimsiú programme is not a 9-5 classroom-based programme. Our team holds online and in person events and training from March to November each year on a range of topics, while providing 1:1 support with our Employability Mentors. The programme is suitable for people who are unemployed, in employment or education. We have aimed to make the programme as flexible as possible for those who have multiple responsibilities. We offer personalised supports to help people reach their employment goals. What the programme covers: Access to tech training, platforms and workshops. 1:1 sessions with our Employability Mentors. Preparation for the workplace – interview preparation and CV workshops. Access to assistive technology. Opportunities to network with employers. Soft skills training – communication, leadership, team work, confidence and more! Mental health and wellbeing. Exploring career options and meeting leaders in industry. Self-advocacy and your rights in the workplace. Transitioning to the workplace. To support and guide us in the roll out of the Cuimsiú Programme, we have an Advisory Council made up of current candidates with lived experience, advocacy organisations, employers, and experts in the field. Alongside working with our candidates, our team supports employers in their own efforts to create more inclusive workplaces. Our Cuimsiú Employer Network provides employers with: Online and in person training Opportunities to share inclusive practices. Opportunities to meet and hear from our candidates. Support and resources from the Cuimsiú Team
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities, Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.evidence: The Objectives of the Programme are: To improve the employment prospects of people with disabilities who are currently distant from the labour market. To build the capacity of employers to recruit, retain and progress people with disabilities within their workforce. To facilitate new partnerships amongst stakeholders (people with disabilities, disability services, employment services and employers) and new approaches to providing employment supports to people with disabilities.
