innovations.name: Aqui Contigo
innovations.lead: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.problem:
The last moment, death, is surrounded by a set of rituals that emphasize pain, loss and suffering. It becomes one of the most memorable and changing moments for people: those who are aware that they are leaving and those who stay. In this way, death is still a taboo and something that is not well assimilated and understood in society. There is no conscious education for life where death is intrinsically present.
In fact, probably as a result of the taboos that still persist around death, society does not have any type of social protection that allows a first-degree relative to care for the terminally ill person full-time, as happens, for example, at the birth of children. , in which parents can take time off to care for their newborn. The social abandonment of patients has as main effects the feeling of loneliness of the patient who leaves without being able to feel the comfort of interacting with those who remain. Families have a feeling of impotence and frustration that adds to the pain of the loss itself, with around 50% ending up needing psychosocial and spiritual intervention, both in the anticipatory mourning phase and in the post-mourning phase, with complications that lead to taking medication and depressive situations.
innovations.description:
The main focus of the “Aqui Contigo” project is on the emotional and family dimension, seeking, in one hand, to provide dignity at the end of life, and on the other and, taking care of those who are helping in their process of loss and mourning, which is often long. and painful. It is important to bear in mind that dignity is an important construct, particularly on the deathbed, where unique and singular support can be provided to those who are dying, their caregivers and their family.
Two musicians and a music therapist. The solution involves analyzing each individual situation, stipulating a careful and individualized plan for musical sessions to promote the dignity of people at the end of their lives and, inevitably, extending to the family and all professional caregivers.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.evidence:
Based on Oliver Holme's phrase “Heal sometimes, relieve often, and comfort always”, "Aqui Contigo" focused on being with others, in sound and music, which contributes for emotional, social, mental and spiritual well-being. Alleviating pain, fear and loss at the moment of Death and Raise Awareness in the Community about this topic, which still presents itself as taboo, so that it is better accepted and understood. The existence of a calm and safe environment influences a dignified death. People in care palliative and/or terminal conditions, their family members and caregivers must be able to live these moments from a different approach. Mediated by sound and music, it is created a privileged linked space in a mostly non-verbal context, moving a large impact on each person and on society.
The Impact observed for those at the end of life is undoubtedly relevant, we can realize, through surrender to the moment, the reduction of loneliness in the most difficult times that the human being goes through, the appreciation of life in these most delicate moments, the awareness that death is a fact and what is important is to give meaning and dignity to life and how important it is to reduce the fear of death and mitigate the sense of loss.
It was also visible to notice the increase in interaction between family and friends during the process, music was an important mediator of these moments, allowing an aproach that values life and its quality until the last breath. Also through it and the construction of a legacy (music CD, songbook of new compositions, concert) was possible to help overcome sadness and find a source of comfort.
authors: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos

innovations.name: ÓPERA IN PRISON: Mozart ON
innovations.lead: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.description: On a global level, this project aims to minimize stigma towards inmates and significantly contribute to the success of their integration, after serving their sentences. At a more individual level, the project aims to provide inmates with socially and communally supported and structured exits, as well as contributing significantly to improving their behavior in prison, reducing the sanctions to which they are subject in the case of misconduct. The big change expected is the increase in the success rate of reintegration processes for young prisoners.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.evidence:
The social intervention through the artistic languages can represent in the life of each subject a great socio-educational significance, contributing to reinforce numerous personal, social, affective, emotional and relational skills.
The social reintegration of young inmates presents a great challenge for professionals, since the period of detention can indeed allow the individual a period of reflection, there are also ties (of friendship, family...) that fall apart, and that, in most cases, it is important to reconcile.
The project "Opera in Prison" searched, through music, theater and dance to promote a strategy of socio-educational intervention that catalyses a socially framed life. This project, funded by the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation, took place in the Leiria Prison (youth), having been promoted by Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos (SAMP). Since the beginning of 2014, a group of 50 inmates.
To understand the impact of this project on the proscess of social reintegbration of young inmates, a research methodology was adopted based on interviews with the various stakholders in the project.
The results presented evidenced the role that artistic languages have played in the lives of young inmates and their families and the way in which they have contributed to a more effective social reintegration.
Keywords: Artistic languages, Young inmates, Social reintegration.
authors: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos

innovations.name: UP! Tutoring support
innovations.lead: UP! Free tutoring in local education initiatives
innovations.problem: The primary issue addressed in the research is the significant educational inequality in Austria, where children from low socio-economic backgrounds have substantially lower chances of achieving educational standards compared to their peers from higher socio-economic backgrounds. This disparity in educational outcomes is rooted in various socio-economic factors that limit access to academic support and resources, thus perpetuating a cycle of disadvantage for children from poorer families.
innovations.description:
The innovative solution proposed involves a structured tutoring program where secondary school students and adult volunteers provide free tutoring to primary school children. The program uses a competency-based training model for the tutors, incorporating visualized-model-centered instruction and practical training scenarios with child actors. This approach ensures that the tutors are well-prepared to offer effective and engaging support, even adapting to remote tutoring during the COVID-19 pandemic with minimal additional training.
UP! is a social innovation in which volunteers from the community are empowered to set up and lead local learning initiatives themselves. All parts of the programme are integrated into the school system or take place in cooperation with companies. The tutors are trained and supervised within the framework of school subjects. In companies, UP! functions as a corporate social responsibility project in which employees help the children as tutors. It is important to note that this programme support children with significant learning deficits individual and based on a development plan.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: UP! Free tutoring in local education initiatives
innovations.evidence:
The project yielded several positive outcomes, including enhanced learning and motivation among the tutees and significant skill development for the tutors. The practice-oriented training model was effective, with tutors rapidly adapting to distance tutoring when necessary. The tutees showed improved academic performance and self-perception as learners. Additionally, the inclusion of all participants in the design and implementation process fostered a strong professional learning community and facilitated smoother implementation.
The entire project was evaluated as part of a dissertation (Educational Design Research) and was assessed very favourably by an external evaluation team ( https://epub.jku.at/obvulihs/content/titleinfo/8905255 ).
ISB Stiftungspreis Bildungsinnovation: Volksschule Concordia Bad Ischl, where UP! Tutoring Support was jointly developed, has been awarded the ISB Stiftungspreis Bildungsinnovation, recognizing it as one of the most innovative schools in Austria for the tutoring support system. Five schools in the category of general education will receive this award.

innovations.name: klooz, learning ecosystem in development
innovations.problem:
Demographic
Specifically rural context, with a concentration of residents in the small urban centers and small numbers of residents in the core villages (Borgloon and Tongeren together have 30…): residents in the core villages are rather the elder population,  they often live alone. Logically there is an increased risk of social isolation. Seniors living alone in rural and aging municipalities are often more vulnerable due to insufficient help at home, mobility barriers and loneliness.
Another challenge is the increased presence of newcomers and families with a migration background who require special attention to integration and bonding with the region.
Economic
Higer than average figures of deprivation and child poverty: in Borgloon and Tongeren the share of children and young people (0-24 years) with an increased health insurance contribution is 18.6%. That is higher than in Limburg and the Flemish average.
Technical profiles are difficult to find and too many short-skilled employees do not have (quality) work. In Borgloon and Tongeren respectively 9.3% and 12% of job seekers are under 25 years old. More than 42% (Borgloon) and 47% (Tongeren) of job seekers have low education. On the other side, there are 602 open jobs in both municipalities (383 temporary + 219 permanent, excluding interim jobs). For the majority (75%), a diploma is not required.(Source: VDAB Limburg 31/05/22.) There is a discrepancy.
Social

innovations.name: #SheDIDIT
innovations.problem: #SheDIDIT’s mission has its origins in the constatation that a lot of talent and potential is going to waste, because some people don’t know how to start their business or where to go. After having two businesses of her own, founder Lien Warmenbol saw that this is mostly the case for women of colour, who are furthest away from the image of ‘the entrepreneur’. There is a mismatch between this group of people and the traditional entrepreneurial organisations.
innovations.description:
SheMeansBusiness ( www.shedidit.be/shemeansbusiness ): individual business coaching in 5 tailor made sessions. 500+ women followed this personal business coaching by one of our 7 coaches, since the start of the program in 2021.
Youthpreneurs ( www.shedidit.be/youthpreneurs ): group program for youngsters where girls (and boys) from 15-30 y/o work towards their business plan/pitch in 10 weeks. 250+ youngsters participated in Antwerp, Genk, Gent and Brussels since the start of the program in 2021.
#SheHUB ( www.shedidit.be/shehub ): inclusive shared conceptstore in Antwerp-Berchem where +- 20 concepts at the time can experiment with the physical sale of their products. 60+ makers and entrepreneurs took part in the program since the opening in October 2022.
Aftercare programs : different offers for growing entrepreneurs, such as #SheFUND (rent-free loan), Power Talks on confidence, master mind programs.
Events and community building ( www.shedidit.be/events ): monthly free workshops (online/offline), network events, co-working, open source database talentpool, online community and online academy.
innovations.target_group: Migrants and ethnic minorities
innovations.evidence:
Impact made from 2018 to 2024 (Q1):
366 youngsters went through our #Youthpreneurs program
720 women where coached in our #SheMeansBusiness program
101 women sold their products through our #SheHUB
We reach over 1 million people through our social media channels
We reached 7.000 girls and women during our workshops and events hosted in Flanders and Brussels
We welcome + 350 in our open source datapool ('Talentpool')

innovations.name: Les Petites Cantines
innovations.problem: Our modern societies are facing the erosion of social bonds, resulting in a significant part of the population feeling abandoned, excluded or useless, no matter if they are rich or poor, young or old, local or exiled.
innovations.description:
Les Petites Cantines design a new type of communal place in the form of restaurants or lunchrooms available to all, offering a new opportunity for social interactions to the inhabitants of a neighborhood. We revolution the way we address loneliness by empowering citizens to become agents of social cohesion and learn again how to create valuable social bonds.
Les Petites Cantines is a network of neighbourhood canteens, where citizen can share meal time to create social links, and experience sustainable food, paying what they want. Inhabitants can cook together, meet people from other generations and different courses of life. Each canteen is financially independant, and run by the inhabitants.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
14 restaurants opened in France
20 other projects are working to open in the next 3 years in France and Belgium
more than 15 000 inhabitants have their membership in the restaurants
more than 125 000 meals served since the beginning of the adventure
35 jobs created
97,5% of the inhabitants feel welcomed just as they are
76% of the inhabitants get aware of the prejudices they attached to strangers
91% of the inhabitants consider free-pricing as a reliable tool for  quality food to become reachable to everyone
more than 1 inhabitant out of 2 has sustainably transformed his comportement when eating

innovations.problem:
The strengthening of the visibility of the Roma through all this extroversion caused negative feelings in part of the local society.
Difficulty in finding human resources in a small society to implement individual actions
innovations.description:
We worked for vulnerable groups with vulnerable groups. The success of the synergy of the programs in the Municipality of Katerini has tangible results. We achieved the visibility of vulnerable groups through all outreach actions.Student dropout, social racism and the level of poverty have now been greatly reduced while employment and the acceptance of the local community, have increased.We, also, emphasize to the fight against racism through school awareness campaign.
We create awareness through information campaigns not only to fight racism but also to defend children's rights. We consider it necessary to implement actions where the central axis is the child, defending their rights in the best possible way. We must respect their inalienable right to develop in a healthy and friendly environment.More specifically, we have managed to defend the child's right to equal access to information. We turn them into active citizens. We organize informative workshops concerning the protection of the environment and the rights of every child.

innovations.name: Brake-Out
innovations.problem:
Young people with disabilities are not given the opportunity to develop their full potential. They grow up in systems that isolate them from their peers and keep them small. Flanders leads with most students in specialized education in Europe. Some young people repeat their last year of secondary school 3 to 8 times because they have no prospect of taking the next step in their lives.  This leads to school fatigue. We see a lot of young people leaving school with drooping shoulders, they have low self-esteem, they think of themselves that they are not good at anything, have no desire for the future and low self-confidence.  Deficit thinking in education is pernicious for all young people. But for young people with disabilities, deficit thinking is most disastrous.  In the current systems, there is too much focus on the disability, the impairment and everything that is difficult.  They are very much brought down by the “waterfall system".  Did you know that young people with disabilities are decided at the age of 12 whether they can do a job later or not.  Too often the expectations are very low and they are prepared for a life in a protected context (read facility) where the focus on care is high.  Young people are thus reduced to objects of care, but no one becomes happy from being well cared for.  Young people with disabilities also want to be meaningful and take on a visible role of importance in society. The potential present in these young people is very much greater than what we see developed in current systems.  Moreover, growing up in systems that segregate them leads to lifelong segregation. However, the right to support and the right to an inclusive life are enshrined in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that Belgium signed in 2009. The UN Convention approaches disability from a human rights perspective. It strives for an inclusive society where people with disabilities can and are allowed to make their own choices as full citizens like everyone else. The convention marked a paradigm shift: people with disabilities are not merely objects of concern, they are citizens with a voice and rights. Yet every day, people with disabilities have to struggle with all kinds of (in)visible barriers. This leads to exclusion and discrimination.
Brake-Out addresses several critical social issues:
Segregation and Low Expectations : a significant number of young people with disabilities are placed in specialized education, often leading to lifelong segregation and low self-esteem.

sections.question: Problem
sections.answer:
Young people with disabilities are not given the opportunity to develop their full potential. They grow up in systems that isolate them from their peers and keep them small. Flanders leads with most students in specialized education in Europe. Some young people repeat their last year of secondary school 3 to 8 times because they have no prospect of taking the next step in their lives.  This leads to school fatigue. We see a lot of young people leaving school with drooping shoulders, they have low self-esteem, they think of themselves that they are not good at anything, have no desire for the future and low self-confidence.  Deficit thinking in education is pernicious for all young people. But for young people with disabilities, deficit thinking is most disastrous.  In the current systems, there is too much focus on the disability, the impairment and everything that is difficult.  They are very much brought down by the “waterfall system".  Did you know that young people with disabilities are decided at the age of 12 whether they can do a job later or not.  Too often the expectations are very low and they are prepared for a life in a protected context (read facility) where the focus on care is high.  Young people are thus reduced to objects of care, but no one becomes happy from being well cared for.  Young people with disabilities also want to be meaningful and take on a visible role of importance in society. The potential present in these young people is very much greater than what we see developed in current systems.  Moreover, growing up in systems that segregate them leads to lifelong segregation. However, the right to support and the right to an inclusive life are enshrined in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that Belgium signed in 2009. The UN Convention approaches disability from a human rights perspective. It strives for an inclusive society where people with disabilities can and are allowed to make their own choices as full citizens like everyone else. The convention marked a paradigm shift: people with disabilities are not merely objects of concern, they are citizens with a voice and rights. Yet every day, people with disabilities have to struggle with all kinds of (in)visible barriers. This leads to exclusion and discrimination.
Brake-Out addresses several critical social issues:
Segregation and Low Expectations : a significant number of young people with disabilities are placed in specialized education, often leading to lifelong segregation and low self-esteem.
Deficit-Based Approach : The current educational and support systems focus heavily on disabilities and limitations, rather than on the strengths and talents of individuals.
Systemic Exclusion : Decisions about a child’s future capabilities are made as early as age 12, often relegating them to low-expectation tracks and preparing them for a life of dependency.
We believe that people with and without disability can live, learn and work together.
Brake-Out helps you build the life YOU want!

innovations.name: JOVE OPORTUNITAT (JOOP)
innovations.problem: In today's society, a significant number of young people are being excluded from social life due to a series of problems such as lack of hope and hope, broken families, serious economic difficulties and absence of policies that listen to each individual. This leads to each person isolating themselves and leaving the educational system and the intention of entering the world of work since everything "does not matter to them." The purpose of JOOP is to ensure that each young person makes a change in attitude, leaving disappointment behind. and frustration over an uncertain future and acquire a series of technical skills through direct work to promote their self-esteem, motivation and positivity. The return to the educational system, mostly to vocational training, will be the objective around which the program is carried out, since through training we will be able to increase the employability of the participating people. With this, JOOP tries to respond to priority 5, which refers to non-formal education for young people at risk of dropping out of the educational system and to the specific objective FSE+4.5 F of the Program, consisting of "Strengthening employability and skills professionals of young people not employed and not integrated into education or training systems.”
innovations.description:
The specific object of the action is the provision of a service for carrying out training and orientation actions (coaching), in groups and individually, for young people with a low level of training, who neither study nor work. The modules that make up each one The training-orientation actions have a total duration of 104 school days. The JOOP program materializes in an action whose primary content is the personal and professional guidance of the young participant, from a comprehensive vision of the person, to allow them to build their own life project.
Module 1: Personal development (attitudinal coaching I):
-Improves “mental strength”:  Self-esteem. Free yourself from labels and recover lost self-esteem, to support personal and professional projects. Don't blame others or the world, don't feel sorry for yourself, don't waste time on things you can't control, don't live in the past, don't be afraid of calculated risks, don't repeat mistakes, don't give up. , not expecting immediate results, tolerance for frustration. Take control over your own life.
-Independence and responsibility. Character formation. Autonomy, self-demand, self-discipline, tenacity, responsible habits. Organization and planning. I control impulsivity and anger, I regulate my emotions, I know how to manage conflicts. Commitment: I commit to something and I keep it, my word can be trusted. Sensible decision making, critical thinking, ability to deliberate and choose. I am honest, I face my mistakes, I accept the consequences. I can change my character.
-I take care of my health: a healthy body for a healthy mind.Healthy lifestyle habits: diet, sport, hygiene. Healthy leisure. Freedom from addictive substances and behaviors: development of protective factors against consumption. Stress and anxiety management techniques
-Domestic curriculum. Relationships in the family context. Tasks, responsibilities. Money management.
-Time management. Establish prioritized tasks and assign times to them. Strategies against procrastination
-Strategies to face change. Resilience.The reality of a world in continuous change. Strategies to adapt and thrive. Overcoming adversity, developing strengths and positive attitudes to face challenges.
-The influence of those around us. Autonomy with respect to the group. How to deal with pressure from “friends”. Distinguish “a good friend.” I know how to say “no” and how to accept “no” for an answer. Affective-sexual relationships: respect and dignity for self and others.
-Gratitude for what was received.Awareness of what I received freely in the program and in daily life, whether from what I received from my family and friends, or from the services that society provides me.
Module 2: Social development (attitudinal coaching II):
-Coexistence agreement. I am in a group, I agree to some rules that we all respect. I greet and say goodbye. Thank you. I apologize. I remain silent to listen, I ask permission, I show with my body language that I respect you. I leave my cell phone when we meet. I come every day, I'm punctual.
-Prosocial habits. Help, share, cooperate, be generous, accept, respect, console the afflicted, encourage the weak, defend the weak.
-The debate. Speaking and listening; argued defense of one's own ideas, attending to and respecting the arguments and ideas of others; how to be convincing, accepting the possibility of being convinced.
-Teamwork, the development of common projects.
-I live in society, I get involved in it. My neighborhood, my town/city, my country.
-I am a citizen. I defend my rights and respect those of others. I have obligations, I comply with the rules, but I can act to change them
-The look at the other. I need others, but there are people who need me. The satisfaction of feeling useful to others, dedicating part of my time to a social purpose. Altruism and empathy versus selfishness and egocentrism.
-I ask myself ethical and moral questions. I want to have things: but not by any means. I am not indiffer
innovations.target_group: NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training)
innovations.evidence:
The results are surprising: 65% of the participants change their vital status and return to the educational system (35%) or join working life (remaining 30%).
Many young people tell us that for the first time in their lives they have felt listened to and cared for personally. Their families thank us for their change in attitude, which is even transformed in a way that changes family coexistence.

innovations.name: Derechos a la vivienda (Rights to Housing)
innovations.problem:
In 2022, 95.3 million people were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU, equivalent to 21.6% of the population, according to Eurostat data on poverty and social exclusion (AROPE rate). This figure remains practically constant compared to 2021, when it stood at 21.7%. In the eighth study on residential exclusion at the European level, FEANTSA and the Abbé Pierre Foundation estimate that 895,000 people in Europe are homeless or housed in temporary emergency collective shelters . These figures represent a 70% increase over the last 10 years. Their latest study, published in September 2023, notes that between 2010 and 2020, the average public spending in the 27 Member States fell by 19%, with Spain among the most significant decreases with 36% less.
According to a study by Eurofund conducted among 180,000 people in the 27 Member States, 3.8% of Europeans reported in the first half of 2021 that they were at risk of losing their housing within the next three months due to inability to pay rent. Additionally, according to Eurostat, 4 out of every 100 people in Europe report having been homeless at least once in their lives.
In Spain, official data about people affected by homelessness and the network addressing this issue reveal alarming figures. Since 2012, this group has increased by more than 5,600 people, rising from approximately 22,900 to over 28,500 in 2022, according to the latest data from the National Statistics. Additionally, the INE survey of centers directed at homelessness estimates that there are currently 20,000 available accommodation places in Spain. These two figures indicate a housing coverage that is only able to address 57% of the need, leaving approximately 15,000 people unserved from the outset.
According to the Survey of centers and services for homeless people, an average of 17,772 people per day were in emergency accommodation centers, which represents a small decrease of 1.3% compared to 2018 but an increase of 30% since 2010.
innovations.description:
The project has successfully implemented several innovative solutions that together make the Housing Rights project a social innovation program in the field of homelessness. The very approach of the project is innovative as it seeks to transcend the management approach to the problem towards a solution-oriented approach, so that people experiencing homelessness can once again have stable housing integrated into the community and a sufficient level of autonomy to freely develop their life projects. To this end, a model has been designed that allows for a chosen and safe transition from shelters to housing-based solutions for achieving autonomy. The implementation of autonomy processes is key in transforming the model, and processes have been initiated with individuals from the deinstitutionalization process carried out in Madrid, from which various lessons have been learned and incorporated into the model. Among the innovative solutions aimed at promoting innovation, the following have been implemented:
Direct transfers: This is designed to financially support clients in the aspects they may need, either to advance their autonomy process or to enable them to exit the program independently. This service provides significant amounts of money directly to clients according to the needs identified by the individuals themselves to achieve this goal. So far, it has only been developed in a pilot experience in Canada and recently piloted by HOGAR SÍ and Provivienda in a smaller experience in Spain. The direct transfer program, designed within the service portfolio, has guaranteed transparency and access for all clients and has demonstrated that providing significant amounts of money associated with an autonomy project generates more financial security and facilitates medium-term processes.
Self-Directed Support Methodology : Designed under the co-production methodology of the Self-Directed Support Model and the first experience in Spain applied to the model with people experiencing homelessness. It represents a significant change in the culture of services and especially in the decision-making processes regarding the supports and benefits that individuals receive. This system is based on the idea that people can manage their own support plan and budget from community resources, thus initiating a deinstitutionalization process that shifts from traditional homelessness care systems based on institutions to a system based on citizenship, individual rights, and free choice. It allows them to address their life plan on an equal footing and with the same rights as any other citizen, activating the necessary services to meet their needs by their choice and not those preselected by the social care system. Therefore, the areas where methodological innovation towards Self-Directed Support has been implemented are: a. Control and decision-making b. Professional roles c. Service flexibility d. Dialogue with the administration
Development and implementation of a rapid rehousing strategy for people who have been homeless for less than three months, focusing on the fastest possible recovery of their autonomy, optimizing their own resources and support networks, providing financial support, and facilitating access to housing solutions independently. The shift in focus towards early detection and intervention is key as it prevents entry into care systems, thus avoiding the chronicity of homelessness.
Integration of technology in support of autonomy : We have committed to integrating technology and digitalization into the relationship between the project participant and the technical support team. A digital skills assessment tool has been designed for both professionals and users, which has been used as a diagnostic tool to detect unmet needs. Based on these results, a web app has been developed that is reducing the digital divide and promoting improvements in support for autonomy.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons
innovations.evidence:
The evaluation of the projects is demonstrating positive results in the effectiveness, efficiency, and impact of the model , supporting the possibility and need for scalability of the project and its innovative proposals, as well as the potential for a change in public policies for the eradication of homelessness.
Pending the final evaluation of the project, intermediate evaluations indicates that better results are being achieved with the profile of the population that has been homeless for a shorter period (less than 6 months), while the results are having a positive impact, but to a lesser extent, on those who have been homeless for more than six months. This evaluation has been conducted using measurements in a control group and an experimental group participating in the projects.
Specifically, the following areas are where improvements in results are being perceived:
Choice and autonomy : People increase their capacity to choose, their autonomy, and self-determination. They are better prepared to start the process of change.
Mental health : The program has rapid positive effects on mental health. Women achieve the best results.
People have a house they value
Deinstitutionalization : Reduction of the resources of the homelessness network attention and reduction in the use of specialized services.
Election : People increase their self-determination.
Autonomy : People are more ready to face change processes.
Economic Efficiency of the project

innovations.name: Museu na Aldeia
innovations.lead: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.problem: The SAMP "Museu na Aldeia" project seeks to offer culture to elderly people in territories with low population density, improving the quality of life for everyone involved. In recent years, there has been an increase in average life expectancy and support networks for older people, however, there is still a clear deficit in care and activities that promote social, psychological, emotional and cultural empowerment, especially isolated elderly people who are still independent. It is in this sense that the "Museu na Aldeia" project arises, which, above all, has as its main objective to help combat and reduce loneliness and isolation, a problem that the current pandemic situation has accentuated, especially in this segment of the population, which previously needed more attention.
innovations.description:
Through a different artistic and cultural program, SAMP professionals, in conjunction with mayors and museum professionals, take and present museum pieces to different communities in the villages. This first meeting allows new approaches, transformations and interpretations of museum objects by elderly people living in the villages. The community is subsequently invited to reflect on the work and relate it to their memories, life experiences and local characteristics.
This process culminates in the materialization of a new work developed by the elderly, together with museum professionals and the SAMP team, which aims to represent both the individual characteristics of each elderly person and their community. The collective work is then inaugurated in the museums involved, through a SAMP Performative Presentation representative of both the museum institution and the community.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: SAMP - Sociedade Artística Musical dos Pousos
innovations.evidence:
Of the 273 elderly people present in sessions, 99 were randomly selected to respond to a social impact questionnaire, with 43.4% considering that Art is very important in their lives and another 43.4% considering it to be completely important. Regarding contact with the Arts, 46.5% considered that the project helped them a lot to have more contact with the Arts, with 40.4% saying that it helped completely with this contact and 12.1% that it helped moderately. Regarding the fact that their ideas were valued, 41.4% considered that they were highly valued and 34.3% completely valued. Regarding the perception of well-being, 53.5% considered that the project contributed completely to their well-being and 38.4% that it contributed a lot. As for the project's contribution to reducing the feeling of loneliness and isolation, 65.6% considered that it contributed completely and 28.3% considered that it contributed a lot. In terms of relational promotion, 45.4% considered that the project completely promoted relationships between community inhabitants, 37.4% considered that it promoted a lot and 5% that it promoted little. Regarding participation in the project, 99% enjoyed participating in it, 97% considered that the project should continue and 98% would participate in this type of project again. In addition to the measuring instruments used, which are quantitative in nature, it was considered important to add a qualitative assessment, to better understand and characterize the effects had and felt by the project participants.
Developing projects in inland locations, improving accessibility, raising awareness of the advantages of creating art in the most remote places, are increasingly pertinent needs, demonstrated during the execution of this project. In this sense, the importance of art and culture being able to occupie more space in our territory is highlighted, with the Museu na Aldeia filling some of this space due to the proximity created between museums and communities, through the programming developed throughout the project. It contributed to the development of closer and more accessible museums. Museums, local authorities, parish councils, local authorities and SAMP all came together for the same purpose. Everyone challenged themselves, everyone left their comfort zone to create bonds with communities and be part of a participatory art project, in networking and partnership.

It is in this sense that the "Museu na Aldeia" project arises, which, above all, has as its main objective to help combat and reduce loneliness and isolation, a problem that the current pandemic situation has accentuated, especially in this segment of the population, which previously needed more attention.
Through a different artistic and cultural program, SAMP professionals, in conjunction with mayors and museum professionals, take and present museum pieces to different communities in the villages. This first meeting allows new approaches, transformations and interpretations of museum objects by elderly people living in the villages. The community is subsequently invited to reflect on the work and relate it to their memories, life experiences and local characteristics.
This process culminates in the materialization of a new work developed by the elderly, together with museum professionals and the SAMP team, which aims to represent both the individual characteristics of each elderly person and their community. The collective work is then inaugurated in the museums involved, through a SAMP Performative Presentation representative of both the museum institution and the community.
Of the 273 elderly people present in sessions, 99 were randomly selected to respond to a social impact questionnaire, with 43.4% considering that Art is very important in their lives and another 43.4% considering it to be completely important. Regarding contact with the Arts, 46.5% considered that the project helped them a lot to have more contact with the Arts, with 40.4% saying that it helped completely with this contact and 12.1% that it helped moderately. Regarding the fact that their ideas were valued, 41.4% considered that they were highly valued and 34.3% completely valued. Regarding the perception of well-being, 53.5% considered that the project contributed completely to their well-being and 38.4% that it contributed a lot. As for the project's contribution to reducing the feeling of loneliness and isolation, 65.6% considered that it contributed completely and 28.3% considered that it contributed a lot. In terms of relational promotion, 45.4% considered that the project completely promoted relationships between community inhabitants, 37.4% considered that it promoted a lot and 5% that it promoted little. Regarding participation in the project, 99% enjoyed participating in it, 97% considered that the project should continue and 98% would participate in this type of project again. In addition to the measuring instruments used, which are quantitative in nature, it was considered important to add a qualitative assessment, to better understand and characterize the effects had and felt by the project participants.
Developing projects in inland locations, improving accessibility, raising awareness of the advantages of creating art in the most remote places, are increasingly pertinent needs, demonstrated during the execution of this project. In this sense, the importance of art and culture being able to occupie more space in our territory is highlighted, with the Museu na Aldeia filling some of this space due to the proximity created between museums and communities, through the programming developed throughout the project. It contributed to the development of closer and more accessible museums. Museums, local authorities, parish councils, local authorities and SAMP all came together for the same purpose. Everyone challenged themselves, everyone left their comfort zone to create bonds with communities and be part of a participatory art project, in networking and partnership.

innovations.name: Timebank Ireland
innovations.problem:
Given risks associated with modern society of diminishing communal interactions, isolation, community breakdown and reductions in social capital. TimeBank strives to actively reverse these trends through proactively supporting new relationships. TimeBank values everybody equally, every person’s time is valued in the same way and everyone is considered to have something to offer. These principles are deeply empowering for all parties and contrast with most charity models where beneficiaries are categorised and often stigmatised.
Timebank Ireland seeks to provide social and practical supports to members as required.
TimeBank Ireland are committed to creating an inclusive and supportive environment for people to connect, share and thrive. Timebanking goes beyond transactions; it is about building lasting relationships, unlocking potential and changing lives. It supports basic needs to be met that mitigate deprivation and stress resulting in a better quality of life and stronger community connections.
For individuals who are isolated, have low income or have weak or no social networks, timebank provides an opportunity to engage with peers in the community to provide practical solutions to real needs.
Timebank Ireland
innovations.description: Innovation The TimeBank model has offered an innovative approach to volunteerism, as the process encourages and facilitates the recipient of voluntary support to recognise that they also have something to offer and to “give back”. This has benefited particularly disadvantaged and vulnerable people and communities in terms of recognising their potential and building their capacity to become more involved in their community and to also reach out and help others. An example of this is given in the Social Impact Study 2023 Case Study 1,(Page 3)– Monica who experiences social isolation and mental health issues and received voluntary support through TimeBank. She is now  giving her time to doing conversational English with Ukrainians and has participated in sewing workshops with a view to transferring these skills.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
In October 2022, there were 391 users of Timebank Ireland with 95% of these members based in County Cork.
Results from the Social Impact study concluded that
When asked about the extent to which involvement with TBI has impacted on their feelings of social connectedness , 95% (n=38) indicated that felt more socially connected.
In relation to improvements in emotional, physical, and mental well-being attributable to TBI, 100% of respondents (n=40) felt that their well-being had improved.
90% of respondents (n=36) felt that TBI had increased their sense of independence .
Using a Social Return on Investment Methodology, TBI over the one-year period November 1st, 2021, to October 31st, 2022, generated a social value of 1:16 . This is based on a Total Present Value of €803,184 created against the input of €50,000. The calculations applied financial proxies to four outcomes for TBI members.

innovations.name: South Aegean Social Inclusion Observatory
innovations.problem: The Regional Social Inclusion Observatory of the South Aegean Region, established under Article 14 of (Greek) Law n. 4445/2016 (A'236), plays a crucial role within the National Mechanism for Coordination, Monitoring, and Evaluation of Social Inclusion and Social Cohesion Policies. The Regional Social Inclusion Observatory of the South Aegean Region addresses several deficiencies identified in local social policy support. By tackling these shortcomings, the Observatory aims to strengthen social inclusion and cohesion, improve the effectiveness of social policies, and support the overall well-being of residents in the South Aegean Region.
innovations.description:
The Observatory implements a holistic approach towards the development of interconnected tools to support its aims in the following areas:
Poverty and Social Exclusion: It targets the pervasive issues of poverty and social exclusion, mapping and analyzing their spatial dimensions to identify the most affected areas and populations.
Social Protection and Welfare Needs: The Observatory identifies and highlights unmet local needs in social protection, welfare, and solidarity policies.
Data Fragmentation and Coordination: It has developed and maintains a database that monitors key socioeconomic indicators in the Region, due to the lack of operation of the Unified Geoinformation System of the National Mechanism.
Labor Market Integration: The Observatory develops and implements tools and indicators to monitor and enhance the social integration processes of beneficiaries, with a specific emphasis on their integration into the labor market and the promotion of economic activity.
Awareness and Information Dissemination: It addresses the lack of awareness and information dissemination by actively informing stakeholders and the public about social inclusion and cohesion policies, ensuring broad engagement and understanding.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion
innovations.evidence:
The Regional Social Inclusion Observatory of the South Aegean Region has accomplished the following:
Conducted four (4) regional income surveys.
Carried out three (3) on-site surveys to record poverty levels in the municipalities (islands) of the region.
Documented significant best practices in the field of social inclusion.
Enhanced its digital presence by creating an electronic portal ( https://socialobservatory.pnai.gov.gr/en/ ) and developing informational and communication applications for the public, including a social data dashboard and a digital assistant.
Implemented eight (8) communication and dissemination activities in the social integration field, including one workshop dedicated on social innovation.
Evidence shows that these efforts have led to enhanced communication among local stakeholders, increased trust in local social support providers and greater awareness of local social integration challenges.

innovations.name: PORT: safe space for victims and survivors of sexual violence
innovations.lead: proFem - centrum pro oběti domácího a sexuálního násilí, o.p.s.
innovations.problem:
Victims and survivors of sexual violence in the Czech Republic are often re-traumatised by the system that is supposed to help them. They face unavailability of services, unprofessional and insensitive treatment, and attitudes that devalue and question their personal experiences. These failures complicate coping with the trauma experienced and prevent victims from returning to a full life. What should be a helping and supportive system is often, in turn, a source of further pain and a deepening of the impact of the violence faced by victims.
Yet data shows that sexual violence is a widespread and serious problem. 58% of women experience some form of violence. As many as one in five women (20%) have experienced rape specifically. And the majority of rape victims (76%) report experiencing impacts on their mental or physical health, relationships, studies, work or even life-threatening consequences as a result of rape (proFem, Sexualised violence: prevalence, impacts and health care costs, 2024).
Just as each victim and survivor is individual, the forms of violence they have experienced or the impacts they face tend to vary. Yet they are expected to recover in a system that does not acknowledge this and address their individual needs and situation. Recovery is not a one-size-fits-all process; it must always begin with an understanding and sensitive response to the needs and wishes of individual victims.
innovations.description:
At proFem, we see and address these critical gaps in the current approach to victims and survivors of sexual violence. Through PORT and its unique services, we are fundamentally changing the way we help victims. We opened this center, the first of its kind, in January 2024, to provide services to survivors of sexual violence and sexual harassment, both those focused on their immediate and long-term needs. The goal of PORT is to improve the quality of care for victims, reduce the risk of retraumatization, and provide appropriate support for the healing process and coping with the trauma experienced by victims of violence. In doing so, we also seek to contribute to the broader goal of proFem, which is to improve social awareness and support for victims and survivors of sexual violence.
We understand that the trauma and impact caused by sexual violence looks different for each victim, and so does their journey back to a full life. At PORT, we offer a wide range of innovative services provided by specially trained professionals. We create a responsive and understanding support system that listens and adapts to victims based on what they want and need at the time. This approach makes proFem and PORT a pioneer in supporting and caring for victims of sexual violence. We emphasize the victim's right to share, cope with and recover from their situation at their own pace and on their own terms, without external pressure or any prejudice or expectations.
At PORT, we also understand that collaborative efforts are key to implementing systemic change and improving the entire system of assistance. That is why we are actively building cooperation with different actors and institutions such as NGOs, police, hospitals as well as international and foreign organizations and platforms. We share our knowledge and practical experience, train in a sensitive approach to victims and raise awareness among the general public about sexual violence.
Thanks to the project "proFem 2.0 - needs analysis and setting up of services for victims of sexual violence" supported by the European Social Fund through OPZ, we were able to create a Functional Specification for the preparation of PORT.
innovations.target_group: Individuals experiencing gender marginalization
innovations.beneficiaries: proFem - centrum pro oběti domácího a sexuálního násilí, o.p.s.
innovations.evidence:
The ProFem 2.0 project represents a significant advancement in supporting victims. Based on an analysis of what works and what does not in the current setup of services for victims of sexual violence, the project focused on addressing issues such as the loss of clients after the first contact, misunderstanding of the role of social workers, and challenges in team communication.
As a result of the project, ProFem developed an interactive tool for trauma psychotherapy, new procedures and tools for direct support of victims of sexual violence, and background materials for the emerging center PORT (Center for Victims of Sexual Violence).
At PORT centre, victims and survivors of sexual violence can find social and legal counselling, crisis intervention, psychotherapeutic support, legal representation, and a room for police interrogation. Crisis accommodation, and a medical room for the collection of evidence and genetic material and testing for sexually transmitted diseases were launched in on November 2024 and are part of comprehensive centre PORT.
Crisis intervention: is a short-term support focused on the "here and now" and improving the current experience at the moment when the client feels overwhelmed by emotions, does not know how to go on, or is unable to perform normal activities.
Social counselling: helps the client to navigate her situation, map her needs and plan steps to get better. The social worker is the client's guide on the path to change and eventually to other PORT services.
Legal counselling and representation: helps the client navigate their rights and the legal avenues available to them. We will help arrange legal representation and accompaniment to court so that she is not alone for the process.
Individual and group therapy: to support the client's mental stability, understanding of her own emotional experience and sense of self-worth and awareness.
Specialized room for police interrogation: allows us to conduct a police interview of the victim in the safety of the PORT, while recording the client's interview, which will be sensitively and professionally conducted by our trained staff. If she decides to report the crime, this interview can be used as evidence.
Crisis accommodation: a safe space to stabilize the client, for up to 7 nights.
Collection and prevention of samples and forensic evidence: is available without the need to immediately decide if the client wants to report the crime. Evidence and samples are sensitively collected and carefully stored by us.
Testing for STDs: enable us to detect possible infection with sexually transmitted diseases. We provide resources and information for their treatment.
During the pilot year of PORT’s operation, we provided comprehensive services to a total of 1,037 clients.
The project provided us with initial information and tools for PORT, but the actual PORT services and further innovation processes from the project supported by the ESF are no longer available.

At PORT centre, victims and survivors of sexual violence can find social and legal counselling, crisis intervention, psychotherapeutic support, legal representation, and a room for police interrogation. Crisis accommodation, and a medical room for the collection of evidence and genetic material and testing for sexually transmitted diseases were launched in on November 2024 and are part of comprehensive centre PORT.
Crisis intervention: is a short-term support focused on the "here and now" and improving the current experience at the moment when the client feels overwhelmed by emotions, does not know how to go on, or is unable to perform normal activities.
Social counselling: helps the client to navigate her situation, map her needs and plan steps to get better. The social worker is the client's guide on the path to change and eventually to other PORT services.
Legal counselling and representation: helps the client navigate their rights and the legal avenues available to them. We will help arrange legal representation and accompaniment to court so that she is not alone for the process.
Individual and group therapy: to support the client's mental stability, understanding of her own emotional experience and sense of self-worth and awareness.
Specialized room for police interrogation: allows us to conduct a police interview of the victim in the safety of the PORT, while recording the client's interview, which will be sensitively and professionally conducted by our trained staff. If she decides to report the crime, this interview can be used as evidence.
Crisis accommodation: a safe space to stabilize the client, for up to 7 nights.
Collection and prevention of samples and forensic evidence: is available without the need to immediately decide if the client wants to report the crime. Evidence and samples are sensitively collected and carefully stored by us.
Testing for STDs: enable us to detect possible infection with sexually transmitted diseases. We provide resources and information for their treatment.
During the pilot year of PORT’s operation, we provided comprehensive services to a total of 1,037 clients.
The project provided us with initial information and tools for PORT, but the actual PORT services and further innovation processes from the project supported by the ESF are no longer available.

innovations.name: Long term care in rural areas
innovations.lead: Centre for Supporting Non-Governmental Organizations, The Prophet Elijah Hospice Foundation in Michałowo, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw
innovations.problem:
The demographic situation in Poland, particularly the advancing aging of the population, calls for actions aimed at seeking and implementing new solutions in the field of accessibility to social and healthcare services. This need particularly affects rural residents, where general adverse demographic trends are compounded by other issues.
Many Polish villages are affected by depopulation, as younger generations move to cities, leaving behind elderly individuals, often alone, living in increasingly sparsely populated areas. As a result, older adults frequently have no close relatives who can assist them with illness and daily care, and the family members who do act as caregivers are often elderly and suffering from health issues themselves.
Additionally, the difficulties with access to public transportation significantly impacts the availability of services (both those provided on-site and those delivered as part of home care, due to the difficulties and costs associated with traveling to the clients).
These barriers also include the relatively lower availability, compared to city residents, of other services provided for example within the social assistance system.
innovations.description:
The home care model is designed for elderly people living in rural areas who are becoming increasingly dependent on others due to conditions like dementia, stroke, or those who don't receive curative treatment.
The model does not focus on improving just one element (e.g., solely working on an empathetic team, motivating neighborly assistance, or helping the caregiver) but proposes a comprehensive home care model for rural areas. In this model, assistance for individuals whose health condition requires care is tailored to their needs.
A new element in providing these services is the expansion of the home care team, consisting of doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, and psychologists, to include caregivers. They play a very important role in the team. Their task is to ensure the overall well-being of the patients. This can involve various activities, including having conversations, doing shopping, or engaging in exercises together. Furthermore, caregivers step in to provide relief for those who look after a sick person every day, such as when they have appointments or errands to run. This also has a positive impact on family relationships,
The introduction of caregivers has helped unburden the workload of medical personnel. It gave possibility of reducing the involvement of qualified specialists in caring for patients - from nurses and physiotherapists to doctors. Caregivers can perform basic nursing tasks for patients, monitor their health status, and conduct recommended exercises with them after a short training conducted by a physiotherapist.
The model combines standard social services with the provision of health services.
In each case, the situation and needs of the patients are assessed by a doctor, who then designs a treatment plan and schedules appropriate specialist visits.
At the beginning of the support, an Individual Service Plan was created for each patient, which was then monitored and modified depending on the changing situation.
It contains support in various areas - more hours of medical and nursing care in medically complex cases, rehabilitation tailored to the patient's condition and needs. In some cases, it was necessary to involve additional specialists, such as speech therapists or dietitians.
The team also educates and trains family members on exercises, caregiving techniques, and methods of care. Another crucial aspect of this home care model in rural areas is collaboration with existing social and health services providers, like family doctors, community nurses, and municipal social welfare center staff. This collaboration involves planning the most effective care for individuals in need, complementing standard services with the specialized care provided by the home care model.
innovations.target_group: Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised, Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Centre for Supporting Non-Governmental Organizations, The Prophet Elijah Hospice Foundation in Michałowo, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw
innovations.evidence:
Implementing the model in the proposed form allows for a comprehensive perspective on the patient's problems – both their health and social needs. Elderly people, especially those living in rural areas, face various challenges aside from illness: loneliness, age-related disabilities, poverty, and sometimes even abuse from relatives. Patients often feel uncomfortable discussing their situation, but regular and attentive contact with the home care team enables the observation of these issues, appropriate response, and incorporation of needs into the individual plan.
Thanks to the carefully designed and comprehensive care provided by a skilled team, patients experience fewer hospitalizations and feel better supported and safer overall. It improved not only their quality of life but also enhanced the well-being of the patients.
Better access to specialist care
Before the hospice team included caregivers, it was solely up to the medical personnel outlined in the regulations (specialist doctor, hospice nurses, physiotherapist, and psychologist) to provide all types of services to patients, even those that didn't necessarily require specialized medical knowledge or skills.
However, with the addition of caregivers to the hospice team, they took over some of the tasks that were previously handled by medical staff. This allowed doctors and nurses to concentrate more on patients who needed medical interventions, while caregivers handled other aspects of patient care.
Ad hoc respite support for family members
The inclusion of professional caregivers made it possible to provide additional support to the family members who care for their loved ones, offering them respite from their daily duties. What is more, patients no longer worried that their illness was keeping their relatives confined at home and prevented them from tending to their own needs.
Reducing the operating costs
Developing a model where certain services previously handled by specialized staff like doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, and psychologists are now carried out by trained caregivers has enabled to decrease the frequency of visits by medical professionals without compromising patient care. Considering the disparity in employment expenses, this adjustment has resulted in approximately a 30% reduction in staffing costs.
In total, the project provided care for 278 individuals. The average age of the recipients was 77 years old.
The model evolved over the years, and its expanded scope was tested as part of the project "To give what is really needed," led by Prophet Elijah Hospice Foundation.
This project was among the seven initiatives financed by the European Commission under the European Programme for Employment and Social Innovation ("EaSI") 2014-2020.
Two significant elements were added to the model:
• Establishing networks of local healthcare and social assistance institutions, as well as other invited institutions, to collaborate within the network.
• Supporting the assistance team by appointing a Coordinator of Care for Dependent Persons.
An important part of the project was also the scientific study, which allowed for monitoring the effect brought about over 2.5 years of the project implementation as well as for gathering good practice and recommendation for institutions acting in this field.
authors: Centre for Supporting Non-Governmental Organizations, The Prophet Elijah Hospice Foundation in Michałowo, The Centre for Supporting Local Activity (CAL) in Warsaw

innovations.name: Café Lebenslust (Café Joy of Life)
innovations.lead: Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales (BMAS), ESF Unit
innovations.problem:
Advancing demographic development in Germany constitutes a special challenge. Over the next few years, too, it will lead to a further rise in the number of older people. It should be stressed that over a relatively short period of time – between 2018-2031 – around 13 million so-called baby boomers will reach retirement age. This term refers to the high-birth-rate years from the mid-1950s to the mid-1960s. This significant increase in the number of people leaving the labour force will place a major strain on existing municipal structures and services for encounters, counselling, education and engagement.
The very different life courses and work histories of baby boomers will exacerbate economic and social inequalities with the risk that more and more older people will feel left behind and social tensions will increase. It has also become apparent that a considerable number of older people are not very familiar or are not familiar at all with technical and digital support options. However, given the penetration of all areas of life by accelerating digitisation, the teaching of digital skills is essential. The transition to the post-employment phase is a crucial factor for later social integration into society. It impacts health, participation, engagement and, in some cases, the economic situation of older people too.
The ESF Plus programme is primarily aimed at workers aged 60 and over who are at risk of or are already affected by exclusion from the labour market. This may also include, for instance, people who are already receiving basic security benefits in line with Book XII of the Social Code, women who want to return to work after assuming family care responsibilities or employees with a migration background.
The programme aims to prevent and combat involuntary loneliness and social isolation, strengthen financial security in old age and support municipal participation structures for older people. Consequently, the funding aims to improve the income and living situation of older employees, both during their active working life and in the post-working phase, and to increase the social participation of older people.
innovations.description:
The programme offers a wide range of services to prepare for retirement. The counselling, educational and leisure activities and the café are open to people who want to make contacts, actively participate and receive new perspectives, impulses and suggestions.
As an intercultural gathering place it offers activities for people over 60 years of age. Activities like consulting services, educational opportunities and leisure offerings are provided. The café addresses people who want to participate, get to know others and are looking for new impulses, perspectives and suggestions. All propositions are accessible and free of charge, designed to empower the participants in all matters concerning the process of getting older.

However, given the penetration of all areas of life by accelerating digitisation, the teaching of digital skills is essential. The transition to the post-employment phase is a crucial factor for later social integration into society. It impacts health, participation, engagement and, in some cases, the economic situation of older people too.
The ESF Plus programme "Strengthening the participation of older people – countering loneliness and social isolation" builds on the goals of the ESF German model programme for the ESF funding period 2014 - 2020 "Strengthening the participation of older people – preventing and fighting loneliness and social isolation in old age" that ran from 1 October 2020 to 30 September 2022.
It is a mobile project with changing locations in the neighbourhood. The idea of supporting solo self-employed people is both novel and innovative because it is not a familiar form of job placement.
This novel idea was reported on in the March 2024 issue of the newsletter of the Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales.

innovations.name: Salary Instead of Pocket Money
innovations.problem:
People with disabilities or multiple challenges in Austria face the difficulty of having little access to the primary labor market and thus their own social insurance after compulsory education, leaving them without entitlement to unemployment benefits and pensions. Typically, these individuals end up in workshops after school or failed placement attempts, where they only receive pocket money and no wages. Aside from social exclusion and lack of their own income, they have no legal claim to pensions in old age and rely on the day structures of disability facilities.
The innovative project focuses primarily on people with disabilities employed in workshops who need comprehensive support for integration into the primary labor market.
innovations.description:
The innovative solution to the problem through our project is the holistic approach and the focus on people with disabilities or mutlieple challenges who are are confronted with a wide range of difficulties when integrating into the labour and currently just supported in workshops in Austria. The holistic approach includes preparing participants through training sessions in small groups (max. 5 people), allowing for need-oriented training units. These training sessions take place four times a week (five if you count the vocational training on Fridays) and focus on public transport training, learning labor market-relevant terms, recognizing personal strengths and abilities, boosting self-confidence and self-responsibility, and preparing for job application phases (creating resumes, practicing interviews, etc.). An action plan is created once the participants' skills profile is defined.
Participants are accompanied by placement staff during their initial trial internships, meaning they practice and consolidate public transport use, and at the internship site, the placement staff provides support. This presence allows the placement staff to reflect with the company on potential job opportunities the participant can take on, creating a win-win situation for both the person with disabilities and the company.
After a short internship (2-3 days), a longer one follows for about 12 weeks. During this time, the participant is accompanied by the placement staff, focusing on achieving the highest possible independence at the internship site. Subsequently, there is a labor leasing for up to six months, provided both parties agree, aiming for permanent employment in the company.
The placement staff remains accessible to the participant during the labor leasing and serves as a contact person for the company for any questions.
The placement staff plays a central role in the project, serving as a mediating, prejudice-reducing, motivating, and clarifying figure for companies and as a direct contact for participants, aligning the needs of both parties to achieve a successful match (employment in the primary labor market).
Additionally, a 360° feedback system is implemented. Participants are surveyed at the beginning, middle, and end of the project using a simple language questionnaire to assess their situation. A social network map is also created at these times to track how the social space of people with disabilities changes when they have a salary instead of pocket money. Relatives and close companions are also surveyed to gain a comprehensive view of the changes in participants' social environments.
innovations.target_group: Individuals with disabilities
innovations.evidence:
The inclusion of people with disabilities or multiple challenges in the primary (general) labor market will:
Break down barriers and prejudices against people with disabilities at a societal level.
Increase self-responsibility and self-determination of people with disabilities and create the conditions for this.
Significantly reduce the dependence of people with disabilities on their relatives or other caregivers.
Employ people with disabilities regularly and pay them wages instead of pocket money for their economic contributions.
Ensure people with disabilities are socially insured and not co-insured with relatives, giving them legal entitlement to pensions and other social benefits in Austria.
Actively integrate people with disabilities into the social space, as they can participate due to their own financial means.
Implement long-overdue aspects (especially paragraph 27) of the UN CRPD in Austria.
