innovations.name: Demola
innovations.lead: Riga Technical University, University of Latvia, Ministry of Education and Science (Latvia)
innovations.problem: Young graduates often struggle with finding their first employment opportunities, in part due to limited work experience, a lack of professional network, and skills mismatches. In Latvia, young people are almost twice as likely to be unemployed compared to the rest of the population (12.2% compared to 7.4% in 2018). It is widely recognised that work-based learning can be an efficient way of addressing labour market imbalances and allowing young people to acquire valuable skills to help them land their first job. Work-based learning is also beneficial for companies, as it allows them to attract creative talent to help them innovate their products and processes at the same time as training a potential pool of new recruits to cover their current and future work force needs. Nevertheless, access to quality work-based learning opportunities remain unequal across the EU.
innovations.description:
Demola is a platform that connect students and companies operating in different fields that can mutually benefit from working together. The main innovation of Demola is that it presents students to companies as potential problem solvers, instead of as young people in need of work experience.
The Demola platform started in Finland in 2014. Demola Latvia was set up in 2015, and is part of an international network of more than 50 universities, 750 000 students and a number of major companies from around the world.
Companies submit an open or specific problem situation for students to address. Students apply to participate in the platform’s activities. Successful applicants are then gathered in teams of five or six and assigned to a specific company and business problem, according to their interests and skills. They participate in workshops on different topics related to marketing and product design, facilitated by the universities involved in the platform. The team is then responsible for presenting potential solutions to the company in a final pitch. If the company is interested in one of the solutions, it can purchase it. The financial compensation is shared among the students according to their workload. The amount of financial compensation per participating student is calculated according to specific criteria, and its distribution is coordinated by the project facilitator.
Participating companies come from a wide range of fields, ranging from marketing to food processing, insurance and logistics. Typical marketing problems that need to be solved include the need to attract new customers, or understanding the productive chain relating to specific products or markets. In one example, the largest Latvian meat processing company challenged students to develop an original concept for their upcoming chain of stores, increasing their competitive advantage, purchasing volume and attracting new customers. In order to compensate students for their work, companies are requested to financially contribute to the activities offered by the platform.
Since 2016, the project in Latvia has been run by the Riga Technical University (RTU) Design Factory and the University of Latvia, with the support of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia. The universities primarily liaise with organisations, facilitate the students’ work, and coordinate the communication aspect of the project (i.e. attracting companies to the platform and managing the application process for both companies and students).
innovations.target_group: Long-term or repeatedly unemployed persons, NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training), Other target groups
innovations.beneficiaries: Riga Technical University, University of Latvia, Ministry of Education and Science (Latvia)
innovations.evidence:
Since 2016, 625 students have applied for the project in Latvia. Of these, 195 students from 15 different secondary education institutes were selected to participate in 50 different cases submitted by the participating companies.
One of the key benefits of the platform is that students can gain practical experience in methods for designing, providing and selling solutions to business problems in different areas. They develop social and professional skills, and enhance their knowledge of the implementation of different business models, as well as methodological and research approaches. Moreover, they learn soft skills such as working in a team, and gain experience in customer-oriented relationships. A number of participating students have gone on to undertake internships at the companies involved in the platform.
The key benefits for companies centre on the opportunity to develop innovative solutions to problems without facing substantial financial risks, since the cost of each solution under this scheme ranges from EUR 1 000 to EUR 3 000.
authors: Riga Technical University, University of Latvia, Ministry of Education and Science (Latvia)
tags: Adaptation of workers and enterprises to change

innovations.name: Opportunities for West II
innovations.lead: Managing Authority Kansen voor West II
innovations.problem: In Rotterdam, the unemployment rate is twice the national average.  In some neighbourhoods in Rotterdam South, unemployment is 150% of the urban average in the country. There is a mismatch between the demand and the supply on the labour market, with only 13% of people finding jobs after receiving social assistance benefits – well below the national average of 22%.
innovations.description:
Kansen voor West II, 2014-2020 (KVWII) – meaning Opportunities for West II – is a programme that aims to address the sluggish progress in economic growth, employment, private research and development (R&D) investment, and energy efficiency in the Western Netherlands. The programme improves the connection between the labour supply and the demand for skills by providing direct funding to business development and innovation, primarily among SMEs. To be eligible for funding, projects must involve SMEs and foster innovation.
KVWII puts special emphasis on piloting and learning what works in tackling unemployment and labour mismatches. This is intended to continuously inform the design of successful new initiatives that bring unemployed individuals into the labour market in a sustainable way.
The 'Slim Made' project (EUR 699 825), for example, trained young people from Rotterdam South in the use of technology, providing job guarantees in the metal and manufacturing industry. It was started by the SME business community, and ran from March 2017 to August 2020, under the direction of the business community in collaboration with the education sector. The innovative aspect of the project stemmed from the fact that academic experts could guide the direction of the training while young people were already working. This aimed to develop a longer-term, more holistic vision for employment for the prospective employee, but in a way that was tailored to the needs of the industry. From 2021 onwards (one year after completion of the project), the seven participating SMEs will provide 21 new jobs per year.
The ‘Connected to South’ (EUR 745 162) project ran from May 2017 to April 2019. It focused on tailoring apprenticeships in the healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors in South Rotterdam to securing training and guaranteed employment for young people above 16 years of age without a job or basic qualification, and recruiting these target groups to enter MBO vocational training (middle-level applied education) up to levels 1 and 2, or to employers struggling to fill vacancies at a lower and elementary professional level. Apprenticeships under the project were unique in that they were developed with regular input from partners from multiple companies, bringing together best practices across the industries. The MBO qualification aimed to deter premature drop out from work due to disinterest, disillusionment with processes and/or lack of professional and financial incentives.
Finally, the Start Engine (EUR 172 714) pilot programme ran from September 2018 to August 2020, and focused on exploring ‘what works’ in staff retention across seven companies in management, HR and education. The companies engaged in direct discussion with educational institutions, employees and job seekers regarding 21st century entrepreneurial skills, in order to determine what was specifically necessary for employees’ personal and professional development in the longer term. With employers and company representatives present, they were able to learn about prospective workers’ priorities, and used this data to inform the design and delivery of tailored professional development schemes. This was innovative in that staff were deployed purely on an evidence basis, while simultaneously operating as a research ‘test’ study for continuous lesson learning.
Through piloting and research, the KVWII programme seeks to build an evidence base on labour potential, entrepreneurship and strategic staff planning in order to understand (and further implement) ‘what works’ in strengthening the demand side of employment.
innovations.beneficiaries: Managing Authority Kansen voor West II
innovations.evidence:
There are currently over 200 projects in place, and many more are in the pipeline in the run up to 2020. Between 2009 and 2013, several ERDF grants (of approximately EUR 50 million in total) were provided to encourage partnerships between enterprise and knowledge. As a result, the percentage of technologically innovative enterprises partnering up with institutions for tertiary education went up from 8% in 2010 to 11% in 2012. Partnerships with public research institutions increased from 7% to 8%. Furthermore, Central Government concluded agreements with the VSNU Association of Universities in the Netherlands and the Netherlands Association of Universities of Applied Sciences to make sure that tackling labour mismatches was embedded in the strategies and activities of these knowledge institutions by 2015.
The ex-ante evaluation of the programme took place between 2012 and 2014, and led to refinement of the indicators for selecting projects to fund. KVWII’s Annual Report (2018 ) indicated that, halfway through implementation, there were 12 ongoing projects committed to the development of labour potential which were making a ‘good contribution’ to the city’s labour mismatch, with marked progress in 2018 ‘thanks to ERDF funding’. Results from an evaluation conducted in 2018 provided more detail on the specific impacts of the projects aiming to strengthen the demand side of employment in Rotterdam.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:
Kansen voor West II, 2014-2020 (KVWII) – meaning Opportunities for West II – is a programme that aims to address the sluggish progress in economic growth, employment, private research and development (R&D) investment, and energy efficiency in the Western Netherlands. The programme improves the connection between the labour supply and the demand for skills by providing direct funding to business development and innovation, primarily among SMEs. To be eligible for funding, projects must involve SMEs and foster innovation.
KVWII puts special emphasis on piloting and learning what works in tackling unemployment and labour mismatches. This is intended to continuously inform the design of successful new initiatives that bring unemployed individuals into the labour market in a sustainable way.
The 'Slim Made' project (EUR 699 825), for example, trained young people from Rotterdam South in the use of technology, providing job guarantees in the metal and manufacturing industry. It was started by the SME business community, and ran from March 2017 to August 2020, under the direction of the business community in collaboration with the education sector. The innovative aspect of the project stemmed from the fact that academic experts could guide the direction of the training while young people were already working. This aimed to develop a longer-term, more holistic vision for employment for the prospective employee, but in a way that was tailored to the needs of the industry. From 2021 onwards (one year after completion of the project), the seven participating SMEs will provide 21 new jobs per year.
The ‘Connected to South’ (EUR 745 162) project ran from May 2017 to April 2019. It focused on tailoring apprenticeships in the healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors in South Rotterdam to securing training and guaranteed employment for young people above 16 years of age without a job or basic qualification, and recruiting these target groups to enter MBO vocational training (middle-level applied education) up to levels 1 and 2, or to employers struggling to fill vacancies at a lower and elementary professional level. Apprenticeships under the project were unique in that they were developed with regular input from partners from multiple companies, bringing together best practices across the industries. The MBO qualification aimed to deter premature drop out from work due to disinterest, disillusionment with processes and/or lack of professional and financial incentives.
Finally, the Start Engine (EUR 172 714) pilot programme ran from September 2018 to August 2020, and focused on exploring ‘what works’ in staff retention across seven companies in management, HR and education. The companies engaged in direct discussion with educational institutions, employees and job seekers regarding 21st century entrepreneurial skills, in order to determine what was specifically necessary for employees’ personal and professional development in the longer term. With employers and company representatives present, they were able to learn about prospective workers’ priorities, and used this data to inform the design and delivery of tailored professional development schemes. This was innovative in that staff were deployed purely on an evidence basis, while simultaneously operating as a research ‘test’ study for continuous lesson learning.
Through piloting and research, the KVWII programme seeks to build an evidence base on labour potential, entrepreneurship and strategic staff planning in order to understand (and further implement) ‘what works’ in strengthening the demand side of employment.

sections.question: Evidence
sections.answer:
There are currently over 200 projects in place, and many more are in the pipeline in the run up to 2020. Between 2009 and 2013, several ERDF grants (of approximately EUR 50 million in total) were provided to encourage partnerships between enterprise and knowledge. As a result, the percentage of technologically innovative enterprises partnering up with institutions for tertiary education went up from 8% in 2010 to 11% in 2012. Partnerships with public research institutions increased from 7% to 8%. Furthermore, Central Government concluded agreements with the VSNU Association of Universities in the Netherlands and the Netherlands Association of Universities of Applied Sciences to make sure that tackling labour mismatches was embedded in the strategies and activities of these knowledge institutions by 2015.
The ex-ante evaluation of the programme took place between 2012 and 2014, and led to refinement of the indicators for selecting projects to fund. KVWII’s Annual Report (2018 ) indicated that, halfway through implementation, there were 12 ongoing projects committed to the development of labour potential which were making a ‘good contribution’ to the city’s labour mismatch, with marked progress in 2018 ‘thanks to ERDF funding’. Results from an evaluation conducted in 2018 provided more detail on the specific impacts of the projects aiming to strengthen the demand side of employment in Rotterdam.

innovations.name: BIP/ZIP CLLD programme
innovations.lead: Housing and Local Development municipal department of the city of Lisbon
innovations.problem: In 2010, the city of Lisbon concluded that some neighbourhoods and territories were affected by higher levels of urban, social and economic deprivation. They launched a territorial mapping study to identify the most deprived areas in the city – called Bairros e Zonas de Intervencao Urbana (BIP/ZIP) in Portuguese – based on economic, urban and environmental indicators in combination with national census data. This analysis was complemented by findings from a survey that identified social and territorial gaps in the city, as well as the most prevalent issues faced by its citizens. The outcome of the study was presented and discussed in a public consultation with local communities. It was determined that 67 municipalities across Lisbon required specific support, through active local involvement and engagement.
innovations.description:
The BIP/ZIP programme is a pilot initiative by the Housing and Local Development municipal department of the city of Lisbon to increase territorial and social cohesion, active citizenship and community involvement. It innovatively promotes local partnerships in deprived neighbourhoods by facilitating the participation of neighbourhood organisations in decision-making processes. It also creates and strengthens local networks within the communities, and runs a funding programme supporting local community initiatives.
BIP/ZIP is organised around annual bidding rounds (editions). To qualify, a project must be pitched by two local partners, have a twelve-month duration, be under EUR 50 000 and be sustained for one year after the funding. BIP/ZIP projects are encouraged to search for other funding sources, such as sponsorship from local enterprises. The BIP/ZIP programme strives to include local actors in the policy process, ensuring that local needs are effectively met. By including a funding component, the BIP/ZIP programme allows initiatives to go beyond solely discussions among stakeholders, to become concrete investments in community development and wellbeing.
Since the start of the programme in 2011, BIP/ZIP, which is entirely financed by the city of Lisbon, has developed a Community-Led Local Development (CLLD) add-on activity. Local organisations receive technical and financial support for the development of their neighbourhoods. The programme encourages the active participation of local organisations that might lack technical expertise such as internet or computer-use, but nonetheless play an active role in the community.
Local co-governance structures called GABIPs (local Offices) have been established under the programme. These are composed of representatives from the local government and an executive committee that includes local authorities, local associations and other actors, depending on the type of projects in the neighbourhood. The GABIPs play a mediating role in policy dialogue down to the local level, involving local stakeholders in decision-making. In doing so, GABIPs facilitate further communication between the local government and its citizens.
innovations.beneficiaries: Housing and Local Development municipal department of the city of Lisbon
innovations.evidence:
By 2019, the programme had funded almost 2 000 local initiatives in 67 BIP/ZIP territories in Lisbon. In total, one fifth of the Lisbon population has participated in the programme, and approximately EUR 12.4 million has funded more than 300 city-wide projects. 610 organisations have participated in BIP/ZIP projects to date. The main beneficiaries of the programme have been local communities who benefit from support and funding for projects that foster inclusion and social cohesion, employment and education. More than 150 private companies, NGOs and local government authorities are a part of the CLLD network.
In 2019, 44 more projects were approved for funding worth EUR 1.6 million which 135 partners will use to promote more than 300 activities in 53 BIP/ZIP neighbourhoods in Lisbon.
The programme is being evaluated and renewed to stay abreast of recent developments. A more permanent programme that enables long-term planning is currently envisioned.

innovations.name: Cleanup day
innovations.problem: The volume of litter in our environment is growing. Our mobile lifestyles have increased the risk of people deliberately or accidentally discarding litter in both urban and rural environments, instead of disposing of it responsibly using the established waste management systems. This has a grave impact, both environmentally and financially. The financial costs associated with cleaning up litter are high. The Clean Europe Network estimates that cleaning up all the current land litter across the European Union could cost around EUR 13 billion .
innovations.description:
The Let’s Do It Foundation organised a national ‘Cleanup Day’ in Estonia to help manage litter in the country by actively engaging citizens to do their part in protecting the environment. The Cleanup Day was crowd-sourced and organised in cooperation with over 500 organisations, from NGOs and public authorities to private companies and IT specialists. The latter were involved in creating an app to map illegal waste locations by enabling citizens themselves to mark locations as they were cleaning litter. The day was promoted through a large, nation-wide communication campaign supported by prominent Estonians and international media coverage.
This innovative solution of involving citizens and organisations in cleaning up litter across the country quickly gained popularity in other countries. The initiative, continually supported by the Let’s Do it Foundation, became global in the form of a World Cleanup Day (WCD) , as part of which 36 million volunteers in 169 countries participated in waste cleanups . It is now a global movement, consisting of grassroots organisations with the same goal of cleaning up different parts of the world.
To facilitate the global reduction of litter pollution, the Let’s Do It Foundation, the data science company SIFR and Microsoft developed an Artificial Intelligence (AI) solution for detecting waste (WADE). This algorithm can analyse images all around the world and detect litter. It is hoped that the solution will become an effective policy tool, allowing decision-makers to access up-to-date information on waste sites to create long-term, effective solutions to waste disposal issues .
Following the national and international success of the cleanup movements, the Let’s Do It Foundation developed a comprehensive ‘Keep It Clean’ plan . The plan provides a strategic approach to tackling the global waste problem and targets individuals, communities and organisations whose joint action can mitigate the waste problem by providing hands-on solutions and practices from the circular economy and Zero Waste movement. It seeks to go beyond regular cleanup activities, acknowledging that the waste problem is deeply rooted within current economic and social structures. The Let’s Do It Foundation provides training and accelerator programmes in which civil society organisations, and Zero Waste ambassadors and trainers can enhance their skills and knowledge to become multipliers of waste-free communities.
innovations.evidence:
During the Estonian Cleanup day, 4% of the total Estonian population collected 10 000 tonnes of garbage. The high turnout demonstrated citizen engagement and successful citizen-led action. It gave the impetus for the Let’s Do It Foundation’s other social and environmental activities. The first cleanup was also deemed extremely efficient, as it was completed in five hours with a budget of EUR 500 000. According to official estimations , the government would have spent more than three years and around EUR 22.5 million to achieve a similar result. [1]
The World Cleanup Day, organised on 15 September 2018, was the biggest civic action against waste in history, lasting 36 hours and gathering 17 million people in 157 countries. This reveals the impressive impact of coordinated, global civic action. The World Waste Platform taps into the power of such collective action; it crowd-sources information on the location of mismanaged waste and litter through 8 different apps.
Cleanup leaders have become more and more interested in dealing with the root causes of waste pollution and thus implementing the ‘Keep It Clean’ plan. In Panama, for example, local leaders have started collecting community bio waste. In Indonesia, public cross-sector discussions on improving waste management are taking place on a CitizenOS platform. Data collected is also being used to improve local policy implementation in Romania, and advocacy in Slovenia.
[1] The calculation was done by keeping track of all in-kind support and volunteer working hours contributed to the organisation of the Clean-up Day.

innovations.name: Look after my parents
innovations.problem: The elderly are at a higher risk of experiencing loneliness and suffering from social isolation than other age groups. This can have negative impacts on their physical and mental wellbeing , including anxiety, depression and intense feelings of vulnerability. Around 6 million people in France are over the age of 75. Of these, one in four lives alone. 300 000 people over the age of 60 are in a situation of social isolation, rarely or never meeting other people from all of their social networks combined (i.e. family, friends, neighbourhood, community network).
innovations.description:
Look after my parents ( Veiller sur mes parents ) is a service, developed by La Poste in 2017, that aims to tackle the social isolation of elderly people through regular social visits from mail delivery staff. La Poste is the largest mail delivery service in France and operates across the country. It has a unique ability to reach individuals in all parts of France, including those in more remote locations. Look after my parents is innovative in that it takes this regular, mainstream service and transforms it into an effective outreach and support service for the most vulnerable.
Service users can select from a range of packages. The most popular is a weekly visit to the elderly individual by the mail carrier. The service relies on an app, which allows the mail carrier to send a short report back to the elderly person’s relatives, or other nominated contacts, keeping the family updated on their relative’s wellbeing. If the elderly person needs specific support or help with a task, the mail carrier can also inform relatives via the app. All relatives on the app are immediately informed when someone has taken care of the task.
Different service packages are available to build onto this basic support. Famileo , another private service, is partnered with La Poste. This service creates a personalised gazette of photos and news from the elderly person’s relatives, via the app. Mail carriers hand out these gazettes on a monthly basis to keep the elderly person in touch with their loved ones, whilst also helping to close the gap between the paper and digital generations . Another service package offers the instalment of a helpline in the elderly person’s home, which they can call in case of emergency.
The mail carriers receive special training, with the support of gerontologists and psycho-gerontologists, to carry out the work. This ensures that they can adequately and effectively manage different situations that may occur during their visits.
This service is the extension of another similar La Poste initiative from 2014, Cohésio, which was also built on the idea of providing visits to the elderly. The difference is that Cohésio users were communities and associations, while the Look after my parents app targets individuals and their families.
innovations.evidence:
Around 40 000 mail carriers were trained before launching the service. The results achieved by October 2019 show that around 7 500 elderly people were using the services, and of these 6 000 were women. The clients’ average age was 82. The visits usually lasted between six and fifteen minutes.
The initiative, however, has been met with some concerns from certain groups, including the La Poste trade union, as they feel that the service commercialises social relations. innovations.name: HomeLab
innovations.lead: Metropolitan Research Institute, Romodrom o.p.s., People in Need Slovakia, Habitat for Humanity Poland, Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta, From Street to Home (Utcáról Lakásba Egyesület), Budapest Institute
innovations.problem: Homelessness, poverty, and a lack of work opportunities are interlinked problems, experienced across four Central and Eastern European countries (CEE) (Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia). Sudden and substantial structural changes and privatisation of the housing market over the last two decades have resulted in poor housing security and limited social accommodation in these countries. The share of households that suffer from severe housing deprivation was 11.7% in these four Member States in 2017 , significantly higher than the EU average (5%).
innovations.description:
HomeLab aimed to support vulnerable households out of their precarious circumstances by helping them to find suitable and affordable housing, simultaneously boosting their employment and social prospects. HomeLab ran from 2016 to 2019 through five pilot projects in Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia, with two pilots in Hungary. The project is based on the innovative Social Rental Enterprise (SRE) model, which asserts that housing and employment problems must be tackled simultaneously. HomeLab provided its service users - individuals excluded from mainstream social services - with frequent follow-ups and strong personal support. This model of providing a number of interlinked social services is innovative and unique, as it marks a shift towards an individual, people-centred approach to tackling complex social issues.
The project was coordinated by the Hungarian Metropolitan Research Institute, and implemented through partnerships with national NGOs located in each of the four participating countries. This included Habitat for Humanity in Poland, People in Need in Slovakia, Romodrom in Czechia, and the Hungarian Charity Service Association and the From Street to Home Association in Hungary.
Through this project, important new partnerships between local governments and civil society organisations were created in all four countries. The NGO sector is frail and underfinanced in the region. These partnerships gave NGOs an opportunity to stabilise their positions. In all the pilot projects, NGOs supported municipalities with valuable outreach expertise to map households in need. Regular public employment services often do not have the necessary hands-on experience and expertise to support particular marginalised groups, like Roma people. The central role of NGOs in the projects was key to providing effective, tailored support for vulnerable groups.
innovations.target_group: Homeless persons, Individuals experiencing poverty or social exclusion, Individuals whose mental health or wellbeing is compromised
innovations.beneficiaries: Metropolitan Research Institute, Romodrom o.p.s., People in Need Slovakia, Habitat for Humanity Poland, Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta, From Street to Home (Utcáról Lakásba Egyesület), Budapest Institute
innovations.evidence:
The monitoring and evaluation activities of the project found that the integrated service provision led to significant improvement in the housing conditions of participants in the pilot projects. Changes in the employment positions of HomeLab clients (compared to the control group) were more varied, but overall significant improvement was registered. HomeLab particularly improved the employment status of both those with inadequate housing, and also vulnerable labour market positions, having less of an impact on those who began in a relatively more stable position. Employment impacts were easier to measure across the five pilots than housing impacts, as the housing situation was very diverse and specific in each pilot, reflecting the different legal requirements of the locality.
Private landlords, as well as municipalities, often see the housing of marginalised groups as a high-risk service. Having HomeLab NGOs as intermediaries between marginalised groups and landlords was seen as a particularly successful factor in breaking down these negative barriers.
Another key result of the project was that it formalised the SRE model in several countries, structurally changing the delivery of housing services to vulnerable groups. In Czechia, Romodrom created the position of a social real estate agent, a professional with in-depth knowledge of the private housing sector, who is able to negotiate with both private landlords and vulnerable clients. In Poland, the initiative not only laid the foundations for an SRE in Warsaw, but led to changes in the national legislation, and to a national call for the support of similar initiatives. In Veszprém, Hungary, partnerships with the Ministry of Interior Affairs were set up to support the housing integration of released prisoners, as well as with the regional public employment agency to support recipients’ participation in EU-funded employment programs and local companies. Social work and debt management services were integrated into the housing support provided by VESZOL, a joint non-profit company of the municipality, and the Hungarian Charity Service Association.
The project also resulted in the creation of strong relations with employers. In Slovakia, People in Need have developed and tested training for companies’ middle managers to prepare them to work with new employees who have limited work history.
authors: Metropolitan Research Institute, Romodrom o.p.s., People in Need Slovakia, Habitat for Humanity Poland, Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta, From Street to Home (Utcáról Lakásba Egyesület), Budapest Institute

innovations.name: Eco-Schools
innovations.problem: The vast majority of Europeans highly value the protection of the environment and are aware of the challenges related to environmental sustainability. However, households in the European Union produce high levels of municipal waste, adding up to 492 kg per person . This illustrates the need to further promote more sustainable habits among European citizens. These habits can be fostered and developed through education.
innovations.description:
Eco-Schools is a global education programme that teaches children about pressing and urgent environmental problems in school. The Eco-Schools programme is the largest global programme implemented in schools that tackles sustainable and environmental issues. The Eco-Schools philosophy is to build on the existing schooling system to deliver a curriculum that covers the environment and sustainable development, using participatory methodologies to empower and inspire pupils.
The concept originated in Germany, Greece, and the United Kingdom in 1994 and was gradually transferred to other countries. The global programme is managed by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE) which is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. This programme is especially wide-reaching in Latvia, as it is the most comprehensive nation-wide school programme on environmental issues.
The programme taps into the resources of local communities, aiming to bring together schools and municipalities with the objective of creating pro-environmental behaviour. Latvian Eco-Schools encourage pupils to pursue sustainable lifestyles in their schools, households, and communities through a variety of activities. Pupils are encouraged to go beyond the classroom and to become active agents of change. For example, one school organised a ‘water day’ competition and invited the local community to clean up the banks of a local river. Participating pre-schools were engaged in reducing food waste and learning more about healthy eating habits.
Participating schools in Latvia must carry out a Sustainability Audit to assess how sustainable their school is based on certain key principles, then develop an Action Plan addressing any sustainability issues with a programme of activities. This is run by a student-led ‘eco committee’, made up of students, teachers, parents and other school staff. Each school must select a topic (such as waste, energy, water, transport, forests, food or biodiversity) on which to build their activities. Pupils monitor and evaluate the programme themselves, and the school integrates the activities into its curriculum via new classes or innovative teaching methods. The school also promotes the programme through events and wider communication, including through local media. As a mark of its dedication to sustainability and the environment, the school must produce an Eco Code. In addition to school-based activities, the Eco-Schools Summer Forum has been running for a decade, and is an important meeting point for teachers and students to discuss and exchange ideas.
Two years after starting the programme, a school will receive a Green Flag. The Eco-Schools' Green Flag is an internationally recognised award for excellence in environmental action and learning. It increases the visibility and prestige of the awarded school and makes it recognisable to the general public.
The foundation is a registered as a non-governmental organisation and is a member of the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE). Membership gives the Latvian Foundation exclusive rights to implement FEE programmes in the country, in adherence with quality and administration criteria. Since 1998, the foundation has been carrying out educational programmes such as Eco-Schools, Young Environmental Reporters, Blue Flag, Green Key and Explore the Forest.
innovations.evidence:
In Latvia, the Eco-Schools programme involves around 20 000 students through more than 200 educational institutions, ranging from primary to higher education. These results represent a success for a country of fewer than 2 million citizens. In 2018, the Eco-Schools Summer Forum brought together 120 teachers from 70 Eco-Schools and more than 100 students. The event’s popularity as a longstanding tradition and the positive experiences of it reported by students and teachers demonstrate the importance of the programme in raising awareness of sustainability among children and the wider community.
Eco-Schools in Latvia has also led to cooperation between different stakeholders , such as municipalities, schools, educational centres, non-governmental organisations, companies, local media, and citizens and their families. Individuals from these groups are involved in a diversity of activities that result in a better understanding of local and global environmental problems, a higher level of participation in civic actions and overall more environmentally-oriented behaviour.

innovations.name: Food and people (ended)
innovations.problem: In rural Denmark, the farming community is diminishing, as local farmers who have been impacted by globalisation cannot afford to scale-up their food production and distribution on their own. The Danish food production sector is very industrialised and centralised, and opportunities for processing farming commodities locally are limited. Under legislation governing food safety, it is not profitable for farmers to establish their own processing facilities, leading to a diminishing farming sector and a rural population facing unemployment and skills depletion.
innovations.description:
Food and People is a social enterprise that promotes sustainable growth and the development of new and established local micro enterprises. It does so by giving farmers access to communal processing facilities, whilst offering skills training and flexible job opportunities to vulnerable individuals, including people with disabilities.
Local farmers can use Food and People’s communal processing facilities for handling, processing, storing and distributing their own produce. Its facilities for food production are situated in a renovated, previously unused agricultural building on Grønnessegaard Manor, an estate in rural Denmark. The facilities comply with European standards for food safety. Farmers can sell their products through the farm shop at the Manor, and food produced through the communal processing facilities is also used for catering, including the delivery of food to local restaurants and cafes.
The project employs people with disabilities who wish to participate in the farming activities that take place in the Grønnessegaard facility and other local farms.  It offers them training and access to flexible work, which would otherwise be difficult for them to find. Workers with disabilities either contact the project themselves, or are referred to the initiative through the local job centre.  All activities involving employees with a disability are designed and managed in partnership with the local municipality and the job centre. This means that people with disabilities have a tailor-made individual plan, detailing the tasks that they are able to perform on the farm, taking into account their individual capabilities.

Access of farmers to the communal processing facilities and to the web shop and showroom to sell local products have facilitated food production and sale and, in turn, boosted the local economy. The project has allowed for the development, marketing, processing and distribution of two innovative, locally-sourced products – the Halsnæs food box and the Halsnæs Christmas box, which are publicised and marketed on the web shop and showroom, further facilitating sales for small local producers.
The new facilities have also been successful in terms of helping to boost the tourism sector. Pop-up restaurants with different themes, food workshops and food markets have opened, and visiting days for companies, institutions, and schools to the operations at Grønnessegaard and other local producers are now popular. sections.question: Problem
sections.answer: In rural Denmark, the farming community is diminishing, as local farmers who have been impacted by globalisation cannot afford to scale-up their food production and distribution on their own. The Danish food production sector is very industrialised and centralised, and opportunities for processing farming commodities locally are limited. Under legislation governing food safety, it is not profitable for farmers to establish their own processing facilities, leading to a diminishing farming sector and a rural population facing unemployment and skills depletion.

sections.question: Description
sections.answer:
Food and People is a social enterprise that promotes sustainable growth and the development of new and established local micro enterprises. It does so by giving farmers access to communal processing facilities, whilst offering skills training and flexible job opportunities to vulnerable individuals, including people with disabilities.
Local farmers can use Food and People’s communal processing facilities for handling, processing, storing and distributing their own produce. Its facilities for food production are situated in a renovated, previously unused agricultural building on Grønnessegaard Manor, an estate in rural Denmark. The facilities comply with European standards for food safety. Farmers can sell their products through the farm shop at the Manor, and food produced through the communal processing facilities is also used for catering, including the delivery of food to local restaurants and cafes.
The project employs people with disabilities who wish to participate in the farming activities that take place in the Grønnessegaard facility and other local farms.  It offers them training and access to flexible work, which would otherwise be difficult for them to find. Workers with disabilities either contact the project themselves, or are referred to the initiative through the local job centre.  All activities involving employees with a disability are designed and managed in partnership with the local municipality and the job centre. This means that people with disabilities have a tailor-made individual plan, detailing the tasks that they are able to perform on the farm, taking into account their individual capabilities.

innovations.name: ResQ Club
innovations.problem: Around 88 million tonnes of food is wasted annually in the European Union. In Finland alone, approximately 120–160 million kilograms of food is wasted by households (about 20–25 kilogrammes per person).  This waste costs the EU an estimated EUR 143 million and has significant negative effects on the environment, as food waste depletes the world of finite natural resources, such as water, and contributes to global warming.
innovations.description:
The Finnish start-up ResQ Club has developed a location-based mobile app that enables consumers to buy surplus food that would otherwise be thrown away by restaurants, cafes, hotels and grocery stores. The food is discounted from 30% up to 100%. The chosen food product can be bought through the app using a payment card or PayPal. Once the transaction has gone through, the consumer is able to pick up the meal whenever they want from a pick-up window set by the supplier, and without having to wait. Restaurants, cafes, and grocery stores can sign up to ResQ Club through the online platform, where they can announce their surplus products and meals. ResQ Club’s overall goal is to limit the amount of food that goes to waste in restaurants to zero.
ResQ adopts a franchising model, but also operates some market areas itself. Its management remains centralised in Finland. All the profits made by ResQ are reinvested back into the company, mostly for hiring purposes.
innovations.evidence:
The benefits of this initiative extend both to restaurants and customers. Consumers are able to buy food that is close to its expiry date, at a reduced price. Restaurants, cafes and grocery stores are able to sell food that would otherwise go to waste. Latest figures show that the app has over 30 000 active monthly users and sells around 80 000 portions of food each month in the cities where ResQ Club is active . The app has been downloaded 800 000 times. A total of 7 000 restaurants, cafes and grocery stores have so far registered on the app, and about 1 300 of them sell food through the platform each week.
According to one grocery store owner , daily food waste at his store ‘has gone down from three shopping carts to half a shopping cart’. ResQ Club helps to save 273 tonnes of CO2 emissions every month ,, which is equivalent to 44 car rides around the world, 227 flights between Helsinki and New York, and 43 tonnes of edible food.
tags: Modernising labour market institutions and services

innovations.name: Cooperative for Ethical Financing (ZEF)
innovations.problem: Since the 2008 economic and financial crisis, there has been heightened interest in socially responsible finance and ethical banking. This is in part due to a lack of confidence in traditional banks caused by the high number of bailouts in the aftermath of the crisis. Additionally, as environmental awareness is rising, people are turning away from traditional banking, which can cause environmental damage through investment in unsustainable development .
innovations.description:
The Cooperative for Ethical Financing (ZEF) is a non-profit organisation based in Croatia, which aims to provide ethical banking alternatives for consumers. ZEF, created in 2014, is the first ethical banking cooperative in Croatia, and uses traditional financial tools to achieve ethical results. ZEF offers a variety of financial instruments to its members, including micro loans for social entrepreneurs, pre-financing for local action groups, and accounting services for cooperatives. By becoming members of the cooperative, individuals and organisations join the market created by ZEF. Members can manage their finances in a way that has a positive social and environmental impact. They can take out loans, crowdfund other members and invest in other members’ projects. Members can also benefit from non-financial services, such as access to business and financial consulting, as well as services that help them to apply for EU grants and other funds focused on socially and environmentally responsible investments. Membership also provides access to a network of members across the country, which facilitates cooperation, the placement of goods and services, and access to education and business consulting. ZEF has also created its own electronic wallet, which enables its members to make internal transactions instantly.
ZEF is a cooperative – its members are co-owners of the bank and can democratically decide on key issues related to the cooperative’s functioning. Of these members, two-thirds are individuals, and one-third are legal entities, such as small- and medium-sized enterprises. Any Croatian citizen or legal entity (except political parties) can become a member of ZEF and thus have ownership over where and how their money is invested.
innovations.evidence:
Overall, ZEF’s impact has been far-reaching, as demonstrated by the fact that it has become the largest cooperative in Croatia, with 1 300 members at present. The combined revenue from the sale of ZEF members’ goods and services exceeds EUR 250 million per year.
According to Goran Jeras, the Cooperative Manager, the main achievement of ZEF has been ‘the creation of an extremely diverse range of participants’, where people from all over the country, with different political views and religious backgrounds, come together to benefit the community through ethical financing. Jeras explains that ‘that kind of trust and social capital is extremely valuable’.
The cooperative also benefits the wider community and the areas in which the ethically responsible projects operate. The cooperative has financed a wide range of activities, from agriculture to architecture projects, and development in the IT, media, and food production sectors. For example, the bank is helping to set up the first green electricity supply in the country.
ZEF is achieving its aims of investing in community development through projects that are financially, socially and environmentally sustainable, and through a network of people who are interested in benefiting their local communities.
tags: Modernising labour market institutions and services

innovations.name: AfB - Social and green IT
innovations.problem: People with disabilities can face multiple obstacles to entering the workplace, often due to stigma or a scarcity of inclusive job positions that can be adapted to their individual abilities. In 2017, there were 7.7 million people of working age with a severe disability in Germany. The disability pay gap and a lack of information about vacancies reduce the chance of people with disabilities finding quality employment. Employers are also sometimes not confident that they will be able to support an employee with a disability and provide them with a barrier-free workspace, and thus do not provide many opportunities for people with disabilities.
innovations.description:
AfB is a social enterprise that aims to create inclusive, barrier-free jobs in refurbishing and reselling used IT hardware. Its innovation lies in its ability to support people with disabilities in their search for employment and to raise awareness amongst employers on disability issues, whilst also helping to reduce the negative environmental impact of IT production and waste. It aims to become one of the leading non-profit IT companies worldwide.
AfB is based on a socially responsible business model sustained by its partnership with over 1 000 corporations, banks and public institutions. AfB collects used IT and mobile hardware, repairs it, certifiably removes stored data, and resells it at a reduced price in AfB stores or online. AfB subsequently provides each partner organisation with a certificate of Corporate Social Responsibility, in which the social and environmental impact of their reused IT hardware is statistically measured (e.g. the collection of 600 notebooks sponsors one workplace for a disabled person). AfB also organises social projects in schools, such as ‘JumP’, which provides schools with more affordable, recycled IT equipment.
AfB works closely with public employment agencies and other organisations to design jobs in which all work processes are inclusive and barrier-free. This includes providing work instructions that are illustrated and in easy-to-read language, ensuring that there are permanent contact people for employees with disabilities, training supervisors to be considerate in stressful situations, and setting up workplaces appropriately for different disabilities. Workplaces for people with visual impairments, for example, can be set up so that sound cues are converted into visual signals (e.g. doorbells, alarm systems). Special workplace equipment can be provided, such as illuminated magnifying glasses, if needed. Light generally plays a major role, with workplaces often illuminated in order to be fully accessible and inclusive.
People with various disabilities and those without disabilities work side-by-side at all stages, from collecting to recycling and reselling. To support staff, AfB provides onboarding programmes tailored to a person’s level of education or job experience. It runs specific workshops for people with disabilities in order to increase their independence and autonomy before entering the labour market. The company also offers a three-year vocational education IT training programme for young people with disabilities. AfB is also involved in social and ecological projects, offering support through IT refurbishment – this includes Joblinge, which provides IT hardware for a work programme that aims to reduce youth unemployment in Germany.
innovations.evidence:
As a result of AfB’s inclusive employment strategy, the company has around 440 employees in 19 different locations, of which approximately half have a disability. Employees are supported by social workers, as well as a representative in the case of severely disabled people. The company has experienced rapid growth over recent years, with 63 employees hired in 2019 alone.
In 2019, AfB processed more than 470 000 pieces of IT equipment and mobile devices, of which 65% were refurbished. It contributed to savings of around 52 300 megawatt hours of energy, 17 000 tonnes of CO2 emissions and 22 900 tonnes of iron. In 2019, it sold more than 13 250 refurbished devices at a reduced price to schools and non-profit organisations.
tags: Equal access to education and training
Social integration of those at risk

innovations.name: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative
innovations.lead: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise, Margarita Vocational Training Centre
innovations.problem: The economic and financial crisis has had a grave impact on public spending in Greece, with large cuts in funding for social services and education. In the northern Athenian suburb of Halandri, five of the nine municipal kindergartens closed down in 2011, leaving over 50 people without work, and the parents of 2 000 pre-school age children with very few childcare options. At the same time, high schools faced cuts, which increased class sizes and negatively affected the quality of teaching.
innovations.description:
The Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise was founded by a committee of parents in 2012. It aims to fill the gaps in public services by empowering and mobilising community members to drive solutions themselves. Through its cooperative model, it responds directly to changing childcare and education needs in the local area, through several initiatives based on one principle – profit-free quality childcare and education that puts the learning of the pupil first.
The cooperative started with a childcare programme in 2012, setting up small schools in private homes to meet the demand for affordable childcare in the area. The programme relies on parent volunteers to keep fees low. In 2013, the cooperative expanded to set up a school of private tuition, which offers classes to high school students preparing for university exams at affordable rates.
The school uses modern educational practices to capture and activate the students’ interest. Teachers and parents have collaborated to create a curriculum that fosters critical thinking and teamwork in the classroom, while addressing each student individually according to their needs and abilities. The objective is to provide quality education with standards such as a child-to-teacher ratio of 8:1 and six-hour working days for educational staff.
innovations.beneficiaries: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise, Margarita Vocational Training Centre
innovations.evidence:
The cooperative employs four full-time paid employees, eight part-time paid employees and ten volunteers. The childcare facility accommodates over 20 children from the neighbourhood.
One of the key benefits of the cooperative is that it has been able to set up additional activities addressing emerging problems in the community. In addition to childcare and private tuition, for example, it set up a parent group coaching programme, which aims to raise public awareness, foster the exchange of opinions, and educate parents and adolescents on a series of general and specialised parenting topics.
Another key benefit of the cooperative was bringing together other stakeholders working in the field – the Margarita Vocational Training Centre, for example, which promotes the social and professional inclusion of young people with learning disabilities. One of the key results of this cooperation is that the cooperative has hired two trainees from the centre who had previously been long-term unemployed. One person with a disability from the centre has since become an employee and a member of the cooperative.
authors: Halandri Parents Social Cooperative Enterprise, Margarita Vocational Training Centre

innovations.name: Impact Hub Athens
innovations.problem:
In recent years, there has been a growing interest in social entrepreneurship across Europe, driven by factors such as economic crises and a collective desire for more inclusive and sustainable economic systems. Social enterprises play a pivotal role in addressing societal challenges, promoting social inclusion, and fostering sustainable development. However, the support structures available to social entrepreneurs—encompassing funding opportunities, capacity building, and knowledge sharing—vary significantly across European countries. In many regions, support remains limited or fragmented, hindering the growth and scalability of social enterprises.​
To address these disparities, the European Commission adopted the Social Economy Action Plan (SEAP) in December 2021, aiming to create the right framework conditions for the social economy to thrive, open up opportunities (including access to finance) and support for capacity building, and enhance recognition of the social economy and its potential. The action plan has a time horizon until 2030, with a mid-term review scheduled for 2025.
Complementing the SEAP, the Commission Expert Group on the Social Economy and Social Enterprises (GECES) advises the European Commission on policies related to the social economy and social enterprises. Currently in its third mandate (2018–2024), GECES assists the Commission in implementing measures from the action plan for the social economy, developing the Transition Pathway for the ‘Proximity and Social Economy’ industrial ecosystem, and preparing legislative proposals. Additionally, GECES facilitates the exchange of best practices and enhances awareness of social economy issues. ​Internal Market SMEs
Despite these efforts, challenges persist, particularly in providing tailored support mechanisms that cater to the diverse needs of social enterprises across different contexts. Strengthening these support structures is essential to unlock the full potential of social entrepreneurship in contributing to Europe's social and economic objectives.
innovations.description:
Impact Hub Athens addresses the absence of structural support for social entrepreneurs by tapping into the unused potential of international networking and knowledge sharing.  Impact Hub is the first global collaborative network of its kind, designed specifically to support and connect social entrepreneurs across the globe, whilst also providing them with co-working space. Membership packages for social entrepreneurs range from EUR 18.00 to EUR 170.00. Membership gives individuals access to both a physical workspace, a vibrant multi-disciplinary community, and a range of services to support them at different stages of their enterprise development.
Impact Hub Athens supports entrepreneurs working in the fields of urbanism, active citizenship, the circular economy, the environment and systemic change for social integration. Its business incubator provides training on capacity building, and workshops on marketing, for more developed enterprises. The Impact Hub supports entrepreneurs at different stages, from the start of an idea (with access to funding through competitions or other financial schemes), right through to the scaling-up of a business initiative through consulting services.
Impact Hub Athens is part of a growing international network. It collaborates with Impact Hubs in other countries to deliver joint activities and share expertise globally. It also works with companies that provide support to Impact Hub training events as part of their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) strategies. For instance, in 2024, Impact Hub Athens launched the Policy Connect initiative, in collaboration with the Google Foundation, to empower the ecosystem of social and environmental innovation in Greece. This series of empowerment events, including Policy Recommendations Focus Groups and Stakeholders Events, aimed to co-create proposals and commitment agreements to strengthen the community of social and environmental entrepreneurship across six regions in Greece.
innovations.target_group: Other target groups
innovations.evidence:
Over the past 10 years, Impact Hub Athens has supported more than 300 social and environmental ventures , trained over 3,000 individuals in entrepreneurship and upskilling, and built a community of over 1,000 members and partners . These social innovators are part of the broader Impact Hub global network, contributing to a culture of collaboration by sharing expertise and co-developing solutions across borders.
Run by a team of 12 full-time experts —including trainers, facilitators, programme managers, researchers, and community builders—Impact Hub Athens hosts a 750 sqm innovation space in central Athens, providing high-quality infrastructure and programming for entrepreneurs and changemakers. Each year, we curate and host over 200 events , including workshops, hackathons, seminars, conferences, networking sessions, and thematic festivals reaching 3,000–5,000 participants.
From 2017 to 2023 , Impact Hub Athens operated Greece’s first Social Economy Market —a 1,500 sqm municipal venue in the Kypseli neighbourhood—proposing and implementing an innovative model rooted in social entrepreneurship and community co-ownership. Selected by the Municipality of Athens , Impact Hub transformed the space into a thriving community hub housing 10 permanent social enterprises , hosting 80+ entrepreneurs through monthly pop-ups , and delivering 50+ cultural events , 20+ educational programmes , and 40+ festivals . This dynamic space engaged over 100,000 visitors and offered weekly educational activities to 230+ students , focusing on digital literacy, intercultural skills, and civic participation.
The Market's success—supported by the European Regional Development Fund —demonstrated how place-based social innovation can deliver sustained economic, cultural, and social impact. The visibility and hands-on work of Impact Hub Athens in this and other projects play a key role in raising awareness about social entrepreneurship, sustainability, and inclusive economic development among policy makers, civil society, and the wider public.

innovations.name: Bio-Village Seeham
innovations.problem: Global emissions from crop and livestock agriculture rose by 16% from 2000 to 2017 . In the EU, 40% of agricultural emissions are nitrous oxide, in part produced by the use of nitrogen fertilisers in conventional farming. Organic farming has been developed as a response to the environmental harm caused by the use of chemical pesticides and synthetic fertilisers in conventional agriculture. It has ecological benefits, in that it can contribute to a more sustainable and environmentally friendly food production system.
innovations.description:
Bio-Village Seeham is the first organic village in Austria that focuses on maintaining and preserving traditional methods of haymaking and organic farming. In 2011, as interest in environmentally friendly lifestyles started to increase, the Seeham municipality began to collaborate with local citizens, farmers and businesses, creating the Bio-Village. The Bio-Village aims to preserve the traditional production of hay milk produced from feeding cows hay and grass mixed with natural herbs, which accounts for only 0.3% of milk produced in the EU. Through this, the Bio-Village promotes community and an environmentally friendly lifestyle, and helps to boost the local economy.

innovations.name: Visits in the Dark
innovations.lead: Czech Radio Endowment Fund, Together with You
innovations.problem: Visually impaired people often struggle to find employment due to a lack of accessible job opportunities. In 2013, there were approximately 102 000 visually impaired people in Czechia, which was around 6% of the population with disabilities. The employment rate of people with any type of disability in 2013 was around 47%.
innovations.description:
Visits in the Dark employs visually impaired people to visit elderly people for 1.5 hours a week. The innovation of the project is the way that it redesigns social support typically provided to visually impaired people, who are normally passive recipients of state support. The project empowers them to become active contributors to society, whilst increasing their skills and autonomy.
The project was set up in 2017 by the Czech Radio Endowment Fund, which has 18 years of experience in working with visually impaired people. To become an employee – a ‘visitor’ – a visually impaired person must have an interest in working with elderly people, have a hobby or a skill to share, and be able to travel independently. The fund carefully matches visitors’ profiles with clients - for example, a visually impaired person who is a talented musician is matched with an elderly person who enjoys listening to music. The service is provided in the elderly person’s home or in a retirement home, where group sessions are often delivered. Activities are based on visitors’ interests and talents, and include playing board games, speaking foreign languages, reading books, listening to music, or going for walks.
Visits are arranged by two coordinators, who have access to the online calendars of employees and can match clients with visitors based on availability and location, through an online platform. Visitors are employed part-time, with flexible working hours, which helps them to adjust gradually to the labour market and gain more independence in their lives. Each employed visitor is provided with a budget, so that they can independently decide on the courses they want to attend in order to develop their knowledge and skills. Courses focus on the development of soft skills such as self-reflection, interpersonal communication and teamwork. The courses offered to the visitors also include first aid, or training focused on computer skills and online tools (e.g. Slack, Google Calendar) used for scheduling the Visits in the Dark.
innovations.beneficiaries: Czech Radio Endowment Fund, Together with You
innovations.evidence:
In total, 27 people have been employed as visitors since the beginning of the project. Currently, the start-up employs 10 visitors, who operate in seven cities across Czechia. Since the beginning of the project, visually impaired people have visited over 600 elderly people and have spent more than 4 200 hours with them. The employees have monthly meetings where they can share their experience with others, which has proved to be an effective team-building activity. Over the years, visually impaired people have gained more responsibility in running the sessions, managing their regular work commitments and attending training courses organised by the Endowment Fund. As a result of this continuous development, five employees were able to become involved in the administrative side of the project, helping to identify new clients, which increased their salary and financial independence.
An evaluation of the project showed that employees gained knowledge and experience in social services and financial independence. The practical courses enhanced their professional and transferable skills and their self-confidence. The project also enabled visually impaired people to become more independent and gain more control over their personal and professional development. Their visual impairment is not seen as a disadvantage, but as something that brings added value. A visitor may be able to help an elderly person to cope with the loss of cognitive functions, including sight, or recommend a suitable aid or adaptation for the household, for example.

innovations.name: Empleando Digital
innovations.lead: Fundacion Secretariado Gitano, Spanish Red Cross, Accenture Foundation
innovations.problem: The demand for digital skills in the workplace is growing rapidly, and it is estimated that 9 out of 10 jobs will require digital skills in the near future . This means that some level of knowledge of advanced digital skills - such as coding or debugging - will be increasingly required for entry into many jobs, barring access to people with low qualifications . For people from vulnerable backgrounds, such as the Roma community, this could mean an increased risk of exclusion from the labour market and further economic hardship if they do not have access to digital and technological training. The Spanish work force lags behind the EU average in terms of digital skills, and this shortcoming is even more pronounced among vulnerable groups.
innovations.description:
EmpleandoDigital (Employing Digital) offers a tailored digital skills training programme for people at risk of social exclusion. The Fundación Secretariado Gitano (FSG) was established in the 1960’s to protect the rights of the Roma community in Spain, improve their living conditions and prevent all kinds of discrimination against this community. The social action NGO achieves this  through a series of programmes including Acceder , which focuses on promoting labour market inclusion among the Roma community through tailored Individual Employment Plans (IEPs) and the establishment of strategic alliances with potential employers. #EmpleandoDigital , launched at the end of 2017, brings the Acceder programme into the digital era, focusing on developing the digital skills of people at risk of social exclusion through a digital skills training scheme. While similar projects exist in Spain, the strength of #EmpleandoDigital lies in the innovative partnership between public, private and non-profit organisations, giving the project access to a range of expertise, as well as funding sources. #EmpleandoDigital was developed as a pilot project by FSG and the Spanish Red Cross, in close collaboration with the Accenture Foundation . The Accenture Foundation provides technical assistance, and high-profile support to the project.
FSG was one of the first social action NGOs to secure funding from the European Union to improve the wellbeing of the Roma community. While the programme is designed to assist any individual at risk of social exclusion, the involvement of FSG has meant that the programme has benefited from expertise on engaging with the Roma community, which makes up 80% of the beneficiaries. The training courses provided to the community aim to improve the digital skills and knowledge, focusing on training the basic digital skills demanded in almost every position today at the labour market, designing innovative training courses in occupations that include new digital components (in logistics, supermarkets, hotels, etc.), creating software development courses (Java/Javascript) adjusted to people with initial low levels of education and experience, or using the virtual reality to improve the training processes in specific employment pathways.
The initiative’s technology partner, Accenture, has designed a range of innovative digital tools to support implementation of the programme, including a data analysis tool to evaluate the effectiveness of actions in Individual Employment Plans. The tool uses data from interventions with over 300 000 beneficiaries of the employment programmes over the past 19 years to predict the probability of actions succeeding in the different IEPs. It also calculates the most successful sequence of activities, based on numerous variable factors of participants. Another tool, ‘+Social value’, aims to measure the social impact of the employment programmes on vulnerable and disadvantaged groups. The tool analyses the effectiveness, efficiency, quality and Social Return On Investment (SROI) of the programmes. A variety of Virtual Reality (VR) tools are also used in training.
innovations.beneficiaries: Fundacion Secretariado Gitano, Spanish Red Cross, Accenture Foundation
innovations.evidence:
From 2017–2019, #EmpleandoDigital was deployed in 12 out of 17 Spanish regions, with over 300 professionals from 26 employment teams in FSG and the Red Cross directly involved in the project. A total of 9 826 people at risk of exclusion participated in the project, improving their digital skills and knowledge. Of these, 5 924 people improved their digital skills through basic courses, and 2 328 have taken an advanced course. A total of 235 people attended one of the 23 courses in occupations that are being modified by digital transformation. Furthermore, 48 people participated in the 4 software development courses in JavaScript and Java – 12 of these are already working in a technical role, 9 of whom have an employment contract of indefinite duration.
The project has also achieved greater recognition and visibility of the challenges facing the Roma community, breaking down stereotypes of vulnerable people and their presence in the labour market and reinforcing the commitment of employers and public employment services to increasing their employability through professional training.
authors: Fundacion Secretariado Gitano, Spanish Red Cross, Accenture Foundation

innovations.name: Portugal Social Innovation
innovations.description:
Portugal Social Innovation (PSI) is a pioneering public policy initiative that aims to promote social innovation and entrepreneurship, and develop the social investment market in Portugal. It does so by encouraging collaboration between investors and social entrepreneurs to promote social innovation projects. The goal of this initiative is to support the development and scaling of new solutions addressing social problems which complement more traditional and conventional ones. To do so, four instruments were created to address the specific financing needs of innovative social organisations and social entrepreneurs, also assuming the active involvement of public and private investors in the process as partners that can contribute to the economic and financial sustainability of the projects.
According to The Economist’s Social Innovation Index 2016 , Portugal is one of only seven countries worldwide that has designed and implemented a national policy on social innovation. PSI is the first initiative in Europe to mobilise EU funds for the use of new financing instruments in the promotion of social innovation and investment, and the construction of this emerging ecosystem. The initiative has been granted EUR 150 million by the European Social Fund as part of the Portugal 2020 Partnership Agreement , which is being used to fund social innovation projects, generally designated as Social Innovation and Social Entrepreneurship Initiatives (SISEI), which are projects that address challenging social problems through the development of new products, services or methodologies with high potential for social impact. The four instruments are aligned with the life cycle of SI projects, addressing their specific needs and potential at different stages of maturity, and promoting as well the development of partnerships between the entrepreneurs and the investors. The four include the following three grant based funding schemes and one financial instrument:
Capacity-Building for Social Investment: grant-based capacity-building instrument that finances the development of management skills in order to help social economy organisations and entrepreneurs to successfully develop social innovation projects. Social investors must present a nonbinding letter of interest.
Partnerships for Impact: strategic/impact philanthropy match-funding scheme to finance the creation and scaling of social innovation projects, co-funded in partnership with social investors (private organisations or public entities like Municipalities) to give greater scale and impact to social innovation projects contributing for a more stable, efficient and sustainable financing model.

Portugal Social Innovation initiative was created in December 2014, within a very specific national context that aligned the needs, the players and the funding.
